title: Moment-Guided Optimizers for Noisy Deep Learning: MGO-SC as a Simple Consistency Gate for Adam-Style Updates
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE Global Emerging Technologies Conference (iGET), Irvine, CA, USA, Oct. 21-25, 2026
summary: Adaptive optimizers are widely used in deep learning, yet their behavior can degrade under heavy stochasticity and label noise where the sign and magnitude of gradients can be unstable. We study MGO-SC (Moment-Guided Optimizer with Sign-Consistency), a lightweight modification of Adam-style methods that derives a coordinate-wise consistency gate from the magnitude of a sign exponential moving average (EMA): coordinates whose gradient sign is stable are trusted, while coordinates whose sign fluctuates are down-weighted. We show that the naive form of this gate, which can only shrink updates, loses effective step size and underperforms when the learning rate is matched to the baseline. We therefore introduce a mean-preserving variant that reallocates trust across coordinates without changing the net per-tensor step magnitude. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, under a matched learning rate and decoupled weight decay, mean-preserving MGO-SC consistently improves over its AdamW baseline across clean, symmetric, and asymmetric label noise (e.g., +1.4 points at 40% symmetric noise; paired bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero; Wilcoxon p<0.01), while adding no second-order information or per-sample filtering. We report matched-seed effect sizes, nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired significance tests, and we release code and raw logs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MGO-SC, a lightweight Adam-style optimizer that down-weights coordinates whose gradient sign fluctuates, and finds that a mean-preserving version improves over AdamW on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 under clean and noisy labels.
AI.motivation: Adaptive optimizers can degrade under heavy stochasticity and label noise, where gradient signs and magnitudes are unstable. The naive consistency gate, which can only shrink updates, loses effective step size and underperforms at a matched learning rate.
AI.method: A coordinate-wise consistency gate is derived from the magnitude of a sign exponential moving average, trusting coordinates with stable gradient sign. The mean-preserving variant reallocates trust across coordinates without changing the net per-tensor step magnitude, and adds no second-order information or per-sample filtering.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, under matched learning rate and decoupled weight decay, mean-preserving MGO-SC consistently improves over its AdamW baseline across clean, symmetric, and asymmetric label noise, e.g. +1.4 points at 40% symmetric noise, with a paired bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero and Wilcoxon p<0.01.
AI.conclusion: The gain is a simple, reproducible modification of Adam-style updates that is robust to label noise, supported by matched-seed effect sizes, bootstrap confidence intervals, paired tests, and released code and logs.

title: What a Weight Update Buys: Leverage Across Training Stages
summary: Post-training moves a language model's weights by about a thousandth of their norm and changes its behavior sharply; pretraining moves them by a third and buys a slow drift. We introduce leverage, an exact measure of what a unit of weight change buys: the Fisher quadratic form of an update, computed with one forward-mode pass per direction, divided by the same form for random directions of the same size at the same checkpoint. Leverage orders released Olmo-3, Tülu-3, Zephyr, and OLMo-2 checkpoints over four orders of magnitude: pretraining windows sit at the random level on prose, SFT five times above it, RL-Zero and RLVR at 400-1,500, and DPO at 400-23,000. With this instrument we find that pretraining accumulates into noise: windows of 30k to 1M steps are no more consequential on prose than random directions of their size, as a noisy quadratic model of SGD predicts. We find that training precision changes what an update looks like: training bf16 parameters without an fp32 master copy freezes 36-99% of coordinates, lowers leverage up to sevenfold, and creates an alignment between update magnitudes and the diagonal Fisher that fp32 training does not show. We derive and verify a law for reuse: the sign-flip null predicts the relative damage of random drop-and-rescale (DARE) at keep rate $p$ as $(1-p)/(p\,\rho_{\mathrm{sign}})$, within a factor of two of measurement wherever DARE succeeds. Two controls make these readings reliable: every controlled SFT and DPO trajectory with fp32 master weights loses leverage as it moves, and two re-runs of a released DPO stage from its anchor with its published recipe land within 1% of the released displacement and 4% of its leverage, where a plain recipe reads five to six times lower; leaving one component out traces the level to the length-normalized loss and its batch size of 128 together.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces leverage, an exact measure of what a unit weight change buys, and uses it to show that pretraining updates act like random noise while post-training updates are far more consequential.
AI.motivation: Post-training changes behavior sharply with tiny weight movement, whereas pretraining moves weights much more with only a slow drift. There is no instrument that quantifies how much behavioral effect a given weight update actually buys.
AI.method: Leverage is defined as the Fisher quadratic form of an update, computed with one forward-mode pass per direction, divided by the same form for random directions of equal size at the same checkpoint. The paper also derives a sign-flip null law for the relative damage of random drop-and-rescale (DARE), and runs controlled SFT and DPO experiments that compare fp32 master weights with bf16 training.
AI.result: Leverage spans four orders of magnitude across Olmo-3, Tulu-3, Zephyr, and OLMo-2 checkpoints: pretraining windows sit at the random level on prose, SFT is about five times above it, RL-Zero and RLVR are at 400 to 1,500, and DPO is at 400 to 23,000. bf16 training without fp32 master copies freezes 36 to 99% of coordinates and lowers leverage up to sevenfold. The DARE law predicts relative damage within a factor of two wherever DARE succeeds.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining accumulates into noise rather than consequential change, and training precision and loss normalization materially affect update leverage, so leverage is a useful diagnostic for reliable measurement of post-training effects.

title: Threshold Compatibility and Support-Selection Diagnostics in Neural Discovery of Partial Differential Equations
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Accurate regression need not yield the correct equation after support selection. For a median/sample-standard-deviation threshold in neural PDE discovery, we derive an exact two-signal retention boundary and a complete-vector perturbation bound. Exact advection-diffusion libraries lose diffusion despite coefficient recovery to numerical precision. True-support refits of forty saved sparse states reduce diffusion error without restoring all derivative accuracy. A fixed sequential threshold ridge comparator recovers exact support in sixty ideal controls but selects extra terms in every learned state. All-fold correct-support candidates are rejected by conditional validation; post hoc energy pooling preserves their higher minimum loss in all sixty states. Supplied-support estimates outperform unchanged selected equations in all 240 physical-residual comparisons on four unused analytic trajectories. With coefficients, observation points and weights fixed, exact replacement of the learned library and target reverses their learned-row ordering in 59/60 states. Weighting both losses also fails the specified Burgers diffusion-benefit criterion at every tested budget. These finite diagnostics distinguish threshold incompatibility, refit damage and score rejection; they establish neither automatic correction nor general recovery or predictive stability.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes threshold-based support selection in neural PDE discovery and shows that accurate regression can still yield an incorrect equation, with diagnostics that separate threshold incompatibility, refit damage, and score rejection.
AI.motivation: Accurate coefficient regression does not guarantee that the correct equation is recovered after support selection, and the causes of such failures in neural PDE discovery are not well characterized.
AI.method: The paper derives an exact two-signal retention boundary and a complete-vector perturbation bound for a median or sample-standard-deviation threshold. It compares against a fixed sequential threshold ridge comparator, runs true-support refits of forty saved sparse states, and evaluates candidates with conditional validation and energy pooling on physical residuals.
AI.result: Exact advection-diffusion libraries lose diffusion despite coefficient recovery to numerical precision. True-support refits reduce diffusion error without restoring all derivative accuracy. The comparator recovers exact support in sixty ideal controls but selects extra terms in every learned state. Supplied-support estimates outperform unchanged selected equations in all 240 physical-residual comparisons on four unused analytic trajectories. Exact library replacement reverses learned-row ordering in 59 of 60 states.
AI.conclusion: The diagnostics distinguish threshold incompatibility, refit damage, and score rejection, but they establish neither automatic correction nor general recovery or predictive stability.

title: Predicate Neuron: Differentiable Quantization of Predicate Relations in Gradient-based Learning
summary: In machine learning, symbolic reasoning approaches often rely on static architectures that hinder integration into deep neural networks and gradient-based optimization. To address this, we introduce the Native Predicate Neuron, a differentiable logic-reasoning neural module that enriches standard architectures with symbolic reasoning capabilities via first-order logic quantization. The proposed neuron models relational logic by learning to alternate between operations using a single trainable parameter. It features a tailored gradient mechanism with a dual-nature formulation: executing hard logical operations during training while maintaining differentiability for backpropagation. By quantizing both its input and choice state, the Predicate Neuron approximates continuous and non-continuous functions, effectively resolving discontinuities that standard deep learning architectures struggle with. We evaluate the Predicate Neuron across Fully-Connected, Convolutional, Recurrent, and Transformer architectures on benchmarks like MNIST and Wikitext. Results show that incorporating Predicate Neurons accelerates convergence, boosts accuracy, and lowers loss in general, with particularly strong improvements in tasks requiring monotonic reasoning or handling discontinuities. Overall, the Predicate Neuron natively integrates into standard neural networks to enable fuzzy logic operations and is available in Keras and PyTorch.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Native Predicate Neuron, a differentiable module that performs first-order logic quantization with a single trainable parameter, and reports faster convergence and better accuracy across several architectures.
AI.motivation: Symbolic reasoning approaches often use static architectures that are hard to integrate into deep networks and gradient-based optimization, and standard architectures struggle with discontinuous functions.
AI.method: The neuron learns to alternate between logical operations using one trainable parameter and quantizes both its input and its choice state. It uses a dual-nature gradient mechanism that executes hard logical operations during training while remaining differentiable for backpropagation.
AI.result: Across fully-connected, convolutional, recurrent, and Transformer architectures on benchmarks including MNIST and Wikitext, adding Predicate Neurons accelerates convergence, boosts accuracy, and lowers loss in general, with particularly strong gains on tasks requiring monotonic reasoning or handling discontinuities.
AI.conclusion: The Predicate Neuron integrates natively into standard networks to enable fuzzy logic operations, and implementations are available in Keras and PyTorch.

title: Selective Transfer Learning for Groundwater Level Anomaly Forecasting: Accuracy-Risk Trade-offs
summary: This work studies context-aware selective transfer learning for multi-well groundwater anomaly forecasting in the Netherlands. Source-domain pretraining can raise average accuracy but is not uniformly reliable: it degrades performance on a substantial fraction of heterogeneous wells. Context-Aware Selective Learning (CASL) uses calibration-trained, constrained contextual blending of frozen no-transfer and fixed-transfer parents. Global Convex Blend uses the same parents with one calibration-fitted weight per seed. The corrected task requires nine consecutive observed monthly inputs and an exact three-calendar-month target, without interpolation. Evaluation covers 457 wells and 13,718 test windows under five predefined seeds, with the four-cell maxsim0.60 source pool frozen using Always-TL validation RMSE alone. Fixed transfer harms 18.38-51.86% of wells. CASL has 0.424-1.084% lower RMSE than No TL, partially rescuing 97.53-99.50% and fully rescuing 23.46-43.78% of fixed-harmed wells. Partial rescue can arise structurally from convex blending and does not establish contextual superiority. Global Convex Blend protects more wells in four seeds, while CASL has slightly lower pooled RMSE in four. Neither dominates: the results support an accuracy-risk trade-off on the fixed split, not rolling deployment validity.

AI.tldr: The paper studies context-aware selective transfer learning for groundwater level anomaly forecasting across 457 Dutch wells and finds an accuracy-risk trade-off rather than a clear winner between selective and global blending.
AI.motivation: Source-domain pretraining raises average accuracy but is not uniformly reliable, since it degrades performance on a substantial fraction of heterogeneous wells.
AI.method: Context-Aware Selective Learning (CASL) uses calibration-trained, constrained contextual blending of frozen no-transfer and fixed-transfer parents. Global Convex Blend uses the same parents with one calibration-fitted weight per seed. The four-cell maxsim0.60 source pool is frozen using Always-TL validation RMSE alone, and evaluation uses 13,718 test windows under five predefined seeds with a fixed target definition.
AI.result: Fixed transfer harms 18.38 to 51.86% of wells. CASL has 0.424 to 1.084% lower RMSE than No TL, partially rescuing 97.53 to 99.50% and fully rescuing 23.46 to 43.78% of fixed-harmed wells. Global Convex Blend protects more wells in four seeds, while CASL has slightly lower pooled RMSE in four.
AI.conclusion: Partial rescue can arise structurally from convex blending and does not establish contextual superiority, so the results support an accuracy-risk trade-off on the fixed split but not rolling deployment validity.

title: Anisotropic Trust Region Warping for Prior-Data Fitted Networks in Bayesian Optimisation
comment: Accepted at the 2026 NeurIPS Workshop on Optimization for Machine Learning (OPT). 18 pages, 12 figures
summary: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) replace the hyperparameter refitting of Gaussian Process (GP) surrogates in Bayesian optimisation with a single forward pass, at the cost of a prior that is fixed at meta-training time. We show empirically that a PFN's predictive log-likelihood falls increasingly behind that of a refitted GP as the objective function's lengthscale grows beyond the mode of the PFN's meta-training prior, and that this deficit carries over to optimisation performance. To correct the mismatch without retraining the network, we introduce Anisotropic Trust Region (ATR) warping. Per-dimension lengthscales are estimated by kernel target alignment, and an affine rescaling of the input space maps the objective onto the lengthscale the PFN expects, with a trust region around the anchor determining which observations are retained, leaving the PFN's $\mathcal{O}(d \cdot N^2)$ inference cost unchanged. On functions drawn from a Matérn-3/2 kernel, ATR warping improves optimisation performance of the PFN at both extremes of the lengthscale range. Our implementation is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Anisotropic Trust Region (ATR) warping, which corrects a Prior-Data Fitted Network's lengthscale mismatch in Bayesian optimisation without retraining, and improves optimisation on Matern-3/2 functions at both ends of the lengthscale range.
AI.motivation: A PFN's predictive log-likelihood falls behind that of a refitted GP as the objective's lengthscale grows beyond the mode of the PFN's meta-training prior, and this deficit carries over to optimisation performance. Retraining the network is costly.
AI.method: Per-dimension lengthscales are estimated by kernel target alignment, and an affine rescaling of the input space maps the objective onto the lengthscale the PFN expects. A trust region around the anchor determines which observations are retained, and the O(d N^2) inference cost is unchanged.
AI.result: On functions drawn from a Matern-3/2 kernel, ATR warping improves the optimisation performance of the PFN at both extremes of the lengthscale range.
AI.conclusion: ATR warping offers a retraining-free correction for PFN prior mismatch in Bayesian optimisation, with the implementation publicly available.

title: Spokes, not a Ring: Revisiting the Weekday Manifold in Language Models
summary: Recent work has hypothesised that large language models may represent some concepts as multi-dimensional manifolds instead of single directions. Using these manifolds to interpret or steer representations often assumes that moving along them corresponds to a continuous change in the represented concept. In this work, we test this continuous manifold assumption on the prototypical weekday manifold. Despite its striking circular geometry, we find that the weekday representations behave more like seven discrete states arranged in a circle than a continuous ring. First, we show that local sensitivity has seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping between representation and behaviour under on-manifold steering. Second, we test whether any concepts are represented along the manifold outside the seven discrete states, and find neither time of day, uncertainty, nor natural text populate the intermediate space. Together, these results challenge the continuous interpretation of the weekday manifold and motivate testing whether movement along other representation manifolds correspond to meaningful changes in model representations and behaviour.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether the weekday representation manifold in language models is a continuous ring and finds instead that it behaves like seven discrete states arranged in a circle.
AI.motivation: Interpreting or steering representations via manifolds assumes that moving along a manifold changes the represented concept continuously, and this assumption had not been tested on the prototypical weekday manifold.
AI.method: The authors measure local sensitivity along the weekday manifold and test on-manifold steering. They also probe whether time of day, uncertainty, or natural text are represented in the intermediate space between weekdays.
AI.result: Local sensitivity has seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping between representation and behaviour under on-manifold steering. Neither time of day, uncertainty, nor natural text populates the intermediate space.
AI.conclusion: The results challenge the continuous interpretation of the weekday manifold and motivate testing whether movement along other representation manifolds corresponds to meaningful changes in behaviour.

title: Responsible Quantum Machine Learning for Medical Imaging: A Fairness Audit Across Sensitive Subgroups
summary: Quantum machine learning (QML) is increasingly explored for medical classification, yet its behaviour under subgroup-aware fairness criteria remains understudied. We present an empirical fairness audit of classical and quantum classifiers for medical imaging, assuming QML is not inherently fair. Two scenarios are evaluated: dermatological lesions on DDI (sensitive attribute: Fitzpatrick skin type) and chest X-rays on CheXpert-derived data (sensitive attribute: age group). Using ResNet-18 embeddings, we train SVM, MLP, QSVM and QCNN under a baseline and three mitigation settings: differentiable Equalized Odds (EO) regularisation, Gradient Reversal Learning (GRL), and both combined. Foundation models (PanDerm, EVA-X) serve as external references. Quantum classifiers may achieve competitive aggregate performance while still exhibiting subgroup disparities. Since a smaller subgroup AUC gap may stem from degrading the best group rather than improving the worst, each mitigation is also tested against a pre-specified non-inferiority margin relative to its baseline. Under this criterion, several configurations with the smallest disparity, notably QCNN with GRL on DDI, are not clinically acceptable due to loss of global discrimination. On DDI, QSVM with GRL+EO performed best and approached PanDerm in the performance/fairness trade-off; on CheXpert, QCNN with GRL achieved the highest aggregate performance but increased disparity, and EVA-X remained stronger. Fairness effects are model- and dataset-dependent, so QML requires empirical subgroup-aware evaluation. All quantum models run in classical simulation; we claim no quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper audits classical and quantum classifiers for medical imaging across subgroups and finds that quantum models can be competitive in aggregate while still showing subgroup disparities, with fairness effects dependent on model and dataset.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning is increasingly explored for medical classification, but its behaviour under subgroup-aware fairness criteria is understudied.
AI.method: SVM, MLP, QSVM, and QCNN are trained on ResNet-18 embeddings under a baseline and three mitigations: differentiable Equalized Odds regularisation, Gradient Reversal Learning, and both combined. Dermatological lesions on DDI (Fitzpatrick skin type) and chest X-rays on CheXpert-derived data (age group) are evaluated, with PanDerm and EVA-X as external references and a pre-specified non-inferiority margin against each baseline.
AI.result: Several configurations with the smallest disparity, notably QCNN with GRL on DDI, fail the non-inferiority criterion due to loss of global discrimination. On DDI, QSVM with GRL+EO performs best and approaches PanDerm in the performance-fairness trade-off. On CheXpert, QCNN with GRL achieves the highest aggregate performance but increases disparity, while EVA-X remains stronger.
AI.conclusion: Fairness effects are model- and dataset-dependent, so QML requires empirical subgroup-aware evaluation. All quantum models run in classical simulation, and the authors claim no quantum advantage.

title: Learning Without Clocks: Partition-Invariant Neural Network
summary: Event cameras, spiking cochleas and similar sensors emit asynchronous events, yet most learning systems first bin them into frames or packets, so the output depends on how the stream was sliced. Networks whose state is updated exactly at every event and evolves in closed form between events are invariant to this slicing. We ask what more makes the output (i) independent of the processing order of simultaneous events and (ii) continuous in the time stamps, even when two events cross in time, while (iii) staying sensitive to temporal order. For arbitrary nonlinear event models we prove that (i) and (ii) are each equivalent to pairwise commutation of the event updates, and that once updates commute, all order dependence comes from their non-commutation with the inter-event dynamics and vanishes linearly in the time lag. This identifies a class of time-mediated non-commutative (TM) models and yields a resolution-robustness bound for any model. We construct the minimal TM layer, a learnable, provably Lipschitz generalization of the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator; prove that no single additive layer can uniformly represent ordered pair interactions, whereas a three-dimensional TM state can; show that each TM layer adds two levels of temporal nesting versus one for additive layers; and give a single-layer higher-order construction (TM-k) and a stacking rule preserving all three properties. We instantiate these results as the Clock-Free Event (CFE) layer, linear in the number of events, give a topology-free variant for temporal point processes with closed-form likelihoods, and specify a preregistered clock-robustness protocol with a physical-time threat model for spike-retiming attacks. In preliminary development-set experiments, the TM state beats an otherwise identical additive state by 3.5-9.1 points on DVS128 Gesture and by 24.5 and 30.6 points on SHD and Speech Commands.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Time-mediated non-commutative (TM) layers and the Clock-Free Event (CFE) layer, which make event-based network outputs invariant to how a stream is sliced and continuous in event timestamps while remaining sensitive to temporal order.
AI.motivation: Event cameras and similar sensors emit asynchronous events, but most learning systems bin them into frames or packets, so the output depends on how the stream was sliced.
AI.method: The authors prove that invariance to event order at simultaneous times and continuity in timestamps are each equivalent to pairwise commutation of event updates, and that order dependence then comes only from non-commutation with inter-event dynamics. They construct a minimal learnable, Lipschitz TM layer as a generalization of the Hassenstein-Reichardt correlator, a three-dimensional TM state, a single-layer higher-order TM-k construction, and a stacking rule.
AI.result: In preliminary development-set experiments, the TM state beats an otherwise identical additive state by 3.5 to 9.1 points on DVS128 Gesture and by 24.5 and 30.6 points on SHD and Speech Commands.
AI.conclusion: The theory yields a linear-in-events layer and a clock-robustness protocol, and the authors argue that TM states provide a principled route to time-slicing-invariant event learning, though the empirical evidence is preliminary.

title: Learning Lotteries with Minimal Stakeholder Violations from Membership Queries
comment: 31 pages, full version of paper at NeurIPS 2026
summary: An AI developer often has several candidate versions of a system and can deploy a mixture of them, sending each request to a randomly chosen version, as in A/B testing. Each stakeholder (e.g., a safety team, a regulator, or a customer with private test data) accepts a mixture exactly when its expected performance (e.g., its rate of harmful replies) meets the stakeholder's own standard, which the developer can learn only by asking whether a proposed mixture is acceptable. We model this as choosing a lottery over $m$ alternatives for $n$ agents, each of whom accepts exactly the lotteries in an unknown halfspace and answers such binary membership queries. While Choo et al. (ICML 2026) sought a lottery that every agent accepts, none may exist when, say, safety and helpfulness requirements conflict, so we minimize the number of rejecting agents. We show that this problem is APX-hard even when all halfspaces are known and all utilities are $0$ or $1$. We then give exact algorithms that run in polynomial time when $m$ is constant, and in quasi-polynomial time when, for a constant $\eta$, some optimal lottery has no accepting agent within $\eta$ of its threshold. When only some agents can be queried, optimizing over a uniform sample of agents gives additive and relative guarantees for the whole population, with a sample size that does not depend on $n$, and a linear program gives a polynomial-time method for any $m$. On the other hand, for $m\ge 3$, a deterministic algorithm that queries only $K$ distinct agents cannot guarantee fewer than $n-K$ extra rejections, and this is achievable; in other words, it can guarantee nothing for the agents it does not ask. Small synthetic experiments indicate that our worst-case bounds are conservative on random instances.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to choose a lottery over candidate AI systems that minimizes the number of stakeholders who reject it, using only membership queries, and gives hardness results together with exact and approximation algorithms.
AI.motivation: Each stakeholder accepts a mixture of AI versions only when its own standard is met, and the developer can learn this only by querying. Conflicting requirements, such as safety and helpfulness, can make a lottery that every agent accepts impossible to find.
AI.method: Agents accept exactly the lotteries in an unknown halfspace, and the authors minimize the number of rejecting agents. They analyze exact algorithms that are polynomial in time for constant m and quasi-polynomial under a threshold margin condition, sampling-based guarantees for querying only some agents, and a linear programming method for any m.
AI.result: The problem is APX-hard even when all halfspaces are known and utilities are 0 or 1. For m at least 3, any deterministic algorithm that queries only K distinct agents cannot guarantee fewer than n minus K extra rejections, and this bound is achievable. Small synthetic experiments suggest the worst-case bounds are conservative on random instances.
AI.conclusion: Querying a limited set of stakeholders gives guarantees only for the agents asked, and the worst-case bounds are conservative on random instances.

title: Depth through Recurrence: Towards Ultra-Efficient On-Device ASR
summary: Modern automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have achieved remarkable accuracy by scaling model depth and capacity, but at the cost of increased memory, energy, and computational demands. On edge devices where ASR is often most needed, such as watches and glasses, deploying such large models is infeasible due to extremely constrained resources. This raises a fundamental question: can we achieve high representational power in deep ASR models without scaling up parameterization? In this work, we revisit the role of depth and identify layer wise representational dynamics, in which most layers learn functionally similar transformations. Motivated by this insight, we propose a block-recurrent ASR architecture that replaces parameterized depth with a small set of recurrent blocks, each consisting of weight-shared layers, thereby preserving effective depth while drastically reducing model size. Through representation-guided grouping and knowledge distillation, block-recurrent models retain the accuracy of large reference models while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Across Open ASR Leaderboard benchmarks, a model with only two shared blocks recovers 97.4% of the accuracy of large models on average. The compact backbone further enables efficient on-device personalization through lightweight MoE-LoRA adaptation, allowing user-specific models to match or surpass the accuracy of general-purpose ASR systems with significantly lower inference cost. By reusing weights across recurrent steps, the proposed architecture reduces memory-access overhead and inference energy consumption. Together, these results show that high quality ASR can be achieved without large parameterization, and that structured recurrence provides a principled path towards ultra-compressed, energy-efficient, and personalized speech recognition on the edge.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a block-recurrent ASR architecture that replaces parameterized depth with a few weight-shared recurrent blocks, retaining most of the accuracy of large models with far fewer parameters for on-device speech recognition.
AI.motivation: High-accuracy ASR scales model depth and capacity, which is infeasible on resource-constrained edge devices such as watches and glasses. Layers in deep ASR models learn functionally similar transformations, suggesting that depth can be obtained without parameters.
AI.method: Representation-guided grouping and knowledge distillation are used to build block-recurrent models in which small sets of weight-shared layers are applied recurrently. Lightweight MoE-LoRA adapters support on-device personalization.
AI.result: Across Open ASR Leaderboard benchmarks, a model with only two shared blocks recovers 97.4% of the accuracy of large models on average, using an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Personalized models can match or surpass general-purpose ASR accuracy at significantly lower inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Weight reuse across recurrent steps reduces memory-access overhead and inference energy, showing that high-quality ASR is achievable without large parameterization.

title: Improving Data-Constrained Scaling with Hyperparameter Transfer and Ensembling
summary: As growing compute budgets outpace the growth of high-quality training data, large language models must be trained with both compute and data constraints in mind. Unfortunately, existing prescriptions for data-constrained scaling suffer from two important limitations. First, past works hold key hyperparameters such as weight decay fixed with scale, despite the fact that optimal hyperparameters vary wildly with model size and number of epochs. Second, past works neglect ensembling, a promising axis for scaling under data constraints. As a surprising consequence, prior prescriptions can lead to loss that increases with compute budget. We address both limitations by fitting power laws that prescribe how to transfer hyperparameters with scale and scaling laws that prescribe how to allocate compute with ensembling. Training on 100M tokens from FineWeb, our recipe reduces validation loss by over 0.15 nats compared to prior recipes, a 14% decrease in perplexity, and achieves monotonic improvements with compute through ensembling. These gains are achieved using prescriptions fit to smaller runs and validated at up to 12$\times$ larger compute budgets.

AI.tldr: The paper fits power laws for transferring hyperparameters across scale and scaling laws for allocating compute to ensembles, and shows that the resulting recipe reduces validation loss under a fixed data budget and improves monotonically with compute.
AI.motivation: Existing data-constrained scaling prescriptions hold key hyperparameters such as weight decay fixed across scale, and they neglect ensembling, so prior prescriptions can lead to loss that increases with compute budget.
AI.method: Power laws prescribe how to transfer hyperparameters with model size and epochs, and scaling laws prescribe how to allocate compute with ensembling. The recipe is fit on smaller runs trained on 100M tokens from FineWeb.
AI.result: The recipe reduces validation loss by over 0.15 nats compared with prior recipes, a 14% decrease in perplexity, and yields monotonic improvements with compute through ensembling. The prescriptions were validated at up to 12 times larger compute budgets.
AI.conclusion: Hyperparameter transfer and ensembling together give a more reliable data-constrained scaling recipe, validated beyond the scale used for fitting.

title: Interpretable neural equation learning for high-dimensional materials data
summary: Equation learning seeks to discover compact, interpretable equations from data using various machine-learning techniques. However, few workflows discover and interpret learned equations in sparse, high-dimensional materials datasets. We present nn-EQL, an equation-learning framework that generates candidate equations through iterative training, pruning, and retraining of a neural network with customizable, user-specified neuron-level activation functions. Candidate equations are ranked using a minimum description length (MDL)-inspired score, balancing error and sparsity, and diagnosed to assess term-wise contributions, input-scaled sensitivities, and uncertainties. We demonstrate nn-EQL on standard AI-Feynman benchmarks as well as multiscale high-dimensional materials datasets such as finite-element simulations of heterogeneous materials, and high-throughput experimental thin-film deposition data. nn-EQL integrates with tabular data and high-dimensional data via standard encoder models, learning equations and providing insight into learned terms. Looking forward, integrating physically interpretable representations, multimodal and multi-fidelity data, and adaptive data acquisition could enable equation learning to formulate and test mechanistic hypotheses.

AI.tldr: The paper presents nn-EQL, an equation-learning framework that discovers and ranks compact equations from sparse high-dimensional materials data via iterative neural network pruning and retraining, scored by an MDL-inspired criterion.
AI.motivation: Few workflows discover and interpret learned equations in sparse, high-dimensional materials datasets, which limits interpretable insight in that domain.
AI.method: Candidate equations are generated by iterative training, pruning, and retraining of a neural network with user-specified neuron-level activation functions. Candidates are ranked by a minimum description length-inspired score balancing error and sparsity, and diagnosed for term-wise contributions, input-scaled sensitivities, and uncertainties. Standard encoder models handle tabular and high-dimensional inputs.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated on standard AI-Feynman benchmarks, multiscale finite-element simulations of heterogeneous materials, and high-throughput experimental thin-film deposition data.
AI.conclusion: Integrating physically interpretable representations, multimodal and multi-fidelity data, and adaptive data acquisition could let equation learning formulate and test mechanistic hypotheses.

title: SAC-GCL: Structure-Aware Compression for Graph Contrastive Learning
summary: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) has achieved remarkable success in self-supervised representation learning by maximizing agreement between augmented views of a graph. Although augmented view generation is the central step in GCL, existing models rely on stochastic augmentation of the input graph, such as edge perturbation and node masking, which lack structural awareness and frequently destroy critical topology or introduce semantically inconsistent views. While recent adaptive methods improve upon random perturbations, they primarily operate on localized node or edge neighborhoods and fail to capture higher-order, macro-level structural organization crucial for graph classification. To address this limitation, we propose Structure-aware Compression for Graph Contrastive Learning (SAC-GCL), a novel framework that employs structural decomposition and graph compression as a principled view generation strategy. Moving beyond random augmentations, SAC-GCL leverages structural decomposition techniques to extract cohesive subgraphs and condense them into supernodes, constructing coarsened graph views that preserve local density and capture higher-level structural patterns while reducing noise and redundancy. We leverage multiple cohesive subgraph models to derive complementary views of the graph, each capturing distinct structural properties. To capture multi-resolution information, a hierarchical view encoder processes these compressed views by initializing super-node features with shared-weight cohesive subgraph embeddings. Our results from extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that structure-aware compression provides a powerful alternative to random perturbations, yielding more robust and discriminative graph representations for graph classification tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SAC-GCL, a graph contrastive learning framework that generates augmented views by compressing cohesive subgraphs into supernodes instead of random perturbations, and reports more robust representations for graph classification.
AI.motivation: Existing graph contrastive learning uses stochastic augmentations that break critical topology, and adaptive methods operate only on local neighborhoods, missing the macro-level structure needed for graph classification.
AI.method: Structural decomposition extracts cohesive subgraphs with several cohesive subgraph models, which are condensed into supernodes to form coarsened complementary views. A hierarchical view encoder initializes super-node features with shared-weight cohesive subgraph embeddings to capture multi-resolution information.
AI.result: Experiments on six benchmark datasets show that structure-aware compression yields more robust and discriminative graph representations for graph classification than random perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Structure-aware compression is presented as a principled alternative to random augmentation for graph contrastive learning.

title: Think Twice: The Metis-1.6 Technical Report
comment: 39 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables. Models and benchmark data: this https URL
summary: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.

AI.tldr: The Metis-1.6 technical report presents two models, Praxis and Logos, trained from scratch on 1.02T tokens, which are competitive on mathematics and reach the Pareto frontier on data and active-parameter efficiency, while being weak at code, instruction following and long context.
AI.motivation: The work asks whether better data, training methods, and architectures can compensate for a smaller parameter count, and it also documents what went wrong during development.
AI.method: Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active) use a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack applied twice per token. Training comprises 804.76B tokens of pretraining, 18B tokens of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B tokens of supervised fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across 40 post-trained benchmarks, Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models and within a point of Qwen3-4B. It ranks second of 30 models in mathematics, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. The authors report that the optimizer configured never ran, attention trained with AdamW throughout pretraining, and a length reward under group-mean normalization inverted its sign once pass rate passed 2/3, which a one-line clamp fixes.
AI.conclusion: Metis-1.6 is modest overall but efficient for its training data and active parameters, and its reported failures and the 10B-token ablations motivate the looped MoRE architecture of Metis-1.7.

title: TERRA: Task-Oriented Edge AI for Regional Fire Detection with Identity-Free Reporting
comment: Accepted for publication at the 16th International Conference on the Internet of Things (IoT 2026)
summary: Distributed fire-monitoring systems may involve many sensing devices reporting over a shared uplink, even though the operational objective is often to identify regions exhibiting evidence of fire rather than to recover device-specific measurements. We introduce TERRA (Task-Oriented Edge Representation and Regional Aggregation), an edge-AI framework that combines task-oriented local inference, identity-free region-tagged reporting, and permutation-invariant regional evidence aggregation. TERRA supports two reporting modes: TERRA-Score, in which each device communicates a quantized local fire probability, and TERRA-Feature, in which it communicates a compact learned representation for receiver-side aggregation using a permutation-invariant DeepSets model. Using all 15 numerical sensing modalities of the distributed indoor EN54 fire-alarm dataset as a proof-of-concept testbed, we evaluate regional inference for an episode-level fire-scenario target under repetition-disjoint three-fold cross-validation. We study representation size, task-payload quantization, report availability, and robustness to missed and false recovered messages. With nine reports and perfect message recovery, TERRA-Feature achieves mean AUPRC 0.990 using a 24-bit task payload, while TERRA-Score achieves 0.987 using only 6 bits; both attain an MDR of 1.81% at FAR $\leq$1%. TERRA-Feature achieves slightly higher AUPRC under reliable recovery, whereas the more compact TERRA-Score is less sensitive to increasing false-message contamination.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TERRA, an edge-AI framework for regional fire detection that reports identity-free, region-tagged evidence and aggregates it with a permutation-invariant model, reaching AUPRC above 0.98 with very small payloads.
AI.motivation: Distributed fire-monitoring systems share an uplink, but the operational goal is to identify regions with fire evidence rather than recover device-specific measurements.
AI.method: TERRA-Score sends a quantized local fire probability from each device, and TERRA-Feature sends a compact learned representation aggregated at the receiver by a permutation-invariant DeepSets model. Evaluation uses the 15 sensing modalities of the EN54 fire-alarm dataset under repetition-disjoint three-fold cross-validation, with varying representation size, quantization, report availability, and message loss or false messages.
AI.result: With nine reports and perfect message recovery, TERRA-Feature achieves mean AUPRC 0.990 with a 24-bit task payload, and TERRA-Score achieves 0.987 with 6 bits. Both reach a miss detection rate of 1.81% at false alarm rate of at most 1%. TERRA-Score is less sensitive to increasing false-message contamination.
AI.conclusion: TERRA-Feature is slightly more accurate under reliable recovery, while the more compact TERRA-Score is more robust to contamination, making task-oriented regional reporting a viable edge design for fire monitoring.

title: Generative modeling for fusion: a large-scale benchmark of stellarator fast-ion simulations
summary: Stellarators offer a promising magnetic confinement approach for achieving controlled nuclear fusion. However, stellarator design remains challenging, as evaluating configuration performance requires computationally expensive, high-fidelity simulations. In particular, key performance metrics derived from guiding center simulations are costly to include directly in the design optimization loop, and are almost exclusively used as diagnostics. Machine learning has the potential to advance fusion research by enabling rapid generation and evaluation of new stellarator configurations. Effectively applying ML for fusion demands large-scale datasets that capture both design diversity and high-fidelity simulation outputs. In this work, we introduce the Benchmark of Stellarator Simulations (BoSS), a dataset of stellarator designs paired with guiding center simulation results and trajectories. The BoSS is the first large-scale dataset of guiding center simulations, containing simulation data for 180,000 distinct magnetohydrodynamic equilibria spanning a wide range of magnetic geometries and confinement properties. To exemplify the utility of ML to accelerate stellarator design, we formulate and address two sets of modeling tasks: generative modeling for designing stellarators with good particle confinement, and surrogate modeling for predicting stellarator heat deposition patterns and particle trajectories. The tasks reveal the potential impact ML can have in the stellarator field and important opportunities to improve the applicability of ML models in the sciences. Our baselines generate diverse, performant stellarators and provide useful surrogate predictions, and point to long-horizon trajectory forecasting and out-of-distribution generation as key directions for future work. The BoSS can be accessed through this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BoSS, a large benchmark of 180,000 stellarator equilibria paired with guiding-center fast-ion simulation results, and shows that generative and surrogate ML models can design and predict stellarator confinement and heat deposition.
AI.motivation: Stellarator design requires expensive high-fidelity guiding-center simulations, which are mostly used as diagnostics rather than in the design loop, and ML for fusion needs large datasets covering design diversity and simulation outputs.
AI.method: The Benchmark of Stellarator Simulations (BoSS) pairs stellarator designs with guiding-center simulation results and trajectories. Two task families are formulated: generative modeling for designing stellarators with good particle confinement, and surrogate modeling for predicting heat deposition patterns and particle trajectories.
AI.result: Baselines generate diverse, performant stellarators and provide useful surrogate predictions. The authors identify long-horizon trajectory forecasting and out-of-distribution generation as key directions for future work.
AI.conclusion: BoSS is presented as the first large-scale dataset of guiding-center simulations and as a resource to improve the applicability of ML models in fusion science.

title: Muon Makes the First Mixture-of-Experts Layer Harder to Balance
comment: 34 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Code and runs: this https URL
summary: Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router. In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less. The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss. On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that Muon, rather than the router, raises the load-balancing bias span of the first MoE layer, driven by a shared direction in the first router's inputs, and that batch-mean subtraction or halving Muon's learning rate mitigates it.
AI.motivation: Open MoE models trained with Muon disagree on whether Muon should also train the router, and the effect of the optimizer on how hard each layer is to balance was not measured.
AI.method: In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, the span of per-layer load-balancing biases, meaning the largest minus the smallest, is tracked across optimizer settings. The authors test moving only the router to AdamW and subtracting the batch mean from router inputs over the first 3,000 steps, and vary Muon's learning rate on the smaller model.
AI.result: At tuned learning rates, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while other layers changed much less. The first router's inputs shared a direction, and its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share after warmup. Subtracting the batch mean removed this overload with little loss change, and halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved loss. Moving only the router to AdamW increased load shifts and slightly raised loss.
AI.conclusion: At this scale the results favour keeping the router on Muon, and the first MoE layer's balance is sensitive to the optimizer acting on the rest of the network.

title: Bi-Phase Training: Learning Efficiently From Scratch
summary: Pre-training foundational models is computationally expensive as models scale. In this work, we introduce Bi-Phase Training (BPT), a parameter-efficient pre-training method that preserves the high-rank learning dynamics observed in full-parameter optimization with substantially reduced trainable parameters. BPT parameterizes each weight update as a composition of constrained high-rank left/right transformations via trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters whose updates are periodically merged into the frozen base weights, resulting in a compounding expansion of accessible directions during training. Across language-model pre-training from scratch (Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B) on FineWeb-Edu (10B and 100B tokens), BPT achieves validation perplexity close to full-parameter baselines while using far fewer trainable parameters; e.g., at the 1.5B scale, BPT uses 66% fewer trainable parameters with only a small validation-perplexity gap. Additionally, a comprehensive evaluation across diverse downstream tasks shows that BPT preserves much of the full-parameterized model's downstream performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Bi-Phase Training (BPT), a parameter-efficient pretraining method that composes constrained high-rank transformations with diagonal matrices and periodically merged low-rank adapters, and approaches full-parameter perplexity with far fewer trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Pretraining foundation models is computationally expensive, and parameter-efficient methods often lose the high-rank learning dynamics seen in full-parameter optimization.
AI.method: Each weight update is parameterized as a composition of constrained high-rank left and right transformations, built from trainable diagonal matrices and low-rank adapters. The adapters are periodically merged into frozen base weights, which expands the accessible update directions over training.
AI.result: Pretraining Qwen2.5 models from 100M to 1.5B parameters and OLMo-2-1B on FineWeb-Edu with 10B and 100B tokens gives validation perplexity close to full-parameter baselines. At 1.5B, BPT uses 66% fewer trainable parameters with a small perplexity gap, and it preserves much of the downstream performance across diverse tasks.
AI.conclusion: BPT offers a parameter-efficient route to pretraining from scratch that retains most of the performance of full-parameter training.

title: Finite-Step Geometry of Marginal-Preserving Velocity Fields in Generative Flows
summary: Generative flows can admit different velocity fields that induce the same continuous marginal evolution but behave differently after numerical discretization. We study this finite-step non-equivalence while keeping the marginal path and numerical method fixed. Projected modified equations characterize the component of local integration error that changes the marginal law and give sufficient conditions for higher marginal convergence order. For affine fixed-shape distributions, we characterize exact finite-step reachability and derive spectral obstructions and sharp nearest-reachable Wasserstein errors. For diffusion probability-flow ODEs, we construct skew-score perturbations that preserve the exact marginal path under exact scores and quantify their leakage under score error. Controlled Gaussian and mixture experiments recover the predicted order, reachability, and obstruction phenomena.

AI.tldr: The paper studies generative flows in which different velocity fields induce the same continuous marginal evolution but behave differently under discretization, and characterizes which marginal-preserving fields give higher finite-step convergence and reachability.
AI.motivation: Velocity fields that share the same continuous marginal path can yield different results after numerical discretization, and this finite-step non-equivalence was not well understood.
AI.method: Projected modified equations characterize the part of local integration error that changes the marginal law, which gives sufficient conditions for higher marginal convergence order. For affine fixed-shape distributions, exact finite-step reachability and spectral obstructions are derived, and for diffusion probability-flow ODEs, skew-score perturbations preserving the exact marginal path are constructed and their leakage under score error is quantified.
AI.result: Controlled Gaussian and mixture experiments recover the predicted order, reachability, and obstruction phenomena.
AI.conclusion: The analysis gives a geometric account of how marginal-preserving velocity fields differ at finite step size, with sharp Wasserstein error bounds for nearest reachable distributions.

title: SAG-Sep: Sparse Augmented Graphs and Onion-Guided Search for Rounded Capacity Cut Separation
comment: 42 pages, 4 figures, 26 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track). Code: this https URL
summary: Rounded capacity cuts (RCCs) are among the most effective cuts for capacitated vehicle-routing relaxations, but exact separation is computationally prohibitive at scale. Existing heuristic and neural separators can be fast, but often fail to produce sufficiently many effective cuts within practical separation budgets. We introduce SAG-Sep, a separator that scores node membership in RCC-inducing subsets across vehicle-count levels from a fractional LP solution in a single encoder forward pass, avoiding the iterative predict-and-coarsen inference used by NeuralSEP-style separators. SAG-Sep encodes the LP solution as a Sparse Augmented Graph (SAG), adding flow-informed multi-hop edges that expose long-range routing structure without densifying attention. Beyond LP-aware sparse encoding, we observe that high-value exact RCCs are typically nested, organizing into onion-like subset families, and SAG-Sep's node scores track subset nesting depth. This motivates Onion-Sweep (OS), a training-free decoder that ranks customers by their scores, evaluates the RCC violation of every prefix of the ranking in one vectorized pass, and emits the most violated prefix of each replica together with a cross-replica family of nested proposals, converting independent node scores into structurally coordinated RCC candidates without a tuned threshold or probing band. On the NeuralSEP benchmark with N=1000 customer instances, SAG-Sep with OS reduces the average root gap by 17.7% relative to the strongest NeuralSEP baseline, while the single-pass SAG-Sep separator achieves a roughly 30-fold per-iteration neural separation speedup. Our findings suggest that LP-aware sparse encoding and the nested structure of high-value cuts are structural patterns worth leveraging in neural separation more broadly.

AI.tldr: SAG-Sep is a neural separator for rounded capacity cuts in capacitated vehicle routing that encodes the LP solution as a Sparse Augmented Graph and scores customers in a single encoder pass, paired with a training-free Onion-Sweep decoder that emits nested cut candidates. On the NeuralSEP benchmark with N=1000 it reduces the average root gap by 17.7% relative to the strongest NeuralSEP baseline and gives a roughly 30-fold per-iteration separation speedup.
AI.motivation: Exact separation of rounded capacity cuts is computationally prohibitive at scale, and existing heuristic and neural separators are fast but often fail to produce enough effective cuts within practical separation budgets, while NeuralSEP-style separators rely on iterative predict-and-coarsen inference.
AI.method: The LP solution is encoded as a Sparse Augmented Graph with flow-informed multi-hop edges, and node scores track the nesting depth of high-value cuts; Onion-Sweep ranks customers by score, evaluates the RCC violation of every prefix of the ranking in one vectorized pass, and emits the most violated prefix plus a cross-replica family of nested proposals without a tuned threshold.
AI.result: On the NeuralSEP benchmark with N=1000 customer instances, SAG-Sep with Onion-Sweep reduces the average root gap by 17.7% relative to the strongest NeuralSEP baseline, and the single-pass SAG-Sep separator achieves a roughly 30-fold per-iteration neural separation speedup.
AI.conclusion: LP-aware sparse encoding and the nested structure of high-value cuts are structural patterns worth leveraging in neural separation more broadly.

title: Self-Supervised Latent Action-Conditioned World Modeling for Time Series
summary: Time-series data play an important role in various tasks, such as weather forecasting, web traffic analysis, and speech recognition. Recently, pioneering studies have increasingly adopted Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) based encoders to learn time-series representations through latent-space prediction. However, they often overlook the underlying factors governing transitions between time-series observations. In this work, we hypothesize that explicitly modeling the information behind changes in time series can facilitate time-series modeling. Building on this hypothesis, we propose ACTS-WM, a self-supervised latent action-conditioned world model framework for time-series analysis. First, we introduce a latent action modeling approach that infers the underlying information behind time-series transitions as latent actions, without requiring explicit action annotations. We then develop a JEPA-based encoder and an action-conditioned world model to predict target time-series representations conditioned on the learned latent actions and task information. We evaluate ACTS-WM across 4 representative tasks on 22 datasets from diverse domains, covering univariate and multivariate forecasting and classification. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ACTS-WM can improve downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders by learning complementary representations.

AI.tldr: ACTS-WM is a self-supervised world-model framework for time series that infers latent actions behind transitions between observations and uses them to condition a JEPA-based predictor. It improves downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders across 4 tasks on 22 datasets.
AI.motivation: JEPA-based time-series encoders learn representations through latent-space prediction but often overlook the underlying factors that govern transitions between time-series observations.
AI.method: A latent action modeling approach infers the information behind time-series transitions as latent actions without requiring explicit action annotations, and a JEPA-based encoder with an action-conditioned world model predicts target representations conditioned on these latent actions and task information.
AI.result: Evaluated on 4 representative tasks across 22 datasets from diverse domains, covering univariate and multivariate forecasting and classification, ACTS-WM improves downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders by learning complementary representations.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling the information behind changes in time series can facilitate time-series modeling.

title: Application of PDE emulators for a multi-material, multi-physics simulation problem
comment: Accepted at ICMLA 2026, Rochester, MI, USA
summary: Machine learning (ML) architectures are being developed for fast emulation of numerical simulators to accelerate both scientific discovery and engineering design. While these approaches are well-tested on popular PDE (partial differential equation) benchmarks, it is necessary to evaluate their performance on datasets that more accurately reflect industrial and engineering applications. We evaluate several computer vision-based architectures trained as surrogate models on a challenging computational physics task involving multiple materials, revealing significant implementation challenges for adapting certain pre-trained models, including transformer-based architectures. For such multi-physics multi-material datasets, our results underscore the importance of learning algorithms designed for sparse and imbalanced data, techniques for adapting spatial encodings and physical consistency metrics, in addition to methods for reducing the cost of generating sufficient training data.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates several computer-vision-based architectures as surrogate models for a multi-material, multi-physics simulation task and finds significant implementation challenges in adapting certain pre-trained models, including transformer-based architectures. It argues that industrial datasets of this kind call for methods for sparse and imbalanced data, adapted spatial encodings, physical consistency metrics, and cheaper generation of training data.
AI.motivation: ML emulators of numerical simulators are well tested on popular PDE benchmarks, but their performance on datasets that more accurately reflect industrial and engineering applications has not been evaluated.
AI.method: Several computer-vision-based architectures are trained as surrogate models on a computational physics task involving multiple materials.
AI.result: The evaluation reveals significant implementation challenges for adapting certain pre-trained models, including transformer-based architectures, on this multi-physics multi-material dataset.
AI.conclusion: For such datasets, learning algorithms designed for sparse and imbalanced data, techniques for adapting spatial encodings, physical consistency metrics, and methods for reducing the cost of generating training data are important.

title: Sometimes less is more: Investigating inductive biases of MLPs and Transformers on noisy k-parity features
summary: We empirically investigate how MLPs and Transformers differ when trained on data sets containing one or more features encoded by noisy k-parity. Noisy k-parity gives us hard synthetic data sets in which we can control the predictivity and availability of every feature. Across a range of data distributions, data scales and model sizes, we find large differences in the training dynamics and inductive biases of the two architectures: Transformers are more robust to noisy features but struggle to learn complex, low-availability features, whereas MLPs show the opposite trend and improve steadily with more data. We also find that, under a fixed training budget, increasing the number of unique training examples can slow Transformer optimisation enough to reduce final accuracy, so that a smaller data set performs better. Training-accuracy results show this is an optimisation-speed effect; it shrinks, but does not vanish, when the budget is scaled with the data set size. By giving precise control over feature predictivity and availability, this testbed offers a clear starting point for understanding when and why Transformers and MLPs learn differently, and for designing data and training budgets that exploit those differences.

AI.tldr: The paper compares MLPs and Transformers trained on synthetic noisy k-parity features and finds that Transformers are more robust to noisy features but struggle with complex low-availability features, while MLPs show the opposite trend. It also finds that under a fixed training budget, more unique training examples can slow Transformer optimisation and reduce final accuracy.
AI.motivation: Understanding when and why Transformers and MLPs learn differently requires a testbed with precise control over feature predictivity and availability.
AI.method: Noisy k-parity is used to build synthetic datasets in which the predictivity and availability of every feature can be controlled, and the two architectures are compared across data distributions, data scales and model sizes.
AI.result: Transformers are more robust to noisy features but struggle to learn complex, low-availability features, whereas MLPs improve steadily with more data. Under a fixed training budget, increasing the number of unique training examples can slow Transformer optimisation enough to reduce accuracy; this effect shrinks but does not vanish when the budget is scaled with data set size.
AI.conclusion: The testbed offers a clear starting point for understanding the inductive biases of the two architectures and for designing data and training budgets that exploit their differences.

title: Separability Is Not Alignability: Representations for Spectrum-to-Molecule Retrieval
comment: 22 pages, 3 figures. Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Representations for the Physical Sciences (RPS). OpenReview: this https URL
summary: Identifying a small molecule from its tandem mass spectrum is limited by paired data. Foundation models offer a way around this scarcity: pretrain a spectrum encoder on unlabeled spectra and a molecule encoder on a large corpus of structures, then align the two frozen representations, as in vision-language and as the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests. We audit this route on MassSpecGym with spectrum encoders retrained free of test-fold contamination. Alignment needs a metric relating distinct molecules, but the objectives that produce spectrum encoders never see molecular structure: we prove that some predictive objectives fix molecular identity without fixing that metric. Moreover, we find that a candidate-based objective rewards a spectrum-independent prior over the benchmark's decoys, which we isolate. What ultimately addresses data scarcity is not architectural: simulated spectra surpass frozen geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper audits aligning frozen spectrum and molecule encoders for spectrum-to-molecule retrieval on MassSpecGym and shows that the objectives producing spectrum encoders do not fix the molecular metric that alignment needs. It finds that simulated spectra surpass frozen geometry, so addressing data scarcity is not an architectural question.
AI.motivation: Identifying a small molecule from its tandem mass spectrum is limited by paired data, and aligning foundation-model encoders pretrained on unlabeled spectra and on molecular structures has been proposed as a way around this scarcity.
AI.method: Spectrum encoders are retrained on MassSpecGym free of test-fold contamination, and the frozen representations are aligned; the paper proves that some predictive objectives fix molecular identity without fixing the metric relating distinct molecules, and isolates a spectrum-independent prior that a candidate-based objective rewards.
AI.result: Some predictive objectives fix molecular identity without fixing the molecular metric needed for alignment, and a candidate-based objective rewards a spectrum-independent prior over the benchmark's decoys. Simulated spectra surpass frozen geometry.
AI.conclusion: What ultimately addresses data scarcity is not architectural; simulated spectra outperform the frozen-representation alignment route.

title: Predicting Sparse Observables in Parameterized Unsteady Flows Using Coarse-Mesh Graph Neural Networks
summary: Full-order surrogates for high-dimensional nonlinear flows are often unnecessary when applications require only selected degrees of freedom. We propose reduced-order models that bypass full-state reconstruction by deploying graph neural networks (GNNs) directly on coarse meshes. Applied to parameterized 2D/3D confined cylinder flows and an unevenly heated cavity over Reynolds/Rayleigh-number ranges, the models generalize to unseen conditions and accurately predict sparse probe locations and integrated quantities. Coarse-mesh GNNs match or outperform finer-mesh surrogates while reducing training time and memory, even for 3D chaotic dynamics. A dynamics-informed adaptive sampling strategy guided by frequency-spectrum variations reduces maximum errors by an order of magnitude versus uniform sampling at negligible cost. Coarse-mesh training also makes noise-augmented multi-step unrolling practical, improving long-horizon autoregressive predictions. The approach outperforms parametric DMD, sparse MLPs, U-Nets, and Fourier neural operators at lower cost, and enables system identification and state estimation from sparse observations. These results show that coarse-mesh representations, adaptive sampling, and noise-augmented unrolled training form an efficient framework for reduced-order modeling of parameterized unsteady flows without solver-resolution reconstruction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes reduced-order models that run graph neural networks directly on coarse meshes to predict sparse observables in parameterized unsteady flows without full-state reconstruction. The coarse-mesh GNNs match or outperform finer-mesh surrogates while reducing training time and memory.
AI.motivation: Full-order surrogates for high-dimensional nonlinear flows are often unnecessary when an application needs only selected degrees of freedom.
AI.method: GNNs are deployed directly on coarse meshes, combined with a dynamics-informed adaptive sampling strategy guided by frequency-spectrum variations and noise-augmented multi-step unrolled training.
AI.result: On parameterized 2D and 3D confined cylinder flows and an unevenly heated cavity, the models generalize to unseen conditions and accurately predict sparse probe locations and integrated quantities. Adaptive sampling reduces maximum errors by an order of magnitude versus uniform sampling, and the approach outperforms parametric DMD, sparse MLPs, U-Nets and Fourier neural operators at lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Coarse-mesh representations, adaptive sampling and noise-augmented unrolled training form an efficient framework for reduced-order modeling of parameterized unsteady flows without solver-resolution reconstruction.

title: Deep learning for non-transvenous ICD screening: tailored neural network architectures, extended experiments, and explainability
summary: This paper studies two non-transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs), namely the Subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) and the Extravascular ICD (EV-ICD). Both avoid the complications of transvenous leads but are prone to oversensing, which can trigger inappropriate shocks associated with increased mortality. Oversensing risk is predicted by the ratio of T- or P-wave amplitude to R-wave amplitude (T:R, P:R), and these ratios vary over a 24-hour period. Yet S-ICD screening uses a single 10-second electrocardiogram (ECG) segment, and the EV-ICD has no formal screening protocol whatsoever. We present a 24-hour ambulatory screening framework for both devices which includes the first T:R analysis in an EV-ICD cohort and the first full evaluation of P:R prediction. We introduce AmpRatioNet, a family of 1D convolutional neural network architectures operating directly on the ECG signal, and benchmark it against the best existing approach - based on 2D phase space reconstruction images. Evaluation uses 4,605 clinician-annotated 10-second segments from 89 patients, with patient-level 10-fold cross-validation and bootstrap confidence intervals. AmpRatioNet-SE demonstrates superior performance on every metric in each setting with no device- or ratio-specific redesign. An explainability analysis against interpretable classical peak labelling algorithms shows that AmpRatioNet-SE's increase in error on oversensing-prone segments is up to 14 times smaller than theirs. Segment-level predictions are aggregated into a 24-hour timeline, extending S-ICD screening beyond 10 seconds and offering a plausible EV-ICD screening pathway pending device-level validation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a 24-hour ambulatory screening framework for the subcutaneous and extravascular ICDs and introduces AmpRatioNet, a family of 1D CNNs operating directly on the ECG, which outperforms the best existing 2D phase-space approach on every metric. Segment-level predictions are aggregated into a 24-hour timeline to extend screening beyond 10 seconds.
AI.motivation: Oversensing in non-transvenous ICDs can trigger inappropriate shocks linked to increased mortality, yet S-ICD screening uses a single 10-second ECG segment and the EV-ICD has no formal screening protocol.
AI.method: AmpRatioNet is benchmarked against the best existing approach, which is based on 2D phase space reconstruction images, for predicting T:R and P:R oversensing ratios, and the segment predictions are aggregated into a 24-hour timeline.
AI.result: Evaluated on 4,605 clinician-annotated 10-second segments from 89 patients with patient-level 10-fold cross-validation and bootstrap confidence intervals, AmpRatioNet-SE performs better on every metric in each setting. Its error increase on oversensing-prone segments is up to 14 times smaller than that of interpretable classical peak labelling algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The framework extends S-ICD screening beyond 10 seconds and offers a plausible EV-ICD screening pathway, pending device-level validation.

title: Towards Generalizing Pretrained All-Atom Representations to Unified Binder Design
summary: PairFormer-based all-atom models demonstrate strong capabilities in biomolecular binder design. However, existing methods often use all-atom representations for modality-specific binder design, such as protein and peptide design. In contrast, recent geometric latent diffusion models pursue unified binder design by representing molecular blocks from different modalities in a shared latent space. These complementary strengths motivate us to investigate how to generalize the use of pretrained all-atom representations to unified binder design. We introduce PairFuse, a parameter-efficient method that enables this generalization through representation fusion. Specifically, we use lightweight layerwise adapters to integrate pretrained all-atom representations into an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model.
