summary: Prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation isolates the two phases of large language model serving, but request-level path selection must account for prefill work, cache reuse, and decode demand. We present DolphinRouting, which learns this choice from end-to-end SLO feedback under a given P/D resource allocation. Requests are clustered by raw prompt length, cache-adjusted input lengths on both worker pools, and output-length information. Offline policy search learns one binary action per cluster. Online feature extraction, cluster assignment, and table lookup select local or remote prefill. We evaluate DolphinRouting on a real PD-disaggregated cluster using three public benchmarks, a mixed workload, and real data. Across the mixed workload and real data, DolphinRouting with $k$-means reduces P90 TTFT by 5.7--7.9\% and P90 TPOT by 2.6--10.1\% relative to Dynamo.

AI.tldr: Presents DolphinRouting, which learns a binary local-or-remote prefill decision per request cluster from end-to-end SLO feedback in prefill-decode disaggregated LLM serving, reducing P90 TTFT relative to Dynamo.
AI.motivation: In prefill-decode disaggregated serving, request-level path selection must jointly account for prefill work, cache reuse, and decode demand.
AI.method: Requests are clustered by raw prompt length, cache-adjusted input lengths on both worker pools, and output-length information; offline policy search learns one binary action per cluster, and online feature extraction, cluster assignment, and table lookup select local or remote prefill.
AI.result: On a real PD-disaggregated cluster with three public benchmarks, a mixed workload, and real data, DolphinRouting with k-means reduces P90 TTFT by 5.7 to 7.9% and P90 TPOT by 2.6 to 10.1% relative to Dynamo across the mixed workload and real data.
AI.conclusion: Cluster-level binary routing learned from SLO feedback is a practical way to improve latency in disaggregated LLM inference serving.

title: Causal-prior-constrained deep learning for rapid-intensification warning of western North Pacific tropical cyclones
comment: 33 pages, including 15 pages of supplementary information; 5 main figures and 6 supplementary figures
summary: Rapid intensification (RI) is one of the most dangerous and unpredictable phases of tropical cyclones, and its environmental and structural drivers are difficult to identify and separate in observations. Here we introduce CausalVisionRI, a causal-prior-constrained deep-learning system for 24-h RI warning in the western North Pacific. It integrates infrared remote sensing imagery, atmospheric and oceanic fields, and an observationally discovered causal graph into a unified model. The graph and eight sign-verified effects on 24-h intensity change provide an auditable causal prior for training. Discovered from 522 cyclones in 2000-2017, it identifies causal pathways linking atmospheric and oceanic conditions, the cyclone's dynamical and structural state, and its 24-h intensity change. On a forward holdout covering 2020-2024 and 3,004 records, the five-member ensemble achieves a Brier skill score (BSS) of 0.259 relative to a fixed development climatology, significantly exceeding four reference systems; the three LDA baselines reach at most 0.105. It also attains higher detection rates than a published knowledge-block scheme and a reconstructed contrastive-learning scheme at matched false-detection rates under our USA 30-kt standard and the published RITCF standard. Ablations show that the graph pathway adds 0.032 BSS across the holdout and 0.063 over 2020-2021, with a significant contribution in one ensemble member. A deep-learning model constrained by observationally discovered causal structure thus offers a new route to physically informed RI warning.

AI.tldr: Presents CausalVisionRI, a causal-prior-constrained deep learning system for 24-hour rapid intensification warning of western North Pacific tropical cyclones, reaching a Brier skill score of 0.259 on a 2020-2024 holdout.
AI.motivation: Rapid intensification is one of the most dangerous and unpredictable phases of tropical cyclones, and its environmental and structural drivers are difficult to identify and separate in observations.
AI.method: Integrates infrared remote sensing imagery, atmospheric and oceanic fields, and an observationally discovered causal graph; the graph and eight sign-verified effects on 24-h intensity change serve as an auditable causal prior for training, with the graph discovered from 522 cyclones in 2000-2017.
AI.result: On a forward holdout of 2020-2024 with 3,004 records, the five-member ensemble reaches BSS 0.259 relative to a fixed development climatology, significantly exceeding four reference systems and the three LDA baselines (at most 0.105); it attains higher detection rates than a published knowledge-block scheme and a reconstructed contrastive-learning scheme at matched false-detection rates; ablation shows the graph pathway adds 0.032 BSS across the holdout and 0.063 over 2020-2021.
AI.conclusion: Constraining deep learning with observationally discovered causal structure offers a physically informed route to rapid intensification warning.

title: How to Loop Your Transformer: Loop Scaling, Specialization, and Parallel Inference
summary: Looping in transformer models reuses weights by repeatedly applying the same transformer, or parts of it, making the model deeper without increasing its parameter count. Whether looping is useful depends on which constraint dominates: model size, training compute, or autoregressive inference efficiency. We study these trade-offs jointly in dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts of the model are looped, how many loops are applied, and how information is passed between loops. Our experiments span models with up to 1B parameters, trained on up to 155B tokens with up to $1.07\times10^{21}$ FLOPs and 32 loops. We find that looping the full transformer generally gives the strongest quality at a fixed parameter budget, whereas looping a middle block of layers gives a better return when training FLOPs are constrained. Adding loops is not uniformly beneficial: gains eventually saturate, reverse, or become unstable. This motivates asking whether forcing every loop to use the same weights limits the benefit of deeper looping. We address this by adding small loop-specific low-rank adapters that improve quality, with larger gains as more loops are added. Looped transformers also suffer a decoding slowdown proportional to the number of loops. Parallel Loop Transformers address this by passing hidden states between loops across adjacent token positions, allowing loop stages to run concurrently. However, in our experiments the original formulation does not consistently retain the quality gains of ordinary looping. We find that preserving the current-token embedding and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before combining them recovers strong performance across model scales and training budgets. Together, these results show that effective looping requires matching the design to the resource constraint and inference setting.

AI.tldr: Studies how looping transformer weights trades off model size, training compute, and inference efficiency, finding full-model looping best at fixed parameters and middle-block looping best under limited training FLOPs, and proposes a modified Parallel Loop Transformer that retains looping gains.
AI.motivation: Looping adds depth without adding parameters, but whether it helps depends on whether model size, training compute, or autoregressive inference efficiency is the binding constraint, and looped decoding slows in proportion to the number of loops.
AI.method: Dense decoder-only transformers trained from scratch, varying which parts are looped, the number of loops, and how information passes between loops; loop-specific low-rank adapters are added to relax full weight sharing; the Parallel Loop Transformer is modified by preserving the current-token embedding and separately normalizing it and the previous-token hidden state before combining them.
AI.result: Experiments span models up to 1B parameters, 155B training tokens, 1.07 x 10^21 FLOPs and 32 loops; looping the full transformer gives the strongest quality at a fixed parameter budget, while looping a middle block gives better return when training FLOPs are constrained; gains can saturate, reverse, or become unstable; loop-specific adapters improve quality, with larger gains as loops increase; the modification recovers strong performance across model scales and training budgets, where the original parallel formulation did not consistently retain the gains of ordinary looping.
AI.conclusion: Effective looping requires matching the design to the binding resource constraint and the inference setting.

title: Factorized Representations of Concurrent Temporal Variables in Pretrained Language Models
summary: Language models often need to maintain multiple contextual variables that evolve independently within a document. Prior work has identified structured representations of individual temporal or contextual quantities, but their joint organization remains less understood. We study this question using controlled documents with independently phased language-switch and topic-change timers. Across ten pretrained checkpoints, both timers are linearly decodable from the same hidden states. Removing a timer-associated centroid plane substantially reduces access to its associated variable while having little effect on the concurrent timer, although the planes are nonorthogonal and contain cross-timer information. Separate timer contributions also explain most reproducible variation among joint-state centroids. These signatures persist from 3 to 51 timer values and across Qwen3 checkpoints from 0.6B to 14B. Schedule position affects continuation probabilities, but the tested centroid displacement produces no consistent timer-specific output effect. Together, these results support approximate factorization based on selective accessibility and approximately additive joint-state geometry in overlapping subspaces.

AI.tldr: Shows that two independently phased temporal variables in pretrained language models are linearly decodable from the same hidden states and approximately factorized into overlapping subspaces, across ten checkpoints and Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 14B.
AI.motivation: Language models must maintain several contextual variables that evolve independently within a document, but how multiple structured temporal or contextual representations are organized jointly remains less understood than for individual ones.
AI.method: Controlled documents with independently phased language-switch and topic-change timers, analyzed through linear decoding of hidden states, removal of a timer-associated centroid plane, and the geometry of joint-state centroids.
AI.result: Both timers are linearly decodable across ten pretrained checkpoints; removing one timer's centroid plane substantially reduces access to its variable while having little effect on the concurrent timer, although the planes are nonorthogonal and contain cross-timer information; separate timer contributions explain most reproducible variation among joint-state centroids; signatures persist from 3 to 51 timer values and across Qwen3 checkpoints from 0.6B to 14B; the tested centroid displacement has no consistent timer-specific output effect.
AI.conclusion: The results support approximate factorization based on selective accessibility and approximately additive joint-state geometry in overlapping subspaces, without a consistent timer-specific output effect for the tested displacement.

title: A Unified Hessian-Guided Framework for Post-Training Quantization
summary: Low-bit quantization enables efficient deployment of large language models by reducing memory footprint and computational cost. Achieving high accuracy at low precision requires selecting quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding decisions. Existing approaches typically optimize these components independently using local reconstruction objectives, which fail to account for the varying impact of quantization errors on downstream predictions. Direct optimization of task-level metrics would provide a more faithful objective, but is challenging due to the discontinuous nature of quantization operations and the high computational cost of evaluating their downstream effects. In this work, we derive a Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization. Based on a tractable Fisher approximation, we formulate a unified post-training quantization framework that enables the joint optimization of quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a common output-sensitivity objective. The resulting method remains practical for modern large language models and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods across both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes a unified post-training quantization framework for LLMs that jointly optimizes quantization ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding under a Hessian-guided, Fisher-approximated output-sensitivity objective, outperforming prior transformation and rounding methods.
AI.motivation: Existing methods optimize these components independently with local reconstruction objectives that ignore how quantization errors affect downstream predictions differently; direct optimization of task-level metrics is hard because quantization is discontinuous and its downstream effects are costly to evaluate.
AI.method: A Hessian-guided approximation of the output change induced by joint weight and activation quantization, made tractable by a Fisher approximation, which allows ranges, linear transformations, and weight rounding to be optimized jointly under a common output-sensitivity objective.
AI.result: The method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art transformation and rounding methods in both channel-wise and block-wise quantization settings, and remains practical for modern large language models.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing all three components under one output-sensitivity objective is a practical route to more accurate low-bit quantization of large language models.

title: Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training
summary: Weight-normalized (WN) training is emerging as a compelling alternative to conventional weight decay (WD), with recent studies reporting substantial pretraining loss gains. We show that these gains are driven primarily by the induced effective learning rate (ELR) trajectory rather than by normalization alone. Matching ELR trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of WN and WD. Schedule design should therefore target ELR rather than the nominal learning rate (LR) alone. Building on this principle, we propose AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay), which combines a theoretically derived $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal LRs over a finite training horizon. We further identify late-stage ELR scheduling as a key source of its gains, because a shared late schedule attenuates the effect of earlier LR choices. Experiments on 128 B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining demonstrate that AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by approximately 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative LR. Applying the same ELR trajectory to WD reproduces the corresponding training dynamics, showing that the benefits extend beyond fixed-norm training and establishing ELR as the principled scheduling object.

AI.tldr: Argues that the gains of weight-normalized training come mainly from its effective learning rate trajectory, and proposes AIR, an affine inverse-square-root schedule that outperforms cosine decay in 128B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining.
AI.motivation: Weight-normalized training is reported to give substantial pretraining loss gains over weight decay, and it is unclear whether these gains come from normalization itself or from the induced effective learning rate trajectory, which schedules should therefore target.
AI.method: Proposes AIR (Affine Inverse-square-Root decay), which combines a theoretically derived 1/sqrt(t) decay with an affine adjustment to satisfy prescribed peak and terminal learning rates over a finite training horizon; matched effective learning rate trajectories are used to compare weight-normalized and weight-decay training.
AI.result: Matching effective learning rate trajectories largely collapses the training loss dynamics of weight-normalized and weight-decay training; on 128B-token Mixture-of-Experts pretraining, AIR outperforms cosine and other candidate schedules in training loss, downstream performance, and hyperparameter robustness, reducing terminal training loss by about 0.01 relative to cosine at matched cumulative learning rate; applying the same trajectory to weight decay reproduces the corresponding dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The effective learning rate, rather than the nominal learning rate, is the principled object for schedule design, and a shared late-stage schedule is a key source of AIR's gains.

title: Is It the Curriculum or Just the Easy Start? Benchmarking Unsupervised Environment Design on Quadrupeds
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures. Code, level space and evaluation suite: this https URL
summary: Unsupervised environment design (UED) methods such as PLR, ACCEL, SFL and PAIRED are compared mostly on 2D mazes, grid worlds and BipedalWalker, while terrain curricula for legged robots are hand-designed and evaluated against a few baselines. We present a benchmark that runs fourteen UED, domain-randomisation and robotics curricula under one protocol on five 3D quadrupeds in MuJoCo MJX: the closed-chain W01-TEK and the open-chain Unitree Go1 and Go2, Google Barkour vB and Boston Dynamics Spot. Levels are vectors of eight interpretable terrain parameters, and all curricula drive the same PPO student at matched environment-step budgets. The evaluation reports success on random and held-out structured terrains, interquartile means with stratified bootstrap intervals, capability envelopes and a level-by-level domination comparison. We compare methods within each robot and report, per level set, the top group of methods not significantly below the best. No method is in the top group on every robot and level set. Methods with easy or low-difficulty training levels, curated or not, fill the top groups on in-distribution random levels of Go1 and Barkour, and of W01-TEK apart from PAIRED+BiBC. The success-driven terrain curriculum from legged-robot practice is in a top group most often, domain randomisation on uniform levels in none, and PAIRED in none outside Spot, where the fourteen methods lie within 3.8 points on random levels of difficulty 0.25. On three robots the leader on in-distribution random levels is not the leader on held-out terrain. We collect the results into a per-robot guide to choosing a curriculum.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks fourteen unsupervised environment design, domain randomization, and robotics curricula under one protocol on five 3D quadrupeds in MuJoCo MJX, finding that no method is in the top group on every robot and level set.
AI.motivation: Unsupervised environment design methods are mostly compared on 2D mazes, grid worlds and BipedalWalker, while terrain curricula for legged robots are hand-designed and evaluated against only a few baselines.
AI.method: Levels are vectors of eight interpretable terrain parameters, and all curricula drive the same PPO student at matched environment-step budgets; evaluation reports success on random and held-out structured terrains, interquartile means with stratified bootstrap intervals, capability envelopes, and level-by-level domination comparisons, with the top group per level set taken as methods not significantly below the best.
AI.result: No method is in the top group on every robot and level set; methods with easy or low-difficulty training levels often fill the top groups on in-distribution random levels; the success-driven terrain curriculum from legged-robot practice is in a top group most often, domain randomization on uniform levels never is, and PAIRED never is outside Spot, where all fourteen methods lie within 3.8 points on random levels of difficulty 0.25; on three robots the leader on in-distribution random levels is not the leader on held-out terrain.
AI.conclusion: The results are collected into a per-robot guide to choosing a curriculum, and in-distribution leaders often do not lead on held-out terrain.

title: Composing and Steering Diffusion Models with Generalized Feynman-Kac Correctors
summary: Diffusion models have become the leading paradigm in generative modeling, yet many applications require sampling from distributions that are not those of any single pretrained model, but are instead defined through combinations of several models, possibly tilted toward high values of a downstream reward. Naively combining the scores of the models yields incorrect samples, while existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets. In this work, we introduce the generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC), a principled framework for sampling from an arbitrary target function of several pretrained diffusion models. We show that the geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function of the models satisfies a Feynman--Kac partial differential equation, and derive its potential in closed form. To evaluate this potential during generation, we further generalize the log-probability ODE to track the density of each model along trajectories driven by a different velocity field. The resulting algorithm operates entirely in the log domain, incorporates reward-based steering at no additional conceptual cost, and corrects the generation on the fly, without retraining or fine-tuning the models. We validate the method on analytic Gaussian models, where it closely matches the ground-truth targets, and on diffusion models trained on MNIST, where it samples from non-trivial combinations of the models and enables effective steering.

AI.tldr: Introduces generalized Feynman-Kac correctors (GFKC) for sampling from arbitrary target functions defined over several pretrained diffusion models, optionally tilted toward a reward, without retraining or fine-tuning the models.
AI.motivation: Many applications need samples from distributions defined by combinations of several diffusion models, possibly tilted toward a reward; naively combining scores yields incorrect samples, and existing corrections are restricted to specific families of targets.
AI.method: Shows that a geometric interpolation between an arbitrary initial function and the target function satisfies a Feynman-Kac PDE and derives its potential in closed form; generalizes the log-probability ODE to track each model's density along trajectories driven by a different velocity field; the algorithm operates entirely in the log domain and corrects generation on the fly.
AI.result: On analytic Gaussian models, samples closely match the ground-truth targets; on diffusion models trained on MNIST, the method samples from non-trivial combinations of the models and enables effective reward steering.
AI.conclusion: GFKC gives a principled, retraining-free way to compose and steer pretrained diffusion models, with reward-based steering included at no additional conceptual cost.

title: SCARL: Sequence Confidence-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves language-model reasoning by scoring sampled responses with a rule-based verifier and reinforcing those that pass. Where a classifier's training couples predicted probability to labels, nothing ties an RLVR policy's confidence in a response to its reward: aligned training would drive responses with the same advantage toward equal confidence, yet the advantage is blind to confidence. Under this sequence-confidence misalignment, a success the policy barely found earns the same update as one it produces with near certainty, and a confident error is corrected no harder than an exploratory one. We propose SCARL (Sequence Confidence-Aligned Reinforcement Learning), which reshapes, but never re-signs, each advantage with the alignment gap between the response's group-relative confidence and the outcome its advantage certifies, normalized into shares of each class's advantage budget. Misaligned samples absorb the force, responses with the same advantage are driven toward equal confidence, and repairing the misalignment doubles as a remedy for the entropy collapse that erodes exploration. SCARL provably reduces to its base estimator when a class's confidences agree, adds no extra passes and one hyperparameter. On Qwen3-4B-Base it lifts average Pass@32 by 2.4 points over DAPO and is best among nine compute-matched methods on both coverage and per-draw accuracy; applied unchanged across four estimators and four backbones, it improves 14 of 16 settings while preserving policy entropy and widening the confidence-correctness separation. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes SCARL, an RLVR method that reshapes each advantage by the gap between a response's group-relative confidence and its outcome, correcting sequence-confidence misalignment; it lifts average Pass@32 by 2.4 points over DAPO on Qwen3-4B-Base.
AI.motivation: In RLVR the advantage ignores the policy's confidence in a response, so a barely found success earns the same update as a near-certain one, and a confident error is corrected no harder than an exploratory one.
AI.method: Reshapes, but never re-signs, each advantage using the alignment gap between group-relative confidence and the outcome its advantage certifies, normalized into shares of each class's advantage budget; it adds no extra passes and one hyperparameter, and reduces to its base estimator when confidences within a class agree.
AI.result: On Qwen3-4B-Base, SCARL lifts average Pass@32 by 2.4 points over DAPO and is best among nine compute-matched methods on both coverage and per-draw accuracy; applied across four estimators and four backbones, it improves 14 of 16 settings while preserving policy entropy and widening the confidence-correctness separation.
AI.conclusion: Repairing sequence-confidence misalignment also counters the entropy collapse that erodes exploration, offering a cheap remedy within RLVR training.

title: IMPACT: Inverter-Informed Multimodal Learning for Photovoltaic Generation Forecasting
summary: This work develops a physics-informed multimodal deep learning framework for 10- to 110-minute-ahead probabilistic photovoltaic power forecasting. The forecasting model is built on a four-branch architecture that separately encodes plant-level temporal history and inverter-level spatial cloud dynamics through a graph attention encoder with a learned adjacency, known-future solar geometry, and the current meteorological state, fused through gated cross-attention. The geometry branch adds two forward-looking physical signals, spatial cloud heterogeneity and inverter ramp-down activity, each empirically weighted toward the horizon where it is most predictive. The decoder anchors its prediction to a smart persistence baseline, learning a horizon-conditioned correction, and the resulting quantile forecasts are calibrated online through a kernel-weighted adaptive conformal calibration step. The proposed model outperforms all 14 baselines, achieving a forecast skill score (FSS) of 0.2950, 0.099 above the next-best model. A branch-composition ablation shows that every branch contributes positively and the model retains substantial skill in challenging overcast and variable sky conditions (FSS 0.198 and 0.255).

AI.tldr: Proposes IMPACT, a physics-informed four-branch multimodal network for probabilistic photovoltaic power forecasting 10 to 110 minutes ahead, reaching a forecast skill score of 0.2950, 0.099 above the next-best of 14 baselines.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic PV forecasting over 10 to 110 minutes requires combining plant-level history, inverter-level spatial cloud dynamics, solar geometry and current weather, along with physically meaningful forward-looking signals.
AI.method: Four branches encode plant temporal history, inverter-level spatial cloud dynamics through a graph attention encoder with a learned adjacency, known-future solar geometry, and the current meteorological state, fused by gated cross-attention; the geometry branch adds spatial cloud heterogeneity and inverter ramp-down activity; the decoder anchors to a smart persistence baseline and learns a horizon-conditioned correction, and quantile forecasts are calibrated online by kernel-weighted adaptive conformal calibration.
AI.result: The model outperforms all 14 baselines with FSS 0.2950, 0.099 above the next-best model; the branch-composition ablation shows every branch contributes positively; FSS is 0.198 in overcast and 0.255 in variable sky conditions.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed branch composition and online conformal calibration yield skilful quantile forecasts that retain substantial skill under challenging sky conditions.

title: NECA: Neighbor Event Curve Augmentation for Multi-Horizon ICU Deterioration Prediction
summary: Early prediction of ICU organ dysfunction events supports timely clinical monitoring and intervention, but estimating short-term organ-specific risk from early ICU records remains challenging due to irregular measurements, heterogeneous clinical variables, and the need to predict risk across multiple future horizons. Existing supervised models usually treat each patient as an isolated sample and do not explicitly use the observed event timing of similar historical patients. We propose Neighbor Event-Curve Augmentation (NECA), a model-agnostic method that retrieves training-set patients with similar early-window profiles and converts their subsequent organ dysfunction event onset times into cumulative event-curve features over 6h, 12h, 24h, and 42h. These features are concatenated with the original patient representation and used by standard downstream predictors. On PhysioNet 2012 and a 4,000-stay MIMIC-IV subset, NECA improves average PR-AUC and ROC-AUC across four organ dysfunction event tasks and seven supervised learners. The largest gain appears for neurological dysfunction events, where task-level average PR-AUC increases from 0.461 to 0.557 on PhysioNet 2012. Ablations show that clinically meaningful retrieval and horizon-specific neighbor risk drive most of the improvement, while the full cumulative curve adds task-dependent temporal context. These results support similar-patient event timing as a structured temporal risk signal for ICU organ dysfunction event prediction. The source code will be publicly released upon acceptance of this paper.

AI.tldr: Proposes NECA, a model-agnostic augmentation that retrieves training patients with similar early ICU profiles and adds cumulative event-curve features built from their subsequent organ dysfunction onset times, improving PR-AUC and ROC-AUC across seven supervised learners.
AI.motivation: Supervised ICU models treat each patient as an isolated sample and do not use the observed event timing of similar historical patients, while estimating organ-specific short-term risk from irregular, heterogeneous early records is challenging.
AI.method: Retrieves training-set patients with similar early-window profiles, converts their subsequent organ dysfunction event onset times into cumulative event-curve features over 6, 12, 24 and 42 hours, and concatenates these features with the original patient representation for standard downstream predictors.
AI.result: On PhysioNet 2012 and a 4,000-stay MIMIC-IV subset, NECA improves average PR-AUC and ROC-AUC across four organ dysfunction event tasks and seven supervised learners; the largest gain is for neurological dysfunction, where task-level average PR-AUC rises from 0.461 to 0.557 on PhysioNet 2012; ablations show that clinically meaningful retrieval and horizon-specific neighbor risk drive most of the improvement.
AI.conclusion: Similar-patient event timing is a structured temporal risk signal for ICU organ dysfunction prediction, and the full cumulative curve adds task-dependent temporal context.

title: Uncertainty-aware Feedback Loop Diagnosis: integrating reinforcement learning and conformal prediction for reliable wafer defect classification
summary: Semiconductor manufacturing is a complex, multi-step process that requires both high precision and low operating costs. Therefore, detecting defects in a high-volume setting is an important component of wafer map analysis for reliable production. However, most state-of-the-art deep learning approaches require a full scan of the surface, which hinders the development of high-throughput inspection systems. To address this problem, we propose Uncertainty-aware Feedback Loop Diagnosis (UFLD), a novel algorithm that employs reinforcement learning for adaptive measurement acquisition and provides a prediction uncertainty level after each step, stopping the process once sufficient information is obtained. Unlike existing methods that rely on ensemble models or auxiliary confidence estimation deep learning models, UFLD utilizes a more parameter-efficient conformal prediction framework to determine the optimal stopping time. The proposed UFLD reduces acquisition time by about $40\%$ and achieves $98.4\%$ inspection accuracy, without requiring an additional learned confidence-estimation network. We validated our approach on the MixedWM38 dataset, demonstrating its advantages over existing adaptive acquisition procedures and standard convolutional neural networks.

AI.tldr: Proposes UFLD, which uses reinforcement learning for adaptive measurement acquisition on wafer maps and conformal prediction to decide when to stop, cutting acquisition time by about 40% at 98.4% inspection accuracy on MixedWM38.
AI.motivation: Most state-of-the-art deep learning approaches for wafer map analysis require a full surface scan, which hinders high-throughput inspection in semiconductor manufacturing.
AI.method: Reinforcement learning chooses successive measurements, and a conformal prediction framework provides a prediction uncertainty level after each step and determines the stopping time, without ensembles or an auxiliary confidence-estimation network.
AI.result: Reduces acquisition time by about 40% and achieves 98.4% inspection accuracy on MixedWM38, outperforming existing adaptive acquisition procedures and standard convolutional neural networks.
AI.conclusion: Conformal prediction can provide a parameter-efficient stopping rule for adaptive, high-throughput wafer defect inspection.

title: A Pretrained Model for Bayesian Filtering in Heterogeneous Dynamical Systems
summary: Filtering has not yet had its foundation-model moment: state estimation is still dominated either by online Bayesian filtering algorithms that require known dy- namics as inputs, or by learning-based neural filters trained from scratch for a single system or parametric family. The core challenge is structural heterogene- ity: dynamical systems differ in their governing dynamics, physical scales, and noise levels, precluding a shared representation space for a reusable filter. To bridge this gap, we introduce FilterFM, the first pretrained model for Bayesian filtering that estimates latent states across heterogeneous dynamical systems with a single checkpoint. FilterFM employs a hierarchical two-level observation se- quence encoder and a prior-to-posterior state-reconstruction module that together handle varying observation and state dimensions across heterogeneous systems, while modeling state uncertainty via quantile prediction. Trained on a mixture of heterogeneous filtering tasks, FilterFM exhibits superior in-domain performance, delivering significant gains in estimation accuracy, runtime efficiency, and noise robustness compared to existing baselines. Beyond in-domain performance, it marks the first model to successfully enable zero-shot filtering on unseen dynamics, bridging the generalization gap in state estimation. Furthermore, we uncover clear scaling behaviors in foundation-model-based Bayesian filtering, which combined with comprehensive component ablation studies, validate the structural optimality of our design and broaden the generalization scope for this research field.

AI.tldr: Introduces FilterFM, a pretrained Bayesian filtering model that estimates latent states across heterogeneous dynamical systems with a single checkpoint and performs zero-shot filtering on unseen dynamics.
AI.motivation: State estimation is still dominated by online Bayesian filters that require known dynamics, or by neural filters trained from scratch for a single system or parametric family, because heterogeneous systems differ in governing dynamics, physical scales and noise levels.
AI.method: A hierarchical two-level observation sequence encoder and a prior-to-posterior state-reconstruction module handle varying observation and state dimensions, with state uncertainty modeled via quantile prediction; the model is trained on a mixture of heterogeneous filtering tasks.
AI.result: FilterFM shows superior in-domain estimation accuracy, runtime efficiency and noise robustness compared with existing baselines, is the first model to enable zero-shot filtering on unseen dynamics, and shows clear scaling behavior, with component ablations supporting the design.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining a single filter across heterogeneous dynamical systems is a viable route to foundation-model-based Bayesian filtering.

title: Framework-Conditional Open Materials Generation
summary: Theoretical predictions of novel materials rely on a variety of techniques, from data-mining-based ion substitution methods to fully de novo generative models. Each approach imposes specific constraints and encounters unique challenges when extrapolating beyond the distribution of known materials to discover new ones. The foremost goal of materials generation is to produce stable, unique, and novel (S.U.N.) structures. Predicted structures that meet these criteria, however, typically result from novel chemical compositions mapped onto known structural prototypes or frameworks. We leverage this heuristic insight to present a new generative paradigm for the de novo prediction of inorganic crystalline materials constrained by their structural framework---i.e., the unit cell shapes and respective particle positions. Our method, termed OMatG-FC (Open Materials Framework-Conditional Generation), learns via a combination of discrete flow matching on the atomic species and stochastic interpolants for the volume scaling of the unit cell lattice, while fixing in-place the fractional coordinates and the unit-volume lattice vectors, dramatically reducing the dimensionality of the problem compared to unconstrained (framework-free) generation. Our method is more flexible than existing prototype-constrained methods, demonstrating capability for discovery of unseen, stable prototypes derived from known structural frameworks. We also investigate the number of unique frameworks in the MP-20 dataset, demonstrating the propensity of duplicate frameworks within the dataset and providing a framework-split version. We benchmark the performance of our model using the LeMat-GenBench suite using three ML interatomic potentials and achieve state-of-the-art S.U.N. rate below the convex hull, eschewing the need to learn atomic packings for materials discovery.

AI.tldr: Proposes OMatG-FC, a generative model for inorganic crystals that is constrained to a fixed structural framework (unit cell shape and fractional coordinates) and learns only atomic species and volume scaling, reaching a state-of-the-art stable-unique-novel (S.U.N.) rate on LeMat-GenBench.
AI.motivation: De novo materials generation is hard because extrapolating beyond known materials is difficult, and S.U.N. structures usually arise from novel compositions placed on known structural prototypes. Existing prototype-constrained methods are less flexible.
AI.method: OMatG-FC combines discrete flow matching over atomic species with stochastic interpolants for unit-cell volume scaling, while the fractional coordinates and unit-volume lattice vectors are fixed in place, greatly reducing the dimensionality compared with framework-free generation.
AI.result: The method discovers unseen stable prototypes derived from known frameworks and achieves state-of-the-art S.U.N. rate below the convex hull on LeMat-GenBench using three ML interatomic potentials. The authors also find many duplicate frameworks in MP-20 and provide a framework-split version of that dataset.
AI.conclusion: Framework conditioning offers a more flexible, lower-dimensional route to materials discovery than prototype-constrained or unconstrained generation, without learning atomic packings.

title: Reinforcement learning for control of partial differential equations
summary: Controlling dynamical systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) remains a challenging task in scientific computing, owing to high-dimensional state spaces, distributed actuation, nonlinear dynamics, and stringent real-time constraints. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for synthesizing feedback controllers that adapt to varying operating conditions and can be deployed efficiently in real-time. This review provides a unified perspective on RL and PDE-constrained optimization, and surveys model-free, model-based, and multi-agent RL approaches to PDE control, with particular emphasis on sample efficiency, generalization across parametric variations, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. Two demonstrative examples, the stabilization of a chaotic system and a flow control problem, illustrate the performance and pitfalls of RL agents in practice. Finally, we discuss evaluation and benchmarking practices, current limitations, and open research directions toward reliable, data-efficient, and scalable RL for scientific computing.

AI.tldr: A review that unifies reinforcement learning and PDE-constrained optimization and surveys model-free, model-based and multi-agent RL for controlling PDE-governed systems, illustrated with two examples.
AI.motivation: PDE control in scientific computing is hard because of high-dimensional states, distributed actuation, nonlinear dynamics and real-time constraints, while RL promises adaptive feedback controllers that can be deployed efficiently.
AI.method: The review is organized by model-free, model-based and multi-agent RL approaches to PDE control, with emphasis on sample efficiency, generalization across parametric variations and scalability, and two demonstrations: stabilization of a chaotic system and a flow control problem.
AI.result: The two demonstrative examples show both the performance and the pitfalls of RL agents in practice. The review also discusses evaluation and benchmarking practices.
AI.conclusion: Reliable, data-efficient and scalable RL for scientific computing remains an open goal, and the review identifies current limitations and research directions toward it.

title: Rural Readiness: Domain Generalization with Adversarially Chosen Domains
summary: Predictive models trained at well-resourced data-rich institutions often fail when deployed in new populations. Motivated by the goal of building clinical diagnosis and decision-making algorithms for data-scarce rural populations using the general knowledge learned from data-rich hospitals, we formulate the fundamental question of \emph{domain generalization with adversarially chosen domains}, which asks a learner to perform on any unseen target domain nearly as well as the worst hypothesis consistent with the evidence from the observed source domains. Assuming only that the hypothesis class contains a "universal" predictor with small error on all $k$ source domains, we characterize the sample complexity of this objective up to logarithmic factors. Letting $d$ denote the VC dimension of the hypothesis class, we find, somewhat surprisingly, that the sample complexity reduces significantly from $\Omega(dk)$ to $O(d)$ under a small relaxation of the learning goal in which, roughly speaking, we allow the learned model to compete with hypotheses that perform well on 99% instead of 100% of the source domains. By applying this insight to the meta-distributional setting, in which source domains are selected according to a distribution on distributions, we obtain a corresponding improvement over known sample complexity upper bounds. We also study the effect of data access to the target domain and show that a small labeled sample from the target domain does not improve the worst-case sample complexity on the source domains.

AI.tldr: Formulates domain generalization with adversarially chosen target domains and characterizes its sample complexity, showing that it drops from Omega(dk) to O(d) under a small relaxation of the learning goal.
AI.motivation: Predictive models trained at data-rich institutions often fail in new populations, such as data-scarce rural clinics. The goal is a learner that performs on any unseen target domain nearly as well as the worst hypothesis consistent with the source domains.
AI.method: The analysis assumes the hypothesis class contains a universal predictor with small error on all k source domains, and characterizes sample complexity in terms of the VC dimension d. It is then extended to a meta-distributional setting in which source domains are drawn from a distribution over distributions.
AI.result: Under the strict goal the sample complexity is Omega(dk), but relaxing it so the learner competes with hypotheses that perform well on 99% rather than 100% of source domains reduces it to O(d), up to logarithmic factors. This improves known upper bounds in the meta-distributional setting. A small labeled sample from the target domain does not improve the worst-case sample complexity on the source domains.
AI.conclusion: A small relaxation of the learning goal yields a significant sample-complexity saving, while a small labeled target sample gives no worst-case benefit.

title: Nonlinear Dynamical Systems as Scalable and Efficient Physical Neural Networks
summary: The rapid growth in the size of state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) models has led to increasing compute demands, spurring the development of energy-efficient hardware accelerators. Physical systems trained to perform ML inference, known as physical neural networks, have been proposed as accelerators in part because of their potential to be highly energy efficient. However, the ML inference accuracies reported in most investigations of physical neural networks have been substantially below the state of the art for conventional digital neural networks. In this work, we show in simulation studies that by applying modern ML training practices, including model compression, various candidate physical neural networks based on nonlinear dynamical systems can achieve accuracies as high as 99.2% on MNIST handwritten-digit recognition. We also show for one dynamical system that using it as the core building block of a parameter-efficient ML architecture inspired by MLP-Mixers enables accuracies of up to 86.4% on CIFAR-10 image classification (92.2% with pretraining and knowledge distillation), compared with 64% for the same system without the mixer architecture. The mixer approach achieved its accuracy while using $>5\times$ fewer trainable parameters than the baseline. Finally, we present back-of-the-envelope estimates for inference energy efficiency and speed when using an example physical dynamical system, suggesting that orders of magnitude improvements may be possible over digital-electronic neural networks.

AI.tldr: Shows in simulation that physical neural networks built from nonlinear dynamical systems can reach 99.2% on MNIST and 86.4% on CIFAR-10 when modern training practices and an MLP-Mixer-inspired architecture are applied.
AI.motivation: Physical neural networks are proposed as energy-efficient ML accelerators, but the inference accuracies reported in most investigations have been well below digital neural networks.
AI.method: Modern ML training practices, including model compression, are applied to candidate physical networks based on nonlinear dynamical systems. For one system, it serves as the core block of a parameter-efficient MLP-Mixer-inspired architecture, and inference energy and speed are estimated with back-of-the-envelope calculations for an example physical system.
AI.result: Accuracy reaches up to 99.2% on MNIST. On CIFAR-10 the mixer architecture reaches 86.4% (92.2% with pretraining and knowledge distillation), compared with 64% for the same system without the mixer, while using more than 5 times fewer trainable parameters than the baseline. The estimates suggest orders-of-magnitude gains in inference energy efficiency and speed may be possible over digital electronics.
AI.conclusion: Physical neural networks may close much of the accuracy gap to digital networks, and their energy advantage could be substantial, although these are simulation studies and estimates.

title: Preserving Utility in Continual LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Projections
summary: Unlearning concerns the task of removing the influence of a sensitive portion of the training data, such as protected, copyrighted or private text, from a model without retraining it from scratch. While unlearning requests happen continuously during a model's lifetime, the vast majority of LLM unlearning methods are ill-suited for iterated removal, yielding steep decay in forgetting and utility upon sequential unlearning. This decay stems from interference between successive updates, as each new deletion can undo earlier ones or push the model further along directions already degraded by them. To address this, we introduce Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a gradient-projection scheme that restricts each update to the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from prior forget sets. This approach provably guarantees first-order non-interference with earlier deletions. COP stores only a low-rank basis per layer, requiring neither past gradients nor previous forget sets, and plugs into unlearning methods that update the model through gradient steps on a differentiable loss without modifying its objective. Experiments on standard LLM unlearning benchmarks (TOFU and RWKU) show that COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, preventing the collapse of standard objectives and forgetting more effectively than continual-specific baselines.

AI.tldr: Introduces Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a gradient-projection method that keeps sequential LLM unlearning from degrading utility by restricting each update to the orthogonal complement of cached activation subspaces from earlier forget sets.
AI.motivation: Most LLM unlearning methods are ill-suited to iterated removal requests, because successive updates interfere with one another and cause steep decay in both forgetting and utility.
AI.method: COP stores only a low-rank basis per layer, without past gradients or previous forget sets, and projects each update onto the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from prior forget sets. It plugs into gradient-based unlearning methods without modifying their objectives.
AI.result: On TOFU and RWKU, COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, prevents the collapse of standard objectives and forgets more effectively than continual-specific baselines.
AI.conclusion: COP gives a practical continual unlearning approach with a provable first-order guarantee of non-interference with earlier deletions.

title: The Precision Wall: An Optimizer-Dependent Boundary for Optimization under Power-Law Measurement Spectra
summary: In low-rank matrix sensing of a rank-$D$ factor $U^\ast \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times D}$, replacing isotropic Gaussian designs with power-law measurement covariance $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(j^{-s})_{j=1}^V$ leaves the Burer--Monteiro landscape free of spurious local minima, yet division-normalised first-order optimizers stall above a critical exponent $s^\ast$. We trace this failure to a numerical precision wall. At the ground truth, the smallest non-gauge expected Hessian eigenvalue scales at leading order as $V^{-(s+1)}D^{-s}$. When this curvature drops below the effective denominator floor $\epsilon_O$ of optimizer $O$, normalisation noise overwhelms rare-direction gradients, yielding the leading-order boundary $s^\ast_O(V, D) = [\log(1/\epsilon_O) - \log V]/\log(VD) + \delta_O$, where $\delta_O$ is a metric-dependent detection lag. With $\delta_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ calibrated on four configurations and frozen, this formula predicts Adam's onset within $0.45$ across all 16 cells of a held-out grid ($V \in \{64,128,256,512\} \times D \in \{4,8,16,32\}$), separates fixed-$VD$ pairs, and distinguishes denominator-precision walls from conditioning and sign-quantisation walls. The approximation fails at $D = 2$, reflects a finite-$D$ spectral crossover, and saturates below $\varepsilon_0 = 10^{-8}$ at a dynamical floor.

AI.tldr: Identifies a numerical precision wall that stalls division-normalised first-order optimizers on low-rank matrix sensing with power-law measurement spectra, and derives a formula that predicts the critical exponent.
AI.motivation: With power-law measurement covariance, the Burer-Monteiro landscape has no spurious local minima, yet normalised optimizers such as Adam stall above a critical exponent, and the cause of this failure was unclear.
AI.method: The smallest non-gauge expected Hessian eigenvalue scales as V^-(s+1) D^-s at the ground truth. When it falls below the optimizer's effective denominator floor, normalisation noise overwhelms rare-direction gradients, which gives a leading-order boundary in V, D and s with a metric-dependent detection lag.
AI.result: With the Adam detection lag calibrated on four configurations and frozen, the formula predicts Adam's onset within 0.45 across all 16 cells of a held-out grid with V in {64, 128, 256, 512} and D in {4, 8, 16, 32}. It separates fixed-VD pairs and distinguishes denominator-precision walls from conditioning and sign-quantisation walls. The approximation fails at D = 2 and saturates below 10^-8 at a dynamical floor.
AI.conclusion: The stall is explained as a denominator-precision effect, and the formula locates where it occurs, with stated limits at D = 2 and at very small floors.

title: Numerical Integration on Bounded Domains via Learned Reflected Diffusions
summary: We study high-dimensional integration on bounded convex domains. Given a non-negative integrand $r$, the goal is to estimate $Z=\int_{D}r(x)\,\mathrm dx$ on $D\subset\mathbb R^d$. Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo does not adapt its evaluation points to the integrand, while effective importance sampling requires a proposal that captures its concentration. Learned diffusion samplers can supply such a proposal, but existing methods are formulated on $\mathbb R^d$ and do not respect the domain constraint $x\in D$. We instead build the proposal from reflected dynamics that stay in $D$ by construction. A reflected diffusion progressively transforms the target distribution toward the uniform distribution on $D$, and a neural score model is trained to reverse this process. A change-of-measure formula for reflected diffusions yields a training objective without additional boundary terms and an unbiased importance-sampling estimator of $Z$. For non-smooth integrands, where reparameterization gradients may be undefined or uninformative, we derive a REINFORCE estimator of the training gradient using Gaussian proposal densities before reflection, without evaluating reflected transition densities or differentiating $r$. We evaluate on numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems, demonstrating strong performance of the proposed method, as well as favorable scaling with the dimension of the problem and the number of points used for the Monte Carlo estimate.

AI.tldr: Proposes a learned reflected-diffusion sampler for integration on bounded convex domains that stays inside the domain by construction and yields an unbiased importance-sampling estimate of the integral.
AI.motivation: Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo does not adapt its points to the integrand, and existing learned diffusion samplers are formulated on R^d and do not respect the domain constraint.
AI.method: A reflected diffusion progressively transforms the target toward the uniform distribution on the domain, and a neural score model is trained to reverse this process. A change-of-measure formula gives a training objective without boundary terms, and a REINFORCE estimator using Gaussian proposal densities before reflection handles non-smooth integrands.
AI.result: The method shows strong performance on numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems, with favorable scaling in problem dimension and in the number of Monte Carlo points.
AI.conclusion: Learned reflected diffusions provide a domain-respecting, adaptive proposal for high-dimensional integration, including for non-smooth integrands.

title: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Mobile Money Scan Messages in Ghana: A Comparative Evaluation of Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and Randon Forest Classifiers
summary: Mobile money (MoMo) is Ghana's preferred retail payment channel, recording GHC518.4 billion in transactions in December 2025 and over 26.7 million active accounts (Graphic Online, 2026). This growth has coincided with increased social-engineering fraud over Short Message Service (SMS) and Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD), where fraudsters impersonate network operators, agents, relatives, or regulators to obtain personal identification numbers (PINs), identity data, or funds. We present a supervised machine-learning pipeline for classifying scam and legitimate Ghanaian MoMo SMS messages using a labelled corpus of 220 messages across 18 scam and legitimate subcategories. Domain-specific normalisation of currency amounts, phone numbers, and USSD codes preceded TF-IDF vectorisation of unigrams and bigrams. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation and a 20% held-out test set, we trained and evaluated Multinomial Naive Bayes, linear support vector machine (SVM), and Random Forest classifiers using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). Held-out accuracy, F1, and AUC were 1.00 for Naive Bayes and linear SVM; cross-validated accuracy averaged 96.6% (+/-3.3), 94.9% (+/-4.6), and 92.0% (+/-4.2). Discriminative n-grams reflected imperative urgency ("send," "claim," "please send") and PIN solicitation ("PIN," "pincode"); legitimate messages featured confirmatory and cautionary language ("balance," "successful," "do not share"). Findings are contextualised in Sub-Saharan African SMS fraud detection, small template-based corpus ceiling effects, and a pathway toward larger naturalistic multilingual corpora. Interpretable classical classifiers achieve high accuracy on structured MoMo scam text and suit carrier- or handset-level filtering in low-resource, on-device settings.

AI.tldr: Compares Multinomial Naive Bayes, linear SVM and Random Forest for classifying scam versus legitimate Ghanaian mobile money SMS messages, with Naive Bayes and linear SVM reaching perfect held-out scores.
AI.motivation: Mobile money is Ghana's preferred retail payment channel, and social-engineering fraud over SMS and USSD that solicits PINs, identity data or funds has grown alongside it.
AI.method: A supervised pipeline classifies 220 labelled messages across 18 scam and legitimate subcategories. Currency amounts, phone numbers and USSD codes are normalised, then TF-IDF unigrams and bigrams are extracted. Evaluation uses stratified five-fold cross-validation and a 20% held-out test set with accuracy, precision, recall, F1, MCC and AUC-ROC.
AI.result: Held-out accuracy, F1 and AUC were 1.00 for Naive Bayes and linear SVM. Cross-validated accuracy averaged 96.6% (+/-3.3), 94.9% (+/-4.6) and 92.0% (+/-4.2) for Naive Bayes, linear SVM and Random Forest respectively. Scam messages were marked by urgent imperative and PIN-solicitation n-grams, and legitimate ones by confirmatory and cautionary phrases.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable classical classifiers are highly accurate on structured scam text and suit carrier- or handset-level filtering in low-resource, on-device settings, although ceiling effects from the small template-based corpus limit how far these scores generalise.

title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
summary: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

AI.tldr: Shows that pretraining, midtraining, SFT and RL can all be cast as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, and builds a unified trainer that mixes static data with RL generations in one system.
AI.motivation: Foundation models are trained in separate stages with changing data and learning algorithms, and the authors argue this algorithmic separation is not fundamental.
AI.method: RL objectives are derived as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, which places all training stages under a single likelihood-based algorithm, unified training. The resulting system mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer.
AI.result: Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage, preserves broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning.
AI.conclusion: The training lifecycle becomes a question of which data to train on, in what proportions and when, with conventional staged training as a special case, laying groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training.

title: An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models
summary: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.

AI.tldr: Introduces exponential residual flows, a deterministic ODE sampler for discrete diffusion models that augments each token with a continuous residual and provably preserves the original marginals.
AI.motivation: Continuous diffusion models have a probability flow ODE that supports accelerated sampling and consistency distillation, and the paper asks whether discrete diffusion models admit an analogous formulation.
AI.method: Each token and position carries a continuous residual that evolves under piecewise-defined ODEs depending on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. A practical discretization is specialized to masked and uniform diffusion.
AI.result: The construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. The deterministic trajectories support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches on code and text generation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A deterministic ODE formulation exists for discrete diffusion, and it supports consistency distillation in this setting.

title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
summary: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: Introduces world2vec, which learns mechanistic latent world models from observations and actions alone, reproducing system dynamics over long horizons with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM.
AI.motivation: World models can achieve strong control without faithfully capturing environment dynamics, which limits their use for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery.
AI.method: The model learns latent dynamics without reward information directly from observations and actions.
AI.result: It achieves state-of-the-art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors.
AI.conclusion: Faithful world models are amenable to scientific discovery as well as control.

title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
comment: Project page can be found here: this https URL
summary: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.

AI.tldr: Shows that the gains attributed to Neural Thickets can be obtained without weight perturbations, using a Perturb-Select-Vote procedure, and that a fully frozen model with a random logit bias matches or exceeds full-weight perturbation on most reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: The Neural Thickets hypothesis explains gains from random Gaussian weight perturbations of pretrained language models as the discovery of nearby task-specific experts in weight space. The authors test whether this geometric explanation is required.
AI.method: Perturbing a single decoder block, or keeping the model frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits, is compared with full-weight perturbation. The authors formalize Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), which generates perturbed predictors, selects high performers on a small validation set and aggregates their predictions. A first-order analysis attributes the effect of small weight perturbations to induced logit shifts, and the study extends to vision.
AI.result: Perturbing one decoder block recovers much of the improvement on language tasks. Logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift in vision, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations add little.
AI.conclusion: The benefits attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead come from output diversity, selection and voting, providing a training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.

title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
summary: An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private. We introduce \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations. We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.

AI.tldr: Proposes propose-filter-release, a general differential privacy primitive that privately filters out atypical records so that noise scales to typical sensitivity rather than worst-case sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Differentially private mechanisms usually scale noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, so a few atypical records can dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would help, but the removal must itself be private.
AI.method: A novel private filtering step needs only a concave friendliness score that measures how well a record fits a dataset, together with a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, meaning private when the changed record fits the remaining data.
AI.result: PFR guarantees standard differential privacy on every input, under public conditions on the number of records. It is instantiated for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, effective resistances of a graph and treatment-rule selection, and FriendlyCore is identified as one of its implementations.
AI.conclusion: PFR is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, that lets noise be calibrated to typical rather than worst-case sensitivity.

title: Accelerated Dataflow: scaling inference in streaming data analytics with efficiency
summary: Streaming data analytics helps businesses identify opportunities and spot risks in a timely fashion. As large language model (LLM) usage grows, people are exploring incorporating agents or LLMs in streaming data pipelines to help find patterns in datasets without supervision or interpret natural languages for content moderation. However, most streaming systems are currently optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU intensive workloads such as performing inference with LLMs. We introduce a system on Google Cloud Dataflow designed to tackle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads with co-designed autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching. This increases throughput 1.5x to 2x for streaming pipelines using LLMs while maintaining similar latency with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.

AI.tldr: Presents a Google Cloud Dataflow system for streaming ML workloads that include LLM inference, using co-designed autoscaling over heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching.
AI.motivation: Streaming systems are optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU-intensive workloads such as LLM inference, which are increasingly placed inside streaming pipelines.
AI.method: Autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools is co-designed with prefix-aware batching to handle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads.
AI.result: For streaming pipelines that use LLMs, throughput increases by 1.5x to 2x while maintaining similar latency, with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing streaming infrastructure with LLM inference can substantially improve throughput and resource efficiency without sacrificing latency.

title: The Best Second Opinion Is Right Where the Primary Is Wrong: Partner Selection for Selective Span Tagging
summary: A span tagger that ranks its outputs by risk can defer the riskiest ones to a person, and a second model can sharpen this ranking. Which second model should it be? Partner selection is conditional, not global: the best second opinion is the model that is right where the primary is wrong. Across eight tagger types, three seeds and three English benchmarks (576 evaluated primary-partner pairings), choosing the partner by held-out accuracy on the primary's errors recovers 82% of the best partner's gain, against 69-70% for span F1 or a random pick. Frozen before a fourth dataset was chosen, the rule replicated there (Spearman 0.40 vs. 0.04 for span F1). Partner value is also directional. The predictive distribution is the second opinion: hard labels discard half of a partner's value, and scoring the served label improves 94% of pairings. Fixed before the fourth dataset was chosen, this score also replicated there. For LoRA-tuned decoders, independently trained partners beat every readout of the primary network. Applied zero-shot to 51 MASSIVE locales, every primary has a helpful trained partner in every locale, and the preferred partner follows competence.

AI.tldr: Shows that the best second-opinion model for selective span tagging is the one that is right where the primary is wrong, and proposes choosing the partner by its held-out accuracy on the primary's errors.
AI.motivation: A span tagger that ranks its outputs by risk can defer the riskiest ones to a person, and a second model can sharpen this ranking, but it is unclear which second model to choose.
AI.method: Partner selection is treated as conditional on the primary's errors. Eight tagger types, three seeds and three English benchmarks give 576 primary-partner pairings, and a fourth dataset was chosen after the rule was frozen. Partners are scored on the predictive distribution rather than hard labels, and independently trained partners are compared with readouts of LoRA-tuned decoders.
AI.result: Choosing by held-out accuracy on the primary's errors recovers 82% of the best partner's gain, against 69-70% for span F1 or a random pick. The rule replicated on the fourth dataset (Spearman 0.40 versus 0.04 for span F1). Scoring the served label improves 94% of pairings. For LoRA-tuned decoders, independently trained partners beat every readout of the primary, and applied zero-shot to 51 MASSIVE locales every primary has a helpful trained partner.
AI.conclusion: Partner value is directional and conditional, and the preferred partner tracks the primary's competence, so error-conditioned selection is the right criterion.

title: Exposure Is Not Commitment: Double-Stratified Evaluation of Latent Monitors for Tool-Using Agents
comment: Accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agents in the Wild (AIWILD); OpenReview: this https URL . 16 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Tool-using language agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, and a growing literature probes model internals to catch unsafe actions before they execute, with sharply conflicting results. We argue much of the conflict is an evaluation artifact, and propose a double-stratification protocol: separate injection exposure from behavioral commitment, in both the evaluation and the training population. On the primary Qwen AgentDojo grid, monitors trained on the naive mixed unsafe-versus-rest contrast mostly learn exposure: they flag exposed trajectories whether or not the agent complies, and barely predict which cases turn unsafe. Retrained on exposed cases only, the same probe families predict the model's own unsafe tool call up to two steps early, the maximum the three-step trajectories admit (logistic AUROC 0.853, matched by a trained TF-IDF text baseline at 0.855). Mistral-7B reaches 0.896 and OLMo-2-7B 0.912; their naive contrasts learn different things: inverted exposure ranking on one, both axes on the other.
