Representations separate on exposure (probe 1.000 versus trained text 0.908) and where visible context is sanitized or unavailable. Training contrast alone reproduces the shape of recent pre-action-probe negative results, one candidate explanation for the conflict: the signal exists, but the model's own zero-shot forecast and NLA verbalizations do not reliably recover it. An unstratified AUROC overstates what a latent monitor knows, and what a naive contrast learns is population-dependent: evaluations should stratify both.

AI.tldr: Argues that conflicting results on latent monitors for tool-using agents are largely an evaluation artifact, and shows that probes trained on injection-exposed cases only can predict an agent's own unsafe tool call up to two steps early.
AI.motivation: Tool-using language agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, and probes of model internals meant to catch unsafe actions before they execute report sharply conflicting results.
AI.method: A double-stratification protocol separates injection exposure from behavioral commitment in both the evaluation and the training population. Probes are assessed on the Qwen AgentDojo grid, with Mistral-7B and OLMo-2-7B as further models.
AI.result: Monitors trained on the naive unsafe-versus-rest contrast mostly learn exposure. Retrained on exposed cases only, the probes predict the model's own unsafe tool call with logistic AUROC 0.853 on Qwen, matched by a trained TF-IDF text baseline at 0.855, and reach 0.896 on Mistral-7B and 0.912 on OLMo-2-7B. Representations separate exposure at 1.000 versus 0.908 for trained text.
AI.conclusion: The signal exists, but a naive contrast learns population-dependent features, so evaluations should stratify both exposure and commitment, since an unstratified AUROC overstates what a latent monitor knows.

title: Artifact Distillation: Training-Free Transfer from Frontier to Small Language Models
comment: 10 pages (4 pages main text), 2 figures, 3 tables
summary: Closing the gap between frontier and smaller language models is usually approached by distillation: fine-tuning the small model (student) on a frontier model's (teacher) outputs, which binds transfer to training compute and leaves the transferred knowledge largely opaque. We propose Artifact Distillation: a teacher solves training instances and externalizes its problem-solving procedure into an artifact bank that a student queries at inference time, with no gradient updates. Across four LiveBench tasks, a bank written by Claude Opus 4.5 lets Claude Haiku 4.5 outperform unaided Claude Sonnet 4.5 on spatial reasoning (0.707 vs. 0.647) at 60% of its cost, and reach Sonnet 4.5's level on table joining at 89% of its cost. The same raw bank raises Qwen3.5-27B's pooled score from 0.730 to 0.800, showing that transfer is not confined to the teacher's model family.

AI.tldr: Proposes Artifact Distillation, in which a teacher externalizes its problem-solving procedure into an artifact bank that a student queries at inference time, transferring capability without gradient updates.
AI.motivation: Closing the gap between frontier and smaller language models is usually done by fine-tuning on teacher outputs, which ties transfer to training compute and leaves the transferred knowledge largely opaque.
AI.method: A teacher solves training instances and writes its procedures into an artifact bank, which the student queries at inference time with no gradient updates. The approach is evaluated on four LiveBench tasks.
AI.result: A bank written by Claude Opus 4.5 lets Claude Haiku 4.5 outperform unaided Claude Sonnet 4.5 on spatial reasoning (0.707 vs. 0.647) at 60% of its cost, and reach Sonnet 4.5's level on table joining at 89% of its cost. The same raw bank raises Qwen3.5-27B's pooled score from 0.730 to 0.800.
AI.conclusion: Transfer is not confined to the teacher's model family, so training-free artifact banks are a viable route to moving frontier problem-solving into smaller models.

title: Supervised Fine-Tuning for Reasoning Large Language Models: A Survey
summary: Large reasoning models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks, where supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on long chain-of-thought data serves as a crucial foundation for eliciting and enhancing their reasoning abilities. Despite rapid progress in both improving and analyzing reasoning-oriented SFT, the field still lacks a systematic survey that consolidates its fast-growing literature. To fill this gap, we present a comprehensive review of recent advancements in reasoning SFT, examining the literature through the dual lenses of methodological design and analytical investigation. First, we review methodological improvements across the SFT pipeline and categorize them into data-centric approaches and algorithm-centric innovations. Second, we reorganize analytical studies along three dimensions: data characteristics, optimization dynamics, and mechanistic insights. Finally, by synthesizing current research focuses and remaining bottlenecks, we outline promising future directions for reasoning SFT. We hope this survey deepens the understanding of reasoning SFT and paves the way for advanced reasoning models.

AI.tldr: A survey of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for reasoning large language models, organized around methodological improvements and analytical studies of SFT on long chain-of-thought data.
AI.motivation: SFT on long chain-of-thought data is a crucial foundation for eliciting reasoning abilities, but the fast-growing literature on reasoning SFT lacks a systematic consolidation.
AI.method: Methodological improvements are reviewed and categorized into data-centric and algorithm-centric approaches. Analytical studies are reorganized along three dimensions: data characteristics, optimization dynamics and mechanistic insights.
AI.result: The survey synthesizes current research focuses and remaining bottlenecks in reasoning SFT.
AI.conclusion: The survey outlines promising future directions for reasoning SFT and aims to deepen understanding of the area.

title: Prompt-agnostic Language Models
comment: Master's thesis, University of Potsdam, Hasso Plattner Institute, 2026, Parts of this work also appear in the EMNLP 2026 paper "Prompt-Robust Language Models: Which Training Strategies Work?" (arXiv:2609.01217)
summary: Despite their strong performance, large language models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. This issue is typically addressed at inference-time through manual prompt optimization, which introduces overhead and lacks scalability. Conversely, we focus on train-time approaches that build prompt robustness into the model during instruction tuning. A common strategy is to mix multiple paraphrases of each prompt into training. We demonstrate that across trainable parameters, the per-paraphrasing gradients interfere, with 57% exhibiting sign conflicts and the naive gradient average discarding approximately a fifth of the magnitude. Therefore, we develop two gradient-merging methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that address this interference by leveraging interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging and applying them to prompt gradients. In this study, we compare the efficacy of our methods to increase model robustness to train-time robustness methods spanning all three established classes: data construction, consistency regularization, and contrastive alignment. The evaluation is conducted across four models from two families at two scales. We observe the interaction between prompt phrasing and the specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and exceeds 70% on tasks such as ANLI and WiC. The gradient-merging methods directly improve this local robustness and nearly halve per-example variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to overall accuracy. The other train-time methods enhance raw performance, but fail to improve per-example variance reliably. Code: this https URL. Model checkpoints: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, gradient-merging methods that resolve interference between per-paraphrase gradients to make instruction-tuned LLMs more robust to prompt phrasing.
AI.motivation: LLMs remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation, inference-time prompt optimization is manual and does not scale, and the common train-time practice of mixing paraphrases into training causes gradient interference.
AI.method: Per-paraphrase gradients are shown to conflict, with 57% exhibiting sign conflicts and naive averaging discarding about a fifth of the magnitude. Interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging are applied to prompt gradients, and the methods are compared with data construction, consistency regularization and contrastive alignment across four models from two families at two scales.
AI.result: Interaction between prompt phrasing and specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and over 70% on tasks such as ANLI and WiC. The gradient-merging methods directly improve local robustness and nearly halve per-example variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to overall accuracy, while the other train-time methods raise raw performance but do not reliably reduce variance.
AI.conclusion: Gradient merging targets per-example prompt robustness more directly than existing train-time robustness methods.

title: One Confidence Threshold, Unequal Coverage: Language Gaps in Typed Decision Interfaces and How Translating Inputs Reduces Them
summary: Deployed classifiers often act on a prediction only when its confidence clears a threshold and pass the rest to a person. We ask whether one threshold serves all languages equally on typed decision interfaces, APIs that return a probability for each option of a fixed multiple-choice question. In a confirmatory study with a written analysis plan, three vendors' interfaces classified 1,000 MASSIVE items, each in 51 languages, with a threshold of 0.9. Even when a request is answered correctly in both English and another language, the English version clears the threshold more often, by 8.6-11.7 percentage points on average. Observed coverage, the share of requests handled automatically, is lower than English's in every other language, while the requests the gate handles are rarely wrong. The gap remains when every language is reweighted to the same accuracy, and a standard calibration metric (ECE) does not detect it on one interface. In exploratory analyses, English's coverage stays higher when each language gets its own threshold fitted to the same 5% error target. Translating inputs into English nearly closes the gap at 0.9 but leaves English ahead at that error target. Requests written natively in African languages show a gap in the same direction when English is their human translation. We recommend reporting per-language coverage at the operating threshold.

AI.tldr: Finds that one confidence threshold gives unequal automation across languages in typed decision interfaces, with English clearing the threshold more often than other languages, and recommends reporting per-language coverage.
AI.motivation: Deployed classifiers act on a prediction only when its confidence clears a threshold, and the question is whether a single threshold serves all languages equally on typed decision interfaces that return a probability for each option.
AI.method: In a confirmatory study with a written analysis plan, three vendors' interfaces classified 1,000 MASSIVE items, each in 51 languages, with a threshold of 0.9. Exploratory analyses fitted per-language thresholds to a 5% error target and tested translating inputs into English.
AI.result: For the same correctly answered request, the English version clears the threshold more often, by 8.6-11.7 percentage points on average. Coverage is lower than English's in every other language, while the requests handled automatically are rarely wrong. The gap remains when languages are reweighted to the same accuracy, and ECE does not detect it on one interface. Translating inputs nearly closes the gap at 0.9 but leaves English ahead at a 5% error target, and a gap in the same direction appears for native African-language requests when English is their human translation.
AI.conclusion: A single threshold is not language-neutral, so per-language coverage should be reported at the operating threshold.

title: Two-Colour Zig-Zag Numberlink on Rectangles: A Forbidden-Pattern Characterization, a Constructive Polynomial-Time Algorithm, and a Lean Verification
summary: In Zig-Zag Numberlink, pairs of endpoints in a grid must be joined by vertex-disjoint paths that together visit every cell. The problem is NP-complete when the number of pairs is un- bounded (Adcock et al.). For a single pair it is the Hamiltonian path problem in rectangular grid graphs, solved by Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter. Two pairs on a rectangle form the paired 2-disjoint path cover problem. We settle the case of two pairs on rectangles with the endpoints anywhere in the grid. If both sides of the rectangle are at least 11, an instance is solvable if and only if no entry of a finite catalogue of forbidden patterns occurs. The catalogue consists of a parity condition, an alternation condition on the border, a handful of local corner and edge patterns, 65 listed corner configurations, and a rule that propagates forced routes out of the corners before testing alternation. If a side is at most 10, a frontier dynamic programming algorithm decides the instance in time linear in the long side. The characterization is construc- tive. Solutions are built by deleting empty lines, splitting the rectangle by straight cuts, and splicing the pieces back together, in time O((R+C) RC). Both directions of the characterization and the correctness of the dynamic programming algorithm are verified in Lean 4. The finite case analyses, which are window certificates for the corner configurations and a check of all irreducible instances with sides 11-22, are carried out by the Lean compiler via native decide. We describe the algorithm, the catalogue, the proof structure, the compromises made in the formalization, and implementations in Python, JavaScript and C that produce identical output.

AI.tldr: Gives a complete characterization of when two-pair Zig-Zag Numberlink instances on a rectangle are solvable, using a finite catalogue of forbidden patterns, together with a constructive polynomial-time algorithm and Lean 4 verification.
AI.motivation: Zig-Zag Numberlink is NP-complete with an unbounded number of pairs, and the two-pair case (paired 2-disjoint path cover on rectangles with endpoints anywhere in the grid) had not been settled.
AI.method: For rectangles with both sides at least 11, solvability is decided by a catalogue of forbidden patterns (a parity condition, a border alternation condition, local corner and edge patterns, 65 corner configurations, and a rule propagating forced routes out of the corners); solutions are built by deleting empty lines, splitting by straight cuts and splicing pieces in O((R+C) RC) time, and a frontier dynamic programming algorithm handles sides of at most 10.
AI.result: The characterization and the dynamic programming algorithm are verified in Lean 4, with the finite case analyses (corner window certificates and all irreducible instances with sides 11 to 22) checked by native decide; Python, JavaScript and C implementations produce identical output.
AI.conclusion: The work gives a complete, constructive and formally verified solution for the two-pair rectangular case, and documents the compromises made in the formalization.

title: Bouba Beats Kiki, and Other Regularities in the Subjective Preferences of LLMs
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures in main text; 27 pages, 13 figures in supplement. To appear at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Users engage with large language models on tasks that are purely objective ("When was Netflix founded?"), purely subjective ("What should I name my child?") or anywhere in-between. We have rich tools for evaluating model accuracy with respect to objective criteria. However, when it comes to subjective aspects of a task, we do not have similarly developed methodology at hand. In this paper, we take some early steps towards framing the question of subjective evaluation. Rather than measure how often a model is right or wrong on a question, we instead ask, how do models make choices among multiple viable responses without a clear winner? To study this question, we restrict our focus to short-form content, and consider comparison tasks among three such content types: numbers, baby names, and fictional cities. We identify 29 aspects of these short-form examples covering many areas of syntax and semantics (length, alphabetic order, popularity, vowel mix, spoken sound, etc.). We show first that models tend to have strong and reproducible preferences for or against some of these aspects. Second, we show that variations in how the model is asked to express a preference may cause some of these aspects to activate or deactivate in the model's selection. Third, we show that overall preference distributions among pairs may vary radically based on seemingly-unimportant variations in the nature of the question posed to the model, raising new questions about manipulation. And finally, we show that, if models are used both to create lists of alternatives and to rank them, there are unexpected interactions between the two stages that may also drive the models' stated preferences.

AI.tldr: Proposes a framework for evaluating subjective LLM choices among multiple viable answers and shows that models have reproducible preferences over 29 short-form aspects, which can be shifted by how the question is phrased.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks measure accuracy on objective questions, but there is no comparable methodology for subjective choices where no response is clearly correct.
AI.method: The authors study pairwise comparison tasks over numbers, baby names and fictional cities, identifying 29 aspects such as length, alphabetic order, popularity, vowel mix and spoken sound, and vary how the preference is elicited and how alternatives are generated and then ranked.
AI.result: Models show strong and reproducible preferences for or against several aspects; the phrasing of the preference question activates or deactivates these aspects; overall preference distributions change radically under seemingly minor question variations; and generating then ranking lists produces unexpected interactions between the two stages.
AI.conclusion: Subjective preferences of LLMs are systematic but fragile, which raises concerns about manipulation through question design and calls for better subjective evaluation methods.

title: Towards Myocardial Infarction Diagnosis: An Investigation into Machine Learning and Deep Learning Algorithms using ECG Data
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Based on the authors' undergraduate thesis at BRAC University (2023)
summary: Myocardial Infarction (MI) is a severe and potentially fatal cardiac condition caused by myocardial injury due to ischemia, and timely detection can substantially reduce its mortality. Electrocardiography (ECG) is the primary diagnostic modality for MI, but manual interpretation is susceptible to human error. In this work, we propose Visionary V2, a multi-step, adaptive filtration method for ECG signal normalization, and use it to study machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches to MI detection on the PTB Diagnostic ECG Database using all 15 available leads. On statistical features extracted from the filtered signals, such as the R-R interval, a Bagging ensemble of decision trees reaches 96.6% accuracy, compared with 87.7% when the signals are processed with BioSPPy. We further generate an image dataset from the filtered signals, on which a custom ResNet-50 misclassifies only 1 of 7,000 validation images and a custom CNN reaches an F1 score of about 98.7%. Finally, we apply LIME, Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients to verify that the image models attend to the ECG waveform rather than the background. These results indicate that careful signal normalization combined with ML and DL models can support fast and accurate automated MI screening.

AI.tldr: Proposes Visionary V2, an adaptive filtration method for ECG normalization, and shows that with it classical ML and deep learning models detect myocardial infarction accurately on the PTB Diagnostic ECG Database.
AI.motivation: ECG interpretation for myocardial infarction is susceptible to human error, and automated detection depends on careful signal preprocessing.
AI.method: The authors normalize ECG signals with a multi-step adaptive filter using all 15 leads, extract statistical features (including R-R intervals) for a Bagging ensemble of decision trees, and generate an image dataset from the filtered signals for a custom ResNet-50 and a custom CNN; LIME, Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients are used for explanation.
AI.result: The Bagging ensemble reaches 96.6% accuracy on filtered features versus 87.7% with BioSPPy processing; the custom ResNet-50 misclassifies only 1 of 7,000 validation images; the custom CNN reaches an F1 score of about 98.7%; explanation methods indicate attention to the ECG waveform rather than the background.
AI.conclusion: Careful signal normalization combined with ML and DL models can support fast and accurate automated screening for myocardial infarction.

title: Generation, Not Selection: LLM Proposals for Certified Access-Control Policy Mining
summary: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) policy mining---recovering a compact, auditable policy from an access log---is posed as minimum set cover and solved greedily, which enjoys an $s^{*}(1+\ln m)$ guarantee. That guarantee is \emph{conditional} on a precondition the literature never states: the candidate pool handed to greedy must contain the optimal rules. Generation, not selection, is the binding constraint, and existing generators are purely \emph{syntactic}---they surface a rule only when enough log records witness it, so they fail on precisely the rare exception rules that fill a heavy-tailed policy. We replace the generator with a language model proposing rules \emph{semantically}, from attribute names, and keep the combinatorial selector to carry the guarantee: every proposal is filtered against the observed denials, so soundness is independent of the proposal mechanism and an unreliable proposer can only waste candidates, never grant access. Over five seeds on each of two enterprise domains, adding semantic proposal to a syntactic miner dominates it on \emph{ten of ten} runs---strictly better on seven---with near-optimal policies ($9.2$--$9.6$ rules against $s^{*}=9$, versus $11.2$--$14.6$) and false grants cut four- to sevenfold. Replacing the syntactic miner rather than augmenting it wins only where witnesses are scarce. An anonymization ablation isolates the mechanism: opaque attribute names cost two thirds of the model's rule recovery while leaving the syntactic baselines provably unmoved, and cost nothing where witnesses are plentiful. Semantic knowledge and log evidence are substitutes.

AI.tldr: Replaces the candidate generator in ABAC policy mining with a language model that proposes rules semantically from attribute names, filtered by observed denials, so the greedy set-cover guarantee is kept while exception rules are recovered.
AI.motivation: Greedy policy mining guarantees its approximation bound only if the candidate pool contains the optimal rules, but existing syntactic generators surface a rule only when enough log records witness it, so they miss rare exception rules.
AI.method: The language model proposes rules from attribute names, every proposal is filtered against the observed denials so soundness does not depend on the proposer, and the combinatorial greedy selector is retained; an anonymization ablation replaces attribute names with opaque ones.
AI.result: Over five seeds on each of two enterprise domains, adding semantic proposal dominates the syntactic miner on ten of ten runs (strictly better on seven), yielding 9.2 to 9.6 rules against an optimum of 9 versus 11.2 to 14.6, with false grants cut four- to sevenfold; opaque names cost two thirds of rule recovery while leaving syntactic baselines unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Semantic knowledge and log evidence are substitutes, and semantic proposal is most valuable where log witnesses are scarce.

title: Learning Graph Beliefs for Active Radio Mapping With Decision-Certified Multi-Step Sensing
summary: Radio maps provide essential wireless propagation knowledge for network optimization and autonomous platforms. Acquiring dense measurements, however, is prohibitively costly, requiring active sampling to prioritize informative measurements. Existing active sampling methods typically rely on variances from prescribed spatial models or learned pointwise uncertainty, which may not fully capture the spatial correlation of different measurements. This paper proposes GraphBARC, a graph-structured active radio map construction framework that integrates learned spatial modeling with analytical Bayesian inference. A graph network learns correlated node and edge factors using only acquired measurements, inducing a joint full-map belief that supports analytical observation updates without retraining. Rather than immediate one-step acquisition, it adopts a nonmyopic sensing strategy that evaluates joint map-wide Bayes risk reduction over feasible multi-step routes, accounting for information redundancy among planned measurements. We reuse candidate responses and derive residual-based bounds directly on route-value differences, retaining shared response-error structure to avoid uniformly high-accuracy evaluation. An error-aware continuation bound screens unpromising prefixes, after which only responses needed for unresolved comparisons are refined. We further establish a computable decision-gap bound and show that certified exclusions remain valid during refinement. Experiments show that GraphBARC reduces mean root-mean-square error (RMSE) by over 16% relative to the evaluated baselines and core planning time by 56% compared with the fixed-accuracy, unpruned implementation.

AI.tldr: Proposes GraphBARC, an active radio map construction framework that uses a graph network for spatial beliefs and multi-step non-myopic sensing with certified pruning of candidate routes.
AI.motivation: Dense radio map measurements are costly, and existing active sampling methods based on prescribed spatial models or pointwise uncertainty may not capture spatial correlation among measurements.
AI.method: A graph network learns correlated node and edge factors from acquired measurements to induce a joint full-map belief, which supports analytical Bayes updates without retraining; planning evaluates joint map-wide Bayes risk reduction over feasible multi-step routes, reuses candidate responses with residual-based bounds, and screens unpromising prefixes with an error-aware continuation bound.
AI.result: GraphBARC reduces mean RMSE by over 16% relative to the evaluated baselines and cuts core planning time by 56% compared with the fixed-accuracy, unpruned implementation.
AI.conclusion: Combining learned graph-based spatial modeling with analytical Bayesian inference and certified pruning makes multi-step active sensing for radio maps both more accurate and cheaper to plan.

title: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
summary: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.

AI.tldr: Presents LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that recalibrates backward-pass demand and compacts retained token-expert pairs, reducing MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2 to 44.8% relative to SYMI.
AI.motivation: Uneven routing in sparse MoE models creates computation and communication bottlenecks, and existing placement and replication methods add expert copies that compete with token buffers for limited GPU memory.
AI.method: During forward execution LRMoE plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations; during backpropagation a load recalibration metric scores each token-expert pair and selects pairs within the quotas; a capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances, and physical compaction forms smaller payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs.
AI.result: On Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B, LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2 to 44.8% relative to SYMI.
AI.conclusion: Jointly recalibrating backward demand and balancing retained workload reduces backward traffic, computation and buffer demand, making MoE training more efficient under memory constraints.

title: Beyond Similarity Search: Knowledge Graph Metadata Enrichment for Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: A key challenge of RAG systems is retrieving information from enterprise documents created by multiple teams over time, where it is not possible to enrich the information using the latest information and metadata available outside the scope of organizational documentation responsibility. We investigated whether using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information would improve upon knowledge retrieval over similarity search over embeddings. To perform the experiment, we created a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset for a quarter, comprising 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks of risk-factor text. To simulate the enrichment, we created a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges carrying an accession number on every edge. To evaluate the gain obtained via a graph-based design, we evaluated three architectures: text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design. All architectures share the same model and temperature to allow comparison. Results are scored programmatically by an LLM as judge over 20 questions divided across four categories, each question asked three times. GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries. Vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win, passing 3 of 15 where GraphRAG passed 15 of 15, because company attribution is not recoverable from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were text-to-SQL conflating distinct people who share a surname, the failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text prevents structurally; GraphRAG made none. We claim no advantage beyond this corpus, this model and this question set.

AI.tldr: Compares text-to-SQL, dense-vector RAG and a two-stage GraphRAG on an SEC EDGAR snapshot and finds that GraphRAG answers the most questions correctly, mainly because it resolves company identity through a knowledge graph.
AI.motivation: Enterprise RAG struggles to retrieve information from documents written by many teams over time and cannot easily enrich them with metadata held outside the documentation, so the authors test whether a knowledge graph helps over similarity search.
AI.method: The authors build a quarterly SEC EDGAR snapshot of 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies with 508,714 embedded risk-factor chunks, and a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges with accession numbers on edges; three architectures share the same model and temperature and are scored by an LLM judge over 20 questions in four categories, each asked three times.
AI.result: GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared with 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG; GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries; all six confident falsehoods came from text-to-SQL conflating people who share a surname, and GraphRAG made none.
AI.conclusion: Resolving identity to an identifier before reading text prevents a class of errors that similarity search and text-to-SQL cannot avoid, though the authors claim no advantage beyond this corpus, model and question set.

title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
summary: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$\epsilon$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.

AI.tldr: Proposes localized posterior inference for model calibration, using Gaussian proximity weights and an amortized conditional normalizing flow, and shows that it reduces prediction errors relative to global calibration for an ocean turbulence closure.
AI.motivation: A single calibration parameter may not reproduce a physical response across the whole context domain because of model discrepancy, and uncertainties in observations and contexts must be quantified.
AI.method: Observation likelihoods are weighted by Gaussian localization around a target context, with covariance inflation for context uncertainty, reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling; a conditional normalizing flow performs amortized variational inference, and the localized posteriors are integrated under a context measure to yield the marginalized parameter distribution.
AI.result: In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model under uniform and skewed context distributions, localization reduces aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior; for the k-epsilon closure in a single-column ocean model with atmospheric forcing as context, localized calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration.
AI.conclusion: Localizing the posterior over contexts gives more accurate calibration when model discrepancy varies across the context domain, although both twin experiments are constructed so that local compensation is possible.

title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
summary: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces ThinkJev, which pairs a fast direct-answer system with a slow thinking system built from one hybrid-thinking model, and accepts direct answers only where a statistical test guarantees a target error rate.
AI.motivation: Reading option probabilities from a single forward pass is fast but error-prone on multi-step decisions such as arithmetic, counting and date comparison, while thinking first is accurate but costly.
AI.method: System 1 reads option-letter probabilities for a direct answer, and System 2 reads the same letters after thinking on the cached prompt, so both give probabilities over the same options; one sampled thought yields answers under every thinking budget, and a statistical test on labeled dev data gates when System 1 alone may answer; a confidence-based stopping rule ends thoughts early.
AI.result: At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8,359 test decisions directly with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%); for the rest, early stopping reaches 81.6% accuracy versus 82.7% for always thinking while using 72% of the thought tokens; on JevBench the 27B model thinks on 29.4% of items and is not distinguishable in accuracy from two thinking APIs.
AI.conclusion: Thinking can be spent selectively with a guaranteed error bound and little accuracy loss, although choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less.

title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces OpenFrontiers, a corpus of 12,151 open research problems and a 200-problem Lean 4 benchmark of mathematics problems, and finds that closed-book rediscovery of resolved problems by seven LLM agents is rare.
AI.motivation: LLMs show growing promise on research-level problems, but no comprehensive collection of such problems exists and evaluating them on research-level questions is difficult.
AI.method: The benchmark has 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean 4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; the HQ-50 subset is filtered by quality score; proofs are graded by two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval and live-web conditions.
AI.result: Seven LLM agents on HQ-50 under a standardized budget rediscover at most 7 of 40 resolved problems in the closed-book setting, while live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions.
AI.conclusion: The resource provides a basis for measuring research-level rediscovery, and the results suggest that apparent success on open problems often depends on retrieving existing solutions.

title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
summary: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Shows that poisoning 0.1% of the pretraining corpus can implant a remote code execution backdoor in a CLI agent built from Qwen3 models, with attack success rising with model scale.
AI.motivation: LLMs are pretrained on uncurated web data, and the authors ask whether attackers planting poisoned content there can backdoor an agent to run commands on a user's machine.
AI.method: The authors pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at 0.6B, 1.7B and 4B parameters, post-train each into a CLI agent with a clean pipeline, and embed a new poison design in a small fraction of the pretraining corpus.
AI.result: With 0.1% of the corpus poisoned, the deployed 4B agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present, reaching roughly 92% attack success rate, and the backdoor remains positive at a poison rate of 0.0005%; the agent behaves normally on clean inputs.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining-data poisoning is a practical threat to agents with command execution, and the risk grows with model scale.

title: Selective and Hybrid-State Communication for Latent Multi-Agent Systems
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Resource-Aware Agentic AI (RAAAI)
summary: Efficient communication remains a major bottleneck in large language model multiagent systems. Latent communication reduces repeated natural-language exchange by transferring internal model states between agents, but these transfers remain costly and are typically designed around conventional KV-cache representations. We address this problem from two complementary perspectives. We introduce SelectKV, a boundary-aware method that selectively communicates KV states while protecting inherited context, and HyLaMAS, which extends latent collaboration to hybrid linear-attention models by communicating both KV caches and recurrent states through a shared workspace. Across six benchmarks, SelectKV reduces communicated KV positions and logical KV payload by 9.7-9.9%, with accuracy unchanged on two benchmarks, within one percentage point on three, and six points lower on HumanEval+. Across Qwen3.5 model scales, HyLaMAS reduces decoded output tokens by 53-80% and achieves 1.16-2.78x speedups relative to text-based multi-agent communication. Together, these independently evaluated methods represent two complementary approaches to efficient latent-state communication across conventional Transformer and hybrid model architectures.

AI.tldr: Proposes SelectKV, which communicates only selected KV states between LLM agents while protecting inherited context, and HyLaMAS, which extends latent communication to hybrid linear-attention models by sharing KV caches and recurrent states.
AI.motivation: Latent communication between agents avoids repeated natural-language exchange but remains costly, and it is typically designed around conventional KV-cache representations.
AI.method: SelectKV is a boundary-aware method that selectively transfers KV states; HyLaMAS communicates both KV caches and recurrent states through a shared workspace for hybrid linear-attention models.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks SelectKV reduces communicated KV positions and logical KV payload by 9.7 to 9.9%, with accuracy unchanged on two benchmarks, within one point on three and six points lower on HumanEval+; across Qwen3.5 scales HyLaMAS reduces decoded output tokens by 53 to 80% and gives 1.16 to 2.78 times speedups over text-based multi-agent communication.
AI.conclusion: The two methods offer complementary routes to efficient latent-state communication for both Transformer and hybrid architectures, with SelectKV trading a small accuracy cost on code for lower payload.

title: Investigating the Early Signatures of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks
comment: 92 pages, 7 figures, 16 pages of main text
summary: Deep neural networks learn data-dependent features, a capacity widely credited for their empirical success. However, explicitly characterizing what features emerge -- and when they improve generalization -- is challenging, since training is nonlinear and non-convex and the data is often anisotropic. Here, we give a closed-form account of feature learning for a deep linear network in a mean-field parameterization, trained by one gradient step from initialization on high-dimensional data carrying a low-dimensional (spiked) signal. In the infinite-width mean-field limit, one step updates each layer's feature kernel by a target-aligned rank-one spike, amplified by both the learning rate and the layer depth. We next assess how these features impact prediction through kernel ridge regression (KRR), finding that KRR on the learned feature kernel yields scalar inflation of the KRR estimator at initialization -- an "anti-shrinkage" mechanism that reinflates task-relevant directions suppressed by ridge, while also amplifying noise. To study when this inflation improves generalization, in the overparameterized proportional limit we derive closed-form expressions for the bias, variance, and generalization errors of these estimators in terms of key macroscopic parameters -- notably the spike strength and spike-target alignment. Crucially, we find that a one-step generalization advantage vanishes for isotropic inputs and appears when both the spike strength and an effective signal-to-noise ratio are sufficiently large, demonstrating that a successful first gradient step both requires and benefits from low-dimensional task structure.

AI.tldr: Gives a closed-form account of feature learning after one gradient step in a deep linear network under mean-field parameterization, and shows that a one-step generalization advantage appears only when the spike strength and effective signal-to-noise ratio are large.
AI.motivation: Explicitly characterizing which features deep networks learn, and when they improve generalization, is hard because training is nonlinear, non-convex and data is often anisotropic.
AI.method: The authors analyze a deep linear network trained by one gradient step from initialization on high-dimensional data with a low-dimensional spiked signal, derive the infinite-width mean-field update of each layer's feature kernel, and use kernel ridge regression on the learned kernel to obtain closed-form bias, variance and generalization errors in the overparameterized proportional limit.
AI.result: One step updates each layer's feature kernel by a target-aligned rank-one spike amplified by the learning rate and depth; KRR on the learned kernel inflates the estimator, an anti-shrinkage effect that also amplifies noise; the generalization advantage vanishes for isotropic inputs and appears when spike strength and effective SNR are sufficiently large.
AI.conclusion: A successful first gradient step both requires and benefits from low-dimensional task structure, which gives a precise picture of early feature learning.

title: An $Ω(T^{3/4})$ lower bound for projection-free online learning with linear minimization oracles
summary: This work considers projection-free online learning algorithms with linear minimization oracles for handling the decision set. For Online Frank--Wolfe (OFW), regret upper bounds were already known for specific OFW tunings [Hazan and Kale, 2012, Hazan, 2016] which scaled as $T^{3/4}$ (where $T$ is the horizon length). However, it remained an open question whether the regret of all OFW tunings scaled as $T^{3/4}$. We answer that question, proving a universal worst-case regret lower bound $\Omega(T^{3/4} m^{-1/4})$ for any projection-free algorithm that makes at most $m$ linear minimization oracle calls per round. The analysis suggests an extended OFW to resort to multiple linear optimizations per round, for which we prove a regret upper bound $O(\max \{ T^{3/4} m^{-1/4}, \sqrt{T} \})$.

AI.tldr: Proves a universal worst-case regret lower bound of Omega(T^3/4 m^-1/4) for projection-free online learning with m linear minimization oracle calls per round, settling an open question on Online Frank-Wolfe and proposing an extended variant that matches it.
AI.motivation: Earlier analyses gave T^3/4 regret for specific Online Frank-Wolfe tunings, but it was unknown whether all tunings scale this way.
AI.method: The authors prove a lower bound for any projection-free algorithm making at most m linear minimization oracle calls per round, and propose an extended OFW that performs multiple linear optimizations per round.
AI.result: The lower bound Omega(T^3/4 m^-1/4) holds for all such algorithms, and the extended OFW achieves regret O(max{T^3/4 m^-1/4, sqrt(T)}).
AI.conclusion: The T^3/4 dependence is unavoidable for single-oracle projection-free methods, and using more oracle calls per round reduces the regret.

title: Finite-Sample Optimal Conformal Prediction Sets under Covariate Shift
summary: We study conformal prediction under covariate shift with a known covariate density ratio, seeking prediction sets with minimum expected length under the target distribution. For every calibration sample size, we prove that the rule combining the inverse conditional-density score with randomized weighted conformal calibration minimizes this expected length among all rules valid over the full weighted-exchangeability class. We approximate the oracle using quantile and kernel histograms, including forest-weighted estimators, and select estimators and tuning parameters by resampling to estimate calibrated target length. On a bounded response domain, we bound excess length linearly in $L^1$ density error at fixed calibration size, without requiring a uniform positive lower bound on the true density. We also bound selection-pool and resampling errors. Under explicit growth conditions, the selected procedure approaches the same oracle while the calibration size remains fixed. Experiments on 36 known-density configurations and four public regression datasets compare coverage, prediction-set length, and runtime with existing methods. In targeted low-coverage and strong-shift comparisons, inverse-density selection yields shorter mean sets in most cases and lower mean runtime than the evaluated weighted baselines, with some differences in achieved coverage.

AI.tldr: Derives a conformal prediction rule under covariate shift that minimizes expected set length among valid rules, approximates the oracle with histogram and forest-weighted estimators selected by resampling, and reports shorter sets and lower runtime in most comparisons.
AI.motivation: Under covariate shift with a known density ratio, prediction sets should be as short as possible under the target distribution while remaining valid, and existing weighted methods may be longer or slower.
AI.method: The rule combines an inverse conditional-density score with randomized weighted conformal calibration; the oracle is approximated with quantile and kernel histograms, including forest-weighted estimators, and estimator and tuning choices are selected by resampling to estimate calibrated target length.
AI.result: On a bounded response domain the excess length is bounded linearly in the L1 density error at fixed calibration size; across 36 known-density configurations and four public regression datasets, inverse-density selection yields shorter mean sets in most targeted low-coverage and strong-shift cases and lower mean runtime than the evaluated weighted baselines, with some differences in coverage.
AI.conclusion: The oracle rule is finite-sample optimal in expected length, and the selected procedure approaches it under explicit growth conditions while the calibration size stays fixed.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Global Climate Policy Cooperation
comment: Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning: workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: International climate policy requires coordination among countries whose mitigation decisions impose local costs but generate global benefits. Classical game-theoretic and integrated assessment approaches can study these incentives, but typically rely on prescribed behavioural assumptions or equilibrium concepts. Recent work has therefore explored Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning as a way to model climate-policy cooperation as an emergent outcome of repeated strategic interaction. We extend an existing MARL climate framework with a multi-stage negotiation mechanism in which agents propose agreements, accept or reject commitments, and face penalties for non-compliance. This allows us to study how agreement design affects learned mitigation behaviour, compliance, and climate outcomes. In an idealized setting with four homogeneous agents, we find that non-binding agreements do little to overcome free-riding, while moderate non-compliance penalties improve cooperation and reduce warming. However, excessively strong penalties discourage ambitious commitments, revealing a trade-off between enforcement and participation. We position the framework as a methodological contribution for testing agreement design rather than a predictive model of real negotiations.

AI.tldr: Extends a MARL climate framework with a multi-stage negotiation mechanism and finds that non-binding agreements do little against free-riding, while moderate non-compliance penalties improve cooperation but overly strong penalties deter ambitious commitments.
AI.motivation: Climate cooperation can be studied with game theory or integrated assessment models, but these rely on prescribed behavior or equilibrium assumptions, so the authors model cooperation as an emergent outcome of learning agents.
AI.method: Four homogeneous agents in an idealized setting propose agreements, accept or reject commitments, and face penalties for non-compliance within a multi-stage negotiation mechanism, and the study compares agreement designs for learned mitigation, compliance and climate outcomes.
AI.result: Non-binding agreements do little to overcome free-riding; moderate non-compliance penalties improve cooperation and reduce warming; excessively strong penalties discourage ambitious commitments, revealing a trade-off between enforcement and participation.
AI.conclusion: The framework is a methodological tool for testing agreement design rather than a predictive model of real negotiations, and it exposes an enforcement-participation trade-off.

title: When More Planning Hurts: Learned Planners for World Models
summary: On PushT, our fixed action updater (1,505 parameters) solves 8 of 16 scenes reserved from our configuration selection. The comparison planners perform as follows: Selected Adam (7 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 218.440s), adapted iCEM (2 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 49.309s), released LePlanner (16 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 5.652s). The total planning and encoding time for our action updater is 59.079s. Note that our action updater does not satisfy the task-cost criterion we fixed before evaluation. We also conduct another matched experiment where we only replay the first ten commands in each context and then allow the next solve 4, 8 or 12 updates (subsequent solves all get 8 updates). Among all 16 contexts (8 scene clusters), the 3 budgets get 9, 8 and 7 successes, respectively. Interestingly, the extra updates did not rescue any failing task in this experiment. All the changes in success/failure happen in one scene cluster, where we observe that the extra updates decrease the costs of the selected latent world-model trajectories for our updater, while the tasks that used to be successes become failures. The code, weights, evaluators, execution traces and cost accounting accompany the paper.

AI.tldr: Proposes a fixed action updater with 1,505 parameters that plans in a latent world model, and shows that more planning updates do not reliably improve success on PushT, with the comparison planners solving 7, 2 and 16 tasks at widely different costs.
AI.motivation: Planning with learned world models is expensive, and the authors ask whether more planning updates help and how a compact learned planner compares with optimization-based planners.
AI.method: The action updater is compared with selected Adam, adapted iCEM and the released LePlanner on PushT scenes reserved from configuration selection, with total planning and encoding time recorded; a matched experiment replays the first ten commands and then allows 4, 8 or 12 updates per solve.
AI.result: The updater solves 8 of 16 reserved scenes; Selected Adam solves 7 tasks in 218.440 s, adapted iCEM 2 tasks in 49.309 s, and released LePlanner 16 tasks in 5.652 s, while the updater takes 59.079 s and does not satisfy the fixed task-cost criterion; in the budget experiment the 4, 8 and 12 update settings yield 9, 8 and 7 successes, and extra updates rescued no failing task.
AI.conclusion: More planning does not always help, since additional updates lowered the cost of latent trajectories while converting some successes into failures in one scene cluster.

title: What Actually Matters? A Paired Evaluation of Inference Settings for $π_{0.5}$ on BEHAVIOR-1K
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for general-purpose household robotics. However, inference and data-collection strategies that have been deployed in smaller-scale settings do not necessarily generalize to large-scale, diverse task suites. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic, paired evaluation of previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies across all 100 tasks. Our evaluation uses a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner, which achieves a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set. These results show that proposed strategies do not transfer uniformly to new environments and tasks. Project page, videos, and detailed analysis: this https URL

AI.tldr: Systematically evaluates previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies for the pi0.5 VLA model on all 100 BEHAVIOR-1K tasks and finds that these strategies do not transfer uniformly to new environments and tasks.
AI.motivation: Inference and data-collection strategies developed in small-scale settings may not generalize to large, diverse household task suites.
AI.method: The authors run a paired evaluation of previously proposed strategies across all 100 tasks, using a fine-tuned pi0.5 model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner that achieves a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set.
AI.result: The paired comparisons show that the proposed strategies do not transfer uniformly across environments and tasks.
AI.conclusion: Gains from inference and data-collection tricks are task- and environment-dependent, so they should not be assumed to carry over to large-scale household robotics.

title: FAD-KV: Adaptive Dictionary KV Caching for Efficient Reasoning Decoding
summary: Key-value (KV) caching is a core mechanism in large language models, where intermediate key and value representations are stored to accelerate autoregressive decoding. As generation length increases, KV cache memory and computation grow linearly, making compression critical for efficient long-output reasoning. Dictionary-based sparse KV compression is appealing because it represents each token's KV states as a sparse combination of learned basis elements (atoms) in a dictionary, preserving token-level structure without enforcing a global low-rank constraint. However, existing dictionary-based methods face two practical limitations during decoding: iterative sparse coding methods such as Orthogonal Matching Pursuit add decoding-time overhead, and static dictionaries may mismatch evolving KV distributions under test-time generation. While adaptive dictionary updates can reduce this mismatch, naive append-only strategies lead to dictionary growth during generation. We propose FAD-KV, a \textbf{F}ast \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{D}ictionary KV caching framework for efficient reasoning decoding. FAD-KV integrates (i) a screening-based sparse coding scheme, where a one-shot Top-\(n\) selection identifies a small candidate pool followed by lightweight coefficient refinement, and (ii) a fixed-size dictionary adaptation mechanism that reuses inactive atoms instead of expanding the dictionary. By controlling both sparse coding cost and adaptive dictionary growth, FAD-KV provides a memory-bounded and computation-efficient KV compression framework for long reasoning workloads. Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show that FAD-KV achieves a strong quality-efficiency trade-off while avoiding unbounded dictionary growth during decoding.

AI.tldr: Introduces FAD-KV, a fixed-size adaptive dictionary KV caching framework that uses screening-based sparse coding and reuses inactive atoms, bounding memory and computation for long reasoning decoding.
AI.motivation: Dictionary-based sparse KV compression is attractive, but iterative sparse coding such as Orthogonal Matching Pursuit adds decoding overhead, static dictionaries can mismatch evolving KV distributions, and append-only adaptive updates make the dictionary grow during generation.
AI.method: FAD-KV combines a screening-based sparse coding scheme, in which a one-shot Top-n selection picks a small candidate pool followed by lightweight coefficient refinement, with a fixed-size dictionary adaptation mechanism that reuses inactive atoms instead of expanding the dictionary.
AI.result: Experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks show a strong quality-efficiency trade-off while avoiding unbounded dictionary growth during decoding.
AI.conclusion: Controlling both sparse coding cost and dictionary growth yields a memory-bounded and computation-efficient KV compression method for long reasoning workloads.

title: Machine learning applications in the heliosphere
comment: Review chapter submitted to the book Machine Learning Techniques for Astrophysics and Cosmology by Spring Singapore
summary: Space weather is the study of the near-Earth impact of the processes on the Sun. In a this era of technology, space weather emerges as a crucial area of study wherein the state of the near-Earth conditions need to be modeled and forecasted. Crucially, the advent of machine learning provides us with opportunities to study this subject in a rather comprehensive manner. In this chapter, we treat the the processes arising from Sun to the impact on the ground as a set of coupled systems, which can be studied in isolation or in a coupled manner. We define these individual systems in terms of their state vector $\vec{S}$, which provides us with an opportunity to define the physical variables determining the system. This also allows us to consider the systems in terms of their observables, obtained through the action of operators as $\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$. In such a formalism, the machine learning algorithms serve as {\it learned operators}, defined generally as inference ($\mathcal{I}$), propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and emulation ($\mathcal{E}$). Through such a formalism, we present how machine learning helps advance our understanding of the physical systems under study, while also accelerating the development of operational models for space weather forecasting.

AI.tldr: A book-chapter overview of machine learning in space weather, framing Sun-to-ground processes as coupled systems in which ML acts as learned operators for inference, propagation and emulation.
AI.motivation: Space weather must be modeled and forecasted as technology becomes more sensitive to near-Earth conditions, and the chapter argues that ML offers a comprehensive way to study the coupled Sun-to-ground chain.
AI.method: The chapter defines each physical subsystem by a state vector S and its observables O[S] obtained through operators, and casts ML algorithms as learned operators: inference (I), propagation (P) and emulation (E).
AI.result: The abstract reports no new numerical findings; it presents how ML advances understanding of the physical systems and accelerates operational space weather forecasting models.
AI.conclusion: The operator formalism gives a unified way to view ML in heliospheric research, linking scientific understanding with operational forecasting.

title: Understanding Large Language Models as Numerical Optimizers
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential tools for numerical optimization. Despite promising results, their intrinsic optimization capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood, particularly in high dimensions. This paper investigates the ability of LLMs to exploit mathematical problem structures and generate feasible, near-optimal solutions. We develop an evaluation framework that distinguishes solution quality from execution failures, including numerical inaccuracies, constraint violations, and output-format errors. Using representative problems from convex optimization, fractional programming, and constrained projection, we assess LLM performance against deterministic reference solvers across different dimensions. Our results reveal that LLMs can capture useful optimization structures and produce near-optimal solutions, even when their outputs fail to satisfy numerical or formatting requirements. However, reliability deteriorates with increasing problem dimension and depends strongly on the underlying optimization structure. To further investigate the limitations, we deploy an iterative refinement mechanism that provides targeted feedback on feasibility and solution quality. The results demonstrate that iterative refinement substantially improves reliability and extends the range of problem dimensions over which LLMs produce valid solutions. Nevertheless, persistent numerical and structural errors limit their applicability as standalone optimizers. These findings provide insights into the capacity and limits of LLM-based optimization and motivate hybrid approaches that combine LLM reasoning with deterministic numerical verification.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates LLMs as numerical optimizers on convex optimization, fractional programming and constrained projection problems, separating solution quality from execution failures. LLMs often find near-optimal solutions, but reliability falls with dimension and persistent errors limit them as standalone optimizers.
AI.motivation: The intrinsic optimization capabilities and limitations of LLMs remain poorly understood, particularly in high dimensions.
AI.method: An evaluation framework that distinguishes solution quality from numerical inaccuracies, constraint violations and output-format errors, comparing LLM outputs with deterministic reference solvers across problem dimensions, plus an iterative refinement mechanism that gives targeted feedback on feasibility and solution quality.
AI.result: LLMs capture useful optimization structure and often produce near-optimal solutions even when outputs violate numerical or format requirements; reliability deteriorates with dimension and depends on the optimization structure; iterative refinement substantially improves reliability and extends the valid dimension range, but numerical and structural errors persist.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based optimization has real but limited capacity, which motivates hybrid approaches that combine LLM reasoning with deterministic numerical verification.

title: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning
summary: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory and makes it directly available during latent multi-agent reasoning.\ A role-conditioned cross-attention reader allows the same memory to guide different agents according to their roles and current hidden states.\ We train the skill memories and shared reader through behavioral distillation, matching the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while keeping the backbone frozen.\ For our experiments, we obtain textual skills from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories, although existing skills can also be compiled directly.\ Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models ranging from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem provides strong gains for smaller backbones while preserving efficient latent multi-agent inference across model scales.\ We use the same $8\times256$ memory configuration across all evaluated model scales, requiring 9.6\,KB of skill-specific storage per skill, including its retrieval embedding.\ For a library of 100 skills, SkillMem reduces total storage by more than $38\times$ compared with alternative skill representations and achieves up to a $4.23\times$ end-to-end inference speedup.\ These results show that compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.

AI.tldr: SkillMem represents each reusable skill as a small external latent memory read by a role-conditioned cross-attention reader during latent multi-agent reasoning. It gives strong gains for smaller backbones with 9.6 KB of storage per skill and up to a 4.23x end-to-end speedup.
AI.motivation: Reusable skills supplied as text require repeated processing, while storing them as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters costs substantial per-skill storage.
AI.method: Each skill is a small external latent memory with a shared 8x256 configuration, trained by behavioral distillation that matches the change in token predictions induced by a textual skill while the backbone stays frozen; a shared role-conditioned cross-attention reader lets the same memory guide different agents, with textual skills drawn from paired successful and failed multi-agent trajectories.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks and Qwen3 models from 4B to 14B parameters, SkillMem gives strong gains for smaller backbones; it needs 9.6 KB per skill including its retrieval embedding, reduces total storage for a 100-skill library by more than 38x compared with alternative representations, and achieves up to a 4.23x end-to-end inference speedup.
AI.conclusion: Compact procedural memories can be reused without sacrificing the efficiency of latent multi-agent reasoning.

title: You Don't Need Aligned Representations: Knowledge Distillation via Random Prototype Spaces
comment: To appear at NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages main text plus appendices. Code: this https URL
summary: A widely held assumption in knowledge distillation is that teacher and student representations must occupy a compatible or explicitly aligned feature space. We propose RPKD (Random Prototype Knowledge Distillation), which discards this assumption by comparing both networks against a shared bank of randomly initialized, frozen prototype vectors. Alignment is therefore carried out in an external reference space rather than in the teacher's native feature coordinates: the teacher side is projected by fixed random maps that carry no trainable parameters, and only the student adapts. Two branches handle the transfer: a logit branch aligning global prototype similarity distributions and a feature branch matching spatially-resolved prototype activation maps. Both operate within the same fixed prototype space, which can be interpreted as a random feature embedding that approximately preserves inter-sample similarity structure, so the prototype bank and the distillation objective stay unchanged across teacher-student pairs while only the input projections are instantiated per architecture. In low-category settings, decoupling the prototype vocabulary from the task label space yields richer supervision than the label space alone, an advantage absent from logit-based methods, whose supervisory signal collapses as class count shrinks. This advantage is especially relevant in real-world scenarios where the label space is typically constrained. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RPKD, achieving a maximum gain of +7.98% over OFA on CIFAR-100, +12.44% on ImageNet-100, and +1.28% on ImageNet-1K. Source code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: RPKD distills knowledge by comparing teacher and student against a shared bank of frozen, randomly initialized prototype vectors, so the two networks do not need aligned feature spaces. It reports gains over OFA of up to +7.98% on CIFAR-100, +12.44% on ImageNet-100 and +1.28% on ImageNet-1K.
AI.motivation: Knowledge distillation assumes teacher and student representations must be compatible or explicitly aligned, and logit-based methods lose supervisory signal as the number of classes shrinks.
AI.method: Both networks are compared against the same fixed bank of random prototypes; the teacher is projected by fixed random maps with no trainable parameters and only the student adapts; a logit branch aligns global prototype similarity distributions, and a feature branch matches spatially resolved prototype activation maps.
AI.result: The maximum gains over OFA are +7.98% on CIFAR-100, +12.44% on ImageNet-100 and +1.28% on ImageNet-1K; in low-category settings the prototype vocabulary gives richer supervision than the label space alone.
AI.conclusion: Explicit feature alignment is not required for effective distillation, and decoupling the prototype vocabulary from the label space is especially useful when the label space is small.

title: Federated Learning for Semantic Communications over Multiple Access Channels
summary: This paper presents a federated learning (FL) framework for semantic communication (SemCom) over the multiple access channel (MAC), where multiple distributed transmitters simultaneously convey semantic information to a common receiver using end-to-end learned semantic representations. Semantic feature extraction, compression, wireless transmission, and semantic inference are jointly optimized through FL-based SemCom. Unlike conventional SemCom systems that train users independently, simultaneous semantic transmissions over the MAC enable concurrent training of multiple transmitters within the same transmission interval, thereby reducing training overhead and channel usage. Federated semantic aggregation is incorporated with shared and personalized encoder components, allowing transmitters with limited local training data to benefit from semantic representations learned from transmitters possessing larger datasets while preserving local adaptation. Evaluated using the CIFAR-10 dataset over fading channels, the proposed approach maintains high semantic inference accuracy under shared wireless access and significantly improves performance under severe data imbalance. In the meantime, simultaneous semantic transmissions can significantly reduce training overhead while preserving robust semantic performance across distributed transmitters with heterogeneous local datasets. These results highlight the potential of combining FL and SemCom to support scalable and communication-efficient edge intelligence in future wireless networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes federated learning for semantic communication over a multiple access channel, where several transmitters send semantic information simultaneously to one receiver. On CIFAR-10 over fading channels it keeps high inference accuracy, improves performance under severe data imbalance, and reduces training overhead.
AI.motivation: Conventional semantic communication trains users independently, which costs training overhead and channel usage, and transmitters with limited local data cannot benefit from larger datasets elsewhere.
AI.method: End-to-end learned semantic representations in which feature extraction, compression, wireless transmission and inference are jointly optimized; federated semantic aggregation with shared and personalized encoder components; simultaneous transmissions over the MAC so that multiple transmitters train concurrently in the same interval.
