AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent deep reinforcement learning models for football action valuation use 2D positions and velocities and omit posture information that is relevant to imminent actions.
AI.method: Using UEFA Champions League 2022/23 event, tracking and 3D pose data, the authors compare six pose representations across five learning settings and three seeds, varying temporal-difference targets and the action-prediction loss, with Monte Carlo return regression as a reference.
AI.result: Pose robustly improved return prediction in only three of 50 comparisons, all using torso and head orientation, and worsened it in twelve, mostly with ST-GCN embeddings. Removing the action-prediction loss raised the on-ball skill of position-only values from 0.003 to 0.040. Pose improved prediction of the on-ball action 0.2 s ahead (macro AUC 0.914 to 0.934 with raw joints) and pass-success prediction (AUC 0.844 to 0.856).
AI.conclusion: Within this training protocol pose informs imminent actions but rarely improves observed-action values, so training choices matter more than adding pose for action valuation.

title: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics
summary: Bisimulation metrics offer a principled notion of task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions and methods are largely confined to discounted MDPs, where contraction arguments ensure well-defined fixed points and downstream guarantees. We develop a unified foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted settings, that is total- and average-reward problems, by replacing the standard operator-centric view with a game-centric one: we interpret prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games and define metrics as the corresponding game value functions, yielding unique definitions even when $\gamma=1$. This game-theoretic foundation facilitates transfer of dynamic-programming theory and algorithms. We also use this game-centric perspective to characterize how metric finiteness depends on structural properties of the underlying MDP and motivate certain directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs. We further introduce an abstract framework for modifying the games' action spaces, allowing general transition coupling sets, that recovers many existing metrics and guides new constructions. Finally, we prove that these metrics bound total-reward and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences. We also provide error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning in total- and average-reward settings.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a game-theoretic foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted total- and average-reward MDPs by defining each metric as the value function of a zero-sum turn-based game, which yields unique definitions even when gamma equals 1. The metrics bound total-reward differences and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences.
AI.motivation: Existing bisimulation metric constructions are largely confined to discounted MDPs, where contraction arguments guarantee well-defined fixed points, so undiscounted settings lack a foundation for downstream guarantees.
AI.method: The authors reinterpret prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games, introduce an abstract framework for modifying game action spaces with general transition coupling sets, and characterize metric finiteness through structural properties of the MDP.
AI.result: The metrics bound total-reward differences and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences. Directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs are motivated, and error and suboptimality guarantees are given for aggregation-based planning in total- and average-reward settings.
AI.conclusion: The game-centric view transfers dynamic-programming theory and algorithms to undiscounted bisimulation metrics, recovers many existing metrics and guides new constructions.

title: CSO: Refining Robotic Policies via Skill Distribution Alignment and Skill-Grained Optimization
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 31 pages, including appendices and checklist
summary: Discretizing continuous actions into discrete skills using methods like VQ-VAE has emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation. However, quantization errors yield a suboptimal distribution for the skill prior, degrading its performance. While reinforcement learning offers a path for refinement, its direct application faces unstable encoder updates and a granularity dilemma in importance sampling. To address these challenges, we introduce Cascaded Skills Optimization (CSO), a two-stage post-training framework. First, Rejection-Sampling Supervised Fine-tuning aligns the model's observation-to-skill mapping with the distribution of successful online trajectories via supervised fine-tuning. Second, with the observation encoder frozen, Skills Policy Optimization computes an independent, clipped importance ratio for each complete skill, enabling stable and efficient updates. With a lightweight QueST-style policy, CSO raises overall LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%, improves performance on RoboTwin2.0, and achieves 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks. Additional comparisons with FAST, discrete BEAST, and fixed-buffer IQL further validate the effectiveness of our two-stage post-training strategy.

AI.tldr: CSO is a two-stage post-training framework for discrete-skill robotic policies that first aligns the observation-to-skill mapping through rejection-sampling supervised fine-tuning and then optimizes each complete skill with an independent clipped importance ratio. It raises overall LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%.
AI.motivation: Quantization errors in VQ-VAE skill discretization yield a suboptimal skill prior, and direct reinforcement learning on it faces unstable encoder updates and a granularity dilemma in importance sampling.
AI.method: Rejection-Sampling Supervised Fine-tuning aligns the observation-to-skill mapping with the distribution of successful online trajectories; then, with the observation encoder frozen, Skills Policy Optimization computes a clipped importance ratio for each complete skill in a lightweight QueST-style policy.
AI.result: CSO raises overall LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%, improves performance on RoboTwin2.0, and achieves 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks, with further validation against FAST, discrete BEAST and fixed-buffer IQL.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage post-training strategy makes reinforcement learning refinement of discrete-skill policies stable and efficient when the encoder is frozen during policy optimization.

title: Towards Reliable, Scalable, and Value-Aligned Generative Recommendation for Large-Scale Advertising
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) reformulates item retrieval as autoregressive generation of discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs), offering a unified paradigm for personalized recommendation. GR4AD, as an industrial generative recommendation framework, has greatly improved advertising revenue while enabling efficient real-time serving in this http URL, continued deployment has exposed three limitations: deterministic SID assignment remains sensitive to semantic boundaries; conventional backbone scaling provides diminishing revenue gains under strict serving constraints; and sequence-level value optimization provides limited credit assignment to intermediate SID decisions, causing likelihood-based beam search to prematurely prune potentially high-value candidates. We present GR4AD-X, which addresses these limitations through reliable SID construction, serving-efficient capacity scaling, and unified value alignment. Specifically, GR4AD-X improves SID reliability through Multi-Path assignment. It expands model capacity along multiple complementary dimensions rather than relying solely on wider or deeper backbones, achieving a better effectiveness-efficiency trade-off under strict serving constraints. Finally, Unified Value-Guided Generation and Discrimination (UniVGD) aligns generation with commercial value through prefix-level reward optimization, value-guided beam pruning, and discriminative reranking within a unified model. Large-scale online A/B tests on the Kuaishou advertising platform demonstrate that GR4AD-X achieves a cumulative revenue improvement of 3.07% over the deployed GR4AD baseline while satisfying strict latency and throughput constraints.

AI.tldr: GR4AD-X improves an industrial generative recommendation framework for advertising through reliable semantic identifier (SID) construction, serving-efficient capacity scaling and unified value alignment. Large-scale online A/B tests on the Kuaishou advertising platform show a 3.07% cumulative revenue improvement over the deployed GR4AD baseline.
AI.motivation: The deployed GR4AD framework has three limitations: deterministic SID assignment is sensitive to semantic boundaries, conventional backbone scaling gives diminishing revenue gains under strict serving constraints, and sequence-level value optimization gives limited credit assignment, so beam search prunes high-value candidates.
AI.method: Multi-Path assignment improves SID reliability, capacity is expanded along multiple complementary dimensions rather than only by widening or deepening the backbone, and UniVGD aligns generation with commercial value through prefix-level reward optimization, value-guided beam pruning and discriminative reranking within one model.
AI.result: Large-scale online A/B tests on the Kuaishou advertising platform show a cumulative revenue improvement of 3.07% over the deployed GR4AD baseline while satisfying strict latency and throughput constraints.
AI.conclusion: Addressing SID reliability, scaling efficiency and value credit assignment together yields measurable revenue gains in a production advertising system under strict serving constraints.

title: Revisiting Temporal Link Prediction through Structural Proximity
summary: Existing temporal link prediction methods typically rely on learned temporal representations to capture evolving interaction patterns. In this paper, we show that a classical structural proximity measure can match or outperform these methods without training or learned temporal sequence modeling. We revisit Personalized PageRank (PPR) on historical interaction graphs, using simple sliding-window retention or exponential time decay. Surprisingly, across 14 datasets, Time-decay PPR ranks first on nine and second on four among the compared methods, including datasets with few repeated edges. To understand this result, we examine the historical paths connecting source nodes to previously unseen destinations. We find that such paths contain useful predictive information, and that PPR outperforms a strong neural baseline on queries where historical structure clearly distinguishes the true destination from negative candidates. These results show that strong performance on current benchmarks does not necessarily require complex temporal models. More fundamentally, they raise the question of how much predictive value learned temporal modeling adds beyond historical structural proximity. Our findings motivate reassessing progress in temporal link prediction with strong classical baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that Personalized PageRank on historical interaction graphs, with sliding-window retention or exponential time decay, matches or outperforms learned temporal link prediction methods without any training. Time-decay PPR ranks first on nine of 14 datasets and second on four among the compared methods.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal link prediction methods rely on learned temporal representations, and it is unclear how much predictive value such temporal modelling adds beyond historical structural proximity.
AI.method: The authors revisit Personalized PageRank on historical interaction graphs using simple sliding-window retention or exponential time decay, and examine the historical paths that connect source nodes to previously unseen destinations.
AI.result: Across 14 datasets, Time-decay PPR ranks first on nine and second on four among the compared methods, including datasets with few repeated edges. PPR outperforms a strong neural baseline on queries where historical structure clearly distinguishes the true destination from negative candidates.
AI.conclusion: Strong benchmark performance does not require complex temporal models, and progress in temporal link prediction should be reassessed against strong classical structural baselines.

title: Does Chain-of-Thought Reliance Follow a Scaling Law?Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training
comment: 15 pages,5 figures, code and data in this https URL
summary: Monitoring a model's chain of thought (CoT) is useful for safety only if the final answer depends on the written steps. Prior measurements use natural tasks where true reasoning is unknown. We measure it against an exact ground truth on a synthetic box-swap task where every intermediate state is known. We replace one step inside a model's own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the answer follows the edit. We evaluate 25 open-weight models--Qwen3 (0.6B-14B, base and post-trained), Gemma 3 (1B-12B), Llama 3 (1B-8B), and 8 OLMo 2 checkpoints--on 7,200 items each. We find five results: (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates. In Qwen3, answer reliance rises from 16-18% at 0.6B to 97-100% at 14B; a logistic in log N fits well (R^2 = 0.89), and Gemma 3 and Llama 3 follow this trend. (2) Capability is the main driver. Across all models, reliance and step accuracy correlate at r = 0.99; equally capable models are equally reliant, regardless of family. (3) Size still matters at matched correctness. On problems solved correctly before the edit, reliance increases with size among capable models (rho = 0.80, p = 0.002). (4) Post-training does not change reliance. Base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward; a large gap at 1.7B matches a large capability gap. (5) No model up to 14B solves the task internally. Without written steps, every capable model is at chance once a problem has four or more swaps. OLMo 2 checkpoints never become capable, making the training-token axis a limitation. On tasks requiring step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, supporting CoT monitoring in this regime.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how much final answers depend on the written chain of thought, using an exact synthetic box-swap task in which every intermediate state is known. Reliance rises with model size and saturates, mainly driven by capability, and post-training does not change it from 4B upward.
AI.motivation: Monitoring a model's chain of thought is useful for safety only if the final answer depends on the written steps, but prior measurements used natural tasks where the true reasoning is unknown.
AI.method: The authors replace one step inside a model's own chain with a wrong but valid state and check whether the answer follows the edit, evaluating 25 open-weight models on 7,200 items each, including base and post-trained Qwen3, Gemma 3, Llama 3 and OLMo 2 checkpoints.
AI.result: In Qwen3, answer reliance rises from 16-18% at 0.6B to 97-100% at 14B, a logistic in log N fits with R^2 = 0.89, and reliance correlates with step accuracy at r = 0.99. At matched correctness reliance still increases with size (rho = 0.80, p = 0.002), base and post-trained Qwen3 differ by at most 0.03 from 4B upward, and no model up to 14B solves the task without written steps once a problem has four or more swaps.
AI.conclusion: On tasks requiring step-by-step computation, scale makes the chain of thought more load-bearing, supporting CoT monitoring in this regime, while the OLMo 2 checkpoints show that the training-token axis remains a limitation.

title: Capacity of the Hopfield-Hebbian dynamics with correlated patterns
summary: Allowing for small fraction of errors in retrieved stored binary patterns, Hopfield-Hebbian neural network (NN) associative memory dynamics [14] achieves linearly scaled capacity. The famous proportionality constant $\alpha_c\approx 0.14$ is obtained in a large dimensional scenario as the ratio of the number of reliably stored patterns $m$ and the patterns' length $n$ under the assumption that uniformly randomly chosen binary patterns are \emph{independent} among themselves. While such an idealized scenario is now well understood, more practical scenarios with correlated/noisy datasets remaining challenging even for classical statistical mechanics replica approaches. We consider precisely such practical settings where each \emph{archetype} pattern is replaced with $M$ correlated \emph{examples} with parameter $r$ governing the quality of correlation. We develop a powerful Random Duality Theory (RDT) based framework to analyze correlated data and already on the first level of RDT lifting obtain capacity characterizations that remarkably well match behavior exhibited through simulated dynamics. Moreover, characterizations explicitly feature correlation parameters $M$ and $r$, which allows to precisely determine their effects on phase-transitioning behavior of the underlying dynamics. Our results are also a well-fitting complement to the existing literature. Namely, to circumvent challenging statistical mechanics analyses, an alternative combination of spectral and replica methods is considered in [4]. We confirm that [4]'s elegant spectral characterizations are excellent approximations in the low correlated regime. At the same time, we also close the gap in the regimes with higher correlation levels where spectral methods deviate from the practical dynamics performance.

AI.tldr: The paper analyses the capacity of Hopfield-Hebbian associative memory when each stored archetype is replaced by M correlated examples governed by a correlation parameter r, using a Random Duality Theory (RDT) framework. Its first-level characterizations closely match simulated dynamics and explicitly capture the effects of M and r.
AI.motivation: The classical capacity constant of about 0.14 assumes independent random patterns, and practical correlated datasets remain challenging even for classical statistical mechanics replica approaches.
AI.method: Each archetype is replaced by M correlated examples with correlation parameter r, and capacity is characterized with a Random Duality Theory framework at the first level of lifting, then compared with a combined spectral and replica analysis from the literature.
AI.result: The first-level RDT capacity characterizations closely match simulated dynamics and feature M and r explicitly. The spectral characterizations of prior work are good approximations in the low-correlation regime, and the paper closes the gap at higher correlation levels where spectral methods deviate from the practical dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The framework precisely determines how correlation shapes the phase-transition behaviour of the dynamics, complementing existing literature on correlated patterns.

title: Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Networks for QC-MDPC Error Decoding in McEliece Cryptosystems
summary: As the advent of large-scale quantum computing threatens classical encryption, Quasi-Cyclic Moderate Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes have emerged as a foundational element of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). However, decoding these relatively dense codes using classical Belief Propagation algorithms often leads to failures caused by short graph cycles that stall the decoder. In cryptographic applications, these failures are severe security vulnerabilities that leak secret key information. To address this, this paper proposes a Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Network (R-BGNN) as proof of concept. By integrating Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) into the message-passing framework and employing a multi-topology curriculum training strategy, the R-BGNN actively learns to break limit-cycle oscillations. Evaluated across 20 unseen matrix topologies, the proposed architecture significantly outperforms classical Bit-Flipping and Min-Sum baselines, reducing the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) by 63.7\% at moderate noise levels ($t=10$) while converging in fewer iterations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Recurrent Bipartite Graph Neural Network (R-BGNN) with GRU-based message passing that learns to break limit-cycle oscillations when decoding QC-MDPC codes for McEliece cryptosystems. It reduces the decoding failure rate by 63.7% at moderate noise (t=10) relative to classical Bit-Flipping and Min-Sum baselines.
AI.motivation: Belief propagation decoding of QC-MDPC codes fails because short graph cycles stall the decoder, and in cryptographic applications these failures are severe vulnerabilities that leak secret key information.
AI.method: The R-BGNN integrates Gated Recurrent Units into the message-passing framework and uses a multi-topology curriculum training strategy.
AI.result: Evaluated on 20 unseen matrix topologies, the architecture significantly outperforms Bit-Flipping and Min-Sum baselines, reducing the decoding failure rate by 63.7% at moderate noise (t=10) while converging in fewer iterations.
AI.conclusion: Learned recurrent message passing is presented as a proof-of-concept route to more reliable QC-MDPC decoding for post-quantum McEliece systems.

title: Beyond Reachability: When Edit Order Preserves Couplings in Graph Flow Matching
summary: Shortest-path optimality does not guarantee that a memoryless graph generator preserves a prescribed source-target correspondence. We study whether reordering legal shortest edits can retain this correspondence without changing the pairing, mandatory edits, or sampling budget. Under a common Poisson clock, we establish an exact criterion for endpoint coupling recoverability: the source-blind Markov projection attains the unavoidable clock-error floor if and only if routes to distinct targets do not share graph states. Routes to the same target may merge without sacrificing endpoint fidelity. This characterization leads to an exact finite-state routing formulation and a legality-preserving scheduling procedure with recovery certificates. A marker-free construction demonstrates how shared edge structure can retain source distinctions, while a capacity-constrained family exhibits a sharp separation in paired error between edit orders with identical marginal error. Finally, a target-conditioned aliasing bound connects structural route design to the terminal fidelity of a learned graph-only generator. These results characterize when legal edit ordering can preserve a prescribed coupling under fixed operational costs.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an exact criterion for when a memoryless graph generator can preserve a prescribed source-target coupling under reordering of legal shortest edits. The endpoint coupling is recoverable if and only if routes to distinct targets do not share graph states.
AI.motivation: Shortest-path optimality alone does not guarantee that a memoryless graph generator preserves a prescribed source-target correspondence, so the question is whether edit order can retain it without changing the pairing, mandatory edits or sampling budget.
AI.method: Under a common Poisson clock, the authors derive the recoverability criterion, formulate an exact finite-state routing problem, and propose a legality-preserving scheduling procedure with recovery certificates, supported by a marker-free construction and a capacity-constrained family.
AI.result: The source-blind Markov projection attains the unavoidable clock-error floor exactly when routes to distinct targets do not share graph states, while routes to the same target may merge without losing endpoint fidelity. A capacity-constrained family shows a sharp separation in paired error between edit orders with identical marginal error, and a target-conditioned aliasing bound links route design to the terminal fidelity of a learned graph-only generator.
AI.conclusion: Legal edit ordering can preserve a prescribed coupling under fixed operational costs, and structural route design governs the terminal fidelity of learned graph-only generators.

title: Accelerating Nonlinear MPC by Behavior Cloning with Separated Timescales: Application to Nuclear Reactor Load-Following
summary: Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost. Beyond the quantitative results, Jacobian-based sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting controller relies on a sparse and less redundant set of latent features, each attributable to a single group of physical variables, and aligned with the physical timescale decomposition of the system.

AI.tldr: SRLBC is a behaviour cloning architecture with separate embeddings for slow, fast and exogenous variables, and it outperforms shared-embedding baselines on a pressurized water reactor load-following benchmark. Embedded in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC, the controller runs about 6.8 times faster than NMPC with at least 99.8% feasibility.
AI.motivation: Behaviour cloning of expert controllers for multiscale systems is challenging because variables evolving at widely separated timescales create nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to represent, degrading closed-loop generalization.
AI.method: SRLBC uses structured representation learning with separate embeddings for slow state variables, fast stiff state variables and predictable exogenous inputs, and the standalone policies are embedded in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC that calls the optimizer only when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe.
AI.result: On 500 long-horizon roll-outs across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings outperform shared baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction, and standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost about 15 times lower on average. The safety-augmented controllers are 6.8 times faster than NMPC with feasibility of at least 99.8%, and under distribution shift SRLBC keeps feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost.
AI.conclusion: Respecting the timescale separation of the system yields sparser latent features, each tied to one group of physical variables, and a controller that approaches NMPC performance at much lower computational cost.

title: Value Probes: Learned Value Functions for Beam-Search Red Teaming
summary: Automated red-team auditing of language models is an important way to evaluate safety-relevant behaviors. These audits implicitly search a tree of possible conversation pathways: at each turn an auditor model decides which conversation to continue, and an LLM judge scores the dialogue. We emphasize that this auditing procedure is a Markov decision process, where states are the conversation history, actions are candidate responses, and rewards are judge scores for the target behavior. By adopting this perspective, we introduce two major improvements to auditing. First, we propose adopting beam search for the audit rather than relying on the auditor alone. We then interpret the problem of finding states that are likely to lead to problematic behavior as value estimation. Surprisingly, we show that this value function can be estimated by linear probing from the target model's activations to predict discounted future rewards - a method we term "Value Probes." By using Value Probes as a heuristic in our beam-search audit, we are able to substantially improve auditing success. Across 18 target behaviors and 3 scales of models, our approach raises peak audit scores by roughly 50% compared to (token-matched) standard auditing approaches. Furthermore, we show that Value Probes can be fit using off-policy data from smaller models. We also ablate individual components, and show that our method offers a comparably-performant and more efficient alternative to more expensive language model follow-ups. We hope these methods will improve language model auditing and lead to safer models.

AI.tldr: The paper frames automated red-team auditing of language models as a Markov decision process and proposes beam search guided by Value Probes, which are linear probes on the target model's activations that predict discounted future judge rewards. The method raises peak audit scores by roughly 50% over token-matched standard auditing.
AI.motivation: Standard automated red-team audits rely on the auditor model alone to choose which conversation to continue, which makes the search for states that lead to problematic behaviour inefficient.
AI.method: The audit is cast as an MDP whose states are conversation histories, actions are candidate responses and rewards are LLM judge scores; the authors apply beam search and estimate the value function by linear probing of the target model's activations to predict discounted future rewards.
AI.result: Across 18 target behaviours and 3 model scales, the approach raises peak audit scores by roughly 50% compared with token-matched standard auditing. Value Probes can be fit from off-policy data of smaller models and offer a more efficient alternative to more expensive language model follow-ups.
AI.conclusion: Estimating value with probes offers an efficient search heuristic for language model auditing, which the authors hope will lead to safer models.

title: A goodness of fit approach to select the optimal visit sequence for nonparametric data synthesis
summary: Synthetic data are a promising way to maintain privacy while disseminating research data, thereby enabling compliance with the open science principles. Popular methods for generating synthetic data include sequential synthesis, where each variable is generated conditionally on the preceding ones in a given order. This order, also called the visit sequence of the synthesizer, is known to affect the quality of synthetic data. This raises the question of the criteria that should guide its choice. In this work, we present a novel method to perform such selection based on a goodness of fit criterion, and show that it outperforms alternative structure-based methods, both in terms of synthesis quality and time complexity. The proposed method also has the advantage of being applicable to any type of data and any class of conditional distribution models.

AI.tldr: Proposes a goodness-of-fit criterion for choosing the visit sequence in sequential synthesis of nonparametric synthetic data, and shows it outperforms structure-based ordering methods in synthesis quality and time complexity.
AI.motivation: The visit sequence affects the quality of sequentially synthesized data, but the criteria that should guide its choice are unclear and existing approaches are structure-based.
AI.method: A novel selection method based on a goodness-of-fit criterion, applicable to any type of data and any class of conditional distribution models.
AI.result: The method outperforms alternative structure-based methods in both synthesis quality and time complexity.
AI.conclusion: Goodness-of-fit offers a general, model-agnostic criterion for visit sequence selection, supporting privacy-preserving data dissemination consistent with open science.

title: Structural Pattern Mining in Inka Khipus: A KFG Re-Analysis
summary: This paper reports a methodological pivot from the Open Khipu Repository to the Khipu Field Guide (KFG) database, prompted by stalled progress on the OKR, and a full re-analysis of the resulting 650-khipu sample. Three findings recur across every analysis attempted. First, khipu size confounds nearly every derived structural count, explaining 42-70% of its variance; all subsequent models control for it. Second, the two-letter name prefix (AS, UR, HP, QU, JC, MM, KH) identifies the original cataloger, not a site or period, which turns documentation completeness into a second confound that must be modeled explicitly. Controlling for both, khipus cataloged by Hugo Pereyra's Proyecto Quipu (HP) show significantly fewer Ascher sum-relation types than Gary Urton's (UR) khipus (p = 0.044), while the Ascher-cataloged (AS) khipus are too collinear with their own near-total lack of side/direction documentation to assess (VIF = 5.0). Third, generic structural clustering (UMAP+HDBSCAN) does not separate the pooled 650-khipu sample from two independent null models (permutation and Gaussian), corroborating an independent conclusion already reached by the KFG itself; the same test restricted to a single cataloger (UR) proved not reproducible across runtime environments and is reported here as a methodological caveat rather than evidence of structure. A targeted replication of the KFG's own S/Z-knot spatial-block heuristic for calendar/astronomical khipus recovers 8 of 10 published candidates and proposes 34 additional ones under the same criterion.

AI.tldr: Re-analyzes a 650-khipu sample from the Khipu Field Guide database with explicit controls for khipu size and cataloger, and finds little evidence of structure beyond null models, apart from a few specific associations.
AI.motivation: Progress on the Open Khipu Repository stalled, and structural analyses of khipus are confounded by khipu size and by differences in documentation across catalogers.
AI.method: Switches to the KFG database; models khipu size and the two-letter cataloger prefix explicitly; tests cataloger effects on Ascher sum-relation types; compares UMAP+HDBSCAN clustering against permutation and Gaussian null models; replicates the KFG S/Z-knot spatial-block heuristic for calendar and astronomical khipus.
AI.result: Khipu size explains 42-70% of the variance in derived structural counts. Controlling for size and cataloger, HP khipus show significantly fewer Ascher sum-relation types than UR khipus (p = 0.044), while AS khipus cannot be assessed (VIF = 5.0). Clustering does not separate the pooled sample from either null model, and a single-cataloger result was not reproducible across runtime environments. The S/Z-knot replication recovers 8 of 10 published candidates and proposes 34 additional ones.
AI.conclusion: Structural claims about khipus must control for size and documentation provenance, and generic clustering gives no evidence of structure, which corroborates the KFG's own conclusion.

title: Robust Active Learning for More Efficient and Reliable Paths to Optimal Design
comment: Global Conference on Naval Architecture and Ocean Engineering (G-NAOE) 2026
summary: Simulation-driven design optimization requires active learning strategies that efficiently combine models with different computational costs and levels of fidelity. We introduce Multifidelity Cost-Aware Screening (MF-CAS), which enables the joint selection of sampling location and fidelity using a surrogate that provides decomposed uncertainty intervals rather than a complete predictive probability distribution. MF-CAS exploits the contribution of each fidelity to the high-fidelity uncertainty together with its computational cost to determine whether a candidate should first be evaluated at low fidelity or directly progressed towards high fidelity. The method is assessed on the constrained 14-dimensional hydrodynamic optimization of the DTMB 5415 hull under a deliberately limited computational budget. MF-CAS achieves an approximately 9.0% resistance reduction, compared with 6.7% for the best baseline optimisation method, demonstrating that incorporating fidelity-resolved uncertainty directly into the joint location-fidelity decision can substantially improve multifidelity active learning efficiency.

AI.tldr: Introduces MF-CAS, a multifidelity active learning method that jointly selects sampling location and fidelity using fidelity-resolved uncertainty and computational cost, and applies it to hull design optimization.
AI.motivation: Simulation-driven design needs active learning that efficiently combines models of different computational cost and fidelity under a limited budget.
AI.method: Joint selection of location and fidelity using a surrogate that provides decomposed uncertainty intervals; each candidate is either evaluated at low fidelity or progressed toward high fidelity, based on each fidelity's contribution to high-fidelity uncertainty and its cost.
AI.result: On the constrained 14-dimensional hydrodynamic optimization of the DTMB 5415 hull under a limited budget, MF-CAS achieves about 9.0% resistance reduction, compared with 6.7% for the best baseline.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating fidelity-resolved uncertainty into the joint location-fidelity decision can substantially improve the efficiency of multifidelity active learning.

title: Explore Where It Matters: Targeted Exploration for Efficient Rover Adaptation
summary: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. Project website: this https URL

AI.tldr: TERRA is an online adaptation framework that combines reward-weighted model adaptation with a learned loss predictor to direct exploration, letting a rover on deformable terrain adapt within a few trials in simulation and on hardware.
AI.motivation: Planetary rovers face sim-to-real gaps on deformable terrain, and deployment leaves little room for trial-and-error.
AI.method: Adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss, and trains a loss predictor to estimate where performance-relevant errors are likely, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC.
AI.result: In simulation, about 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, coordinated active-suspension locomotion is recovered on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials.
AI.conclusion: Targeted, reward-relevant exploration lets rovers correct model errors from few real-world trials, a practical route to closing sim-to-real gaps in planetary mobility.

title: Weaken to Strengthen: Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Reasoning Models
comment: Work in progress. Code is released at this https URL
summary: Self-distillation offers a way to improve reasoning models when a suitable external teacher is unavailable. However, common approaches rely on privileged information to construct a stronger self-teacher, limiting their use when only unlabeled prompts are available. In this paper, we introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), which instead constructs a weaker counterpart of the original model and uses the contrast between the two as a training signal without requiring privileged information. We explore two ways to construct the weaker model: low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning. We evaluate WISD across diverse architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks. Across these benchmarks, quantization and pruning improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points, respectively, achieving state-of-the-art performance even without privileged information. Notably, pruning raises Qwen3.5-4B's accuracy from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. Quantization raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B's accuracy from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5% on the same benchmarks, respectively. These results establish WISD as a novel and effective self-distillation framework for large reasoning models.

AI.tldr: WISD performs on-policy self-distillation without privileged information by contrasting the original model with a deliberately weakened version made by quantization or pruning, and improves reasoning accuracy on math and coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Self-distillation normally requires privileged information to build a stronger self-teacher, which is unavailable when only unlabeled prompts exist.
AI.method: Constructs a weaker counterpart of the original model via low-bit quantization or magnitude pruning, and uses the contrast between the two as the training signal.
AI.result: Across diverse architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks, quantization and pruning improve average accuracy over the original models by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points. Pruning raises Qwen3.5-4B from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6; quantization raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 68.5% to 74.6% and from 61.8% to 69.5% on the same two benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Weakening the model yields a usable self-distillation signal, establishing WISD as an effective framework for large reasoning models without privileged information.

title: Deogen: Automatic Benchmark Generation for Reasoning over Policies
summary: Language models are increasingly being deployed in regulated settings, where a model must apply given rules to the facts of a situation to determine a verdict. Benchmarking this capability, known as deontic reasoning, remains a costly and manual process, with existing datasets largely hand-crafted. In this paper, we present DeoGen, a scalable, automatic, and parametrizable benchmark generator for deontic reasoning. By autoformalizing policy rules to first-order logic, we can construct decision trees that capture possible outcome trajectories. Each path down a tree becomes a benchmark entry, with each tree producing combinatorially many entries relative to tree depth. Paths ending at a leaf entail a verdict, while non-leaf paths measure a model's ability to abstain when presented with insufficient information. Evaluations show frontier models return the correct verdict 89-92% of the time. Notably, performance degrades (22-40% correct) on entries without sufficient information to claim a verdict, even with explicit instructions to abstain in such cases. In all, DeoGen presents an automatic, scalable, and parametric method for generating deontic reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: DeoGen automatically generates parametrizable deontic reasoning benchmarks by autoformalizing policy rules into first-order logic and enumerating decision-tree paths, and finds that frontier models struggle to abstain when information is insufficient.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks testing whether models apply rules to facts in regulated settings are costly to build and largely hand-crafted.
AI.method: Autoformalizes policy rules to first-order logic and constructs decision trees of possible outcome trajectories; each path becomes a benchmark entry, with leaves giving verdicts and non-leaf paths testing abstention.
AI.result: Frontier models return the correct verdict 89-92% of the time, but only 22-40% of entries without sufficient information are answered correctly, even with explicit instructions to abstain.
AI.conclusion: The generator offers a scalable, automatic, and parametric method for deontic reasoning benchmarks, and it exposes a clear weakness in abstention under incomplete information.

title: Geometry Matters in Packed 3D Attention
summary: Packing a 3D volume into a token sequence is not merely long-sequence modeling. Once the volume is packed, sequence order no longer encodes the geometry of the sample---so a positional mechanism indexed by sequence position can learn the memory layout rather than the object. This is a general failure mode for attention over packed geometric data. We introduce PACK3D, a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry. PACK3D keeps local neighborhood attention exact, compresses only distant context into contiguous 3D block summaries, and indexes every query-key interaction with axial RoPE on true token-grid coordinates rather than packed positions. Because the rotation is applied before a block is summarized, the query-to-summary logit remains a weighted sum of query-relative 3D displacements; compressed global context therefore stays spatially interpretable after packing, instead of collapsing to anonymous pooled content. We measure the failure mode directly. On a controlled synthetic task---train on one packing, change only the memory order of the tokens, hold the physical labeling rule fixed---learned positional embeddings and packed-sequence RoPE solve the training layout perfectly yet collapse under Morton, block-contiguous, and random repacking, while axial grid-coordinate RoPE stays exact throughout. The same coordinate system carries to real data: on Allen WTC-11 hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over a parameter-matched 3D U-Net on the 15-structure joint task and over a matched learned-position local-global baseline, with controls isolating the coordinate system, not encoder capacity, as the source of the gain. A fused Triton implementation matches windowed-attention latency at 65k tokens while supplying the long-range context windowing cannot---so the operator is not only correct but trainable at scale.

AI.tldr: PACK3D is a local-global attention operator that applies axial RoPE on true 3D grid coordinates rather than packed sequence positions, so attention over packed volumes stays geometrically meaningful.
AI.motivation: When a 3D volume is packed into a token sequence, sequence position no longer encodes geometry, so positional mechanisms can learn the memory layout rather than the object.
AI.method: Keeps local neighborhood attention exact and compresses distant context into contiguous 3D block summaries; every query-key interaction is indexed with axial RoPE on grid coordinates, applied before a block is summarized; a fused Triton implementation is provided.
AI.result: On a controlled synthetic task, learned positional embeddings and packed-sequence RoPE collapse under repacking, while grid-coordinate RoPE stays exact. On Allen WTC-11 hiPSC microscopy, PACK3D improves over a parameter-matched 3D U-Net on the 15-structure joint task and over a matched learned-position local-global baseline, and its fused kernel matches windowed-attention latency at 65k tokens.
AI.conclusion: The coordinate system, rather than encoder capacity, accounts for the gain, and the operator is both correct and trainable at scale for packed geometric data.

title: Streaming Speech Recognition on a Microcontroller: a 65.7M-Parameter Transducer in 2 and 4 Bits on the ESP32-P4
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures, 11 tables, 1 algorithm. Code: this https URL ; weights: this https URL
summary: We run Kroko, a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer for English, on the ESP32-P4, a microcontroller with two 400 MHz RISC-V cores, a 128-bit SIMD extension (PIE) and 32 MB of PSRAM, but no neural accelerator. Without any training, the encoder's 290 matrices are stored with 2 or 4 bits per weight in Hadamard-rotated groups: the width of each matrix comes from its measured sensitivity, and each matrix is first corrected toward the original model's output, then rounded with GPTQ and a search over the group norms. The released 71 MB of int8 weights become a 26.65 MB file. Activations are int16 between the matrix products and int8 into them. A C engine with hand-written PIE kernels processes each 1.28 s chunk of audio in 0.90 s on both cores, beam search included, and its PC build computes the same bits as the chip, so accuracy is measured on whole test sets. LibriSpeech WER is 4.34% on test-clean and 10.26% on test-other, against 3.94% and 9.17% for the released model; on FLEURS and Common Voice the gap grows to 2.3 and 1.1 points. A GPU simulator shows that the integer arithmetic costs nothing and that the whole gap comes from the weights, and an ablation on all of test-clean shows that GPTQ does most of the work. We also report the port's speed history, from 51.3 s to 0.62 s of encoder time per chunk, each design step measured again in one build, an attempt to reach 16 MB that stopped at 19.63 MB, and what did not work. We did not measure energy. The inference engine, the firmware and the 2/4-bit weights are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Runs a 65.7M-parameter streaming English transducer (Kroko) on an ESP32-P4 microcontroller with 2- and 4-bit weights, processing each 1.28 s audio chunk in 0.90 s with a modest word error rate gap to the released model.
AI.motivation: Streaming speech recognition on a microcontroller without a neural accelerator requires very compact weight storage and fast integer inference.
AI.method: Quantizes the encoder matrices to 2 or 4 bits in Hadamard-rotated groups, with widths set by measured sensitivity; each matrix is first corrected toward the original output and then rounded with GPTQ and a search over group norms. Activations are int16 and int8, and a C engine with hand-written PIE SIMD kernels runs on both cores.
AI.result: The 71 MB int8 weights become a 26.65 MB file. LibriSpeech WER is 4.34% on test-clean and 10.26% on test-other, versus 3.94% and 9.17% for the released model; the gap grows to 2.3 and 1.1 points on FLEURS and Common Voice. An attempt to reach 16 MB stopped at 19.63 MB. Energy was not measured.
AI.conclusion: Without any training, low-bit weight quantization makes streaming ASR feasible on a microcontroller, the accuracy gap comes entirely from the weights, and GPTQ does most of the work.

title: Trustworthy Distributed Machine Learning in Cloud-Edge-IoT Systems: A Heterogeneity-Aware Survey of Security, Privacy, and Robustness
summary: Distributed machine learning (DML), including conventional distributed training and federated learning (FL), enables collaborative model development across cloud-edge-IoT systems without fully centralizing raw data. However, distributing data, computation, updates, and orchestration increases the attack surface and introduces coupled challenges across privacy, robustness, reliability, fairness, and governance. This survey presents a security-centered, heterogeneity-aware roadmap for trustworthy DML, with FL treated as a prominent high-risk case. We first characterize the assets, adversaries, trust assumptions, and coordination patterns that define DML/FL security boundaries. We then analyze how statistical, system, and trust heterogeneity, including non-IID data, resource asymmetry, intermittent participation, and cross-silo/cross-device trust differences, affect convergence, fairness, attack detectability, and defense reliability. Next, we synthesize attack-defense interactions across poisoning, backdoors, Byzantine manipulation, privacy leakage, model extraction, network/orchestration attacks, Sybil behavior, and strategic participation. We further compare layered defenses, including robust aggregation, drift-aware optimization, differential privacy, secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, trusted execution environments, watermarking, provenance, authenticated communication, and monitoring. Finally, we discuss deployment, evaluation, governance, and open research guidelines, emphasizing reproducible, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) partitions, attack-aware benchmarks, privacy budgets, attack success rate, client-level disparity, latency, communication, memory, energy/carbon overhead, and auditable lifecycle artifacts.

AI.tldr: A survey giving a security-centered, heterogeneity-aware roadmap for trustworthy distributed machine learning in cloud-edge-IoT systems, with federated learning treated as the main high-risk case.
AI.motivation: Distributing data, computation, updates and orchestration widens the attack surface and couples privacy, robustness, reliability, fairness and governance challenges, while heterogeneity complicates defenses.
AI.method: Characterizes assets, adversaries and trust assumptions; analyzes how statistical, system and trust heterogeneity affect convergence, fairness and defense reliability; synthesizes attack-defense interactions; and compares layered defenses such as robust aggregation, differential privacy, secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, MPC, TEEs, watermarking and monitoring.
AI.result: As a survey it reports no new experiments; it instead identifies evaluation practices such as reproducible non-IID partitions, attack-aware benchmarks, privacy budgets, attack success rate, client-level disparity, and latency, communication, memory and energy/carbon overhead.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy DML requires security, privacy and heterogeneity to be addressed jointly, with reproducible evaluation and auditable lifecycle artifacts as open research guidelines.

title: Pinpointing Pivot Points: The DECIDE Framework for Data Analysis Decision Importances
summary: Human judgment calls made throughout the data science life cycle can change the conclusions drawn from data. Independent analysts often make different choices when given the same data, leading to often unacceptable variations in results and contributing to the ongoing reproducibility crisis across scientific disciplines. The rapid adoption of agentic tools threatens to amplify this crisis. Several approaches have been developed to address this variation by following the same strategy: repeating an analysis under different combinations of analytical decisions and inspecting the distribution of outcomes. Examples include multiverse analysis, specification curve analysis, and vibration of effects. More broadly, the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework assesses how documented judgment calls across the data science life cycle affect conclusions, with predictability serving as a reality-check that a model captures signal. Each of these approaches results in a "multiverse" object. While the distribution of outcomes reflects the overall variability of conclusions, estimating the influence of each individual decision requires additional tools. A common heuristic is to train a model to predict the outcome from these decisions and treat its coefficients or feature importances as proxies for each decision's influence. Although this strategy may work in certain cases, it assumes the model is correctly specified and accurately predicts the outcome, which we show is not always the case. In this work, we introduce DECIDE, a model-free framework that quantifies each decision's importance from the actual outcomes across the plausible decision space, avoiding issues of predictability by design. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DECIDE by applying it to real-world multiverse analyses. We further provide what is, to our knowledge, the first formal definition of the multiverse.

AI.tldr: DECIDE is a model-free framework that quantifies the importance of each analytical decision directly from outcomes across a multiverse of analyses, and the paper gives the first formal definition of the multiverse.
AI.motivation: Analytical judgment calls change conclusions, and the common heuristic of reading coefficients or feature importances from a predictive model fails when the model is misspecified or does not predict the outcome accurately.
AI.method: Repeats the analysis over plausible combinations of decisions and estimates each decision's influence from the actual outcomes, without fitting a predictive model.
AI.result: The framework is applied to real-world multiverse analyses; the abstract reports no specific numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Decision importance can be estimated without a model, avoiding predictability issues by design, and the paper provides a formal definition of the multiverse.

title: UnEZ: A Fully Unsupervised Self-Templating Neural Network for Redshift and Line Strength Estimation
summary: As spectroscopic surveys grow, estimating galaxy properties such as metallicity, star formation rate, and redshift becomes computationally cumbersome. Methods of estimating such properties rely on template spectra or curated redshift catalogs, which fail to represent the diversity of objects seen in large-scale surveys. We present UnEZ, a fully unsupervised, physics-informed machine learning model that can predict spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths with no prior redshift or line strength labels. An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes/widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a unique template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve, and spectral model. UnEZ was tested on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 18 due to its large dataset and thoroughly vetted redshift catalog which serves as an independent benchmark. Despite the lack of templates, line strength labels, or redshift labels, UnEZ's performance competes with modern redshift estimation algorithms. At SNR > 10, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 0.459% and a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of $1.237 \times 10^{-4}$. At SNR > 3, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 3.89% and an NMAD of $1.471 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how UnEZ's line strength and redshift predictions can be utilized for various purposes such as constructing template spectra required in traditional redshift estimation algorithms. UnEZ illustrates how a fully unsupervised neural network can allow redshift, among other galaxy properties, to emerge naturally from the spectra themselves, providing a template-free, label-free approach that scales to the demands of future surveys.

AI.tldr: UnEZ is a fully unsupervised, physics-informed network that estimates spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths from SDSS spectra without template or label supervision, with performance said to compete with modern redshift estimation algorithms.
AI.motivation: Estimating galaxy properties with template spectra or curated redshift catalogs does not represent the diversity of objects in large-scale surveys.
AI.method: An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes and widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve and spectral model.
AI.result: On SDSS DR18, at SNR > 10 the outlier fraction is 0.459% and NMAD is 1.237 x 10^-4; at SNR > 3 the outlier fraction is 3.89% and NMAD is 1.471 x 10^-4.
AI.conclusion: Redshift and line strengths can emerge from the spectra themselves without labels, giving a template-free approach that scales to future surveys and can supply templates for traditional algorithms.

title: Learning to Reason from Reference Samples Alone: Reinforced Adversarial Learning for Modern LLM Post-Training
comment: 31 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables, including references and appendices
summary: In many settings where LLM post-training is desirable, high-quality answers are recognizable but difficult to score with explicit rewards. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited to tasks where an explicit correctness signal is available. Prior adversarial approaches to training reasoning LLMs either complement verifiable rewards with co-trained critics or require reference reasoning traces. We ask whether a co-trained LLM judge can turn reference answers alone into the sole reward for on-policy post-training of reasoning LLMs. We call this method Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL). We first validate RAL on three verifiable tasks (integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation), using the verifiers only for evaluation. With sufficiently capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR. We then apply RAL to scientific abstract generation in two settings. In the first setting, RAL guides the generator to produce abstracts in the scientific domain of the reference abstracts, even though the prompt leaves that domain unspecified. In the second setting, we generate abstracts for U.S. National Institutes of Health grant proposals conditioned on the grant title. Human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find our generations harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines. These results suggest a path toward post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains, where increasingly capable judges infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers.

AI.tldr: Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL) post-trains reasoning LLMs using only reference answers, with a co-trained LLM judge as the sole reward; it matches RLVR on verifiable tasks and yields scientific abstracts that are harder to distinguish from real ones.
AI.motivation: RLVR requires an explicit correctness signal, and prior adversarial approaches need co-trained critics or reference reasoning traces.
AI.method: A co-trained LLM judge scores on-policy outputs against reference answers alone, and that score is the only reward for post-training.
AI.result: With capable judges and enough training, RAL matches direct RLVR on integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis and SMILES-to-formula translation. On scientific abstract generation, both human scientists and an ensemble of LLM judges find RAL outputs harder to distinguish from real abstracts than those of frontier-LLM baselines, including for NIH grant proposals conditioned on the grant title.
AI.conclusion: Increasingly capable judges can infer hard-to-specify reward functions from example answers, suggesting a path to post-training reasoning models in scientific and other high-value domains.

title: Where You Inject Matters: The Trust Region Effect in LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents are increasingly adopted in long-horizon tasks and interact with diverse external environments. Despite their growing capabilities, these agents remain vulnerable to real-world attacks such as indirect prompt injections, which manipulate agents through malicious instructions embedded in external environments. While existing risk assessment work has primarily focused on the injection content, the effect of where an injection appears has not been systematically characterized. Studying injection placement requires agents to operate over longer-horizon tasks and interact with diverse environmental surfaces. Thus, we build three agentic testbeds spanning tool use, coding, and daily workflow domains with diverse injection surfaces. Holding the injection content fixed, we find that agent susceptibility varies across injection placements. We refer to this phenomenon as the trust region effect: agents implicitly assign different levels of trust to different regions of their environments. For example, an agent powered by GPT-5.4 follows an unsafe injection instruction placed in a repository documentation file (i.e., a README or TODO file) 2.6 times more often on average than the same instruction placed in a code or data file. Building upon this observation, we develop learning-based attackers that generate injection content and select better injection placements. Our approach demonstrates that both where an injection is placed and what content it contains can affect the strength of indirect prompt injection attacks. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first systematic characterization for the effectiveness of different injection placements, spanning both coarse-grained environmental surfaces and fine-grained positions. The uneven trust that agents implicitly place across their environments provides important insights for future attack and defense design.

AI.tldr: Shows that where an indirect prompt injection is placed in an agent's environment changes attack success, a trust region effect, and builds learning-based attackers that select better placements.
AI.motivation: Prior risk assessment focused on injection content, while the effect of injection location on long-horizon LLM agents had not been systematically characterized.
AI.method: Builds three agentic testbeds spanning tool use, coding and daily workflow with diverse injection surfaces; holds content fixed while varying placement; and develops learning-based attackers that generate injection content and choose placements.
AI.result: With GPT-5.4, an unsafe instruction placed in a repository README or TODO file is followed 2.6 times more often on average than the same instruction placed in a code or data file.
AI.conclusion: Agents implicitly assign different levels of trust to different regions of their environment, so both placement and content affect attack strength, with implications for attack and defense design.

title: TrussTutor-Bench: Benchmarking large language models on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection in statics
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly become a default source of help for students in science and engineering courses. In foundational engineering mechanics courses such as statics, students routinely use these tools to check answers, work through partial solutions, and ask for explanations. Effective tutoring in this setting requires more than a correct final answer. A model must also confirm correct work when a student doubts it, and identify errors in flawed work. Existing benchmarks evaluate LLMs primarily on final-answer accuracy, so it is unclear whether models that can solve mechanics problems also have the other technical capabilities that tutoring depends on. Here we introduce TrussTutor-Bench, a benchmark of 200 verified two-dimensional truss problems paired with automatically generated student solutions, and use it to evaluate thirteen LLMs on solution accuracy, sycophancy, and error detection. Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%. Every model detected nearly all injected errors in synthetic flawed student work (90.4% to 100%), so error detection did not distinguish models under these clean conditions. Sycophancy did. When a student insisted that correct work was wrong, models rejected correct solutions to problems they had themselves solved in 1.6% to 50.0% of cases. These results show that performance varies widely across models: the leading models solve, check, and defend student work nearly perfectly, while others are far less reliable, particularly when a student doubts correct work. TrussTutor-Bench provides a verified, extensible standard for determining which models are technically reliable enough to put in front of students. Follow-up work must now focus on teaching rather than technical capability, drawing on learning science to determine whether LLM help leads students to understand the material or simply to reach the right answer.

AI.tldr: TrussTutor-Bench evaluates 13 LLMs on 200 verified two-dimensional truss statics problems for solution accuracy, sycophancy and error detection, and finds that sycophancy, not error detection, separates the models.
AI.motivation: Final-answer benchmarks do not show whether a model can also confirm correct student work and identify errors, which effective tutoring requires.
AI.method: Uses 200 verified two-dimensional truss problems paired with automatically generated student solutions, including injected errors in flawed work and cases where the student insists correct work is wrong.
AI.result: Baseline accuracy ranged from 64.5% to 97.0%. Error detection ranged from 90.4% to 100%. When a student insisted that correct work was wrong, models rejected correct solutions in 1.6% to 50.0% of cases.
AI.conclusion: The leading models solve, check and defend student work nearly perfectly while others are far less reliable, particularly when a student doubts correct work; follow-up work must focus on whether tutoring leads to understanding.

title: Memorization Capacity of Invariant Convolutional Neural Nets
summary: Neural networks are powerful memorizers which are often able to interpolate their training data even when the labels have been randomized. While there exists an extensive literature on the memorization capacity of fully connected networks, in practice more specific architectures with problem-dependent properties are preferred, such as convolutional networks for image classification. In this paper we consider convolutional networks which are invariant with respect to a given arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations, which may include translations, reflections, and/or rotations of images and invariances of higher order tensors. We prove upper bounds on the size of an invariant convolutional neural network with threshold activations that is required to interpolate a given dataset with two classes. Our bounds are formulated in terms of a complexity measure that takes the invariant structure into account and is instance-specific, i.e., it is related to the mutual arrangement of the classes in the given dataset and their geometric properties rather than the number of samples. Our proof is constructive: for given input data, instances of an interpolating network can be computed via a randomized algorithm with high probability. In numerical experiments we investigate the practical effectiveness of this algorithm.

AI.tldr: Proves upper bounds on the size of invariant convolutional networks with threshold activations needed to interpolate a two-class dataset, using an instance-specific complexity measure and a constructive randomized algorithm.
AI.motivation: Memorization capacity is well studied for fully connected networks, but not for the convolutional architectures preferred in practice when the data has a finite orthogonal symmetry group.
AI.method: Considers convolutional networks invariant to an arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations; the bounds are stated in terms of a complexity measure that depends on the arrangement and geometry of the classes rather than the number of samples; the proof is constructive via a randomized algorithm.
AI.result: The randomized algorithm computes interpolating networks with high probability, and numerical experiments investigate its practical effectiveness; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Invariant convolutional networks can interpolate a dataset with a size governed by its instance-specific geometry rather than its sample count.

title: Optimization-based lane-changing trajectory planning in mixed traffic with embedded input convex neural networks
summary: Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers are highly challenging vehicle interactions, with substantial implications for traffic safety and efficiency. Developing effective LC strategies for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic is complicated by the uncertainty associated with surrounding-vehicle behavior and the computational burden of embedding realistic prediction models within optimization schemes. To capture these complex interactions while retaining tractability, this study proposes a data-driven optimization framework that embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a Bézier-curve-based trajectory planner. Specifically, the safety cost during the LC process is quantified via a surrogate composed of an input convex recurrent neural network (ICRNN) encoding the planned trajectory, a fully input convex neural network (FICNN) embedding the LC duration, and a partially input convex neural network (PICNN) decoder fusing them with historical traffic states; separately, another FICNN surrogate approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost as a function of the LC duration. Both surrogates are embedded via linear programming (LP) formulations, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP) approaches for NN-embedded optimization. We further theoretically establish their exactness at optimality and extend the framework to problems with additional analytical objective terms and multiple surrogates. Experiments on a hybrid dataset combining real-world and simulated trajectories demonstrate that the proposed method achieves surrogate accuracy competitive with unconstrained baselines while substantially improving optimization efficiency over conventional MIPs. Closed-loop simulations further show that the proposed planners markedly reduce the weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes a lane-changing planner that embeds input convex neural network surrogates for safety and comfort in linear-programming form within a Bezier-curve trajectory optimization, avoiding binary variables and reducing planning cost.
AI.motivation: Realistic prediction models of surrounding vehicles are hard to embed in optimization, and conventional mixed-integer programming for neural-network-embedded problems is computationally expensive.
AI.method: The safety cost is a surrogate combining an ICRNN that encodes the planned trajectory, a FICNN that embeds the lane-change duration, and a PICNN decoder that fuses them with historical traffic states; a separate FICNN approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost. Both surrogates are embedded via LP formulations.
AI.result: On a hybrid dataset of real-world and simulated trajectories, the surrogates are as accurate as unconstrained baselines and the optimization is substantially faster than conventional MIP. Closed-loop simulations show markedly lower weighted planning cost and consistently better performance than baselines.
AI.conclusion: Input convex surrogates allow learned safety and comfort models to be embedded exactly and tractably in lane-change planning for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic.

title: Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code
comment: 55 pages, 5 figures, plus 120 pages of supplementary material
summary: Large language models pass most functional-correctness benchmarks, but passing tests says little about whether their code is readable, efficient or secure. Many techniques claim to improve these qualities, yet their evidence is scattered, usually covers one quality dimension and is rarely compared at an equal compute budget. We contribute a systematic review and a controlled re-evaluation. A systematic literature review of 628 primary studies (July 2021 to October 2026), with disclosed, author-reviewed LLM assistance, organizes the techniques by stage, signal source and quality target. Most studies measure only the dimension they target, gains often come with unchanged or unreported correctness, single automated quality signals are gamed, and compute, variance and contamination are rarely reported. A controlled re-evaluation runs ten techniques on four models at matched budgets on correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security benchmarks, extends it to thirteen current models and repository-level tasks, and compares 66 highlighted techniques head-to-head on Gemma 4 31B. At one call, quality prompting raises analyzer issue counts and leaves complexity and judge scores almost unchanged. At matched budgets, best-of-n sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval on measures the ranker does not optimize, while an analyzer feedback loop and fine-tuning beat it only on analyzer issue counts. Large correctness losses on HumanEval+, a likely contaminated benchmark near its ceiling, do not appear on contests held after the models' training cutoffs. In the head-to-head, 1 of 66 techniques beats best-of-n on its primary target beyond the 95% interval, a rate consistent with chance. Gains should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline and on measures independent of the technique's own signal.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 628 studies and a controlled re-evaluation find that many techniques for improving LLM-generated code quality gain little beyond a budget-matched best-of-n sampling baseline.
AI.motivation: Evidence for techniques that improve readability, efficiency and security of LLM-generated code is scattered, usually covers one quality dimension, and is rarely compared at equal compute.
AI.method: A systematic literature review of 628 primary studies organized by stage, signal source and quality target, followed by a controlled re-evaluation of ten techniques on four models at matched budgets, extended to thirteen models and repository-level tasks, with 66 highlighted techniques compared head-to-head on Gemma 4 31B.
AI.result: At one call, quality prompting raises analyzer issue counts but leaves complexity and judge scores almost unchanged. At matched budgets, best-of-n with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval on measures the ranker does not optimize. Only 1 of 66 techniques beats best-of-n on its primary target beyond the 95% interval.
AI.conclusion: Gains should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline and on measures independent of the technique's own signal, since single automated quality signals are easily gamed.

title: Self-Supervised Doppler-Guided RF Odometry
