Subtrajectory Balance relates potential differences to forward and backward transition densities across subtrajectories of different lengths. The model is jointly trained with answer supervision, CoT supervision, and representation distillation. Experiments on arithmetic and deductive reasoning show increasing solution coverage with larger sampling budgets across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, as well as improvements on several structural OOD benchmarks. Trajectory analyses reveal progressive divergence among sampled latent paths and higher mean relative potentials for correct trajectories across arithmetic benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SubLAT learns stochastic exploration in continuous latent reasoning by coupling a relative answer potential with Subtrajectory Balance, increasing solution coverage with larger sampling budgets on arithmetic and deductive reasoning.
AI.motivation: Continuous latent reasoning can sample multiple paths, but stochasticity alone does not ensure exploration toward useful reasoning paths.
AI.method: SubLAT couples a relative answer potential, which compares the answer support of sampled states against replacement states with a correctness signal at the terminal state, with Subtrajectory Balance, which relates potential differences to forward and backward transition densities across subtrajectories. Training jointly uses answer supervision, CoT supervision and representation distillation.
AI.result: On arithmetic and deductive reasoning, solution coverage increases with sampling budget on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, with improvements on several structural OOD benchmarks. Trajectory analyses show progressive divergence among sampled latent paths and higher mean relative potentials for correct trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Potential-guided subtrajectory balance is an effective way to direct stochastic latent exploration toward correct reasoning.

title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets
summary: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.

AI.tldr: An energy accounting of speculative decoding in production SGLang serving on H100 and H200 GPUs finds that its energy saving depends on acceptance, shrinks as batch size grows, and becomes a loss at large batches with block drafters.
AI.motivation: Facility power limits LLM serving, and speculative decoding reduces weight reads per token, but the energy it saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted, which varies by target model, drafter, text and language.
AI.method: Speculative decoding is measured under production conditions (SGLang with CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64, across 5 corpora, for several target models and drafting schemes.
AI.result: Every drafter accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and fewer on Romansh than on English. On dense models verification dominates energy cost. The saving shrinks as batch grows; at large batches block drafters push verification into the compute-bound regime, where speculation becomes a loss, and low acceptance raises energy per token. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation, and speculation adds savings only when acceptance is high, leaving little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.
AI.conclusion: Speculative decoding saves energy only at high acceptance and moderate batch sizes, and batching alone is often the stronger lever for energy per token.

title: Rimuru: Unified Memory Management for Modern LLM Serving via Elastic Expert Offloading
summary: Modern LLMs strain device memory through large model weights and attention states, particularly in resource-constrained scenarios. Existing systems separately provision memory for model weights and attention states, imposing fixed fixed boundaries that cannot adapt to the changing memory demands of workloads. Under heavy workloads, insufficient state capacity limits request concurrency and reduces throughput; under light workloads, idle memory in one region cannot be reallocated to another, wasting device memory. Meanwhile, modern LLM architectures introduce heterogeneous tensors with diverse layouts and lifetimes, further complicating memory management. These problems motivate unified memory management for heterogeneous tensors. However, a shared pool alone does not make memory directly reusable across tensors with different allocation granularities and execution layouts. This paper presents Rimuru, a modern LLM serving system that unifies memory management through elastic expert offloading. Rimuru establishes a shared page pool to enables elastic memory sharing across heterogeneous tensors. To accommodate different allocation granularities, Rimuru introduces memory views that allow each tensor type to interpret the shared memory space using its own page size and page table. Furthermore, Rimuru combines huge-page alignment with a multi-level page allocator that splits and merges pages, enabling cross-type capacity reuse. A page-table-aware fused MoE kernel directly accesses non-contiguous expert weights, avoiding copy overhead. Building on these mechanisms, Rimuru employs a workload-aware adjuster that dynamically reallocates pages across tensor types according to runtime demands. Implemented on top of vLLM, Rimuru remains compatible with modern LLMs. Evaluations show that Rimuru achieves up to 19.03x baseline throughput and reduces TTFT by 98.1% on average.

AI.tldr: Rimuru is an LLM serving system built on vLLM that unifies memory for model weights and attention states through a shared page pool and elastic expert offloading, reporting up to 19.03x baseline throughput and a 98.1% average reduction in TTFT.
AI.motivation: Separately provisioned memory for weights and attention states is fixed, so heavy workloads limit concurrency while light workloads waste idle memory, and heterogeneous tensors with different layouts and lifetimes complicate reuse.
AI.method: A shared page pool with memory views lets each tensor type interpret the pool with its own page size and page table; huge-page alignment with a multi-level allocator splits and merges pages; a page-table-aware fused MoE kernel reads non-contiguous expert weights without copying; and a workload-aware adjuster reallocates pages across tensor types according to runtime demand.
AI.result: Implemented on top of vLLM and compatible with modern LLMs, Rimuru achieves up to 19.03x baseline throughput and reduces TTFT by 98.1% on average.
AI.conclusion: Unified, workload-adaptive memory management with elastic expert offloading substantially improves LLM serving throughput and latency under memory constraints.

title: Multistep and Multivariate Time Series Explainability with GradientSHAP: A Wind Power Case Study
summary: As the effects of climate change become increasingly apparent, the demand for renewable energy sources such as wind power continues to grow. However, renewables' variable and intermittent nature presents significant challenges in their integration into energy grids. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool to address these issues. Still, its adoption in the energy sector has been hindered by the opacity of many AI models, which often function as black boxes. This paper introduces a carefully adapted GradientSHAP approach to provide interpretability for multivariate, multistep wind power forecasting -- a largely underexplored area. This capability is critical for day-ahead grid management and, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to apply GradientSHAP in the context of wind power forecasting. To address the inherent dimensionality, we developed novel visualizations that deliver both local and global explanations, uncovering intricate relationships between environmental factors, site-specific conditions, and temporal dynamics. While GradientSHAP is not an out-of-the-box solution, our findings demonstrate that, with thoughtful handling of SHAP values and domain expertise, it can offer valuable insights into model behaviour, supporting more informed and trustworthy decision-making. Nevertheless, its complexity poses challenges for practical implementation. Future research should focus on streamlining these interpretability methods to make them more actionable for routine deployment in critical energy applications.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts GradientSHAP to explain multivariate, multistep wind power forecasts, introducing visualizations that give local and global explanations, and reports that the method is informative but complex to apply in practice.
AI.motivation: Wind forecasting models are often opaque black boxes, and interpretability for multivariate, multistep wind power forecasting is largely unexplored, although it is critical for day-ahead grid management.
AI.method: A carefully adapted GradientSHAP approach with new visualizations that address the high dimensionality and reveal relationships among environmental factors, site-specific conditions and temporal dynamics.
AI.result: The abstract reports qualitative findings only: with careful handling of SHAP values and domain expertise, the method yields insights into model behaviour. No numerical results are stated.
AI.conclusion: GradientSHAP can support more informed and trustworthy forecasting decisions, but its complexity means the methods need streamlining before routine deployment.

title: Deep Learning Based Behavioral Drift Modeling for Continuous Biometric Authentication
summary: This research proposes a two-level keystroke dynamics authentication system that provides defense-in-depth security through continuous behavioral drift monitoring. Level 1 employs fixed-text password authentication using Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) with contrastive learning and population-based training (PBT), achieving 3.77% EER for high-security login verification. Upon successful authentication, Level 2 continuously monitors user typing during natural free-text sessions using a 4-Model Deep Learning Ensemble. If suspicious behavioral drift is detected during monitoring, the system re-authenticates the user by returning to Level 1, providing a feedback loop against session hijacking and behavioral anomalies. The system explicitly models long-term behavioral drift through the fixed-text component's PBT mechanism, which adapts to temporal variations in password typing patterns. This research leverages free-text (Buffalo dataset) and fixed-text (GREYC dataset) keystroke dynamics datasets, extracting temporal and spatial features including hold times, up-down latencies, down-down intervals, and trigram patterns. The final system achieves 96%+ accuracy for fixed-text authentication (3.77% EER) and 83.53% True Acceptance Rate (TAR) at 5% False Acceptance Rate (FAR) for free-text continuous authentication (10.05% EER), demonstrating superior performance and strong resistance to impostor attacks through continuous behavioral monitoring.

AI.tldr: A two-level keystroke dynamics authentication system uses a TCN with contrastive learning and population-based training for fixed-text login, and a four-model ensemble for continuous free-text monitoring that re-authenticates the user when behavioral drift is detected.
AI.motivation: Single-point authentication does not protect against session hijacking or behavioral anomalies, and long-term drift in typing patterns must be modeled.
AI.method: Level 1 performs fixed-text password authentication with a TCN, contrastive learning and population-based training (PBT). Level 2 monitors free-text typing with a 4-model deep learning ensemble, and suspicious drift returns the user to Level 1. Features include hold times, up-down latencies, down-down intervals and trigram patterns, drawn from the Buffalo and GREYC datasets.
AI.result: Fixed-text authentication reaches 3.77% EER and over 96% accuracy; free-text continuous authentication reaches 83.53% TAR at 5% FAR, with 10.05% EER.
AI.conclusion: Two-level keystroke authentication with drift-aware re-authentication offers defense-in-depth against session hijacking and impostor attacks.

title: Continuous-Action World Models: Learning Cross-Embodiment Spatiotemporal Dynamics Priors
summary: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.

AI.tldr: CoAWM learns a shared latent function space for robot actions that transfers across embodiments and control frequencies, pretrained on heterogeneous trajectories and connected to a world-model backbone that predicts end-effector actions at any query time.
AI.motivation: Robot experience is hard to transfer across embodiments and execution frequencies, and pretraining has been limited by heterogeneous trajectory data.
AI.method: In stage one, function pretraining maps trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. In stage two, this space is connected to a world-model backbone conditioned on observations, language instructions and robot state to predict a latent action function, which a single decoder evaluates at any query time.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results.
AI.conclusion: Separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.

title: OCCAMS: A Multi-Task Learning-Based Investigation of the CMB Power Spectra
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, plus appendices. Comments are welcome
summary: How many latent variables are needed to fit the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature and polarisation power spectra when a neural network is given no cosmological model, and to what extent do they map onto the standard cosmological parameters? We use multi-task learning with variational autoencoders trained on CLASS-generated spectra (TT, TE, EE) over $2\le\ell\le2500$. No cosmological model is built into the network, and the number of latent variables, $L$, is varied over $L=5$, $6$ and $7$. Their fits are compared to the Planck 2018 data using $\hat{\chi}^2$, AIC, BIC and Bayesian evidence. Their correspondence with cosmological parameters is measured with normalised mutual information post-training. The loss weights are set within a single training run by uncertainty weighting, with the weight of the disentanglement term either fixed (semi-automated, SA) or learned (completely automated, CA). The reconstruction loss is split over multipole ranges in three configurations that separate the roles of temperature and polarisation and of the low- and high-$\ell$ ranges. In four of the six combinations of configuration and strategy, the fit improves from $L=5$ to $L=6$ and not beyond, and $L=6$ is the best, or close to the best, in five of the six cases. So, six latent variables are needed, as many as the free parameters of the standard, model-dependent approach. SA gives clearer disentanglement, while CA needs no a priori choice of the disentanglement weight and has the higher evidence at $L=5$ and $6$: the two strategies are points on a trade-off between interpretability and fit to the data. Notably, the latent variables for $\tau$ and $A_s$ share almost no information in any model, consistent with large-scale polarisation separating the two, as in standard analyses. A deep-learning approach can thus give a compact, data-driven parametrisation of the CMB spectra.

AI.tldr: Multi-task variational autoencoders trained on CLASS-generated CMB spectra, with no built-in cosmology, find that six latent variables are needed to fit the TT, TE and EE spectra, and that these latents correspond only partly to standard cosmological parameters.
AI.motivation: The question is how many latent variables a neural network needs to fit CMB temperature and polarisation power spectra without a cosmological model, and how far those latents map onto standard cosmological parameters.
AI.method: Multi-task learning with variational autoencoders on TT, TE and EE spectra over multipoles 2 to 2500, with latent sizes of 5, 6 and 7, compared with Planck 2018 data using reduced chi-squared, AIC, BIC and Bayesian evidence. Loss weights are set by uncertainty weighting, with the disentanglement weight either fixed (semi-automated, SA) or learned (completely automated, CA). Correspondence with parameters is measured by normalised mutual information.
AI.result: In four of the six configuration-strategy combinations the fit improves from L=5 to L=6 and not beyond, and L=6 is best or close to best in five of six cases. SA gives clearer disentanglement, while CA needs no a priori choice of weight and has higher evidence at L=5 and 6. The latent variables for tau and A_s share almost no information in any model.
AI.conclusion: About six latent variables suffice, matching the free parameters of the standard model-dependent approach, giving a compact, data-driven parametrisation of the CMB spectra.

title: Adaptive search with path-constrained mobile sensors using multi-arm bandits
summary: We study a constrained sequential decision problem for detecting regions of interest from noisy online measurements collected by a team of energy-constrained mobile sensors. The sensor motion is restricted to a precomputed set of feasible paths that satisfy mobility constraints, limited available energy by requiring return to charging stations, and avoidance of known obstacles. We cast the resulting active path selection as a multi-armed bandit problem and propose an iterative search algorithm that adaptively assigns paths using confidence bounds computed from the collected data. We also propose a graph-based method to construct low-cardinality path covers under the team's constraints. We establish finite-time and anytime probabilistic correctness guarantees for the proposed algorithm, derive non-asymptotic upper bounds on the times required to detect all regions of interest and to label all nodes, and show that these bounds match algorithm-independent lower bounds up to constant factors for a broad class of problem instances. Using numerical simulations, we illustrate the behavior of the proposed approach and the effect of path redundancy and team size on search performance.

AI.tldr: A bandit-based search algorithm adaptively assigns feasible paths to energy-constrained mobile sensors to detect regions of interest, with finite-time correctness guarantees and detection and labelling time bounds that match algorithm-independent lower bounds up to constant factors for a broad class of instances.
AI.motivation: Energy-constrained sensor teams must find regions of interest from noisy online measurements while respecting mobility limits, charging requirements and known obstacles.
AI.method: Active path selection is cast as a multi-armed bandit over a precomputed set of feasible paths, using confidence bounds computed from collected data. A graph-based method constructs low-cardinality path covers under the team's constraints.
AI.result: The algorithm has finite-time and anytime probabilistic correctness guarantees, and its detection and labelling time bounds match lower bounds up to constant factors for a broad class of problems. Simulations illustrate how path redundancy and team size affect search performance.
AI.conclusion: Bandit-based path selection over low-cardinality path covers is a principled, near-optimal approach to constrained sensor search.

title: Soil Moisture Estimation in Precision Agriculture: A Knowledge Distillation Approach
summary: Accurate soil moisture estimation is critical for precision agriculture, influencing irrigation, fertilization, and harvesting strategies. Traditional methods primarily rely on meteorological and soil property data, while recent approaches incorporate visual modalities such as aerial and geospatial imagery. However, these high-resolution images are expensive and computationally demanding to analyze. In this work, we propose Soil Moisture Distillation (SMD), a Knowledge Distillation (KD)-based multimodal learning framework that leverages unimodal teachers to enhance multimodal soil moisture estimation. SMD surpasses not only traditional multimodal fusion techniques, including MIS-ME, but also outperforms unimodal models, demonstrating the benefits of guided unimodal knowledge transfer. Additionally, we conduct a comparative analysis of soil patches and crop images, showing that crop images provide superior visual cues, leading to improved prediction accuracy. SMD achieves a 2% improvement in MAPE for soil patches and 1.2% for crops over state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of leveraging both meteorological and visual data through knowledge distillation for enhanced soil moisture forecasting.

AI.tldr: Soil Moisture Distillation (SMD) uses knowledge distillation from unimodal teachers to improve multimodal soil moisture estimation, with a 2% MAPE improvement on soil patches and 1.2% on crops over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: High-resolution aerial and geospatial imagery is expensive and computationally demanding, while meteorological and soil property data alone may limit prediction accuracy in precision agriculture.
AI.method: A knowledge distillation framework in which unimodal teachers guide a multimodal model, compared against multimodal fusion techniques including MIS-ME and unimodal models. The authors also compare soil patch imagery with crop imagery as visual inputs.
AI.result: SMD surpasses traditional multimodal fusion, including MIS-ME, and also outperforms unimodal models, with a 2% MAPE improvement for soil patches and 1.2% for crops over state-of-the-art baselines; crop images provide superior visual cues.
AI.conclusion: Guided unimodal knowledge transfer through distillation makes multimodal soil moisture forecasting more accurate, and crop imagery is the more informative visual modality.

title: Learning developmental dynamics from lineage context
summary: A central goal of biology is to predict the dynamics of multicellular systems. Lineage context (the states of a cell's sisters, cousins, etc.) could inform these predictions, but how best to leverage it remains unclear. Here we introduce lineage inpainting, a generative modeling approach that uses lineage context with tree-structured transformers and stochastic interpolants to model cell state dynamics across lineage trees. Applied to a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, it recovers dynamics not resolved by gene expression alone, including multiple transcriptional convergence events where distinct lineages are drawn to a common state. Despite being fit on unperturbed development, lineage inpainting can generate hypotheses about perturbation responses by simulating counterfactuals. These simulations agree in many cases with observed developmental phenotypes, including a single-cell measurement of the Tbx5 knockout response. Our results show that lineage information provides a rich source of context for learning multicellular dynamics.

AI.tldr: Introduces lineage inpainting, a generative model that uses lineage context with tree-structured transformers and stochastic interpolants to predict cell state dynamics across lineage trees. It recovers dynamics that gene expression alone does not resolve and generates counterfactual perturbation hypotheses that partly agree with observed phenotypes.
AI.motivation: Predicting multicellular dynamics is a central goal of biology, and lineage context (the states of a cell's sisters, cousins and so on) could inform these predictions, but how best to use it remained unclear.
AI.method: Lineage inpainting combines tree-structured transformers with stochastic interpolants, is fit on unperturbed development in a lineage-traced transcriptional atlas of mouse embryogenesis, and is used to simulate counterfactuals.
AI.result: The model recovers dynamics not resolved by gene expression alone, including several transcriptional convergence events where distinct lineages move to a common state; its simulated counterfactuals agree in many cases with observed developmental phenotypes, including a single-cell measurement of the Tbx5 knockout response.
AI.conclusion: Lineage information is a rich source of context for learning multicellular dynamics.

title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures with Methods. We will release the fully supplementary information in the second update soon
summary: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce \emph{neural triage decoding}, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the \texttt{Triage} decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

AI.tldr: Proposes neural triage decoding, a neural decoder for ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes that adaptively allocates computation based on syndrome consistency. It reaches accuracy comparable to near-optimal algorithmic decoders while cutting decoding latency by roughly one to two orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: High-rate qLDPC codes reduce physical qubit overhead, but existing decoders are either accurate yet slow, and neural decoders had not been demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes.
AI.method: A local neural message-passing network predicts corrections quickly, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections for the remaining shots; the design is inspired by an analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder.
AI.result: The Triage decoder decodes ultra-high-rate codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, with accuracy comparable to near-optimal algorithmic decoders; the analysis reveals a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor, and the neural decoders are shown to be robust to mismatched error priors.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive neural decoding is a promising route to fast, accurate and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

title: Discovering Interpretable Acoustic Features in Autoregressive Voice-Cloning TTS Models
summary: Voice-cloning TTS models synthesize an unseen speaker's voice from brief speech prompts, but it remains unclear which acoustic properties they represent and use. We introduce a feature-based interpretability framework for autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models, analyzing features from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), PCA, and random directions via sparse probing, steering, and quantitative auto-interpretability. We focus on Qwen3-TTS and extend probing and steering to $5$ additional models to test generalization across architectures. These models encode concepts like pitch, energy, noise, and accent, but sparse prediction and steering are effective only for some concepts. Strong probing does not always translate to steering or vice-versa. SAEs are useful for sparse probing of human-labelled concepts and novel-concept discovery, while PCA is competitive for dense probing and steering. Auto-interpretability finds $684$ automatically validated SAE features in Qwen3-TTS covering speaker clusters, speaking style, and recording conditions beyond known concepts. Overall, we perform a comprehensive interpretability study of autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models.

AI.tldr: Presents a feature-based interpretability framework for autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models, using sparse autoencoder features, PCA and random directions. The models encode concepts such as pitch, energy, noise and accent, but sparse prediction and steering work only for some concepts.
AI.motivation: It is unclear which acoustic properties voice-cloning TTS models represent and use when synthesizing an unseen speaker's voice from brief speech prompts.
AI.method: Sparse probing, steering and quantitative auto-interpretability are applied to SAE features, PCA components and random directions, focusing on Qwen3-TTS and extending probing and steering to five additional models to test generalization across architectures.
AI.result: Strong probing does not always translate into steering, or the reverse; SAEs are useful for sparse probing of human-labelled concepts and novel-concept discovery, while PCA is competitive for dense probing and steering. Auto-interpretability finds 684 automatically validated SAE features in Qwen3-TTS covering speaker clusters, speaking style and recording conditions.
AI.conclusion: The paper gives a comprehensive interpretability study of autoregressive voice-cloning TTS models, showing that what can be probed and what can be steered are different questions.

title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
summary: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

AI.tldr: Introduces MSafeTemp, a 60-language safety alignment corpus built with a template-based augmentation pipeline that fills culturally localized entities into translated safe templates. It shows that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety and that template-augmented training improves safety beyond English.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment for LLMs focuses heavily on English, which damages low-resource language performance, and existing open training datasets are often small or do not follow region-localized harmful topics.
AI.method: Safe templates are extracted from harmful prompts, translated, and their slots filled with culturally authentic harmful and benign entities, producing large-scale multilingual refusal and benign corpora.
AI.result: For several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, and culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses; augmenting safety training data with templates yields higher diversity and quality of alignment and improved safety performance beyond English.
AI.conclusion: The released corpus and pipeline are intended to support safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
comment: 84 pages, 19 figures, 3 tables. Code: this https URL (tags neopic-arxiv-v1, neopic-arxiv-v1-nufft); analysis scripts: this https URL
summary: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an $O(N_p)$ method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.

AI.tldr: Introduces NEOPIC, a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of particles to learn the field solve in particle-based kinetic plasma simulations, evaluated at particle positions without grid deposition. It works as a plug-and-play field solver and reproduces standard electrostatic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Grid-based neural operators require deposition onto a mesh, which aliases the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations.
AI.method: The operator is evaluated at particle positions on the empirical measure, requiring no mesh or tree; it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes, and the particle noise in training data acts as an implicit regularizer.
AI.result: The discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any particle number, and the error analysis separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors. The method is O(Np) with constants set by the architecture alone. Experiments on 2D and 3D electrostatic benchmarks (Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap) confirm the theory, and a single model trained on several mini-apps captures all of them and stays stable up to twice the training time window.
AI.conclusion: The results point towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.

title: Homebrewed SLMs: Autoregressive and Masked Diffusion Language Models Built at Home for Portuguese
comment: 34 pages, 14 figures, 13 tables. Code and notebooks: this https URL
summary: Building a language model of one's own no longer requires a data centre. This tutorial trains one from scratch, tokenizer included, on one consumer GPU, and shows how to tell whether it is good for the tasks of a specialist domain. It proposes no new method. It releases a tested Python package and two notebooks in Brazilian Portuguese with autoregressive and masked diffusion generation on one network, a preregistered comparison protocol, legal tasks built from text alone with a Kneser-Ney floor and public yardsticks, reference numbers for models of 11 to 12M parameters, and a catalogue of defects that only measurement revealed. On Brazilian prose and federal laws, at minutes per run, the autoregressive mode peaks at 64 epochs over the same text and then memorises it, while masked diffusion improves up to 256. At their best points on test, the diffusion bound exceeds the autoregressive likelihood by 0.06 bits per byte, within the preregistered minimum effect. On held-out laws and on acts published after training, the model ties a 6-gram floor in likelihood on the same windows, and it loses to the floor at continuing those acts. It beats the floor at detecting tampered text, and fills cross-references more often than the floor and public models of 160M and 630M parameters, only in decrees, a genre absent from training, where those scorers stay near or below chance, and in filling the blank only when each group weighs the same, since per item it ties the 630M model. On laws, the public models, trained with about 5x10^2 to 10^5 times its compute, lead in tampered text and continuation. The blind human reading is preregistered and not part of this version.

AI.tldr: A tutorial that trains small Brazilian Portuguese language models (11 to 12M parameters) from scratch, tokenizer included, on one consumer GPU, with autoregressive and masked diffusion generation in one network. It proposes no new method and reports measurements on Brazilian prose and federal laws.
AI.motivation: Building and assessing a specialist-domain language model is usually assumed to require a data centre; the paper aims to show that it can be done on consumer hardware with reliable measurement for Portuguese legal tasks.
AI.method: The paper releases a tested Python package and two notebooks, a preregistered comparison protocol, legal tasks built from text alone with a Kneser-Ney floor and public yardsticks, and reference numbers for the small models.
AI.result: The autoregressive mode peaks at 64 epochs and then memorises the text, while masked diffusion improves up to 256 epochs; at their best test points the diffusion bound exceeds the autoregressive likelihood by 0.06 bits per byte, within the preregistered minimum effect. On held-out laws the model ties a 6-gram floor in likelihood but loses to it at continuing acts; it beats the floor at detecting tampered text and fills cross-references more often than the floor and the public 160M and 630M models, but only in decrees, a genre absent from training, where those scorers stay near or below chance. Public models trained with far more compute lead in tampered text and continuation on laws.
AI.conclusion: The paper documents a reproducible small-model pipeline and a catalogue of defects that only measurement revealed; the blind human reading is preregistered and not part of this version.

title: TRACER, a time-to-event EHR foundation model for disease detection across health systems
summary: Foundation models trained on longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can predict clinical diagnoses years in the future, making them a potential tool for disease screening. We developed TRACER (Temporal Risk Assessment with Clinical EHR Representations), a decoder-based foundation model pretrained on data from over 4.5 million patients from four health systems, and evaluated it on 16 incident diseases at 1-, 2-, and 5-year horizons in more than 2 million patients from two health systems excluded from model development. In contrast to typical evaluations that focus on global metrics (e.g., AUROC), we measured performance at the low false-positive rates that are realistic for screening. We found that TRACER retained its discrimination in external health systems, and at 95% specificity, the patients it flagged were up to eight times more likely to be diagnosed within a year than unselected patients. Evaluating at this operating point also revealed what global metrics alone did not: detection and false-alert burden varied across diseases and health systems, even when discrimination appeared stable. Our results illustrate the potential of foundation models for screening and underscore the need for evaluation in health systems excluded from development to assess disease detection and false-alert burden at levels appropriate for intended clinical use.}

AI.tldr: TRACER is a decoder-based EHR foundation model pretrained on over 4.5 million patients that predicts 16 incident diseases at 1-, 2- and 5-year horizons. At 95% specificity, the patients it flagged were up to eight times more likely to be diagnosed within a year than unselected patients.
AI.motivation: Foundation models on longitudinal EHRs could support disease screening, but global metrics such as AUROC do not reflect performance at the low false-positive rates that screening requires, and validation in external health systems is often missing.
AI.method: The model is pretrained on data from four health systems and evaluated on more than 2 million patients from two health systems excluded from development, with performance measured at low false-positive rates.
AI.result: Discrimination is retained in external health systems, and at 95% specificity the flagged patients were up to eight times more likely to be diagnosed within a year; detection and false-alert burden varied across diseases and health systems even when discrimination appeared stable.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models show potential for screening, and evaluation in health systems excluded from development is needed to assess detection and false-alert burden at levels appropriate for clinical use.

title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
summary: Realistic, fast robotics simulations could enable large-scale training of embodied AI models that transfer to the real world. However, despite decades of progress, available simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena. The core bottleneck is that creating better simulations requires significant expert effort and therefore does not scale. To address this, we introduce Gym-Anything for Robotics, a framework in which coding agents create realistic robotics simulations. Our core insight is that simulation creation is a coding agent task, so improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations. We select simulations based on U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, define what makes a good simulation and a good task, and develop an adversarial creation-audit loop that checks each simulation and task against these definitions. Using this pipeline, we build RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments of varying difficulty. Even the best frontier models fail on every RoboWorld test task, achieving an average reward of only 0.06. Building on RoboWorld, we introduce several new ways for frontier models to improve, including in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher that reads the simulator state and teaches a student in context, self-assisted learning from the model's own privileged experience, and code policies that generate demonstrations across varied scenes to train vision-language-action models (VLAs) such as $\pi_{0.5}$. Each of these substantially improves performance. We release our pipeline, RL environments, and benchmark to facilitate future research. Code and data are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Gym-Anything for Robotics uses coding agents to create robotics simulations, producing RoboWorld, a set of 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments. Even the best frontier models fail every RoboWorld test task, averaging a reward of 0.06, but the proposed improvement methods substantially raise performance.
AI.motivation: Realistic robotics simulations are needed for large-scale training of embodied AI models, but building them requires expert effort that does not scale, and existing simulations cover only a narrow range of real-world tasks and physical phenomena.
AI.method: Simulations are selected by U.S. GDP data to cover economically valuable physical work, good simulations and tasks are defined, and an adversarial creation-audit loop checks each one; improvements include in-context learning across repeated attempts, a privileged teacher, self-assisted learning, and code policies that generate demonstrations for VLAs such as pi0.5.
AI.result: The best frontier models achieve an average reward of only 0.06 on RoboWorld test tasks, failing every one; each of the new improvement methods substantially improves performance.
AI.conclusion: Improvements in coding agents translate directly into richer and more faithful simulations, and the pipeline, RL environments and benchmark are released.

title: Multistatic ISAC with Deep Learning-Based Clutter Suppression for 5G and Beyond
summary: Integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) systems using 5G and beyond signals of opportunity enable joint wireless sensing and communication using shared infrastructure and spectrum resources. While multistatic ISAC can increase sensing coverage with spatially distributed receivers, dense and dynamic clutter can significantly degrade bistatic range and Doppler estimation, leading to errors in target localization and velocity estimation. This paper presents a multistatic ISAC framework with clutter suppression for high-fidelity estimation of target position and velocity. Distributed clutter is modeled with randomly located scatterers with varying Doppler spreads and radar cross sections to capture dense and dynamic clutter effects. A broad range of conventional signal processing baselines are evaluated for clutter suppression, showing limited robustness under strong clutter conditions. To address this limitation, deep learning-based clutter suppression methods are introduced to improve robustness against dense and dynamic clutter by employing residual and attention-enhanced deep neural network architectures that directly enhance target responses from clutter-contaminated observations. These methods substantially outperform conventional approaches in target position and velocity estimation across diverse clutter conditions in multistatic ISAC.

AI.tldr: Presents a multistatic ISAC framework using 5G and beyond signals of opportunity, with deep learning-based clutter suppression built on residual and attention-enhanced networks. The learned methods substantially outperform conventional approaches in target position and velocity estimation under dense, dynamic clutter.
AI.motivation: Dense and dynamic clutter degrades bistatic range and Doppler estimation, causing errors in target localization and velocity estimation, and conventional signal processing baselines show limited robustness under strong clutter.
AI.method: Distributed clutter is modeled with randomly located scatterers with varying Doppler spreads and radar cross sections, and deep neural networks with residual and attention modules directly enhance target responses from clutter-contaminated observations.
AI.result: The learned methods substantially outperform conventional approaches in target position and velocity estimation across diverse clutter conditions in multistatic ISAC.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning-based clutter suppression improves the robustness of multistatic ISAC for high-fidelity sensing of target position and velocity.

title: Difficulty Calibration Across Time for Membership Inference in Diffusion Models
summary: Modern diffusion models are trained on massive datasets that often include copyrighted or private images. Membership inference attacks (MIAs) address this by testing whether a given image was in a model's training set. The standard approach scores an image by its reconstruction loss and flags low-loss images as members. This often fails because some images are simply easier to reconstruct than others, so a simple unseen image can score a lower loss than a complex training image. Difficulty calibration separates memorization from how difficult an image is to begin with. We show how to calibrate along two axes of time: training time and diffusion time. First, across training time, we introduce Reference-Model Calibration (RMC), which compares a fine-tuned model's loss against an earlier checkpoint. This cleanly isolates newly memorized data and gives near-perfect auditing, even without text captions. Since earlier checkpoints are not always available, we next present Temporal Self-Calibration (TSC), which calibrates across diffusion time using only a single model. Our key observation is that an image's difficulty persists across noise levels, whereas memorization is localized in time. By comparing the loss at a target timestep against neighboring timesteps from the same model, TSC attenuates image difficulty using the model's own trajectory. Empirically, our methods beat the state of the art by a wide margin, and unlike most existing attacks, generalize across different model parameterizations such as $x$-, $v$-, and $\epsilon$-prediction models. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes difficulty calibration for membership inference on diffusion models: Reference-Model Calibration across training time and Temporal Self-Calibration across diffusion time. Both methods beat the state of the art by a wide margin and generalize across x-, v- and epsilon-prediction models.
AI.motivation: Standard loss-based membership inference flags low-loss images as members, but some images are simply easier to reconstruct, so an unseen simple image can score a lower loss than a complex training image.
AI.method: RMC compares a fine-tuned model's loss with an earlier checkpoint to isolate newly memorized data; TSC calibrates the loss at a target timestep against neighboring timesteps of the same model, exploiting that image difficulty persists across noise levels while memorization is localized in time.
AI.result: RMC gives near-perfect auditing even without text captions; TSC, which needs only a single model, beats the state of the art by a wide margin and, unlike most existing attacks, generalizes across x-, v- and epsilon-prediction models.
AI.conclusion: Separating memorization from intrinsic image difficulty gives a stronger and more general way to audit diffusion models for the membership of training data.

title: Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model
summary: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Solving the resulting problem poses a second difficulty, because it can accommodate only a few scenarios, and an independent sample of that size is likely to omit the rare realizations on which the worst case concentrates. We therefore build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new realizations from the learned nominal, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights that correct the draws back to the model. On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering the ball at the learned nominal rather than at the record lowers cost under distribution shift, at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model class captures structure that lets it extrapolate beyond the record. The advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the structure the model has learned.

AI.tldr: Proposes a KL-divergence ball for distributionally robust optimization centered at a learned density model instead of the empirical record, with adaptive scenario generation that alternates between solving a finite problem and drawing importance-weighted samples from the model. Centering at the learned nominal lowers cost under distribution shift when data is scarce.
AI.motivation: Divergence balls around the empirical distribution only reweight observed realizations, while transport balls also hedge against off-record realizations the data-generating process cannot produce; a small independent scenario sample is also likely to miss the rare realizations where the worst case concentrates.
AI.method: The ambiguity set is a KL ball around a density model fitted to the record, which lets the adversary up-weight unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them; scenarios are built adaptively, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights correcting the draws back to the model.
AI.result: On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering at the learned nominal lowers cost under distribution shift at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model captures structure that allows extrapolation; the advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the learned structure.
AI.conclusion: The learned nominal helps mainly when data is scarce and the model class captures structure it can extrapolate, and the benefit fades when either condition fails.

title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures; under review at ICLR 2027
summary: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

AI.tldr: Introduces SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients, so output detail grows without lengthening the global attention sequence. It matches or beats a FLOPs-matched JiT control on ImageNet and on DPG-Bench text-to-image generation at lower cost.
AI.motivation: Pixel-space generative Transformers use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and increasingly expensive global attention, although high-frequency detail does not necessarily need global communication.
AI.method: Each anchor is split into slots with disjoint DCT bands; only the lowest-frequency slot per anchor joins global attention while all slots interact locally, and a spatial head adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, with the generative state, target and loss kept in pixel space.
AI.result: On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot reaches a final FID comparable to the FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster; on ImageNet-512 it improves FID by 2.84 with 3.9% fewer FLOPs and comes within 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation it surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.
AI.conclusion: Spectral slots decouple output detail from the length of the global attention sequence, offering a cheaper route to finer detail in pixel-space generation.

title: MesoCraft: a web-based tool for interactive procedural modeling of mesoscale biological structures
summary: Biological models bring the molecular world of cells into view, enabling experts and the public to explore and understand biological discoveries. Building mesoscale models requires organizing many molecular components into spatial arrangements that can be revised as evidence and interpretations develop. We present MesoCraft, a browser-based tool for structural biologists centered on interactive procedural modeling. User-defined rules generate collections of molecular instances, while a geometry-node editor and visual feedback support authoring and revision of their spatial relationships. Beyond model construction, MesoCraft integrates exploration and communication, enabling researchers to inspect molecular organization and create guided animations that highlight key spatial relationships. By connecting modeling, exploration, and explanation in a unified workflow, MesoCraft allows insights gained during exploration and communication to inform iterative model refinement, supporting the development of mesoscale models into visual narratives of cellular organization. A demonstrative deployment of the tool is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MesoCraft is a browser-based tool for interactive procedural modeling of mesoscale biological structures, in which user-defined rules generate molecular instances that can be edited in a geometry-node editor. It also supports exploration and guided animations, linking modeling, exploration and explanation in one workflow.
AI.motivation: Mesoscale biological models require organizing many molecular components into spatial arrangements that must be revised as evidence and interpretations develop, and modeling, exploration and communication are typically separate activities.
AI.method: A browser tool centered on user-defined rules that generate collections of molecular instances, a geometry-node editor with visual feedback for authoring and revising spatial relationships, and features to inspect molecular organization and create guided animations.
AI.result: The abstract reports a demonstrative public deployment of the tool and gives no quantitative evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Connecting modeling, exploration and explanation lets insights from exploration and communication inform iterative model refinement, supporting mesoscale models as visual narratives of cellular organization.

title: HyperIntent: Tracking Intent Shifts for Efficient Reasoning on Dynamic Textual Graphs
summary: Dynamic web interactions continuously evolve as new edges arrive, offering large language models (LLMs) great potential for reasoning over edge-level temporal semantics. However, continuously arriving edges are often repetitive, obscuring the key structures that truly reflect temporal changes and limiting the efficiency of LLMs. A key insight is that beneath the dense stream of edge arrivals lies a sparse evolution of temporal intent, enabling LLMs to be responsively triggered only when such intent shifts, while otherwise inheriting the previous state. To this end, we propose a hypergraph-based framework named HyperIntent, which enhances dynamic graph reasoning by parsing differentiated intents, quantifying their temporal discrepancies, and performing shift-triggered semantic updating. Experimental results on destination node retrieval and future link prediction demonstrate that HyperIntent consistently achieves the best overall performance, with average relative Hits@1 gains of 34.0% and 25.4% over vanilla TGAT and DyGFormer, respectively. Meanwhile, HyperIntent reduces LLM token consumption by 54.4%-95.9% across six datasets while achieving leading predictive performance. In-depth studies further confirm the necessity of shift triggering for identifying structural and semantic temporal changes. The code will be made publicly available upon completion of the review process.

AI.tldr: HyperIntent is a hypergraph-based framework for reasoning over dynamic textual graphs that triggers LLM updates only when a sparse temporal intent shifts and otherwise inherits the previous state. It improves destination node retrieval and future link prediction while cutting LLM token consumption by 54.4% to 95.9%.
AI.motivation: Continuously arriving edges in dynamic web interactions are often repetitive, which obscures the structures that reflect real temporal change and makes invoking LLMs on every edge inefficient.
AI.method: The hypergraph framework parses differentiated intents, quantifies their temporal discrepancies, and performs shift-triggered semantic updating, so the LLM is invoked only when intent shifts.
AI.result: On destination node retrieval and future link prediction, HyperIntent achieves the best overall performance, with average relative Hits@1 gains of 34.0% over vanilla TGAT and 25.4% over DyGFormer, and it reduces LLM token consumption by 54.4% to 95.9% across six datasets.
AI.conclusion: Shift-triggered updating is necessary for identifying structural and semantic temporal changes, making LLM-based dynamic graph reasoning both accurate and efficient.

title: Neural Explicit Shape Representation
summary: Existing neural 3D representations separately address continuous surface modeling, efficient image synthesis, or object-specific compression. They do not jointly provide the explicit surface queries required by ray tracing and a structured output space that can be predicted across objects. We introduce NeuOctree, a neural explicit representation that directly predicts whether and where a ray intersects a surface, together with its normal and albedo. NeuOctree stores shared features at the corners of sparse octree voxels and interpolates them into a continuous local field. A lightweight decoder with recurrent intersection-guided sampling refines each query near the predicted surface, enabling direct surface rendering without mesh extraction or texture baking and accommodating open, non-watertight geometry. The same octree structure supports both compact per-object optimization and a shared octree CNN that constructs renderable assets from colored point clouds without per-object fitting. Across seven meshes and four storage budgets, NeuOctree achieves the lowest positional error in 24 of 28 comparisons while retaining competitive normal accuracy, and substantially improves joint geometry--appearance reconstruction over N-BVH and VQAD. The feedforward model constructs a representation in 0.05 seconds and transfers from Objaverse to ShapeNet without retraining. We further demonstrate ray-traced rendering and image-conditioned generation, showing that NeuOctree provides a common output space for neural inference and direct surface rendering. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: NeuOctree is a neural explicit representation that stores shared features at the corners of octree voxels and directly predicts whether, where and how a ray intersects a surface, together with its normal and albedo. It enables direct surface rendering without mesh extraction, and its feedforward model builds a representation in 0.05 seconds.
AI.motivation: Existing neural 3D representations separately address continuous surface modeling, efficient image synthesis and object-specific compression, and do not jointly provide the explicit surface queries that ray tracing requires together with a structured output space predictable across objects.
AI.method: Shared features at sparse octree voxel corners are interpolated into a continuous local field, and a lightweight decoder with recurrent intersection-guided sampling refines each query near the predicted surface; a shared octree CNN builds renderable assets from colored point clouds without per-object fitting.
AI.result: Across seven meshes and four storage budgets, NeuOctree achieves the lowest positional error in 24 of 28 comparisons with competitive normal accuracy, and substantially improves joint geometry-appearance reconstruction over N-BVH and VQAD. The feedforward model builds a representation in 0.05 seconds and transfers from Objaverse to ShapeNet without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The octree structure provides a common output space for neural inference and direct surface rendering, demonstrated through ray-traced rendering and image-conditioned generation.

title: UniffordInteractor: Reasoning the Unified Affordance for Human and Multi-Object Interaction
comment: 13 pages, 11 figures. Published in ACM Transactions on Graphics (Proceedings of SIGGRAPH Asia 2026)
summary: Deriving plausible and dynamic Human Object Interaction (HOI) has gained tremendous progress in Embodied AI and Immersive AR/VR. While existing HOI methods have effectively explored human interaction with individual or fixed objects, they still show limitations in complex multi-object interaction scenes. Meanwhile, previous approaches focus more on the contact information held by human-object relation, overlooking the significance of the contact situation of various entities (i.e., object-object). To address these limitations, we propose UniffordInteractor, a Reasoning-then-Interacting framework that leverages unified affordance for realistic and long-horizon human and multi-object interaction modeling. At the reasoning stage, we devise a Unified Affordance Reasoner (UAR) that employs a fine-tuned 3D Multimodal Large Language Model for unified object-centric affordance prediction. At the interacting stage, we propose Hierarchical Interaction Generator (HIG), which formulates the interaction generation as a hierarchical (e.g., root to body to hand to objects) autoregressive prediction, conditioned on the obtained unified affordance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniffordInteractor surpasses SOTA counterparts in human and multi-object interaction generation.

AI.tldr: UniffordInteractor is a Reasoning-then-Interacting framework for human and multi-object interaction that predicts unified object-centric affordance with a fine-tuned 3D multimodal LLM and generates hierarchical autoregressive interactions conditioned on it. It surpasses state-of-the-art methods in human and multi-object interaction generation.
AI.motivation: Existing HOI methods handle individual or fixed objects well but are limited in complex multi-object scenes, and they focus on human-object contact while overlooking object-object contact situations.
AI.method: A Unified Affordance Reasoner uses a fine-tuned 3D multimodal LLM for unified affordance prediction, and a Hierarchical Interaction Generator formulates generation as autoregressive prediction from root to body to hand to objects, conditioned on the unified affordance.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that UniffordInteractor surpasses state-of-the-art counterparts in human and multi-object interaction generation; the abstract gives no specific figures.
AI.conclusion: Unified affordance reasoning supports more realistic and long-horizon modeling of human and multi-object interaction.

title: Mastering Multi-State Dynamics: Continuum Damage and Viscoplastic MPM for RL-Based Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation of multi-state materials needs a simulator that handles large deformation, topology change, and two-way contact between tools and materials while staying fast enough to drive online reinforcement learning. We present MG-CD-MPM, a tool-centered localized extension of CD-MPM. The implicit Ginzburg-Landau phase-field damage system is solved on a local patch by preconditioned conjugate gradients using a geometric-multigrid V-cycle as the preconditioner. The background MPM discretization remains uniform: only the damage solve is localized. Two-way rigid-tool coupling converts MPM contact impulses into forces and torques on the tool, exposing material resistance directly to the policy. The resulting Gym-like simulator covers soft solids, brittle materials, granular media, and viscoplastic or semi-fluid media within a unified per-particle constitutive layer. We demonstrate cutting, scooping, and shoveling in six scenes, combining scripted tool motions with PPO policies trained on two cutting tasks.

AI.tldr: MG-CD-MPM is a tool-centered localized extension of CD-MPM that solves the implicit phase-field damage system only on a local patch, using a geometric-multigrid-preconditioned conjugate gradient solver, to give a fast Gym-like simulator for RL-based dexterous manipulation. PPO policies trained on two cutting tasks are demonstrated across six scenes.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation of multi-state materials needs a simulator that handles large deformation, topology change and two-way tool-material contact while staying fast enough to drive online reinforcement learning.
AI.method: The background MPM discretization stays uniform and only the damage solve is localized, with a geometric-multigrid V-cycle as preconditioner; two-way rigid-tool coupling converts MPM contact impulses into forces and torques on the tool, and a unified per-particle constitutive layer covers several material types.
AI.result: The simulator covers soft solids, brittle materials, granular media and viscoplastic or semi-fluid media, and demonstrates cutting, scooping and shoveling in six scenes that combine scripted tool motions with PPO policies trained on two cutting tasks; the abstract gives no speed figures.
AI.conclusion: Exposing material resistance directly to the policy through contact forces makes the simulator suited to learning dexterous material manipulation.

title: Greenscapes: Optimized Vegetation Configurations in Cities
comment: 18 pages (11 main paper + 7 supplementary material), 15 figures, 5 tables. Project page: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Vegetation plays a central role in cities, serving functional roles such as balancing shade and sky exposure, shaping the microclimate, carbon sequestration, and providing acoustic screening. Furthermore, aesthetic choices in landscape styles (formal, modernist, picturesque) are important for citizens' well-being and should be considered in the design of urban landscapes. In this paper, we present a novel method for placing vegetation, ranging from shrubs to large trees, in 3D urban scenes. Our method uses individual lots as input and employs a conditioned Vision-Language Model (VLM) to generate a top-down rendering of vegetation, placing large trees, small trees, and shrubs on lawn areas. This rendering is then converted into a 3D scene by detecting individual plants and selecting appropriate 3D assets. To refine the proposed configurations, we define an optimization loop that keeps the VLM-generated positions fixed after a deterministic feasibility repair and uses CMA-ES to optimize per-instance scale transformations along with discrete vegetation asset substitutions. To define the objective function for the optimization, we evaluate the generated 3D scenes with efficient surrogate models of shade and path-based acoustic exposure. Furthermore, we render in-scene views at each optimization step to compute view-dependent perceptual descriptors, enabling the generation of both aesthetic and functional vegetation layouts for urban scenes.

AI.tldr: Presents a method that places vegetation, from shrubs to large trees, in 3D urban scenes: a conditioned VLM generates a top-down vegetation layout, which is then refined by CMA-ES against surrogate shade and acoustic exposure objectives and perceptual descriptors computed from in-scene renders.
AI.motivation: Vegetation in cities serves functional roles such as shade, microclimate, carbon sequestration and acoustic screening, and landscape style matters for citizens' well-being, so urban vegetation design should weigh both functional and aesthetic goals.
AI.method: Individual lots are input to a conditioned VLM that renders a top-down vegetation layout, which is converted into 3D by detecting plants and selecting assets; after deterministic feasibility repair the VLM positions are fixed, while CMA-ES optimizes per-instance scale transformations and discrete asset substitutions against efficient surrogate models of shade and path-based acoustic exposure, with view-dependent perceptual descriptors computed at each step.
AI.result: The abstract describes the pipeline and its objectives but reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The approach aims to produce both aesthetic and functional vegetation layouts for urban scenes.

title: Walk on Multiscale Media: Compiling Editable and Composable Transport Medium Prefabs for Monte Carlo PDE Solvers
summary: Monte Carlo PDE solvers enable mesh-free pointwise queries, but repeatedly traversing heterogeneous media is costly, particularly in scenes with reusable or dynamically changing materials. We introduce Walk on Multiscale Media (WoMM), which compiles fine-scale transport into reusable, editable and composable transport prefabs. A probabilistic interpretation of multiscale finite-element bases and condensed operators yields coarse transitions retaining fine-scale material effects. Each prefab combines port-level operators, entrance-dependent exit distributions, and Poisson-marked trajectory records, enabling incremental updates for overlapping absorption fields, gradient-field steering through path reweighting and transient diffusion. Integrated with conventional Walk-on-Spheres in a hybrid continuous--discrete solver, these prefabs accelerate repeated pointwise PDE queries and support interactive material edits without repeatedly solving the fine-scale problem.

AI.tldr: WoMM compiles fine-scale transport in heterogeneous media into reusable, editable and composable transport prefabs for Monte Carlo PDE solvers, so repeated pointwise queries do not require re-solving the fine-scale problem. Integrated with Walk-on-Spheres in a hybrid solver, the prefabs accelerate repeated queries and support interactive material edits.
AI.motivation: Monte Carlo PDE solvers enable mesh-free pointwise queries, but repeatedly traversing heterogeneous media is costly, particularly in scenes with reusable or dynamically changing materials.
AI.method: A probabilistic interpretation of multiscale finite-element bases and condensed operators yields coarse transitions that retain fine-scale material effects; each prefab combines port-level operators, entrance-dependent exit distributions and Poisson-marked trajectory records, supporting incremental updates, gradient-field steering through path reweighting and transient diffusion.
