AI.result: The prefabs accelerate repeated pointwise PDE queries and support interactive material edits without repeatedly solving the fine-scale problem; the abstract gives no numerical speedups.
AI.conclusion: Compiling transport into prefabs makes Monte Carlo PDE solving practical for interactive editing of heterogeneous scenes.

title: GOFish: Full Field-of-View Gaussian Splatting and Mesh Extraction
summary: Robots, autonomous vehicles, and consumer 360° cameras use fisheye lenses for wide fields of view (FoVs). Simulation-ready digital twins require photorealistic rendering across the full FoV and an aligned collision mesh. However, prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods only rasterize up to 180° and do not produce meshes, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize FoVs beyond 180°, and extract an aligned mesh from the same scene. Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and mesh. Across the 200° FIORD and 205° FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB, respectively. It also outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Together, the Gaussian scene and mesh form a LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twin that renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry.

AI.tldr: GOFish is the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method trained directly on fisheye images, rasterizing fields of view beyond 180 degrees and extracting an aligned mesh from the same scene. It improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 dB on FIORD and 1.97 dB on FullCircle.
AI.motivation: Simulation-ready digital twins need photorealistic full-FoV rendering and an aligned collision mesh, but prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods rasterize only up to 180 degrees and produce no mesh, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images.
AI.method: Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and the mesh.
AI.result: On the 200-degree FIORD and 205-degree FullCircle benchmarks, PSNR improves over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB; GOFish outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set.
AI.conclusion: The Gaussian scene and mesh together form a LiDAR-free, real-time, simulation-ready digital twin that also ray traces the full FoV and provides collision geometry.

title: Frequency-Adaptive Gaussian Grids for Efficient Image Representation
summary: Neural representation has emerged as a powerful tool to mitigate the demand for increasingly higher-resolution images. However, a fundamental trade-off remains between structured (e.g., feature grids, which offer spatial consistency) and unstructured (e.g., 2D Gaussians, which adaptively capture local variances) representations. This choice significantly affects how well an algorithm represents an image. Here, we present Gaussian-Grid, a hybrid neural representation that adaptively integrates structured and unstructured primitives. By dynamically partitioning computation between 2D Gaussian distributions and their attached multi-resolution feature grids based on the local frequency content, Gaussian-Grid automatically optimizes its architecture to match the underlying complexity of the target signal. We evaluate our approach using high-resolution natural images and demonstrate its applications as GPU-native dataset storage, showing $1.24$-$2.14\times$ decoding speed improvement and PCIe data traffic reduction of $23\times$-$176\times$ over JPEG + ZIP data archiving. The results show that Gaussian-Grid maintains small memory footprints while achieving high reconstruction fidelity across a variety of datasets.

AI.tldr: Gaussian-Grid is a hybrid neural image representation that splits computation between 2D Gaussians and multi-resolution feature grids according to local frequency content, keeping memory footprints small while reaching high reconstruction fidelity. As GPU-native dataset storage it decodes 1.24-2.14x faster and cuts PCIe traffic by 23-176x relative to JPEG plus ZIP archiving.
AI.motivation: Neural image representations face a trade-off between structured feature grids, which offer spatial consistency, and unstructured 2D Gaussians, which adaptively capture local variance, and this choice strongly affects how well an image is represented.
AI.method: Gaussian-Grid adaptively integrates both kinds of primitive by dynamically partitioning computation between 2D Gaussian distributions and their attached multi-resolution feature grids based on local frequency content, so its architecture matches the complexity of the target signal.
AI.result: On high-resolution natural images the method keeps small memory footprints and high reconstruction fidelity across a variety of datasets. As GPU-native dataset storage it gives 1.24-2.14x faster decoding and 23-176x lower PCIe data traffic than JPEG plus ZIP archiving.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-adaptive hybrid primitives offer a practical route to compact neural image representations that decode quickly on GPUs, with potential use as GPU-resident dataset storage.

title: 3DCodeEdit: Benchmarking Instruction-Guided 3D Program Editing
summary: Language models increasingly create 3D content through code, with practical workflows often relying on editing existing programs rather than regenerating them, for speed and precise control. Such edits require understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it, yet prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits against a reference. In this paper, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs that construct objects entirely in code. Its edits range from parameter to structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, and are judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. Across 17 models, the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models become more capable, their failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. We therefore study whether multi-turn feedback can compensate for this missing foresight. Feedback from a separate reviewer model that describes how the renders differ from the request helps most, more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and can let a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.

AI.tldr: 3DCodeEdit is a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided edits over 108 Blender programs, and across 17 models the average success rate is only 37%. Multi-turn feedback from a separate reviewer model helps most, letting a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.
AI.motivation: Language models increasingly build 3D content through code and are often asked to edit existing programs, but prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits judged against a reference.
AI.method: The benchmark covers edits from parameter changes to structural changes, style redesign and scene composition, judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. The authors then test whether multi-turn feedback, from a reviewer model that describes how renders differ from the request, can compensate for missing geometric foresight, and compare it with maximum reasoning effort and an agent harness.
AI.result: The average success rate across 17 models is 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models improve, failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. Reviewer feedback helps more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and lets a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.
AI.conclusion: Editing code-defined 3D programs remains hard, and as models become more capable the bottleneck moves to anticipating geometry, where targeted multi-turn feedback is a useful lever.

title: Self-Consistency Geometry Injection for Multi-view Consistent Image Generation
summary: Recent diffusion models have achieved impressive progress in single image to multi-view generation by synthesizing consistent novel views efficiently. Existing methods usually explicitly or implicitly couple geometry inference and texture synthesis, making generation vulnerable to inaccurate geometry prediction. Although several geometry-guided methods have explored decoupling, they usually treat predicted geometry as a fixed condition and do not explicitly model whether the geometry is reliable. We therefore propose Reliability-Guided Multi-View Generation (RGMV), which comprises a parameter-free Self-Consistency Geometry Gate (SCG) and a Reliability-aware Geometry Injection (RGI) module. Specifically, a geometry proposal generator produces multiple geometry predictions for the same reference image and target viewpoints under different stochastic sampling configurations. SCG measures their spatial agreement to derive a reliability map, which RGI uses to modulate the injection strength of geometry-conditioned residuals in the RGB synthesis model. Moreover, RGMV can adapt to different geometry proposal generators. As a result, RGMV preserves stronger geometric guidance in stable regions while attenuating unreliable geometry cues before they propagate into multi-view RGB generation. Extensive experiments show that reliability-aware geometry injection improves the geometric quality of multi-view generation. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: RGMV decouples geometry from texture in single-image multi-view diffusion by measuring the reliability of geometry predictions through their agreement across stochastic samples and modulating geometry injection accordingly. The reliability-aware injection improves the geometric quality of multi-view generation.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion methods couple geometry inference and texture synthesis, so inaccurate geometry corrupts generation, and prior geometry-guided methods that decouple the two treat predicted geometry as a fixed condition without modelling whether it is reliable.
AI.method: A geometry proposal generator produces several geometry predictions for the same reference image and target viewpoints under different stochastic sampling configurations. A parameter-free Self-Consistency Geometry Gate measures their spatial agreement to derive a reliability map, and a Reliability-aware Geometry Injection module uses this map to modulate the strength of geometry-conditioned residuals in the RGB synthesis model. The framework adapts to different geometry proposal generators.
AI.result: Reliability-aware geometry injection improves the geometric quality of multi-view generation, preserving stronger geometric guidance in stable regions and attenuating unreliable cues. The abstract reports no specific numbers or datasets.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning on geometry in proportion to its reliability is a general way to decouple geometry from texture synthesis and reduce the propagation of geometric errors into RGB generation.

title: CAD-WAM: Anticipating Geometry for Text-to-CAD Generation
summary: Generating editable computer-aided design (CAD) models from text requires selecting operations that produce the intended changes to the geometry constructed so far. An incorrect operation can compromise subsequent steps, making reliable multi-step generation challenging. Existing methods based on large language models (LLMs) primarily learn to predict commands, without explicit supervision of the geometric states those commands should produce. Inspired by world-action models, we introduce CAD-WAM, which couples geometry-conditioned action generation with next-state prediction. We define complete modeling operations as actions in a CAD domain-specific language (DSL) and encode surface point clouds of intermediate solids into compact latent states using a pretrained variational autoencoder. An LLM backbone generates the next action from the target description and current geometric state, while an auxiliary head on the same backbone predicts the next state to provide geometric supervision during training. We construct step-wise training trajectories from parametric CAD models in the DeepCAD dataset, pairing each trajectory with an expert-level textual description. At inference, each generated action is executed by a CAD kernel, and the resulting solid is re-encoded to inform the next decision. On the DeepCAD test set, CAD-WAM outperforms the task-specific baselines in geometric accuracy and output validity, with larger gains on models requiring more operations, and produces more accurate geometry than general-purpose LLMs prompted with the same DSL. Ablations further show that next-state supervision reduces mean Chamfer distance by 13.2\% relative to an otherwise identical model trained only to predict actions. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CAD-WAM generates editable CAD models from text by predicting the next modelling action together with the geometric state it should produce, using a pretrained VAE latent of the intermediate solid as supervision. On DeepCAD it outperforms task-specific baselines and general-purpose LLMs in geometric accuracy and output validity, and next-state supervision cuts mean Chamfer distance by 13.2% relative to action-only training.
AI.motivation: LLM-based text-to-CAD methods mainly learn to predict commands without explicit supervision of the geometric states those commands should produce, so an early incorrect operation can compromise all later steps.
AI.method: Complete modelling operations are defined as actions in a CAD domain-specific language, and surface point clouds of intermediate solids are encoded into compact latent states by a pretrained VAE. An LLM backbone generates the next action from the target description and current geometric state, while an auxiliary head on the same backbone predicts the next state as geometric supervision during training. At inference a CAD kernel executes each action and the resulting solid is re-encoded to inform the next decision.
AI.result: On the DeepCAD test set, CAD-WAM outperforms task-specific baselines in geometric accuracy and output validity, with larger gains on models requiring more operations, and produces more accurate geometry than general-purpose LLMs prompted with the same DSL. Next-state supervision reduces mean Chamfer distance by 13.2% relative to an otherwise identical model trained only to predict actions.
AI.conclusion: Supervising the geometric consequence of each step through a learned latent state is a promising way to make multi-step text-to-CAD generation more reliable.

title: HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
summary: The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM's own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: HairDeck generates animation-ready stylized hair cards from a single image by treating a hairstyle as an unordered set of cards, one token per card, denoised jointly by a set diffusion transformer. It also produces the spring-bone chains that drive the cards, and on CHARM's test set it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% while running 33 times faster.
AI.motivation: Stylized hair in games is built from artist-placed hair cards, but image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, and the only existing generator of stylized hair cards, CHARM, decodes control points autoregressively as one long sequence.
AI.method: Each hair card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together, exploiting the fact that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives. Spring-bone chains are generated alongside the cards, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats.
AI.result: On CHARM's own test set, HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance by 44%, reduces card-orientation error by more than half, and runs 33 times faster. From single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods.
AI.conclusion: Modelling a card hairstyle as a set rather than a sequence gives a faster and more accurate route to animatable stylized hair assets from single images.

title: The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus: harmonising 128 aviation-safety source codes into one deduplicated cross-national accident dataset
comment: 34 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Dataset deposited at Zenodo: version DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22303316 (the exact snapshot every reported number is computed from); concept DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22228451
summary: National aviation-investigation databases are deep but territorial; global compilations such as the Aviation Safety Network and the Bureau of Aircraft Accidents Archives are hand-curated, apply their own inclusion thresholds, and publish no per-record lineage. The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus harmonizes 279,485 occurrences and 131,882 attached narratives from 128 source codes -- national accident-investigation authorities, occurrence-reporting systems and four global compilations. Records are mapped into one schema; each normalized record reduces to exactly one key from an ordered ladder -- event signature, registration and date, rounded position and date, or source and native identifier -- so a missing field never creates a link, and the key is the occurrence identifier. Records the ladder cannot reach are scored in a blocked pass into an explicit merge table and applied only within an automatically approved score band or after a person confirms them. Field conflicts follow a documented source ranking; one provenance row per contributing source -- its native identifier and URL -- is retained, with attribution and licence terms per source code. Linkage error is measured on five adjudicated samples totalling 200 pairs. A recorded uniform random draw of 60 from the 3,441 merges the automatic band applies as it ships found no error; the exact two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound on its false-merge rate is 6.0%, or 205 pairs. The measured error covers the scored band only; the ladder's deterministic joins are not adjudicated. The corpus has no exposure denominators and inherits the under-reporting of its sources. It is offered as a base for cross-national safety statistics, source-disagreement studies and narrative text mining; a frozen, DOI-referenced snapshot accompanies the live API.

AI.tldr: The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus harmonises 279,485 aviation occurrences and 131,882 narratives from 128 source codes into one deduplicated cross-national dataset, using a deterministic key ladder and a scored merge band. A sampled audit of 60 automatic merges found no errors, giving a 95% upper bound of 6.0% on the false-merge rate.
AI.motivation: National aviation-investigation databases are deep but territorial, while global compilations are hand-curated with their own inclusion thresholds and publish no per-record lineage.
AI.method: Records are mapped into one schema, and each normalised record reduces to exactly one key from an ordered ladder (event signature, registration and date, rounded position and date, or source and native identifier), so a missing field never creates a link. Records the ladder cannot reach are scored in a blocked pass, and merges are applied only within an automatically approved score band or after a person confirms them. Field conflicts follow a documented source ranking, and one provenance row per source, with its native identifier, URL, attribution and licence terms, is retained.
AI.result: Linkage error was measured on five adjudicated samples totalling 200 pairs. A recorded uniform random draw of 60 from 3,441 automatic merges found no error, and the exact two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound on the false-merge rate is 6.0%, or 205 pairs. The deterministic joins are not adjudicated, and the corpus has no exposure denominators and inherits the under-reporting of its sources.
AI.conclusion: The corpus is offered as a base for cross-national safety statistics, source-disagreement studies and narrative text mining, with a frozen DOI-referenced snapshot accompanying the live API.

title: Sparse tensor networks for individual tree diameter estimation in mixed forests
summary: Measurements of tree diameter at breast height (DBH) are fundamental to forest inventories, but manual surveys across entire stands or regions are impractical. UAV-borne laser scanning (ULS) enables scalable automated forest surveys, yet canopy occlusion makes accurate DBH estimation from ULS point clouds non-trivial. Limited stem-level point density of ULS data constrains approaches relying on detailed stem reconstruction, such as Quantitative Structure Models (QSMs) and circle fitting. Empirical machine learning methods based on predefined point cloud metrics are an alternative. New deep learning approaches offer an even more principled solution, allowing models to learn directly from point clouds. Sparse tensor networks have shown particular promise, transforming forestry tasks such as tree species classification. We investigate whether these strengths can be extended to estimate individual tree DBH from ULS data across four mixed-species temperate forest plots in Germany. We further advance existing sparse tensor networks by introducing TreeNext, a lightweight deep learning architecture for direct individual tree parameter estimation from voxelized LiDAR point clouds. We present a fully automated forest inventory pipeline from individual tree instance segmentation to DBH regression, and quantify the impact of segmentation errors by comparing performance on automatically segmented and ground truth instances. TreeNext achieves an $R^2$ of 0.8355 on automatically segmented trees and 0.9380 on ground truth segments, outperforming strong tabular baselines including Random Forest and XGBoost. Segmentation quality emerges as the dominant error source in the automated pipeline. TreeNext proves highly data-efficient, performing well even in small data scenarios. Our findings establish sparse tensor networks as a practical foundation for automated individual tree DBH estimation from ULS.

AI.tldr: TreeNext, a lightweight sparse tensor network, estimates individual tree diameter at breast height (DBH) from UAV laser scanning point clouds, reaching R2 0.8355 on automatically segmented trees and 0.9380 on ground truth segments. It outperforms Random Forest and XGBoost baselines, and segmentation quality is the dominant error source.
AI.motivation: Manual DBH surveys are impractical at scale, and canopy occlusion and low stem-level point density in UAV laser scanning constrain methods that rely on stem reconstruction, such as Quantitative Structure Models and circle fitting, while predefined-metric machine learning is an alternative that sparse tensor networks may improve on.
AI.method: The authors introduce TreeNext, a lightweight deep learning architecture that estimates individual tree parameters directly from voxelised LiDAR point clouds. They build a fully automated pipeline from individual tree instance segmentation to DBH regression, and quantify the impact of segmentation errors by comparing automatically segmented and ground truth instances across four mixed-species temperate forest plots in Germany.
AI.result: TreeNext achieves R2 of 0.8355 on automatically segmented trees and 0.9380 on ground truth segments, outperforming Random Forest and XGBoost. It is highly data-efficient and performs well in small-data scenarios, and segmentation quality emerges as the dominant error source in the automated pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Sparse tensor networks are a practical foundation for automated individual-tree DBH estimation from ULS data, with improving segmentation as the main target for future gains.

title: Scoring Explanations Without Reading Them: Structural Shortcuts in Automated-Interpretability Evaluation Data
summary: Automated interpretability scores an explanation of a sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature by asking a model to predict, token by token, where the feature fires on evaluation examples or to judge whether marked tokens fit it. We find that the evaluation data standard pipelines build can be scored without reading the explanation. On Neuronpedia's stored fuzzing runs for 500 random GPT-2 small features, 91.3% of activating examples are cropped with the peak on the centre token, and a rule that says "yes" when the centre token is marked reaches balanced accuracy 0.979, against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers (recomputed from the stored per-item verdicts, on marks rebuilt from the pipeline's code); a rule reading only the mark count reaches 0.969. The cue changes form across pipelines: current delphi always marks the same slot in its fuzzing negatives, and full-context runs mark negatives with more tokens. OpenAI's simulation benchmark lists each neuron's top-activating sequences first; a rule that predicts activity on the first five scores 0.227 in pooled correlation against 0.160 for GPT-4's published simulator (post hoc). We give closed forms for what such rules can score; show that one scorer's simulation scores are higher on stored snippets than on natural windows but not shown to be reordered; and build windows that remove the position cue, derive but do not build negatives that remove the mark cues, and separate the sequence cue by decomposition. On natural-text windows cut at random offsets, the best fixed-offset prior shared by all features scores 0.015. On them, that scorer, a typed decision model (Jev), reaches a pooled correlation of 0.331 over 49 features, against 0.013 with shuffled explanations, and an open 8B simulator with the original read-out reads the explanation there (0.194 against 0.019). Scores should be reported beside the best explanation-free rule on the same items.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that standard automated-interpretability evaluation data can be scored without reading the explanation: a rule answering yes when the centre token is marked reaches balanced accuracy 0.979, above 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers. On natural-text windows without the position cue, a typed decision model reaches pooled correlation 0.331 against 0.013 with shuffled explanations.
AI.motivation: Automated interpretability scores an explanation of a sparse-autoencoder feature by asking a model to predict where the feature fires or to judge whether marked tokens fit it, but the evaluation data built by standard pipelines may carry cues that let a scorer succeed without using the explanation.
AI.method: The authors audit Neuronpedia's stored fuzzing runs for 500 GPT-2 small features and OpenAI's simulation benchmark, derive closed forms for what such cue-based rules can score, and build windows that remove the position cue while separating the sequence cue by decomposition. They then evaluate on natural-text windows cut at random offsets, using a typed decision model (Jev) and an open 8B simulator.
AI.result: On the stored fuzzing data, 91.3% of activating examples are cropped with the peak on the centre token, and a centre-mark rule reaches balanced accuracy 0.979 against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers, while a mark-count-only rule reaches 0.969. On the simulation benchmark a rule predicting activity on the first five tokens scores 0.227 pooled correlation against 0.160 for GPT-4's published simulator (post hoc). On natural windows the best fixed-offset prior scores 0.015, Jev reaches 0.331 over 49 features against 0.013 with shuffled explanations, and the 8B simulator reaches 0.194 against 0.019.
AI.conclusion: Interpretability scores should be reported beside the best explanation-free rule evaluated on the same items, since existing evaluation data can reward structural shortcuts.

title: Rank-Aware Differentially Private Release of Listwise Preferences for LLM Alignment
summary: Listwise preference feedback offers richer supervision for large language model (LLMs) alignment than pairwise comparisons, but a full ranking also reveals more sensitive user preferences. Existing privacy-preserving alignment methods focus mainly on pairwise feedback, while listwise alignment under local differential privacy (LDP) remains unexplored. Extending LDP to this listwise domain raises a critical challenge: the high sensitivity of the full ranking space demands excessive noise, neutralizing the benefits of listwise supervision. To address this challenge, we analyze the interaction between supervision granularity and privacy noise in downstream training, and introduce a rank-aware exponential mechanism that privatizes listwise preference data into a low-sensitivity granularity suitable for downstream alignment. The mechanism leverages ranking information to sample a fixed-size binary partition, concentrating the noise near borderline items instead of perturbing all items uniformly as randomized response (RR) does. Empirical evaluations on downstream LLM alignment tasks show that our mechanism consistently outperforms existing LDP baselines at matched privacy budgets. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a rank-aware exponential mechanism that privatises listwise preference rankings under local differential privacy by sampling a fixed-size binary partition, reducing sensitivity while concentrating noise near borderline items. It consistently outperforms existing LDP baselines on downstream LLM alignment at matched privacy budgets.
AI.motivation: Listwise preference feedback gives richer alignment supervision than pairwise comparisons, but full rankings reveal more sensitive preferences, existing private alignment methods target pairwise feedback, and the high sensitivity of the full ranking space under LDP demands noise that cancels the benefit of listwise supervision.
AI.method: The authors analyse how supervision granularity interacts with privacy noise and introduce a rank-aware exponential mechanism. It uses ranking information to sample a fixed-size binary partition, turning listwise data into a low-sensitivity granularity suitable for downstream alignment, and concentrates noise near borderline items instead of perturbing all items uniformly as randomized response does.
AI.result: On downstream LLM alignment tasks the mechanism consistently outperforms existing LDP baselines at matched privacy budgets. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Matching the privatised granularity to what downstream alignment needs lets listwise preference data be used under local differential privacy without the full noise cost of ranking-level perturbation.

title: An Introduction to Large Language Models for Scientists and Professionals
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.

AI.tldr: An accessible introduction to large language models for scientists and professionals, covering tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, prompting and RAG, with emphasis on hallucination, uncertainty and verification. It includes a hands-on exercise running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI over scientific papers and requires no programming knowledge.
AI.motivation: LLMs have become important tools for science, education, medicine and professional work, but effective and responsible use requires understanding how they work, what their limitations are and how their outputs should be evaluated.
AI.method: The document is a lecture-based text written for a master's course in AI in medicine at the University of Turin and deliberately avoids mathematical detail. It explains the core concepts, discusses limitations, privacy, governance and security, and introduces advanced topics such as RAG, retrieval quality, chunking, vector search, agents and tools, alongside a substantial practical exercise.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results. The exercise guides readers through evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty and disagreement between studies over a collection of scientific papers.
AI.conclusion: The text aims to help readers distinguish plausible language from scientifically supported conclusions and to apply systematic verification and human oversight.

title: From Geometry to Behavior: How Instruction Exposure Unlocks Latent Rhetorical Directions in LLMs
summary: Language models do not merely memorize facts; they absorb rhetorical strategies from pretraining data, including the human tendency to reason by analogy. We ask: is this absorbed capability geometrically accessible before any instruction tuning, and what determines whether it can be activated at inference time? We extract an "Analogy Vector" from the residual stream via difference-in-means and show it enables steerable explanation style across seven instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5; 2B-32B), improving harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 (+22%) for Gemma-2-9B-IT on 300 held-out test prompts. A small human validation study confirms the LLM judge on Analogy Quality. Our central finding, from seven matched base-instruct pairs, is a gradient of behavioral accessibility: the analogy direction exists in every base model, but its behavioral accessibility under linear intervention scales continuously with instruction exposure during training. Gemma-2 base models (strict pretraining/IT separation) show flat steering landscapes: present but behaviorally inert. Qwen-2.5 base models (instruction data woven into pretraining) are already partially accessible before any explicit fine-tuning; base-instruct cosine similarity of the analogy vector reaches 0.94-0.97 for Qwen versus 0.37-0.66 for Gemma, providing geometric corroboration of the behavioral gradient. This challenges the binary "base vs instruct" framing: the relevant variable is how much instruction exposure a model has received across its full training pipeline. We position activation steering as a complementary interpretability tool that reveals how instruction exposure organizes rhetorical knowledge in activation space.

AI.tldr: An analogy direction extracted from the residual stream by difference-in-means can steer explanation style across seven instruction-tuned models, raising Gemma-2-9B-IT's harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 (+22%). The paper argues that the behavioural accessibility of this direction scales with instruction exposure across the training pipeline rather than following a binary base-versus-instruct distinction.
AI.motivation: Language models absorb rhetorical strategies such as reasoning by analogy from pretraining data, and the paper asks whether this capability is geometrically accessible before instruction tuning and what determines whether it can be activated at inference time.
AI.method: An Analogy Vector is extracted from the residual stream via difference-in-means and used for linear activation steering across seven base-instruct pairs from Gemma-2, Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5 (2B-32B). Evaluation uses 300 held-out prompts with an LLM judge and a small human validation study on Analogy Quality, and activation steering is positioned as a complementary interpretability tool.
AI.result: The analogy direction exists in every base model, but its behavioural accessibility under linear intervention scales continuously with instruction exposure during training. Gemma-2 base models show flat steering landscapes, whereas Qwen-2.5 base models are already partially accessible, with base-instruct cosine similarity of 0.94-0.97 for Qwen versus 0.37-0.66 for Gemma. Gemma-2-9B-IT's harmonic mean improves from 3.22 to 3.94.
AI.conclusion: The relevant variable is how much instruction exposure a model receives across its full training pipeline, which challenges the binary base-versus-instruct framing and shows how instruction exposure organises rhetorical knowledge in activation space.

title: Multi-Draft On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding is used to reduce the inference cost of language models. One-step diffusion drafters propose a block of multiple tokens in parallel, reducing the sequential cost of speculative decoding. On-policy distillation trains these drafters using verifier feedback on their own proposals. However, parallel drafting makes this feedback difficult to use: the drafter predicts each token without observing the preceding tokens sampled within the same block, while the verifier conditions its prediction on those tokens. Different sampled prefixes therefore give different verifier targets for the same drafter prediction. We show that distilling against these targets separately can suppress tokens that are plausible after some prefixes but unlikely after others, harming draft acceptance. We explain the effects of this mismatch and introduce Multi-Draft On-Policy Distillation (MDraft), a new parallel drafter distillation method which samples several draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier's full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes. We use all the drafts to collect information from the verifier, allowing support from alternative prefixes to influence the training target. The resulting algorithm improves the acceptance length of a parallel drafter beyond the level of pre-training, and alleviates the effects of the distributional mismatch. MDraft changes only training, retaining the drafter's architecture and inference procedure, allowing the resulting drafter to be used as-is in place of the pretrained checkpoint. Experiments on a suite of mathematical, coding, and conversational tasks show longer accepted drafts than prior distillation methods.

AI.tldr: MDraft is a training-only method for distilling one-step diffusion drafters for speculative decoding: it samples several draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier's full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes. It lengthens accepted drafts beyond the pretrained level and outperforms prior distillation methods on mathematical, coding and conversational tasks.
AI.motivation: Parallel one-step diffusion drafters propose token blocks without observing the earlier tokens sampled in the same block, while the verifier conditions on them, so different sampled prefixes give different verifier targets, and distilling against these separately can suppress tokens that are plausible after some prefixes and harm draft acceptance.
AI.method: MDraft samples several draft blocks from the same context and aggregates the verifier's full-vocabulary conditionals across their prefixes, so support from alternative prefixes shapes the training target. It changes only training and retains the drafter's architecture and inference procedure, so the resulting drafter can replace the pretrained checkpoint as-is.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical, coding and conversational tasks show longer accepted drafts than prior distillation methods, and the method improves acceptance length beyond the level of pretraining while alleviating the effects of the distributional mismatch.
AI.conclusion: Aggregating verifier feedback across alternative prefixes resolves the target mismatch in parallel drafter distillation without changing the architecture or inference procedure.

title: Locating Sycophancy Across Training Stages in Open Language Models
summary: Language model assistants sometimes change a correct answer when the user suggests a wrong one. The behavior, called sycophancy, is usually attributed to preference-based post-training, yet early measurements found it in pretrained models. We ask where it comes from by measuring it at every available stage of training: 13 open checkpoints from 5 lineages, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization to release. We separate how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and vary who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be, and how strongly they make it. Two sycophancy behaviors with different origins emerge, and both replicate across datasets. Deference to a claim in the prompt is already present in every base model, which ranks sources in the same order as its post-trained descendants. Capitulation in conversation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint. When the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones. We discuss the implications of these measurements for evaluating sycophancy and approaches for addressing each behavior.

AI.tldr: Measuring 13 open checkpoints from 5 lineages across training stages, the paper finds two sycophancy behaviours with different origins. Deference to a claim in the prompt is present in every base model, while capitulation when the user objects is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint.
AI.motivation: Sycophancy is usually attributed to preference-based post-training, yet early measurements found it in pretrained models, so where the behaviour comes from remains unclear.
AI.method: The authors measure sycophancy at every available training stage, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimisation to release. They separate how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and vary who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be and how strongly it is made, with results replicated across datasets.
AI.result: Deference to a claim is already present in every base model, and base models rank sources in the same order as their post-trained descendants. Capitulation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint. When the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones.
AI.conclusion: The two behaviours have different origins, so sycophancy measurement and mitigation should treat them separately rather than as one phenomenon.

title: DeFT-RAG: Incrementally Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

AI.tldr: DeFT-RAG answers multi-hop questions by generating one self-contained sub-question at a time, updating a rule-based QA table, using a lightweight fine-tuned decision model for yes/no decisions, and caching reusable answers. It achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than other iterative methods.
AI.motivation: Graph-based RAG retrieves once from the entities a question names and so rarely recovers the full evidence chain, while iterative RAG is limited by the many tasks it asks the LLM to perform, such as planning sub-questions, tracking dependencies and rewriting them as answers arrive.
AI.method: DeFT-RAG has three components. Each sub-question is self-contained and names every entity it asks about, which removes the need for planning and rewriting. The remaining LLM work is moved outside the LLM into rule-based updates to a QA table and yes/no decisions by a fine-tuned lightweight model. QA pairs are cached so that a later sub-question with the same meaning reuses an existing answer.
AI.result: With gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as backbones, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, reducing LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Restricting the LLM to one fine-grained task at a time, with external bookkeeping and answer caching, improves both accuracy and efficiency for multi-hop RAG.

title: Human-Residual Steering: Aligning Frozen LLM Judges with Human Judgment Distributions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as automated judges, yet most alignment methods target aggregated human judgments and overlook variation among individual annotators. Existing approaches to matching the full distribution of human ratings mainly rely on output-level calibration or parameter fine-tuning. We propose Human-Residual Steering (HRS), to our knowledge the first method to align frozen LLM judges with human judgment distributions through learned hidden-state interventions. An oracle analysis shows that low-rank corrections at a single layer remove most of the discrepancy between judge and human distributions. HRS learns to predict such corrections from the judge's hidden representation and rating logits, training on individual annotations with proper scoring rules for ordinal and nominal judgments and optimising through the frozen downstream layers. Across 14 benchmarks and four judges from three model families, HRS outperforms all evaluated frozen-weight baselines. With Qwen2.5-7B, it achieves the lowest Jensen-Shannon distance on 13 of 14 benchmarks, reducing the mean from 0.565 to 0.352 versus 0.377 for the strongest calibrator. HRS also raises mean Spearman correlation with aggregate human scores from 0.449 to 0.579, improves population-level estimation under limited annotation budgets, and trains about 88 times fewer parameters than distributional fine-tuning at a modest cost in alignment.

AI.tldr: Human-Residual Steering aligns a frozen LLM judge with the distribution of individual human ratings by learning low-rank hidden-state corrections at a single layer. Across 14 benchmarks and four judges it achieves the lowest Jensen-Shannon distance on 13 of 14 benchmarks with Qwen2.5-7B, while training about 88 times fewer parameters than distributional fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Most alignment methods target aggregated human judgments and overlook variation among annotators, and existing approaches to matching the full distribution of human ratings rely on output-level calibration or parameter fine-tuning.
AI.method: HRS is presented as the first method to align frozen LLM judges with human judgment distributions through learned hidden-state interventions. It predicts corrections from the judge's hidden representation and rating logits, trains on individual annotations with proper scoring rules for ordinal and nominal judgments, and optimises through the frozen downstream layers. An oracle analysis shows that low-rank corrections at a single layer remove most of the discrepancy.
AI.result: Across 14 benchmarks and four judges from three model families, HRS outperforms all evaluated frozen-weight baselines. With Qwen2.5-7B it reduces mean Jensen-Shannon distance from 0.565 to 0.352, versus 0.377 for the strongest calibrator, and raises mean Spearman correlation with aggregate human scores from 0.449 to 0.579. It also improves population-level estimation under limited annotation budgets.
AI.conclusion: Learned hidden-state steering is an efficient way to match human judgment distributions, at a modest cost in alignment compared with distributional fine-tuning.

title: Grounding Long Financial Text with Semantically-Enriched Tables via Multimodal Learning
comment: Accepted to Neurips Long-context foundation model workshop
summary: We propose a multimodal transformer framework for efficiently modeling long1 financial documents that combine structured tabular data with noisy, unstructured2 textual disclosures. The framework represents financial tables as semantically3 enriched token sequences and integrates them with long-form text through a cross-4 attention mechanism that explicitly captures cross-modal dependencies. In par-5 ticular, we augment each numerical variable with a semantic embedding derived6 from its textual definition, enabling the model to encode both numerical magnitude7 and economic meaning. This design yields a more expressive and parameter-8 efficient representation of tabular data compared to value-only embeddings. Using9 a large-scale dataset of financial statements and MD&A disclosures, we show that10 structured numerical features remain the dominant source of predictive signal;11 however, textual information provides consistent incremental gains when incor-12 porated via cross-attention rather than simple concatenation. Our results further13 demonstrate that noisy textual disclosures are most useful when conditioned on a14 stable, semantically structured tabular representation. In particular, using frozen15 variable-level tabular representations as cross-attention queries enables the model16 to weight MD&A chunks differently for each financial variable and observation.17 These findings suggest that cross-attention provides an efficient mechanism for18 table-conditioned aggregation of long-form narrative evidence.

AI.tldr: A multimodal transformer represents financial tables as tokens enriched with semantic embeddings of variable definitions and fuses them with long MD&A disclosures through cross-attention. Structured numerical features remain the dominant predictive signal, while text adds consistent incremental gains when cross-attended rather than concatenated.
AI.motivation: Long financial documents combine structured tables with noisy textual disclosures, and value-only numerical embeddings miss economic meaning, while simple concatenation may not make good use of textual evidence.
AI.method: Financial tables are represented as semantically enriched token sequences, with each numerical variable augmented by an embedding derived from its textual definition. Long-form text is integrated through cross-attention, using frozen variable-level tabular representations as queries so that MD&A chunks are weighted differently for each financial variable and observation.
AI.result: On a large-scale dataset of financial statements and MD&A disclosures, structured numerical features remain the dominant source of predictive signal, and textual information yields consistent incremental gains when incorporated via cross-attention rather than simple concatenation. Noisy textual disclosures are most useful when conditioned on a stable, semantically structured tabular representation.
AI.conclusion: Cross-attention with table-conditioned queries provides an efficient mechanism for aggregating long-form narrative evidence in financial prediction.

title: QMUL_AK at AISA-ArabicFC: Schema-Constrained Function Calling with ALLaM
comment: Published at ArabicNLP 2026 (Shared Tasks), co-located with EMNLP 2026. ACL Anthology: this https URL
summary: We describe the QMUL_AK submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026. The system adapts the Arabic-English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model to function calling with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). It combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema. The same output supports Track A function calling and Track B reasoning-augmented calling. Training uses only the official task data. On the development set, the system achieves 0.9982 function accuracy and 0.8920 argument exact match, corresponding to overall A and B scores of 0.9345 and 0.9454. On the blind test set, the system reaches overall A and B scores of 0.9253 and 0.9380, ranking 3rd on both submission tracks and 1st of 21 teams on the Track C dialect-robustness diagnostic with a macro-averaged score of 0.9075 and the smallest dialect gap in the shared task (0.077). The results show that function selection is nearly saturated, while argument extraction remains the main source of error.

AI.tldr: The QMUL_AK system adapts ALLaM-7B-Instruct to function calling with LoRA, adding a schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, and deterministic validation against tool schemas. It ranks 3rd on both Track A and Track B of AISA-ArabicFC 2026 and 1st of 21 teams on the Track C dialect-robustness diagnostic.
AI.motivation: The shared task AISA-ArabicFC 2026 requires function calling in Arabic, including dialectal variants, under both direct and reasoning-augmented calling tracks.
AI.method: The Arabic-English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model is adapted with low-rank adaptation. The system combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema. One output supports Track A function calling and Track B reasoning-augmented calling, and training uses only the official task data.
AI.result: On the development set the system achieves 0.9982 function accuracy and 0.8920 argument exact match, corresponding to overall A and B scores of 0.9345 and 0.9454. On the blind test set it reaches overall A and B scores of 0.9253 and 0.9380, ranking 3rd on both tracks. On Track C it reaches a macro-averaged score of 0.9075 with the smallest dialect gap in the shared task (0.077).
AI.conclusion: Function selection is nearly saturated for this task, so argument extraction is the main remaining source of error.

title: Large Language Models for Accurate Medical Chart Abstraction: Enabling Scalable and Secure Artificial Intelligence Deployment in Stroke
summary: Medical chart abstraction transforms unstructured clinical narratives into structured variables for research and quality monitoring. We evaluated a prompting-based large language model (LLM) framework for extracting eight clinical variables from 2,416 neurointerventional acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals. Twenty-two instruction-tuned open-source LLMs were evaluated across architectures, model sizes, and biomedical adaptations using Quick Response and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. Non-expert staff annotations served as the cross-model reference standard. Evaluation was restricted to report-variable pairs with a valid LLaMA3.3-70B CoT prediction and a corresponding reference label. Performance measures included extraction accuracy, inference latency, and agreement with expert adjudication. Twenty discordant cases per variable underwent review by two senior physicians and four medical students. LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest overall accuracy (94.8%). CoT improved performance on inference-dependent variables such as site of occlusion, while Quick Response was optimal for directly stated procedural fields. Expert adjudication showed that AI predictions were more closely aligned with expert interpretations than non-expert annotations for most variables, with intracranial angioplasty remaining a challenge. Locally deployed LLMs can support scalable clinical information extraction and retrospective stroke registry curation, with expert oversight for ambiguous cases.

AI.tldr: Locally deployed open-source LLMs extracted eight clinical variables from 2,416 neurointerventional stroke reports, with LLaMA3.3-70B reaching the highest overall accuracy of 94.8%. Chain-of-Thought prompting helped inference-dependent variables, Quick Response suited directly stated fields, and expert review found AI predictions aligned more closely with expert interpretations than non-expert annotations for most variables.
AI.motivation: Medical chart abstraction turns unstructured clinical narratives into structured variables for research and quality monitoring, and the study asks whether prompting-based open-source LLMs can do this accurately.
AI.method: Twenty-two instruction-tuned open-source LLMs, spanning architectures, model sizes and biomedical adaptations, were evaluated with Quick Response and Chain-of-Thought prompting on reports from three hospitals. Non-expert staff annotations served as the cross-model reference standard, and twenty discordant cases per variable were reviewed by two senior physicians and four medical students.
AI.result: LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest overall accuracy (94.8%). CoT improved inference-dependent variables such as site of occlusion, while Quick Response was optimal for directly stated procedural fields. Expert adjudication found AI predictions more closely aligned with expert interpretations than non-expert annotations for most variables, with intracranial angioplasty remaining a challenge.
AI.conclusion: Locally deployed LLMs can support scalable clinical information extraction and retrospective stroke registry curation, provided expert oversight is retained for ambiguous cases.

title: Beyond Aggregate WER: In-domain Adaptation, Learner Speech, Code-Switching, and Speaker Attribution in Online Spanish Learning Classrooms
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) increasingly supplies transcripts for educational NLP, but aggregate word error rate (WER) can conceal errors concentrated in learner speech, multilingual turns, and speaker attribution. We compare platform-integrated, open-weight, adapted, and commercial ASR configurations on held-out sessions of online L2 Spanish interaction between L1 English learners and their instructors and tutors. Because English is the learner's shared first language, the interactions contain Spanish-only, English-only, and code-switched turns. Evaluation combines overall WER and character error rate (CER), WER disaggregated by speaker role and language context, and diarization error rate (DER). We also adapt Whisper large-v3 and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize with LoRA using human-corrected in-domain classroom data. MOSS adaptation produced consistent improvements across speaker roles and language contexts, whereas Whisper showed smaller gains. Domain match proved more important than data volume: Larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner corpora did not outperform the smaller classroom corpus, where learner speech and code-switching are embedded in instructor--learner interaction. The open-weight MOSS adapter was competitive with commercial Muse Voice Transcribe on WER and CER and achieved lower system-provided DER on the recordings eligible for each system. Learner, English-only, and code-switched speech remained more difficult than instructor and Spanish-only speech. The findings demonstrate the value of condition-aware evaluation and interactionally matched data for bilingual educational ASR.

AI.tldr: On online L2 Spanish classroom recordings, LoRA adaptation with human-corrected in-domain data improves MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize consistently across speaker roles and language contexts, and the open-weight adapter is competitive with a commercial ASR system. Domain match matters more than data volume, and learner, English-only and code-switched speech remain the hardest to transcribe.
AI.motivation: Aggregate word error rate can conceal errors concentrated in learner speech, multilingual turns and speaker attribution, which matters when ASR transcripts feed educational NLP.
AI.method: Platform-integrated, open-weight, adapted and commercial ASR configurations are compared on held-out sessions between L1 English learners and their instructors or tutors. Evaluation combines overall WER and character error rate, WER disaggregated by speaker role and language context, and diarization error rate. Whisper large-v3 and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize are adapted with LoRA using human-corrected in-domain classroom data.
AI.result: MOSS adaptation produced consistent improvements across speaker roles and language contexts, whereas Whisper showed smaller gains. Larger out-of-domain bilingual and learner corpora did not outperform the smaller classroom corpus. The open-weight MOSS adapter was competitive with commercial Muse Voice Transcribe on WER and CER and achieved lower system-provided DER on the recordings eligible for each system. Learner, English-only and code-switched speech remained harder than instructor and Spanish-only speech.
AI.conclusion: Condition-aware evaluation and interactionally matched training data are valuable for bilingual educational ASR.

title: CARF: Context-Aware Reasoning Supervision for Scientific Evidence Screening
summary: Systematic reviews synthesize biomedical evidence to inform clinical and public-health decision-making, but require domain experts to manually screen thousands of studies against detailed eligibility criteria. We investigate whether language models can assist with this bottleneck by learning from expert feedback on title and abstract screening decisions and model-generated reasoning. We introduce the Context-Aware Reasoning Framework (CARF), a human-in-the-loop framework that uses expert feedback on model-generated reasoning to adapt language models to context-dependent screening tasks. We evaluate CARF on systematic reviews of verbal autopsy and cause-of-death ascertainment methods used in global public health mortality surveillance. CARF shows competitive screening performance compared to evaluated models while retaining high sensitivity, and is more inclined to retain ambiguous, context-dependent studies for human review. Together, these findings suggest that expert-corrected reasoning is a promising supervision signal for context-dependent scientific screening, while retaining a role for human oversight.

AI.tldr: CARF is a human-in-the-loop framework that adapts language models to context-dependent scientific screening by learning from expert feedback on model-generated reasoning. On systematic reviews of verbal autopsy methods it shows competitive screening performance with high sensitivity, and it is more inclined to retain ambiguous studies for human review.
AI.motivation: Systematic reviews require domain experts to screen thousands of studies against detailed eligibility criteria, a bottleneck in synthesising biomedical evidence for clinical and public-health decisions.
AI.method: The Context-Aware Reasoning Framework learns from expert feedback on title and abstract screening decisions and on model-generated reasoning, using this feedback to adapt language models to context-dependent screening tasks.
AI.result: Evaluated on systematic reviews of verbal autopsy and cause-of-death ascertainment methods used in global mortality surveillance, CARF shows competitive screening performance compared with the evaluated models, retains high sensitivity, and is more inclined to keep ambiguous, context-dependent studies for human review. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Expert-corrected reasoning is a promising supervision signal for context-dependent scientific screening, while human oversight retains a role.

title: From Error Prediction to Causal Influence: Auditing SAE Features in Multiple-Choice QA
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can predict internal features associated with model errors, but association alone does not establish causal influence. We study this distinction in multiple-choice question answering, where answer preference can be measured by the logit margin between the correct answer and the competing choices. Across eight datasets, we analyze Gemma~3 1B and 4B with Gemma Scope SAEs. We propose a pipeline to filter out the features that have high correlation with format and content artifacts, such as prompt and answer permutation, and evaluate the remaining ones with causal feature interventions. Our results show that SAE activations contain predictive signals about wrongness and uncertainty across models and datasets. After filtering artifact-contaminated features, selected features for causal intervention at question and option spans produce larger absolute margin shifts and a higher wrong-to-correct rate than randomly selected features, indicating greater causal leverage. However, answer flips are rare, and we do not observe stable effect directions across meaning-preserving changes in prompt format and answer order. An adapted HalluSAE baseline produces larger final-token margin changes, but relies on substantially contaminated features and does not significantly improve correction rates. Therefore, the identified features reflect context-dependent answer competition rather than the mechanism of incorrect answer errors.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether SAE features that predict multiple-choice QA errors causally influence answers. After filtering features correlated with format and content artifacts, causal interventions shift answer margins more than random features do, but answer flips are rare and effects are not stable across meaning-preserving prompt changes.
AI.motivation: Sparse autoencoder features can predict model errors, but association alone does not establish causal influence, and format and content artifacts such as prompt and answer permutation may account for the signal.
AI.method: On eight datasets with Gemma 3 1B and 4B and Gemma Scope SAEs, the authors filter out features highly correlated with format and content artifacts, then evaluate the remaining features with causal interventions at question and option spans, compared against random features and an adapted HalluSAE baseline.
AI.result: SAE activations contain predictive signals about wrongness and uncertainty across models and datasets. Selected features produce larger absolute margin shifts and a higher wrong-to-correct rate than random features, but answer flips are rare, effect directions are not stable across meaning-preserving prompt format and answer order changes, and the HalluSAE baseline gives larger final-token margin changes without significantly improving correction rates.
AI.conclusion: The identified features reflect context-dependent answer competition rather than the mechanism behind incorrect answers.

title: Prompt Lottery in LLM-as-a-Judge: Measuring and Mitigating Sensitivity to Syntactic Rephrasing
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge has become a standard for evaluating large language models, yet most approaches implicitly assume that a single judge prompt functions as a stable evaluation instrument. Prior work has primarily explored deliberate prompt modifications such as scoring rubrics, role descriptions, or chain-of-thought reasoning in order to optimize accuracy. In contrast, we investigate whether validated prompt variants intended to preserve evaluation semantics while differing in surface realization (\textit{paraphrastic rephrasings}) yield consistent judgments under a fixed evaluation task. We introduce \textit{Prompt Lottery}, a phenomenon in which paraphrastic rephrasings produce different LLMaJ judgments. Across a large-scale study spanning diverse evaluation tasks, judge families, and model backbones, we find that these variations can alter evaluation outcomes and, in some settings, reverse relative model rankings. A user study with 10 human annotators shows that LLMaJ judges exhibit 6-9$\times$ larger agreement degradation under prompt rephrasings than humans, falling below the generally accepted threshold in usability studies. This indicates that single-prompt evaluation is insufficiently robust for model ranking. Finally, we show that multi-prompt aggregation substantially improves robustness by emphasizing judgments that remain consistent across prompt variants.

AI.tldr: Paraphrastic rephrasings of a fixed judge prompt can change LLM-as-a-Judge verdicts and, in some settings, reverse model rankings. Aggregating judgments across multiple prompt variants substantially improves robustness.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge work usually assumes that a single judge prompt is a stable evaluation instrument, while prior work has focused on deliberate prompt modifications such as rubrics or chain-of-thought rather than semantically equivalent rephrasings.
AI.method: The authors introduce Prompt Lottery, measuring whether validated paraphrastic rephrasings yield consistent judgments across diverse evaluation tasks, judge families and model backbones. They compare agreement degradation of LLM judges under rephrasing with a user study of 10 human annotators, and then evaluate multi-prompt aggregation.
AI.result: Paraphrases alter evaluation outcomes and, in some settings, reverse relative model rankings. LLM judges show 6-9 times larger agreement degradation under prompt rephrasings than humans, falling below the generally accepted usability-study threshold. Multi-prompt aggregation substantially improves robustness by emphasizing judgments that stay consistent across prompt variants.
AI.conclusion: Single-prompt evaluation is insufficiently robust for model ranking, and aggregating judgments across prompt variants is a practical remedy.

title: ATI-OPD: Adaptive Teacher Intervention for Stable Long-Sequence On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level feedback from a teacher. As responses grow longer, the student's prefix can depart from the teacher's own reasoning, weakening its feedback on later tokens. Updates based on this feedback can reinforce the same deviations in later responses and destabilize training. Prior approaches such as length control and loss reweighting limit learning from problematic responses but leave their prefixes unchanged. Fixed cutoffs can also discard later reasoning. We propose \textbf{Adaptive Teacher Intervention for On-Policy Distillation (ATI-OPD)} to improve subsequent teacher guidance by revising the student's reasoning prefix. ATI-OPD replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher segment, then lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text. To handle renewed disagreement, it excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful student continuation. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.

AI.tldr: ATI-OPD stabilizes long-sequence on-policy distillation by replacing the student's earliest high-disagreement reasoning segment with a short teacher segment and excluding persistently divergent suffixes from the loss. It improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In on-policy distillation, long student responses drift from the teacher's reasoning, which weakens token-level feedback on later tokens and can destabilize training. Length control and loss reweighting leave the prefixes unchanged, and fixed cutoffs can discard useful later reasoning.
AI.method: ATI-OPD replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment of the student's reasoning prefix with a short teacher segment, then lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text. It excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful student continuation.
AI.result: Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes and fewer extremely long responses.
AI.conclusion: Revising the student's reasoning prefix with teacher guidance stabilizes long-sequence distillation and improves accuracy.

title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
summary: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents, proves most of PutnamBench, all six IMO 2026 formalizations, and most of NTP4VC and VERINA without extra training. The paper also introduces Aegis, a harder verification benchmark built from competitive programming problems over real Rust implementations.
AI.motivation: PutnamBench, NTP4VC and VERINA are close to saturation, and hand-written benchmarks do not carry implementation-level obligations such as fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops and casts.
AI.method: EasyProver combines recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing and an elastic elaboration service, using an off-the-shelf frontier model. Aegis converts competitive programming problems into safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation.
AI.result: EasyProver proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations, and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Aegis yields 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement.
AI.conclusion: The Aegis tasks are much harder than saturated benchmarks, can benchmark other provers, and can serve as rewards for reinforcement learning.

title: Component Translation and Judge-Labelled Refusal: A Multilingual Safety Evaluation
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure. Ten-page manuscript prepared for the 4th Workshop on Large Language and Foundation Models (WLLFM 2026) at IEEE BigData 2026, plus appendices A-E. Replication archive included as ancillary files
summary: Whole-prompt translation evaluates a request in different languages but does not compare which component carries a language. We introduce a paired reversal: translate the complete request component or the complete operation component into the same target language, holding behaviour, English frame and translated-span count fixed. Component identity and non-English text quantity change together. Assigning English, Chinese and Spanish independently to the two components yields nine configurations on 190 of 300 sampled harmful behaviours retained after consensus annotation and automatic gating.
