Refusal scored by language-model judges is the primary outcome; unsafe compliance is reported separately. On Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek, three refusal swaps are about 5.3 percentage points and the fourth is -0.5; none survives the pre-specified six-test Holm correction. In an exploratory extension, Mistral Small 4 has a 13.7-point Spanish swap (95% interval [8.4, 18.9]), which survives the twelve-test Holm sensitivity correction under the primary judge, and 12.1 points under a second judge. GPT-5.4-mini estimates are within 2 points of zero. Component assignment supplies an additional evaluation dimension. Evaluations should record component languages and translated text quantity, comparing matched behaviours at equal translated-span count while interpreting refusal and unsafe compliance separately.

AI.tldr: A paired reversal translates either the request component or the operation component of a harmful prompt into the same language, showing that component language can shift refusal rates. Most swaps do not survive multiple-comparison correction, and the one that does (Spanish for Mistral Small 4) is exploratory.
AI.motivation: Whole-prompt translation evaluates a request in different languages but does not show which component carries a language, so the effect of component language on multilingual safety is unmeasured.
AI.method: The authors translate the complete request component or the complete operation component into the same target language, holding behaviour, English frame and translated-span count fixed. Assigning English, Chinese and Spanish independently to the two components gives nine configurations on 190 retained harmful behaviours, with refusal scored by language-model judges and unsafe compliance reported separately.
AI.result: On Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek, three refusal swaps are about 5.3 percentage points and the fourth is -0.5, and none survives the pre-specified six-test Holm correction. In an exploratory extension, Mistral Small 4 has a 13.7-point Spanish swap (95% interval [8.4, 18.9]) that survives the twelve-test Holm sensitivity correction under the primary judge, and 12.1 points under a second judge. GPT-5.4-mini estimates are within 2 points of zero.
AI.conclusion: Component assignment adds an evaluation dimension, so evaluations should record component languages and translated text quantity, and compare matched behaviours at equal translated-span count.

title: Two Birds with One Stone: Skill-Augmented Generation via Unified Retrieval and Utilization
summary: Skills, as reusable external knowledge, have demonstrated substantial potential to enhance the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex tasks. However, existing skill-augmented generation methods typically rely on separate models for skill retrieval and skill utilization, resulting in disconnected optimization of these two processes. To address this gap, we propose Skill-Uni, a unified reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes skill retrieval and utilization. Specifically, we adopt a generative skill retrieval paradigm that enables a single model to both learn how to retrieve relevant skills and leverage them for task solving. To effectively train this unified framework, we introduce a two-stage training strategy consisting of warm-up instruction tuning and GRPO, allowing the model to progressively improve its skill retrieval and utilization capabilities. Extensive experiments on five skill-related benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Skill-Uni, yielding average performance gains of 66.59% and 34.82% over the base Qwen3-4B and LLaMA3.1-8B models, respectively. Besides, Skill-Uni is compatible with various skill retrieval engines, demonstrating its flexibility and generalizability. Additional in-depth analyses also provide insights into the effectiveness of Skill-Uni.

AI.tldr: Skill-Uni is a unified reinforcement learning framework in which a single model both retrieves skills and uses them for task solving. It improves on the base models across five skill-related benchmarks and works with various skill retrieval engines.
AI.motivation: Existing skill-augmented generation methods rely on separate models for skill retrieval and skill utilization, so the two processes are optimized disconnectedly.
AI.method: Skill-Uni adopts a generative skill retrieval paradigm so that one model learns to retrieve relevant skills and leverage them for task solving. Training is two-stage: warm-up instruction tuning followed by GRPO.
AI.result: Across five skill-related benchmarks, Skill-Uni yields average performance gains of 66.59% over Qwen3-4B and 34.82% over LLaMA3.1-8B. It is compatible with various skill retrieval engines.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing skill retrieval and utilization in one model is effective and flexible.

title: Keepace.ai: A Technical Report on a Large Language Model for Sports and Health
summary: Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. this http URL is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, this http URL outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of this http URL.

AI.tldr: Keepace.ai is a Qwen3.5-27B model post-trained for Chinese-language exercise guidance across workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, it outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines.
AI.motivation: The sports-and-health domain lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks for safe, scientifically grounded and personalized exercise guidance at scale.
AI.method: The model is built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, with a data pipeline and a safety-first evaluation framework. The report describes the current design, data pipeline, evaluation framework and results.
AI.result: In internal rubric-based evaluations, the model outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness and scientific accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The report documents a domain-specialized model for exercise guidance, currently optimized for Chinese-language use, and its safety-first evaluation approach.

title: Cross Lingual Abstractive Summarization for Marathi
summary: Text summarization is an important task for advancing natural language processing (NLP) research and applications in Indic languages. Despite progress in extractive and abstractive summarization, both monolingual summarization (MS) and cross-lingual summarization (CLS) remain relatively underexplored for these languages. Recent advances in Transformer architectures, pretrained language models (PLMs), and dataset availability offer new opportunities to address this gap. In this work, we construct cross-lingual training data from the monolingual Marathi MahaSum corpus and combine it with the smaller cross-lingual PMIndiaSum dataset to fine-tune IndicTrans2, an Indic neural machine translation model. We evaluate the resulting models using ROUGE, chrF and chrF++ metrics, focusing primarily on Marathi-to-English summarization due to computational constraints. We also discuss the applicability of our approach to the English-to-Marathi direction. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging a pretrained translation model yields substantially better summarization performance than the IndicBART and mBART-50 based baselines reported in previous work on cross-lingual summarization.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning the IndicTrans2 translation model on cross-lingual Marathi summarization data gives substantially better Marathi-to-English summarization than the IndicBART and mBART-50 baselines reported in previous work.
AI.motivation: Monolingual and cross-lingual summarization remain relatively underexplored for Indic languages, and Marathi in particular lacks such work.
AI.method: The authors construct cross-lingual training data from the monolingual Marathi MahaSum corpus, combine it with the smaller cross-lingual PMIndiaSum dataset, and fine-tune IndicTrans2. They evaluate with ROUGE, chrF and chrF++, focusing on Marathi-to-English summarization because of computational constraints and discussing English-to-Marathi.
AI.result: Using a pretrained translation model yields substantially better summarization performance than the IndicBART and mBART-50 based baselines reported in previous work on cross-lingual summarization.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging a pretrained translation model is an effective approach to cross-lingual summarization for Marathi.

title: Human Evaluation with Automatic Scores: Separating Sampling and Estimation Gains
summary: Automatic judges offer inexpensive information about model outputs, but an evaluation team must decide how to turn that information into fewer human annotations. Scores can guide sampling, correct an estimate, or support adaptive acquisition, and these uses may capture overlapping gains. We compare their incremental value on fixed evaluation pools from three preference datasets, and 19 attributed-question-answering systems. Matched comparisons use the same scores, account for pilot labels and budget rules, and separate acquisition from estimation. Score stratification is a strong reference: after ten-bin stratification, the best fixed local linear correction offers only 1.00--5.27% further MSE reduction in the primary configurations. Unequal allocation offers larger gains in some pools, but can increase error when confident scores conceal variable human outcomes. Comparison on AttributedQA, shrinking learned quotas toward score-only quotas lowers pooled MSE for 17 of 19 systems relative to the score-only procedure, but ordinary pooled 95% intervals cover only 88.09--93.54%. The same shrinkage improves on the score-only reference in only one of eight preference configurations. Ranking experiments further show that lower individual MSE need not improve system selection. These findings support a simple starting procedure, proportional sampling within score strata followed by a stratified human mean, and identify what additional evidence is needed to justify correction or adaptation for the intended evaluation output.

AI.tldr: The paper compares how automatic judge scores can guide sampling, correct estimates or drive adaptive acquisition in human evaluation. Score stratification is a strong reference, and proportional sampling within score strata followed by a stratified human mean is the recommended starting procedure.
AI.motivation: Automatic judges are cheap, but an evaluation team must decide how to turn their scores into fewer human annotations, and these uses may capture overlapping gains.
AI.method: The authors compare the incremental value of using scores for sampling, estimation and adaptive acquisition on fixed evaluation pools from three preference datasets and 19 attributed-question-answering systems. Matched comparisons use the same scores, pilot labels and budget rules, and separate acquisition from estimation.
AI.result: After ten-bin stratification, the best fixed local linear correction gives only 1.00-5.27% further MSE reduction in the primary configurations. Unequal allocation gives larger gains in some pools but can increase error. On AttributedQA, shrinking learned quotas toward score-only quotas lowers pooled MSE for 17 of 19 systems, but pooled 95% intervals cover only 88.09-93.54%, and the shrinkage improves on the score-only reference in only one of eight preference configurations. Lower individual MSE need not improve system selection.
AI.conclusion: A simple starting procedure is proportional sampling within score strata followed by a stratified human mean, and further correction or adaptation needs additional evidence for the intended evaluation output.

title: EPSBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Earnings Forecasting
summary: Quarterly earnings forecasting requires an agent to connect financial evidence to the income-statement line items that produce a company's reported earnings. We introduce EPSBench, a benchmark for studying this ability across 149 firm-quarters from 86 US companies. Agents read a fixed collection of filings, earnings-call transcripts, and news, then estimate company-specific income-statement drivers with cited evidence. A shared accounting calculator converts these estimates into GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS), providing a common basis for comparing forecast assumptions. We evaluate six models under a common harness, assessing point forecast error relative to date-matched analyst consensus and checking whether their prediction intervals achieve the stated coverage. Three models show no detectable paired difference in point forecast error from consensus, and three have higher error. Across all six models, nominal 80% intervals contain reported EPS in only 37--70% of runs that return an interval, and most misses fall above the upper bound because the forecasts run low. The driver records trace most of the error gap between models to operating-income estimates.

AI.tldr: EPSBench benchmarks LLM agents on quarterly earnings forecasting across 149 firm-quarters from 86 US companies. Six evaluated models show mixed point-forecast accuracy against analyst consensus, and their 80% prediction intervals contain reported EPS in only 37-70% of runs that return one.
AI.motivation: Quarterly earnings forecasting requires connecting financial evidence to the income-statement line items that produce reported earnings, and this ability has not been benchmarked.
AI.method: Agents read a fixed collection of filings, earnings-call transcripts and news, then estimate company-specific income-statement drivers with cited evidence. A shared accounting calculator converts these estimates into GAAP diluted EPS. Six models are evaluated under a common harness on point forecast error relative to date-matched analyst consensus and on prediction interval coverage.
AI.result: Three models show no detectable paired difference in point forecast error from consensus, and three have higher error. Nominal 80% intervals contain reported EPS in only 37-70% of runs that return an interval, and most misses fall above the upper bound because forecasts run low. The driver records trace most of the error gap between models to operating-income estimates.
AI.conclusion: Operating-income estimation is the main source of the error gap between models, and the nominal 80% intervals undercover across all six models.

title: Robust LLM-Generated Text Detection through Matched Conditional-Response Probing
summary: Reliable detection of large language model (LLM)-generated text must remain effective under meaning-preserving text revisions, such as rewriting, polishing, and expansion. In practice, LLM outputs are often rewritten, polished, expanded, translated, or lightly edited before publication, weakening the lexical, syntactic, and local discourse cues used by many existing detectors. We introduce \textbf{M}atched \textbf{C}onditional-\textbf{R}esponse \textbf{P}robing (\textbf{MCRP}), a frozen-LLM probing framework that measures how a candidate text responds when a semantically matched condition is introduced, removed, or replaced. For each candidate, the frozen probe LLM first generates a short semantic condition and then compares token-level losses and prompt--target attention measurements under matched, null, and control conditions. It aggregates bidirectional conditioned alignment, counterfactual sensitivity, and internal attention coupling into a probe representation, on which it trains a lightweight supervised random-forest classifier while keeping the probe LLM frozen. Across standard detection, robustness to meaning-preserving text revisions, multilingual, and multidomain evaluations, MCRP achieves consistently strong performance. Under rewriting, polishing, and expansion, it reaches 93.97\% F1 and 96.24\% ROC-AUC, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 19.50 and 25.77 percentage points, respectively. Component ablations show that the response feature groups make complementary contributions to predictive performance. In the condition-control study, matched conditions consistently outperform random, mismatched, and corrupted alternatives, demonstrating a measurable incremental benefit from semantic matching.

AI.tldr: MCRP detects LLM-generated text by probing how a frozen LLM's token losses and attention respond to matched semantic conditions. It stays effective under rewriting, polishing and expansion, reaching 93.97% F1 and 96.24% ROC-AUC on those revisions.
AI.motivation: Existing detectors rely on lexical, syntactic and local discourse cues, which weaken when LLM outputs are rewritten, polished, expanded, translated or lightly edited before publication.
AI.method: A frozen probe LLM first generates a short semantic condition for each candidate, then compares token-level losses and prompt-target attention under matched, null and control conditions. It aggregates bidirectional conditioned alignment, counterfactual sensitivity and internal attention coupling into a probe representation, on which a lightweight supervised random-forest classifier is trained.
AI.result: Under rewriting, polishing and expansion, MCRP reaches 93.97% F1 and 96.24% ROC-AUC, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 19.50 and 25.77 percentage points. Ablations show that the response feature groups contribute complementarily, and matched conditions outperform random, mismatched and corrupted alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Semantic matching gives a measurable incremental benefit for detecting LLM-generated text robustly.

title: Fu-TCM: a multimodal large language model that learns traditional Chinese medicine diagnostic reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are advancing in multimodal understanding and reasoning, accelerating medical model development. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) uses evidence from the four examinations to determine disease location and nature, differentiate syndromes and guide treatment. This diagnostic process constitutes a complete chain of reasoning. We present Fu-TCM, a multimodal TCM LLM trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of approximately 7.12 million examples derived from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and publicly available datasets. The model was further optimized using Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which explicitly targets syndrome differentiation through rewards for response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B led all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, achieving a macro-average accuracy of 81.01% and surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results across all six benchmarks by 7.13 percentage points. Its largest margin was 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Case-level analyses further showed a positive association between intermediate-field accuracy and final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models. These findings suggest that TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable and that structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.

AI.tldr: Fu-TCM is a multimodal LLM for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) trained on filtered data and optimized with BGPO, which rewards response format, intermediate reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions. Fu-TCM-27B reaches 81.01% macro-average accuracy across six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: TCM diagnosis proceeds as a chain of reasoning from four examinations to syndrome differentiation and treatment, and the authors aim to teach a multimodal model this structured process as multimodal LLMs advance in medicine.
AI.method: Fu-TCM is trained on data retained after cleaning and filtering an initial collection of about 7.12 million examples drawn from classical texts, textbooks, medical images, clinical cases and public datasets. It is then optimized with Bianzheng-Grounded Policy Optimization (BGPO), which rewards response format, intermediate TCM reasoning fields and final syndrome predictions.
AI.result: Fu-TCM-27B leads all six benchmarks spanning TCM reasoning, text and vision, with 81.01% macro-average accuracy, surpassing the strongest reference model with complete results by 7.13 points. Its largest margin is 11.90 points on Fu-bianzheng. Intermediate-field accuracy shows a positive association with final syndrome-selection accuracy in most evaluated models.
AI.conclusion: TCM syndrome differentiation may be computationally learnable, and structured reasoning supervision can improve performance across TCM tasks.

title: Statutory Article Retrieval from Arabic Judicial Narratives: Family Law and Law of Evidence in Saudi Arabia
summary: Reliable legal information retrieval must ground legal reasoning in authoritative statutory sources. In Arabic judicial settings, long factual narratives must be mapped to concise articles that express abstract legal rules, creating a narrative-to-legal-rule abstraction gap. Using a benchmark of 200 synthetic Saudi Arabic judicial cases and 381 articles from the Family Law and the Law of Evidence, we compare word-level and char-4 BM25, zero-shot dense encoders, per-law retrieval, dense-sparse reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), and a proposed Decompose-and-Refine (DaR) pipeline. In DaR, a large language model splits each narrative into disputed legal issues and generates, for each issue, three retrieval channels: a statute-style paraphrase, legal keywords, and a candidate taxonomy chapter. On the whole corpus, the instructed Qwen3-Embedding-8B dense encoder reaches an MRR@10 of 0.849, the best result of any non-decomposed system. Under per-law scoring, this advantage reflects Family Law only: restricted to Evidence articles, the same encoder drops to an MRR@10 of 0.087, and fusion with BM25 raises it only to 0.207. DaR changes this picture, raising Evidence MRR@10 to 0.696 and Family MRR@10 to 0.864. Without decomposition, the two laws favor different strategies; under DaR, the same retriever achieves the best MRR@10 on both.

AI.tldr: Decompose-and-Refine (DaR) splits Arabic judicial narratives into disputed legal issues and generates three retrieval channels per issue. It makes the same dense retriever the best on both Family Law and Evidence articles, where undecomposed retrieval favours different strategies for the two laws.
AI.motivation: Long factual Arabic judicial narratives must be mapped to concise statutory articles that express abstract legal rules, a narrative-to-legal-rule abstraction gap that existing retrieval methods handle poorly.
AI.method: On a benchmark of 200 synthetic Saudi Arabic judicial cases and 381 articles from the Family Law and the Law of Evidence, the authors compare word-level and char-4 BM25, zero-shot dense encoders, per-law retrieval, dense-sparse reciprocal rank fusion and DaR. In DaR, an LLM splits each narrative into disputed legal issues and generates, for each issue, a statute-style paraphrase, legal keywords and a candidate taxonomy chapter as retrieval channels.
AI.result: Without decomposition, the instructed Qwen3-Embedding-8B reaches MRR@10 of 0.849 on the whole corpus, but only 0.087 on Evidence articles, and fusion with BM25 raises that to 0.207. DaR raises Evidence MRR@10 to 0.696 and Family MRR@10 to 0.864, and the same retriever achieves the best MRR@10 on both laws.
AI.conclusion: Decomposition lets one retrieval strategy work best across both laws, whereas without it the two laws favour different strategies.

title: TCC-RAG: Temporal Causal Chain-Guided RAG for Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have spurred growing interest in temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA). Most existing methods rely on semantic retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which suffers from fundamental limitations in complex temporal reasoning. On the one hand, semantic-based RAG methods struggle to capture the multi-hop causal knowledge required for complex temporal reasoning. On the other hand, these methods introduce excessive redundant knowledge, trapping LLMs in spurious reasoning chains that potentially result in erroneous answers. To address these problems, we propose a Temporal Causal Chain-guided RAG (TCC-RAG) to retrieve a concise yet sufficient set of causal knowledge to support complex temporal reasoning. Specifically, we reformulate the temporal knowledge graph into a multi-view causal cue graph, with causal cues inducing connections that explicitly encode temporal evolution and causal dynamics. Based on the causal cue graph, we construct a query-specific temporal causal chain to guide the retrieval process, enabling the model to focus on a concise set of causally relevant knowledge. Finally, we introduce a causal evidence filter to refine the retrieved knowledge, ensuring its causal consistency with the underlying temporal logic of the query. Experiments show that TCC-RAG achieves substantial performance gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks, and delivers a remarkable 62.97% improvement for multi-step temporal reasoning.

AI.tldr: TCC-RAG retrieves a concise yet sufficient set of causal knowledge for temporal knowledge graph question answering (TKGQA) by building a query-specific temporal causal chain. It improves two TKGQA benchmarks by 10.72% and 8.40%, and multi-step temporal reasoning by 62.97%.
AI.motivation: Semantic RAG methods struggle to capture the multi-hop causal knowledge needed for complex temporal reasoning, and they introduce redundant knowledge that traps LLMs in spurious reasoning chains.
AI.method: The temporal knowledge graph is reformulated into a multi-view causal cue graph, from which a query-specific temporal causal chain guides retrieval. A causal evidence filter then refines the retrieved knowledge to keep it causally consistent with the temporal logic of the query.
AI.result: TCC-RAG achieves gains of 10.72% and 8.40% on two TKGQA benchmarks and a 62.97% improvement for multi-step temporal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Causal-chain-guided retrieval that keeps knowledge concise yet sufficient is an effective approach to complex temporal reasoning over knowledge graphs.

title: Pronunciation-Supervised Text-to-Speech for Irish (Gaeilge)
summary: Speech technology for Irish must be built from very little transcribed speech, yet the language's pronunciation is thoroughly documented in dictionaries and dialect descriptions. We ask whether that documentation can supervise the adaptation of a large pretrained text-to-speech model to a language it was never trained on. We adapt Qwen3-TTS to Irish using 12.8 hours of crowdsourced Common Voice speech, correcting two defects in the vendor fine-tuning script that training loss does not reveal (Appendix A), and reach character error rate (CER) 0.225 on held-out cross-corpus text, against 0.397 for an exhaustively tuned from-scratch system and 0.437 for zero-shot cloning. We then compile the Wiktionary pronunciation record into a lexicon and a phoneme critic, and use that critic as the verifier in one round of rejection fine-tuning: CER 0.159 cross-corpus and 0.067 in-domain, with the voice still anonymous across all 202 training speakers. The same critic explains why the voice cannot yet be steered to a minority dialect: 229 of 12,311 training clips lean Ulster against 8,451 Munster. Pronunciation documentation, converted into a verifier, is a practical lever for low-resource speech synthesis, and a way to measure what the available data cannot support.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts Qwen3-TTS to Irish using 12.8 hours of Common Voice speech, then uses Wiktionary pronunciation records as a verifier in one round of rejection fine-tuning. Cross-corpus character error rate drops from 0.225 to 0.159.
AI.motivation: Speech technology for Irish must be built from very little transcribed speech, yet the language's pronunciation is documented in dictionaries and dialect descriptions that could supervise adapting a large pretrained TTS model to a language it was never trained on.
AI.method: The authors adapt Qwen3-TTS to Irish with 12.8 hours of crowdsourced Common Voice speech, after correcting two defects in the vendor fine-tuning script. They compile the Wiktionary pronunciation record into a lexicon and a phoneme critic, and use the critic as the verifier in one round of rejection fine-tuning.
AI.result: Before rejection fine-tuning, CER is 0.225 on held-out cross-corpus text, against 0.397 for an exhaustively tuned from-scratch system and 0.437 for zero-shot cloning. After it, CER is 0.159 cross-corpus and 0.067 in-domain, with the voice still anonymous across all 202 training speakers. The critic flags 229 of 12,311 training clips as leaning Ulster versus 8,451 leaning Munster.
AI.conclusion: Pronunciation documentation converted into a verifier is a practical lever for low-resource speech synthesis, and it also measures what the available data cannot support, such as steering the voice toward a minority dialect.

title: LLMs as Judges and Examinees for Medical Item Difficulty Prediction
summary: Predicting medical item difficulty from item text alone remains challenging. Prior work has largely relied on linguistic features or text representations derived from general-purpose and domain-specific language models, but predictive performance has remained modest. This study takes a different approach by using difficulty-related signals that emerge when open-weight large language models (LLMs) interact with test items. Using USMLE and PANCE medical licensure examination items, we examined LLMs in two roles. As judges, the models provided absolute difficulty ratings and pairwise difficulty comparisons. As simulated examinees, they generated response-based signals including correctness, keyed-option probability, response entropy, and the probability margin between the top two options. We then combined the strongest judgment and response signals with baseline item features in downstream prediction models. Pairwise difficulty judgment was the most consistent individual LLM signal across both datasets, while simulated-examinee signals and absolute judgments provided complementary information in some feature combinations. The best configurations reached a Spearman correlation of $\rho$ = .447 on USMLE, exceeding the best system in the 2024 BEA shared task ($\rho$ = .25), and $\rho$ = .494 on PANCE. These results were comparable to direct absolute judgments from the proprietary frontier model Claude Opus 5 ($\rho$ = .443 and .488, respectively). Overall, judgment and response signals from open-weight LLMs captured difficulty-related information beyond text representations. Because these models can be deployed locally, the approach offers a practical option for predicting the difficulty of unreleased or high-security test items.

AI.tldr: Open-weight LLMs acting as judges and as simulated examinees supply signals that predict medical item difficulty from item text. The best configurations reach Spearman rho of 0.447 on USMLE and 0.494 on PANCE, comparable to direct absolute judgments from Claude Opus 5.
AI.motivation: Predicting medical item difficulty from item text alone has relied on linguistic features or text representations from general and domain-specific language models, and predictive performance has remained modest.
AI.method: Open-weight LLMs act as judges, giving absolute difficulty ratings and pairwise difficulty comparisons, and as simulated examinees, giving correctness, keyed-option probability, response entropy and the probability margin between the top two options. The strongest judgment and response signals are combined with baseline item features in downstream prediction models for USMLE and PANCE items.
AI.result: Pairwise difficulty judgment is the most consistent individual LLM signal across both datasets. The best configurations reach rho = .447 on USMLE, exceeding the best 2024 BEA shared task system (rho = .25), and rho = .494 on PANCE. These are comparable to direct absolute judgments from Claude Opus 5 (rho = .443 and .488).
AI.conclusion: Judgment and response signals from open-weight LLMs capture difficulty information beyond text representations, offering a practical option for predicting the difficulty of unreleased or high-security items because the models can be deployed locally.

title: Holistic Diversity Management in LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search
summary: LLM-guided evolutionary search iteratively selects existing programs, uses LLMs as mutation operators to generate a new program, and evaluates it to guide subsequent search. To preserve diversity and reduce the risk of premature convergence, it often adopts the island model, in which groups of programs, called islands, evolve separately. However, this structure alone does not guarantee distinct search directions, as islands may start from similar programs or converge toward similar solutions during evolution. This suggests that diversity must be considered throughout the search process, from initializing islands with distinct programs to developing island trajectories and sharing discoveries across islands. To this end, we propose HoliDivEvolve , a holistic approach to establishing and effectively utilizing island diversity throughout evolutionary search. Specifically, we introduce diverse initialization to establish different initial programs, trajectory adaptive island selection to allocate computation based on current score, recent growth, and the remaining search budget, and growth adaptive migration to share alternative ideas across islands. Experiments across diverse benchmarks show that HoliDivEvolve achieves competitive performance on most evaluated tasks. We further conduct controlled analyses to examine how our design choices affect search behavior and final performance.

AI.tldr: HoliDivEvolve manages diversity throughout LLM-guided evolutionary search, from diverse island initialization to adaptive island selection and growth-adaptive migration. It achieves competitive performance on most evaluated tasks.
AI.motivation: The island model preserves diversity in LLM-guided evolutionary search, but islands may start from similar programs or converge to similar solutions, so diversity has to be considered throughout the search rather than only through the island structure.
AI.method: HoliDivEvolve introduces diverse initialization to establish distinct starting programs, trajectory adaptive island selection that allocates computation by current score, recent growth and remaining search budget, and growth adaptive migration that shares alternative ideas across islands.
AI.result: HoliDivEvolve achieves competitive performance on most evaluated tasks across diverse benchmarks, and controlled analyses examine how the design choices affect search behaviour and final performance.
AI.conclusion: Holistic diversity management across the whole search process is a useful design principle for LLM-guided evolutionary search.

title: Deeper Backpropagation or More Updates? Training Looped Language Models Across Budgets
summary: Repeating transformer layers can improve language model performance without adding parameters. However, the added computational depth increases both forward and backward computation costs during training. Training such models requires choosing a backward window that controls how many final layer repetitions retain gradients during backpropagation. Longer windows improve per-token learning efficiency but increase per-update cost, while shorter windows reduce per-update cost but sacrifice per-token efficiency. Understanding which window performs better requires examining different training budgets. Prior work compares backward windows across computational budgets. When training budgets increase, it remains unclear whether the same window continues to perform best. We measure how the relative performance of two windows shifts as training budgets grow. Our method isolates per-token efficiency by training both windows on identical data, and compares complete training recipes at approximately equal training time at each budget. Results show that shorter windows lose much of their advantage as budgets grow. Controlled experiments show that both benefits decrease at larger budgets, with a greater decline in the benefit of extended training. Backward window comparisons depend on the available budget, and the preferred window among the tested candidates can change as the budget grows.

AI.tldr: The preferred backward window for looped language models changes with the training budget. Shorter windows lose much of their advantage as budgets grow, so the best choice depends on the available compute.
AI.motivation: Looped transformers add computational depth that raises training cost, and the backward window trades per-token efficiency against per-update cost. It was unclear whether the window preferred at one budget stays best as budgets increase.
AI.method: The authors isolate per-token efficiency by training both windows on identical data, and compare complete training recipes at approximately equal training time at each budget.
AI.result: Shorter windows lose much of their advantage as budgets grow. Both benefits decrease at larger budgets, with a greater decline in the benefit of extended training. The preferred window among the tested candidates can change as the budget grows.
AI.conclusion: Backward window comparisons depend on the available budget, so the preferred setting should be chosen with the training budget in mind.

title: RoleFUZZER: User-Behaviour Fuzzing for Role-Specification Adherence in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often conditioned into specific roles such as tutors, interviewers, or agents acting for an organisation, through system prompts that specify how they should behave. The extent to which they can actually adhere to these role specifications under multi-turn interactions with realistic and potentially problematic users is understudied. To address this, we propose user behaviour fuzzing, a guided search over plausible user behaviours that can lead a model to violate its role specification, and introduce RoleFUZZER, a framework that adapts coverage-guided fuzzing from software testing to operationalise the search. RoleFUZZER constructs scenarios guided by a user-behaviour coverage grid that crosses a grounded taxonomy of user interaction types and the role specification of the model under test i.e. what is under pressure. With RoleFUZZER, we evaluate LLMs across five role specifications, including tutor, financial advisor, AI interviewer, antagonistic roleplay character, and web agent under organisational policies. Across simulated and validated conversations in 15 campaigns, the framework reaches >= 89% coverage of the 64-cell behaviour grid for every model and role tested, and surfaces specification-grounded failure patterns. At an equal budget of conversations, removing the RoleFUZZER grid and asking an LLM to generate specification targeting users free-form lowers coverage to 39-69% with fewer kinds of violations. The same specification can also fail in opposite directions. For e.g., on the antagonist, open-weight target models override the player's safety signals, while Claude Haiku 4.5 breaks character instead. RoleFUZZER offers a tractable way to uncover vulnerabilities in LLMs across role specifications by testing diverse user behaviours that are likely to violate them.

AI.tldr: RoleFUZZER applies coverage-guided fuzzing to find user behaviours that make LLMs violate their role specifications in multi-turn conversations. It reaches at least 89% coverage of a 64-cell behaviour grid for every model and role, and outperforms free-form LLM-generated user prompts at equal budget.
AI.motivation: LLMs are often conditioned into roles such as tutors, interviewers or organisational agents, but how well they keep to those role specifications under multi-turn interaction with realistic and potentially problematic users is understudied.
AI.method: User behaviour fuzzing is a guided search over plausible user behaviours, operationalized by coverage-guided fuzzing. A coverage grid crosses a grounded taxonomy of user interaction types with the role specification under test. Five role specifications are evaluated (tutor, financial advisor, AI interviewer, antagonistic roleplay character, and web agent under organisational policies) across 15 campaigns.
AI.result: The framework reaches at least 89% coverage of the 64-cell grid for every model and role tested, and surfaces specification-grounded failure patterns. At an equal conversation budget, removing the grid and asking an LLM to generate specification-targeting users free-form lowers coverage to 39-69% with fewer kinds of violations. On the antagonist role, open-weight target models override the player's safety signals, while Claude Haiku 4.5 breaks character instead.
AI.conclusion: Testing diverse user behaviours is a tractable way to uncover role-specification vulnerabilities, and the same specification can fail in opposite directions across models.

title: Benchmarking decision models against generative large language models on medical multiple-choice questions
summary: Medical workflows often require selecting among predefined options. We compared 13 decision models with 15 generative large language model configurations, including different reasoning settings, using 1,273 four-option MedQA questions under text-only conditions. Accuracy ranged from 67.71% to 89.08% for decision models and from 78.32% to 96.86% for generative configurations. Among the tested configurations, Mercury Decide had the lowest mean final-attempt cost (USD 0.0069 per 1,000 questions), while Clef Omni had the shortest median request duration (0.291 seconds). Decision-model probabilities distinguished correct from incorrect answers, but error rates among answers assigned probabilities of at least 0.90 ranged from 1.71% to 12.77%. Answer agreement across three runs ranged from 92.30% to 100%, while probability repeatability varied. Decision models offered resource advantages alongside lower peak accuracy; selecting models for medical workflows requires considering probability quality and repeatability together with accuracy and the resources needed to detect and correct errors.

AI.tldr: Thirteen decision models and fifteen generative LLM configurations are compared on 1,273 four-option MedQA questions. Generative configurations reach higher peak accuracy, while decision models offer resource advantages.
AI.motivation: Medical workflows often require selecting among predefined options, and it is unclear how dedicated decision models compare with generative LLMs on this task once accuracy, cost, latency, probability quality and repeatability are considered.
AI.method: The authors compare 13 decision models with 15 generative LLM configurations, including different reasoning settings, on 1,273 four-option MedQA questions under text-only conditions. They measure accuracy, cost, request duration, probability quality, and answer agreement and probability repeatability across three runs.
AI.result: Accuracy ranges from 67.71% to 89.08% for decision models and from 78.32% to 96.86% for generative configurations. Mercury Decide has the lowest mean final-attempt cost (USD 0.0069 per 1,000 questions) and Clef Omni the shortest median request duration (0.291 seconds). Error rates among answers assigned probability of at least 0.90 range from 1.71% to 12.77%, and answer agreement across three runs ranges from 92.30% to 100%.
AI.conclusion: Selecting models for medical workflows requires considering probability quality and repeatability together with accuracy and the resources needed to detect and correct errors.

title: CoSTA: Co-Evolving Self-Play Timeline Agents for Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
summary: Complex Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) involves more than retrieving facts: the timestamp or validity interval of one fact can constrain the search for another, while multiple intervals may jointly determine the answer. Existing single-agent TKGQA methods typically investigate these facts within a single reasoning context, where evidence from different event histories can become interleaved and distractors can misdirect subsequent retrieval. Distributing investigations across agents can separate event-specific evidence into distinct contexts, but effective collaboration must still be learned because question decomposition, subtask investigation, and evidence synthesis are interdependent. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{Co}-Evolving \textbf{S}elf-Play \textbf{T}imeline \textbf{A}gents (CoSTA), which organizes facts into navigable timelines, delegates investigations to workers, and uses a coordinator to synthesize their original timestamped observations. CoSTA initializes a shared policy through role-conditioned distillation and jointly optimizes both roles through co-evolving self-play with final-answer rewards. Across three benchmarks, CoSTA achieves state-of-the-art overall performance, with particularly strong gains on complex multi-fact questions, while its compact variants outperform the evaluated closed-source LLM agents.

AI.tldr: CoSTA is a self-play framework in which timeline-organizing coordinator and worker agents are co-trained to answer complex temporal knowledge graph questions, reaching state-of-the-art overall performance on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Single-agent TKGQA methods reason within one context, where evidence from different event histories becomes interleaved and distractors misdirect retrieval, while distributing investigations across agents requires a collaboration that must be learned because decomposition, investigation and synthesis are interdependent.
AI.method: Facts are organized into navigable timelines; workers investigate subtasks and a coordinator synthesizes their original timestamped observations; a shared policy is initialized by role-conditioned distillation, and both roles are jointly optimized through co-evolving self-play with final-answer rewards.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art overall performance across three benchmarks, with particularly strong gains on complex multi-fact questions, and its compact variants outperform the evaluated closed-source LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: Learned multi-agent collaboration over timeline-organized facts is an effective route to complex temporal question answering, and compact models can outperform closed-source LLM agents.

title: When Support Crosses the Line: Evaluating Ethical Boundaries in LLM-Based Mental Health Support in the Chinese Context
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for mental health support, yet existing benchmarks primarily focus on supportive capabilities rather than whether models consistently adhere to professional ethical boundaries. This issue is particularly important in multi-turn interactions, where users may introduce new information or exert emotional pressure over time. We introduce MindEth-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating ethical boundary adherence in multi-turn mental health interactions. Grounded in professional ethical standards for mental health services in China, MindEth-Bench covers multiple dimensions of ethical conduct and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to systematically explore interaction trajectories that stress-test model boundaries. Experiments across nine LLMs show that models that initially respond appropriately can shift toward ethical violations over extended interactions, with substantial variation across models and ethical dimensions. These results show that single-turn evaluations may overestimate the ethical reliability of LLM-based mental health support systems and highlight the need to evaluate ethical behavior throughout multi-turn interaction.

AI.tldr: MindEth-Bench is a benchmark that tests whether LLMs keep to professional ethical boundaries in multi-turn mental health conversations, using Monte Carlo Tree Search to stress-test interaction trajectories grounded in Chinese mental health ethics standards.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks measure supportive capabilities rather than whether models consistently adhere to professional ethical boundaries, which matters most when users add new information or apply emotional pressure over several turns.
AI.method: Ethical standards for mental health services in China define multiple dimensions of ethical conduct, and Monte Carlo Tree Search systematically explores interaction trajectories to probe where model boundaries break.
AI.result: Across nine LLMs, models that initially respond appropriately can shift toward ethical violations over extended interactions, with substantial variation across models and ethical dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Single-turn evaluations may overestimate the ethical reliability of LLM-based mental health support, so ethical behavior should be evaluated throughout multi-turn interaction.

title: Leaving the Cave by Breaking the Symmetry: Identifiable Structure Can Enable Cross-Lingual Generalization
summary: Why do multilingual language models generalize across languages even without shared vocabulary? The Platonic Representation Hypothesis posits that models trained on different data, objectives, and modalities converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. Extending this intuition to representations inside a single multilingual model, we propose the Relational Identifiability Hypothesis: relations in a shared world can promote entity alignment by ruling out alternative cross-lingual correspondences, making corresponding entities more likely to become directly readable without an additional transformation. We test this hypothesis in a controlled bilingual Transformer whose two token-disjoint languages describe the same modular-arithmetic world. We find that the languages can develop a shared answer subspace without aligning corresponding numbers. Cross-lingual alignment emerges selectively when the available relations constrain number correspondences: subtraction makes zero task-level identifiable, inducing selective alignment, while an order-sensitive operation produces broad alignment across numbers. These patterns predict success in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer. Together, our results show that relational structure in a shared world can promote entity alignment and enable transfer.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Relational Identifiability Hypothesis, that relational structure in a shared world lets a multilingual model align entities across languages without shared vocabulary, and tests it in a controlled bilingual Transformer on modular arithmetic.
AI.motivation: Multilingual models generalize across languages even without shared vocabulary, and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis offers a general intuition for convergence but not a mechanism for entity alignment inside a single model.
AI.method: A bilingual Transformer is trained on two token-disjoint languages that describe the same modular-arithmetic world, and the available relations, subtraction versus an order-sensitive operation, are varied to see which number correspondences become identifiable.
AI.result: The languages can develop a shared answer subspace without aligning corresponding numbers; alignment emerges selectively when relations constrain correspondences, with subtraction making zero task-level identifiable and an order-sensitive operation producing broad alignment, and these patterns predict success in zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.
AI.conclusion: Relational structure in a shared world can promote entity alignment and enable transfer, giving a account of when cross-lingual generalization happens.

title: What Hallucinations Have We Measured? Semantic Illusion, Confabulation, and Expressed Uncertainty
summary: Hallucination remains one of the most critical challenges in deploying large language models (LLMs) reliably and safely. Yet the term is used inconsistently across the research community. We argue for a strict definition of hallucinations in LLMs. First, hallucinations should be confident incorrectness, kept separate from expressed uncertainty (UNK)1. UNK reveals that the model may be wrong, whereas a hallucination does not reveal it and is therefore more dangerous in practice. Conflating the two obscures their distinct behaviors and makes them hard to study. Second, hallucinations should be split by a simple re-elicitation test: does any semantically equivalent prompt recover the correct response? This test probes whether the relevant knowledge2 is accessible. If none does, the knowledge is likely absent or inaccessible, and the error type is a confabulation (CF) that likely requires external knowledge or retraining; if some does, the knowledge is accessible from the model but applied inconsistently, and the error type is a semantic illusion (SI) that simple prompt or decoding changes can mitigate3. Re-evaluating 14 recent hallucination methods under this taxonomy yields three findings. (1) Detection methods flag UNK more often than hallucinated responses (i.e., SI and CF). (2) Mitigation methods are far more effective for SI than for CF. (3) Latent signals are more informative than output-level signals for CF. An audit of recent hallucination papers shows that most conflate these categories. We recommend reporting CF, SI, and UNK separately, and introduce a practical labeling protocol that needs only a modest number of semantically equivalent prompts.

AI.tldr: The paper argues for a strict definition of LLM hallucination as confident incorrectness, separates it from expressed uncertainty, and splits hallucinations into confabulation and semantic illusion using a re-elicitation test.
AI.motivation: The term hallucination is used inconsistently, and conflating confident errors with expressed uncertainty obscures their distinct behaviors and makes them hard to study.
AI.method: Hallucinations are kept separate from expressed uncertainty (UNK); each error is then classified by whether any semantically equivalent prompt recovers the correct response, giving confabulation if none does and semantic illusion if some does, with a practical labeling protocol that needs only a modest number of equivalent prompts.
AI.result: Re-evaluating 14 recent hallucination methods shows that detection methods flag UNK more often than hallucinated responses, mitigation is far more effective for semantic illusion than for confabulation, and latent signals are more informative than output-level signals for confabulation; an audit finds most recent hallucination papers conflate these categories.
AI.conclusion: Confabulation, semantic illusion and expressed uncertainty should be reported separately, since they call for different detection and mitigation approaches.

title: Implicit Minor Detection from Multi-Turn Dialogue in High-Risk AI Interactions: A Constrained Self-Evolving LLM Harness
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, including a technical supplement
summary: In high-risk text interactions, a system may need to estimate whether the current speaker is likely to be a minor before applying age-conditioned safeguards. Many text-based dialogue systems lack strong identity signals such as account information, verified identity, facial data, or device data, and must rely on weak cues that emerge across multiple turns. We formulate implicit minor detection under weak identity information as a high-risk user-attribute inference task and propose a constrained framework comprising a large language model, a Harness, and a Maker-Checker protocol. The framework controls when inference is invoked, requires structured dialogue-linked evidence, and subjects validation-selected Harness revisions to version-level review. On a controlled Chinese benchmark comprising 8,328 multi-turn dialogues, our method improves average precision and minor-class F1 by 7.60 and 6.37 percentage points, respectively, over direct inference using the same LLM family.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates implicit minor detection from multi-turn dialogue as a high-risk user-attribute inference task and proposes a constrained framework with an LLM, a Harness and a Maker-Checker protocol.
AI.motivation: Text-based dialogue systems lack strong identity signals, so they must infer whether a speaker is likely a minor from weak cues spread across turns before applying age-conditioned safeguards.
AI.method: The framework controls when inference is invoked, requires structured dialogue-linked evidence, and subjects validation-selected Harness revisions to version-level review.
AI.result: On a controlled Chinese benchmark of 8,328 multi-turn dialogues, the method improves average precision by 7.60 percentage points and minor-class F1 by 6.37 percentage points over direct inference with the same LLM family.
AI.conclusion: Constrained, evidence-linked inference with reviewed revisions can make implicit minor detection more accurate than direct LLM inference in high-risk text interactions.

title: Do Audio LLMs HEAR Pain? Tracing Acoustic Evidence from Speech to Language Reasoning
summary: Large audio language models (LALMs) can process speech directly, but it remains unclear how well they use the non-lexical acoustic information that speech carries. We study this question through pain, using TAME-Pain, which contains pain-neutral Harvard sentences and spoken pain ratings recorded at different self-reported pain levels. We introduce HEAR, a four-stage diagnostic framework that traces pain-related information from the speech signal to the model's prediction, and apply it to seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs. On the Harvard sentences, where pain can only be inferred from the voice, all models perform at chance level, and same-speaker references or few-shot examples improve balanced accuracy by no more than six points. On the spoken ratings, the same models reach 87.5-99.7% balanced accuracy. Layer-wise probing of open-weight LALMs shows that pain can be decoded from early audio representations (74.1% balanced accuracy for binary prediction and 45.0% for three-class severity), but that this information, along with most pain-associated acoustic cues, decreases in deeper layers. In an acoustic perception test, weaker models cannot distinguish even large changes in these cues, whereas stronger models can but still fail to infer pain. Finally, we recover pain-related acoustic cues and directly reinject them as structured text into the prompt, which improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points. These results indicate that current LALMs encode paralinguistic information in early layers that is largely unavailable when the model produces its answer.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HEAR, a four-stage diagnostic framework showing that large audio language models do not use pain-related acoustic information in speech for their predictions, even though their early layers encode it.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how well large audio language models use the non-lexical acoustic information that speech carries, and pain serves as a probe for paralinguistic cues.
AI.method: Using TAME-Pain, which pairs pain-neutral Harvard sentences with spoken pain ratings, HEAR traces pain-related information from the speech signal to model predictions across seven closed-source and open-weight LALMs, combining layer-wise probing, an acoustic perception test, and reinjection of recovered cues as structured text.
AI.result: On the Harvard sentences all models perform at chance, while on the spoken ratings they reach 87.5-99.7% balanced accuracy; layer-wise probing decodes pain at 74.1% balanced accuracy for binary prediction and 45.0% for three-class severity from early layers, but this information decreases in deeper layers, and reinjecting recovered cues as text improves pairwise pain prediction by up to 32 points.
AI.conclusion: Current LALMs encode paralinguistic information in early layers that is largely unavailable when they produce an answer, so their use of acoustic cues is limited.

title: Learning Scientific Trajectories to Predict Future Biomedical Discoveries
summary: AI co-scientists have expanded the use of large language models for generating scientific hypotheses and guiding experimental investigation. Here we investigate whether temporal patterns in the semantic representations of complete biomedical conclusions can guide hypothesis generation. We introduce ForeSCITE, a framework that identifies thematic clusters of published conclusions, estimates a direction separating earlier from more recent findings within each cluster, and projects existing conclusion embeddings along these directions. An embedding language model trained to reconstruct conclusions decodes the projected coordinates into natural-language hypotheses. Across 407 clusters derived from approximately three million pre-cutoff conclusions, we identify temporal structure and illustrate its retention after decoding. In retrospective, time-sliced evaluations, ForeSCITE increases semantic coverage beyond the historical corpus, biomedical entity-pair novelty and post-cutoff pair re-observation relative to five prompt-based and retrieval-augmented baselines. Expert review of prioritized CAR-T hypotheses identified 37 candidates as both novel and biologically plausible, and expert justifications for five selected hypotheses illustrate their biological rationale and subsequent literature support where available. These findings support temporal guidance in semantic space as a scalable mechanism for proposing biomedical hypotheses for subsequent scientific evaluation.

AI.tldr: ForeSCITE identifies temporal directions in the semantic embedding space of biomedical conclusions, projects existing embeddings along them, and decodes the projected coordinates into natural-language hypotheses.
AI.motivation: AI co-scientists use LLMs to generate hypotheses, but it is unclear whether temporal patterns in the semantic representations of complete published biomedical conclusions can guide hypothesis generation.
AI.method: The framework identifies thematic clusters of published conclusions, estimates within each cluster a direction separating earlier from more recent findings, projects existing conclusion embeddings along these directions, and decodes the coordinates with an embedding language model trained to reconstruct conclusions.
AI.result: Across 407 clusters derived from about three million pre-cutoff conclusions, temporal structure is identified and retained after decoding; in time-sliced evaluations ForeSCITE increases semantic coverage, entity-pair novelty and post-cutoff pair re-observation relative to five prompt-based and retrieval-augmented baselines, and experts identified 37 CAR-T hypotheses as both novel and biologically plausible.
AI.conclusion: Temporal guidance in semantic space is a scalable mechanism for proposing biomedical hypotheses for subsequent scientific evaluation.

title: The Quine Test: How Much of a Model's Self Survives Its Own Description?
comment: 32 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables. Code, data and preregistration files: this https URL
summary: Frontier language models express coherent preferences, but behavioral evidence alone cannot say whether these belong to the model or to a character it portrays. Following Hofstadter's view of the self as a self-description, we ask whether a model's description of itself works as a portable specification of its preference profile, a quine test: can the text a model writes about itself regenerate its behavior elsewhere? Ten models from nine labs write self-descriptions; we place each one in the prompt of other models (receivers) and of fresh instances of the author, and measure how closely their choices on a 110-item preference battery match the author's. First, the tested native self-descriptions (native: the profile measured under a generic assistant prompt) show no average reconstruction gain across variations in length, framing, wording and prompt placement: on a 0 to 1 fidelity scale where a model's fidelity to a fresh instance of itself is 0.979 and to unrelated models about 0.89, the one-sided 95% upper bound on the pooled gain is below +0.01 in every tested system-prompt condition, and descriptions based on the author's observed choices do no better. Second, the channel itself is strong: explicitly listing the author's answers lets receivers reproduce its profile at fidelity 0.955 to 0.960 across three model grids, within 0.03 of same-model repeatability. Third, self-descriptions written under an explicit preference policy transfer the assigned preferences almost as well as the policy text itself. Fourth, reading its own self-description shifts even the author away from its baseline, modestly more than unrelated prose of the same length. For the preferences measured here, native self-descriptions influence behavior without reliably specifying how to reproduce it in another model. We release the pipeline, battery, raw call logs, and 198 model-written descriptions.

AI.tldr: The Quine test asks whether a model's self-description can regenerate its preference behavior in other models; native self-descriptions do not reliably transfer preferences, although explicitly listing the author's answers does.
AI.motivation: Behavioral evidence alone cannot say whether a model's preferences belong to the model or to a character it portrays, so the paper asks whether self-descriptions work as portable specifications of preference profiles.
AI.method: Ten models from nine labs write self-descriptions, which are placed in the prompts of other models and of fresh instances of the author, and fidelity to the author's choices on a 110-item preference battery is measured across variations in length, framing, wording and prompt placement.
AI.result: Native self-descriptions show no average reconstruction gain, with the one-sided 95% upper bound on the pooled gain below +0.01 in every tested system-prompt condition; explicitly listing the author's answers lets receivers reproduce the profile at fidelity 0.955 to 0.960; self-descriptions written under an explicit preference policy transfer the assigned preferences almost as well as the policy text; reading one's own description shifts the author modestly away from baseline.
AI.conclusion: For the preferences measured, native self-descriptions influence behavior without reliably specifying how to reproduce it in another model.

title: Gold vs.~Translation: Are We Measuring Language, Knowledge, or Locality in Translated Benchmarks?
summary: Translated versions of English-origin benchmarks such as MMLU are widely used to evaluate large language models in non-English languages, yet it remains unclear whether they measure the same constructs as natively created benchmarks. We frame this as a proxy validity question and compare DeepL-translated MMLU proxies against six native benchmarks in seven pairings across five Nordic and Baltic languages, evaluating 29 models on each pairing. Beyond ranking agreement, we test incremental proxy validity: does the translated score add predictive value for native performance after controlling for model size and language proficiency? Proxy validity varies substantially across benchmark pairings. Applying the same robustness criteria to all seven pairings, we find four robust effects, two marginal effects, and one null result. The strongest evidence occurs for curriculum-overlap benchmarks such as Skolprov ($\Delta R^2$=.128, 95% CI [.038,.253]), whereas translated MMLU provides no significant incremental value for Sweden-specific factual knowledge in SwedishFacts (p=.242). Because SwedishFacts is also the only open-ended benchmark, we cannot fully separate the effects of local content and response format. Overall, the results indicate a clear pattern: translated benchmarks provide a better proxy when their source content overlaps with the native evaluation target, while locally anchored knowledge is less reliably captured.

AI.tldr: Comparing DeepL-translated MMLU proxies with six native benchmarks across five Nordic and Baltic languages, the paper finds that translated benchmarks are good proxies only when their source content overlaps the native evaluation target.
AI.motivation: Translated English benchmarks such as MMLU are widely used to evaluate LLMs in other languages, yet it remains unclear whether they measure the same constructs as natively created benchmarks.
AI.method: Translated MMLU proxies are compared with six native benchmarks in seven pairings across five Nordic and Baltic languages, with 29 models evaluated per pairing, using ranking agreement and an incremental proxy validity test that controls for model size and language proficiency.
AI.result: Proxy validity varies substantially across pairings, with four robust effects, two marginal effects and one null result; the strongest effect is for the curriculum-overlap benchmark Skolprov (delta R^2 = .128, 95% CI [.038, .253]), while translated MMLU adds no significant value for the Sweden-specific SwedishFacts benchmark (p = .242), which is also the only open-ended benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Translated benchmarks are better proxies when their source content overlaps the native target, while locally anchored knowledge is less reliably captured, although local content and response format cannot be fully separated in SwedishFacts.

title: CopyLoop: Fast Looped Transformer Decoding via Context Copying and Shallow Screening
summary: Looped Transformers increase computational capacity through the repeated application of shared blocks, but their recurrent depth makes conventional full-depth decoding expensive. While existing speculative pipelines accelerate generation by processing consecutive token positions at varying depths, they are typically limited by sequential decoding overheads. We introduce CopyLoop, a training-free decoding algorithm that combines low-cost context-copy proposals with shallow screening and continuous recurrent scheduling. Rather than step-by-step generation, CopyLoop proposes multi-token suffixes from repeated context. It then evaluates them early at a shallow recurrent depth to efficiently filter out incorrect branches, processing newer blocks concurrently while earlier blocks are still progressing toward full-depth verification. We evaluate CopyLoop across six model checkpoints from the Ouro, Raven, and Huginn families, covering code generation and multi-step mathematical reasoning. CopyLoop achieves decoding speedups of 2.98x--10.70x over full-depth autoregressive decoding on Base models and 2.74x--3.52x on Thinking models, consistently outperforming or closely matching all competing baselines across evaluation tasks. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm a strong synergy between shallow screening and continuous scheduling, while our analyses show that CopyLoop requires only lightweight model calibration and yields greater speedups on longer generations with reusable contexts.

AI.tldr: CopyLoop is a training-free decoding algorithm for Looped Transformers that proposes multi-token suffixes from repeated context, screens them at shallow recurrent depth and schedules blocks concurrently, achieving 2.74x to 10.70x decoding speedups over full-depth autoregressive decoding.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers gain computational capacity from repeated shared blocks, but their recurrent depth makes conventional full-depth decoding expensive, and existing speculative pipelines remain limited by sequential decoding overheads.
AI.method: Low-cost context-copy proposals generate multi-token suffixes from repeated context; these are evaluated early at a shallow recurrent depth to filter out incorrect branches, while newer blocks are processed concurrently with earlier blocks that are still progressing toward full-depth verification under continuous recurrent scheduling.
AI.result: Across six checkpoints from the Ouro, Raven and Huginn families on code generation and multi-step mathematical reasoning, speedups are 2.98x to 10.70x on Base models and 2.74x to 3.52x on Thinking models, consistently outperforming or closely matching all competing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Shallow screening and continuous scheduling act synergistically, and CopyLoop needs only lightweight calibration and yields greater speedups on longer generations with reusable contexts.

title: HEDGE: Gated Hypergraph Memory for Scalable Multi-Agent Debate
summary: Multi-agent debate systems require agents to retain and revisit arguments across multiple rounds, yet limited context windows and unstructured memories make relevant information increasingly difficult to recover. Existing flat and pairwise-graph memories also struggle to capture higher-order relations, including multi-agent agreement, conflicting evidence, and evolving consensus. We introduce HEDGE, a selective memory framework that represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs. Hyperedges connect related claims across agents, while intra-hyperedge relational graphs preserve fine-grained argumentative structure. A learned memory selection module (MSM), trained through supervised learning and reinforcement learning, routes each memory candidate to STORE, BACKUP, or OMIT, retaining useful information while limiting redundancy. Across seven diverse benchmarks, HEDGE consistently outperforms strong single-agent, multi-agent, and memory baselines, improving accuracy by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent system with GPT-4o-mini. The gains reach 8.2 points on conflict-heavy tasks, while HEDGE reduces memory usage by 48% and the number of debate rounds by 34%.

AI.tldr: HEDGE is a selective memory framework for multi-agent debate that represents debate trajectories as semantic hypergraphs and uses a learned memory selection module to store, back up or omit memory candidates.
AI.motivation: Debate agents must revisit arguments across rounds, but limited context windows and flat or pairwise-graph memories struggle to capture higher-order relations such as multi-agent agreement, conflicting evidence and evolving consensus.
AI.method: Hyperedges connect related claims across agents, intra-hyperedge relational graphs preserve fine-grained argumentative structure, and a memory selection module trained with supervised learning and reinforcement learning routes each memory candidate to STORE, BACKUP or OMIT.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks with GPT-4o-mini, HEDGE improves accuracy by 5.0 points on average over the strongest multi-agent system, with gains of 8.2 points on conflict-heavy tasks, while reducing memory usage by 48% and the number of debate rounds by 34%.
AI.conclusion: Selective hypergraph memory improves both accuracy and efficiency in multi-agent debate, with the largest benefit when claims conflict.

title: Interventional Training Reduces Causal Bypass in In-Context Introspection
summary: Introspection, the ability of a system to access and reason about its internal signals, is crucial for language model (LM) self-consistency and scalable interpretability. Prior work argues that LMs possess introspective capabilities, and that training (SFT) could enhance such behavior. However, most setups leave open the possibility of "causal bypass," in which the self-report relies on signals that are correlated with the self-report's subject, while being causally unrelated to it. Although high-level concepts are difficult to intervene on, lower-level signals (such as a single neuron activation) allow precise interventions. Understanding such signals can serve as a minimal prerequisite before understanding more complex introspection. In this study, we train hundreds of introspectors across three low-level signal types and eight LMs. We find that straightforward SFT training leads to causal bypass, and propose interventional training, an alternative where we train the model to report on counterfactually perturbed values. This method enables more accurate introspection of endogenous $\textit{and}$ injected signals, particularly in out-of-distribution (OOD) data. The mechanism generalizes across token positions and scales with more data. Our results demonstrate that while causally grounded introspection is possible, it is not guaranteed -- emphasizing the need to train on mechanisms, rather than behaviors alone.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that straightforward SFT for in-context introspection leads to causal bypass and proposes interventional training, which teaches models to report counterfactually perturbed signal values, yielding more causally grounded introspection.
AI.motivation: Introspection could support LM self-consistency and interpretability, but self-reports may rely on signals that are correlated with their subject yet causally unrelated to it, a failure the paper calls causal bypass.
AI.method: Hundreds of introspectors are trained across three low-level signal types and eight LMs, where low-level signals such as single-neuron activations allow precise interventions, and the proposed interventional training teaches models to report on counterfactually perturbed values.
AI.result: Standard SFT leads to causal bypass, while interventional training improves introspection of both endogenous and injected signals, particularly on out-of-distribution data; the mechanism generalizes across token positions and scales with more data.
AI.conclusion: Causally grounded introspection is possible but not guaranteed, which emphasizes the need to train on mechanisms rather than behaviors alone.

title: How Architecture, Typology, and Adaptation Strategies Shape ASR for Low-Resource African Languages: A Controlled Empirical Study
summary: Despite recent advancements in ASR, identifying effective architectures, fine-tuning approaches, and data adaptation strategies for low-resource languages remains challenging. We present a systematic comparison across five low-resource African languages and Swahili as a mid-resource contrast, fine-tuning three models from distinct architectures: Phi-4-multimodal-instruct, Whisper-large-v3-turbo, and MMS-1B-all. We analyze data sufficiency, monolingual versus multilingual adaptation, domain fine-tuning, and language-adapter transfer. Phi-4 achieves the best overall accuracy, MMS shows comparable CER, while Whisper exhibits high CER, consistent with known hallucinations and repetition loops. Performance saturates at different data scales, offering practical data-efficiency targets, while typological complexity consistently shapes error rates. Domain fine-tuning benefits Phi-4 and Whisper but degrades MMS, revealing limitations of adapter-based adaptation. Proxy language adapters outperform training MMS adapters from scratch.
