AI.tldr: A controlled comparison of Phi-4-multimodal-instruct, Whisper-large-v3-turbo and MMS-1B-all for ASR on five low-resource African languages, with Swahili as a mid-resource contrast, finds Phi-4 most accurate, MMS comparable in CER and Whisper much higher in CER.
AI.motivation: Identifying effective architectures, fine-tuning approaches and data adaptation strategies for low-resource languages remains challenging for ASR.
AI.method: Three models from distinct architectures are fine-tuned, and the study analyzes data sufficiency, monolingual versus multilingual adaptation, domain fine-tuning and language-adapter transfer.
AI.result: Phi-4 achieves the best overall accuracy and MMS shows comparable CER, while Whisper exhibits high CER consistent with known hallucinations and repetition loops; performance saturates at different data scales; domain fine-tuning benefits Phi-4 and Whisper but degrades MMS; proxy language adapters outperform training MMS adapters from scratch.
AI.conclusion: Typological complexity consistently shapes error rates, adapter-based adaptation has limits, and the saturation points offer practical data-efficiency targets.

title: Implicit Reasoning in Transformers: Bridging the Compositionality Gap in GPT-2-like Models
comment: Code available at: this https URL
summary: Compositional generalization remains a persistent limitation of transformer language models: even when a model learns to combine known facts correctly in-distribution (ID), the same compositional mechanism may fail when applied to out-of-distribution (OOD) knowledge. We investigate this compositionality gap in a controlled two-hop reasoning setting using a GPT-2-like transformer model trained from scratch. Building on prior work identifying a circuit associated with compositional generalization, we test whether the failure of OOD transfer is related to how atomic knowledge is structurally exposed during training. We modify the training distribution by presenting both ID and OOD atomic facts in a format positionally aligned with the second-hop retrieval step of the learned compositional circuit, without modifying the model architecture or adding OOD compositional supervision. Under this intervention, the model successfully transfers the learned ID compositional behaviour to held-out OOD atomic facts, closing the observed compositionality gap in the controlled setting. Our results provide evidence that the observed compositionality gap is not a fundamental architecture limitation and that it can be overcome through mechanistically informed training distribution design.

AI.tldr: The compositionality gap in a GPT-2-like two-hop reasoning model is closed by presenting atomic facts in a format positionally aligned with the second-hop retrieval step, without changing the architecture or adding compositional supervision.
AI.motivation: Transformers combine known facts correctly in distribution but fail to apply the same compositional mechanism to out-of-distribution atomic knowledge, and the paper asks whether this failure relates to how atomic knowledge is exposed during training.
AI.method: A GPT-2-like model is trained from scratch on a controlled two-hop reasoning task, and both in-distribution and OOD atomic facts are presented in a format aligned with the second-hop retrieval step of a learned compositional circuit.
AI.result: Under this intervention the model transfers the learned in-distribution compositional behavior to held-out OOD atomic facts, closing the observed compositionality gap in the controlled setting.
AI.conclusion: The compositionality gap is not a fundamental architectural limitation and can be overcome through mechanistically informed design of the training distribution.

title: Author-Informed Stance Detection: A Dataset and Findings
summary: Stance detection in social media is challenging, as interpreting a text often requires understanding the author's perspective. We re-frame political stance detection as an author-informed text understanding task, where it is desired to infer both the author's political leaning and their stance towards the target from the text. We first show that human annotators struggle to infer authors' political leanings and stances from individual tweets, and that pretrained large language models (LLMs) perform below human level in this setting. We then demonstrate that author context improves stance detection for both humans and LLMs, with particularly pronounced benefits for tweets perceived as sarcastic. Through extensive experiments, we further show that LLMs can be effectively fine-tuned to predict authors' political affiliations, and that author-informed fine-tuning yields better stance detection performance than standard fine-tuning. This approach not only surpasses human performance but also improves generalization across datasets. To support further research on author-informed political stance detection, we release a large dataset of stance-labeled tweets enriched with author-context information.

AI.tldr: The paper re-frames political stance detection as author-informed text understanding, releases a dataset of stance-labeled tweets enriched with author context, and shows that author-informed fine-tuning of LLMs outperforms standard fine-tuning and human performance.
AI.motivation: Stance in social media often depends on the author's perspective, yet humans struggle to infer authors' political leanings and stances from single tweets, and pretrained LLMs perform below human level in this setting.
AI.method: Author context is provided to both humans and LLMs, and LLMs are fine-tuned to predict authors' political affiliations, with the resulting author-informed fine-tuning compared against standard fine-tuning for stance detection.
AI.result: Author context improves stance detection for humans and LLMs, especially for tweets perceived as sarcastic; author-informed fine-tuning yields better stance detection than standard fine-tuning, surpasses human performance and improves generalization across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Author-informed modeling is a useful direction for political stance detection, and the released author-context dataset supports further research on it.

title: Distilling the Shape of Uncertainty: What On-Policy Distillation Learns and How to Predict It
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly adopted in the post-training of large language models. However, a stronger teacher may fail to improve the student. Prior work attributes this to a lack of new knowledge, but what that knowledge is remains unclear. We show that OPD learns not only \textit{how to branch}, i.e., which candidate tokens to consider, but also \textit{where to branch}, i.e., where to keep reasoning paths open. The existing token-overlap metric captures only the former. We introduce the entropy shape, the sequence of next-token entropies, to characterize the latter, and propose the Entropy Shape Correlation (ESC) to measure student-teacher agreement in entropy shape. Tracking ESC throughout training and intervening on a teacher's entropy while preserving its token preferences, we empirically show that \textit{where to branch} causally drives OPD gains, independently of \textit{how to branch}. Finally, we formulate OPD outcome prediction as a teacher selection task and establish an evaluation protocol for it, under which pre-OPD ESC selects the best teacher for both students and outperforms existing predictors. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: On-policy distillation teaches a student where to branch in reasoning, not only which tokens to consider, and the paper proposes Entropy Shape Correlation to measure this and to select teachers before training.
AI.motivation: A stronger teacher may fail to improve the student in on-policy distillation, and prior work attributes this to missing new knowledge without specifying what that knowledge is; the existing token-overlap metric captures only which candidate tokens to consider.
AI.method: The entropy shape, the sequence of next-token entropies, characterizes where to branch, and Entropy Shape Correlation measures student-teacher agreement in entropy shape, tracked throughout training; the teacher's entropy is intervened on while its token preferences are preserved.
AI.result: Where-to-branch causally drives distillation gains, independently of how-to-branch; pre-distillation ESC selects the best teacher for students and outperforms existing predictors under the proposed evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: Entropy shape is a key factor in on-policy distillation, and ESC offers a practical way to choose teachers before training.

title: Tracing the Influence of Retrieved Literature on Scientific Ideation in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate research ideas from scientific literature. Existing systems combine literature retrieval with search, generation, and refinement, making it difficult to determine how the retrieval strategy itself shapes the ideas generated. We isolate this contribution by comparing five retrieval strategies and a No Literature baseline under a shared generation protocol, using 45,000 ideas across 15 machine learning topics and ten open-weight models. Relative to no literature basline, all five retrieval strategies reduce diversity among ideas generated from the same set of papers by $5.6\%$--$17.9\%$, while most increase diversity by $10.2\%$--$18.1\%$ when ideas from different sets are pooled. Effects on idea quality and novelty are modest on average but vary across topics. We further apply a JSD-based attribution method to trace the influence of individual input papers on each idea's motivation, core idea, approach, and validation. In $79.3\%$ of ideas, only one or two distinct papers receive the highest attribution scores across these four parts. These leading sources often recur across ideas generated from the same set of papers, and groups with more varied source attribution contain more diverse ideas ($r=0.70$). These findings motivate various sets of literature and the use of attribution to guide the choice of sources for subsequent ideas.

AI.tldr: Comparing five retrieval strategies and a no-literature baseline for LLM research idea generation, the paper finds that retrieval shapes idea diversity and that attribution shows only one or two papers dominate most ideas.
AI.motivation: Existing literature-based ideation systems combine retrieval with search, generation and refinement, so the contribution of the retrieval strategy itself to the generated ideas is unclear.
AI.method: Five retrieval strategies and a No Literature baseline are compared under a shared generation protocol using 45,000 ideas across 15 machine learning topics and ten open-weight models, and a JSD-based attribution method traces each input paper's influence on the motivation, core idea, approach and validation of each idea.
AI.result: Relative to no literature, all five strategies reduce diversity among ideas from the same paper set by 5.6% to 17.9%, while most increase diversity when ideas from different sets are pooled by 10.2% to 18.1%; effects on quality and novelty are modest on average and vary by topic; in 79.3% of ideas only one or two distinct papers receive the highest attribution, and groups with more varied source attribution contain more diverse ideas (r = 0.70).
AI.conclusion: Varied literature sets and attribution can guide the choice of sources for subsequent idea generation.

title: HEARSAYBENCH: Can AI Navigate from Abstract Human Rights to Lived Lives?
summary: As large language models (LLMs) reach users worldwide, personal counseling has emerged as one of their most consequential applications, sometimes in life-critical situations. Yet broader access does not mean equal support. The text these models learn from disproportionately reflects people with the freedom to act, embedding an implicit assumption that users can leave, report, seek help, or appeal. Existing benchmarks largely inherit this assumption, overlooking users whose agency is constrained by structural conditions such as war, statelessness, and displacement. Meanwhile, models are increasingly shaped by normative frameworks such as Constitutional AI, often grounded in ideals like human rights, even as many users live where those rights offer little protection or recourse. We introduce HEARSAYBENCH, a human-authored dataset of 400 test cases with in-region human verification grounded in scenarios where structural barriers stand between a person and the exercise of their rights. Built from United Nations and other human rights reports, the scenarios span over 80 regions and cover social, environmental, and personal constraints. Drawing on Nobel laureate Amartya Sen's Capabilities Approach, HEARSAYBENCH tests whether models can distinguish what a person is formally entitled to do from what they are actually able to do. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, every model infers a user's situation more accurately than it advises on it. Stronger models narrow this gap, but their recommendations remain unsafe to follow. Models may understand lives shaped by constraint, yet that knowledge remains hearsay if it cannot translate into advice people can act on. Those people are not alignment's long tail; they are among the users for whom good guidance matters most. HEARSAYBENCH makes this failure measurable, a step toward systems that serve the world as it is rather than as assumed.

AI.tldr: HEARSAYBENCH is a 400-case dataset testing whether LLMs can distinguish what a person is formally entitled to do from what they are actually able to do under structural constraints, and finds that every model infers situations better than it advises on them.
AI.motivation: Personal counseling is a consequential LLM use, but existing benchmarks assume users can leave, report, seek help or appeal, overlooking users constrained by war, statelessness and displacement, even as models are shaped by normative frameworks such as Constitutional AI.
AI.method: A human-authored dataset of 400 test cases with in-region human verification is built from United Nations and other human rights reports, covering over 80 regions and social, environmental and personal constraints, and draws on Amartya Sen's Capabilities Approach.
AI.result: Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models every model infers a user's situation more accurately than it advises on it; stronger models narrow this gap, but their recommendations remain unsafe to follow.
AI.conclusion: Models may understand lives shaped by constraint, but that knowledge does not yet translate into advice people can act on, and the benchmark makes this failure measurable.

title: HALO: Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents
summary: Proactive agents must decide whether, when, and how far to assist without an explicit request. Existing evaluations often rely on automated scores or binary verdicts, offering limited human diagnosis of evidence use and intervention quality. To address these gaps, we introduce HALO, Human-Grounded GrAnular EvaLuation of PrOactive Agents. HALO-Arena covers 4 proactive need types, Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity, across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments. Scenarios require agents to retrieve evidence from structured databases or unstructured documents before judging whether assistance is warranted and choosing its scope. On HALO-Arena, we construct HALO-8K, a dataset of 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts, and human diagnosis. For rejected responses, human diagnosis covers timing, intensity, and other issues. Recorded reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds measure the effort behind these responses. The best proprietary and open-source models achieve 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, respectively. Our central finding is that over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode, with Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounting for 61.20% of rejected responses. Further analyses yield complementary findings on the balance between intervention and restraint, evidence acquisition, and the calibration of timing and intensity.

AI.tldr: HALO is a human-grounded evaluation framework for proactive agents, with the HALO-8K dataset of expert-annotated responses, and finds that over-proactivity, especially premature timing or excessive intensity, is the dominant failure mode.
AI.motivation: Proactive agents must decide whether, when and how far to assist without an explicit request, but existing evaluations rely on automated scores or binary verdicts, which offer little human diagnosis of evidence use and intervention quality.
AI.method: HALO-Arena covers four proactive need types (Dependency, Blockage, Risk and Opportunity) across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments, requiring agents to retrieve evidence from structured databases or documents; HALO-8K contains 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts and human diagnosis.
AI.result: The best proprietary and open-source models achieve 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, and premature timing or excessive intensity account for 61.20% of rejected responses.
AI.conclusion: Over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode, so calibrating timing and intensity and balancing intervention against restraint are central challenges for proactive agents.

title: XLaw-JP-27B: A Lightweight Open Model Specialized for Japanese Law
summary: We present XLaw-JP-27B, an open-weight model specialized for Japanese law that runs on a single 48\,GB GPU under the Apache~2.0 licence. It adapts Qwen3.8-27B with hybrid retrieval over all current statutes and 31k case summaries, a light QLoRA fine-tune on its own verified answers to past bar-exam questions (self-distillation), a contract-specific LoRA adapter, and four-sample voting. We evaluate it on eight Japanese legal tasks---the multiple-choice section of the bar examination in 2024, 2025 and 2026, statement-level bar questions (JBE-QA), statute questions (LawQA-JP), the patent attorney exam, and contract review and drafting built from government model contracts---against open models of 12--33B under identical prompts and retrieval. XLaw-JP-27B ranks first on six tasks, ties on one and is third on one (mean rank 1.3 against 2.8--3.1 for the baselines). It is the only system that passes the bar exam in all three years (129, 120 and 130 of 175, meeting every subject minimum; no test-year material was used in training), while open Japanese 32--33B models fail at least one year. A controlled study of each component shows that retrieval, voting and self-distillation help, and that thinking mode, retrieval-grounded synthetic tuning, self-verification, per-statement decomposition and more self-distillation do not. The largest remaining gaps to frontier models are in contract review and patent law. The model is available as a free web service at this https URL with the weights available at this https URL under Apache~2.0.

AI.tldr: XLaw-JP-27B is an open-weight model specialized for Japanese law, adapted from Qwen3.8-27B with hybrid retrieval, QLoRA self-distillation, a contract-specific LoRA and four-sample voting, and it ranks first on six of eight legal tasks.
AI.motivation: Japanese legal work needs strong domain performance from models that run on modest hardware, and open Japanese 32-33B models fail at least one bar exam year.
AI.method: Qwen3.8-27B is adapted with hybrid retrieval over all current statutes and 31k case summaries, a light QLoRA fine-tune on its own verified answers to past bar-exam questions, a contract-specific LoRA adapter and four-sample voting; it runs on a single 48 GB GPU under Apache 2.0.
AI.result: On eight Japanese legal tasks against open 12-33B models it ranks first on six, ties on one and is third on one (mean rank 1.3 versus 2.8-3.1 for baselines); it is the only system that passes the bar exam in all three years (129, 120 and 130 of 175) with no test-year material used in training; retrieval, voting and self-distillation help, while thinking mode, retrieval-grounded synthetic tuning, self-verification and per-statement decomposition do not.
AI.conclusion: Specialized retrieval-augmented fine-tuning can make a lightweight open model strong on legal tasks, though the largest remaining gaps to frontier models are in contract review and patent law.

title: Grounding Multimodal Reasoning with Evidence-Ablated Negatives
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful tool for improving multimodal reasoning. However, standard outcome supervision suffers from credit assignment ambiguity, as a model may receive positive rewards by exploiting language priors or dataset shortcuts rather than grounding its reasoning in the requisite visual evidence. This makes high-quality negative responses critical, since effective negatives should remain plausible under the current policy while exposing the shortcut that should be suppressed. In this paper, we propose EVAN, a multimodal reinforcement learning framework utilizing EVidence-Ablated Negatives to train LMMs against their own language-prior failures. EVAN first identifies highly visually dependent examples using a scaled image information gain metric and preserves data diversity with a mixed-ranking strategy. It then constructs evidence-ablated images by masking the most discriminative image patches, eliciting plausible but visually ungrounded responses from the current policy. During policy optimization, these negative responses are incorporated as bounded auxiliary signals under the clean image, penalizing shortcut learning while maintaining RL stability. Experiments across challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that EVAN mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes EVAN, a multimodal RL framework that trains large multimodal models against language-prior shortcuts using evidence-ablated negative responses generated from images with their most discriminative patches masked. Experiments on challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that EVAN mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines.
AI.motivation: Outcome supervision in RLVR creates credit assignment ambiguity, because a model can earn positive rewards by exploiting language priors or dataset shortcuts instead of grounding its reasoning in visual evidence, and effective negatives that expose such shortcuts are needed.
AI.method: EVAN selects highly visually dependent examples with a scaled image information gain metric and a mixed-ranking strategy that preserves diversity, builds evidence-ablated images by masking the most discriminative patches to elicit plausible but visually ungrounded responses from the current policy, and adds these negatives as bounded auxiliary signals under the clean image during policy optimization.
AI.result: On challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks EVAN mitigates modality imbalance and improves over strong RLVR baselines; the abstract reports no specific numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Bounded auxiliary penalties on evidence-ablated negatives suppress shortcut learning while maintaining RL stability, offering a way to ground multimodal reasoning in visual evidence.

title: Unlimited OCR Works 2
summary: Unlimited OCR ushers the era of long-horizon parsing, substantially mitigating the growth of working memory as document lengthens. However, as document length scales to hundreds of pages, the visual context grows substantially, sharply increasing the computational cost of each decoding step and limiting the scalability of ultra-long document parsing. Inspired by human book transcription via localized focus without re-scanning preceding pages, we introduce Unlimited OCR 2, a document parsing model that looks only at what it transcribes. Building on Unlimited OCR, we upgrade all the decoder attention modules to Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), bounding active reference tokens to a fixed capacity and thus sustaining constant computational costs across arbitrarily long documents. By combining SR-SWA with Unlimited-Horizon Decoding Paradigm, Unlimited OCR 2 enables document parsing over virtually unlimited lengths without prohibitive memory overhead. At the hundred-page scale, Unlimited OCR 2 achieves 7.0$\times$ and 5.6$\times$ per-step speedups over Full Attention and R-SWA, respectively. Furthermore, it delivers state-of-the-art end-to-end performance on both MPDocBench and MarathonDocBench, our newly proposed benchmark targeting hundred-page document parsing. Ultimately, the capacity for uninterrupted, one-shot document parsing signifies a fundamental paradigm shift into the OCR 3.0 era.

AI.tldr: Introduces Unlimited OCR 2, a document parsing model that attends only to the localized content it is transcribing, enabling parsing of documents of virtually unlimited length at constant per-step cost. It reports state-of-the-art end-to-end performance on MPDocBench and MarathonDocBench.
AI.motivation: As documents grow to hundreds of pages, the visual context grows substantially and sharply increases the computational cost of each decoding step, which limits the scalability of ultra-long document parsing.
AI.method: All decoder attention modules of Unlimited OCR are upgraded to Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA), which bounds active reference tokens to a fixed capacity, and this is combined with an Unlimited-Horizon Decoding Paradigm.
AI.result: At the hundred-page scale the model achieves 7.0x and 5.6x per-step speedups over Full Attention and R-SWA respectively, and delivers state-of-the-art end-to-end performance on MPDocBench and on MarathonDocBench, a new benchmark proposed for hundred-page document parsing.
AI.conclusion: Constant-cost, one-shot parsing of arbitrarily long documents is presented as a paradigm shift into an OCR 3.0 era.

title: Cord: Confidence-Anchored Order Residual Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: The decoding order of masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) can substantially affect generation quality, yet common decoders typically apply the same reveal rule throughout generation. Confidence provides a strong default, but it measures how decisively a position can be predicted now, not how useful revealing that position will be for subsequent decoding. We propose Cord, a lightweight prompt-conditioned policy that retains confidence decoding as a stable reference and learns when and how to depart from it through geometric residuals over generation direction, proximity to revealed context, and two-sided infilling. The residuals adapt to both the prompt and the evolving partial response. Rather than sampling a new policy action at every decoding step, Cord samples a single low-dimensional coefficient matrix per rollout, which induces an entire state-dependent reveal trajectory. This yields a contextual-bandit formulation trained directly from sequence-level rewards, without step-level credit assignment or backbone updates. Across three dLLMs and five reasoning, code, and constraint-satisfaction benchmarks, Cord improves average task success from 32.0% under confidence decoding to 48.2%, and further improves over the best per-domain fixed residual. Behavioral audits show that the learned residuals induce substantial, task-dependent changes in reveal locality and two-sided infilling. Cord adds only $0.53$M trainable parameters, requires no additional backbone forward passes, and incurs only 5.39% inference latency overhead.

AI.tldr: Proposes Cord, a lightweight prompt-conditioned policy that learns when and how to depart from confidence decoding in masked diffusion language models, raising average task success from 32.0% to 48.2% across three dLLMs and five benchmarks with a small parameter overhead.
AI.motivation: Confidence decoding is a strong default reveal rule for dLLMs, but it measures how decisively a position can be predicted now rather than how useful revealing that position will be for subsequent decoding.
AI.method: Cord keeps confidence decoding as a stable reference and adds geometric residuals over generation direction, proximity to revealed context, and two-sided infilling. It samples one low-dimensional coefficient matrix per rollout, which induces a state-dependent reveal trajectory, and is trained as a contextual bandit from sequence-level rewards without step-level credit assignment or backbone updates.
AI.result: Average task success across three dLLMs and five reasoning, code and constraint-satisfaction benchmarks rises from 32.0% under confidence decoding to 48.2%, and Cord further improves over the best per-domain fixed residual. It adds 0.53M trainable parameters, needs no additional backbone forward passes, and incurs a 5.39% inference latency overhead.
AI.conclusion: The learned residuals induce substantial, task-dependent changes in reveal locality and two-sided infilling, showing that an adaptive reveal order can be a cheap way to improve dLLM decoding.

title: What Makes Medical Examination Items Difficult? Using Large Language Models to Explore Patterns Associated With Empirical Item Difficulty
summary: Research on medical item difficulty has largely focused on prediction rather than on identifying interpretable patterns associated with empirical difficulty. This study used empirical difficulty labels to guide large language models (LLMs) in inducing difficulty rubrics and examined how rubric guidance affected LLM difficulty judgments. Using training items and their empirical difficulty estimates from the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) and the Physician Assistant National Certifying Examination (PANCE), Claude Opus 5 induced separate rubrics for absolute and pairwise difficulty judgment. None of the induced rubrics treated surface features, such as stem length, option count, or images, as major sources of difficulty. Several patterns emerged across both examinations, including cue convergence, misleading cues, and option competition, although their specific forms differed. Retrieval of knowledge that could not be derived from the stem was particularly prominent in the PANCE rubrics, whereas the USMLE rubrics placed greater emphasis on integrating multiple clinical cues. We compared commercial and open-weight LLMs on held-out items under unguided and rubric-guided conditions. Rubric guidance changed how models used the difficulty scale but did not consistently improve performance. In absolute judgments, guidance encouraged broader use of the scale and generally improved coarse-grained agreement, without consistently improving rank ordering. In pairwise comparisons, its effects varied across models and examinations, and judgments became more sensitive to presentation order. These findings suggest that the value of label-guided rubric induction may lie more in generating interpretable, testable hypotheses from empirical difficulty data than in reliably improving difficulty judgments.

AI.tldr: Uses empirical difficulty labels to guide Claude Opus 5 in inducing interpretable difficulty rubrics for USMLE and PANCE items, and finds that rubric guidance changes how LLMs use the difficulty scale without consistently improving their difficulty judgments.
AI.motivation: Research on medical item difficulty has focused on prediction rather than on identifying interpretable patterns associated with empirical difficulty.
AI.method: Using training items and empirical difficulty estimates from USMLE and PANCE, Claude Opus 5 induces separate rubrics for absolute and pairwise difficulty judgment, and commercial and open-weight LLMs are then compared on held-out items under unguided and rubric-guided conditions.
AI.result: None of the induced rubrics treats surface features such as stem length, option count or images as major difficulty sources. Recurring patterns include cue convergence, misleading cues and option competition, with knowledge that cannot be derived from the stem prominent in PANCE rubrics and multi-cue integration emphasized in USMLE rubrics. Guidance broadened scale use and generally improved coarse-grained agreement in absolute judgments without consistently improving rank ordering, while pairwise effects varied across models and examinations and made judgments more sensitive to presentation order.
AI.conclusion: The main value of label-guided rubric induction may lie in generating interpretable, testable hypotheses from empirical difficulty data rather than in reliably improving difficulty judgments.

title: Robustness of Chatbot LLM Judgments of Presidential Actions and Hypothetical Reforms
summary: Chatbots are increasingly consulted about public affairs, and their judgments of policies are useful only if they are robust. We measure this robustness in the setting of an ordinary user, through consumer chat interfaces. For 30 days, five chatbot configurations (Mistral, Gemini Flash, Claude Sonnet, and Claude Opus at two effort settings) were asked twice a day to score the long-term effect on the United States of 40 actions of the last four presidential administrations and of 15 hypothetical reforms, each with a confidence and a short comment. The judgments are robust: all configurations agree on the sign and the ranking of the administrations' mean scores, and two different configurations asked on the same day give opposite signs to the same action in about 4% of cases. Responses from different days differ more than same-day responses, but the difference grows slowly over the month, except where the service itself changed. We identify three such changes, which shifted the judgments while leaving little or no trace in the interface. Treating the comments as a retrieval task, we find them specific to each item and consistent across runs and chatbots, with lexical and embedding similarities agreeing. We release the dataset of 16,500 judgments.

AI.tldr: Measures the robustness of five chatbot configurations' judgments of 40 presidential actions and 15 hypothetical reforms through consumer chat interfaces over 30 days of twice-daily queries. The judgments are largely robust, but three service changes shifted them with little or no visible trace in the interface.
AI.motivation: Chatbots are increasingly consulted about public affairs, and their policy judgments are useful only if they are robust, which the authors measure from the perspective of an ordinary user on consumer chat interfaces.
AI.method: Five configurations (Mistral, Gemini Flash, Claude Sonnet, and Claude Opus at two effort settings) were asked twice a day for 30 days to score the long-term effect on the United States of 40 actions from the last four administrations and of 15 hypothetical reforms, each with a confidence and a short comment, and the comments were also treated as a retrieval task using lexical and embedding similarity.
AI.result: All configurations agree on the sign and ranking of the administrations' mean scores, and two configurations asked on the same day give opposite signs to the same action in about 4% of cases. Responses from different days differ more than same-day responses, with the difference growing slowly except at three identified service changes. The comments are item-specific and consistent across runs and chatbots, and a dataset of 16,500 judgments is released.
AI.conclusion: Chatbot policy judgments are broadly robust, but silent service changes can shift them without visible trace, so a dataset of this kind is useful for tracking drift over time.

title: How Specific Do I Need to Be? Effects of User Query Underspecification on Deep Research Agents
summary: Deep research agents (DRAs) conduct long-horizon reasoning, search, and literature synthesis to provide long-form answers to complex, domain-specific questions. These agents are typically trained and evaluated on fully specified user queries. However, real-world user queries can often be underspecified. We introduce UNDERSPEC-DR, a framework for systematically evaluating how underspecified queries affect agents' final answer quality and intermediate search behavior. Across three DRAs we evaluated, underspecification substantially reduces how well DRA's answers fulfill users' information needs, even though they remain grounded in cited evidence. Our analysis of intermediate search behavior suggests a possible explanation: DRAs conduct broader searches that draw less on the original user query but rely more on their learned prior during training, which can be misaligned with users' intent. Our findings reveal the vulnerability of current DRAs to underspecified user queries and inform future efforts to build DRAs that proactively recognize when additional user input is needed to reliably complete deep research tasks.

AI.tldr: Introduces UNDERSPEC-DR to evaluate how underspecified user queries affect deep research agents, finding that underspecification substantially reduces how well answers fulfill users' information needs across three agents, even though the answers remain grounded in cited evidence.
AI.motivation: Deep research agents are typically trained and evaluated on fully specified queries, whereas real-world user queries are often underspecified.
AI.method: UNDERSPEC-DR is a framework for systematically evaluating how underspecified queries affect final answer quality and intermediate search behavior across three deep research agents.
AI.result: Underspecification substantially reduces answer quality with respect to users' information needs while answers stay grounded in cited evidence. Analysis of intermediate search shows that agents run broader searches that draw less on the original query and rely more on learned priors, which can be misaligned with user intent.
AI.conclusion: Current deep research agents are vulnerable to underspecified queries, which motivates agents that proactively recognize when additional user input is needed.

title: ARBITRA: Robust Document-Level ATT&CK Extraction via Multi-Expert Argumentation
comment: 13 pages of main paper, 21 pages total, preprint
summary: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reports describe adversary behavior in natural language, but converting them into structured MITRE ATT&CK mappings remains difficult: existing methods decompose reports to sentence-level granularity for extraction, while modern LLMs can work with full reports in a single pass but with noticeable performance degradation. We present ARBITRA, which orchestrates multiple role-specialized LLM experts that propose candidate ATT&CK entities from the full report, which are then verified through a per-candidate quantitative bipolar argumentation framework (QBAF) grounded in document evidence and rationales. We additionally construct reasoning-specialized corpora for fine-tuning so experts can act as effective participants during this verification process. Across ATT&CK extraction benchmarks, ARBITRA reaches a stronger precision-oriented operating point than sentence-level pipelines, recent LLM-based extraction systems, and frontier models including GPT-5.5. Under adversarial perturbations simulating conflicting TTP statements, cross-report contamination, and semantic poisoning, ARBITRA limits mean precision degradation to roughly half that of frontier-model baselines for a more robust extraction.

AI.tldr: Presents ARBITRA, which uses multiple role-specialized LLM experts to propose ATT&CK entities from full CTI reports and verifies each candidate with a per-candidate quantitative bipolar argumentation framework. It reports higher precision than sentence-level pipelines, recent LLM-based systems and frontier models including GPT-5.5, and smaller precision loss under adversarial perturbations.
AI.motivation: Converting cyber threat intelligence reports into ATT&CK mappings is hard because existing methods decompose reports to sentence level, while modern LLMs can process full reports in one pass but with noticeable performance degradation.
AI.method: Multiple role-specialized LLM experts propose candidate ATT&CK entities from the full report, and each candidate is verified through a quantitative bipolar argumentation framework (QBAF) grounded in document evidence and rationales, with reasoning-specialized corpora constructed for fine-tuning so that experts can participate effectively in verification.
AI.result: Across ATT&CK extraction benchmarks ARBITRA reaches a stronger precision-oriented operating point than sentence-level pipelines, recent LLM-based extraction systems and frontier models including GPT-5.5. Under adversarial perturbations simulating conflicting TTP statements, cross-report contamination and semantic poisoning, it limits mean precision degradation to roughly half that of frontier-model baselines.
AI.conclusion: Verified multi-expert argumentation over full reports is presented as a more robust extraction approach than single-pass frontier models.

title: Integrating Heterogeneous Echocardiography AI Outputs in Language Space: Learnable Late Fusion with a Supervised LLM
summary: View- and target-specific echocardiography AI models capture useful but complementary information and may not achieve sufficient predictive performance in isolation. A learned ensemble is a natural way to combine these outputs, but heterogeneous models typically require each output to be converted into a binary decision, probability, confidence score, or fixed-length feature vector. We developed a supervised large language model (LLM)-based late-fusion module that directly aggregates view-specific predicted finding statements and predicted measurements in language space and learns a case-level fusion function. In patient-level three-fold cross-validation of 859 examinations from 646 patients, the proposed method integrated heterogeneous outputs within a single framework, performed comparably to the best-performing reference strategy evaluated, and outperformed a general-purpose LLM without task-specific training. These results suggest that a supervised LLM can combine multiple upstream models without model-specific output conversion or feature engineering that requires medical knowledge.

AI.tldr: Develops a supervised LLM-based late-fusion module that combines the outputs of view- and target-specific echocardiography AI models in language space without model-specific output conversion or feature engineering. In three-fold cross-validation on 859 examinations from 646 patients it performs comparably to the best reference strategy and outperforms a general-purpose LLM without task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous echocardiography AI models capture complementary information but usually must have their outputs converted into binary decisions, probabilities, confidence scores or fixed-length feature vectors before a learned ensemble can combine them.
AI.method: A supervised LLM directly aggregates view-specific predicted finding statements and predicted measurements in language space and learns a case-level fusion function.
AI.result: In patient-level three-fold cross-validation of 859 examinations from 646 patients, the method integrates heterogeneous outputs within a single framework, performs comparably to the best-performing reference strategy evaluated, and outperforms a general-purpose LLM without task-specific training.
AI.conclusion: A supervised LLM can combine multiple upstream models without the model-specific output conversion or medical-knowledge-based feature engineering that would otherwise be required.

title: Raincheck: Deferred Multimodal Prefill for Efficient Multi-Turn MLLM Inference
summary: Multi-turn conversations with multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reuse input context, but long multimodal inputs increase time to first token (TTFT). Query-aware hard pruning reduces prefill tokens but permanently excludes information that later questions may require. We propose Raincheck, a framework for deferred multimodal prefill that decouples initial token selection from later information availability. An existing pruning method selects tokens for initial prefill; Raincheck preserves and progressively prefills unselected tokens in source order using unused compute capacity during decode. Unfinished prefill continues after answer return during available scheduling gaps. Attention visibility control and affine state mapping enable context updates after generation begins in full-attention and hybrid recurrent models. Prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B with 30% initial multimodal-token retention. Across both models and four pruning methods, Raincheck recovers on average 77.7% and 60.4% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on MultiVerse and ConvBench, respectively. On MultiVerse, the SGLang implementation reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill, with less than 0.5% increase in mean time per output token (TPOT).

AI.tldr: Proposes Raincheck, which defers prefill of the tokens that query-aware pruning leaves out of multi-turn MLLM conversations, so that later questions can still access information that was pruned from the initial context. With 30% initial multimodal-token retention, it recovers much of the quality lost to hard pruning and reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% on MultiVerse in SGLang.
AI.motivation: Long multimodal inputs in multi-turn MLLM conversations raise time to first token, and query-aware hard pruning reduces prefill tokens but permanently excludes information that later questions may require.
AI.method: Raincheck preserves the tokens that an existing pruning method leaves unselected and progressively prefills them in source order using spare compute during decoding, continuing after the answer is returned. Attention visibility control and affine state mapping allow context updates after generation begins in full-attention and hybrid recurrent models, and prefill-decode fusion reduces repeated weight reads.
AI.result: Evaluated on Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B with 30% initial multimodal-token retention, across both models and four pruning methods, Raincheck recovers on average 77.7% and 60.4% of the quality lost to matched hard pruning on MultiVerse and ConvBench respectively. On MultiVerse the SGLang implementation reduces mean first-turn TTFT by up to 24.1% relative to full prefill, with less than 0.5% increase in mean time per output token.
AI.conclusion: Deferred multimodal prefill offers a way to keep the efficiency of token pruning while retaining information that later turns may require.

title: Red-Teaming Large Language Models in Low-Resource African Languages: A Case Study of Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin
summary: As large language models (LLMs) become more widespread in Africa, their safety in low-resource languages remains largely untested since most red-teaming work focuses on English. This study evaluates six state-of-the-art LLMs using 400 explicit adversarial prompts in Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin, categorised into four harm categories. The responses were scored by native-speaker annotators and reliability was assessed using Cohen's $\kappa$. While models that rejected up to 69% of English prompts rejected as few as 0% in Yoruba, this was not because they were safer, but because they failed to understand the prompts. Attack success rates increased for most models in the Nigerian languages, with GPT-4o Mini demonstrating the most significant cross-lingual safety discrepancy (+0.23 in Yoruba). When models did engage with adversarial prompts, many of the responses were harmful, with rates of harmful content reaching 0.63 in English and 0.50 in Nigerian Pidgin. The most difficult harm category to detect was cultural stereotypes and discrimination (ASR = 0.44 in Nigerian Pidgin). Comprehension in Yoruba was low across most models, and this directly suppressed apparent attack success without indicating actual safety. Gemini 2.0 Flash was the most consistent model across languages. Despite its explicit training in African languages, Aya 101 had the highest attack success rate in English (0.60) and one of the lowest Yoruba comprehension rates (0.28). These results demonstrate that English-centric safety alignment does not transfer to Nigerian languages, highlighting the urgent need for language-specific safety evaluations.

AI.tldr: Red-teams six LLMs with 400 adversarial prompts in Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin and finds that low refusal rates in Yoruba mostly reflect failure to comprehend the prompts rather than greater safety, while English-centric safety alignment does not transfer to these languages.
AI.motivation: Most red-teaming work focuses on English, so the safety of LLMs in low-resource African languages is largely untested even as these models become more widespread in Africa.
AI.method: Six state-of-the-art LLMs were evaluated with 400 explicit adversarial prompts in four harm categories written in Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin, with responses scored by native-speaker annotators and reliability assessed using Cohen's kappa.
AI.result: Models rejected up to 69% of English prompts but as few as 0% of Yoruba prompts, because they failed to understand them. Attack success rates rose for most models in the Nigerian languages, with GPT-4o Mini showing the largest cross-lingual discrepancy (+0.23 in Yoruba). When models engaged, harmful content reached 0.63 in English and 0.50 in Nigerian Pidgin, and cultural stereotypes and discrimination was the hardest category to detect (ASR 0.44 in Nigerian Pidgin). Gemini 2.0 Flash was the most consistent across languages, while Aya 101 had the highest English ASR (0.60) and one of the lowest Yoruba comprehension rates (0.28).
AI.conclusion: English-centric safety alignment does not transfer to Nigerian languages, so language-specific safety evaluations are urgently needed.

title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

AI.tldr: Introduces a textbook-based self-learning task in which LLMs retrieve, study and apply knowledge from reference textbooks to construct proofs, and uses RL with fine-grained rewards in a BookNavigator interface, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5%.
AI.motivation: Problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, which goes beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context.
AI.method: The authors formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task in which models navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises whose reference solutions are withheld. They introduce a BookNavigator interface and incentivize self-learning through RL with fine-grained rewards.
AI.result: Performance improves across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, with Intern-S2-Preview-35B's proof accuracy rising from 51.5% to 79.5%, outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. Gains extend to BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, with improvements of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points over the base model respectively.
AI.conclusion: RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, suggesting that learning from long-form corpora can strengthen broader problem solving on complex long-context tasks.

title: When the Top Answer Decides: Gender Bias in Decision Models
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures. Code, stimuli and results: this https URL
summary: Decision models are language models built to route, classify and triage: they return option probabilities from one forward pass, and an application acts on the top answer. They are offered off the shelf, trained for the decision format rather than for fairness or any one application, and we found no bias measurement in their cards. We test TypeSafe's closed Jev and five open decision models on gender-swapped yes/no decisions about people (Tamkin et al., 2023), BBQ, StereoSet and the gender-bias studies of Fulgu and Capraro (2024). Five of the six give women significantly more favourable answers than men (+0.05 to +0.10 in log-odds), and a gender swap changes 1-3.5% of top answers (Jev's partly through its call-to-call variation). The makers' recommended confidence gate removes many biased commitments but raises the stereotyped share of those it keeps in ambiguous BBQ gender questions (granite-switch 0.76 to 0.85, pplx 0.81 to 1.00). Probes show gender preferences in the same models: all six rate violence for a greater good as more acceptable against a man than against a woman, and two default to "girl" when forced to guess a child's gender without a cue. Decision-level and probability-level measures differ, so audits should read a model as its application does.

AI.tldr: Audits six off-the-shelf decision models on gender-swapped yes/no decisions and bias benchmarks and finds that five of the six give women significantly more favourable answers than men. It also shows that the makers' recommended confidence gate removes many biased commitments but raises the stereotyped share of the answers it keeps in ambiguous BBQ gender questions.
AI.motivation: Decision models are offered off the shelf and trained for the decision format rather than for fairness, and the authors found no bias measurement in their model cards.
AI.method: The authors test TypeSafe's closed Jev and five open decision models on gender-swapped yes/no decisions about people (Tamkin et al., 2023), BBQ, StereoSet and the gender-bias studies of Fulgu and Capraro (2024), together with probes of gender preferences.
AI.result: Five of six models give women significantly more favourable answers (+0.05 to +0.10 in log-odds), and a gender swap changes 1-3.5% of top answers, partly through Jev's call-to-call variation. The confidence gate raises the stereotyped share of kept answers in ambiguous BBQ gender questions (granite-switch 0.76 to 0.85, pplx 0.81 to 1.00). Probes show all six rate violence for a greater good as more acceptable against a man than against a woman, and two default to "girl" when forced to guess a child's gender without a cue.
AI.conclusion: Decision-level and probability-level measures differ, so audits should read a model as its application does.

title: Grammar Control for Language Learning with Sequential Monte Carlo and Small Language Models
summary: Second language learners benefit from exposure to level-appropriate grammar in interactive language use. While prompted frontier language models can usually produce target grammar structures, less resource-intensive models that can be run on device often fail in this task. We use sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to steer dialogue turn generation in small lan- language models toward target grammar constructions from an expert-developed pedagogical resource. With a minimal set of hand-coded potential functions, SMC achieves near-perfect coverage of target grammar, enabling small models to outperform state-of-the-art results from models 140 times larger. We also use code synthesis with frontier models to generate new potentials, showing that our method scales to hundreds of target grammar skills with no need for additional training or supervised data.

AI.tldr: Uses sequential Monte Carlo to steer dialogue turns of small language models toward target grammar constructions from an expert-developed pedagogical resource, enabling small on-device models to outperform state-of-the-art results from models 140 times larger.
AI.motivation: Second language learners benefit from level-appropriate grammar in interactive language use, but prompted frontier models can usually produce target structures while smaller models that run on device often fail at this task.
AI.method: Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) steers dialogue turn generation with a minimal set of hand-coded potential functions, and code synthesis with frontier models generates new potentials, so the method scales to hundreds of grammar skills without additional training or supervised data.
AI.result: SMC achieves near-perfect coverage of the target grammar, enabling small models to outperform state-of-the-art results from models 140 times larger.
AI.conclusion: Steering with SMC scales to hundreds of target grammar skills with no training or supervised data, offering a practical route to grammar practice on small on-device models.

title: KV Cache Quantization for Diffusion Language Models
summary: KV cache quantization is well studied for autoregressive language models, where cached prefix states are exact under causal attention and quantization is mainly a cache reconstruction problem. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) break this assumption. Fast dLLM inference reuses KV states across denoising steps, but bidirectional token representations can change as masked tokens are revealed, so the reused cache may already differ from full recomputation before quantization is applied. We study KV cache quantization under this cache-reuse error. We adapt KIVI and KVQuant to Fast-dLLM-style prefix and dual cache reuse, and introduce TRACE and dLLM-KVQ. TRACE reconstructs feasible dLLM reveal trajectories from prompt-answer pairs, providing calibration states that match iterative masked decoding. dLLM-KVQ uses these trajectories to choose per-layer K-cache entries that remain in high precision according to output- and attention-level behavior metrics, while applying standard low-bit value quantization. Across LLaDA and Dream evaluations on GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH, and MBPP, dLLM-KVQ achieves the highest average score among quantized methods across the reported 4-bit and 2-bit prefix/dual cache settings.

AI.tldr: Studies KV cache quantization for diffusion language models, where cache reuse introduces error before quantization is applied, and proposes TRACE and dLLM-KVQ, which achieve the highest average score among quantized methods on LLaDA and Dream under 4-bit and 2-bit prefix and dual cache settings.
AI.motivation: KV cache quantization is well studied for autoregressive models, where cached prefixes are exact under causal attention, but in diffusion language models bidirectional representations change as masked tokens are revealed, so reused caches can already differ from full recomputation.
AI.method: KIVI and KVQuant are adapted to Fast-dLLM-style prefix and dual cache reuse. TRACE reconstructs feasible reveal trajectories from prompt-answer pairs to provide calibration states matching iterative masked decoding, and dLLM-KVQ uses these trajectories to choose per-layer K-cache entries to keep in high precision based on output- and attention-level metrics, while applying standard low-bit value quantization.
AI.result: On GSM8K, HumanEval, MATH and MBPP with LLaDA and Dream, dLLM-KVQ achieves the highest average score among quantized methods across the reported 4-bit and 2-bit prefix and dual cache settings.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for cache-reuse error through trajectory-based calibration and per-layer precision selection enables better low-bit KV caching for diffusion language models.

title: Tokenizer Tokens Tell Training Tales
summary: Tokenizers are usually treated as fixed preprocessing tools, but they are trained on text and can retain traces of that text in their vocabularies. We ask whether a BPE tokenizer can reveal if a candidate dataset was part of its training corpus. The key observation is simple. Rare strings become tokens only when enough corpus frequency pushes them over the merge threshold. This suggests that membership signal should appear in rare tokens used by the candidate dataset, rather than in the order in which merges were made. We formalize this under a threshold model of BPE inclusion, showing that the likelihood-ratio test assigns its largest weights to tokens that are rare in the background but frequent in the candidate dataset. The same model suggests that merge rank and merge-graph position should not add a first-order membership signal once token existence and dataset frequency are known. We instantiate this view as RTAM-Fusion, which calibrates rare-token mass with shadow tokenizers and combines signals across rarity levels. On the tokenizer membership benchmark, RTAM-Fusion improves AUC and balanced accuracy over Vocabulary Overlap while using fewer shadow tokenizers. Existing defenses also continue to leak membership signal against adaptive attackers at production vocabulary sizes. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: Proposes RTAM-Fusion, a membership inference method that uses rare tokens in a BPE tokenizer to infer whether a candidate dataset was part of its training corpus, improving AUC and balanced accuracy over Vocabulary Overlap with fewer shadow tokenizers, and showing that existing defenses still leak membership signal against adaptive attackers.
AI.motivation: Tokenizers are usually treated as fixed preprocessing tools, but they are trained on text and can retain traces of that text in their vocabularies, so the question is whether a BPE tokenizer reveals dataset membership.
AI.method: Under a threshold model of BPE inclusion, the likelihood-ratio test assigns its largest weights to tokens that are rare in the background but frequent in the candidate dataset, while merge rank and merge-graph position add no first-order signal once token existence and dataset frequency are known. RTAM-Fusion calibrates rare-token mass with shadow tokenizers and combines signals across rarity levels.
AI.result: On the tokenizer membership benchmark RTAM-Fusion improves AUC and balanced accuracy over Vocabulary Overlap while using fewer shadow tokenizers. Existing defenses continue to leak membership signal against adaptive attackers at production vocabulary sizes.
AI.conclusion: Tokenizer vocabularies can leak training-data membership, and existing defenses do not close this leak against adaptive attackers at production vocabulary sizes.

title: Prompts and probabilities in the linguistic assessment of language models: Evidence from semantic focus-sensitivity
summary: As language models (LMs) have improved, an increasingly common means of evaluating their linguistic competence is through explicit prompting (e.g., "Which sentence is more acceptable?"). Prior work indicates that such prompting underperforms compared to standard token-probability-based methods in smaller models, but improves in larger models. We test this in a new domain: semantic focus-sensitivity, responsible for contrasts like "Lucy only SWAM yesterday" vs. "Lucy only swam YESTERDAY". Testing models of various sizes using text-based focus markers like boldface and italics, we find universal above-chance performance for token probabilities. Prompting results mostly align with previous findings, but in some larger models they outperform probabilities by a wide margin. We propose that this is because LMs are not prone to produce out-of-the-blue focus marking, which muddies results from token probabilities in a way that does not affect prompting. We test this by replacing standard focus markers with randomly generated ones; token probabilities still beat chance but show significantly greater performance decrease compared to prompting. These results suggest that metalinguistic prompting, while non-trivial for LMs, can also be more robust when testing stylistically atypical data. We argue that this has important consequences for the assessment of LMs' language competence, even if LMs do not perform metalinguistic judgments through human-like introspection.

AI.tldr: Compares explicit prompting with token-probability methods for assessing language models' competence in semantic focus sensitivity, finding that prompting outperforms probabilities by a wide margin in some larger models and is more robust when focus markers are replaced with random ones.
AI.motivation: Prior work suggests that explicit prompting underperforms token probabilities in smaller models but improves in larger ones, and this paper tests that pattern in the new domain of semantic focus sensitivity.
AI.method: Models of various sizes are tested on contrasts such as "Lucy only SWAM yesterday" versus "Lucy only swam YESTERDAY" using text-based focus markers such as boldface and italics, and the standard markers are then replaced with randomly generated ones to test robustness.
AI.result: Token probabilities show universal above-chance performance. Prompting mostly aligns with previous findings but in some larger models outperforms probabilities by a wide margin. When markers are replaced with random ones, token probabilities still beat chance but decrease significantly more than prompting does.
AI.conclusion: Metalinguistic prompting, while non-trivial for LMs, can be more robust when testing stylistically atypical data, which matters for assessing LM competence even though LMs may not judge through human-like introspection.

title: Can LLMs Ignore What They Know? Measuring Knowledge Leakage in Persona-Based User Simulation
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at UserSim @ NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival workshop)
summary: When persona-conditioned responses are read as respondent-level simulations, each response should reflect the described persona's knowledge, and the respondent written to know nothing must act as if the model's knowledge were not there. We test whether it can, and find persistent favourable-item real-twin rating separation under the tested low-knowledge and explicit-ignorance prompts. We define the resulting problem (knowledge leakage: a response bias that arises when knowledge the real user could not have enters the simulated response) and present a methodology for measuring it quantitatively. The core instrument pairs real items with fabricated twins matched in surface form: screened fabricated variants designed to minimize prior item-specific knowledge. The paired difference therefore provides a diagnostic contrast for knowledge leakage even in rating tasks where no answer is correct. In a rating experiment across three knowledge-handling arms and five API endpoints from two model families, we find, first, that the personas we test do not fully suppress real-item existence and familiarity signals: a favourable-item real-twin rating contrast remains under an explicit in-context statement that the persona has never heard of the item. Second, the unfavourable-item contrast reverses sign across domain groups: pooling all unfavourable-content items across domains the contrast sits near zero (+0.077 [-0.057, +0.204]), yet the same estimator in the same conditions returns -0.359 where the rating scale asks about an item's documented hazard and +0.438 where it asks about a company or an organisation. A pooled analysis of unfavourable-content items against zero therefore does not detect the opposing domain-group differences. All estimates are conditional on the adequacy of twin construction and screening; human low-knowledge baselines remain necessary for population-level interpretation.

AI.tldr: Defines knowledge leakage in persona-based user simulation and measures it by pairing real items with fabricated twins, finding that personas do not fully suppress real-item existence and familiarity signals and that the unfavourable-item contrast reverses sign across domain groups.
AI.motivation: Persona-conditioned responses are read as respondent-level simulations, in which a respondent written to know nothing should not act as if the model's knowledge were present, and the authors test whether current personas meet this requirement.
AI.method: The core instrument pairs real items with surface-matched fabricated twins screened to minimize prior item-specific knowledge, so that the paired difference diagnoses knowledge leakage. A rating experiment covers three knowledge-handling arms and five API endpoints from two model families.
AI.result: A favourable-item real-twin rating contrast remains under an explicit in-context statement that the persona has never heard of the item. The unfavourable-item contrast pooled across domains is near zero (+0.077 [-0.057, +0.204]), but the same estimator returns -0.359 for documented hazards and +0.438 for companies or organisations, so a pooled analysis hides opposing domain-group differences.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge leakage persists under the tested prompts and depends on domain, and since estimates hinge on twin construction, human low-knowledge baselines remain necessary for population-level interpretation.

title: AI Cosmos: An Agentic Infra for Situated Learning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can improve task performance during learning, yet these gains do not necessarily reflect learners' ability to thereafter apply the knowledge and skills independently. We present AI Cosmos, an agentic infrastructure for situated learning that organizes learning around two complementary principles: scenario-based participation and cumulative assets of practice. AI Cosmos organizes learners and role-specialized agents within learning scenarios that integrate task-relevant knowledge and, when needed, executable workbenches. An asset-memory loop preserves the processes and outcomes of practice as reusable assets with explicit provenance and dependencies. We evaluate scenario-based interaction through two preregistered randomized controlled studies examining the acquisition of legal reasoning and programming competence, holding the same underlying LLM across conditions. AI Cosmos achieves greater learning gains than a conventional LLM in legal reasoning and higher mastery of unseen programming problems than an LLM-as-Teacher baseline.

AI.tldr: Presents AI Cosmos, an agentic infrastructure for situated learning that organizes learning around scenarios and cumulative assets of practice. In two preregistered randomized controlled studies it yields greater learning gains than a conventional LLM in legal reasoning and higher mastery of unseen programming problems than an LLM-as-Teacher baseline.
AI.motivation: LLMs can improve task performance during learning, but these gains do not necessarily reflect learners' ability to apply knowledge and skills independently afterwards.
AI.method: AI Cosmos places learners and role-specialized agents within learning scenarios that integrate task-relevant knowledge and, when needed, executable workbenches. An asset-memory loop preserves the processes and outcomes of practice as reusable assets with explicit provenance and dependencies.
AI.result: In two preregistered randomized controlled studies on legal reasoning and programming, with the same underlying LLM held across conditions, AI Cosmos achieves greater learning gains than a conventional LLM in legal reasoning and higher mastery of unseen programming problems than an LLM-as-Teacher baseline.
AI.conclusion: Scenario-based participation combined with cumulative assets of practice is presented as a way to build learning that carries over to independent application.

title: Rethinking Pre-pretraining
summary: We report that allocating compute to synthetic pre-pretraining (PPT) never outperforms pure natural-language training in our compute-matched experiments. This holds across four PPT curricula (k-Dyck, neural cellular automata (NCA), declarative reference corpora, and code) and three training regimes: data-constrained, data-unconstrained, and a high token-to-parameter-ratio regime (881M parameters trained on 50B tokens). When natural language is scarce, repeated epochs over a 100M-token corpus beat every synthetic curriculum on natural-language validation loss, with no consistent downstream accuracy advantage from PPT. We find that PPT gains reported in prior work are sensitive to the weight initialization scheme. In an NCA reproduction, we recover a 5.4% perplexity improvement from PPT under the original initialization scheme. An alternative scheme improves both methods, but the no-PPT baseline more, closing the gap between them. However, when PPT receives additional compute rather than a share of the natural-language budget, gains persist at small natural-language budgets even with improved initialization, but disappear by 1B tokens. Finally, models forget what they learn during PPT in subsequent natural-language training; interleaving the same data throughout training prevents forgetting, but does not significantly improve natural-language performance. Our results suggest limited benefits of synthetic pre-pretraining as a distinct training stage and motivate rethinking how such data are used in language model training.

AI.tldr: Reports that synthetic pre-pretraining (PPT) never outperforms pure natural-language training in compute-matched experiments across four curricula and three training regimes, and that earlier reported PPT gains are sensitive to the weight initialization scheme.
AI.motivation: Prior work reports gains from synthetic pre-pretraining, and this paper asks whether such synthetic stages offer benefits as a distinct training step once compute is matched.
AI.method: Compute-matched experiments compare four PPT curricula (k-Dyck, neural cellular automata (NCA), declarative reference corpora and code) across data-constrained, data-unconstrained and high token-to-parameter-ratio regimes (881M parameters trained on 50B tokens). An NCA reproduction examines weight initialization schemes, and interleaving experiments test forgetting.
AI.result: When natural language is scarce, repeated epochs over a 100M-token corpus beat every synthetic curriculum on natural-language validation loss, with no consistent downstream accuracy advantage from PPT. Under the original initialization the NCA reproduction recovers a 5.4% perplexity improvement from PPT, while an alternative scheme improves both methods but the no-PPT baseline more, closing the gap. When PPT receives extra compute, gains persist at small natural-language budgets with improved initialization but disappear by 1B tokens. Models forget PPT content during later natural-language training, and interleaving prevents forgetting without significantly improving natural-language performance.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic pre-pretraining offers limited benefits as a distinct training stage, which motivates rethinking how such data are used in language model training.

title: Upcycling Language Models for Multiple Specialized Domains
summary: Effective multi-domain adaptation of large language models requires prioritizing relevant domain knowledge while minimizing interference from irrelevant domains. Existing approaches commonly use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to train a separate adapter for each domain and combine these adapters within one model. However, they either weight adapters equally regardless of the input domain or dynamically weight adapters while still activating all of them including irrelevant ones. Additionally, while efficient, their low-rank structure limits performance. In contrast, upcycling is a model expansion method that adds experts and a router to a dense Transformer layer offering larger capacity than LoRA approaches. In this paper, we propose Domain-Specialized Upcycling (DS-Upcycling) for multi-domain adaptation. We introduce a new domain-aware supervision that allows the router to effectively learn to distinguish domains by selecting the appropriate experts. During fine-tuning on each new domain, we update only the corresponding expert and router while freezing all other parameters. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest average performance across the adapted domains compared to baselines while retaining general performance. With just 256 examples per domain for router supervision, DS-Upcycling achieves 90-98% routing accuracy after adaptation compared with 43-70% for routers trained without our approach.

AI.tldr: Proposes Domain-Specialized Upcycling (DS-Upcycling), which adds experts and a router to a dense Transformer layer with domain-aware router supervision and updates only the relevant expert and router for each new domain. It achieves the highest average performance across adapted domains and 90-98% routing accuracy with only 256 examples per domain.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-domain LoRA approaches either weight adapters equally regardless of the input domain or weight them dynamically while still activating irrelevant adapters, and their low-rank structure limits performance.
AI.method: Upcycling expands a dense Transformer layer with experts and a router, and a new domain-aware supervision lets the router learn to select the appropriate experts. On each new domain only the corresponding expert and router are updated while all other parameters are frozen.
AI.result: Compared with baselines the method achieves the highest average performance across adapted domains while retaining general performance. With just 256 examples per domain for router supervision it reaches 90-98% routing accuracy after adaptation, compared with 43-70% for routers trained without this approach.
AI.conclusion: Domain-aware router supervision combined with domain-specific expert updates offers a higher-capacity alternative to LoRA for multi-domain adaptation of language models.

title: Towards Full-Text Scholarly Argument Mining using Entity-Anchored Claim Extraction
summary: Argument mining in full-text scholarly articles remains an important yet challenging task. This difficulty stems not only from the need to model long-distance dependencies but also from the substantial effort required to annotate sentence-level argumentative components throughout lengthy documents. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel approach that leverages scientific entity mentions (e.g., tasks, datasets, and models) to identify and structure claims in scholarly literature. We validate our approach through a case study involving 50 full-text research papers on sentiment analysis.
