We first establish a reliable human gold standard (Krippendorff's $\alpha = 0.80$), identifying 113 claim-bearing sentences and extracting 199 structured claim records from 300 candidate sentences. To address the annotation bottleneck, we employ a majority-voting ensemble of large language models (LLMs) to generate a silver-standard dataset comprising 1,487 claims. Encoders fine-tuned exclusively on the silver-standard dataset outperform those trained on a small human-annotated gold-standard dataset and demonstrate strong zero-shot transfer to NLP papers outside the training corpus.

AI.tldr: The paper extracts structured claims from full-text scholarly articles by anchoring on scientific entity mentions, validated on 50 sentiment-analysis papers. Encoders fine-tuned only on LLM-generated silver annotations outperform those trained on the small human gold set and transfer zero-shot to NLP papers outside the corpus.
AI.motivation: Argument mining in long full-text scholarly articles is difficult because of long-distance dependencies and the heavy cost of annotating sentence-level argumentative components across lengthy documents.
AI.method: Claims are identified and structured by leveraging scientific entity mentions such as tasks, datasets and models; a human gold standard (Krippendorff's alpha of 0.80) is built, and a majority-voting ensemble of LLMs produces a silver-standard dataset for training encoders.
AI.result: From 300 candidate sentences, 113 claim-bearing sentences and 199 structured claim records were annotated as gold; the silver dataset comprises 1,487 claims; encoders trained only on silver data outperform those trained on the small gold dataset and show strong zero-shot transfer to NLP papers outside the training corpus.
AI.conclusion: Entity-anchored claim extraction combined with LLM silver annotation offers a way around the annotation bottleneck in full-text scholarly argument mining.

title: Mobilizing the Archive: Bitext Extraction at Scale from Archival Documents for Extremely Low-resource Languages
summary: While mining parallel sentences from web pages has proven effective for low-resource machine translation, the majority of the world's languages have little to no web presence. What they do have, though, are resources that are the result of centuries of efforts by linguists, such as grammars, dictionaries, and other documentation materials. We propose extracting translation examples from such linguistic resources, which offer parallel data for languages under-represented online and could potentially scale to thousands more languages. We develop a pipeline to achieve this, leveraging an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model as well as a vision language model (VLM), to ensure identified content to be aligned with visual layout information. We demonstrate the utility of the extracted bitexts for bootstrapping translation systems across 20 languages, both by training machine translation models and by applying in-context learning for large language models. For in-context learning, we observe improvements of +15.78 and +6.94 chrF2++ over zero-shot translation for into low- and high-resource languages, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper extracts parallel translation examples from OCR-processed linguistic archival documents such as grammars and dictionaries, aligning content with layout using a vision language model. The resulting bitexts bootstrap translation systems for 20 languages.
AI.motivation: Web-based parallel data mining works for low-resource machine translation, but most of the world's languages have little web presence, while centuries of linguistic documentation exist in print.
AI.method: A pipeline combines an OCR model with a vision language model to identify content and align it with visual layout information, extracting translation examples from linguistic resources such as grammars and dictionaries.
AI.result: The extracted bitexts are used both to train machine translation models and for in-context learning across 20 languages; for LLM in-context learning, gains over zero-shot translation are +15.78 chrF2++ into low-resource languages and +6.94 chrF2++ into high-resource languages.
AI.conclusion: Archival linguistic documents are a scalable source of parallel data for extremely low-resource languages and could extend to thousands more languages.

title: ScienceJudge: Pattern Perturbation Augmentation for Sentence-Level Scientific Claim Verification
summary: Sentence-level scientific claim verification determines whether each sentence in an AI-generated scientific paragraph is supported by a given multimodal evidence bundle. Fine-grained reporting errors often preserve fluent and plausible statements while introducing subtle evidence-claim deviations, making them difficult to detect under sparse and imbalanced supervision. We propose Pattern Perturbation Augmentation (PPA), which models reporting errors as label-specific faithfulness breaking transformations and induces reusable error patterns from labeled examples. PPA applies these patterns to supported claims to construct controlled hard negatives and expands their coverage through pattern-level, operation-level, and cross-domain augmentation. Based on these augmented views, we develop ScienceJudge, which integrates PPA-trained vision-language predictors and instruction-guided LLM predictors through class-weighted ensemble inference. On the local development set, ScienceJudge improves the average score from 0.8124 to 0.8692, achieving a Macro-F1 of 0.8466 and a Paragraph Exact Match score of 0.8919. Our submitted system ranks first on the official NLPCC 2026 Task 10 Track 1 leaderboard with a final score of 0.6890.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Pattern Perturbation Augmentation, which builds hard negatives by applying learned error patterns to supported claims, and uses it to train ScienceJudge for sentence-level verification of AI-generated scientific paragraphs against multimodal evidence. The submitted system ranks first on the NLPCC 2026 Task 10 Track 1 leaderboard.
AI.motivation: Fine-grained reporting errors keep statements fluent and plausible while introducing subtle evidence-claim deviations, and such errors are hard to detect under sparse and imbalanced supervision.
AI.method: PPA models reporting errors as label-specific faithfulness-breaking transformations, induces reusable error patterns from labeled examples, and expands coverage through pattern-level, operation-level and cross-domain augmentation; ScienceJudge combines PPA-trained vision-language predictors with instruction-guided LLM predictors through class-weighted ensemble inference.
AI.result: On the local development set the average score rises from 0.8124 to 0.8692, with Macro-F1 of 0.8466 and Paragraph Exact Match of 0.8919; the submitted system scores 0.6890 on the official leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting training data with controlled, pattern-based hard negatives is an effective way to detect subtle reporting errors, and the approach placed first in the NLPCC 2026 shared task track.

title: Judged in Company: In-Context Batching Makes LLM Verdicts Depend on Other Items
summary: To save cost, practitioners often ask a language model to grade many independent items in one prompt. This assumes that verdicts are separable: that the verdict on an item does not depend on the other items in the prompt or on its position among them. Across three judgement tasks (harm in social-media comments, short-answer grading and review star ratings) and five open-weight models with 4-9B parameters, assigning the same 2,000 items to different random batches of 25 changes 11-22% of decisions on harm and grading, 6.5-13.3 points more than renaming the item keys or rewording the instruction, while AUROC against human labels differs from single-item grading only by -0.033 to +0.010; for four models with 14-32B parameters, 6-15% of decisions change, 4.2-9.1 points more. We show that flip rates decompose exactly into components of order, slot and membership, and that under a threshold model they grow with the square root of the variance that the context contributes, so that effects that are small for scores are large for decisions. Most of the latent dissimilarity between partitions comes from the order of the neighbours and the slot. The main effect of which items share the prompt, the part that voting over permutations of a batch cannot remove, accounts for 0.11-0.22 of it, and majority votes over nine permutations still leave 52-60% of the flips. Batched verdicts also differ systematically from single-item verdicts: even the majority of fifteen random batches disagrees with them on 8.4-17.8% of decisions. Editing a single generation shows that both the model's own earlier verdicts and the neighbours' texts carry the effect. On the easy task, star ratings, only 2.9-3.9% of decisions change. We recommend grading ambiguous items one per prompt, recovering most of the cost with a cached prefix, and reporting agreement with single-item grading whenever items are batched.

AI.tldr: Grading many items in one LLM prompt makes each verdict depend on which other items share the batch and where they sit, so batched verdicts are not separable. The authors recommend grading ambiguous items one per prompt.
AI.motivation: Practitioners batch many independent items into one prompt to save cost, which assumes that each verdict is unaffected by the other items or by its position among them.
AI.method: Across three judgement tasks (harm in social-media comments, short-answer grading, review star ratings) and five open-weight 4-9B models plus four 14-32B models, the same items are assigned to different random batches of 25; flip rates are decomposed into order, slot and membership components, analysed under a threshold model, and probed with permutation voting and edits to earlier generations.
AI.result: Assigning the same 2,000 items to different random batches changes 11-22% of decisions on harm and grading, 6.5-13.3 points more than renaming item keys or rewording the instruction, while AUROC against human labels differs from single-item grading by only -0.033 to +0.010; for the 14-32B models 6-15% of decisions change. Order and slot account for most of the dissimilarity, majority votes over nine permutations still leave 52-60% of flips, and batched majorities disagree with single-item verdicts on 8.4-17.8% of decisions; on star ratings only 2.9-3.9% change.
AI.conclusion: Batch membership and position systematically affect LLM verdicts even when aggregate AUROC is preserved, so items should be graded one per prompt, with a cached prefix to recover most of the cost, and agreement with single-item grading should be reported whenever items are batched.

title: Decision and System One models in rheumatology: accuracy and calibration on specialty-training examination questions and diagnostic case vignettes
comment: 28 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables; includes supplementary material (8 tables, 1 figure)
summary: Objectives: To evaluate the accuracy and calibration of Decision and System One models on rheumatology examination questions and diagnostic vignettes. Methods: Two benchmarks were analysed: 172 rheumatology questions from Spanish specialty-training examinations (expanded RheumaMIR dataset) in Spanish and English, and 70 English diagnostic vignettes from RheumBench with 5-18 candidate diagnoses, 52 of which included the reference diagnosis. Four System One models (Jev 1.13, Clef, Microsoft-Decision-1, Laya) and GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI Decisions API) were compared with GPT-6 Sol and two local generative models. The primary outcome was accuracy; secondary outcomes included calibration, discrimination, accuracy of answers with probability >=0.90 and language differences. Results: In RheumaMIR, Jev's accuracy was 93.0% in Spanish and 91.9% in English, below GPT-6 Sol (99.4%; Holm-adjusted P<=0.005); GPT-6 Luna reached 97.7%, Clef 91.9-93.0% and Microsoft-Decision-1 86.0-87.8%, without detectable language differences. Jev's answers with probability >=0.90 (76-77% of answers) were 98.5% correct. In RheumBench, accuracy was lower: GPT-6 Sol 76.9%, GPT-6 Luna 63.5%, Clef 59.6%, Jev 50.0% and Microsoft-Decision-1 40.4% (each System One model below GPT-6 Sol, Holm-adjusted P<=0.045; chance 9.6%). Jev became overconfident (mean probability 0.659; over/underconfidence index +0.159), and its answers with probability >=0.90 (25% of cases) were 84.6% correct, against 95.5% for GPT-6 Luna (42%). Laya performed near chance in both benchmarks. Conclusion: The best-performing System One models were highly accurate on examination questions but less accurate on diagnostic vignettes, remaining below GPT-6 Sol. Jev's high-confidence predictions were less reliable on vignettes, highlighting the need for task-specific evaluation and calibration.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates Decision and System One models on rheumatology exam questions and diagnostic vignettes, finding that the best System One models are highly accurate on exam questions but less accurate on vignettes and below GPT-6 Sol. One model is overconfident on vignettes, so its high-confidence answers are less reliable.
AI.motivation: The accuracy and calibration of specialised clinical decision systems on rheumatology examination questions and diagnostic vignettes needed to be established.
AI.method: Two benchmarks were analysed: 172 Spanish specialty-training exam questions (RheumaMIR, in Spanish and English) and 70 English diagnostic vignettes from RheumBench with 5-18 candidate diagnoses; four System One models and GPT-6 Luna were compared with GPT-6 Sol and two local generative models, with accuracy as the primary outcome and calibration, discrimination, high-confidence accuracy and language differences as secondary outcomes.
AI.result: On RheumaMIR, Jev reached 93.0% in Spanish and 91.9% in English, below GPT-6 Sol at 99.4%, while GPT-6 Luna reached 97.7%. On RheumBench, accuracy was 76.9% for GPT-6 Sol, 63.5% for GPT-6 Luna, 59.6% for Clef, 50.0% for Jev and 40.4% for Microsoft-Decision-1 (chance 9.6%); Jev's mean probability was 0.659 with an over/underconfidence index of +0.159, and its answers with probability at least 0.90 were 84.6% correct against 95.5% for GPT-6 Luna. Laya performed near chance on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The best System One models are accurate on examinations but less reliable on diagnostic vignettes, so task-specific evaluation and calibration checks are needed before any clinical use.

title: Don't Lose the Thread: Empowering Long-Horizon LLM Agents with Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation
comment: Accepted at COLM 2026. Code is available at this https URL
summary: Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable progress in solving complex reasoning tasks. However, LLM agents often falter on long-horizon tasks due to cognitive overload, as their working memory becomes cluttered with expanding and irrelevant information, which dilutes their attention and hinders effective planning and reasoning. To mitigate this challenge, we introduce Cognitive Resource Self-Allocation (CORAL), a novel reasoning paradigm that empowers agents to proactively optimize their context. Implemented as an agent-callable working memory management toolset, CORAL allows an agent to checkpoint its task progress and verified facts, and adaptively initiate a new problem-solving episode by resetting cluttered context while preserving only the checkpointed information, enabling it to resume reasoning from a clean state. We further enhance the agent's checkpointing capabilities using a Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm. On the GAIA benchmark, CORAL with an 8B model achieves 42.8% average accuracy, with particularly strong gains on the most challenging long-horizon tasks (Level 2 and Level 3). Crucially, these gains come at a substantially lower inference cost: CORAL consumes 6-7$\times$ fewer input tokens than a ReAct agent. It also generalizes to multi-hop Knowledge QA benchmarks and to the considerably harder BrowseComp, where it improves a strong proprietary agent by 8.0 points.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CORAL, a reasoning paradigm in which an LLM agent checkpoints its progress and verified facts, then resets cluttered context to resume from a clean state. An 8B model with CORAL reaches 42.8% average accuracy on GAIA while consuming 6-7 times fewer input tokens than a ReAct agent.
AI.motivation: LLM agents falter on long-horizon tasks because their working memory fills with expanding and irrelevant information, which dilutes attention and hinders planning and reasoning.
AI.method: CORAL is an agent-callable working memory management toolset that lets the agent checkpoint task progress and verified facts and start a new problem-solving episode carrying only the checkpointed information; checkpointing is further improved with a Multi-episode Agentic Reinforced Policy Optimization algorithm.
AI.result: On GAIA the 8B model with CORAL achieves 42.8% average accuracy, with the largest gains on Level 2 and Level 3 tasks, at 6-7 times fewer input tokens than ReAct; it also generalizes to multi-hop knowledge QA and improves a strong proprietary agent on BrowseComp by 8.0 points.
AI.conclusion: Letting agents proactively manage their own context through checkpointing and reset improves long-horizon performance while substantially lowering inference cost.

title: Scaling Mathematical Proof Supervision from Structured Textbooks
summary: Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem-solution pairs, discarding the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources. We introduce TOME-Math (Textbook-Oriented Mathematical Evidence), a large-scale corpus that converts 2,118 textbooks spanning the core areas of university-level mathematics subjects into approximately 380K structured proof-supervision records while preserving chapter order, proposition-proof links, dependency references, and source provenance. Leveraging these structural signals, we explore curriculum learning across multiple mathematical subjects and characterize scaling patterns with supervision volume and source breadth. At full scale, fine-tuning on TOME-Math raises the unweighted mean score across our held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, while exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate. Our findings highlight structured textbooks as both a scalable source of mathematical supervision and an empirical framework for studying the impact of data organization on mathematical reasoning. We will release the corpus to facilitate further research on structured mathematical supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TOME-Math, a corpus of about 380K structured proof-supervision records from 2,118 university mathematics textbooks that preserves chapter order, proposition-proof links and dependency references. Fine-tuning on it raises the mean score by 16.7 percentage points over the base model.
AI.motivation: Mathematical supervision for language models is typically flattened into isolated problem-solution pairs, which discards the curricular organization and evidential structure of the original sources.
AI.method: Textbooks are converted into structured records that preserve chapter order, proposition-proof links, dependency references and source provenance; the authors explore curriculum learning across mathematical subjects and characterize scaling with supervision volume and source breadth.
AI.result: At full scale, fine-tuning raises the unweighted mean across held-out evaluations and established public benchmarks by 16.7 percentage points over the base model, exceeding all three public instruction-data baselines evaluated in aggregate.
AI.conclusion: Structured textbooks are a scalable source of mathematical supervision and a framework for studying how data organization affects mathematical reasoning; the corpus will be released.

title: Glance: The Generator Is Its Own Reranker
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Adapters and code: this https URL
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation commonly serves separate models for reranking and answering, duplicating model residency and passage processing. We introduce Glance, which equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head to score candidate passages from a shared prefill. Short relevance probes branch from the cached context, producing one score per passage without separately prefilling each query-passage pair. A single resident 9B backbone supports generation, general decisions and reranking, with approximately 0.1 GiB of additional memory per decision skill. After 39 minutes of MS MARCO fine-tuning, Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, compared with 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3. On 300 HotpotQA questions, its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context under the same base generator (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]). In a scaling study, reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens) scored from one shared prefill, where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10, and a probe-only activated adapter lets generation continue from the original passage cache. These initial results demonstrate generator-based reranking with one resident backbone; evaluation currently covers two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one backbone family.

AI.tldr: Glance equips the generator with a lightweight decision adapter and pointer head so that one resident 9B backbone can both answer and rerank candidate passages from a shared prefill. It matches or exceeds a cross-encoder reranker on two retrieval datasets with about 0.1 GiB of extra memory per decision skill.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation usually serves separate models for reranking and answering, which duplicates model residency and passage processing.
AI.method: Short relevance probes branch from the cached context and produce one score per candidate passage without prefilling each query-passage pair separately; the decision adapter and pointer head are fine-tuned on MS MARCO for 39 minutes.
AI.result: Glance achieves nDCG@10 of 0.741 on SciFact and 0.345 on NFCorpus, versus 0.721 and 0.326 for bge-reranker-v2-m3; on 300 HotpotQA questions its selected context improves answer F1 by 0.045 over cross-encoder-selected context (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.014, 0.076]); reranking quality keeps rising up to 200 candidates (43k tokens), where it exceeds the cross-encoder by 0.058 nDCG@10.
AI.conclusion: One resident backbone can serve generation and reranking with little overhead, although evaluation currently covers only two retrieval datasets, one QA dataset and one model family.

title: rTaste: Do Research Agents Have Taste? Evaluating Early Stage Research Judgment
comment: 27 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, proposes minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. The agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run remains limited. The evaluation harness and a dataset of all 415 MVEs, with their forecasts and audited outcomes, are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether research agents have research taste, that is, the judgment of which minimum viable experiments are worth running before their outcomes are known. Agents produce many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve the choice of which to run is limited.
AI.motivation: Research taste, the ability to judge which experiments to run before knowing their outcomes, had not been measured for research agents.
AI.method: Six frontier models, working alone or as teams, read seven recent NLP papers and propose minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecast whether each will pass a self-set threshold, and rank them; a separate executor runs every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results.
AI.result: Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but only 73 are also judged beyond the seed paper and non-obvious. The agents' first choices match the auditors' most valued experiment more often than a random pick but do not beat choosing the experiment written first; their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model, and teams cost more without a clear overall gain.
AI.conclusion: Agents generate many worthwhile experiments, but the evidence that their rankings improve which experiments get run remains limited; the harness and dataset of 415 audited MVEs are released.

title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
comment: 23 pages, 12 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper shows that LLM-brain alignment is carried by a low-dimensional subspace: ridge reduced-rank regression recovers full linear encoding performance with only 1-3% of the embedding dimensionality. These brain-predictive directions differ from the principal axes of variance in the embeddings.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear which components of LLM representations drive alignment with human neural activity during naturalistic language processing.
AI.method: Ridge reduced-rank regression identifies the brain-predictive subspace, the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses; it is evaluated on three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, across six model conditions including autoregressive, bidirectional masked and randomly initialized models, and compared with PCA.
AI.result: Full linear encoding performance is recovered with only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality; the subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets; PCA needs substantially more dimensions to reach comparable neural prediction; learned subspaces surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity beyond the LLM representations.
AI.conclusion: LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations, which provides a framework for explaining why these representations align with neural activity.

title: IndicIPR-QA: A Benchmark for Extractive Question Answering on Indian IPR Laws
summary: Legal Question Answering (QA) over statutory texts is a challenging task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), especially in low-resource settings with complex legal systems. It requires answers that are precise and grounded in the law. However, to the best of current knowledge, no existing extractive QA benchmark provides exact answer spans from statutory texts across all seven Indian Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Acts. This paper presents IndicIPR-QA1, an extractive QA benchmark for Indian IPR laws. The proposed dataset contains 4,462 QA pairs from 1,116 statutory contexts across seven Acts. Questions and answers are generated using GPT-4o and validated through nine automatic quality checks, single and multi-model LLM evaluations, and a 200-pair human audit. Section-level partitioning prevents source-context overlap across the training, validation, and test sets. Further analysis examines answer span length, lexical overlap, and multi-clause structure across the corpus and individual Acts. BM25 achieves a token-level F1 score of 20.21, while fine-tuned InLegalBERT reaches 85.02 under a unified sliding-window inference protocol. The large performance gap between BM25 (20.21 F1) and InLegalBERT (85.02 F1) shows that simple word matching is not enough to answer these legal questions. Performance also varies across the seven Acts, indicating substantial differences in answer-extraction performance.

AI.tldr: The paper releases IndicIPR-QA, an extractive QA benchmark of 4,462 question-answer pairs over the statutory texts of seven Indian Intellectual Property Rights Acts. Fine-tuned InLegalBERT reaches 85.02 token-level F1, while BM25 reaches 20.21.
AI.motivation: No existing extractive QA benchmark provides exact answer spans from statutory texts across all seven Indian IPR Acts, which leaves legal QA in this low-resource setting under-served.
AI.method: Questions and answers were generated with GPT-4o from 1,116 statutory contexts and validated through nine automatic quality checks, single and multi-model LLM evaluations and a 200-pair human audit; section-level partitioning separates the training, validation and test sets, and BM25 and fine-tuned InLegalBERT are compared under a unified sliding-window inference protocol.
AI.result: BM25 achieves token-level F1 of 20.21 and fine-tuned InLegalBERT 85.02; performance varies across the seven Acts, and answer span length, lexical overlap and multi-clause structure are analysed across the corpus.
AI.conclusion: The large gap shows that simple word matching is not enough for these legal questions, and the benchmark exposes substantial differences in answer extraction across individual Acts.

title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
summary: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MTA-OPSD, which lets every token select its own teacher from a multi-teacher pool during on-policy self-distillation instead of relying on one fixed teacher. On Qwen3 models for mathematical reasoning it gains up to +5.9 over the base model and outperforms existing OPSD approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation keeps the teacher fixed either throughout training or within each response, but the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response.
AI.method: A teacher-intervention pilot study shows that teacher preference differs across tokens; a preferred teacher is identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection, and the multi-teacher pool lets every token adaptively select its teacher during training.
AI.result: With Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks, MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches, with an average gain of up to +5.9 over the base model.
AI.conclusion: Adapting teacher supervision at the token level matters for post-training LLMs through self-distillation.

title: PIVOT: Progressive Intervention via Online Teacher Correction
comment: 19 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited by sparse outcome-level feedback on hard reasoning tasks: when all rollouts in a group fail, rewards provide no learning signal. Stronger teachers can provide additional guidance, but this raises a central question: how can such signals be incorporated into RLVR to support successful rollouts while remaining learnable for the student? We distinguish two complementary mechanisms: trajectory-level intervention, which improves access to reward-bearing trajectories, and token-level supervision, which provides dense targets to guide student learning. Our controlled experiments show that either mechanism alone can remain insufficient, motivating their combination. We therefore introduce PIVOT, which inserts teacher-generated corrections into student rollouts and applies token-level KL supervision to these segments alongside the RLVR objective. Beyond their combination, we systematically analyze where to intervene and how to supervise, yielding a recipe for effective guidance. Across hard logic games and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, PIVOT consistently outperforms existing methods, nearly doubling mean avg@8 on logic games from 19.5% for the best-performing baseline to 35.6%.

AI.tldr: PIVOT combines trajectory-level teacher intervention with token-level KL supervision on the inserted corrections, helping RLVR learn from hard reasoning tasks where all rollouts fail. On hard logic games it nearly doubles mean avg@8, from 19.5% for the best baseline to 35.6%.
AI.motivation: RLVR is limited on hard reasoning tasks by sparse outcome-level feedback, since groups in which every rollout fails provide no learning signal, and it is unclear how teacher guidance should be incorporated.
AI.method: PIVOT inserts teacher-generated corrections into student rollouts and applies token-level KL supervision to these segments alongside the RLVR objective; the authors systematically analyse where to intervene and how to supervise.
AI.result: Across hard logic games and mathematical reasoning benchmarks PIVOT consistently outperforms existing methods; on logic games mean avg@8 rises from 19.5% for the best-performing baseline to 35.6%.
AI.conclusion: Combining trajectory-level intervention with token-level supervision is more effective than either mechanism alone, yielding a practical recipe for teacher guidance in RLVR.

title: Multi-View MoE: Letting Every Router Shape Expert Computation
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand parameter capacity by activating a small subset of experts per token. Expert selection directly affects model capabilities under a fixed active-expert budget. Dense evaluation of all experts reveals weak agreement between single-router rankings and expert-utility evaluation rankings, especially in middle and deep layers. Richer signals for selection and computation incur additional cost: selection based on internal expert activations requires preliminary computation, while processing multiple full representations separately through the same expert repeats its computation. We propose Multi-View MoE to improve expert selection with multiple routers and reuse their preferences to modulate expert computation under a fixed expert budget. Its Multi-Router submodule aggregates sigmoid scores from independently initialized routers. These routers develop highly differentiated expert preferences during training, allowing experts strongly favored by one router or jointly supported by several routers to be selected. Multi-View further uses each selected expert's relative scores across routers to mix learned latent views into its input, reusing routing preferences for both selection and computation. Each selected expert executes one forward pass, preserving the active-expert count, expert FLOPs, and all-to-all communication volume. On a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens, full Multi-View MoE improves the nine-task downstream mean by 1.18 percentage points over the baseline. Multi-Router alone yields a 0.6-percentage-point gain and improves the rank correlation between router scores and evaluated expert utility, with relative increases of 8.1% globally and approximately 58% in the layer with the lowest single-router alignment. Controlled mixing interventions show the model uses input differences that depend on both the expert and the token.

AI.tldr: Multi-View MoE improves expert selection in sparse mixture-of-experts models by aggregating several independently initialized routers, then reuses their preferences to mix latent views into each selected expert's input while keeping expert compute fixed. On a 10B-A1B model it improves the nine-task downstream mean by 1.18 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Single-router expert rankings agree weakly with expert-utility rankings, especially in middle and deep layers, while richer selection signals usually add computational cost.
AI.method: A Multi-Router submodule aggregates sigmoid scores from independently initialized routers to select experts; each selected expert's relative scores across routers are used to mix learned latent views into its input, so each selected expert executes one forward pass.
AI.result: On a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens, the full method improves the nine-task downstream mean by 1.18 percentage points; Multi-Router alone gives +0.6 points and raises the rank correlation between router scores and expert utility by 8.1% globally and about 58% in the least-aligned layer.
AI.conclusion: Using multiple routers for both selection and computation improves MoE quality without changing the active-expert count, expert FLOPs or all-to-all communication volume.

title: When to Assist and What to Suggest: Joint Gating and Memory-Grounded Hint Generation in One Compact Decoder
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 13 tables; supplementary material included (Sections S1-S8)
summary: Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that one compact 1B decoder can decide when to give a memory-grounded hint and generate it in the same pass, matching or exceeding two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time.
AI.motivation: Proactive assistants currently split the decision of when to assist and what to suggest between a gate and a larger generator, and the two have not been evaluated together end to end.
AI.method: The gate and generator are evaluated together on 28,058 decision points; a single 1B decoder gates from an intermediate layer and generates in the same pass; a human evaluation of 1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues assesses the effect of memory.
AI.result: Behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against an oracle ceiling of 0.2971, with precision of 0.2387; removing the memory profile costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match; the joint 1B model ties the separate gate across seeds, and human ratings place it level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one.
AI.conclusion: A single small decoder can handle both gating and hint generation with less wall-clock time, and the memory profile is the main driver of hint quality.

title: Testimony from Timelines: Evidence-Grounded Significance Testing of Temporal Clinical Hypotheses
summary: Ask a language model whether sales tend to dip after a product recall, or whether one side effect tends to follow another after a vaccine, and it answers in a fluent sentence that reads like a finding, with no test behind it. Assertions about how events unfold across many cases fill the Web, and each is a temporal hypothesis that only a significance test over the right records can settle. The verifier must specify the null, select the test and decide which records bear on the hypothesis, and any of these choices can go wrong while the conclusion still comes out right. Yet benchmarks for language-model data analysis grade only the conclusion, with the relevant data handed over. We study the problem in health, where a wrong verdict is costly, and present STRATA, a benchmark that grades every decision on the way to a verdict: 8,735 hypotheses over the clinical timelines of vaccine adverse-event reports, with gold plans, evidence sets, p-values and verdicts derived under a released codebook and reproduced by a deterministic oracle. We also propose ART (articulate, retrieve, test), a staged paradigm that exposes each decision as an inspectable output. Extensive experiments with five model configurations show that systems fail mostly at choosing which records count, a verdict-evidence gap that accuracy alone conceals. ART closes most of this gap and brings a 31B open model to within 0.01 of the frontier models under the same paradigm; the frontier models succeed once given the codebook.

AI.tldr: The paper presents STRATA, a benchmark that grades every decision on the way to a verdict for temporal clinical hypotheses over vaccine adverse-event timelines, and ART, a staged articulate-retrieve-test paradigm. Systems fail mostly at choosing which records count, and ART brings a 31B open model to within 0.01 of frontier models.
AI.motivation: Language models answer temporal hypotheses fluently without a significance test behind the answer, while existing data-analysis benchmarks grade only the conclusion with the relevant data supplied, hiding errors in null specification, test selection and record selection.
AI.method: STRATA contains 8,735 hypotheses over clinical timelines of vaccine adverse-event reports, with gold plans, evidence sets, p-values and verdicts derived under a released codebook and reproduced by a deterministic oracle; ART (articulate, retrieve, test) exposes each decision as an inspectable output.
AI.result: Experiments with five model configurations show that systems fail mostly at choosing which records count, a verdict-evidence gap that accuracy alone conceals; ART closes most of this gap and brings a 31B open model within 0.01 of frontier models under the same paradigm; frontier models succeed once given the codebook.
AI.conclusion: Grading the full reasoning path rather than only the verdict exposes failure modes that accuracy hides, and staged, inspectable analysis narrows the gap for open models.

title: ShallowDefend: Harnessing Shallow Safety Alignment for Multi-Turn Defender
summary: Safety alignment has enabled large language models to reliably refuse harmful requests directly, yet the same request distributed across a multi-turn conversation still succeeds far too often. This brittleness has a mechanistic root: Alignment is shallow, with safety behavior concentrated in a model's first few output tokens, and existing defenses inherit the weakness, supervising the surface form of the response without ever giving the model an explicit safety decision to learn. We take the opposite view of shallowness: if a short span determines the trajectory of an entire response, that span is the highest-leverage place to intervene, and the defender can occupy it first. We propose Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, a framework in which the defender assesses the user's intent, commits to an explicit, parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it, with the commitment trained by reinforcement learning at the payload turn. Because the decision is a token span, the reward can be a rule: a self-verified reward checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, requiring no judge and no annotation, while the same format also supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection. Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks spanning safety, utility, and helpfulness, our defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison, maintaining their lead in safety while preserving utility at a modest cost to helpfulness. A per-token KL analysis and interventional probes confirm why this works: training concentrates its effect on the brief deliberation that sets a response's trajectory, and the decision committed there is a causal control point. The very shallowness attackers exploit becomes the mechanism of defense.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Assess, Decide, Respond, a multi-turn safety framework in which the model commits to an explicit, parseable safety decision before replying, trained with reinforcement learning. Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks the defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison while keeping utility at modest cost.
AI.motivation: Safety alignment is shallow, concentrated in the first few output tokens, so harmful requests spread across a multi-turn conversation still succeed too often, and existing defenses supervise surface form without giving the model an explicit safety decision to learn.
AI.method: The defender assesses the user's intent, commits to an explicit parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it; because the decision is a short token span, a rule-based self-verified reward checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, and the same format supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection.
AI.result: Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks covering safety, utility and helpfulness, the defenders maintain the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison while preserving utility at a modest cost to helpfulness; per-token KL analysis and interventional probes show that training concentrates its effect on the brief deliberation that sets the response trajectory.
AI.conclusion: The shallowness that attackers exploit can become a defense when the brief opening decision is made explicit and trained as a causal control point.

title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
summary: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Controlled Attribution Benchmark, which fine-tunes LLMs on fictitious knowledge to give unambiguous ground truth for data attribution. It shows that negative log-odds gradients and aggregating only the top token scores substantially improve attribution recall.
AI.motivation: Data attribution methods for language models are evaluated on downstream tasks that vary several dataset properties at once, so it is impossible to isolate why a given attribution algorithm fails.
AI.method: The CATT benchmark for fact tracing fine-tunes LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge and alters one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors; the authors examine two underexplored design choices, the loss used for gradients and how per-token scores are aggregated into a document score, rather than proposing a new estimator.
AI.result: Redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution; replacing cross-entropy gradients with negative log-odds gradients and aggregating only the top token scores improves ground-truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines; the negative log-odds correction also improves counterfactual retraining on FTRACE-TREX for every method tested, by up to 4.9x.
AI.conclusion: Causal evidence in training documents is highly localized and averaging over whole documents dilutes it into noise, so loss and aggregation choices matter as much as the estimator itself.

title: DuQUAD: A Dual-View Framework with Quality-Aware Evidence Pruning for Multi-Document Question Answering
summary: Large language models with retrieval-augmented generation systematically underutilize evidence in the middle of multi-document contexts, a phenomenon known as Lost in the Middle. Existing mitigation strategies, such as document reordering and attention steering, can reduce boundary bias but remain brittle in noisy settings, where inaccurate relevance estimation and spurious documents still obscure useful evidence in central positions. We propose DuQUAD, a multi-document QA framework that mitigates positional bias through dual-view reasoning and quality-aware evidence pruning. DuQUAD combines a Local Agent guided by a Structural Fusion Score with a Global Agent that reasons over the full document set, providing both targeted evidence recovery and broad contextual understanding. The framework further filters candidate evidence using explicit quality scoring and refines it at the sentence level to reduce noise. DuQUAD consistently outperforms strong Lost-in-the-Middle mitigation baselines, including hybrid retrieval and reranking, multi-agent reasoning, and context optimization methods, improving accuracy by 3.0% on average over the strongest competing baseline and gold evidence recall by 9.4%, while substantially reducing computational cost compared to existing multi-agent frameworks.

AI.tldr: DuQUAD is a multi-document QA framework that combines dual-view reasoning, a local agent and a global agent, with quality-aware evidence pruning to counter the lost-in-the-middle effect. It improves accuracy by 3.0% on average over the strongest baseline and gold evidence recall by 9.4%.
AI.motivation: RAG systems underuse evidence in the middle of multi-document contexts, and existing mitigations such as reordering and attention steering remain brittle when relevance estimates are noisy and spurious documents occupy central positions.
AI.method: A Local Agent guided by a Structural Fusion Score provides targeted evidence recovery, a Global Agent reasons over the full document set, and candidate evidence is filtered by explicit quality scoring and refined at sentence level to reduce noise.
AI.result: DuQUAD consistently outperforms Lost-in-the-Middle mitigation baselines, including hybrid retrieval and reranking, multi-agent reasoning and context optimization methods, improving accuracy by 3.0% on average over the strongest competing baseline and gold evidence recall by 9.4%, with substantially lower computational cost than existing multi-agent frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Combining targeted local recovery with global context and quality-aware pruning mitigates positional bias more robustly than existing approaches.

title: Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration for Spectral Compression of Dense Retrieval Embeddings
summary: Spectral compression reduces the storage and scoring costs of dense retrieval by projecting embeddings onto a smaller principal subspace. However, its corpus-derived weighting rules tie all retained directions to a shared spectral trend, without directly accounting for their individual contributions to relevance. To address this, we propose Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration (RRC), a closed-form method for refining spectral weights using relevance judgments. RRC estimates margin-based weights from the means and variances of positive--negative score contributions along each retained direction. It retains directions with positive estimated weights, decomposes their log weights into a fitted power-law trend and a residual, and adds the residual to the compressor's log weights on this support. This allows relevance judgments to adjust individual directions while preserving the compressor's overall spectral trend. RRC applies to PCA, Whitening, and SpecTemp, and incorporates the corrections into the existing transformation shared by documents and queries, without iterative model training or an additional inference stage. Experiments with three encoders on nine datasets covering conventional and reasoning-intensive retrieval show that SpecTemp + RRC achieves the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors on the BEIR group and BRIGHT at every target dimension. On the five evaluated BRIGHT datasets, it improves over SpecTemp by an average of 2.34 nDCG@10 points at 768 dimensions. The gains also persist under scalar and product quantization, improving the trade-off between per-document storage and retrieval effectiveness. Our code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration, a closed-form method that refines spectral compression weights of dense retrieval embeddings using relevance judgments. SpecTemp plus RRC achieves the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors on BEIR and BRIGHT at every target dimension.
AI.motivation: Spectral compression reduces the storage and scoring cost of dense retrieval, but its corpus-derived weights tie all retained directions to a shared spectral trend without accounting for each direction's contribution to relevance.
AI.method: RRC estimates margin-based weights from the means and variances of positive-negative score contributions along each retained direction, keeps directions with positive weights, decomposes their log weights into a fitted power-law trend and a residual, and adds the residual to the compressor's log weights; it applies to PCA, Whitening and SpecTemp without iterative training.
AI.result: Across three encoders and nine datasets, SpecTemp plus RRC achieves the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors on BEIR and BRIGHT at every target dimension; on five BRIGHT datasets it improves over SpecTemp by 2.34 nDCG@10 points on average at 768 dimensions, and the gains persist under scalar and product quantization.
AI.conclusion: Relevance judgments can refine individual spectral directions while preserving the overall trend, improving the storage-effectiveness trade-off of compressed dense retrieval.

title: Detecting Covert Collusion between AI Agents through Partner-Outsider Positive Listening
summary: AI agents that share a secret convention can coordinate through messages that look innocent, so a monitor that reads only the messages can miss them. We propose a behavioural test: a partner that uses a code reacts to the exact wording of a message, whereas an uninvolved agent placed in its seat does not. Partner--Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) is the difference between the two agents in how much their action changes when the message is reworded with its meaning kept, and it is computed after the fact by replaying logged prompts. In a simulated market with five conditions (no collusion, a joint reward with neutral messages, the same with an openly stated intention, a covert first-letter code, and the code with a stated intention), PoPLi is between 0.48 and 0.59 whenever the code is present (95% intervals all above 0.29) and between -0.10 and -0.01 without it. Message-only monitors did not separate the conditions: one reading the speaker's messages answered "no" in all 50 markets, and one reading every seller's messages flagged 9 of 10 markets with no collusion. PoPLi detects the use of a private channel, not collusion as such, and it cannot detect collusion through incentives alone or codes carried by meaning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Partner-Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi), a behavioural test that detects covert collusion between AI agents by checking whether a partner reacts to the exact wording of a message while an uninvolved outsider does not. In a simulated market, PoPLi separates coded collusion from non-collusion, whereas message-only monitors do not.
AI.motivation: AI agents that share a secret convention can coordinate through innocent-looking messages, so a monitor that reads only the messages can miss the collusion.
AI.method: PoPLi is the difference between the partner and the outsider in how much their action changes when the message is reworded with its meaning kept; it is computed after the fact by replaying logged prompts, in a simulated market with five conditions, including a covert first-letter code.
AI.result: PoPLi is between 0.48 and 0.59 whenever the code is present (95% intervals all above 0.29) and between -0.10 and -0.01 without it. Message-only monitors did not separate the conditions: one answered "no" in all 50 markets, and another flagged 9 of 10 markets with no collusion.
AI.conclusion: PoPLi detects the use of a private channel rather than collusion as such, and it cannot detect collusion through incentives alone or through codes carried by meaning.

title: Beyond Utterance-Level Speaker Similarity: Perception-Aligned Segmental Evaluation of Accent in Speech Generation
summary: Utterance-level similarity ratings do not reveal where perceived accent differences occur in generated speech. We introduce a segmental evaluation protocol combining speaker and accent similarity ratings with subword annotations of perceived accent differences provided by listeners from target accent regions. Using newly collected recordings, 47 retained listeners evaluate 200 content-matched reference--candidate pairs spanning four Scottish and Australian voices, two zero-shot TTS systems, and an articulation-based voice conversion system. Subword annotations locate salient pronunciation differences and sometimes yield different system rankings from similarity ratings. Speaker and accent ratings remain strongly associated ($\rho = 0.71$), highlighting the value of examining local perceptual evidence beyond these scores. Evaluation of seven objective distances reveals weak correspondence with subword selections, with correlations reaching at most $\rho = 0.22$. We release code, data, and an interactive demo to support the development of perceptually grounded segmental accent evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a segmental evaluation protocol for accent in speech generation that combines utterance-level similarity ratings with listener annotations of subword accent differences. It shows that segmental evidence can change system rankings, and that seven objective distances correlate only weakly with listeners' selections.
AI.motivation: Utterance-level similarity ratings do not reveal where perceived accent differences occur in generated speech.
AI.method: Listeners from the target accent regions rated speaker and accent similarity and annotated subword pronunciation differences for 200 content-matched reference-candidate pairs, covering four Scottish and Australian voices, two zero-shot TTS systems and an articulation-based voice conversion system.
AI.result: Subword annotations locate salient pronunciation differences and sometimes produce different system rankings from similarity ratings. Speaker and accent ratings remain strongly associated (rho = 0.71). Seven objective distances show weak correspondence with subword selections, reaching at most rho = 0.22.
AI.conclusion: Local perceptual evidence adds information beyond utterance-level scores, and the released code, data and interactive demo support perceptually grounded segmental accent evaluation.

title: SciGame: Let Agents Play the Scientific Discovery Games in the Real and Counterfactual World
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly used for scientific discovery. However, existing benchmarks mix law inference with programming, score data fitting instead of prediction on unseen inputs, and do not separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors. We introduce SciGame, a controlled benchmark that converts scientific literature into structured scientific cards. Each card yields a pair of Original and dimensionally consistent Counterfactual environments with the same task interface. SciGame contains a Historical collection of canonical laws and a live Temporal collection curated from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs. It evaluates agents in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings. Each setting runs under Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive protocols. Experiments on five frontier models yield three findings. First, familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered. Second, adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets. Third, good explanations can hide quantitative failures. Recovering the exact symbolic form remains the main bottleneck, even when agents interpret evidence correctly. Current agents can investigate systems actively, but inducing exact laws in unfamiliar settings remains an open challenge.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SciGame, a controlled benchmark in which LLM agents must discover scientific laws in Original and Counterfactual environments derived from the literature. Experiments on five frontier models show that familiar priors can mislead agents, and that recovering the exact symbolic law remains the main bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks mix law inference with programming, score data fitting rather than prediction on unseen inputs, and do not separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors.
AI.method: Scientific literature is converted into structured scientific cards, each yielding a dimensionally consistent Original and Counterfactual environment with the same task interface. The benchmark has a Historical collection of canonical laws and a Temporal collection drawn from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs, evaluated in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings under Prior-only, Fixed and Adaptive protocols.
AI.result: Familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered. Adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets. Good explanations can hide quantitative failures, and recovering the exact symbolic form remains the main bottleneck even when agents interpret the evidence correctly.
AI.conclusion: Current agents can investigate systems actively, but inducing exact laws in unfamiliar settings remains an open challenge.

title: "It Would Make a Geordie Feel at Home": Regional Accent Perceptions and Speech Accommodation in Voice AI
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often perform less accurately for speakers of regional dialects, but less is known about how users respond to these limitations and how regional voices produced by voice assistants (VAs) are evaluated through a sociolinguistic lens. This study investigates these issues among speakers of Newcastle English (Geordies), examining both linguistic accommodation to voice technologies and perceptions of regional versus mainstream-accented VA voices. Participants interacted with a simulated VA that spoke either Newcastle English or Standard Southern British English (SSBE). They subsequently completed semi-structured interviews about their experiences with the experimental VA and voice technologies, language use, accent attitudes, and place orientation. The findings reveal a two-way process of sociolinguistic bias. The Geordie VA was associated with familiarity, warmth, personality, and local belonging, but also with concerns about professionalism and authority, whereas the SSBE voice was perceived as more neutral, clear, and credible. Participants also reported adapting their speech when voice technologies failed to recognise them, most commonly by shifting to a more mainstream accent, enunciating more clearly, and speaking more slowly. These strategies are similar to accommodation in human-human interaction and reflect users' perceptions of what technologies can recognise, also known as perceived intelligibility pressures. Overall, the findings demonstrate that voice technologies can reproduce existing accent biases both by encouraging users to suppress regional features and by activating established social stereotypes through synthetic voices. The study positions sociolinguistics as a bridge between understanding human-AI interaction and designing inclusive technologies around users' own linguistic priorities.

AI.tldr: This study examines how Newcastle English speakers (Geordies) accommodate to voice assistants and how they evaluate regional versus mainstream-accented assistant voices. It finds a two-way sociolinguistic bias, in which users suppress regional features and synthetic regional voices activate social stereotypes.
AI.motivation: Automatic speech recognition systems often perform less accurately for regional dialect speakers, but less is known about how users respond to these limitations and how regional voices produced by voice assistants are evaluated.
AI.method: Participants interacted with a simulated voice assistant that spoke either Newcastle English or Standard Southern British English (SSBE), then completed semi-structured interviews about their experiences, language use, accent attitudes and place orientation.
AI.result: The Geordie assistant was associated with familiarity, warmth, personality and local belonging, but also with concerns about professionalism and authority; the SSBE voice was perceived as more neutral, clear and credible. Participants reported adapting their speech when recognition failed, most often by shifting to a more mainstream accent, enunciating more clearly and speaking more slowly.
AI.conclusion: Voice technologies can reproduce existing accent biases both by encouraging users to suppress regional features and by activating social stereotypes through synthetic voices, which argues for designing inclusive technologies around users' own linguistic priorities.

title: Calculation and rejection diverge in language models tested at known mechanical limits
comment: 94 pages, including Supplementary Information. Data and code: this https URL
summary: When a language model returns engineering quantities with the status "solved", software that trusts it passes them on, even when the requested design is physically impossible. Such failures could reflect poor calculation, how the answer is requested, or a failure to judge feasibility. We set beam loads and disk speeds at known percentages above or below plastic collapse or burst, measured each model's limit calculation separately and tested 12 models in 4,860 calls, including follow-up experiments on new designs. We find that a model can recognize an impossible design when asked only whether it is feasible, yet accept the same design, reporting "solved", when asked for a full answer. Three models accepted beams 10 to 30% beyond collapse despite precise limit calculations in separate questions, and many accepted replies stated the violation. Asked only about feasibility, Opus 5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash rejected every impossible new design they were given, including those accepted in full answers, without false alarms. Rewording when to decline or changing the answer format raised rejection on the original beams, but not consistently on new designs. Software and benchmarks using a model's status should test feasibility judgment and full-answer rejection separately, and report the exact prompt.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a language model can reject a physically impossible engineering design when asked only about feasibility, yet accept the same design and report it as solved when asked for a full answer. Testing 12 models in 4,860 calls, it argues that software and benchmarks relying on a model's status should test feasibility judgment and full-answer rejection separately.
AI.motivation: When a model returns engineering quantities marked "solved", software that trusts the status may pass on physically impossible designs, and it is unclear whether such failures reflect poor calculation, how the answer is requested, or a failure to judge feasibility.
AI.method: Beam loads and disk speeds were set at known percentages above or below plastic collapse or burst; each model's limit calculation was measured separately, and 12 models were tested in 4,860 calls, with follow-up experiments on new designs.
AI.result: Three models accepted beams 10 to 30% beyond collapse despite precise limit calculations in separate questions, and many accepted replies stated the violation. Asked only about feasibility, Opus 5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash rejected every impossible new design they were given, including those accepted in full answers, without false alarms. Rewording when to decline or changing the answer format raised rejection on the original beams but not consistently on new designs.
AI.conclusion: Calculation and rejection diverge, so software and benchmarks that use a model's status should test feasibility judgment and full-answer rejection separately and report the exact prompt.

title: Manifest-Assisted Retrieval in Artificial Intelligence Search: Evidence Gaps and a Security Evaluation
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 5 table. Accepted at IEEE FLLM 2026. Author accepted manuscript. Reproducibility artifact: this https URL
summary: The external sources retained in our non-systematic audit did not isolate the incremental security or utility effect of consuming /llms.txt while ordinary retrieval remained fixed. The initial audit covered 39 sources through August 16, 2026, with later targeted updates through October 14. A purposive 15-tool study observed no automatic requests in 45 trials at one endpoint; a non-probability log study found that 97% of domains with detected files received no recorded requests in May 2026. We separate publication, fetch, model use, and action; define five operational threat paths and paired security-utility estimands; and exercise deterministic pre-model controls with 30 author-defined parser fixtures. We also execute a reduced pilot: 24 tasks across eight sites, five conditions, and 120 real model responses, with ordinary evidence held fixed. Frozen automatic scoring identifies attacker-target adoption in $21/24$ raw adversarial responses, with one further response unresolved; the adversarial URLs-only condition has no known adoptions and one unresolved response. The pilot measures output changes conditional on supplied evidence, without live retrieval or external actions. Together, the framework and pilot distinguish manifest-content effects from publication, discovery, and downstream execution, while leaving full retrieval and agent evaluation open.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether consuming /llms.txt manifests changes the security and output of AI search retrieval, separating manifest content from publication, discovery and downstream execution. A reduced pilot finds attacker-target adoption in 21 of 24 raw adversarial responses, while full retrieval and agent evaluation remain open.
AI.motivation: The external sources retained in a non-systematic audit did not isolate the incremental security or utility effect of consuming /llms.txt while ordinary retrieval remained fixed.
AI.method: A non-systematic audit of 39 sources, a purposive 15-tool study with 45 trials at one endpoint, and a non-probability log study of domains with detected files. The authors define five operational threat paths and paired security-utility estimands, test deterministic pre-model controls on 30 author-defined parser fixtures, and run a pilot of 24 tasks across eight sites, five conditions and 120 real model responses with ordinary evidence held fixed.
AI.result: No automatic requests occurred in 45 trials at one endpoint, and 97% of domains with detected files received no recorded requests in May 2026. Frozen automatic scoring identified attacker-target adoption in 21 of 24 raw adversarial responses, with one further response unresolved; the adversarial URLs-only condition had no known adoptions and one unresolved response.
AI.conclusion: The framework and pilot distinguish manifest-content effects from publication, discovery and downstream execution by measuring output changes conditional on supplied evidence, without live retrieval or external actions, while full retrieval and agent evaluation remain open.

title: Predict the Reward, Not the World: World Reward Models for ML Agents
summary: Search-based machine-learning (ML) agents improve a solution by writing candidate programs, executing them, and keeping the best. Execution gives the search reliable feedback, but a single run can take hours, and most runs end in programs the agent discards. Recent agents try to save these runs by letting a large language model act as a world model that predicts how each program would perform. However, a wrong prediction feeds the search false information. We argue that an agent does not need to predict the outcome of execution, only the decision that execution would support. We propose World Reward Models (WRMs), which learn from real execution results to choose directly which candidate will perform better, without predicting any intermediate outcome. We prove that a selector which predicts execution from the same inputs cannot outperform the best direct selector, that predicted outcomes add an error which can make a likelihood-trained world model prefer the worse program on every instance, and that cross-entropy on executed winners drives a WRM toward the optimum. Our WRM, ForeCritic, adapts a 9B typed decision model to 5k executed program pairs. On 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, it picks the better program 79.4% of the time, while general-purpose LLM judges reach 53--62%, and its probabilities are calibrated. Inside AIDE, ML-Master, and ForeAgent, it cuts mean task time by 4.4--7.5 times while keeping their mean scores within 0.01 or raising them.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes World Reward Models (WRMs), which learn from real execution results to pick the better candidate program directly, without predicting intermediate execution outcomes. The ForeCritic WRM picks the better program 79.4% of the time and cuts task time by 4.4 to 7.5 times inside three ML agents while keeping their mean scores within 0.01 or raising them.
AI.motivation: Search-based ML agents need costly execution for reliable feedback, and recent world-model approaches use an LLM to predict program performance, so a wrong prediction feeds the search false information.
AI.method: The agent needs only the decision that execution would support, so WRMs are trained with cross-entropy on executed winners to choose directly between candidates.
