AI.conclusion: An evidence-citing, self-auditing LLM pipeline can outperform trained machine learning for pediatric diabetes outcome prediction, and its cited evidence is interpretable enough for clinicians to reach similar judgments.

title: Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success
summary: Tool-use benchmarks often score agents by final task success, but terminal outcomes can obscure whether the intermediate tool-call trajectory was executable. We propose prefix executability as a trajectory-level evaluation protocol for tool-using agents. The protocol measures whether every prefix of a predicted tool-call sequence remains executable under tool schemas, state preconditions, and data dependencies, and summarizes reliability using Prefix Executability Curves (PEC), First-Error Depth (FED), Trajectory Executability Rate (TER), horizon-normalized AUC-PEC, and Recovery Rate (RR). We instantiate the protocol on stratified samples from BFCL-v3 multi-turn and ToolSandbox, and on the complete Airline/Retail base splits of $\tau^3$-bench. We observe that outcome-only and prefix-level rankings diverge: agents whose execution is conditioned on an unverified plan often achieve higher point-estimate final success than non-plan-conditioned baselines while substantially lowering TER and AUC-PEC. These divergences are precisely the failure modes that prefix executability is designed to expose: they reveal whether apparent success rests on an executable trajectory, where invalidity first enters, and whether success follows recovery from an earlier failure. As a validation intervention, explicit pre-execution plan checking can improve executable-prefix survival while maintaining competitive terminal success. These results show that final success alone is insufficient for evaluating tool-use agents and that prefix-level executability provides an actionable reliability signal for comparing agents, diagnosing failures, and assessing validation mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes prefix executability, a trajectory-level protocol that checks whether every prefix of a tool-call sequence remains executable. It shows that outcome-only and prefix-level rankings diverge, and that explicit pre-execution plan checking improves executable-prefix survival while keeping terminal success competitive.
AI.motivation: Tool-use benchmarks score agents by final task success, which can hide whether intermediate tool calls were executable. Terminal outcomes alone are therefore insufficient for judging reliability.
AI.method: The protocol checks whether each prefix of a predicted tool-call sequence is executable under tool schemas, state preconditions and data dependencies. It summarizes reliability with Prefix Executability Curves (PEC), First-Error Depth (FED), Trajectory Executability Rate (TER), horizon-normalized AUC-PEC and Recovery Rate (RR). It is instantiated on stratified samples from BFCL-v3 multi-turn and ToolSandbox, and on the full Airline and Retail base splits of tau3-bench.
AI.result: Agents whose execution is conditioned on an unverified plan often achieve higher point-estimate final success than non-plan-conditioned baselines, while substantially lowering TER and AUC-PEC. Explicit pre-execution plan checking improves executable-prefix survival while keeping terminal success competitive.
AI.conclusion: Final success alone is insufficient for evaluating tool-use agents, and prefix-level executability is an actionable reliability signal for comparing agents, diagnosing failures and assessing validation mechanisms.

title: Training language models in simulation for psychiatric intake
comment: 76 pages, 8 figures, 15 tables (27 pages main text, 7 main figures, 2 main tables)
summary: In psychiatric practice, the clinical intake interview remains a primary diagnostic instrument, requiring the clinician to establish rapport while disentangling complex, overlapping presentations. Here, we show that multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation environments improves language model performance on structured text-based psychiatric intake, spanning history-taking, differential diagnosis, and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study ($N = 60$ matched scenario pairs, 120 encounters) comparing the RL-trained agent against its identically prompted base model, 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients while a separate panel of 15 independent, board-certified psychiatrists scored the de-identified transcripts. The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched scenario pairs ($p < 0.0001$), with gains on an adapted clinical-examination rubric ($d_z = 0.77$, $p < 0.0001$), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%, $p < 0.001$), and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%, $p < 0.001$). Across 127 psychiatrist-validated simulated intake scenarios, the trained agent nearly doubled its base model's clinical rubric score (0.706 vs. 0.379; composite reward 0.564 vs. 0.294, $p < 0.0001$). To systematically probe conversational safety, we established two Delphi-consensus taxonomies, of clinical safety risks and relational competencies, from which 256 challenging adversarial presentations were derived; we find that training in simulation environments more than halved under-triage of acute safety risks (12.9% vs. 30.5%, $p < 0.0001$). Simulation environments thus provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, with gains that transferred to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that multi-turn reinforcement learning in simulated environments improves an LLM's structured psychiatric intake, and that the trained agent beats its base model in a randomized, double-blind crossover study with 32 psychiatrists. Training also more than halves under-triage of acute safety risks in adversarial presentations.
AI.motivation: The clinical intake interview is a primary diagnostic tool in psychiatry, requiring rapport-building alongside disentangling complex presentations. The authors ask whether simulation-based RL can train language models for this task, and whether the training improves safety under adversarial presentations.
AI.method: Multi-turn RL is run in simulation environments covering history-taking, differential diagnosis and initial management planning. In a randomized, double-blind crossover study with 60 matched scenario pairs (120 encounters), 32 board-certified psychiatrists role-played standardized patients, and 15 independent psychiatrists scored de-identified transcripts. Two Delphi-consensus taxonomies of clinical safety risks and relational competencies were used to derive 256 adversarial presentations.
AI.result: The trained agent outperformed the base model in 76.7% of matched pairs (p below 0.0001), with gains on the clinical-examination rubric (d_z 0.77), patient-centered communication (82.0% vs. 65.2%) and differential diagnosis appropriateness (68.3% vs. 33.3%). Across 127 validated simulated scenarios, the clinical rubric score rose from 0.379 to 0.706, and the composite reward from 0.294 to 0.564. Under-triage of acute safety risks fell from 30.5% to 12.9%.
AI.conclusion: Simulation environments provide a controlled testbed for training and stress-testing psychiatric conversational agents, and the gains transfer to psychiatrist-enacted encounters, though residual gaps require safeguards and clinician oversight.

title: FIRME: Registry-Anchored Memory Graphs for Evolving, Heterogeneous Investor Knowledge
comment: 20 pages. Accepted at the 3rd Workshop on LLMs and Generative AI for Finance (AI4F) at ACM ICAIF 2026 (non-archival)
summary: Financial AI workflows that reuse investor knowledge need persistent memory that integrates observations across sources and periods without losing identity or provenance. In a knowledge graph, recurring observations may use different surface forms, fragmenting relationship histories and preventing evidence from accumulating. We introduce Fusion and Identity Registry for Memory Evolution (FIRME), a registry-anchored memory graph that reconciles incoming observations to persistent canonical relationships and retains their source, time, and context. Within periods, rule-based fusion links investor-call discussions to portfolio cash-flow signals, directly or through a fixed product-topic ontology. Across periods, canonical identities and persistent aliases direct recurring observations to the same relationship history; deterministic updates summarize reinforcement, inactivity, and reactivation. We evaluate FIRME on proprietary investor-call and cash-flow records and on S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts. Compared with a historical registry that retains canonical identities and semantic fallback but omits alias memory, FIRME increases final-period Correct Match Rate by 7.8-12.1 percentage points across four dataset-backend settings under a fixed-judge and fallback-review protocol. A blinded human audit of 200 incoming observations per setting finds Correct Match Rate gains of 9.0-16.5 points and reattachment-recall gains of 22.5-29.0 points, with higher observed merge precision in all four samples. A separate audit finds valid evidence paths for 293 of 300 outputs from full within-period fusion in the investor-call setting. Extraction-faithfulness and round-trip diagnostics assess source grounding and preservation of extractor-derived graph content.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FIRME, a registry-anchored memory graph that reconciles incoming financial observations to persistent canonical relationships while retaining source, time and context. It increases Correct Match Rate over a registry baseline without alias memory, and blinded audits confirm the gains.
AI.motivation: Financial AI workflows that reuse investor knowledge need persistent memory that integrates observations across sources and periods. In knowledge graphs, recurring observations may use different surface forms, which fragments relationship histories and prevents evidence from accumulating.
AI.method: FIRME uses a registry of canonical identities and persistent aliases to direct recurring observations to the same relationship history, with deterministic updates that summarize reinforcement, inactivity and reactivation. Within periods, rule-based fusion links investor-call discussions to portfolio cash-flow signals, directly or through a fixed product-topic ontology. It is evaluated on proprietary investor-call and cash-flow records and on S&P 500 earnings-call transcripts.
AI.result: Compared with a historical registry that retains canonical identities and semantic fallback but omits alias memory, FIRME raises final-period Correct Match Rate by 7.8 to 12.1 percentage points across four dataset-backend settings. A blinded audit of 200 observations per setting finds Correct Match Rate gains of 9.0 to 16.5 points and reattachment-recall gains of 22.5 to 29.0 points. A separate audit finds valid evidence paths for 293 of 300 outputs from within-period fusion in the investor-call setting.
AI.conclusion: Registry-anchored identities with alias memory allow financial knowledge graphs to accumulate evidence coherently across periods, with grounding preserved and verified by audits.

title: Agentic University: Collaborative Agents for Personalized Learning
summary: Large language models support personalized tutoring, content generation, and adaptive learning paths. However, capability development requires these resources and interactions to form a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner. A central challenge is to align goals, activities, and assessment while using learning evidence to decide what should follow. We introduce Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization and instantiate it in Agentic University (AU). In AU, learners participate as organization members and work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program. The program connects personal goals, learning activities across modalities, and layered assessment, while learner feedback and performance guide subsequent support. Our evaluation shows advantages in program organization, assessment design, and revision quality. Users achieved larger mean assessment gains (12.19 versus 5.61 points on a 50-point scale) and reported stronger cognitive support. This work contributes an organizational approach to adaptive learning that makes learner participation a continuing basis for multi-agent coordination. The Agentic University project is available at \href{this https URL}.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Human-Participatory Multi-Agent Organization and instantiates it as Agentic University, where learners work with specialized agents to maintain a revisable Capability Program. Users achieved larger assessment gains than the comparison condition and reported stronger cognitive support.
AI.motivation: LLM-based personalized tutoring and content generation do not by themselves form a coherent learning process that evolves with the learner. Aligning goals, activities and assessment, and using learning evidence to decide what follows, remains a central challenge.
AI.method: In Agentic University, learners participate as members of the organization alongside specialized agents. The Capability Program connects personal goals, learning activities across modalities and layered assessment, and learner feedback and performance guide subsequent support.
AI.result: Evaluation shows advantages in program organization, assessment design and revision quality. Users achieved mean assessment gains of 12.19 versus 5.61 points on a 50-point scale, and reported stronger cognitive support.
AI.conclusion: Making learner participation a continuing basis for multi-agent coordination offers an organizational approach to adaptive learning.

title: On the Fundamental Limits of Prefill-Based Decoding Length Prediction
summary: Predicting how many tokens a large language model (LLM) will decode, using only prefill-phase hidden states, is a key primitive for inference scheduling. We show that current benchmarks conflate predictor quality with task hardness: when the target model, dataset, or sampling configuration changes, reported accuracy collapses even though the predictor is unchanged. We trace this instability to an overlooked error source---the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding---and derive bounds that every prefill-side method must obey. Our analysis treats decoding as a stopped stochastic process. The per-step stopping probability of a response is not constant but ramps up over hundreds of steps, so the decode length inherits a central limit theorem from the many local decisions that determine where a response ends; this yields per-prompt normality with an explicit error term, together with an affine variance law $\sigma=\alpha\mu+b$ whose slope is the coefficient of variation of the number of response segments. Empirically, the normal law reproduces the per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent, and the residual departures from normality (mild right skew, slight excess kurtosis) are the ones predicted by the sampling-noise correction. Under fixed model, data, and sampling conditions, a broad design space of predictors (MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label, and Mixture-of-Experts variants) converges to similar performance close to the bound, confirming that \emph{system error dominates model error}. We argue for a benchmarking protocol that fixes the model, data, and sampling parameters and that reports relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones. Code and analysis tools are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that benchmark results for predicting LLM decode length from prefill hidden states conflate predictor quality with task hardness and decoding stochasticity. It derives bounds for prefill-side methods and argues for a benchmarking protocol that fixes model, data and sampling settings.
AI.motivation: Predicting decode length from prefill-phase hidden states is key to inference scheduling, but reported accuracy collapses when the target model, dataset or sampling configuration changes, even though the predictor is unchanged. The authors trace this to the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding, which is overlooked.
AI.method: Decoding is treated as a stopped stochastic process, in which the per-step stopping probability ramps up over hundreds of steps. This yields a central-limit-theorem normality of decode length per prompt, with an explicit error term and an affine variance law sigma = alpha mu + b. Empirical checks cover MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label and Mixture-of-Experts predictors.
AI.result: The normal law reproduces per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent. Residual departures from normality are consistent with the predicted sampling-noise correction. Under fixed model, data and sampling conditions, the predictors converge to similar performance close to the bound.
AI.conclusion: System error dominates model error, so benchmarks should fix model, data and sampling parameters and report relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones.

title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
summary: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Ramanujan Challenge submissions on research-level number theory problems, comparing AI models, computer algebra systems and formal tools. It also introduces an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline that reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6%.
AI.motivation: As AI's mathematical abilities improve, meaningful benchmarks are moving to research-level mathematics. Judging complex proofs reliably at scale is itself a challenge, since one-shot LLM judgment is error-prone.
AI.method: The Challenge contains research-level number theory problems with checkable numerical formulas, including unpublished results and open conjectures. The authors analyze submissions from AI models, computer algebra systems and formal tools, and introduce an AI-assisted pipeline that assesses semantic and logical correctness of natural language proofs, CAS code and Lean formalizations.
AI.result: The pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% compared with one-shot LLM judgment, and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. Some correct submissions are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and one published open conjecture was proved.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.

title: Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns
comment: Published at EDM 2025 (18th International Conference on Educational Data Mining), short paper. 7 pages
summary: This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Models to simulate counselling clients in educational role-plays in comparison to human role-players. Initially, we recorded role-playing sessions, where novice counsellors interacted with human peers acting as clients, followed by role-plays between humans and clients simulated by Mistrals Mixtral 8x7b using 4-bit quantization. These interactions were analysed with a counselling communication pattern system at sentence level. We investigated two key questions: (1) to what extent LLM-generated responses replicate authentic conversational dynamics and (2) whether counsellors' communication behaviour differs when interacting with human versus LLM-simulated clients. The findings highlight both similarities and differences in the application of counselling patterns across scenarios, showing the potential of LLM-based role-playing exercises to enhance counselling competencies and to identify areas for further refinement in virtual client simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper compares human role-players with Mixtral 8x7b-simulated clients in online counselling role-plays, analyzing sentence-level counselling communication patterns. It finds both similarities and differences in how counsellors behave with human versus LLM clients.
AI.motivation: LLMs could simulate counselling clients for training novice counsellors, but it is unclear how authentic their conversational dynamics are compared with human role-players.
AI.method: Novice counsellors held role-plays with human peers acting as clients, and then with clients simulated by Mixtral 8x7b using 4-bit quantization. Both sets of interactions were analyzed at sentence level with a counselling communication pattern system, addressing how well LLM responses replicate authentic dynamics and whether counsellor behavior differs by client type.
AI.result: The findings show both similarities and differences in the application of counselling patterns across the two scenarios.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based role-play has potential to enhance counselling competencies and to reveal areas for refining virtual client simulations.

title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
summary: Building and scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web environments requires reliable task-completion verification for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Typical automated approaches prompt vision-language models (VLMs) to judge trajectories or generate programs to inspect application state. However, both rely on partial views of complex digital environments. VLM judges are restricted to supplied observations, while generated programs depend on accessible state. These views can omit decisive evidence or leave completion judgments unsupported. Tailoring separate verifiers to different platforms and access settings adds further engineering cost. We present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verification through agentic exploration. It treats verification as dynamic evidence gathering and assessment within a shared procedure for online and offline settings across platforms and observation modalities. After inspecting the available context to construct a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Further analyses connect these gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration.

AI.tldr: VeriCUA is a platform-agnostic framework that verifies whether computer-using agents completed a task by treating verification as agentic exploration, selecting GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements. It improves agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines in online and offline settings.
AI.motivation: Existing automated verifiers rely on partial views: VLM judges see only the supplied observations, and generated programs depend on accessible application state. Tailoring separate verifiers to each platform and access setting adds engineering cost.
AI.method: After inspecting the available context to build a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules, within one shared procedure for online and offline settings and all platforms and observation modalities.
AI.result: Agreement with reference labels improves over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Analyses link the gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration.
AI.conclusion: A single exploration-based verifier can serve data curation, evaluation and reinforcement learning for desktop, mobile and web computer-using agents without per-platform verifier engineering.

title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
summary: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.

AI.tldr: TextSeal2 is a distortion-free watermark for LLMs that keeps its signal under speculative decoding, preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. It detects more watermarked 100-token and 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain at matched diversity or acceptance rate.
AI.motivation: Its predecessor TextSeal restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip, and the detector then averages scores from both keys without knowing which key was used, which is suboptimal.
AI.method: TextSeal2 merges two or more keys into a single virtual key coupled to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula, so any number of keys, including publicly shared ones, can be merged without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, keyed drafts are verified with one more exponential race run on the leftovers of the draft races; by memorylessness this reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly.
AI.result: At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of 10^-3, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate. Evaluated on three LLMs.
AI.conclusion: TextSeal2 combines exact target-model output distribution, preserved diversity and stronger detection in both standard and speculative decoding, without post-logits optimization.

title: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments
summary: Web agents require diverse, executable, and resettable website environments for reproducible training and evaluation. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, while generative construction can diverge from specified real websites. Capture-and-replay preserves observations, with interaction coverage constrained by captured content and replay capabilities. We present WebAnything, a fully automated framework that reconstructs source-grounded, reusable Web environments from real URLs without per-site manual implementation or repair after initial setup and authorization. An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources, and interaction outcomes; an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture. We construct 244 website artifacts across 14 application domains and 53 categories, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties, and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: WebAnything is a fully automated framework that rebuilds source-grounded, reusable web environments from real URLs without per-site manual work after initial setup. It constructs 244 website artifacts and 12,984 executed and accepted tasks, and fine-tuning on its trajectories improves several web-agent benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Web agents need diverse, executable, resettable environments. Human-assisted mirrors demand per-site engineering, generative construction can diverge from the specified real websites, and capture-and-replay constrains interaction to captured content and replay capabilities.
AI.method: An Explorer-Builder collects browser-observable structures, resources and interaction outcomes, and an independent verifier checks frozen candidates and guides local repair or targeted source recapture.
AI.result: Across 14 application domains and 53 categories, 244 artifacts support 12,984 accepted tasks. Compared with human-assisted WebHarbor, WebAnything achieves higher aggregate scores on three fidelity metrics, with 12 wins, two ties and no losses in a blind audit. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improves REAL success by 9.9 percentage points, Odysseys-Easy Rubric Avg and Task Avg by 6.25 and 6.32 percentage points, and WebArena-Verified Overall success by 13.33 percentage points under the fixed harness.
AI.conclusion: Automated reconstruction of real websites can supply scalable, reusable and resettable training and evaluation environments for web agents.

title: What Does an Ontology Catch? Curated, LLM-Generated and Data-Derived Ontologies as Checkers of LLM Agents over Knowledge Graphs
summary: LLM agents that answer questions over Web knowledge graphs are increasingly wrapped in checks derived from the graph's ontology, on the assumption that a formal schema makes a reliable judge. Yet a checker can be wrong as well: it can miss errors, and it can flag correct answers and push the agent into "fixing" them. Whether a curated ontology is worth its cost as such a judge, and how it compares with an ontology an LLM writes or a schema mined from the data, is unknown. We make the checker itself the object of study. Across curated, LLM-generated and data-derived ontologies, used as prompt context, as a checker, or both, and across open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph of nearly $10^{9}$ triples, we account for what ontology-derived checks catch and what they wrongly flag. We show how each source trades caught errors against false alarms, how a curated schema used as published can contradict its own data, which errors structural checks miss, and whether combining sources or giving the agent the checker's specific feedback pays off. On UniProt, the curated ontology flags more correct answers than either an ontology derived from the data or one an LLM derives from a summary of the data with masked identifiers. On real agent answers, its flags are only marginally more precise than random flags.

AI.tldr: The paper studies ontologies used as checkers of LLM agents that answer questions over knowledge graphs, comparing curated, LLM-generated and data-derived ontologies. Each source trades caught errors against false alarms, and on real agent answers the curated ontology's flags are only marginally more precise than random flags.
AI.motivation: LLM agents over web knowledge graphs are increasingly wrapped in ontology-derived checks on the assumption that a formal schema makes a reliable judge, yet a checker can miss errors or flag correct answers, and whether a curated ontology is worth its cost as a judge was unknown.
AI.method: The checker itself is the object of study: curated, LLM-generated and data-derived ontologies are used as prompt context, as a checker, or both, with open-weight and proprietary agents on public graphs and a private graph of nearly 10^9 triples.
AI.result: On UniProt, the curated ontology flags more correct answers than either a data-derived ontology or an LLM-derived ontology built from a summary of the data with masked identifiers. A curated schema used as published can contradict its own data, and structural checks miss some errors. On real agent answers, the curated ontology's flags are only marginally more precise than random flags.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-derived checks should not be assumed to be reliable judges of agent answers without measuring their false alarms, and combining sources or giving specific checker feedback is assessed as a possible improvement.

title: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis
comment: ACM TheWebConf2027 8 pages main content 4 pages appendix
summary: AI agents can now write software from a plain-English description, but code that runs is not the same as code that does what was asked. This gap matters most for smart contracts, the programs behind Web3 applications that move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed. We ask how to check whether an AI-written contract behaves as it should, and where the requested behavior gets lost. We design an evaluation built on execution rather than opinion. We replay the same transactions on an AI-written contract and on the original it should reproduce and measure how often they agree. We test every grading tool on planted mistakes, compare against an answer key written without the description, and audit our own scorer until known wrong answers cannot pass. Common methods, such as AI judges and standard analysis tools, miss obvious mistakes, and scoring choices matter too. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines. We then propose an elicitation-first architecture. Before writing code, the agent asks the client a short checklist of questions, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code. Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. To our knowledge, this is the first study in smart contract synthesis to gather missing requirements before generation and check the result against an independently written executable model. The lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs. We release our tools, 600 tasks and all results.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how often AI-written smart contracts reproduce the behavior requested in plain-English descriptions, using execution-based replay of transactions. It proposes an elicitation-first architecture that asks clarifying questions before coding and checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key.
AI.motivation: AI agents can write code that runs, but running code is not the same as code that does what was asked. The gap matters most for smart contracts, which move money on a blockchain and cannot be fixed once deployed, and common checks such as AI judges and standard analysis tools miss obvious mistakes.
AI.method: Each AI-written contract is evaluated by replaying the same transactions as the original contract and measuring agreement. Grading tools are tested on planted mistakes, and the answer key is written without the description. The proposed agent asks the client a short checklist of questions before writing code, checks the contract against an independently written executable answer key, and returns disagreements to the client instead of silently rewriting code.
AI.result: Asking first matters far more than reviewing or patching afterwards, across three AI models, while automated security fixes often break requested behavior. Checking only the functions every system includes hid about half the difference between pipelines, and scoring choices matter. A few well-chosen questions recover much of what a short description omits, and their value can be estimated without the original contract. The paper releases its tools, 600 tasks and all results.
AI.conclusion: Gathering missing requirements before generation and checking the result against an independently written executable model is presented as a method whose lessons extend to any setting where AI agents turn requests into programs.

title: Evaluating and improving AI agents for sequencing protocol understanding
summary: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays. We introduce LibStructBench, a document-grounded benchmark for reconstructing sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. Our experiments show that frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the underlying language model produced larger average performance differences than switching agent harnesses, with a statistically significant difference only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out molecular-workflow improvement in the tested trajectory. These findings highlight the need for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.

AI.tldr: LibStructBench is a document-grounded benchmark for whether agents can reconstruct the exact sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows specified by sequencing protocols. Frontier agents often produce approximately correct reconstructions but remain unreliable at exact reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing scientific-agent benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents reconstruct the exact molecular structures and generation workflows specified by sequencing protocols, a capability critical for analyzing customized sequencing assays.
AI.method: The benchmark is document-grounded and tests reconstruction of sequencing-library structures and molecular workflows. The authors compare swapping the underlying language model with swapping the agent harness, test added knowledge, and test autonomous accumulation of procedural rules and cross-protocol examples.
AI.result: Agents are unreliable at exact reconstruction, particularly in molecular-state representation and workflow connectivity. Switching the language model produced larger average differences than switching harnesses, significant only for molecular-state reconstruction. Additional knowledge improved oligo-family recovery in a small pilot without improving mean molecular-workflow scores. Autonomous rule accumulation showed non-monotonic validation performance and no mean held-out workflow improvement in the tested trajectory.
AI.conclusion: The findings call for more controlled and verifiable approaches to scientific reasoning about molecular processes in complex experimental protocols.

title: Seq@K: Evaluating Language Models Under Sequential Feedback
summary: Language-model agents differ fundamentally from prior intelligent systems in their ability to learn from natural language in context. This capability enables agents to iteratively refine their answers in response to feedback, a prevalent mode of operation in modern agentic workflows. However, the community primarily ranks models by metrics such as Pass@1 or Pass@K, which cannot capture how they utilize feedback on prior attempts. We introduce Seq@K, a natural evaluation protocol that measures whether a model can solve a problem within K sequential attempts, provided feedback after each previous failure. Unlike multi-turn agentic benchmarks that examine long-horizon planning, Seq@K isolates and formalizes the core capability of refinement from feedback. We evaluate Seq@K on a suite of 7 benchmarks and 16 frontier models, and show that Seq@K reveals a materially different model-selection landscape: under Seq@K, (1) model rankings often differ, (2) the Pareto frontiers admit more efficient configurations and (3) the gains from choosing the optimal model configuration can widen or shrink relative to those of Pass@K. We further show that analyzing model trajectories under Seq@K helps characterize iterative refinement behavior, such as the rate at which models address issues raised in feedback, or how rigidly they hold onto their own answers. Finally, we study how the nature of feedback affects models' iterative refinement, showing that practitioners must carefully design and benchmark the feedback loops of iterative agentic systems. Together, these results establish how Seq@K offers a more faithful metric for intelligent systems that typically operate in such feedback loop, and the necessity to consider Seq@K in evaluating models for these systems.

AI.tldr: Seq@K is an evaluation protocol that measures whether a language model solves a problem within K sequential attempts, receiving feedback after each failure. Across 7 benchmarks and 16 frontier models it reveals a materially different model-selection landscape than Pass@K.
AI.motivation: Models are ranked by metrics such as Pass@1 or Pass@K, which cannot capture how they use feedback on prior attempts, even though iterative refinement from feedback is a prevalent mode in agentic workflows.
AI.method: Seq@K isolates the core capability of refinement from feedback, unlike multi-turn agentic benchmarks that test long-horizon planning. Trajectories under Seq@K are analyzed to characterize refinement, such as the rate at which models address feedback and how rigidly they hold to their own answers, and the nature of feedback is varied.
AI.result: Under Seq@K, model rankings often differ, Pareto frontiers admit more efficient configurations, and the gains from choosing the optimal configuration can widen or shrink relative to Pass@K.
AI.conclusion: Seq@K is a more faithful metric for intelligent systems that operate in feedback loops, and the feedback loops of iterative agentic systems must be carefully designed and benchmarked.

title: What Constitutes Food Similarity? Visual Representations and Retrieval in Indian Cuisine
summary: Food similarity underlies retrieval, recommendation, substitution, and other food computing tasks, yet food representations are typically evaluated by identity preservation. We ask what happens to food similarity beyond identity: how different visual representations organize foods into relational neighborhoods, what culinary relationships these neighborhoods reveal or obscure, and how consistently these structures emerge across representations. Indian cuisine provides a challenging setting in which visually similar foods may have different culinary identities, while foods within a culinary family can vary substantially in appearance. Using an expanded Khana dataset and seven pretrained visual representations spanning convolutional, transformer-based, self-supervised, and image-text aligned models, we evaluate image-to-image retrieval and image-to-dish neighborhoods, examining culinary-family structure, contrast cases, and cross-representation agreement. We also aggregate image representations to compare dish-level visual similarity across models and against recipe-derived similarity for the same dishes. Image-level neighborhoods vary substantially across representations, including similarities across culinary-family boundaries. At the dish level, aggregation reveals common visual structure despite local variation, but this structure corresponds less strongly with recipe-derived similarity. These findings show that recognition performance alone cannot characterize relational structure: food similarity depends on representation, modality, and abstraction level rather than being a fixed property of the food collection. Understanding these structures is therefore a prerequisite to combining multiple food information modalities into a coherent notion of similarity.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how seven pretrained visual representations organize Indian dishes into similarity neighborhoods, finding that image-level neighborhoods vary substantially across representations. Dish-level visual structure corresponds less strongly to recipe-derived similarity.
AI.motivation: Food representations are typically evaluated by identity preservation, which says little about what happens to food similarity beyond identity or how relational structure relates to culinary relationships.
AI.method: Using an expanded Khana dataset and seven pretrained visual representations (convolutional, transformer-based, self-supervised and image-text aligned), the authors evaluate image-to-image retrieval and image-to-dish neighborhoods, examine culinary-family structure and contrast cases, and aggregate image representations to compare dish-level visual similarity across models and against recipe-derived similarity.
AI.result: Image-level neighborhoods vary substantially across representations, including similarities across culinary-family boundaries. Aggregation reveals common visual structure at the dish level despite local variation, but this structure corresponds less strongly with recipe-derived similarity.
AI.conclusion: Food similarity depends on representation, modality and abstraction level rather than being a fixed property of the food collection, so recognition performance alone cannot characterize relational structure.

title: Verification Learning Theory: A Process Model of Checking and Retention in AI-Assisted Judgment
summary: Accurate AI assistance can improve immediate judgments while reducing opportunities to practise the operations needed for independent performance. Verification Learning Theory (VLT) formalises this possibility for claim-evaluation practice followed by correct, independent, rule-specific feedback. The model links perceived assistant reliability to evidence checking and links the history of those checks to retained rule use. Its strict form assumes that task demands and perceived reliability influence learning only through checking, with equal learning per genuine check. It therefore predicts that perceived fallibility can improve delayed unaided judgment even without observed assistant errors, and that this advantage disappears when checking is already required and performed. Rule-specific gains and forecasts from checking histories provide further tests. Simulations examine the consequences and parameter dependence of these commitments; they do not constitute empirical validation. Comparisons with depth-of-processing and feedback-encoding accounts identify where predictions diverge and where the accounts remain observationally equivalent. The framework specifies experiments that can test the proposed mechanism and separates retention of practised rules from the broader problem of recognising which rule applies to a new claim.

AI.tldr: Verification Learning Theory is a process model in which perceived assistant reliability drives evidence checking, and the history of those checks drives retained rule use. It is a theoretical and simulation study and does not constitute empirical validation.
AI.motivation: Accurate AI assistance can improve immediate judgments while reducing opportunities to practise the operations needed for independent performance, and this possibility needs a formal account for claim-evaluation practice.
AI.method: The model formalises claim-evaluation practice followed by correct, independent, rule-specific feedback, and it links perceived reliability to checking and checking history to retained rule use. Simulations examine its consequences and parameter dependence, and it is compared with depth-of-processing and feedback-encoding accounts.
AI.result: No empirical validation is reported; simulations only. The strict form predicts that perceived fallibility can improve delayed unaided judgment even without observed assistant errors, and that this advantage disappears when checking is already required and performed. Rule-specific gains and forecasts from checking histories provide further tests.
AI.conclusion: The framework identifies where its predictions diverge from rival accounts, specifies experiments that could test its mechanism, and separates retention of practised rules from recognising which rule applies to a new claim.

title: The Anatomy of Socio-Demographics in Pluralistic Offensiveness Modeling: When and Where It Helps, and the Role of Reasoning
summary: Subjective judgments such as offensiveness often vary substantially across individuals, motivating pluralistic modeling approaches that incorporate annotators' socio-demographic information to capture this variation. However, prior findings on the benefits of socio-demographic information for pluralistic modeling are mixed, calling for a systematic analysis of both its effectiveness and the mechanisms through which it improves prediction. In this work, we study $\textbf{when}$ and $\textbf{where}$ socio-demographics benefit pluralistic offensiveness modeling, as well as $\textbf{the role of explicit reasoning}$ in leveraging this information. Across three multi-annotator datasets with prompted and trained LLMs, we first show that demographic gains are small and inconsistent for individual predictions but become clearer at the group and population levels, because aggregation attenuates the idiosyncratic variation that masks small but systematic demographic signals. Second, using a reasoning and prediction format that explicitly decomposes individual judgment into an overall baseline and a demographic-specific deviation, we show that the gains arise from both components: demographic information improves baseline estimation and enables meaningful demographic-specific shifts, and interventions show that better component estimates improve final predictions. Finally, comparing direct demographic conditioning with explicit reasoning about how the text interacts with annotator demographics, we find that reasoning yields more accurate baseline and shift estimates as well as final predictions, whereas conditioning alone rarely produces informative shifts. These results suggest that the mixed evidence in prior work may partly stem from individual-level evaluation, and that the value of socio-demographic information depends on both how it is evaluated and how models are guided to use it.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when and where socio-demographic information helps pluralistic offensiveness modeling, and shows that explicit reasoning about how a text interacts with annotator demographics gives the most accurate estimates. Demographic gains are small and inconsistent for individual predictions but clearer at group and population levels.
AI.motivation: Prior findings on the benefits of socio-demographic information for pluralistic modeling of subjective judgments are mixed, and the mechanisms through which it helps needed systematic analysis.
AI.method: A reasoning and prediction format decomposes individual judgment into an overall baseline plus a demographic-specific deviation. It is compared with direct demographic conditioning across three multi-annotator datasets, using prompted and trained LLMs.
AI.result: Gains come from both the baseline estimate and the demographic-specific shifts, and better component estimates improve final predictions. Reasoning yields more accurate baseline and shift estimates and final predictions, whereas conditioning alone rarely produces informative shifts.
AI.conclusion: Mixed prior evidence may partly stem from individual-level evaluation, and the value of socio-demographic information depends on both how it is evaluated and how models are guided to use it.

title: FilingLoop: Evaluating and Evolving LLM Agents for Corporate Disclosure Review and Revision
summary: Public disclosure repositories such as SEC EDGAR support informed investment through web access to corporate filings. Supporting their review with language model agents requires discovering unstated deficiencies across related documents, acquiring missing company facts, and verifying that requested revisions satisfy evidence-backed requirements. Existing financial question-answering evaluations provide limited evidence of these interactive capabilities. We introduce \textbf{FilingLoop}, an interactive benchmark and a self-evolving agent framework for corporate disclosure review and revision. Grounded in historical U.S.\ Securities and Exchange Commission correspondence, FilingLoop reconstructs 380 predominantly IPO review tasks from 96 companies under distinct information constraints. An evaluator separate from the acting agents scores final filings and responses against 6,099 eligible requirements and audits unsupported claims and harmful revisions. Our framework couples iterative review and revision within each case with procedural learning across cases, converting requirement-level evaluation feedback into role-specific guidance without updating model weights. Updates affect only subsequent cases, allowing procedural adaptation to be assessed without retrying scored tasks. On the evaluated stream, evolution increases requirement fulfillment from 24.28\% to 27.96\% and full comment resolution from 16.90\% to 20.75\%, with a 5.8\% increase in total cost over the fixed-policy variant. FilingLoop connects the concerns an agent discovers with the company facts it obtains and the revisions it commits, providing requirement-level feedback for procedures used in later review tasks.

AI.tldr: FilingLoop is an interactive benchmark and self-evolving agent framework for reviewing and revising corporate disclosures, built from 380 mostly IPO SEC review tasks across 96 companies. Procedural learning across cases raises requirement fulfillment from 24.28% to 27.96% without updating model weights.
AI.motivation: Supporting SEC filing review with language model agents requires discovering unstated deficiencies across documents, acquiring missing company facts and verifying revisions, but existing financial question-answering evaluations provide limited evidence of these interactive capabilities.
AI.method: Tasks are reconstructed from historical SEC correspondence under distinct information constraints. A separate evaluator scores final filings and responses against 6,099 eligible requirements and audits unsupported claims and harmful revisions. Iterative review and revision within each case is coupled with procedural learning across cases, which converts requirement-level feedback into role-specific guidance; updates affect only subsequent cases.
AI.result: On the evaluated stream, evolution raises requirement fulfillment from 24.28% to 27.96% and full comment resolution from 16.90% to 20.75%, at a 5.8% increase in total cost over the fixed-policy variant.
AI.conclusion: Linking discovered concerns, acquired facts and committed revisions through requirement-level feedback offers a route to procedural adaptation that can be assessed without retrying scored tasks.

title: Beyond Low-Pass Dynamics: Frequency-Selective Spiking Reservoirs with Resonant Neurons
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 30 pages (10 main text), 4 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Spiking reservoir computing combines the training efficiency of fixed recurrent reservoirs with the energy efficiency of event-driven inference, where computation is triggered by sparse spikes rather than executed densely at every timestep. However, existing spiking reservoirs almost exclusively rely on Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons, whose low-pass dynamics limit their ability to distinguish information encoded at different temporal frequencies. We introduce HRF-Res, a liquid state machine in which LIF neurons are replaced by a heterogeneous population of Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire (HRF) neurons. These neurons exhibit intrinsic oscillatory dynamics and selectively respond to input frequencies, enabling the reservoir to capture frequency-specific temporal patterns. The result is more discriminative representations and higher classification accuracy than LIF-based reservoirs, achieved without sacrificing the energy efficiency of spiking computation, with up to 19x lower energy consumption than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir. Evaluated on ten benchmarks spanning time series, sequential images, audio spike trains, and neuromorphic vision, HRF-Res achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods. These results demonstrate that introducing frequency-selective dynamics into spiking reservoirs improves representational quality and classification performance while preserving their inherent energy efficiency.

AI.tldr: HRF-Res is a liquid state machine in which LIF neurons are replaced by a heterogeneous population of Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire neurons, giving frequency-selective spiking dynamics. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods on ten benchmarks, with up to 19x lower energy than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir.
AI.motivation: Existing spiking reservoirs almost exclusively use Leaky Integrate-and-Fire neurons, whose low-pass dynamics limit their ability to distinguish information encoded at different temporal frequencies.
AI.method: LIF neurons are replaced by a heterogeneous population of Harmonic Resonate-and-Fire neurons, which have intrinsic oscillatory dynamics and selectively respond to input frequencies, so the reservoir captures frequency-specific temporal patterns while remaining event-driven.
AI.result: The reservoir yields more discriminative representations and higher classification accuracy than LIF-based reservoirs, with up to 19x lower energy consumption than an equivalent non-spiking oscillatory reservoir. Evaluated on ten benchmarks spanning time series, sequential images, audio spike trains and neuromorphic vision, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among spiking reservoir methods.
AI.conclusion: Introducing frequency-selective dynamics into spiking reservoirs improves representational quality and classification performance while preserving their energy efficiency.

title: VerifiedLab: Harnessing Knowns for Unknowns
summary: Across human history, knowledge has undergone several transitions, from orality to writing and then to digital archives. At each transition, humans established new conventions to preserve knowledge for the new era. Nowadays, as research agents are increasingly deployed for laboratory experiments, knowledge is crossing another boundary: from records written for humans to those for machines. In this work, we introduce VerifiedLab, a multi-agent harness framework for this human-to-machine transition of knowledge. VerifiedLab transforms research output from passive artifacts into active systems that accelerate downstream use, adoption and prediction of future trends. In VerifiedLab, a team of AI scientists with distinct roles reasons over records verified field by field: a principal investigator plans, a librarian computes the evidence directly from the records, specialists draft, and a gate and a critic check each claim against the measured reliability of its data before the harness decides whether to release or withhold it. We demonstrate the efficacy of VerifiedLab through extensive experiments on perovskite solar cells: VerifiedLab recovers known physical trends, anticipates devices reported a year later, and lets AI scientists inherit the literature together with a measure of how far it can be trusted. By scaling the inference-time verification compute, VerifiedLab introduces a new pathway for knowledge dissemination and machine harness for AI co-scientists.

AI.tldr: VerifiedLab is a multi-agent harness that converts research output into machine-usable records, with AI scientists releasing or withholding each claim according to the measured reliability of its data. On perovskite solar cells it recovers known physical trends and anticipates devices reported a year later.
AI.motivation: As research agents are deployed for laboratory experiments, knowledge must move from records written for humans to records usable by machines, and existing research outputs are largely passive artifacts.
AI.method: A team of AI scientists with distinct roles reasons over records verified field by field: a principal investigator plans, a librarian computes evidence directly from the records, specialists draft, and a gate and a critic check each claim against the measured reliability of its data before the harness decides whether to release or withhold it.
AI.result: On perovskite solar cells, VerifiedLab recovers known physical trends, anticipates devices reported a year later, and lets AI scientists inherit the literature together with a measure of how far it can be trusted.
AI.conclusion: Scaling inference-time verification compute offers a new pathway for knowledge dissemination and a machine harness for AI co-scientists.

title: GARDEN: Generalist Autonomous Reward Design Through Evidence Navigation for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.

AI.tldr: GARDEN develops one LLM-written reward program for a family of cooperative multi-agent scenarios and transfers it unchanged to scenarios unseen during design. It raises task returns by 58.2% and 52.5% over default rewards on two Overcooked kitchen layouts and raises the mean win rate in two SMAX combat scenarios from 51.0% to 89.9%.
AI.motivation: Intermediate rewards for cooperative MARL are usually hand-designed and must be repeated whenever the environment or team changes, and LLM-written rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting.
AI.method: An LLM reward engineer investigates environment code, training records and agent behavior and tests draft rewards in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. The resulting reward program is transferred unchanged to related scenarios.
AI.result: On unseen Overcooked and SMAX scenarios, returns rise by 58.2% and 52.5% over default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios rises from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeds the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection.
AI.conclusion: A single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.

title: GAUSS: A Workload-Aware Analytical and Monte-Carlo Simulator for LLM Inference Serving
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference has become an operational workload that fleets must provision, monitor, and bill against latency service-level objectives (SLOs). A single throughput number cannot answer the questions operators actually face, because generative serving couples two phases with very different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the effective service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before aggregate throughput saturates. We present GAUSS, a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-between-tokens (TBT), together with the sustainable request rate, for a given workload, engine, and accelerator. GAUSS pairs calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode with a Lindley-recurrence model of queueing under stochastic arrivals and estimates performance by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace. This lets GAUSS reason about workloads, routing policies, and hardware that have never been deployed, and to capture the latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample. We describe the model and show how it supports operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.

AI.tldr: GAUSS is a workload-aware analytical and Monte-Carlo simulator that predicts the full distributions of time-to-first-token and time-between-tokens, and the sustainable request rate, for LLM inference serving. It targets latency tails that trace-driven simulators systematically under-sample, including for workloads, engines and hardware never deployed.
AI.motivation: A single throughput number cannot answer operators' SLO questions, because prefill and decode have different service characteristics, continuous batching reshapes the service process, and user-visible tail latency can degrade long before throughput saturates. Trace-driven simulators under-sample these tails.
AI.method: Calibrated, phase-specific latency surfaces for prefill and decode are paired with a Lindley-recurrence queueing model under stochastic arrivals, and performance is estimated by ensemble Monte-Carlo sampling rather than by replaying a single trace.
AI.result: The abstract reports no numerical results. It describes support for operating-point selection, traffic segmentation, and shortest-remaining-processing-time scheduling capacity questions that trace-driven simulators cannot address.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble Monte-Carlo simulation with phase-specific latency models lets operators reason about capacity, routing policies and tail latency for workloads and hardware that have not been deployed.

title: Algorithmic Bias from the Perspectives of Healthcare Professionals
summary: This paper focuses on algorithmic bias of machine learning and artificial intelligence applications in healthcare information systems. Based on the quantitative data and qualitative comments from a survey and interviews with healthcare professionals, who have different job roles (e.g., clinical vs. administrative), this study provides findings about the relationships between algorithmic bias, perceived fairness, and the intended acceptance and adoption of ML algorithms and algorithm generated outcomes. The results suggest that the opinions of healthcare professionals toward the causes of algorithmic bias, the criteria of algorithm assessment, the perceived fairness, and bias mitigation approaches may vary depending on their job roles, perspectives, tasks, and the algorithm characteristics. More research is needed to investigate algorithmic bias to ensure fairness and equality in healthcare.

AI.tldr: A survey and interviews with healthcare professionals show that their views on algorithmic bias, perceived fairness and acceptance of ML outcomes vary with job role. The paper calls for further research to ensure fairness and equality in healthcare.
AI.motivation: Algorithmic bias in machine learning and AI applications in healthcare information systems can affect perceived fairness and intended adoption, and the paper examines how healthcare professionals see it.
AI.method: A survey combining quantitative data with qualitative comments, together with interviews, with healthcare professionals in different job roles, such as clinical and administrative.
AI.result: Professionals' opinions on the causes of bias, the criteria for assessing algorithms, perceived fairness and mitigation approaches may vary with job role, perspective, tasks and algorithm characteristics. The paper reports relationships among algorithmic bias, perceived fairness and intended acceptance and adoption.
AI.conclusion: Perceptions of algorithmic bias differ across healthcare roles, and more research is needed to ensure fairness and equality in healthcare.

title: Assessing Language Models for Scientific Applications: Inertial Confinement Fusion as a Use Case
summary: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluations of scientific fluency, physical reasoning, and quantitative analyses. Using inertial confinement fusion (ICF) as a test case, we have developed an expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation, and equation formulation. Responses have been evaluated using deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. We compared a variety of out-of-the-box closed-source and open-source large language models with Prospero, a model specialized through combined domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning for ICF. We also conducted initial retrieval-assisted evaluations. Prospero improved its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Frontier models achieved the highest aggregate scores, but critical physics errors persisted, particularly in numerical calculations. We note that domain-specific performance can improve through specialization, but benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but yielded no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests further illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions and model validity. Based on these findings, we recommend evaluating existing domain capabilities and retrieval benefits before committing to substantial additional specialization.

AI.tldr: An expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions on inertial confinement fusion shows that Prospero, a domain-specialized model, improves its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model. Frontier models score highest overall but still make critical physics errors, particularly in numerical calculations.
AI.motivation: Advancing language models for specialized scientific applications requires evaluating scientific fluency, physical reasoning and quantitative analysis in the target domain.
AI.method: An expert-curated benchmark of 250 questions spanning qualitative reasoning, numerical calculation, symbolic derivation and equation formulation, scored with deterministic numerical and symbolic checks together with language-model judges. Closed-source and open-source models are compared with Prospero, which is specialized through domain-adaptive pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, and initial retrieval-assisted evaluations are run.
AI.result: Prospero improves its aggregate score by 10.7 percentage points over its base model, with gains across all question types. Retrieval improved performance for a smaller model but gave no statistically significant improvement for a frontier model. Two scientific stress tests illustrate useful capabilities and the need for expert assessment of physical assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Domain capabilities and retrieval benefits should be evaluated before committing to substantial additional specialization, since benchmark gains alone do not establish scientific reliability.

title: PromptSense: Sentiment-Aware Mental Health Chatbot with Dynamic Prompting
summary: Current Large Language Models (LLMs)-based mental health chatbots often lack sufficient empathy, contextual awareness, and safety mechanisms, potentially leading to ineffective or harmful interactions. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates sentiment and depression analysis with a rule-based filtering mechanism prior to model inference. By dynamically constructing prompts based on emotional and risk-related insights, the framework aims to significantly improve the contextual relevance, empathy, and risk-aware of model-generated responses. We evaluated four model strategies and two prompt engineered variants across qualitative metrics such as empathy, helpfulness, clarity, relevance, safety, as well as toxicity assessments using the Perspective API. Experimental results indicate that the prompt engineering approaches outperforms DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8\% and 1.1\% respectively.

AI.tldr: PromptSense is a mental health chatbot framework that runs sentiment and depression analysis plus a rule-based filter before model inference, then builds prompts from the resulting emotional and risk insights. Its prompt engineering variants outperform DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8% and 1.1% respectively.
AI.motivation: LLM-based mental health chatbots often lack sufficient empathy, contextual awareness and safety mechanisms, which can make interactions ineffective or harmful.
AI.method: Sentiment and depression analysis together with a rule-based filtering mechanism run before inference, and prompts are constructed dynamically from the emotional and risk-related insights. Four model strategies and two prompt-engineered variants are evaluated.
AI.result: Prompt engineering approaches outperform DSFT and RLAIF by 1.8% and 1.1% respectively, judged on empathy, helpfulness, clarity, relevance and safety, with toxicity assessed using the Perspective API.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, risk-aware prompt construction is presented as a way to improve the relevance, empathy and safety of mental health chatbot responses.

title: AI-Driven Digital Twin Framework for Warehouse Logistics Automation Optimization
comment: ICRA 2026 Workshop Advances and Challenges in AI-Driven Automation and Robotic System Integration with Digital Twins
summary: In recent years, warehouse logistics optimization has increasingly focused on intelligent, data-driven systems to enhance operational efficiency. Conventional static product placement strategies are being progressively replaced by dynamic slotting approaches that can adapt to real-time variations in warehouse conditions. In this work, we present a novel framework that employs a reinforcement learning agent integrated within a FlexSim-based Digital Twin environment for real-time product placement optimization. The proposed agent continuously learns from streaming operational data, enabling it to reduce picking time while improving overall system throughput. The simulation environment models a four-zone warehouse layout with forklift-based material handling and leverages the Asset Administration Shell framework to ensure seamless interaction between the learning agent, physical asset, and the digital twin. Experimental evaluation demonstrates substantial performance gains, with the proposed approach achieving a 29.66\% reduction in average picking time, a 35.42\% increase in throughput, and an 18.54\% decrease in travel distance.

AI.tldr: A reinforcement learning agent integrated with a FlexSim digital twin learns product placement from streaming operational data in a four-zone warehouse. It reports a 29.66% reduction in average picking time, a 35.42% increase in throughput and an 18.54% decrease in travel distance.
AI.motivation: Conventional static product placement is being replaced by dynamic slotting that adapts to real-time warehouse conditions, and the paper targets this adaptive placement problem.
AI.method: An RL agent within a FlexSim-based digital twin continuously learns from streaming data for real-time product placement. The Asset Administration Shell framework links the learning agent, the physical asset and the digital twin, and the simulated warehouse has four zones with forklift-based material handling.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves a 29.66% reduction in average picking time, a 35.42% increase in throughput and an 18.54% decrease in travel distance.
AI.conclusion: Digital-twin-based reinforcement learning with streaming operational data gives substantial efficiency gains in the simulated warehouse evaluated.

title: Too Hard, Too Easy, Just Right: Performance-Driven Challenge Adaptation in Virtual Reality Firefighter Training
