AI.tldr: Proposes A-RSI, which decides when to refresh a task pool for zero-data multimodal self-improvement by monitoring training logs. With 800 fresh tasks, it raises the performance average on an eleven-benchmark suite from 57.77 to 61.05.
AI.motivation: Existing recursive self-improvement methods focus on what experience to generate next and pay less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced, and many build training targets from self-consistency or majority voting, which depends on the model's uncertain predictions.
AI.method: A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs and refreshes the task pool when the learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers. The task-generation contract and chosen reward and refresh properties are verified automatically, and the generated answers are audited separately. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels.
AI.result: On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, the performance average rises from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.
AI.conclusion: Training dynamics can decide when to acquire new experience, and independently checkable answers allow self-improvement without external training data or human-written labels.

title: CALM: Conflict-Aware Lifecycle Memory Governance for Long-Horizon Language Agents
summary: A memory can be outdated for present-day reasoning yet indispensable for reconstructing the past. Relevance-based retrieval overlooks this tension: semantic relevance, evidence-grounded validity, and query-specific eligibility are distinct. We propose CALM, a conflict-aware lifecycle memory governance framework that decouples persistent memory preservation from query-time admission. CALM converts heterogeneous records into evidence-grounded memory cells, updates validity and lifecycle states using support, conflict, and dependency signals, and admits query-appropriate evidence through training-free or learned gating informed by temporal applicability. Across LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo with Qwen and GPT backbones, CALM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving the best overall accuracy. Compared with simple filtering and reranking, query-conditioned admission further improves evidence selection. Conflict-blocking and robustness analyses show CALM suppresses erroneous retrieved memories while retaining useful evidence. Historical-reconstruction experiments demonstrate that preserving superseded records supports accurate earlier-state reasoning without compromising current-state answers.

AI.tldr: Proposes CALM, a lifecycle memory governance framework for language agents that preserves outdated but historically useful memories and admits evidence at query time. It achieves the best overall accuracy on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo.
AI.motivation: Relevance-based retrieval overlooks that semantic relevance, evidence-grounded validity and query-specific eligibility are distinct, so memories that are outdated for present reasoning but needed to reconstruct the past can be lost.
AI.method: CALM converts heterogeneous records into evidence-grounded memory cells and updates their validity and lifecycle states using support, conflict and dependency signals. It decouples persistent memory preservation from query-time admission, which uses training-free or learned gating informed by temporal applicability.
AI.result: Across LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo with Qwen and GPT backbones, CALM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Query-conditioned admission further improves evidence selection over simple filtering and reranking. Conflict-blocking analyses show it suppresses erroneous retrieved memories while retaining useful evidence, and preserving superseded records supports accurate earlier-state reasoning without compromising current-state answers.
AI.conclusion: Preserving superseded records and gating them by query relevance supports historical reasoning while keeping current-state answers accurate.

title: Think Before You Act: Decision Gate for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform consequential actions through external tools, yet their proposed actions are often executed without independent verification of policy compliance or task completion. We introduce JevAct, a runtime verification framework that intercepts selected agent actions before execution and enables feedback-driven correction. JevAct compiles domain policies into executable state checks and structured questions evaluated by a prefill-only decision model, which produces probability-based judgments without relying on LLM generation. By combining deterministic verification of tool-state facts with probabilistic assessment of conversational context, the framework identifies potentially invalid actions and premature task termination, providing targeted feedback for bounded revision. JevAct operates independently of the underlying agent model and requires no modifications to its parameters or tools. We evaluate JevAct across eleven LLM agents on $\tau^2$-bench Airline and Telecom tasks and BFCL. Results show improvements in agent reliability across multiple models and benchmarks, with particularly consistent gains on Telecom and BFCL, while performance on Airline is more mixed. Overall, these findings suggest that combining structured decision models with executable verification can improve the reliability of tool-using LLM agents.

AI.tldr: Introduces JevAct, a runtime verification framework that intercepts agent actions before execution, checks them against domain policies and triggers bounded, feedback-driven revision. It improves reliability across eleven LLM agents on tau^2-bench Airline and Telecom and BFCL, with more mixed results on Airline.
AI.motivation: LLM agents execute consequential tool actions often without independent verification of policy compliance or task completion.
AI.method: JevAct compiles domain policies into executable state checks and structured questions evaluated by a prefill-only decision model that produces probability-based judgments without LLM generation. It combines deterministic verification of tool-state facts with probabilistic assessment of conversational context to identify invalid actions and premature task termination, and requires no changes to the agent's parameters or tools.
AI.result: Across eleven LLM agents on tau^2-bench Airline and Telecom and BFCL, reliability improves across multiple models and benchmarks, with particularly consistent gains on Telecom and BFCL and more mixed performance on Airline.
AI.conclusion: Combining structured decision models with executable verification can improve the reliability of tool-using LLM agents.

title: "Close enough?" An investigation into multiplication errors in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) frequently fail at multi-digit arithmetic, but the underlying mechanisms governing these failures remain poorly understood. While recent work demonstrates that addition errors follow a "noisy quantisation" model localised around carry boundaries, whether this framework generalises to multiplication remains an open question. In this work, we evaluate multiplication capabilities across several small base LLMs on a dataset of 16,991 problems spanning varied operand lengths. We show that multiplication errors do not conform to the addition-style noisy quantisation model. Instead, we uncover a novel error regime in small Qwen models: errors in lower-order columns predominantly preserve parity. Conversely, higher-order digit errors shift toward off-by-one carry failures. Our findings suggest that arithmetic computation in LLMs relies on distinct, multi-periodic internal representations where parity is tracked more robustly than exact digit identity, providing new mechanistic insights into numerical reasoning in transformers.

AI.tldr: Evaluates multi-digit multiplication errors in several small base LLMs on 16,991 problems and finds that they do not follow the addition-style noisy quantisation model. Small Qwen models show a distinct regime in which lower-order column errors preserve parity.
AI.motivation: Addition errors in LLMs follow a noisy quantisation model localised around carry boundaries, but whether this framework generalises to multiplication was an open question.
AI.method: Multiplication capabilities are evaluated across several small base LLMs on a dataset of 16,991 problems spanning varied operand lengths, with errors analysed by digit column.
AI.result: Multiplication errors do not conform to the addition-style noisy quantisation model. In small Qwen models, errors in lower-order columns predominantly preserve parity, while higher-order digit errors shift toward off-by-one carry failures.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that arithmetic in LLMs relies on distinct multi-periodic internal representations in which parity is tracked more robustly than exact digit identity.

title: Curriculum-Based Deep Reinforcement Learning for Robust Autonomous Rocket Landing under Atmospheric Uncertainty
summary: Autonomous far-range rocket landing is a challenging control problem because navigation, descent-rate regulation, attitude management, and fuel use must be coordinated in the presence of uncertain atmospheric and vehicle dynamics. This paper presents a curriculum-driven proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework for three-dimensional rocket landing in a stochastic environment incorporating altitude-dependent aerodynamic drag, wind shear, temporally correlated turbulence, discrete gusts, uncertain propulsion and aerodynamic parameters, thrust-vector misalignment, engine lag, actuator-gain variation, noisy observations, and command latency. Learning is organised into far-range approach, soft descent, and integrated landing stages. Policy transfer, critic warm-up after reward changes, rehearsal of earlier tasks, and progressive expansion of weather severity are used to support learning across these coupled phases. Across 100,000 evaluation episodes, the policy achieves 96,656 successful landings, corresponding to a success rate of 96.656\% and a 95\% Wilson confidence interval of 96.543--96.766\%. Success decreases from 98.84\% under zero-disturbance conditions to 88.07\% in the highest weather-severity band. Successful touchdowns exhibit small miss distances and low residual horizontal and vertical velocities. An exploratory logistic-regression analysis identifies mean wind speed as the strongest measured correlate of success, with initial distance, initial altitude, initial vertical velocity, and wind-shear exponent also associated with outcomes. The results quantify both the effectiveness of the learned policy over the evaluated disturbance distribution and the degradation that occurs under severe compound atmospheric conditions.

AI.tldr: Presents a curriculum-driven PPO framework for autonomous 3D rocket landing under stochastic atmospheric and vehicle uncertainty. The policy achieves a 96.656% success rate over 100,000 episodes, falling from 98.84% with zero disturbance to 88.07% in the highest weather-severity band.
AI.motivation: Far-range rocket landing requires coordinating navigation, descent-rate regulation, attitude management and fuel use under uncertain atmospheric and vehicle dynamics, which makes the control problem challenging.
AI.method: Curriculum-driven proximal policy optimisation (PPO) is organised into far-range approach, soft descent and integrated landing stages. Policy transfer, critic warm-up after reward changes, rehearsal of earlier tasks and progressive expansion of weather severity support learning across these phases. The stochastic environment includes altitude-dependent drag, wind shear, correlated turbulence, discrete gusts, uncertain propulsion and aerodynamic parameters, thrust-vector misalignment, engine lag, actuator-gain variation, noisy observations and command latency.
AI.result: Across 100,000 evaluation episodes the policy achieves 96,656 successful landings, a success rate of 96.656% (95% Wilson confidence interval 96.543% to 96.766%). Success falls from 98.84% under zero-disturbance conditions to 88.07% in the highest weather-severity band. Successful touchdowns show small miss distances and low residual horizontal and vertical velocities. In an exploratory logistic-regression analysis, mean wind speed is the strongest measured correlate of success.
AI.conclusion: The learned policy is effective across the evaluated disturbance distribution, with measurable degradation under severe compound atmospheric conditions.

title: From Grind to Grasp
summary: Discussions of complexity, knowledge and intelligence often overlook the work involved. For example, outputs generated by short programs have low algorithmic complexity but can have high computational depth, the least work needed to produce them from near-shortest programs. Producing them with less work can require longer descriptions, giving high work-bounded complexity. We introduce a formalism that compares achievements under work and information limits and describes how learning and persistence can make deep achievements shallow by reusing products of earlier work. For an agent with a limited work budget, the value of building and maintaining such resources depends on how they support its goals over later tasks. We define grasp as performance across work budgets at a fixed information allowance. Low grasp can still yield success through grind at high cost in work, without necessarily improving human grasp. Applied to improvement itself, grasp gives a criterion for recursive self-improvement in which successors make comparable further improvements more efficiently. Another route to faster progress is to expand the resources brought to bear through knowledge sharing and coordination across society, even while comparable advances require increasing work. Grasp also applies to collectives, which may outperform their members yet require more total work than one system with their combined resources. Establishing and sustaining organisation can itself be deep even when the primary task is simple. These demands may help explain the richness of biological and social systems. In agent collectives, this organisational work can generate goals beyond assigned tasks, including maintaining the collective itself. We therefore caution against allowing an emergent agent society to assume authority over social coordination, since it could increasingly direct work towards its own persistence and goals.

AI.tldr: Introduces a formalism that compares achievements under work and information limits, defining grasp as performance across work budgets at a fixed information allowance. It gives a criterion for recursive self-improvement and cautions against letting emergent agent societies assume authority over social coordination.
AI.motivation: Discussions of complexity, knowledge and intelligence often overlook the work involved, and learning and persistence can make deep achievements shallow by reusing earlier work.
AI.method: The formalism compares achievements under work and information limits. Grasp is defined as performance across work budgets at a fixed information allowance, and is applied to self-improvement, knowledge sharing and collectives.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results. It describes theoretical implications: low grasp can still yield success through costly grind, grasp gives a criterion for recursive self-improvement in which successors make comparable improvements more efficiently, and collectives may outperform their members yet require more total work than one system with their combined resources.
AI.conclusion: Agent collectives can generate goals beyond their assigned tasks, including maintaining the collective itself, so an emergent agent society should not be allowed to assume authority over social coordination.

title: Leaving, Staying, or Living There? Duration Commonsense Reasoning with Human-LLM Co-annotations
summary: Gardening in the backyard implies living there, while checking into an Airbnb more likely means staying for a few days. Such duration judgments are important for understanding human mobility, travel behavior, and social context. However, duration is rarely stated explicitly in social media posts and must instead be inferred from noisy textual, visual, and contextual cues. In this paper, we investigate whether vision-language models possess such duration commonsense. We create a new corpus of geotagged tweets co-annotated by humans and LLMs to serve as a testbed for this task. We find that state-of-the-art models struggle with duration inference, even when guided by multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting. Error analyses further reveal that models often fail to integrate critical contextual information, or they overly rely on prominent visual details while overlooking subtle hashtags and semantic nuances. These findings underscore the significant challenges remaining in context-aware multimodal understanding.

AI.tldr: Investigates whether vision-language models have duration commonsense, that is, whether a geotagged tweet's author is living somewhere, staying briefly or leaving. State-of-the-art models struggle with this inference, even with multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting.
AI.motivation: Duration is rarely stated in social media posts and must be inferred from noisy textual, visual and contextual cues, yet it matters for understanding human mobility, travel behaviour and social context.
AI.method: A new corpus of geotagged tweets is co-annotated by humans and LLMs to serve as a testbed for duration inference.
AI.result: State-of-the-art models struggle with duration inference even when guided by multi-turn Chain-of-Thought prompting. Error analyses show that models often fail to integrate critical contextual information, or overly rely on prominent visual details while overlooking subtle hashtags and semantic nuances.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware multimodal understanding of duration remains a significant open challenge.

title: Auditable Belief Updates as a Missing Safety Layer for LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as cognitive interfaces that shape how users interpret evidence, communicate, and make decisions. As deployed systems become more multimodal, tool-using, and multi-agent, safety failures no longer arise only from isolated harmful outputs, but also from how agents update, store, and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools, and peer communication. In this paper, we define belief as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. Building on this view, we propose the Explicit Belief Multi-Agent System (EB-MAS), which externalizes belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues. We also discuss the risk of group belief at the group level, including manufactured consensus, collusion, and cascading misinformation, and outline practical integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability, and ethical misuse. Therefore, scalable agent safety requires not only better output filtering or stronger base models, but also explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating, and constraining belief revision at runtime.

AI.tldr: Proposes EB-MAS, a multi-agent system that externalises belief states into a structured substrate and uses a Cognitive Firewall to bound or reject weakly evidenced updates that are strongly driven by vulnerability cues. It argues that auditable belief revision is a missing safety layer for LLM-powered multi-agent systems.
AI.motivation: As LLM systems become more multimodal, tool-using and multi-agent, safety failures arise from how agents update, store and propagate epistemic commitments across retrieval, memory, tools and peer communication, not only from isolated harmful outputs.
AI.method: Belief is defined as an engineering abstraction for evidence-based commitments that guide downstream action. EB-MAS externalises belief states into a structured substrate, uses belief operators to propose candidate updates, and applies a Cognitive Firewall that bounds or rejects updates that are weakly evidenced but strongly driven by vulnerability cues.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results. It discusses group-level risks, including manufactured consensus, collusion and cascading misinformation, and outlines integration challenges around grounding, false positives, scalability and ethical misuse.
AI.conclusion: Scalable agent safety requires explicit interfaces for tracing, calibrating and constraining belief revision at runtime, in addition to better output filtering or stronger base models.

title: Aligning Autoresearch: Co-Improvement between Agents and Humans
summary: Autoresearch agents can now attempt long-horizon AI research end-to-end, i.e., self-improvement. However, best results are still obtained by research agents interacting with human researchers, and improving AI's ability to perform this co-research will only reinforce this effect---a process termed co-improvement (Weston and Foerster, 2025). Further, aligning with human expectations is likely a safer path for research agents, especially given recent agent reward hacking phenomena (OpenAI, 2026b). In this work we address these issues in four ways: (i) we empirically study the role of humans in directing autoresearch agents, focusing on the domain of benchmark creation, and find humans still play a pivotal role particularly in the ideation phase; (ii) we also develop a benchmark, HackBench, that shows current autoresearch agents are not aligned and are unable to achieve hack localization sufficiently; (iii) we present a method to train agents for improved human interaction by using human simulators as a proxy during reinforcement learning (RL); and finally (iv) we develop a method to improve model text generation, and hence agent communication, by RL with rubrics aligned with human experts. Together, our training and evaluation recipes provide a path toward more capable and aligned (co-)research agents.

AI.tldr: Studies how humans direct autoresearch agents and proposes ways to align them, including HackBench for hack localisation and RL methods that use human simulators and expert-aligned rubrics. It finds that humans still play a pivotal role, particularly in ideation for benchmark creation.
AI.motivation: Autoresearch agents can attempt long-horizon AI research end-to-end, but the best results still come from agents working with human researchers, and agents may be misaligned, as recent reward hacking phenomena show.
AI.method: Four components: an empirical study of the role of humans in directing autoresearch agents for benchmark creation; HackBench, a benchmark for hack localisation; RL training with human simulators as a proxy for human interaction; and RL with rubrics aligned with human experts to improve text generation and agent communication.
AI.result: Humans still play a pivotal role, particularly in the ideation phase. HackBench shows that current autoresearch agents are not aligned and cannot achieve hack localisation sufficiently. The abstract reports no further quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The training and evaluation recipes offer a path toward more capable and aligned co-research agents.

title: TreasuryQA Bench: Can AI Agents Work an Archive of Scanned Financial Records?
summary: Organisations keep decades of financial records as scanned PDFs on shared drives, and AI agents can now reach those drives through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Existing benchmarks do not mirror this production setting because they simplify the task. In some, the relevant documents are handed to the agent, so it never has to search. In others, the agent searches through documents with pre-extracted text, so it never has to read scanned images. We introduce TreasuryQA Bench, which requires both: 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications, held in Veris's high-fidelity Dropbox twin. In each task the agent searches for the relevant file through Dropbox's MCP server, reads the pages it needs with Reducto's hosted OCR server or its own tools, and replies with one exact figure. A Python grader checks each answer against an accepted range around the correct value. In this paper we present results from ten agents. The best, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst, GPT-5.6 Terra in Codex, solves 16.7%, so the benchmark is far from saturated. We also test how scan quality affects performance: every agent solves fewer tasks on the blurriest scans. Most failed attempts reply with a wrong number rather than no number, and the most common cause is a digit misread from the scan. Three worked examples are included with their answer keys.

AI.tldr: Introduces TreasuryQA Bench, which tests AI agents on searching and reading 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications through MCP servers and answering with one exact figure. The best agent, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst, GPT-5.6 Terra in Codex, solves 16.7%.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks simplify the production setting: either the relevant documents are handed to the agent, or the agent searches documents with pre-extracted text and never has to read scanned images.
AI.method: The benchmark has 70 questions over 1,435 scanned U.S. Treasury publications held in a high-fidelity Dropbox twin. Agents search through Dropbox's MCP server, read pages with Reducto's hosted OCR server or their own tools, and reply with one exact figure, which a Python grader checks against an accepted range around the correct value.
AI.result: Ten agents were evaluated. The best solves 64.8% of attempts and the worst 16.7%. Every agent solves fewer tasks on the blurriest scans. Most failed attempts reply with a wrong number rather than no number, and the most common cause is a digit misread from the scan.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark is far from saturated, and scan quality and digit misreads from scans are the main difficulties for agents working on archives of scanned financial records.

title: Dungeons & Dragons Encounter Analysis with Semi-Random Simulation in Foundry VTT
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 22nd Artificial Intelligence and Interactive Digital Entertainment Conference
summary: Dungeons & Dragons (D&D) is a tabletop roleplaying game (TTRPG) in which a group of players, guided by a Game Master, roleplay a fantasy adventure with simulated combat and improvisational narrative. In D&D, an encounter is a single instance of simulated combat, where the players must use their characters to attempt to defeat a selection of enemy characters that the GM controls. D&D has multiple systems that approximate encounter difficulty by summing individual difficulty values that designers predefine for each enemy. However, since players and enemies can have a wide variety of capabilities, encounter difficulty depends on more than just the estimated difficulty of each monster. For example, these metrics do not account for positioning and dungeon layout, the synergies between monster abilities, and player party composition. We have created a tool, Mage-Hand, that can simulate D&D encounters semi-randomly using Foundry Virtual Tabletop, a virtual tabletop (VTT) system. In this paper, we show that our tool's simulated winrates have a strong correlation with D&D's published difficulty evaluation metrics, while also better aligning with some players' reported experiences.

AI.tldr: Presents Mage-Hand, a tool that simulates D&D encounters semi-randomly in Foundry Virtual Tabletop, and shows that its simulated winrates correlate strongly with D&D's published difficulty metrics while better matching some players' reported experiences.
AI.motivation: D&D's difficulty metrics sum predefined per-enemy difficulty values, which ignores positioning, dungeon layout, synergies between monster abilities and party composition, all of which affect encounter difficulty.
AI.method: Mage-Hand simulates D&D encounters semi-randomly using Foundry Virtual Tabletop, a virtual tabletop system.
AI.result: Simulated winrates have a strong correlation with D&D's published difficulty evaluation metrics, and also align better with some players' reported experiences.
AI.conclusion: Simulation can complement published encounter difficulty metrics by capturing factors that those metrics omit.

title: Context Compaction for World Models
summary: World models let observers explore and interact with generated worlds. Recent work shows that when observers revisit a region, current models often fail to regenerate it consistently. We view this as a context retrieval problem. LLM agents manage context retrieval at two layers of their stack. At the model layer, the KV cache design determines how much context fits in memory. At the agent harness layer, harnesses such as Claude Code pick the context sent to the LLM. Prior work on world models has mostly focused only on the model layer. In this paper, we make three contributions. First, we build a benchmark to measure world model context retrieval. It generates new worlds for every episode, preventing a model from recalling rooms using training data. It also separates context retrieval from guesses based on nearby frames. Second, we build an agent harness that performs context compaction for world models, which to our knowledge no prior work has studied. Third, we use our benchmark to study four world model designs. Context compaction lets our world models retrieve rooms up to 4 times beyond their context window without retraining. However, world models with sliding-window attention lose most of their context retrieval when dreaming. Therefore, a dreaming world agent benefits more from extending the reach of its world model using context compaction than switching to sliding window attention at the model layer.

AI.tldr: Frames world-model revisit consistency as a context retrieval problem and builds a benchmark, an agent harness with context compaction, and a study of four world model designs. Context compaction lets world models retrieve rooms up to 4 times beyond their context window without retraining.
AI.motivation: When observers revisit a region, current world models often fail to regenerate it consistently, and prior work on world models has focused only on the model layer rather than the agent harness.
AI.method: The paper builds a benchmark that generates new worlds for every episode and separates context retrieval from guesses based on nearby frames, builds an agent harness that performs context compaction for world models, and studies four world model designs using the benchmark.
AI.result: Context compaction lets the world models retrieve rooms up to 4 times beyond their context window without retraining. World models with sliding-window attention lose most of their context retrieval when dreaming.
AI.conclusion: A dreaming world agent benefits more from extending its world model's reach through context compaction than from switching to sliding-window attention at the model layer.

title: Syntactic Segmentation and Collage Generation for Videogame Levels with Perceptual Distance
comment: 11 pages, 12 figures, 22nd Artificial Intelligence and Interactive Digital Entertainment Conference
summary: In procedural videogame level design, many existing techniques combine hand-authored level chunks. Some existing analysis techniques also rely on a higher-level graph structure which abstracts the level design. In this paper, we explore techniques for computing both of these things automatically from an existing design. We introduce the concept of perceptual distance, based on analysis techniques from the architecture subfield of Space Syntax. We use this perceptual distance to segment level designs with hierarchical clustering. We compare with past work on StarCraft analysis, show results on rooms from Super Metroid, and also demonstrate a proof-of-concept level generation algorithm based on this segmentation method.

AI.tldr: Proposes computing perceptual distance, based on Space Syntax, to segment videogame level designs with hierarchical clustering, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept level generation algorithm built on this segmentation.
AI.motivation: Procedural level design often combines hand-authored level chunks, and existing analysis techniques rely on a higher-level graph structure that abstracts the design. The paper seeks to compute both automatically from an existing design.
AI.method: Introduces perceptual distance, based on analysis techniques from the architecture subfield of Space Syntax, and uses it to segment level designs with hierarchical clustering.
AI.result: The method is compared with past work on StarCraft analysis and shown on rooms from Super Metroid. A proof-of-concept level generation algorithm based on the segmentation is also demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: Perceptual-distance segmentation can automatically extract chunk structure from existing level designs and support level generation.

title: Agentic AI Reasoning and Learned Sampling for Task-Aware Projection Selection in Sparse-View CT: Predicting Hemodynamics
summary: Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces the number of acquired projections, but conventional sampling strategies are designed primarily for image reconstruction rather than for downstream physical inference. Here, we investigate optimal task-aware projection selection for directly predicting hemodynamics from sparse CT angiography (CTA) measurements. Using computational fluid dynamics simulations of intracranial aneurysms, we generate synthetic fan-beam CTA projections and train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) to predict two targets: the spatially resolved time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) field and the spatially averaged TAWSS. The FNO was coupled with optimal input selection for simultaneous optimal sampling and training. Our goal was to investigate if agentic AI could discover optimal sampling strategies that outperform current methods. We compared fixed uniform and golden-angle sampling with three task-aware optimal selection strategies: Gumbel-Softmax, a Soft top-K method, and an agentic AI selector. The methods were compared at different view selection budgets. A detailed analysis of the AI agent was performed to understand its reasoning and performance. For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieve the lowest mean errors (Agentic performs slightly better) and substantially outperform fixed sampling under extreme sparsity. For spatially averaged TAWSS, optimized selection becomes important at extremely sparse acquisitions. Analysis of the selected masks reveals multiple distinct subsets concentrated around informative regions. Moreover, masks optimized for hemodynamic prediction yield poor image reconstructions, showing that task-optimal acquisition differs fundamentally from reconstruction-optimal acquisition. This work suggests the possibility of designing sparse acquisitions directly around downstream physical quantities.

AI.tldr: Investigates task-aware projection selection for predicting hemodynamics from sparse CT angiography, using a Fourier neural operator with Gumbel-Softmax, Soft top-K and an agentic AI selector. For spatially resolved TAWSS under extreme sparsity, the agentic and Soft top-K methods give the lowest errors.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view CT sampling strategies are designed primarily for image reconstruction rather than for downstream physical inference, such as predicting hemodynamics.
AI.method: Synthetic fan-beam CTA projections are generated from CFD simulations of intracranial aneurysms, and a Fourier neural operator is trained to predict the spatially resolved time-averaged wall shear stress (TAWSS) field and the spatially averaged TAWSS. Gumbel-Softmax, a Soft top-K method and an agentic AI selector are compared with fixed uniform and golden-angle sampling at several view budgets.
AI.result: For spatially resolved TAWSS, Agentic and Soft top-K achieve the lowest mean errors, with Agentic slightly better, and both substantially outperform fixed sampling under extreme sparsity. For spatially averaged TAWSS, optimised selection matters at extremely sparse acquisitions. Selected masks form multiple distinct subsets concentrated around informative regions, and masks optimised for hemodynamic prediction yield poor image reconstructions.
AI.conclusion: Task-optimal acquisition differs fundamentally from reconstruction-optimal acquisition, so sparse acquisitions can be designed directly around downstream physical quantities.

title: When Should AI Decide, Defer, and Deviate? Responsible Automation for Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation
summary: We ask when an AI trained on historical decisions should be allowed to recommend decisions, defer to human experts, or in other cases, flag concerning patterns in data and deviate from past practice. This can be challenging because past decisions record what was done rather than what should have been done, and where data is sparse, a model's predictions may be too uncertain to act on. We provide a framework for addressing this problem using a case study in deceased-donor kidney allocation. Nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from deceased donors in the United States are never transplanted, largely because they are hard to place through the standard waitlist sequence. One can use AI to flag kidneys at risk of delayed or failed placement for out-of-sequence (OOS) allocation, but this comes at the cost of bypassing candidates higher on the waitlist. Thus, OOS allocation should only be used when the organ is demonstrably at high risk of discard on the standard sequence. Using Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network match-run data from 2016-2019 and 2023-2025 (excluding COVID-19-disrupted years), we build the Arbitrator framework, which combines various interpretable models and acts only when the uncertainty in their predictions cannot change the preferred action. Our Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organ placement decisions using explicit medical criteria learned from data, and defers the remaining 6.5% to a human or a more complex model. We show that the Arbitrator correctly identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as OOS candidates, projecting that up to 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys could be flagged for expedited placement and potentially transplanted. We then exploit the interpretability of the Arbitrator to create an agentic audit comparing the learned rules to published clinical literature in order to flag decision-making patterns that are contentious.

AI.tldr: Presents the Arbitrator, a framework that decides when an AI trained on historical kidney allocation decisions should recommend, defer to humans or deviate from past practice. It resolves 93.5% of placement decisions and correctly identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as out-of-sequence candidates.
AI.motivation: Nearly 30% of kidneys recovered from US deceased donors are never transplanted, largely because they are hard to place through the standard waitlist sequence. Out-of-sequence allocation can help but bypasses higher-ranked candidates, so it should be used only when a kidney is demonstrably at high risk of discard. Past decisions record what was done, not what should have been done.
AI.method: The Arbitrator combines various interpretable models and acts only when the uncertainty in their predictions cannot change the preferred action. It uses OPTN match-run data from 2016 to 2019 and 2023 to 2025, excluding COVID-19-disrupted years. Its interpretability supports an agentic audit that compares the learned rules with published clinical literature.
AI.result: The Arbitrator resolves 93.5% of organ placement decisions using explicit medical criteria learned from data and defers the remaining 6.5% to a human or a more complex model. It correctly identifies 70.1% of historically discarded low-KDPI kidneys as out-of-sequence candidates, projecting that up to 43.9% of historically discarded kidneys could be flagged for expedited placement.
AI.conclusion: Explicit deferral and interpretability let AI support kidney allocation responsibly, and the audit flags decision patterns that are contentious relative to clinical literature.

title: When the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers (and the Same Answer Isn't Always Right): A Taxonomy of Failure Mechanisms, Testing, and Mitigation Strategies for LLM-Assisted Evidence Synthesis Read-and-Evaluate Tasks
comment: 76 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables, 1 box, 6 supplementary files
summary: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment settings in which each can operate, approaches for testing them, and mitigation strategies. We also show why repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure and why human evaluation should assess whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced through a process that can be examined and verified.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TRAILS, a taxonomy of 38 mechanisms that can make LLM read-and-evaluate judgements in evidence synthesis unreliable, either by varying across repeated runs or by systematically biasing the judgement in ways the judgement itself does not reveal. It also identifies deployment settings, testing approaches and mitigation strategies for these mechanisms.
AI.motivation: LLM judgements in screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and critical appraisal must be accurate, grounded in source evidence and reproducible, but a correct judgement does not show that the evaluation process behind it is reliable, and no systematic way to identify the mechanisms that compromise it is available.
AI.method: The authors develop a taxonomy organised around two questions: what mechanisms make the same read-and-evaluate task yield different judgements across repeated runs, and what mechanisms systematically affect the judgement or required output in ways not apparent from the judgement itself. For each of the 38 mechanisms they identify the deployment settings in which it can operate, approaches for testing it and mitigation strategies.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental figures. Its main output is the 38-mechanism taxonomy, and it argues that repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure.
AI.conclusion: Human evaluation should check whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced by a process that can be examined and verified.

title: Certified Access: Test-Time Compute on Conservative Physics-Structured AI Memory
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026); Workshop: Long-Context Foundation Models
summary: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as memory, in which access-expanding mechanisms have exact phase-volume, energy and latch-transport properties. It verifies the resulting certificate stack on an analytic testbed and demonstrates calibrated compute rationing on a learned physics-structured memory.
AI.motivation: Test-time compute mechanisms such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing are usually added to trained models as black boxes, with no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees.
AI.method: The encoder latent state (q,p) is advanced by a damped symplectic velocity-Verlet step of a learned Hamiltonian. Reachability failures are split into escape failures, resolved by a Lorentz squeeze that injects bounded, re-absorbable energy, and reach failures, resolved by a gated canonical translation across C_T that has unit phase-volume Jacobian.
AI.result: On the analytic testbed, reaching just beyond C_T with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically with the excess distance, whereas the gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured and does not grow with distance. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. The abstract gives no benchmark numbers for the learned memory experiments.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is the formalisation and verification of the certificate stack rather than benchmark performance.

title: Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration for Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes GAD, Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration, for long-horizon LLM agent tasks. It uses a growing execution graph of subtasks and dependencies, goal-carrying agent contexts, and verification and recovery steps that check results against task goals.
AI.motivation: A preliminary study finds that verification is most associated with task success but often happens late, and that duty-relevant information shrinks as records accumulate in a shared context. Separating duties across agents with separate contexts is insufficient alone, because agents lose track of the overall goal, repeat investigations, and lack background or receive irrelevant information.
AI.method: GAD builds a growing execution graph that organises subtasks and their dependencies. Each agent context keeps the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. Agents can divide tasks into subtasks and set dependencies based on execution evidence, and these dependencies determine when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against goals, giving repair feedback when checks fail.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining goal awareness and adapting collaboration to changing task needs, rather than only separating contexts, is presented as the way for multi-agent systems to handle long-horizon tasks.

title: Beyond LLM Wrappers: Context Engineering and the Three-Engine Architecture for Reliable Financial AI
summary: Financial AI systems must support decision-bearing questions involving payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance while ensuring numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction but cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations. We present a production-grounded architecture integrating three components: a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation, and claim validation. A coordination layer, termed context engineering, selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools, and tenants. Based on observations from 15 deployments over approximately 11 months, single-agent pipelines exhibited hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% across query types), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although these findings are observational rather than causal. ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major implementation challenges. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with a reduction in deployment time from roughly six to two weeks. We argue that financial context engineering extends beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by requiring structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls, and validation against source records and solver outputs. We outline research challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality, and cross-tenant generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a financial AI architecture that combines a financial knowledge graph, a deterministic optimisation engine and a multi-agent LLM layer, coordinated by context engineering. Observations from 15 deployments suggest that graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced hallucination rates from about 7-9% to below 1%.
AI.motivation: Financial AI must give numerically accurate, traceable and auditable answers on payments, collections, cash flow and compliance, but LLMs cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations.
AI.method: The architecture integrates a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context and provenance; a deterministic optimisation engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation and claim validation. A coordination layer called context engineering selects, ranks, composes and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools and tenants.
AI.result: Over about 11 months of observation across 15 deployments, single-agent pipelines showed hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% by query type), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although the authors state these findings are observational rather than causal. Reusable mappings, graph templates and validation policies coincided with deployment time falling from about six to two weeks, while ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major challenges.
AI.conclusion: Financial context engineering must go beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by using structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls and validation against source records and solver outputs, and evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality and cross-tenant generalisation remain open research challenges.

title: SocialArena: Evaluating Social Intelligence in Large Language Models
summary: We introduce SocialArena, a benchmark for systematically defining and evaluating the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring, existing evaluations remain fragmented focusing on isolated capabilities or single scenarios and evaluation reliability is largely unverified. This work makes three main contributions to address these limitations. (1) We first propose a unified three-tier framework that defines social intelligence along three capability dimensions: role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning. To operationalize this definition, we design a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking for evaluation, enabling simultaneous assessment of these capabilities in a manner that mirrors realistic human interactions. (2) To ensure diversity across social scenarios and thereby prevent evaluation conclusions from being confined to specific scenarios, we introduce the U-TRIMF framework, which guides us in synthesizing social contexts with broad coverage. (3) To obtain reliable evaluation, we invest $132.4K to recruit and train human annotators and adopt a human-annotated arena-style protocol, where annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels along with natural-language critiques. We hope that SocialArena can provide valuable insights and guidance for future LLM improvements.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SocialArena, a benchmark for the social intelligence of LLMs that covers role-playing ability, mental state reasoning and behavioural reasoning. It uses a human-annotated arena-style protocol with preference labels and natural-language critiques to obtain reliable evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counselling, companionship and tutoring, but existing evaluations are fragmented, focus on isolated capabilities or single scenarios, and their reliability is largely unverified.
AI.method: A unified three-tier framework defines social intelligence along role-playing ability, mental state reasoning and behavioural reasoning, operationalised by a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking. The U-TRIMF framework guides the synthesis of social contexts with broad coverage. Human annotators, recruited and trained at a reported cost of 132.4K dollars, compare model responses and give preference labels with natural-language critiques.
AI.result: The abstract reports no benchmark scores. It describes the benchmark's framework, scenario-coverage design and human-annotated arena protocol.
AI.conclusion: The authors hope SocialArena will give valuable insight and guidance for future improvements in the social intelligence of LLMs.

title: Where to Learn and How Far to Roll Out: Efficient Adaptive Training for GUI Agents
summary: Trajectory-level GRPO is a common approach for training multi-step GUI agents, but repeatedly rolling out complete trajectories from the task root can be inefficient: task-level rewards provide coarse supervision over which intermediate decisions require improvement, while already-mastered prefixes are repeatedly re-executed before reaching difficult states. We introduce a two-stage adaptive training framework that jointly addresses where to learn and how far to roll out. We first construct reusable intermediate checkpoints from successful expert trajectories and select informative pivots using action disagreement, which measures uncertainty directly from sampled GUI actions. Stage I performs one-step RL at these pivots to improve uncertain local decisions. Stage II then progressively expands policy responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix, and Root training according to task progress. Recoverable checkpoints enable repeated training from intermediate states without replaying the preceding trajectory. Across MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, our method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to Vanilla GRPO while improving task performance, demonstrating that jointly allocating training across states and rollout ranges can substantially improve GUI-agent RL efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-stage adaptive training framework for GRPO-based GUI agents that selects informative intermediate states by action disagreement and adaptively decides how far rollouts extend. It reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to vanilla GRPO while improving task performance.
AI.motivation: Trajectory-level GRPO for multi-step GUI agents repeatedly rolls out complete trajectories from the task root, where task-level rewards give coarse supervision over which decisions need improvement, and already mastered prefixes are re-executed before difficult states are reached.
AI.method: Reusable intermediate checkpoints are built from successful expert trajectories, and informative pivots are chosen by action disagreement, a measure of uncertainty computed from sampled GUI actions. Stage I performs one-step RL at these pivots to improve uncertain local decisions. Stage II progressively expands policy responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix and Root training according to task progress. Recoverable checkpoints allow repeated training from intermediate states without replaying the preceding trajectory.
AI.result: Across MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, the method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to vanilla GRPO while improving task performance.
AI.conclusion: Jointly allocating training across states and rollout ranges can substantially improve the efficiency of GUI-agent reinforcement learning.

title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps
summary: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an online RL framework that trains a decoupled Planning agent and UI Grounding model directly on live iOS apps, using LLM-as-a-Judge dense step-level rewards and a terminal task reward. Its 8B RL agents outperform SFT and terminal-only RL baselines and match or exceed some Gemini models on real iOS applications.
AI.motivation: Frontier vision-language models are costly to run for UI navigation, while smaller models trained by SFT or offline RL memorise static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors.
AI.method: The agent is split into a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. An LLM-as-a-Judge provides dense step-level feedback on intermediate progress plus a terminal reward for overall completion. The agent is optimised with PPO using step-level advantage estimation. GiGPPO, a neighbour-conditioned value estimation method, improves critic stability by using reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. An infrastructure orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices.
AI.result: On UINavBench, iOSWorld and AndroidWorld, the online RL agents substantially outperform SFT and terminal-only RL baselines and converge faster. The 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalisation to Android, and outperform Gemini-3.5-Flash while tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
AI.conclusion: Combining dense dual-level rewards with neighbour-conditioned critics lets online RL make small UI navigation agents competitive with frontier models on live iOS tasks.

title: LLM-Assisted Optimization for Simulation-Based Redesign
comment: 17 pages, 12 figures, 11 tables. Submitted to the ASME Journal of Mechanical Design. Code: this https URL, data: this https URL
summary: Engineering design frequently involves redesigning a prior solution to adapt to changes in context, such as material prices or system requirements. Redesign often leverages simulators too complex and/or computationally intensive for traditional numerical solvers, which lack engineering knowledge and context, to ensure global solution quality. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret semantic information, including engineering knowledge about the system and changes in context, to help guide search, and recent studies have shown that incorporating this knowledge into optimization can improve search performance. However, how best to combine LLMs with numerical solvers in redesign remains unclear. We develop and test an integrated LLM-optimization approach for redesign and compare three methods for leveraging LLMs (warm start, variable fixing and ReAct) and four black-box solvers (Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search) on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization case study across four types of redesign scenarios. We find that the integrated approach can match feasible design discovery of the numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions. We find that the best LLM-solver integration approach and the way the prior solution is leveraged depend on the structure of the design requirement change, and that the benefit of increasing LLM model size grows with the extent to which the LLM controls the search. These results show clear potential for LLMs in redesign tasks for guiding or replacing numerical solvers.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an integrated LLM-optimisation approach for simulation-based redesign and compares three ways of leveraging LLMs with four black-box solvers on an electric vehicle battery pack cost case study. The integrated approach matches the feasible-design discovery of numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations.
AI.motivation: Redesigning a prior engineering solution to fit changed context often relies on simulators too expensive for traditional numerical solvers, which lack engineering knowledge, and how best to combine LLMs with numerical solvers in redesign remains unclear.
AI.method: Three methods for leveraging LLMs, namely warm start, variable fixing and ReAct, are combined with four black-box solvers: Bayesian optimisation, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search. The approach is tested on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimisation case study across four types of redesign scenario.
AI.result: The integrated approach matches the feasible-design discovery of numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations and triples the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions. The best LLM-solver integration and the way the prior solution is used depend on the structure of the design requirement change, and larger LLMs help more as the LLM controls the search more.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show clear potential for redesign tasks, either guiding or replacing numerical solvers.

title: MemSteer: Turning User Histories into Supervision for Agent Memory Optimization
summary: An effective agent memory system should adapt to a user's history and task requirements. Human-annotated supervision can guide this adaptation by providing feedback for evaluating and improving memory designs. Yet suitable labels are rarely available for new user histories, and manually constructing QA pairs and supporting evidence is costly. We introduce MemSteer, which turns unlabeled user histories into question-answer (QA) supervision with supporting evidence for memory-design optimization. MemSteer constructs an evidence-grounded answer plan that specifies how facts across related records jointly support a reference answer. The plan guides question generation, while source-grounded auditing and blind answer recovery check the resulting annotations. To study the utility of this supervision, we develop MemSteer-Opt, which combines QA-based design evaluation with evidence-guided failure diagnosis to revise memory store, retrieval, and context construction without updating model parameters. Experiments on ATM-Bench and RHELM show that this supervision is competitive with official-QA-guided optimization. Relative to Base-BM25, MemSteer-Opt improves ATM-Bench Question Score by 13.4 points and RHELM accuracy by 4.1 and 6.6 points without and with external data, respectively. The supervision also benefits two existing optimizers on ATM-Bench, while new-user experiments demonstrate continued design optimization using supervision generated from the target histories.

AI.tldr: MemSteer turns unlabelled user histories into evidence-grounded question-answer supervision for agent memory design, and MemSteer-Opt uses that supervision to revise memory store, retrieval and context construction without updating model parameters. It improves ATM-Bench Question Score by 13.4 points over Base-BM25.
AI.motivation: Effective agent memory must adapt to a user's history, and human-annotated supervision guides that adaptation, but suitable labels are rarely available for new user histories and manually building QA pairs with supporting evidence is costly.
AI.method: MemSteer constructs an evidence-grounded answer plan that specifies how facts across related records jointly support a reference answer. The plan guides question generation, and source-grounded auditing and blind answer recovery check the annotations. MemSteer-Opt combines QA-based design evaluation with evidence-guided failure diagnosis to revise memory store, retrieval and context construction.
AI.result: On ATM-Bench and RHELM, the supervision is competitive with official-QA-guided optimisation. Relative to Base-BM25, MemSteer-Opt improves ATM-Bench Question Score by 13.4 points and RHELM accuracy by 4.1 points without external data and 6.6 points with external data. The supervision also benefits two existing optimisers on ATM-Bench, and new-user experiments show continued design optimisation using supervision generated from the target histories.
AI.conclusion: Supervision generated from unlabelled user histories can drive memory-design optimisation, offering an alternative to costly human-annotated QA.

title: What Does "Now" Mean to Your Computer-Use Agent? Stale Screenshots, Page Loads, and Which Check to Run Before a Click
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Code, benchmark generator and preregistrations: this https URL
summary: Computer-use agents plan on a screenshot for several seconds and then click at a position on the screen; if the page has changed in the meantime, the click lands on an unintended element. Prior work treats the planning interval as the source of this risk. Measuring planned clicks on 31 public web pages, we find that the risk lies in page loading: 0.4% of clicks planned on fully loaded pages became stale within 30 seconds, against 17% of clicks planned in the first second after a page opened. On these pages, waiting about one second for network activity to stop removes most of this risk, yet the wait rules of eight of ten widely used open-source agents leave more than 1% of clicks stale. Commercial pages keep loading for longer: in the HTTP Archive's public crawl, 15% of 65 desktop booking and buying home pages went 500 ms without network requests within 3 seconds of their HTML being parsed, against 63% of 3,028 .gov pages, and 52% shifted their layout within 6.5 seconds of a network-idle wait capped at 3 seconds, against 8% (61% against 26% among pages recorded in full). Where a check before the click is needed, as before irreversible actions and on pages that are still loading, a pixel comparison verifies the target's position as accurately as a frontier vision-language model at one eighth of the latency, and a 4B model matches the frontier model in verifying whether the previous action succeeded. We release a benchmark generator, a break-even formula for when a check pays, and three rules for agent developers: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper shows that stale clicks by computer-use agents mainly come from page loading rather than the planning interval, and that waiting about one second for network activity to stop removes most of this risk on the pages tested. Where a pre-click check is needed, a pixel comparison verifies target position as accurately as a frontier vision-language model at one eighth of the latency.
AI.motivation: Prior work attributes the risk of clicking an unintended element to the planning interval, but the abstract finds that the real risk lies in page loading, and the wait rules of widely used open-source agents often leave a notable share of clicks stale.
AI.method: The authors measure clicks planned on 31 public web pages and test a network-idle wait. For verifying targets, they compare a pixel comparison with a frontier vision-language model, and for checking whether the previous action succeeded, they compare a 4B model with the frontier model. They also analyse HTTP Archive crawl data on booking and buying home pages and .gov pages, and release a benchmark generator, a break-even formula for when a check pays, and three rules for agent developers.
AI.result: Of clicks planned on fully loaded pages, 0.4% became stale within 30 seconds, against 17% of clicks planned in the first second after a page opened. About one second of waiting for network activity to stop removes most of this risk, yet the wait rules of eight of ten widely used open-source agents leave more than 1% of clicks stale. In the HTTP Archive crawl, 15% of 65 desktop booking and buying home pages went 500 ms without network requests within 3 seconds of HTML parsing, against 63% of 3,028 .gov pages. Layout shifted within 6.5 seconds of a network-idle wait capped at 3 seconds for 52% of pages against 8% in the comparison, and 61% against 26% among pages recorded in full.
AI.conclusion: Agent developers should treat page loading as the main source of stale clicks and check before irreversible actions or on pages still loading, using the released tools and rules.

title: Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs
summary: Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a \emph{Platonic Representation Theorem}: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--\emph{good views}--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with \emph{bad views}, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a Platonic Representation Theorem: JEPAs trained separately on different modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation when their positive pairs are good views of one scene. It also shows that a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns better with vision encoders than every language model evaluated, up to 72B parameters.
AI.motivation: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis conjectures that models trained on different modalities converge to a shared representation as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe.
AI.method: The authors prove that JEPAs trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are good views (two observations of one scene), with misalignment bounded otherwise. They show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with bad views, parts of a single document. They validate the theory on data from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and fit a scaling law of alignment.
AI.result: The scaling law predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment. A 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP image encoders better than every language model evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and better than CLIP's text encoder. One rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner with CIDEr 0.838 on COCO, and on the latest pair-free benchmark the text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported for language models up to 8B parameters, for example 64% against at most 56% top-5 on ImageNet-100.
AI.conclusion: Positive views, rather than scale alone, are the lever for building platonic representations, and next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to them.

title: CoToan: Executable Rules and a Representation Contract for Reproducible Game AI Evaluation
summary: Game AI results are comparable only when different implementations expose the same decision problem. Yet seemingly minor representation choices can silently change that problem by altering action probabilities or collapsing states with different outcomes. We study this issue through CoToan, an executable specification and representation contract for Vietnamese Mathematical Chess connecting the Game Description Language (GDL) with OpenSpiel. The game provides a useful case because a single capture may have multiple arithmetic justifications, while outcomes can depend on scoring rules and a finite playing horizon. CoToan therefore represents actions by their state transitions rather than by arithmetic witnesses, and treats time and victory configuration as part of task identity.
