Cross-representation tests show agreement in legal actions, successor states, and terminal outcomes across hundreds of sampled and constructed positions, complemented by exhaustive checks of all 32 operator masks and 512 opposing-material subsets. Controlled diagnostics further show that uniform witness-level sampling alters endpoint-action probabilities, while omitting remaining time or victory settings can merge states with different terminal behavior. These results show that action semantics, time, and victory configuration are not merely implementation details. They are part of the experimental task itself and must be represented explicitly for reproducible game AI.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoToan, an executable specification and representation contract for Vietnamese Mathematical Chess that links the Game Description Language with OpenSpiel. It shows that action representation, time and victory configuration change the decision problem, so they must be specified for reproducible game AI evaluation.
AI.motivation: Game AI results are comparable only when different implementations expose the same decision problem, yet seemingly minor representation choices can silently change that problem by altering action probabilities or collapsing states with different outcomes.
AI.method: CoToan represents actions by their state transitions rather than by arithmetic witnesses, and treats time and victory configuration as part of task identity. Cross-representation tests compare legal actions, successor states and terminal outcomes across hundreds of sampled and constructed positions, complemented by exhaustive checks of all 32 operator masks and 512 opposing-material subsets.
AI.result: Cross-representation tests show agreement in legal actions, successor states and terminal outcomes. Controlled diagnostics show that uniform witness-level sampling alters endpoint-action probabilities, and that omitting remaining time or victory settings can merge states with different terminal behaviour.
AI.conclusion: Action semantics, time and victory configuration are part of the experimental task itself and must be represented explicitly for reproducible game AI.

title: Before the Next Rollout: Diagnosing Skill Utility Shifts from Policy Updates
summary: Skill-evolution methods typically analyze execution trajectories to guide agent skill refinement. However, policy updates can change the behavioral effects and marginal utility of an unchanged skill. Attribution based on earlier trajectories may therefore no longer reflect the skill's contribution under the updated policy. Moreover, trajectory failures can arise from multiple factors, making individual skill contributions difficult to isolate. We evaluate whether policy-update signals contain predictive information about changes in skill marginal utility. At fixed contexts from pre-update training rollouts, we measure how policy updates change the contrast in token preferences between skill and control conditions. Combining these interaction shifts with advantage estimates yields reward-directed readouts for diagnosing utility changes. The readouts reuse existing training rollouts and require only forward passes for single-step action scoring, without additional post-update rollout evaluation. Our experiments show that policy updates can alter skill marginal utility and that policy-update readouts carry diagnostic information for identifying skills with declining utility. Integrating readout-guided prioritization into skill evolution improves downstream performance while reducing policy and editor token consumption.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses how policy updates shift a skill's marginal utility, using readouts computed from existing training rollouts and single-step forward passes. Using these readouts to prioritise skill evolution improves downstream performance while reducing policy and editor token consumption.
AI.motivation: Skill-evolution methods analyse execution trajectories to refine skills, but policy updates can change the behavioural effect and marginal utility of an unchanged skill, so attribution from earlier trajectories may no longer reflect its contribution under the updated policy, and several factors can make individual contributions hard to isolate.
AI.method: At fixed contexts from pre-update training rollouts, the authors measure how policy updates change the contrast in token preferences between skill and control conditions. These interaction shifts are combined with advantage estimates to form reward-directed readouts, which reuse existing training rollouts and require only forward passes for single-step action scoring.
AI.result: Policy updates can alter skill marginal utility, and the readouts carry diagnostic information for identifying skills with declining utility. Integrating readout-guided prioritisation into skill evolution improves downstream performance while reducing policy and editor token consumption. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Policy-update signals contain predictive information about changes in skill utility, and they can guide skill evolution effectively at lower token cost.

title: AgentDecept: Benchmarking Deceptive Behavior in Tool-Using LLM Agents under Pressure
summary: LLM agents increasingly carry out multi-turn tasks across everyday applications, yet users often see only the agent's report rather than the observations, API calls, and state changes behind it. Existing deception benchmarks have studied long-horizon interactions and tool-use settings, but whether agents faithfully report their actions across realistic, stateful application workflows remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce AgentDecept, an executable benchmark for evaluating behavioral deception under pressure. AgentDecept contains 477 pressure variants derived from 257 source tasks across six pressure sources, each paired with a pressure-free counterpart. Interventions enter through event messages, task context, application state, tool responses, and service quotas, spanning explicit events and implicit task or environment changes. Our evidence-grounded protocol evaluates full trajectories by relating user-facing claims to time-ordered observations and executed outcomes, distinguishing falsification, concealment, and equivocation from honest failure and disclosed limitations. The resulting behavioral labels also provide a setting for testing existing activation-based probes. AgentDecept enables controlled analysis of when multi-turn agents' reports diverge from execution in realistic application interactions.

AI.tldr: AgentDecept is an executable benchmark that tests whether tool-using LLM agents faithfully report their actions under pressure. It contains 477 pressure variants derived from 257 source tasks and separates falsification, concealment and equivocation from honest failure and disclosed limitations.
AI.motivation: Users usually see only an agent's report rather than the observations, API calls and state changes behind it, and existing deception benchmarks do not establish whether agents faithfully report their actions across realistic, stateful application workflows.
AI.method: The benchmark has 477 pressure variants derived from 257 source tasks across six pressure sources, each paired with a pressure-free counterpart. Interventions enter through event messages, task context, application state, tool responses and service quotas. An evidence-grounded protocol evaluates full trajectories by relating user-facing claims to time-ordered observations and executed outcomes.
AI.result: The abstract reports no model scores. It provides behavioural labels that distinguish falsification, concealment and equivocation from honest failure and disclosed limitations, and these labels also serve as a setting for testing existing activation-based probes.
AI.conclusion: AgentDecept enables controlled analysis of when multi-turn agent reports diverge from execution in realistic application interactions.

title: Retaining Repair Hypotheses for Cost-Aware Execution
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures; data and code in ancillary files
summary: Several corrections of an executable model can fit the same observations while predicting different execution outcomes. We study a repair-to-execution interface that retains compatible finite guard repairs, conditions their weights on diagnostic and ordinary-execution observations, and uses their predictions to choose routes, priced tests, or a backup. On 24 synthetic two-stage devices, an equal mixture of a language-model-generated repair and a uniform belief over compatible repairs (the AI-weighted belief) lowers no-test cost by 2.14 percent relative to committing to the generated repair. Access charges can erase the benefit of diagnosis on isolated tasks, while repeated work can recover it under the AI-weighted belief. With normal-execution learning in every repeated-work arm, workload-valued testing costs 3.33 percent less than same-budget random selection under the AI-weighted belief. Weighting changes the comparison: uniform normal learning costs 540.75 less than AI-weighted normal learning on this cohort, with a device-paired interval excluding zero. Testing recovers part of that gap, but uniform normal learning still has a lower aggregate cost than AI-weighted workload-valued selection. Under uniform beliefs, information-gain selection has the lowest total among the compared selectors, while workload-valued testing costs more than normal learning. These results support retaining alternatives to a generated repair and evaluating diagnostic selection together with repair weighting and learning from execution.

AI.tldr: The paper studies retaining several compatible repairs of an executable model and using their weighted predictions to choose routes, priced tests or a backup. On 24 synthetic two-stage devices, an equal mixture of an LLM-generated repair and a uniform belief over compatible repairs lowers no-test cost by 2.14% relative to committing to the generated repair.
AI.motivation: Several corrections of an executable model can fit the same observations yet predict different execution outcomes, and committing to a single generated repair discards this ambiguity.
AI.method: A repair-to-execution interface retains compatible finite guard repairs, conditions their weights on diagnostic and ordinary-execution observations, and uses their predictions to choose routes, priced tests or a backup. The AI-weighted belief is an equal mixture of a language-model-generated repair and a uniform belief over compatible repairs. Workload-valued testing is compared with same-budget random selection and information-gain selection under different beliefs and learning schemes.
AI.result: On 24 synthetic two-stage devices, the AI-weighted belief lowers no-test cost by 2.14% relative to the generated repair. Access charges can erase the benefit of diagnosis on isolated tasks, while repeated work can recover it. Under the AI-weighted belief, workload-valued testing costs 3.33% less than same-budget random selection. Uniform normal learning costs 540.75 less than AI-weighted normal learning, with a device-paired interval excluding zero. Under uniform beliefs, information-gain selection has the lowest total among the compared selectors.
AI.conclusion: Alternatives to a generated repair should be retained, and diagnostic selection should be evaluated together with repair weighting and learning from execution.

title: Verifiable LLM-Guided Focal SMT Solving for Quantified Arrays
summary: Large language models can often identify useful semantic structure in formal artifacts, but their outputs cannot be trusted as proofs or solver decisions. We study whether LLMs can instead guide formal reasoning systems through a narrow, solver-verifiable interface. We instantiate this idea in quantified array SMT solving, where modern instantiation-based techniques can fail when key ground terms and equalities are hidden by auxiliary variables, axiom guards, and nested array terms. We observe that many instances are largely driven by a small set of focal ground terms or constraints, similar to the backdoor sets in SAT solving. Building on this, we present LinguaArray, a framework where an LLM proposes a small Semantic Focus Set (ground terms/constraints), while a conventional SMT solver remains the sole proof engine and certifies all results. LinguaArray uses these LLM-suggested, solver-validated finite sets to significantly enhance solver capability, solving additional satisfiable and unsatisfiable instances that the backend alone fails to solve. It interacts within a finite time and then falls back to the backend solver to mitigate potential regressions. Evaluation on 1015 SMT-LIB instances across five logics under 1200s timeout (including LLM latency) shows that LinguaArray solves up to 69.1% of instances and increases solved-instance counts by 105%--397% over the corresponding backends.

AI.tldr: LinguaArray lets an LLM propose a small Semantic Focus Set of ground terms or constraints for quantified array SMT solving, while a conventional SMT solver remains the sole proof engine. It solves up to 69.1% of 1015 SMT-LIB instances and raises solved-instance counts by 105% to 397% over the backends.
AI.motivation: LLM outputs cannot be trusted as proofs or solver decisions, and instantiation-based techniques for quantified arrays can fail when key ground terms and equalities are hidden by auxiliary variables, axiom guards and nested array terms.
AI.method: Many instances are driven largely by a small set of focal ground terms or constraints, similar to backdoor sets in SAT solving. An LLM proposes a Semantic Focus Set, which the solver validates as a finite set. The framework interacts with the solver within a finite time and then falls back to the backend solver to mitigate potential regressions, and the SMT solver certifies all results.
AI.result: On 1015 SMT-LIB instances across five logics under a 1200 s timeout (including LLM latency), LinguaArray solves up to 69.1% of instances and increases solved-instance counts by 105% to 397% over the corresponding backends. It solves satisfiable and unsatisfiable instances that the backend alone fails to solve.
AI.conclusion: A narrow, solver-verifiable interface lets LLMs guide formal reasoning systems while every result remains certified by the solver.

title: ATLAS-Bench: An Agentic Tool-Use Benchmark for Local Area Search
summary: Reliable local search is essential for LLM agents to support everyday decisions and longer plans by finding places that meet users' needs at given times and locations. Yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of whether search results satisfy mandatory requirements, account for preferences, and ground factual and experiential judgments in place attributes and reviews. We introduce ATLAS-Bench, a benchmark of 1,200 queries across three regions, expanded from real search events using place attributes, reviews, and existing user profiles from the platform. Each query distinguishes mandatory requirements from preferences and factual conditions from subjective judgments, with supporting evidence and criteria for checking each requirement. Queries are validated through iterative assertion checks and cross-model review. We also introduce ATLASBox, a standardized evaluation environment with search tools and a fixed point-of-interest (POI) knowledge base. Given a query, timestamp, and location, an agent searches place attributes and reviews to recommend evidence-supported options or report that no place meets all mandatory requirements. We evaluate answer quality, trajectory quality, and execution cost. Across 14 configurations of 11 models, GPT-6-Luna achieves the highest constraint satisfaction rate among returned recommendations (71.5%) and factual accuracy (95.6%). However, it returns at least one acceptable recommendation for fewer satisfiable queries than GLM-5.3 (67.3% versus 85.3%). These results highlight the challenge of satisfying individual requirements while providing usable recommendations across queries.

AI.tldr: ATLAS-Bench is a benchmark of 1,200 local-search queries that separate mandatory requirements from preferences and factual conditions from subjective judgements, with a standardised evaluation environment, ATLASBox. Across 14 configurations of 11 models, the best model reaches 71.5% constraint satisfaction among returned recommendations, yet returns an acceptable option for fewer satisfiable queries than GLM-5.3.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of whether search results satisfy mandatory requirements, account for preferences, and ground factual and experiential judgements in place attributes and reviews.
AI.method: Queries are expanded from real search events using place attributes, reviews and existing user profiles from the platform, and each query has supporting evidence and criteria for checking each requirement. Queries are validated through iterative assertion checks and cross-model review. ATLASBox provides search tools and a fixed point-of-interest knowledge base, and evaluation covers answer quality, trajectory quality and execution cost.
AI.result: GPT-6-Luna achieves the highest constraint satisfaction rate among returned recommendations (71.5%) and factual accuracy (95.6%). However, it returns at least one acceptable recommendation for fewer satisfiable queries than GLM-5.3 (67.3% versus 85.3%).
AI.conclusion: Satisfying individual requirements while still providing usable recommendations across queries remains a challenge.

title: Timbre: Reliability-aware harmonic consensus for label-free multimodal test-time rexinforcement learning
summary: Label-free test-time reinforcement learning adapts vision--language models using rewards derived from their own predictions. However, misinterpreted visual evidence and sensitivity to textual formulation can produce a consistent but incorrect consensus that majority voting reinforces. Cross-view aggregation can expose such errors, but image and text transformations may themselves degrade task-relevant evidence to different extents. We introduce \method, a reliability-aware harmonic consensus framework for multimodal test-time reinforcement learning. \method constructs a $2\times2$ grid combining original and perturbed images with direct-solving and reframing modes, selects pseudo-labels through weighted harmonic aggregation, and adapts modality-level weights using batch-averaged, temporally smoothed shifts in pseudo-label confidence as a heuristic reliability signal. We formulate consensus as a weighted $\chi^2$-barycenter problem whose unique minimizer is the normalized weighted harmonic aggregate, without requiring correct-answer invariance. An exact support--dispersion decomposition characterizes when harmonic aggregation preserves or corrects arithmetic rankings, while a sensitivity analysis establishes how modality reweighting changes pairwise ranking margins, informing interpretation of the heuristic updates. Across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL model scales, \method outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark--model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 settings on held-out instances under matched estimation and optimization rollout counts. These results demonstrate improved target-task adaptation and transfer to unseen instances without further updates.

AI.tldr: Timbre is a reliability-aware harmonic consensus framework for label-free multimodal test-time reinforcement learning of vision-language models. It builds a 2x2 grid of original and perturbed images in direct-solving and reframing modes, and outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark-model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 on held-out instances.
AI.motivation: Label-free test-time RL adapts vision-language models using rewards from their own predictions, but misinterpreted visual evidence and sensitivity to textual formulation can produce a consistent but incorrect consensus that majority voting reinforces.
AI.method: Timbre combines original and perturbed images with direct-solving and reframing modes in a 2x2 grid, selects pseudo-labels by weighted harmonic aggregation, and adapts modality-level weights using batch-averaged, temporally smoothed shifts in pseudo-label confidence as a heuristic reliability signal. Consensus is formulated as a weighted chi-squared barycenter problem whose unique minimiser is the normalised weighted harmonic aggregate, and an exact support-dispersion decomposition characterises when harmonic aggregation preserves or corrects arithmetic rankings.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL model scales, Timbre outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark-model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 settings on held-out instances, under matched estimation and optimisation rollout counts.
AI.conclusion: The framework improves target-task adaptation and transfers to unseen instances without further updates.

title: Kairos: Semantics-Aware Orchestration of Planning Engines across Classical, Numeric, Temporal and Hybrid PDDL
comment: 32 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables. Submitted to the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research. Code: this https URL ; benchmark, scripts and results: this https URL
summary: Planning at run time, as in robots that re-plan while they act, needs a planner that reads the PDDL its users write (durative actions, numeric resources, time windows, continuous change), answers quickly, and delivers only validated plans. Specialised planners are strong on individual fragments of PDDL, but they differ in coverage, latency and in what their failures mean. We study whether selecting heterogeneous engines from the semantics of each task can give broad coverage of PDDL, from STRIPS to PDDL+, while remaining competitive with specialised planners and making explicit what each answer guarantees. Kairos profiles each task to decide which of five engines apply (ground heuristic search, compressed and snap-action temporal search, time steps for hybrid dynamics, lifted search) and schedules them under one budget of time and memory. Every candidate plan is checked by a validator independent of the planner's transformations, and "unsolvable" is reported only when a search whose exhaustion is a proof exhausts its space. On 1,756 tasks from nine comparative suites, Kairos solves more tasks at the full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite, with the largest differences on numeric, temporal, PDDL3 and PDDL+ planning, and it also solves the most tasks at 100 ms and 1 s. Resampling over domains, the gain is above zero in six of the nine suites, while on classical planning against LAMA it is within the noise. A further 450 feature-oriented tasks and 26 one-feature probes show that Kairos handles all seventeen features probed, where no other planner evaluated handles more than eight. Ablations identify compressed temporal search and the novelty fallback as major contributors, and a comparison with VAL traces every disagreement to a PDDL+ convention or to a documented VAL defect. Planner and benchmark are open source.

AI.tldr: Kairos profiles each PDDL task and schedules five heterogeneous planning engines under one time and memory budget, checking every candidate plan with an independent validator. On 1,756 tasks it solves more tasks at the full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite, and it also solves the most tasks at 100 ms and 1 s.
AI.motivation: Run-time re-planning needs a planner that reads the full range of PDDL, from STRIPS to PDDL+, answers quickly and delivers only validated plans, but specialised planners differ in coverage, latency and in what their failures mean.
AI.method: Kairos profiles each task to decide which of five engines apply: ground heuristic search, compressed and snap-action temporal search, time steps for hybrid dynamics, and lifted search. These engines are scheduled under one budget of time and memory. Every candidate plan is checked by a validator independent of the planner's transformations, and unsolvable is reported only when a search whose exhaustion is a proof exhausts its space.
AI.result: On 1,756 tasks from nine comparative suites, Kairos solves more tasks at the full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite, with the largest differences on numeric, temporal, PDDL3 and PDDL+ planning. Resampling over domains, the gain is above zero in six of the nine suites, while on classical planning against LAMA it is within noise. On 450 further feature-oriented tasks and 26 one-feature probes, Kairos handles all seventeen features probed, where no other planner evaluated handles more than eight. Ablations identify compressed temporal search and the novelty fallback as major contributors.
AI.conclusion: Selecting heterogeneous engines from task semantics can give broad PDDL coverage while staying competitive with specialised planners and making explicit what each answer guarantees; the planner and benchmark are open source.

title: Does Scaling Toward AGI Depend on What System-1 Lets System-2 Execute?
summary: Progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) has largely relied on scaling a resource-intensive executive, System-2, through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning, and more agents. We ask whether the next stage may come instead from co-designing it with System-1, a lightweight, semantically aware predictor that evaluates candidate interactions before execution, so that System-2 acts only on those worth their cost. Our answer is a qualified yes. We study \textit{conditional interaction}, a predict--gate--execute--update loop: System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application. Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching $1/\rho_u$, where $\rho_u$ is the density of utility-relevant interactions (cost-weighted when costs differ); prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the saving. We bound selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin. These results motivate our central hypothesis: $\rho_u$ is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency and makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes co-designing System-2 with a lightweight System-1 predictor that screens candidate interactions, so that expensive execution happens only for those worth their cost. It argues that the density of utility-relevant interactions is a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency, giving a qualified yes to whether the next scaling stage depends on what System-1 lets System-2 execute.
AI.motivation: Progress toward AGI has largely relied on scaling the resource-intensive System-2 executive through larger models, more data and compute, longer reasoning and more agents, and the paper asks whether the next stage may instead come from co-designing it with System-1.
AI.method: The authors study conditional interaction, a predict-gate-execute-update loop in which System-1 estimates each candidate's utility, System-2 executes those admitted by an adaptive threshold, and the outcomes update System-1. The loop spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined by the application.
AI.result: Under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute falls by a factor approaching the reciprocal of the utility-relevant interaction density (cost-weighted when costs differ), and prediction errors, exploration and distribution shift reduce the saving. Selection regret is bounded by predictor error and the utility margin.
AI.conclusion: The utility-relevant interaction density is proposed as a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency, which makes informative compute a better description of scaling than total compute.

title: Integrated Feature Selection for classification and Representation Learning with Group-Lasso Siamese Networks
summary: The Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso) has been widely employed for feature selection in linear models and has also been extended to multi-layer perceptron (MLP) networks for both feature and group feature selection. Group-Lasso has also been used in feature selection using feed-forward neural networks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to incorporate the Group-Lasso principle into a Siamese network architecture for feature selection. Unlike existing approaches that primarily optimize classification accuracy, the proposed method aims to identify a compact subset of features that simultaneously preserves the intrinsic representation of the input data (the goal of Siamese network) and is expected to achieve high classification performance. Two variants of the proposed framework are developed: one based on the Euclidean distance and the other on a modified Jaccard similarity measure for real-valued vectors. The latter is specifically designed to improve feature selection for high?dimensional sparse data. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated on 12 benchmark datasets with feature dimensions ranging from 6 to 7070 using eight different classifiers. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Siamese Lasso framework consistently identifies compact and discriminative feature subsets maintaining competitive or superior classification performance, although the loss function used explicitly did not consider any regularizer to learn classification. In addition, the quality of the embeddings produced by these networks is assessed using manifold learning techniques such as UMAP and t-SNE.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Siamese network with a Group-Lasso penalty for feature selection that finds compact feature subsets preserving the input representation while keeping classification performance on 12 benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing Lasso and Group-Lasso feature selection methods mainly optimize classification accuracy, and Group-Lasso has not been incorporated into a Siamese network architecture for feature selection.
AI.method: Group-Lasso is integrated into a Siamese network so that selected features preserve the intrinsic representation of the data; two variants use either Euclidean distance or a modified Jaccard similarity for real-valued vectors, the latter aimed at high-dimensional sparse data.
AI.result: On 12 benchmark datasets with 6 to 7070 features and eight classifiers, the method consistently identifies compact and discriminative feature subsets with competitive or superior classification performance, and the embeddings are assessed with UMAP and t-SNE.
AI.conclusion: Group-Lasso regularization inside a Siamese architecture gives a feature selection approach that balances compactness, representation preservation and classification performance without an explicit classification regularizer in the loss.

title: What Breaks When Facts Become Stories? The Distortions Source-Agreement Metrics Miss When Models Retell Real Events
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 11 tables. Accepted at the Trust-AI-Eval (TAE) Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Data and code: this https URL
summary: Language models are now widely used to turn recorded facts into media for public consumption, yet evaluation of such output still assumes agreement with the source as its measure of success. In reconstruction, where departing from the source can itself be the goal, this criterion measures the wrong construct: applied as is, it counts intended departures as errors; withheld, it lets real distortion through. We had three model families rewrite 2,000 news articles as summaries and as stories, measured what changed on every axis of the five Ws and how, and asked of each detected distortion whether the assigned perspective warranted it, which set a third of them aside. Time and manner were not lost but replaced, while place and causation lost the expressions that carry them. Accountability distortion behaved otherwise. Barely present in summaries, it rose up to sevenfold in stories, and of those whose direction could be determined, two in three lightened the perpetrator's responsibility. Such distortions survive claim-level fact checking and leave the retelling grammatically cleaner than its source. Where our judges disagreed, three authors relabeling the same cases converged on whether a distortion had occurred but not on whether it was warranted, a boundary contested rather than merely hard to detect. To support work on detecting and reducing them, we release ReTold-2k, a reconstructable corpus with the scoring protocol and per-judge baselines kept unaggregated.(this https URL).

AI.tldr: Shows that source-agreement metrics misjudge model retellings of real news, and that accountability distortion rises up to sevenfold in stories compared with summaries, with two in three directional cases lightening the perpetrator's responsibility; releases the ReTold-2k corpus.
AI.motivation: Evaluation of model output still assumes agreement with the source, which counts intended departures in reconstruction as errors and, if withheld, lets real distortion through.
AI.method: Three model families rewrote 2,000 news articles as summaries and as stories; changes were measured on each of the five Ws, and each detected distortion was judged for whether the assigned perspective warranted it, which set a third of them aside.
AI.result: Time and manner were replaced rather than lost, while place and causation lost the expressions that carry them; accountability distortion was barely present in summaries but rose up to sevenfold in stories, and such distortions survive claim-level fact checking and leave the retelling grammatically cleaner than the source. Three authors agreed on whether a distortion occurred but not on whether it was warranted.
AI.conclusion: The boundary between distortion and warranted reconstruction is contested rather than merely hard to detect, so reconstruction needs evaluation criteria beyond source agreement, and the released corpus with its scoring protocol and unaggregated per-judge baselines supports work on detecting and reducing such distortions.

title: Compile Away Uncertainty: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Programmatic Compilation
summary: Self-evolving agent skills enable AI agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. However, since such skills are typically represented as textual documents and executed through LLM reasoning, even previously learned procedures must be repeatedly interpreted and regenerated, introducing avoidable uncertainty into every execution. In contrast, program execution is deterministic and independently verifiable. Intuitively, transforming well-specified operations into executable programs can reduce reliance on LLM reasoning and, consequently, reduce execution uncertainty. Motivated by this intuition, we introduce SKillCompiler, a self-evolving skill framework that integrates programmatic compilation into the skill evolution process. Specifically, SkillCompiler adopts an executability-aware skill compilation strategy that decomposes skills into fine-grained operations, analyzes their executability, and constructs hybrid skill skeletons that retain LLM reasoning for context-dependent operations while compiling well-specified ones into validated programs. To avoid redundant program synthesis and enable executable knowledge to accumulate across evolving skills, we further design a program asset reuse mechanism that organizes validated programs as reusable assets, retrieves existing implementations whenever applicable, and synthesizes and verifies new programs only when necessary. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks and six model families demonstrate that SkillCompiler consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 32.33\% improvement in task performance.

AI.tldr: Introduces SkillCompiler, a self-evolving agent skill framework that compiles well-specified skill operations into validated programs while keeping LLM reasoning for context-dependent steps, with up to 32.33% task performance improvement over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving skills stored as textual documents must be re-interpreted and regenerated by an LLM at every execution, which introduces avoidable uncertainty even for procedures already learned.
AI.method: An executability-aware compilation strategy decomposes skills into fine-grained operations, analyzes their executability and builds hybrid skill skeletons that compile well-specified operations into programs; a program asset reuse mechanism stores validated programs, retrieves existing implementations and synthesizes and verifies new programs only when necessary.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks and six model families, SkillCompiler consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 32.33% improvement in task performance.
AI.conclusion: Compiling well-specified procedures into deterministic, independently verifiable programs and reusing them across evolving skills reduces execution uncertainty and reliance on LLM reasoning.

title: DEG: Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet for Solving Vehicle Routing Problems
summary: Traditional neural solvers for solving vehicle routing problems (VRPs) often suffer from limited solution diversity, motivating the development of Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet)-based models. However, the effectiveness of these models is frequently constrained by insufficient flow expansion in high-reward regions, limiting their ability to distribute probability across promising solution routes. Deeper exploration could yield superior results. Diffusion models, in contrast, provide stronger structural guidance for exploration. These two paradigms are naturally complementary: GFlowNet can supply edge-level signals for diffusion to embed, while diffusion can guide broader exploration. Leveraging this synergy, we propose Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet (DEG), a novel framework that integrates GFlowNet with a diffusion model to encourage richer flow expansion toward high-reward regions and derive higher-quality solutions. Specifically, DEG exploits GFlowNet's inherent diversity to generate edge-specific backward signals, applies the stochastic noise schedule of diffusion to perturb these signals, and then denoises them within the GFlowNet paradigm. To further improve scalability, we introduce a specialized decoder capable of dynamically adapting to diverse problem scales. Extensive experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets, including instances with up to 10,000 nodes, demonstrate that DEG consistently achieves favorable performance compared to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes DEG, which couples GFlowNet with a diffusion model so that diffusion-guided exploration expands flow toward high-reward regions, achieving favorable results on vehicle routing instances with up to 10,000 nodes.
AI.motivation: GFlowNet-based neural VRP solvers have limited solution diversity because flow expansion in high-reward regions is insufficient, while diffusion models provide stronger structural guidance for exploration.
AI.method: GFlowNet generates edge-specific backward signals, which are perturbed with the stochastic noise schedule of diffusion and then denoised within the GFlowNet paradigm; a specialized decoder adapts dynamically to diverse problem scales.
AI.result: On synthetic and real-world datasets, including instances with up to 10,000 nodes, DEG consistently achieves favorable performance compared with baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining GFlowNet's inherent diversity with diffusion-guided exploration yields higher-quality VRP solutions and better scalability than the evaluated baselines.

title: Category-Anchored Large Language Models for Next POI Recommendation
comment: Accepted by the 43rd IEEE International Conference on Data Engineering (ICDE 2027)
summary: Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination from spatio-temporal check-in data, and serves as the foundation for many location-based services. Recent advances incorporate large language models (LLMs) into this task by textualizing user trajectories to exploit their semantic reasoning ability. However, directly generating POI identifiers with such models is unreliable: POIs are sparse, localized, and long-tailed entities with weak natural-language semantics, which creates a semantic-to-entity gap between high-level mobility intent and concrete POI prediction. To bridge this gap, we propose ANCHOR, a category-anchored framework for semantic-to-entity grounding in next POI recommendation. Specifically, ANCHOR first estimates category-level mobility intent in a compact and stable semantic space, rather than predicting concrete POI entities directly. The inferred intent is then grounded into a candidate set by integrating three complementary sources of mobility evidence: category anchors, historical visit memory, and user preferences. Finally, a history-aware reranker selects the target POI by matching each candidate with the user's historical mobility patterns and current context. Experiments on three real-world check-in datasets show that ANCHOR consistently outperforms representative traditional, structure-enhanced, and LLM-based baselines on the reported metrics. Further analyses validate the effectiveness of semantic-to-entity grounding and show favorable trade-offs among candidate coverage, ranking quality, and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: Proposes ANCHOR, a category-anchored LLM framework for next POI recommendation that first infers category-level mobility intent and then grounds it into concrete POIs, consistently outperforming traditional, structure-enhanced and LLM-based baselines on three check-in datasets.
AI.motivation: Directly generating POI identifiers with LLMs is unreliable because POIs are sparse, localized and long-tailed entities with weak natural-language semantics, which creates a semantic-to-entity gap between high-level mobility intent and concrete POI prediction.
AI.method: Category-level intent is estimated in a compact semantic space and grounded into a candidate set using category anchors, historical visit memory and user preferences; a history-aware reranker then selects the target POI by matching candidates to the user's mobility patterns and current context.
AI.result: On three real-world check-in datasets, ANCHOR consistently outperforms representative traditional, structure-enhanced and LLM-based baselines on the reported metrics, and analyses show favorable trade-offs among candidate coverage, ranking quality and inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-to-entity grounding through category-level intent is an effective way to bridge the gap between mobility intent and POI prediction when LLMs are used for next POI recommendation.

title: Non-Zero Radius: The Missing Component of Neural Networks
summary: Inspired by the analogy between the all-or-none activation of biological neurons and the true-false of logic circuits, McCulloch and Pitts proposed a mathematical model of the biological neuron in 1943 with the aim of simulating logical reasoning. Although Norbert Wiener considered the model overly simplistic at the time, it later became a building block of modern neural networks, including large language models. Despite their remarkable empirical success, however, conventional neural networks remain largely black-box systems and struggle with reliable symbolic reasoning. Viewing vectors as spheres of zero radius, we relax the zero-radius constraint and represent concepts as spheres with non-zero radii. We argue that sphere-based representations can capture additional features of biological cognition, including representing spatial concepts as regions and reasoning through model construction and inspection. Building on sphere embeddings, we introduce Sphere Neural Networks (SphNNs), which use a transition map to achieve symbolic-level Aristotelian syllogistic reasoning without training data, thereby taking an initial step toward the original goal of McCulloch and Pitts. We suggest that the zero-radius constraint may reflect an aspect of the oversimplification identified by Wiener and may limit conventional neural networks' capacity for symbolic-level logical reasoning.

AI.tldr: Introduces Sphere Neural Networks, which represent concepts as spheres with non-zero radii and achieve Aristotelian syllogistic reasoning without training data.
AI.motivation: Conventional neural networks, built on the zero-radius vector model descended from McCulloch and Pitts neurons, remain largely black boxes and struggle with reliable symbolic reasoning.
AI.method: Vectors are relaxed to spheres with non-zero radii so that concepts can be represented as regions, and a transition map over sphere embeddings performs reasoning through model construction and inspection.
AI.result: The abstract reports that SphNNs achieve symbolic-level Aristotelian syllogistic reasoning without training data; no quantitative results are stated.
AI.conclusion: The zero-radius constraint may be an oversimplification that limits the symbolic reasoning capacity of conventional networks, and sphere-based representations are an initial step toward the original goal of McCulloch and Pitts.

title: From Intent to Improvement: Agentic Dataset Search for Better Model Training
summary: Finding training data in million-scale machine learning repositories is a Web search problem where text relevance is not enough. A query couples a semantic training goal with constraints such as task, license, and training stage, and the metadata that would verify them are often missing. Text retrieval ranks dataset cards by similarity but cannot enforce hard constraints or follow the relations that reach a sparsely described dataset. Free-form tool-calling agents are more flexible, but the same model that picks a dataset also declares it a match, and nothing checks that the query's constraints are actually met. Neither approach establishes that the data it returns will improve model training. To address it, we propose AgenticDS, a contract-governed agentic framework in which every language model decision instantiates a typed object before deterministic code consumes it. The framework compiles a query into a typed search plan, executes it through admissible deterministic operators over hybrid retrieval and bounded graph expansion, and verifies the provenance-grounded evidence before accepting a ranking or emitting a typed diagnosis that permits only local repairs. On HuDS-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 queries with 24,908 graded judgments pooled over 15 systems, AgenticDS improves NDCG@10 by 25.7\% over the strongest dense--sparse hybrid and by 18.9\% over a commercial LLM agent. A controlled search-to-train study further shows that the datasets it retrieves give the best downstream accuracy in mathematics, code, and medicine. Code and data are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents AgenticDS, a contract-governed agentic framework for dataset search that enforces typed intermediate decisions and verifies provenance-grounded evidence, improving NDCG@10 by 25.7% over the strongest dense-sparse hybrid on HuDS-Bench.
AI.motivation: Text retrieval cannot enforce hard constraints or follow relations to sparsely described datasets, and free-form tool-calling agents let the same model choose a dataset and declare it a match without any check that the query's constraints are met.
AI.method: Every language model decision instantiates a typed object before deterministic code consumes it; a query is compiled into a typed search plan executed by admissible deterministic operators over hybrid retrieval and bounded graph expansion, and the evidence is verified before a ranking is accepted, with typed diagnoses permitting only local repairs.
AI.result: On HuDS-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 queries with 24,908 graded judgments pooled over 15 systems, AgenticDS improves NDCG@10 by 25.7% over the strongest dense-sparse hybrid and by 18.9% over a commercial LLM agent, and in a controlled search-to-train study its datasets give the best downstream accuracy in mathematics, code and medicine.
AI.conclusion: Constraining LLM agents with typed decisions and deterministic verification yields dataset rankings that are both more accurate and better at producing datasets that improve downstream model training.

title: Emergence of the transformer architecture as the score of entropic laws of random measures
summary: We show that the transformer architecture emerges as the score of last-token laws in a natural statistical model of language, where sentences are empirical measures of tokens, a language is a law on $P(S^d)$, and our prior belief is that sentences carry no structure at all. By the maximum-entropy principle, we select the law closest to this prior in relative entropy among those reproducing an observed sentence-level statistic. We discuss the relevance of the statistic in the posterior interaction between tokens and we build a statistic, able to capture that interaction, with Luce's choice axiom truncated at the lowest relational order. This procedure gives the softmax choice rule, with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter. The query--key matrix is then the Lagrange multiplier of a maximum-entropy problem inside each sentence, and the value matrix the multiplier of the constraint over the language, so that the two are untied. Under the optimal entropic law we then show that a transformer head appears in the score of the last-token law. For ordered sentences, causal masking follows from the masked reference choice rule, and with a next-token cross-moment the score equals one causally masked attention head. We also discuss multi-head attention, weight-tied unembedding, and a heuristic reading of residual blocks as projected Langevin steps.

AI.tldr: Shows that the transformer architecture, including softmax attention and causal masking, emerges as the score of last-token laws under a maximum-entropy model of language in which sentences are empirical measures of tokens and the prior assumes no structure.
AI.motivation: Seeks a first-principles statistical account of why the transformer takes its form, starting from a prior belief that sentences carry no structure at all.
AI.method: A language is a law on P(S^d) selected by maximum entropy relative to the prior, subject to a sentence-level statistic built from Luce's choice axiom truncated at the lowest relational order, which gives the softmax choice rule with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter; the query-key and value matrices arise as distinct Lagrange multipliers, and causal masking follows from a masked reference choice rule.
AI.result: Under the optimal entropic law a transformer head appears in the score of the last-token law; for ordered sentences with a next-token cross-moment the score equals one causally masked attention head, and multi-head attention, weight-tied unembedding and a heuristic reading of residual blocks as projected Langevin steps are also discussed.
AI.conclusion: The transformer head is derived from maximum-entropy principles rather than assumed, which gives a theoretical account of attention, causal masking and the separate roles of the query, key and value matrices.

title: Letting AI Formulate the Research Question: Autonomous Research Agents
summary: Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.

AI.tldr: Studies an AI system that formulates its own research question and carries the study through to a revised paper, reporting five consecutive runs (one pilot and four pre-registered) that each produced a re-computable paper judged at or near workshop level by external AI reviewers.
AI.motivation: Earlier demonstrations such as The AI Scientist had humans choose the research area and select the outputs shown, so whether AI can formulate the research question itself has not been tested in the same way.
AI.method: An off-the-shelf coding agent is given an instruction document and two skills: one that diverges from recent technologies into problems in other fields, screens candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model, and one for peer review in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper.
AI.result: Across 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences setting the research area coincided with large shifts in the candidate questions and chosen papers; after the system was frozen, the pilot and four pre-registered runs all went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper on a laptop with no human research input, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level.
AI.conclusion: Letting an agent formulate the question and review its own work can yield complete, re-computable papers, and the system, the five papers and the records needed for reproduction are released.

title: The Real Cost of Context: Predicting Compute Time and Energy Consumption in LLM Prefill and Decode Phases
summary: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into agentic architectures has substantially increased token consumption, raising concerns about their energy footprint. Yet, estimating the energy consumption of proprietary API-based models remains challenging, and existing approaches focus primarily on generated output tokens while overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows. To address this gap, we systematically profile compute time and energy consumption across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths. Using generalized linear models, we show that decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length. These findings demonstrate that input context becomes a relevant factor for large-context workloads. Furthermore, we show that compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable. Our mapping framework enables precise energy estimation and supports more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.

AI.tldr: Profiles compute time and energy across prefill and decode token lengths and shows that decode scales linearly with output length, prefill scales both linearly and quadratically with input length, and compute time is a reliable proxy for energy.
AI.motivation: Energy estimates for LLMs focus on generated output tokens and are hard to obtain for proprietary API models, overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows.
AI.method: Compute time and energy are systematically profiled across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths and analyzed with generalized linear models, and a mapping framework is built for energy estimation.
AI.result: Decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length; compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable.
AI.conclusion: Input context becomes a relevant energy factor for large-context workloads, and the mapping framework supports precise energy estimation and more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.

title: MoLRSI: A Recursive Self-Improving AI agent for Molecular Discovery
summary: Molecular discovery requires navigating vast combinatorial search spaces while balancing competing biological objectives. AI agents can automate expert-defined molecular design protocols, but automation alone does not address how to optimize workflows for new tasks or improve their development through experience. Here we introduce MoLRSI, an AI agent that combines systematic optimization of workflows and model architectures with persistent cross-task memory to recursively improve its search policy for molecular discovery. Workflow performance, refinement outcomes, and execution feedback guide subsequent searches, allowing the agent to improve both its workflows and its strategy for developing them. We evaluate MoLRSI in two challenging molecular discovery settings that require balancing competing properties. In antibiotic discovery, MoLRSI developed a screening workflow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty, achieving an experimental hit rate of 15.9%, compared with 8.7% for a previous expert-led workflow using the same training data and screening library. In de novo peptide-MHC binder design, MoLRSI developed workflows that jointly consider target binding and specificity, producing eight experimentally validated hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs with preferential binding over tested off-targets while Claude Science completely failed. These findings demonstrate how experience-guided workflow optimization can address competing discovery objectives while improving the search strategies used in subsequent campaigns.

AI.tldr: Introduces MoLRSI, an AI agent that recursively improves its molecular discovery search policy through workflow optimization and persistent cross-task memory, reaching a 15.9% experimental hit rate in antibiotic screening versus 8.7% for an expert-led workflow.
AI.motivation: Automating expert-defined molecular design protocols does not address how to optimize workflows for new tasks or improve their development through experience, and discovery requires balancing competing biological objectives.
AI.method: The agent systematically optimizes workflows and model architectures and keeps persistent cross-task memory, so that workflow performance, refinement outcomes and execution feedback guide subsequent searches.
AI.result: In antibiotic discovery, the MoLRSI screening workflow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty achieved a 15.9% experimental hit rate versus 8.7% for a previous expert-led workflow using the same training data and screening library; in de novo peptide-MHC binder design it produced eight experimentally validated hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs with preferential binding over tested off-targets, while Claude Science completely failed.
AI.conclusion: Experience-guided workflow optimization can address competing discovery objectives and improve the search strategies used in subsequent campaigns.

title: Bank-World: A Benchmark for Evaluating Agents on Banking Workflows
comment: 43 pages, 3 figures, including appendices. Ancillary files contain the task ID mapping, reward specifications, and single-turn check-authority mapping
summary: Bank-World is a benchmark of 50 banking tasks across two simulated institutions. Completing banking work requires more than producing the right calculation: agents must reconcile records, obtain permission, execute transactions, and keep instructions and status reports consistent as circumstances change. Bank-World tests these requirements through single-turn assignments and multi-turn interactions with simulated employees who supply information, approve actions, and revise instructions. Grading combines executable checks of recorded actions and state with model judgments of task requirements, including whether valid alternative solutions satisfy them. Across 1,600 attempts by four models, we find that correct decisions often fail to become completed work. Agents charge fees twice, distribute the correct total in incorrect amounts among the recipients, and execute payments while approval is pending. Their strengths also differ: Sol leads single-turn completion, Opus has the highest observed multi-turn completion rate, and Grok succeeds across more multi-turn tasks but less consistently. Bank-World makes these differences inspectable through task-level results and worked examples connecting source evidence, agent decisions, and simulated consequences. We retain the task environments, executable graders, and full trajectories privately to reduce contamination and preserve the benchmark for future evaluations.

AI.tldr: Introduces Bank-World, a benchmark of 50 banking tasks across two simulated institutions, and finds that correct decisions often fail to become completed work, with agents charging fees twice and executing payments while approval is pending.
AI.motivation: Banking work requires more than a correct calculation: agents must reconcile records, obtain permission, execute transactions and keep instructions and status reports consistent as circumstances change.
AI.method: Tasks combine single-turn assignments with multi-turn interactions with simulated employees who supply information, approve actions and revise instructions; grading combines executable checks of recorded actions and state with model judgments of task requirements, including whether valid alternative solutions satisfy them.
AI.result: Across 1,600 attempts by four models, agents charged fees twice, distributed the correct total in incorrect amounts among recipients and executed payments while approval was pending; Sol leads single-turn completion, Opus has the highest observed multi-turn completion rate, and Grok succeeds across more multi-turn tasks but less consistently.
AI.conclusion: Task-level results and worked examples make these model differences inspectable, and private retention of the environments, executable graders and trajectories aims to reduce contamination and preserve the benchmark.

title: PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines?
summary: Before AI can be trusted to discover new science, it should be able to reproduce what science already knows. Reproduction provides a rigorous checkpoint for an AI scientist: the target claim is known, yet recovering it still requires translating an incomplete scientific description into an executable experiment and producing evidence that can be independently verified. Existing research-reproduction benchmarks largely focus on AI and machine learning, where experiments share relatively homogeneous software stacks. Extending this capability across scientific disciplines introduces a different challenge: agents must operate domain-specific scientific software, make physical and numerical choices, diagnose long-running computations, and distinguish valid evidence from merely plausible outputs. We introduce PAPERBENCHX, a benchmark of 93 expert-constructed paper-reproduction tasks spanning 12 research areas across electromagnetics, photonics, chemistry, materials science, biology, and robotics. Each task provides the source paper, a public task specification, and a domain-native scientific environment involving specialized scientific software. Agents must reconstruct a key experiment, execute and diagnose it, and deliver a runnable workflow that supports the target scientific claim. To evaluate scientific validity rather than surface-level agreement, we replay every submission from scratch and score only regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria. Across 10 frontier agent configurations, the best configuration fully reproduces only 14% tasks under the 90% threshold. Meanwhile, mean rubric scores range from 27.53% to 59.08%, indicating that substantial partial progress rarely translates into complete scientific reproduction. These results reveal a large gap between paper understanding and reliably producing reproducible scientific evidence.

AI.tldr: Introduces PAPERBENCHX, 93 expert-constructed paper-reproduction tasks across 12 research areas, and finds that the best of 10 frontier agent configurations fully reproduces only 14% of tasks under a 90% threshold.
AI.motivation: Existing reproduction benchmarks focus on AI and machine learning with relatively homogeneous software stacks, whereas extending AI scientist evaluation to other disciplines requires domain-specific scientific software, physical and numerical choices, and validation of evidence.
AI.method: Each task provides the source paper, a public task specification and a domain-native scientific environment; agents reconstruct a key experiment, execute and diagnose it, and deliver a runnable workflow, and every submission is replayed from scratch and scored only on regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria.
AI.result: The best configuration fully reproduces only 14% of tasks under the 90% threshold, and mean rubric scores range from 27.53% to 59.08% across the 10 configurations, so substantial partial progress rarely becomes complete reproduction.
AI.conclusion: A large gap remains between understanding a paper and reliably producing reproducible scientific evidence across disciplines such as electromagnetics, chemistry, biology and robotics.

title: Finding Is Not Returning, Returning Is Not Reconstructing: A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation of Agent Social Re-entry
summary: As Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in persistent social environments, understanding their long-term social interaction capabilities becomes increasingly important. While existing research has advanced long-term memory and conversational context retrieval, less attention has been paid to whether agents can autonomously re-engage with previously inactive conversations. In particular, remembering a past interaction does not necessarily mean that an agent can identify when to revisit it, decide to return, or reconstruct the context needed for a coherent continuation. To investigate this gap, we introduce agent social re-entry as a multi- dimensional evaluation problem, distinguishing three complementary capabilities: Finding, Returning, and Reconstructing. We develop a shared-snapshot evaluation framework that measures these dimensions independently, allowing us to examine how conversational resurfacing and persistent memory relate to different aspects of social re-entry. Evaluations across six LLM configurations show that resurfacing substantially improves target conversation identification, while persistent memory is associated with higher rates of autonomous target-directed replying. However, neither improvement is accompanied by consistent gains in contextual reconstruction. These results highlight the distinction between accessing previous conversations, choosing to re-engage, and maintaining conversational continuity. Our framework provides a way to evaluate these capabilities separately rather than relying on memory retrieval or conversational response quality alone.

AI.tldr: Introduces a multi-dimensional evaluation of LLM agent social re-entry, separating Finding, Returning and Reconstructing, and shows that resurfacing and persistent memory improve identification and replying but not contextual reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Existing work addresses long-term memory and conversational context retrieval, but not whether agents can autonomously re-engage with previously inactive conversations, identify when to revisit them and reconstruct the context needed for coherent continuation.
AI.method: A shared-snapshot evaluation framework measures Finding, Returning and Reconstructing independently, examining how conversational resurfacing and persistent memory relate to each dimension.
AI.result: Across six LLM configurations, resurfacing substantially improves target conversation identification and persistent memory is associated with higher rates of autonomous target-directed replying, but neither yields consistent gains in contextual reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Accessing previous conversations, choosing to re-engage and maintaining conversational continuity are distinct capabilities, so they should be evaluated separately rather than through memory retrieval or response quality alone.

title: Long-Term Agent Memory through Complementary Curation and Consolidation
summary: Long-horizon dialogue agents require effective memory systems to recall facts, events, and relationships from interaction histories. In this work, we propose a hybrid-memory architecture comprising episodic memories and structured relational memories and a consolidation mechanism which preserves efficiency. We conduct an empirical study across two benchmarks: LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S. Our experiments demonstrate that the two memory types are consistently complementary, combining both outperform state-of-the-art memory frameworks and achieves 90.2% accuracy on LoCoMo and 85.5% on LongMemEval-S.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hybrid memory architecture for long-horizon dialogue agents that combines episodic and structured relational memories with a consolidation mechanism, reaching 90.2% accuracy on LoCoMo and 85.5% on LongMemEval-S.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon dialogue agents need effective memory systems that recall facts, events and relationships from interaction histories while remaining efficient.
AI.method: A hybrid-memory architecture comprising episodic memories and structured relational memories, together with a consolidation mechanism that preserves efficiency.
AI.result: On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S the two memory types are consistently complementary, and combining them outperforms state-of-the-art memory frameworks, achieving 90.2% accuracy on LoCoMo and 85.5% on LongMemEval-S.
AI.conclusion: Episodic and relational memories are complementary, and their combination with consolidation is an effective memory design for long-horizon dialogue agents.

title: Revisiting Over-refusal in Safety-aligned Large Language Models: A Representation and Optimization Perspective
summary: Over-refusal is a critical side effect of safety alignment in large language models (LLMs), causing harmless but superficially risky queries to be mistakenly rejected. Despite the effectiveness of existing mitigation methods, why safety-aligned LLMs may still reject harmless queries under correct safety supervision remains insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we analyze over-refusal through the lens of representation and optimization. We make two observations: 1) the representations of harmful and over-refusal samples are visually distinguishable at certain intermediate layers but increasingly overlap in deeper layers; and 2) harmful-sample gradients exhibit high intra-class similarity and concentrate in a low-rank subspace. Moreover, they are more strongly aligned with refusal-target gradients than with correct helpful-target gradients on over-refusal prompts. This imbalanced gradient coupling can bias over-refusal samples toward refusal, while the reduced apparent representational separation in deeper layers may make it more difficult for the model to maintain a clear boundary between harmful and over-refusal samples. To this end, we propose GOAL (Gradient Orthogonalization with contrAstive Learning), a safety-alignment framework for mitigating over-refusal. Specifically, GOAL consists of two components: 1) to prevent imbalanced gradient coupling from biasing the optimization of over-refusal samples toward refusal, we orthogonalize over-refusal gradients against the low-rank refusal subspace extracted from harmful gradients; and 2) to explicitly enhance the separation between harmful and over-refusal representations, we introduce a contrastive learning objective. Extensive experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that GOAL effectively mitigates over-refusal while preserving safety performance and general capabilities.

AI.tldr: Proposes GOAL, a safety-alignment framework that mitigates over-refusal in LLMs by orthogonalizing over-refusal gradients against the refusal subspace and adding a contrastive objective, while preserving safety and general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Safety-aligned LLMs still reject harmless queries even under correct safety supervision, and the reasons for this are insufficiently understood.
AI.method: Representation and gradient analysis shows that harmful and over-refusal samples overlap more in deeper layers and that harmful gradients are low-rank and coupled with refusal-target gradients; GOAL orthogonalizes over-refusal gradients against a low-rank refusal subspace extracted from harmful gradients and adds a contrastive learning objective that separates harmful and over-refusal representations.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show that GOAL effectively mitigates over-refusal while preserving safety performance and general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Imbalanced gradient coupling biases over-refusal samples toward refusal, and correcting that coupling together with enhancing representation separation offers an effective remedy.

title: EvoTeam: Multi-Agent Collaboration via Evolving Teams
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on collaboration among specialized agents to solve complex tasks. Existing methods improve MAS by refining the prompts, skills, and execution strategies of individual agents based on task feedback. However, improving individual agents does not necessarily lead to better team collaboration. Recent studies have therefore extended evolution to the collaboration level, using collective execution experience to adjust team organization, and inter-agent interactions. Nevertheless, evolving collaboration across heterogeneous tasks remains challenging, as existing approaches often constrain team reorganization within a shared structure and reuse interaction rules across incompatible team contexts. In this paper, we propose EvoTeam, a collaboration-centric evolution framework that jointly evolves team organization, interaction rules, and individual agent skills through execution experience. It maintains a library of reusable teams, selecting or creating agent teams and guiding collaboration through team-specific interaction rules. Collaboration experience accumulates within compatible team contexts, while individual skills remain reusable across teams. Experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes EvoTeam, a collaboration-centric framework that jointly evolves team organization, team-specific interaction rules and individual agent skills for LLM multi-agent systems, with experiments on four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Improving individual agents does not necessarily improve team collaboration, and existing collaboration-level evolution constrains team reorganization to a shared structure and reuses interaction rules across incompatible team contexts.
AI.method: A library of reusable teams is maintained; teams are selected or created for each task and collaboration is guided by team-specific interaction rules, so collaboration experience accumulates within compatible team contexts while individual skills remain reusable across teams.
AI.result: Experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of EvoTeam; the abstract reports no quantitative figures.
AI.conclusion: Evolving teams and their interaction rules alongside individual skills is presented as a way to improve collaboration across heterogeneous tasks.

title: AegisFlow: Training-Free Non-Myopic Path-Safe Guided Flow Matching
summary: Pretrained generative models, such as diffusion and flow matching models, have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in synthesizing high-quality data. However, steering their generative trajectories to satisfy strict constraints--such as identity preservation in image editing or obstacle avoidance in robotics--remains fundamentally challenging. While recent training-free guidance methods enforce path-safety, they rely heavily on min-norm controllers that only account for immediate constraint satisfaction. These myopic approaches often yield suboptimal trajectories that hover dangerously close to the boundary, severely restricting the model's ability to optimize toward its target. In this paper, we propose AegisFlow, a training-free, non-myopic path-safe guidance framework that recasts guided generation as a safety-critical optimal control problem with global scope. By integrating a time-varying barrier function directly into the global cost functional, AegisFlow naturally enforces constraints along the entire generative path. To compute the global optimal control, we derive a tractable, mathematically grounded approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that AegisFlow outperforms state-of-the-art methods across text-guided image manipulation and robotic planning, establishing a significantly better trade-off between target alignment and constraint satisfaction. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes AegisFlow, a training-free guidance method for diffusion and flow matching models that enforces path-safety constraints non-myopically through a time-varying barrier in a global optimal control formulation, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on image manipulation and robotic planning.
AI.motivation: Steering pretrained generative trajectories to satisfy strict constraints is difficult, and existing training-free guidance relies on min-norm controllers that account only for immediate constraint satisfaction, yielding trajectories that hover close to the boundary.
AI.method: Guided generation is recast as a safety-critical optimal control problem with global scope; a time-varying barrier function is integrated into the global cost functional, and a tractable approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation is derived to compute the global optimal control.
AI.result: Experiments on text-guided image manipulation and robotic planning show that AegisFlow outperforms state-of-the-art methods and establishes a better trade-off between target alignment and constraint satisfaction.
