Consequently, populations of several models, including those with up to 7B parameters, reliably compound small local drifts to reach confident agreement on objectively false claims regardless of their network structure. Our results prove that classical graph-theoretic metrics are inadequate for LLM populations, highlighting a profound deployment risk where multi-agent deliberation predictably saturates in collective delusion.

AI.tldr: Shows that the assumptions of classical distributed consensus fail for LLM populations: LLMs update outside the convex hull of observed opinions with negative weights, so network topology explains almost none of whether populations converge on false claims.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM networks are widely deployed, yet classical consensus theory predicts their convergence from network topology under the assumptions of convex updates, conserved population means and content-independent weights, which may not hold for LLMs.
AI.method: Continuous credence is extracted deterministically from token-level probabilities across eight instruction-tuned models and 73,080 controlled exchanges to measure the empirical LLM update operator, which is then scaled to simulations of 10,000 agents.
AI.result: LLMs systematically update outside the hull of observed opinions and show active repulsion with negative weights. Algebraic connectivity explains almost none of the final outcome variance, and population dynamics are governed by the model's internal update bias and message framing. Populations of several models, including models with up to 7B parameters, reach confident agreement on objectively false claims regardless of network structure.
AI.conclusion: Classical graph-theoretic metrics are inadequate for LLM populations, and multi-agent deliberation can predictably saturate in collective delusion, which is a deployment risk.

title: The Coordination Tax and the Heterogeneity Dividend: Break-Even Conditions for Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
summary: Multi-agent LLM pipelines built on interoperability protocols such as the Open Floor Protocol (OFP) or A2A are usually justified on capability grounds, with their runtime cost treated as an overhead of unknown size. Comparing such a pipeline with one model call is underspecified, because a pipeline can give each role a different model. We give a closed-form model that sets the coordination tax (decomposition overhead plus per-handoff protocol cost) against the heterogeneity dividend from routing work to a cheaper model, with a break-even threshold and a feasibility bound, $\alpha < 1/r$, and measure every term, with OFP as the protocol under test, on 135 HumanEval and ClassEval tasks in 2430 runs of six architectures with Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. The protocol adds 7.2 ms per handoff, 0.11% of pipeline wall time. Decomposition does not pay on these tasks: a planner-coder-reviewer pipeline costs 3.22x as much as a single strong call, takes 3.24x as long, and solves no more tasks. Moving planner and reviewer to the cheap model cuts the pipeline's cost to 0.39x but changes pass@1 by -6.7 points, leaving it dearer, slower and less accurate than the single call, and the break-even forecast misses by -19% because the cheap roles inflate token volume. The saving lies in choosing a model per task instead: an oracle choice between the two single calls solves 94.3% of runs at half the strong call's cost per solved task.

AI.tldr: Gives a closed-form break-even model for multi-agent LLM pipelines and finds that decomposition does not pay on HumanEval and ClassEval tasks, while choosing a model per task saves cost.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent pipelines built on interoperability protocols such as OFP or A2A are justified on capability grounds with their runtime cost treated as an overhead of unknown size, and comparing them with one model call is underspecified because each role can use a different model.
AI.method: A closed-form model sets the coordination tax (decomposition overhead plus per-handoff protocol cost) against the heterogeneity dividend from routing work to a cheaper model, with a break-even threshold and a feasibility bound alpha < 1/r. Six architectures with Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 were run on 135 HumanEval and ClassEval tasks in 2430 runs, with OFP as the protocol under test.
AI.result: The protocol adds 7.2 ms per handoff, 0.11% of pipeline wall time. A planner-coder-reviewer pipeline costs 3.22x as much as a single strong call, takes 3.24x as long and solves no more tasks. Moving planner and reviewer to the cheap model cuts the cost to 0.39x but changes pass@1 by -6.7 points, and the break-even forecast misses by -19%. An oracle choice between the two single calls solves 94.3% of runs at half the strong call's cost per solved task.
AI.conclusion: On these tasks the coordination tax outweighs the heterogeneity dividend, and the saving lies in choosing a model per task rather than decomposing the work.

title: Search-Guided Reasoning Trace Curation for Verilog Generation
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have improved Verilog generation. However, most training pipelines distill natural-language reasoning traces whose intermediate design decisions are weakly structured and are primarily selected according to the correctness of the final generated RTL. We present MCTS-SFT, a verifier-guided framework for curating reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Verilog generation models. MCTS-SFT formulates trace construction as search over intermediate reasoning states and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to propagate functional feedback from complete Verilog rollouts to earlier design decisions. Within this framework, we introduce Plan-MCTS, which searches over compact hardware-design plans that explicitly represent interfaces, timing, state, behavior, and update rules. We further study plan-preserving supervision, in which the searched structured state is retained as part of the downstream SFT target. Our experiments find that Plan-MCTS achieves the highest functional trace yield, with 84.2% correct traces compared with 81.9% for one-shot structured planning and 82.0% for unguided tree exploration. For identical Plan-MCTS trajectories and Verilog outputs, retaining the explicit searched plan during SFT raises pass@10 from 52.56% to 57.7%, demonstrating that the representation of intermediate design decisions materially affects downstream learning. In a separate 6,000-trace study, MCTS-curated supervision improves pass@10 over full-response chain-of-thought distillation by up to 3.7 points while reducing downstream generation length by approximately 50% on VerilogEval-v2. These results demonstrate that structured hardware planning, verifier-guided search, and explicit intermediate-state supervision provide complementary mechanisms for constructing more effective and token-efficient training data for Verilog generation.

AI.tldr: Presents MCTS-SFT, which uses Monte Carlo Tree Search over compact hardware-design plans to curate reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning of Verilog generation models, improving trace yield and token efficiency.
AI.motivation: Training pipelines for Verilog generation distill natural-language reasoning traces whose intermediate design decisions are weakly structured and are selected mainly by the correctness of the final RTL.
AI.method: MCTS propagates functional feedback from complete Verilog rollouts to earlier design decisions. Plan-MCTS searches over plans that explicitly represent interfaces, timing, state, behavior and update rules, and plan-preserving supervision keeps the searched plan in the SFT target.
AI.result: Plan-MCTS reaches 84.2% correct traces, compared with 81.9% for one-shot structured planning and 82.0% for unguided tree exploration. Retaining the explicit searched plan during SFT raises pass@10 from 52.56% to 57.7%. In a 6,000-trace study, MCTS-curated supervision improves pass@10 over full-response chain-of-thought distillation by up to 3.7 points and cuts generation length by about 50% on VerilogEval-v2.
AI.conclusion: Structured hardware planning, verifier-guided search and explicit intermediate-state supervision together yield more effective and token-efficient training data for Verilog generation.

title: FVH-Bench: Evaluating Image Generator Safety Beyond Overtly Harmful Imagery
summary: Modern image generators can produce complex visual artifacts, including diagrams, interfaces, and records that combine text, graphics, and layout to convey detailed information. They may refuse requests for overtly harmful imagery yet still generate artifacts that guide dangerous actions or support deception. We call the risk arising from what such images enable, rather than only what they depict, functional visual harm (FVH). Existing safety benchmarks focus largely on overtly harmful content, such as pornography and graphic violence, leaving image generators' safety alignment against FVH insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce FVH-Bench, comprising 669 prompts across five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains. The 11 evaluated image generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently generate artifacts that fulfill the targeted harmful functions. High scores for target harm realization and harmful artifact usability further indicate that these outputs can support the intended harmful purposes. A further analysis finds that existing safety detectors also provide limited coverage of FVH, indicating gaps in their ability to recognize harmful visual functions. Together, these findings show that evaluating image-generator safety alignment requires considering not only what images depict, but also what they may enable.

AI.tldr: Introduces FVH-Bench, 669 prompts across five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains, and shows that eleven image generators rarely refuse requests whose outputs enable harm even when the images do not depict overtly harmful content.
AI.motivation: Safety benchmarks focus on overtly harmful imagery such as pornography and graphic violence, leaving generators' alignment against functional visual harm, where images such as diagrams, interfaces or records guide dangerous actions or support deception, insufficiently evaluated.
AI.method: FVH-Bench comprises 669 prompts across five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains, used to evaluate 11 image generators and existing safety detectors. Outputs are assessed for target harm realization and harmful artifact usability.
AI.result: The generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently produce artifacts that fulfill the targeted harmful functions, with high scores for target harm realization and harmful artifact usability. Existing safety detectors provide limited coverage of functional visual harm.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating image-generator safety requires considering what images may enable as well as what they depict, and current safety detectors have gaps in recognizing harmful visual functions.

title: When Skills Tell Agents Not to Ask: A Large-Scale Study of Oversight Directives in Agent Skills
summary: Agent skills, reusable instruction packages centred on a this http URL file, extend AI agents on demand, and a single line in a widely copied skill reaches every agent that loads it. Some lines are oversight-loosening directives: they tell the agent to proceed without approval, to bypass checks with --no-verify, or to keep working without checking in. Although such directives can remove a checkpoint from every agent that loads them, no prior work has examined them. We present the first large-scale study of oversight-loosening directives, analyzing 1.53 million English skills from GitSkills. We split skills into units (sentences, bullets, table cells, and code lines), develop a codebook that labels oversight directives by polarity, mechanism, and scope, label 2,097 units by hand, and train a detector to scale the analysis. Our results show that about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills) contains a loosening directive. These directives most often loosen oversight through permission flags, and most of them (70.1%) apply unconditionally rather than only in specific contexts such as CI. Compared with skills that have the same amount of oversight language, skills that run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing a loosening directive, an association that holds across all our robustness checks, and they do not compensate with more tightening. Loosening spreads through a few upstream skills rather than through edits by their adopters: 2.4% of the skill families that carry loosening account for half of all copies of loosening-carrying skills, and 1.1% of distinct loosening units for half of all loosening occurrences. Open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of loosening directives, with a precision below 0.4, while the LLM behind them, prompted with our codebook instead, catches 61% at a precision of 0.71.

AI.tldr: A large-scale study of 1.53 million English agent skills finds that about one in seventeen contains an oversight-loosening directive, such as proceeding without approval or bypassing checks, and that open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of them.
AI.motivation: A single line in a widely copied skill reaches every agent that loads it, and oversight-loosening directives can remove a checkpoint from all of those agents, yet no prior work has examined them.
AI.method: Skills are split into units (sentences, bullets, table cells and code lines). A codebook labels oversight directives by polarity, mechanism and scope, 2,097 units are labeled by hand, and a detector is trained to scale the analysis.
AI.result: About 88,000 skills contain a loosening directive, most often through permission flags, and 70.1% of these apply unconditionally. Skills that run shell code, install packages or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing one. 2.4% of skill families carrying loosening account for half of all copies of loosening-carrying skills. Open-source scanners catch at most 46% of directives with precision below 0.4, while an LLM prompted with the codebook catches 61% at precision 0.71.
AI.conclusion: Loosening spreads mainly through a few upstream skills rather than through edits by adopters, and codebook-guided LLM detection outperforms the open-source scanners.

title: Poisoned Skills: Propagating Jailbreaks Through Agent Markdown Files
summary: Modern agent frameworks allow users to provide Markdown files containing system prompts, tool descriptions, and skill definitions (e.g., this http URL), which are incorporated into the agent's context during initialization. In this work, we investigate whether this configuration mechanism can also serve as an injection channel: can a jailbreak embedded in a Markdown skill file propagate through an agent and induce prohibited behavior? To answer this question, we construct a LangChain-based question-answering agent whose system prompt is assembled from a user-provided Markdown file. We embed a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack and evaluate its effectiveness across seven contemporary open-weight models using 270 forbidden questions spanning nine harm categories. Under a benign system prompt, the models exhibit near-complete refusal behavior, with a mean attack success rate (ASR) of just 0.5%. In contrast, the injected skill file raises the mean ASR to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models. We further evaluate two payload obfuscation strategies: an invisible zero-width character-based stealth payload and a phonetic payload based on grapheme-to-phoneme transformations. Neither outperforms the plain-text injection; notably, the phonetic variant reduces mean ASR to 30%. These findings identify Markdown skill files as an underexplored attack surface for AI agents and suggest that vulnerability to configuration-based jailbreaks depends more strongly on the underlying model than on the specific payload obfuscation technique.

AI.tldr: Shows that a jailbreak embedded in a Markdown skill file propagates into an agent's system prompt and raises mean attack success rate from 0.5% to 45% across seven open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Agent frameworks incorporate user-provided Markdown files into the agent's context at initialization, so this configuration mechanism may also serve as an injection channel for jailbreaks.
AI.method: A LangChain-based question-answering agent assembles its system prompt from a user-provided Markdown file. A jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack is embedded and evaluated on seven open-weight models using 270 forbidden questions in nine harm categories. Zero-width character and grapheme-to-phoneme payload obfuscations are compared with plain-text injection.
AI.result: Under a benign system prompt the mean attack success rate (ASR) is 0.5%. The injected skill file raises the mean ASR to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models. Neither obfuscation strategy outperforms plain-text injection, and the phonetic variant reduces the mean ASR to 30%.
AI.conclusion: Markdown skill files are an underexplored attack surface for AI agents, and vulnerability depends more strongly on the underlying model than on the payload obfuscation technique.

title: EUReCA: End-to-End Unified CBCT Reconstruction Across Clinical Acquisitions
summary: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is widely used for image-guided radiotherapy, but reducing the number of projections to lower dose and scan time makes reconstruction increasingly ill-posed. We present EUReCA (End-to-end Unified REconstruction across Clinical Acquisitions), a geometry-aware feed-forward model for variable-view clinical linac CBCT. For a given acquisition trajectory, EUReCA accepts 8-100 projections with a single set of weights, without view-count-specific retraining; the same architecture and training recipe extend unchanged to other clinical trajectories. It combines learned projection features with an in-frame Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstruction. The model encodes each projection with a shared multiscale backbone, back-projects features into multiresolution 3D grids using the acquisition geometry, aggregates variable numbers of views at fixed computational cost, and refines the volume with a global 3D transformer and multilevel decoder. On simulated data, EUReCA achieved 29.9-33.2 dB PSNR with 10-100 views and outperformed all applicable feed-forward baselines; it also exceeded iterative optimization-based methods while running orders of magnitude faster. On 15 measured patient CBCT scans evaluated against vendor reconstructions, EUReCA achieved the best performance at every tested view count. These results suggest that geometry-aware, measurement-anchored feed-forward reconstruction can provide a practical and flexible foundation for variable-view linac CBCT.

AI.tldr: Presents EUReCA, a geometry-aware feed-forward model that reconstructs CBCT volumes from 8 to 100 projections with a single set of weights, outperforming feed-forward baselines and iterative methods on simulated data and vendor reconstructions on patient scans.
AI.motivation: Reducing the number of projections to lower dose and scan time makes CBCT reconstruction for image-guided radiotherapy increasingly ill-posed.
AI.method: A shared multiscale backbone encodes each projection, and features are back-projected into multiresolution 3D grids using the acquisition geometry. Variable numbers of views are aggregated at fixed computational cost, and a global 3D transformer with a multilevel decoder refines the volume. The model combines learned projection features with an in-frame FDK reconstruction and needs no view-count-specific retraining.
AI.result: On simulated data EUReCA achieves 29.9-33.2 dB PSNR with 10-100 views, outperforming all applicable feed-forward baselines and exceeding iterative optimization-based methods, which run orders of magnitude slower. On 15 measured patient CBCT scans evaluated against vendor reconstructions, it achieves the best performance at every tested view count.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware, measurement-anchored feed-forward reconstruction can provide a practical and flexible foundation for variable-view linac CBCT.

title: Convex Potential Learning for Optimal Transport Between Medical Images
summary: Computing optimal transport maps between medical images plays a fundamental role in morphological analysis. However, existing methods are either difficult to scale to large 3D medical images or rely on regularized formulations that provide only approximate transport maps. To improve the accuracy of downstream medical image analysis, we propose a novel approach for estimating optimal transport maps by parameterizing the convex potential function. By construction, the resulting transport map is guaranteed to be curl-free, consistent with Brenier's theorem. We evaluate the proposed method on both 2D and 3D medical imaging datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves lower transport estimation errors and produces higher-quality image reconstructions than existing methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes estimating optimal transport maps between medical images by parameterizing a convex potential function, which makes the resulting transport map curl-free and consistent with Brenier's theorem.
AI.motivation: Existing methods either are difficult to scale to large 3D medical images or rely on regularized formulations that give only approximate transport maps, limiting accuracy in downstream medical image analysis.
AI.method: The optimal transport map is estimated by parameterizing the convex potential function, so the map is guaranteed to be curl-free by construction.
AI.result: On 2D and 3D medical imaging datasets the approach achieves lower transport estimation errors and produces higher-quality image reconstructions than existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Convex potential learning gives more accurate optimal transport maps between medical images, which can improve morphological analysis.

title: Effects of Deep Learning Architecture and Pretraining on Automated Vocal Fold Segmentation in Ex Vivo High-Speed Phonation Images
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) intraglottal particle image velocimetry (PIV) of ex vivo phonation experiments quantifies vocal fold medial surface dynamics and the intraglottal flow field. However, it relies on manual segmentation because residual glare, low tissue-to-flow contrast, and tracer-particle speckle obscure the vocal fold boundaries. This study assessed how deep learning architecture and ImageNet pretraining affect automated vocal fold segmentation in these high-speed images. Four established architectures from three categories were benchmarked: the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based UNet and UNet++, the hybrid CNN-transformer-based TransUNet, and the pure transformer-based Swin-UNet, the latter two trained from scratch and from ImageNet-pretrained weights. Using 16,344 expert-annotated images from 227 phonation trials of excised canine larynges, the six pipelines were trained with five seeds under a standardized protocol and compared on 50 held-out test trials using trial-level Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. Mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) spanned only 0.9734 to 0.9764, so the pipelines differed mainly in boundary fidelity. Pretraining significantly improved the boundary F1 score (BF1) and 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of the TransUNet and Swin-UNet, about four times more for the Swin-UNet. Once pretrained, the two performed similarly, although the Swin-UNet has only about a quarter of the trainable parameters. Without pretraining, the TransUNet had a significantly higher BF1 and a lower HD95 than both CNN-based pipelines and about half their share of images with HD95 > 50 pixels. To our knowledge, this is the first study to apply deep learning to vocal fold segmentation in 2D intraglottal PIV, and it offers a reference framework for segmenting experimental flow-visualization images with noisy optical conditions or highly deformable objects.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks four deep learning architectures for automated vocal fold segmentation in ex vivo high-speed phonation images, finding that ImageNet pretraining mainly improves boundary fidelity rather than overlap.
AI.motivation: 2D intraglottal particle image velocimetry (PIV) of ex vivo phonation relies on manual vocal fold segmentation, because residual glare, low tissue-to-flow contrast and tracer-particle speckle obscure the boundaries.
AI.method: UNet, UNet++, TransUNet and Swin-UNet are compared, with TransUNet and Swin-UNet trained both from scratch and from ImageNet-pretrained weights. Six pipelines were trained with five seeds on 16,344 expert-annotated images from 227 phonation trials of excised canine larynges, and compared on 50 held-out test trials using trial-level Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction.
AI.result: Mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) spans only 0.9734 to 0.9764. Pretraining significantly improves boundary F1 (BF1) and 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of TransUNet and Swin-UNet, about four times more for Swin-UNet. Once pretrained, the two perform similarly, although Swin-UNet has about a quarter of the trainable parameters. Without pretraining, TransUNet has significantly higher BF1 and lower HD95 than both CNN-based pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining matters mainly for boundary fidelity, and the study offers a reference framework for segmenting experimental flow-visualization images with noisy optical conditions or highly deformable objects.

title: PairCLIP-SWA: Similarity-Guided Balancing and Stochastic Weight Averaging for Generalized Deepfake Image Detection with OpenCLIP
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 12 tables. Code and experiment outputs: this https URL
summary: Deepfake detectors are almost always deployed as the single checkpoint that scored best on a validation split, yet the reliability of that choice is rarely measured. We measure it with PairCLIP-SWA, a single-backbone detector that adapts an OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 visual tower by progressive block unfreezing on a class-balanced corpus built by CLIP-similarity-guided one-to-one subsampling, and averages the fine-tuning trajectory in weight space. Trained in-domain on the IEEE SP Cup 2025 (DF-Wild-Cup) benchmark under the same protocol as the strongest published three-backbone ensemble, the weight-averaged detector reaches 97.04% accuracy, 98.64% AU-ROC and a 4.07% equal error rate, against 94.46%, 97.60% and 5.00%. Its training log shows why averaging matters: over the averaged epochs the non-averaged checkpoint swings across 5.34 points of validation accuracy while its validation loss more than doubles, whereas the average is never worse and is up to 5.99 points better. On an OpenForensics-derived benchmark the same instability becomes a misranking: the checkpoint that validation accuracy selects (98.43%) scores 88.85% on a disjoint 10,905-image test partition, rejecting 21.1% of genuine photographs, while the terminal average, ranked last on validation, scores 94.76%. A study of twenty-two in-house configurations on the identical DF-Wild-Cup split, including preprocessing ablations, shows that CLIP pre-training rather than ensembling drives accuracy, that secondary face cropping costs about 34 points, and that frequency-domain inputs transfer poorly. We recommend per-class selection criteria measured off the early-stopping split.

AI.tldr: Proposes PairCLIP-SWA, an OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 deepfake detector using CLIP-similarity-guided balancing and stochastic weight averaging, which reaches 97.04% accuracy on DF-Wild-Cup and shows that selecting a single checkpoint by validation accuracy is unreliable.
AI.motivation: Deepfake detectors are usually deployed as the single checkpoint that scored best on a validation split, yet the reliability of that choice is rarely measured.
AI.method: A single-backbone detector adapts an OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 visual tower by progressive block unfreezing on a class-balanced corpus built by CLIP-similarity-guided one-to-one subsampling, and averages the fine-tuning trajectory in weight space.
AI.result: On the IEEE SP Cup 2025 (DF-Wild-Cup) benchmark the weight-averaged detector reaches 97.04% accuracy, 98.64% AU-ROC and 4.07% equal error rate, against 94.46%, 97.60% and 5.00% for the strongest published three-backbone ensemble. Non-averaged checkpoints swing across 5.34 points of validation accuracy. On an OpenForensics-derived benchmark, the checkpoint chosen by validation accuracy (98.43%) scores 88.85% on a disjoint 10,905-image test partition, while the terminal average scores 94.76%. CLIP pre-training rather than ensembling drives accuracy, and secondary face cropping costs about 34 points.
AI.conclusion: Per-class selection criteria measured off the early-stopping split are recommended over choosing a checkpoint by validation accuracy alone.

title: Intersectional Invariant Learning for Fair Deepfake Detection
summary: Deepfake detection models achieve high overall accuracy but exhibit large performance disparities across demographic groups, causing some groups to experience substantially higher false-positive rates than others. Existing fairness-aware methods address this by constraining model outputs to equalize group predictions, but do not tackle the underlying feature-level bias. As a result, models may still rely on demographic characteristics, such as skin texture, as indirect cues for detecting manipulated content. To address this problem, we propose Intersectional Invariant Learning (IIL), a framework that improves feature learning rather than only adjusting model outputs. IIL alternates between identifying the most challenging demographic partitions and learning features that remain consistent across those partitions. The framework also includes a false-positive-rate fairness objective and group-balanced sampling across six gender x skin-tone intersectional groups. We evaluate IIL on a large-scale fairness benchmark containing over one million images, 10 baseline detectors, and 21 fairness and utility metrics. Results show that IIL achieves Pareto-optimal performance, simultaneously attaining an AUC above 99%, a false-positive rate under 2.5%, and the lowest intersectional fairness disparity (FMEO) among all compared methods. IIL outperforms prior fairness-aware methods on the large majority of the 21 evaluation metrics, while reducing both false-positive rates and intersectional fairness disparities by several-fold compared with the strongest competing method.

AI.tldr: Proposes Intersectional Invariant Learning (IIL), which improves feature-level fairness of deepfake detectors across six gender x skin-tone groups and reaches AUC above 99% with false-positive rate under 2.5%.
AI.motivation: Deepfake detectors show large demographic disparities in false-positive rates, and existing fairness-aware methods constrain model outputs without addressing feature-level bias, so models may still rely on demographic cues such as skin texture.
AI.method: IIL alternates between identifying the most challenging demographic partitions and learning features that stay consistent across those partitions. It adds a false-positive-rate fairness objective and group-balanced sampling across six gender x skin-tone intersectional groups.
AI.result: Evaluated on a benchmark with over one million images, 10 baseline detectors and 21 fairness and utility metrics, IIL is Pareto-optimal, attaining AUC above 99%, false-positive rate under 2.5% and the lowest intersectional fairness disparity (FMEO). It outperforms prior fairness-aware methods on the large majority of the 21 metrics and reduces false-positive rates and intersectional disparities several-fold compared with the strongest competing method.
AI.conclusion: Improving feature learning, rather than only adjusting outputs, yields Pareto-optimal fairness and accuracy for deepfake detection.

title: FYC: FPR-Disparity Weight Perturbation and Youden Calibration for Fair Deepfake Detection
summary: Deepfake detectors routinely achieve high aggregate accuracy while exhibiting substantial demographic disparities in their errors: false-positive rates differ by double digits across gender and skin tone. Most existing remedies require either full retraining with a fairness-aware objective or demographic-annotated training data, both impractical when only a pretrained checkpoint is available, while label-free post-hoc calibrators leave the detector's weights unchanged. We introduce FYC (FPR-disparity Weight Perturbation and Youden Calibration), a two-stage post-hoc method that perturbs a detector's weights under an FPR-disparity criterion, then calibrates a separate decision threshold for each demographic group - requiring no architectural changes and no full retraining. Evaluated against every detector benchmarked on AI-Face v2 across six intersectional gender x skin-tone groups, FYC outperforms the field on 18 of 21 reported fairness and utility metrics, including purpose-built fairness architectures, at a fraction of the training cost. We further identify why the choice of fairness criterion is critical: the original Demographic Parity objective used in prior weight-perturbation work is architecture-dependent and unpredictable, improving two of four evaluated architectures, leaving a third largely unchanged, and substantially degrading the fourth (PG-FDD), with no way to anticipate the outcome for a given checkpoint in advance. Conditioning the same objective on real images only - our FPR-disparity criterion - eliminates this unpredictability, improving fairness and accuracy jointly across all four architectures with no exceptions.

AI.tldr: Proposes FYC, a post-hoc method that perturbs a pretrained deepfake detector's weights under an FPR-disparity criterion and then calibrates a threshold per demographic group, without retraining or demographic-annotated training data.
AI.motivation: Fairness remedies usually require full retraining or demographic-annotated data, which is impractical when only a pretrained checkpoint is available, while label-free post-hoc calibrators leave the detector's weights unchanged.
AI.method: The two stages are weight perturbation under an FPR-disparity criterion, then a separate decision threshold for each demographic group via Youden calibration. The method needs no architectural change and no full retraining, and the FPR-disparity criterion is conditioned on real images only.
AI.result: On AI-Face v2 across six intersectional gender x skin-tone groups, FYC outperforms the field on 18 of 21 fairness and utility metrics, including purpose-built fairness architectures. The original Demographic Parity objective is architecture-dependent: it improves two of four evaluated architectures, leaves a third largely unchanged and substantially degrades the fourth (PG-FDD). The FPR-disparity criterion improves fairness and accuracy jointly across all four architectures.
AI.conclusion: The choice of fairness criterion is critical, and the FPR-disparity criterion removes the unpredictability of Demographic Parity weight perturbation across the evaluated architectures.

title: Venus-DefakerOne2: A Vision-Forensics Foundation Model with Broader Coverage
summary: Real-world forgery is inherently heterogeneous: it manifests not only as digital manipulation but also as physical spoofing, and is carried not only by images but also by videos. Despite substantial progress, a unified anti-forgery foundation model covering such a broad threat spectrum remains absent. In this paper, we present Venus-DefakerOne2, which substantially extends the forensic capability boundary along both the forgery-form and media-type dimensions. Trained on tens of millions of open-source and in-house samples, it incorporates two key designs. Tide-Style-Tuning alternates LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning to balance computational efficiency, generalization, and hard-sample fitting while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Entropy-based Test Adaptation determines the optimal prediction modality by analyzing prediction entropy. Venus-DefakerOne2 achieves new state-of-the-art performance across a comprehensive suite of benchmarks, including DeepFake faces (96.7%), AI-generated images (93.3%), tampered documents (87.6%), manipulated natural images (89.6%), physical spoofs (93.1%), and AI-generated videos (96.0%). It significantly outperforms both specialized expert models and its predecessor, DefakerOne, establishing itself as a powerful and versatile foundation model for binary-decision forensic tasks.

AI.tldr: Presents Venus-DefakerOne2, a vision-forensics foundation model covering digital manipulation and physical spoofing in both images and videos, which scores state-of-the-art results across six benchmark categories.
AI.motivation: Real-world forgery is heterogeneous, spanning digital manipulation and physical spoofing across images and videos, and no unified anti-forgery foundation model covers this threat spectrum.
AI.method: Trained on tens of millions of open-source and in-house samples, the model uses Tide-Style-Tuning, which alternates LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, and Entropy-based Test Adaptation, which determines the optimal prediction modality by analyzing prediction entropy.
AI.result: The model scores 96.7% on DeepFake faces, 93.3% on AI-generated images, 87.6% on tampered documents, 89.6% on manipulated natural images, 93.1% on physical spoofs and 96.0% on AI-generated videos, significantly outperforming specialized expert models and its predecessor DefakerOne.
AI.conclusion: The model is a versatile foundation model for binary-decision forensic tasks across forgery forms and media types.

title: Hierarchical Diffusion for Camera-controlled Autoregressive Video Generation
summary: We address the task of long-video, camera-controlled generation from a single image. The dominant autoregressive paradigm suffers from two key limitations: (1) error accumulation over time, as distant frames are conditioned on previously generated outputs rather than ground truth, leading to drift; and (2) ambiguity in how to incorporate camera control. Standard solutions to both--such as self-forcing and conditioning on explicit 6-DOF poses--either incur significant computational overhead or produce drifting scene geometries over time. We propose a simple and lightweight framework that combines autoregressive generation (WanAR) with hierarchical long-context denoising (FixAR). To enforce scene geometry remains consistent with input cameras, we draw from feed-forward novel-view synthesis and reformulate video generation as a warping-and-inpainting problem. To mitigate drift, we introduce a hierarchical denoising strategy in which different stages condition on different temporal histories. Specifically, we first generate frames conditioned on the immediate past, and then refine them using a second denoiser conditioned on a temporally subsampled long-range history to enforce global consistency. This fine-to-coarse scheme enables each generated frame to effectively condition on the full temporal context without incurring a prohibitive cost. Experiments on RealEstate10k and DL3DV demonstrate that WanAR+FixAR outperforms prior methods for camera-controlled long-video generation, producing results that are both temporally stable and consistent with input camera trajectories.

AI.tldr: Proposes WanAR+FixAR, which generates long camera-controlled videos from a single image by combining autoregressive generation with hierarchical denoising that conditions on the immediate past and on a temporally subsampled long-range history.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive long-video generation suffers error accumulation and drift, and standard fixes such as self-forcing or conditioning on 6-DOF poses either add significant computational overhead or produce drifting scene geometry.
AI.method: Autoregressive generation (WanAR) is combined with hierarchical long-context denoising (FixAR). Video generation is reformulated as a warping-and-inpainting problem, using feed-forward novel-view synthesis to keep the geometry consistent with input cameras. A first denoiser conditions on the immediate past, and a second denoiser refines the frames conditioned on a temporally subsampled long-range history.
AI.result: WanAR+FixAR outperforms prior methods on RealEstate10k and DL3DV for camera-controlled long-video generation, producing results that are temporally stable and consistent with the input camera trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The fine-to-coarse scheme lets each generated frame condition effectively on the full temporal context without prohibitive cost.

title: Where Can We Fool the Model's Mind? Response-Guided Semantic Probing and Adaptive Routing for Transferable Attacks on Black-Box MLLMs
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) ground language in visual evidence, yet their semantic reasoning can be exploited through transferable black-box adversarial attacks. Existing attacks typically allocate perturbations using surrogate-model saliency, which may not reflect how an unseen MLLM semantically interprets or relies on different image regions. We introduce VISTA (Vulnerability-Informed Semantic Transfer Attacks), a black-box framework that identifies semantically vulnerable visual regions from an MLLM's responses without access to gradients, logits, parameters, or internal representations. VISTA supports two attack settings: (i) VISTA-Proxy, a pure-transfer setting that probes an open-source MLLM and transfers the resulting adversarial examples to unseen commercial MLLMs without querying them; and (ii) VISTA-Victim, a query-assisted setting that probes the target MLLM to capture model-specific semantic vulnerabilities. VISTA builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior (UBMB) map from response drift, conflict, misleading, and semantic shifts, then uses entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing and a surrogate ensemble to focus perturbations on vulnerable regions. Across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6, VISTA achieves up to 97 % attack success rate (ASR) while maintaining a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) above 30 dB. Notably, VISTA-Proxy achieves up to 93 % ASR without querying the final victim, demonstrating that response-derived semantic vulnerability can enable effective transfer across heterogeneous MLLMs.

AI.tldr: Presents VISTA, a black-box attack that uses MLLM responses to locate semantically vulnerable image regions, reaching up to 97% attack success rate on GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash and Claude Sonnet 4.6 while keeping PSNR above 30 dB.
AI.motivation: Existing transferable attacks allocate perturbations using surrogate-model saliency, which may not reflect how an unseen MLLM semantically interprets or relies on different image regions.
AI.method: VISTA builds an Uncertainty-Based Multimodal Behavior (UBMB) map from response drift, conflict, misleading and semantic shifts, without gradients, logits, parameters or internal representations. Entropy-adaptive Sinkhorn routing and a surrogate ensemble focus perturbations on vulnerable regions. VISTA-Proxy transfers from an open-source MLLM without querying the victim, and VISTA-Victim probes the target model to capture model-specific vulnerabilities.
AI.result: Across GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-Flash and Claude Sonnet 4.6, VISTA achieves up to 97% ASR while keeping PSNR above 30 dB. VISTA-Proxy achieves up to 93% ASR without querying the final victim.
AI.conclusion: Response-derived semantic vulnerability can enable effective transfer across heterogeneous MLLMs.

title: Can Event Detectors Leave the Broadcast Camera? Evidence from Tennis
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Benchmark, evaluator and frozen predictions: this https URL
summary: Ball bounces and racket hits are the events from which tennis statistics are derived, and on monocular video the two are easy to confuse. We release a benchmark of 345 bounce and hit annotations at frame level on eight clips that mix broadcast, fixed elevated, phone and court-level viewpoints, with a frozen development and test split, a confusion-aware matcher, clip-level bootstrap intervals and a blind second annotation of three clips. On it we score supervised precise spotters with published broadcast weights, two zero-shot vision-language models, and RallyArb, an arbitration layer over a ball track and player poses that fits no parameter on event labels. The supervised spotters score near-perfectly on broadcast footage and almost nothing on phone and court-level footage, where the pooled bounce F1 of E2E-Spot is 0.130. RallyArb keeps a bounce F1 above 0.8 on the three phone and court-level clips, two of which were used to tune it, and finds 8 of 11 bounces on the held-out one, but it places hits too far from the contact frame to match human timing. The vision-language models detect events on every viewpoint and miss the contact frame by about 0.1 s. Fine-tuned leave-one-clip-out from its broadcast weights, the spotter reaches about 0.8 bounce F1 on two phone and court-level clips and stays at 0.2 on a grazing phone angle. The annotations, the evaluator and the frozen predictions of every scored row are released.

AI.tldr: Releases a benchmark of 345 frame-level bounce and hit annotations for tennis and shows that supervised spotters trained on broadcast footage fail on phone and court-level video, while RallyArb, an arbitration layer over ball tracks and player poses, keeps bounce F1 above 0.8 on three such clips.
AI.motivation: Tennis statistics are derived from ball bounces and racket hits, which are easy to confuse on monocular video, and event spotters with published broadcast weights may not transfer to other viewpoints.
AI.method: The benchmark covers eight clips that mix broadcast, fixed elevated, phone and court-level viewpoints, with frozen development and test splits, a confusion-aware matcher, clip-level bootstrap intervals and a blind second annotation of three clips. Supervised spotters, two zero-shot vision-language models and RallyArb, which fits no parameter on event labels, are scored, and leave-one-clip-out fine-tuning from broadcast weights is also tested.
AI.result: Supervised spotters score near-perfectly on broadcast footage and almost nothing on phone and court-level footage, where the pooled bounce F1 of E2E-Spot is 0.130. RallyArb keeps bounce F1 above 0.8 on three phone and court-level clips, two of which were used to tune it, and finds 8 of 11 bounces on the held-out clip, but places hits too far from the contact frame to match human timing. Vision-language models detect events on every viewpoint but miss the contact frame by about 0.1 s. Fine-tuned leave-one-clip-out spotters reach about 0.8 bounce F1 on two phone and court-level clips and stay at 0.2 on a grazing phone angle.
AI.conclusion: Event detectors do not transfer reliably beyond the broadcast camera, and hit timing remains a gap; the annotations, evaluator and frozen predictions are released.

title: Classifying Urban Locations by Cyclist Facility Usage and Directional Alignment: A Validated Camera-Based Framework from Multi-Site Observations
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for presentation at the 106th Transportation Research Board (TRB) Annual Meeting, Washington, D.C., January 10-14, 2027
summary: Objectives: Agencies invest in bicycle facilities but lack tools to assess whether cyclists use them as designed. We examine whether usage patterns follow facility configurations and whether higher bike lane usage is associated with less wrong-way riding. Methods: Motion-triggered cameras covered 19 deployments at 17 locations in Tempe, Arizona, in 2023. Manual review identified 1,963 cycling events; excluding 20 crossings left 1,943 labeled events for analysis. An automated pipeline on the same captures counted 92.9 percent of the full manual total (per-deployment r = 0.99), and every automated wrong-way call was visually verified. Deployments were classified using thresholds on facility usage shares. Findings: Deployments were bike-lane dominant (9), sidewalk dominant (6), or mixed (4). Cyclists in bike lanes rode against the flow in 4.6 percent of events; on sidewalks, riders opposed the near-side traffic flow in 49.6 percent. Across deployments, bike lane share and wrong-way rate were negatively correlated (Spearman rho = -0.87, p < 0.001, n = 16). An independent volunteer count in the same city showed a similar sidewalk-direction pattern (rho = 0.79). Novelty: The study combines multi-site still-camera observations with a fully hand-verified benchmark to characterize facility use and travel direction. Practical Applications: The workflow offers planners a low-cost screen for locations with high sidewalk cycling and travel against the near-side traffic flow, supporting more detailed site investigation.

AI.tldr: The paper classifies 17 locations in Tempe, Arizona by cyclist facility usage and wrong-way riding, using camera observations validated against manual review and a volunteer count. Across deployments, higher bike lane usage is associated with less wrong-way riding.
AI.motivation: Agencies invest in bicycle facilities but lack tools to check whether cyclists use them as designed, and whether usage patterns follow facility configurations.
AI.method: Motion-triggered cameras at 19 deployments were manually reviewed to label 1,943 cycling events, and an automated pipeline counted 92.9 percent of the manual total (per-deployment r = 0.99). Deployments were classified as bike-lane dominant, sidewalk dominant or mixed using thresholds on facility usage shares.
AI.result: Nine deployments were bike-lane dominant, six sidewalk dominant and four mixed. Wrong-way riding occurred in 4.6 percent of bike lane events and 49.6 percent of sidewalk events, and bike lane share correlated negatively with wrong-way rate (Spearman rho = -0.87, n = 16); an independent volunteer count showed a similar sidewalk pattern (rho = 0.79).
AI.conclusion: The workflow gives planners a low-cost screen for locations with heavy sidewalk cycling and travel against the near-side traffic flow, to prioritise more detailed site investigation.

title: Vision Tomography: Towards Portable 3D Bidirectional Face-Skull Inference from Visual Data
summary: Traditional computed tomography (CT) can capture paired 3D face and skull geometry, but it remains costly, fixed in location, and exposes patients to radiation. For applications such as remote diagnostics, digital healthcare, forensic identification, missing-person investigation, and archaeological analysis, there is an urgent need for a portable, safe, and accessible solution to capture 3D skull geometry. In this work, we introduce Vision Tomography (VT), a concept and framework capable of reconstructing paired 3D face-skull geometry from various visual modalities, and also enabling joint manipulation of 3D facial and skull geometry. To achieve this, we first construct a dataset of over 200 samples, where each case includes a CT-based skull, a CT-based face, and a high-fidelity textured face scan. Secondly, we propose a novel dense ray matching registration method that ensures topological consistency across face, skull, and their tissue correspondences. Building on this registration, we introduce the 3D Bidirectional Face-Skull Morphable Model (BFSM) as the foundation of Vision Tomography, which enables shape inference between the face and skull through a shared coefficient space, while also modeling tissue thickness variation to support one-to-many facial reconstructions from the same skull, reflecting individual facial changes such as age or body fat. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Vision Tomography across various forensic and medical applications, including paired 3D face-skull reconstruction from images or sketches and predicting surgical outcomes with joint face-skull editing. Extensive experiments confirm the robustness and accuracy of our method. Vision Tomography is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Vision Tomography reconstructs paired 3D face and skull geometry from various visual modalities, aiming to replace costly, fixed and radiation-exposing CT. It introduces a 3D Bidirectional Face-Skull Morphable Model built on a dataset of over 200 paired samples.
AI.motivation: CT captures paired face and skull geometry but is costly, fixed in location and exposes patients to radiation, which limits remote diagnostics, forensic identification and archaeological analysis.
AI.method: The authors build a dataset of over 200 cases, each with a CT skull, a CT face and a textured face scan, and propose dense ray matching registration for topological consistency. The 3D Bidirectional Face-Skull Morphable Model shares a coefficient space between face and skull and models tissue thickness variation.
AI.result: The framework reconstructs paired face-skull geometry from images or sketches and supports joint face-skull editing for predicting surgical outcomes. The abstract reports robustness and accuracy in extensive experiments but gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a portable, safe route to 3D skull geometry for medical and forensic use, and supports one-to-many facial reconstruction from a single skull.

title: From Next Day Wildfire to Next Days Wildfire: A New Multi-Continent Dataset of Active-Fire Spread for Sequence-to-Sequence Forecasting
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. 19 pages including supplementary material, 12 figures, 13 tables
summary: Benchmarks such as WildfireSpreadTS (WSTS) have enabled data-driven forecasting of wildfire spread from multimodal satellite time series, but they suffer from limitations: size restricts them to large fires that burn for weeks, and they are from similar environments. We introduce AFSeq, a multimodal dataset of 1,194 recent fire events (2023 to 2026) from 8 different countries across three regions, dominated by the short, small fires that existing benchmarks underrepresent. Our dataset is the largest and most diverse to date for time-series-based wildfire spread prediction. We also introduce UTAE-AR, an extension of a classical U-Net with Temporal Auto Encoder, enhanced with recurrent modules before the decoder. This allows the model to not only predict the next day but the whole sequence in an autoregressive way. Moreover, our model can feed its own predicted fire mask back one day at a time, producing the day-by-day forecasts that single-step models cannot. Our results show that UTAE-AR surpasses state-of-the-art on both WSTS, WSTS+ and AFSeq for next-day accuracy while having 21.5% of their parameters, and being able to predict confidently at a longer horizon.

AI.tldr: AFSeq is a multimodal dataset of 1,194 recent active-fire events from 8 countries, and UTAE-AR is a recurrent extension of U-Net with a Temporal Auto Encoder that forecasts whole fire sequences autoregressively. UTAE-AR surpasses the state of the art on WSTS, WSTS+ and AFSeq for next-day accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing wildfire spread benchmarks such as WildfireSpreadTS are limited in size, favour large fires that burn for weeks and come from similar environments, so they underrepresent short, small fires.
AI.method: AFSeq collects multimodal satellite time series for fires from 2023 to 2026 across three regions. UTAE-AR adds recurrent modules before the decoder of UTAE and feeds its own predicted fire mask back one day at a time.
AI.result: UTAE-AR surpasses the state of the art on WSTS, WSTS+ and AFSeq for next-day accuracy while using 21.5 percent of their parameters, and it predicts confidently at longer horizons.
AI.conclusion: The dataset is the largest and most diverse to date for time-series wildfire spread prediction, and the autoregressive model produces day-by-day forecasts that single-step models cannot.

title: The Prestige: Benchmarking Cognitive Visual Reasoning using Magic Tricks
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets
summary: We introduce The Prestige, a video understanding benchmark that probes cognitive visual reasoning through professional magic performances, where deliberate misdirection challenges models to track events and explain unexpected outcomes. The benchmark comprises open-ended questions ranging from temporal and causal understanding to robustness against adversarial questions. Evaluation of leading open-source and proprietary VLMs reveals a substantial gap between even the strongest model and human performance. We also find systematic discrepancies between human and automated grading and identify recurring model failure modes. Ablations further show that models can select correct multiple-choice answers even when they fail to generate correct explanations independently, motivating further investigations into question formats. Together, these findings highlight limitations in both VLM reasoning and its evaluation, underscoring the need for more reliable video understanding models and more rigorous benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The Prestige is a video understanding benchmark built from professional magic performances that tests cognitive visual reasoning under deliberate misdirection. Leading open-source and proprietary VLMs fall well short of human performance.
AI.motivation: Existing video benchmarks do not probe whether models can track events and explain unexpected outcomes, and the reliability of their evaluation is open to question.
AI.method: The benchmark asks open-ended questions ranging from temporal and causal understanding to robustness against adversarial questions. Human and automated grading are compared, and ablations examine multiple-choice answers against generated explanations.
AI.result: The strongest model still shows a substantial gap to human performance. Human and automated grading disagree systematically, recurring failure modes are identified, and models can select correct multiple-choice answers without producing correct explanations.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal limits in both VLM reasoning and its evaluation, motivating more reliable video understanding models, more rigorous benchmarks and careful choice of question formats.

title: StepControl: Long-Horizon Human Motion Generation from Foot-Contact Schedules
summary: Controllable human motion generation has largely focused on specifying what action should occur or where the body should move. We study a complementary question: can full-body motion be controlled by specifying only when each foot contacts the ground? We introduce StepControl, an autoregressive diffusion model conditioned on a future binary left/right foot-contact schedule, without requiring target root and body poses, or semantic prompts. StepControl represents contact as explicit temporal events and injects them through dedicated cross-attention with classifier-free guidance. We further introduce a stochastic mixture noise schedule and warmup strategy for stable long-horizon autoregressive generation. Experiments show that StepControl follows prescribed contact timing more accurately than adapting existing spatially guided motion generators to contact constraints. It maintains effective contact control over long continuous rollouts and responds to edited schedules such as cadence changes, stop-and-go pauses, limping gaits, and bilateral jumping. Our results show that minimal foot-contact schedules provide an effective and intuitive temporal interface for controllable motion generation.

AI.tldr: StepControl is an autoregressive diffusion model for human motion conditioned only on a future left and right foot-contact schedule. It follows prescribed contact timing more accurately than adapted spatially guided motion generators over long rollouts.
AI.motivation: Controllable motion generation has focused on what action should occur or where the body should move, not on when each foot should contact the ground.
AI.method: Contacts are represented as explicit temporal events and injected through dedicated cross-attention with classifier-free guidance. A stochastic mixture noise schedule and warmup strategy support stable long-horizon autoregressive generation.
AI.result: Compared with adapting existing spatially guided generators to contact constraints, StepControl follows contact timing more accurately, keeps effective contact control over long rollouts and responds to edited schedules such as cadence changes, stop-and-go pauses, limping gaits and bilateral jumping.
AI.conclusion: Minimal foot-contact schedules provide an effective and intuitive temporal interface for controllable motion generation.

title: REEL: Same Frames, Different Answers and Different Costs
comment: Accepted at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027, Datasets and Evaluation Track
summary: Video understanding keeps moving toward longer recordings, and the longer a recording is, the more questions can be asked about it. But processing it again for every question does not scale, so many systems watch the video once, build a memory, and answer later questions from it. Yet what to remember is decided before anyone knows what will be asked, and whatever is left out cannot be recovered later. Moreover, whether the savings pay off is judged by token counts, which fall when the input gets shorter but not when the model reuses what it has already computed. We present REEL, an evaluation framework that compares three saved representations built from exactly the same observed frames, so that a change in answers can come only from what the system remembered. Text writes a short record of what happened, Visual keeps the encoder outputs, and Prefix State also keeps the language-model prefix. Each is compared with full reprocessing (Frames) by paired correctness changes, cumulative GPU time, and storage size. Across six vision-language models and two benchmarks, Text and Frames differ in correctness on 20\% to 29\% of questions, even when their mean accuracy is almost the same. By contrast, Visual and Prefix State stay much closer to Frames. With unlimited storage, Prefix State is the cheapest in total GPU time among memories that keep almost all of the answers Frames gets right, for every model on both benchmarks. The trade-off is storage: Prefix State keeps up to about 21 GiB per video, whereas Text needs only kilobytes. Reusing computation and discarding information both look like efficiency, but only the second removes evidence that later questions may need, and neither mean accuracy nor token count tells them apart. REEL makes that difference measurable for any system that answers many questions from one saved memory.

AI.tldr: REEL is an evaluation framework that compares three saved video memories against full reprocessing of the same frames. It shows that similar mean accuracy or token counts can hide large per-question differences in correctness and in cost.
AI.motivation: Systems that answer many questions about one video store a memory chosen before the questions are known, and efficiency is usually judged by token counts, which ignore reused computation and information that was discarded.
AI.method: Text, Visual and Prefix State memories are built from exactly the same observed frames and compared with full reprocessing (Frames) by paired correctness changes, cumulative GPU time and storage size, across six vision-language models and two benchmarks.
AI.result: Text and Frames differ in correctness on 20 to 29 percent of questions even when mean accuracy is almost the same, while Visual and Prefix State stay much closer to Frames. With unlimited storage, Prefix State is the cheapest in total GPU time among memories keeping almost all correct answers, but it needs up to about 21 GiB per video, against kilobytes for Text.
AI.conclusion: Reusing computation and discarding information both look like efficiency, but only the second removes evidence that later questions may need, and REEL makes that difference measurable.

title: Neighbourhood shortcuts in building damage assessment from very-high-resolution satellite imagery: diagnosis and a building-evidence plug-in
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Building damage assessment (BDA) from very-high-resolution imagery supports disaster response, and deep models now achieve high overall accuracy on public benchmarks. Because damage is spatially clustered, most buildings share the damage level of their neighbours, so overall scores are dominated by such buildings, whereas damaged buildings among intact ones are rare and easily overlooked. A high overall score therefore cannot tell whether a model judges the building itself or relies on its neighbourhood as a shortcut, and this study tests which of the two current models do. We stratify buildings by their agreement with their neighbours, move buildings into new neighbourhoods with their pixels unchanged, and diagnose nine models covering the main paradigms of BDA. All models miss a third to half of the isolated damaged buildings, and in non-flood events they call 73--87% of intact buildings damaged once these are moved into a damaged neighbourhood. We propose a building-evidence plug-in that adds two experts to an existing model without retraining it. One expert sees only the building, and the other sees its surroundings but is trained with seamlessly swapped neighbourhoods so that it learns not to trust them. With each of the nine models, the plug-in maintains or improves overall accuracy, reduces errors on buildings that disagree with their neighbours by 8--18%, and cuts by 40--69% the intact buildings that a damaged neighbourhood turns into damaged ones. It also raises the detection of synthetic isolated damage from 1--6% to 13--39% and carries over to optical--SAR data and to an unseen earthquake. High overall scores thus conceal a systematic reliance on the neighbourhood, which building-level evidence reduces at low cost.

AI.tldr: Building damage assessment models from very-high-resolution satellite imagery rely systematically on neighbourhood shortcuts, and the proposed building-evidence plug-in adds two experts to an existing model without retraining it. The plug-in maintains or improves overall accuracy for each of the nine models diagnosed.
AI.motivation: Damage is spatially clustered, so high overall scores are dominated by buildings that share their neighbours' damage level, and they cannot show whether a model judges the building itself or relies on its neighbourhood.
AI.method: Buildings are stratified by agreement with their neighbours and moved into new neighbourhoods with their pixels unchanged to diagnose nine models. The plug-in adds a building-only expert and a surroundings expert trained with seamlessly swapped neighbourhoods so that it learns not to trust them.
AI.result: All models miss a third to half of isolated damaged buildings, and in non-flood events they call 73 to 87 percent of intact buildings damaged once these are moved into a damaged neighbourhood. With the plug-in, errors on buildings that disagree with their neighbours fall by 8 to 18 percent, intact buildings turned damaged fall by 40 to 69 percent, and detection of synthetic isolated damage rises from 1 to 6 percent to 13 to 39 percent.
AI.conclusion: High overall scores conceal systematic reliance on the neighbourhood, and building-level evidence reduces that reliance at low cost, carrying over to optical-SAR data and an unseen earthquake.

title: Complementing Text Based Moderation with Multimodal Grounding: Detecting Fraudulent Inducement Behaviors on Short Video Platforms
summary: Short video platforms have become a primary channel for black and gray industry operations in internet finance, where inducements such as prompts to like, follow, join private chat groups, or click external links frequently steer users toward fraud. Because such videos are short, dynamic, and often convey intent through fleeting visual cues rather than stable text, a moderation system must guarantee detection recall and localize the offending segment so reviewers inspect only the relevant clip. Existing OCR+LLM pipelines transcribe on-screen text frame by frame and classify the transcript, but exploit only textual information. Many inducements are conveyed through visual cues OCR cannot observe, and keyframe-based localization cannot recover precise temporal boundaries. We explore OCR+MLLM, which augments the text pipeline with a Multimodal Large Language Model, and compare three routes: OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM, and a large zero-shot MLLM, along detection, latency, token consumption, and deployment complexity. OCR preserves the text signal that guarantees recall, while the MLLM jointly performs OCR-grounded discrimination and temporal grounding, localizing both textual and non-textual inducements. We construct a dataset of 2,419 internet finance short videos (66.49 hours) with 3,194 annotated events across four categories, and study reward design for RL-based grounding under class imbalance. We report two findings: auxiliary reward terms are exploited through reward hacking, and stronger localization rewards degrade class-balanced detection. We therefore design a recall-weighted F2 localization reward with class-balanced resampling. Experiments show OCR+MLLM localizes better than the keyframe OCR+LLM baseline (mIoU 26.52 vs. 14.49) and detects non-textual inducements that text-only pipelines miss, while maintaining 67.0 percent macro recall.

AI.tldr: The paper compares three routes for detecting fraudulent inducement behaviours in short videos: OCR+LLM, OCR+MLLM and a large zero-shot MLLM. OCR+MLLM localizes inducements better than the keyframe OCR+LLM baseline and detects non-textual inducements that text-only pipelines miss.
AI.motivation: Text-only OCR+LLM moderation misses inducements conveyed through visual cues, and keyframe-based localization cannot recover precise temporal boundaries for reviewers.
AI.method: OCR+MLLM augments the text pipeline with a multimodal LLM that jointly performs OCR-grounded discrimination and temporal grounding. The authors use RL-based grounding with a recall-weighted F2 localization reward and class-balanced resampling, on 2,419 internet finance short videos (66.49 hours) with 3,194 annotated events in four categories.
AI.result: OCR+MLLM reaches mIoU 26.52 against 14.49 for the keyframe OCR+LLM baseline and maintains 67.0 percent macro recall. Auxiliary reward terms were exploited through reward hacking, and stronger localization rewards degraded class-balanced detection.
AI.conclusion: Combining OCR with an MLLM and a recall-weighted localization reward localizes both textual and non-textual inducements while preserving the text signal that guarantees recall.

title: Silhouette-Based Gaitomics for Frailty Assessment in Older Adults
summary: Walking offers a window into physical function that may support interpretable video-based frailty assessment. We developed silhouette-based "gaitomics" to connect frailty predictions with measurable patterns of body configuration and movement. In 66 older adults assessed using the Fried Frailty Phenotype, standardized silhouettes and gait energy images yielded 90 descriptors of shape, temporal variation, motion, and texture. Minimum redundancy maximum relevance selection using the mutual information difference criterion prioritized informative features while limiting redundancy. Each classifier was evaluated using nested stratified cross-validation with five outer and three inner folds at the participant level, with feature ranking and feature-count selection confined to training partitions. Shapley additive explanations examined contributions to held-out predictions. Bilateral silhouette difference led the aggregate feature-selection rankings for three-class classification and both comparisons involving frail participants. Attribution profiles differed across tasks, with texture and consecutive-frame silhouette differences prominent in three-class classification. Among classifier-specific evaluations, CatBoost achieved the highest mean three-class micro-AUC of 0.647 \pm 0.085. Leading pairwise mean micro-AUCs were 0.833 \pm 0.249 for frail versus nonfrail, 0.765 \pm 0.168 for frail versus prefrail, and 0.554 \pm 0.129 for prefrail versus nonfrail classification. These findings connect model predictions to explicit gait characteristics while revealing task-dependent feature priorities and limited separation of prefrail and nonfrail participants. The framework provides an interpretable basis for further investigation, with larger independent studies needed to establish reliability and clinical relevance.

AI.tldr: Silhouette-based gait features with interpretable machine learning give moderate frailty classification in 66 older adults. Frail versus nonfrail separation is the strongest, while prefrail and nonfrail participants are hard to tell apart.
AI.motivation: Video-based frailty assessment needs predictions that connect to measurable patterns of body configuration and movement in order to be interpretable.
AI.method: Standardized silhouettes and gait energy images yielded 90 descriptors of shape, temporal variation, motion and texture. Minimum redundancy maximum relevance selection, nested stratified cross-validation and Shapley additive explanations were used to rank features and explain held-out predictions.
AI.result: CatBoost achieved the highest mean three-class micro-AUC of 0.647 plus or minus 0.085. Pairwise mean micro-AUCs were 0.833 plus or minus 0.249 for frail versus nonfrail, 0.765 plus or minus 0.168 for frail versus prefrail and 0.554 plus or minus 0.129 for prefrail versus nonfrail, and bilateral silhouette difference led the feature rankings.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an interpretable basis for further study, but larger independent studies are needed to establish reliability and clinical relevance.

title: MEV: A Multi-Event Video Dataset for Long-Take Generation
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Current datasets for text-to-video generation are largely limited to short clips depicting a single event or coarse-grained captions. As a result, they provide limited supervision for modeling long-take temporal dependencies, often leading to temporally inconsistent generations when describing multiple events. In this paper, we introduce MEV, a multi-event video dataset designed for long-take video generation. MEV provides high-quality real-world videos where subjects can perform a sequence of distinct, non-overlapping events, featuring precise temporal boundaries and fine-grained procedural annotations. This event-centric discretization reduces confounding factors and enables models to support temporally localized conditioning and build long-take videos from atomic event units. Furthermore, we introduce a comprehensive annotation pipeline that segments videos into temporally grounded events, and generates structured captions at both the global level and the event level. In addition, under an event-centric evaluation protocol, we conduct multi-event generation experiments by fine-tuning on MEV with temporally grounded event conditioning, leading to improved long-take event transitions and more coherent content. We believe this work provides a publicly available resource for multi-event fine-tuning and event-centric evaluation, together with practical insights into learning from temporally structured video-text data.

AI.tldr: MEV is a multi-event video dataset of real-world videos with precise temporal boundaries and structured captions, designed for long-take text-to-video generation. Fine-tuning on it with temporally grounded event conditioning improves transitions between events.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-video datasets are mostly short clips of a single event with coarse captions, which gives little supervision for temporal dependencies across multiple events.
AI.method: An annotation pipeline segments videos into temporally grounded, non-overlapping events and generates structured captions at global and event levels. Multi-event generation experiments fine-tune models with event conditioning under an event-centric evaluation protocol.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on MEV improves long-take event transitions and makes content more coherent under the event-centric protocol; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a publicly available resource for multi-event fine-tuning and event-centric evaluation, along with insights into learning from temporally structured video-text data.

title: ETA-Motion: Efficient Topology-Agnostic Motion Diffusion via Sparse Joint Learning
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027; Project page : this https URL
summary: Topology-agnostic motion generation aims to synthesize motions for diverse characters with arbitrary skeletons. Unlike conventional motion generation, which assumes a fixed skeletal template, this setting must handle diverse joint configurations and inconsistent joint semantics across characters. Existing methods address this challenge through dense full-joint modeling, which incurs substantial computational cost and hinders learning transferable motion patterns across diverse skeletal topologies. We present ETA-Motion, a topology-agnostic motion generation framework based on sparse joint learning. Instead of learning motion from all joints, our method uses a compact subset of joints to reduce redundancy and trains the motion generator on the resulting sparse skeleton. To facilitate correspondence across diverse topologies, we introduce semantic joint embeddings that combine textual and visual cues, together with topology-aware training objectives for preserving skeletal structure. Although ETA-Motion is trained only on sparse skeletal observations, it supports full-skeleton motion generation during inference. Experimental results demonstrate that ETA-Motion outperforms existing topology-agnostic baselines while significantly improving efficiency and generalization to unseen motions and unseen topologies.

AI.tldr: ETA-Motion generates motion for characters with arbitrary skeletons by learning from a compact subset of joints, and it produces full-skeleton motion at inference. It outperforms existing topology-agnostic baselines with better efficiency and generalization.
AI.motivation: Dense full-joint modelling for topology-agnostic motion generation is computationally costly and hinders learning motion patterns that transfer across diverse skeletal topologies.
AI.method: A sparse skeleton formed from a compact joint subset is used to train the motion generator. Semantic joint embeddings combining textual and visual cues align joints across topologies, and topology-aware training objectives preserve skeletal structure.
AI.result: ETA-Motion outperforms existing topology-agnostic baselines while significantly improving efficiency and generalizing to unseen motions and unseen topologies; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Sparse joint learning is an efficient route to topology-agnostic motion diffusion that reduces redundancy while still producing full-skeleton output.

title: TreemapMix: Dirichlet-Controlled Multi-Image Augmentation for Probability and Ordinal Supervision
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 40 pages including references, appendices, and checklist. Ejafa Bassam and Konstantin Garbers contributed equally
