However, verifying that these transformations preserve visual consistency, defined as the preservation of an object's intrinsic visual attributes, including geometry, texture, color, and fine-grained details, remains a largely unsolved problem. This challenge is particularly pronounced at scale, where manual inspection is infeasible and automated quality assessment (AutoQA) could become essential. In this work, we introduce Visual Consistency Assessment for Product Image Editing (V-CAPE), a large-scale dataset for evaluating visual consistency in generative image editing. The dataset consists of 40K unique source-target product image pairs, each annotated with binary accept/reject labels and structured failure modes capturing fine-grained inconsistencies such as geometric distortions, pose errors, and identity mismatches. V-CAPE combines real-world edited images with a synthetic subset constructed from 3D assets, enabling both realistic evaluation and controlled analysis. Vision-language models (VLMs) across all evaluated size categories on AutoQA achieve accuracy below 65%, indicating that the dataset poses a substantial challenge regardless of model scale. Our results highlight fundamental limitations of current models in verifying visual consistency under transformation, positioning V-CAPE as a benchmark for advancing fine-grained image editing evaluation.

AI.tldr: V-CAPE is a 40K-pair dataset of source and target product images labeled accept or reject for visual consistency in generative image editing, with structured failure modes. Vision-language models achieve below 65% accuracy on automated quality assessment regardless of model scale.
AI.motivation: Verifying that generative image edits preserve an object's intrinsic attributes, such as geometry, texture, color and fine-grained details, remains largely unsolved, and manual inspection is infeasible at scale.
AI.method: The dataset combines real-world edited product images with a synthetic subset constructed from 3D assets, with each source-target pair annotated with binary accept/reject labels and structured failure modes such as geometric distortions, pose errors and identity mismatches.
AI.result: Vision-language models across all evaluated size categories achieve accuracy below 65% on AutoQA, indicating the dataset poses a substantial challenge regardless of model scale.
AI.conclusion: Current models have fundamental limitations in verifying visual consistency under transformation, positioning V-CAPE as a benchmark for fine-grained image editing evaluation.

title: TRIM: Temporal Run-Time Monitoring of 3D Object Detection via Activation Statistics
comment: 6 pages. Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE 23rd International Conference on Smart Communities: Improving Quality of Life using AI, Robotics and IoT (HONET)
summary: Reliable perception is essential to intelligent transportation systems, yet deep neural networks can silently miss safety-critical objects while continuing to produce apparently plausible outputs. Existing run-time monitors for 3D object detection generally assess each frame independently and therefore cannot exploit the temporal evolution of occlusion, point sparsity, and scene complexity. We present TRIM, a lightweight temporal monitor that detects missed-object failures without modifying or retraining the underlying detector. TRIM summarises intermediate activations using compact channel-wise statistics and processes short sequences of these summaries with a temporal convolutional network. Experiments on NuScenes show that temporal monitoring improves AUROC from 0.686 to 0.704 and reduces the false alarm rate at 95% recall from 0.818 to 0.759 compared with single-frame monitoring. Early and intermediate backbone features provide the strongest monitoring signal, while the temporal inference head requires only 0.159 ms on a CPU.

AI.tldr: TRIM is a lightweight temporal run-time monitor that detects missed-object failures in 3D object detection by processing short sequences of channel-wise activation statistics with a temporal convolutional network. On NuScenes it raises AUROC from 0.686 to 0.704 over single-frame monitoring.
AI.motivation: Existing run-time monitors for 3D object detection assess each frame independently and cannot exploit the temporal evolution of occlusion, point sparsity and scene complexity, while deep networks can silently miss safety-critical objects.
AI.method: TRIM summarizes intermediate activations with compact channel-wise statistics and processes short sequences of these summaries with a temporal convolutional network, without modifying or retraining the underlying detector.
AI.result: On NuScenes, temporal monitoring improves AUROC from 0.686 to 0.704 and reduces the false alarm rate at 95% recall from 0.818 to 0.759 compared with single-frame monitoring; early and intermediate backbone features give the strongest monitoring signal, and the temporal inference head requires 0.159 ms on a CPU.
AI.conclusion: Temporal monitoring of activation statistics offers an efficient way to flag missed objects in 3D object detection without changes to the detector.

title: inkGround: Benchmarking Fine-grained Visual Grounding Capabilities of Vision-Language Models for Cursive Handwriting in the Wild
summary: Human handwriting is produced as an ordered sequence of pen movements, but an offline image keeps only the final ink. Handwriting trajectory recovery aims to restore the ordered stroke points and their pen-up/pen-down transitions. Existing image-trajectory pair datasets are recorded with digitizing tablets under controlled conditions, which limits writer coverage and stylistic diversity. Moreover, there is no benchmark that measures the visual grounding capabilities of general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for the stroke trajectory recovery task. In this work, we introduce inkGround, a benchmark for stroke trajectory recovery from full-page, camera-captured handwriting. inkGround pairs 537 page images (~18.7k words, ~163k strokes) with reference trajectories produced by a pretrained offline-to-online model, filtered by OCR agreement, and verified by human raters. Because these references are pseudo-labels that represent one plausible pen trajectory, we also evaluate VLMs on the IAM-OnDB dataset, which provides recorded pen trajectories. We cast the task as text-conditioned point grounding: given a page image and a target word, the model must locate the word and output its ordered stroke points. Outputs are scored by trajectory fidelity (DTW, Chamfer distance), readability of the rendered strokes (Accurate Rate, Correct Rate), and style similarity. We benchmark four open-source and three frontier closed-source VLMs with a shared in-context prompt. Closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produce legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also holds on IAM-OnDB.

AI.tldr: inkGround is a benchmark for recovering ordered pen trajectories from full-page, camera-captured handwriting, cast as text-conditioned point grounding for vision-language models. Closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produce legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also holds on IAM-OnDB.
AI.motivation: Existing image-trajectory datasets are recorded on digitizing tablets under controlled conditions, which limits writer coverage and stylistic diversity, and no benchmark measures the visual grounding ability of general-purpose VLMs for stroke trajectory recovery.
AI.method: The benchmark pairs 537 page images (about 18.7k words, about 163k strokes) with pseudo-label reference trajectories from a pretrained offline-to-online model, filtered by OCR agreement and verified by human raters. Given a page image and a target word, a model locates the word and outputs its ordered stroke points under a shared in-context prompt, scored by DTW and Chamfer distance, Accurate Rate and Correct Rate, and style similarity; IAM-OnDB, which provides recorded pen trajectories, serves as a second evaluation set.
AI.result: Four open-source and three frontier closed-source VLMs were benchmarked; the closed-source models, notably Gemini-3.1-Pro, produced legible trajectories close to the reference, and this ranking also held on IAM-OnDB.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark gives a measure of fine-grained visual grounding for handwriting trajectory recovery, showing that frontier closed-source VLMs lead on this task and that evaluation against pseudo-labels agrees with evaluation against recorded trajectories.

title: RuleForge: Inferring and Instantiating Latent Visual Rules as Executable Programs
summary: Visual rule reasoning asks whether multimodal models can recover an abstract concept from a few examples. Existing studies either infer rules from visual examples but evaluate only classification or verbalization, or supervise executable generation with rules provided as input. Consequently, the relationship between visual rule understanding and reliable rule instantiation remains insufficiently explored. We present Bongard-Forge100k, a controlled benchmark, together with RuleForge, a backbone-agnostic framework that jointly learns visual rule understanding and rule-conditioned executable generation. The benchmark contains 108,797 problems: 86,000 for training, 19,297 for testing familiar rules, and 3,500 for testing held-out rule compositions. The framework progresses through rule-understanding training, joint understanding and scene-program supervision, and refinement via execution-grounded reinforcement learning with Understanding Replay. Executing generated programs under multiple random seeds provides verifiable feedback on executability, rule satisfaction, diversity, and robustness. With UniLIP as the primary backbone, RuleForge improves multiple-choice accuracy over the base model by 20.93 percentage points on familiar rules and 28.42 percentage points on held-out rule compositions, while increasing scene-level rule satisfaction on familiar rules from 2.91% to 70.99%. Additional experiments on InternVL3.5, Qwen3-VL, and Show-o2 demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed training data and framework across diverse multimodal architectures.

AI.tldr: Bongard-Forge100k is a controlled benchmark of visual rule reasoning with 108,797 problems, and RuleForge is a backbone-agnostic framework that jointly learns visual rule understanding and rule-conditioned executable program generation. With UniLIP as backbone, RuleForge raises multiple-choice accuracy by 20.93 and 28.42 percentage points on familiar rules and held-out rule compositions, respectively.
AI.motivation: Existing studies either infer rules from visual examples but evaluate only classification or verbalization, or supervise executable generation with rules given as input, so the relationship between visual rule understanding and reliable rule instantiation remains insufficiently explored.
AI.method: The framework proceeds through rule-understanding training, joint understanding and scene-program supervision, and refinement via execution-grounded reinforcement learning with Understanding Replay. Generated programs are executed under multiple random seeds to give verifiable feedback on executability, rule satisfaction, diversity, and robustness. The benchmark has 86,000 training problems, 19,297 test problems for familiar rules, and 3,500 test problems for held-out rule compositions.
AI.result: With UniLIP as the primary backbone, RuleForge improves multiple-choice accuracy over the base model by 20.93 points on familiar rules and 28.42 points on held-out rule compositions, and raises scene-level rule satisfaction on familiar rules from 2.91% to 70.99%. Gains are also reported on InternVL3.5, Qwen3-VL, and Show-o2.
AI.conclusion: The training data and framework transfer across diverse multimodal architectures, indicating that coupling visual rule understanding with execution-verified program generation is an effective route to reliable rule instantiation.

title: A 211K Parameter Foundation Model: Genetic Prompting in Neural Cellular Automata
summary: The scale of modern foundation models enables broad task generalization. In medical imaging, where segmentation demands vary widely across clinical contexts, such flexibility is invaluable. But current models, such as SAM trade adaptability for scale, locking their utility behind high-end infrastructure and leaving behind the low-resource environments most in need of diagnostic support. To bridge this gap, we introduce Foundational-NCA, a lightweight foundation model capable of adapting to a wide range of medical segmentation tasks without retraining. Built on Neural Cellular Automata (NCA), Foundational-NCA incorporates gradient-based learning with genetic optimization over a latent task space, using a compact task vector to guide predictions. This enables dynamic adaptation via a genetic prompt mechanism, allowing the model to generalize across tasks while keeping the parameter count magnitudes lower at just 211 thousand, compared to SAM-based models with 38.9 to 636 million parameters. We evaluate Foundational-NCA on 15 trained and 6 entirely unseen segmentation tasks from the TotalSegmentator dataset, achieving an average Dice score of 84.5% on known tasks and 60.4% on unseen ones. These results demonstrate that task generalization is possible in ultra-compact models, laying the groundwork for resource-efficient, deployable foundation models in clinical environments where infrastructure is limited. By reducing model size by over 180 times, Foundational-NCA takes a step toward a more equitable future for medical AI, one where powerful tools are within reach of every healthcare setting.

AI.tldr: Foundational-NCA is a 211-thousand-parameter foundation model built on Neural Cellular Automata that adapts to many medical segmentation tasks without retraining. It reaches an average Dice of 84.5% on 15 trained tasks and 60.4% on 6 unseen tasks from TotalSegmentator.
AI.motivation: Foundation models such as SAM trade adaptability for scale, with 38.9 to 636 million parameters, which keeps them dependent on high-end infrastructure and leaves low-resource clinical settings without diagnostic support.
AI.method: The model combines gradient-based learning with genetic optimization over a latent task space, using a compact task vector to guide predictions. A genetic prompt mechanism enables dynamic adaptation to each task while keeping the parameter count very small.
AI.result: On 15 trained and 6 entirely unseen segmentation tasks from the TotalSegmentator dataset, the model achieves an average Dice score of 84.5% on known tasks and 60.4% on unseen tasks, with a model size more than 180 times smaller than SAM-based models.
AI.conclusion: Task generalization is achievable in ultra-compact models, pointing toward resource-efficient, deployable foundation models for clinical environments with limited infrastructure.

title: Beyond Region Memory: Local Point Tracking for Vocal Cord Localization in Video Laryngoscopy
summary: Reliable vocal-cord localization in emergency video laryngoscopy remains visually challenging due to rapid tissue deformation, specular highlights, and instrument occlusions. We propose Local Point Tracking (LPT), a robust framework that combines a single-frame detector, local point propagation, and stateless mask refinement. LPT follows a localize first, snap second pipeline. First, a single-frame semantic detector generates sparse anchors, within which LPT initializes local query points (SAM-supported by default, with a regular grid as fallback). A point-propagation module tracks these points through detector-missed frames and recovers temporal bounding boxes from their geometry. Second, because point-derived boxes can be loose around the visible boundary, a box-snap step refines the selected box to the target boundary. This decomposition keeps temporal state in local point coordinates rather than a stateful mask or whole-region representation, while the spatial refinement module handles single-frame boundary precision without feeding mask errors back into temporal memory. Extensive evaluations on two distinct datasets demonstrate that our proposed LPT method achieves strong overall performance against existing baselines, with the best mAP_50, success AUC, and missing rate on both datasets. Furthermore, ablation studies confirm that point tracking primarily enhances temporal tracking robustness, while box-snap refinement effectively improves boundary tightness.

AI.tldr: Local Point Tracking (LPT) localizes vocal cords in emergency video laryngoscopy by detecting sparse anchors in single frames, propagating local query points through frames the detector misses, and snapping the resulting boxes to the target boundary. It achieves the best mAP_50, success AUC, and missing rate on two datasets.
AI.motivation: Reliable vocal-cord localization in video laryngoscopy is hard because of rapid tissue deformation, specular highlights, and instrument occlusions, and region-based temporal memory entangles temporal tracking with mask errors.
AI.method: The framework follows a localize-first, snap-second pipeline. A single-frame semantic detector produces sparse anchors, from which LPT initializes local query points (SAM-supported by default, with a regular grid as fallback). A point-propagation module tracks the points and recovers temporal bounding boxes from their geometry, and a box-snap step refines each box to the target boundary. Temporal state is kept in local point coordinates rather than in a stateful mask.
AI.result: Across two distinct datasets, LPT achieves strong overall performance against existing baselines, with the best mAP_50, success AUC, and missing rate on both. Ablations show that point tracking mainly improves temporal robustness and box-snap refinement mainly improves boundary tightness.
AI.conclusion: Separating temporal tracking in point coordinates from single-frame boundary refinement improves both robustness and precision of vocal-cord localization without feeding mask errors back into temporal memory.

title: OneScene-Bench: Do Vision-Language Models Integrate Evidence Across Views?
comment: Accepted at LM4RWD Workshop, Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2026
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly process multiple views of the same scene, but it remains unclear whether they integrate these observations into a coherent scene-level representation. Existing multi-image evaluations do not isolate this capability, as tasks may admit correct solutions through independent per-view processing without requiring cross-view correspondence. We introduce OneScene-Bench, a controlled benchmark designed to explicitly distinguish when cross-view integration is necessary. Our benchmark evaluates three complementary capabilities on real-world multi-view scenes: unique object counting, cross-view consistency, and spatial reasoning. For counting, we control object overlap across views to separate cases solvable by simple per-view aggregation from those requiring instance-level correspondence. For consistency, we introduce localized edits in shared and view-specific regions, testing whether models distinguish genuine scene contradictions from differences caused by viewpoint and visibility. For spatial reasoning, we construct object relations that require combining spatial evidence across viewpoints to compare physical proximity. We evaluate twelve state-of-the-art open-weight and proprietary VLMs and find that counting accuracy drops substantially on complementary views, ranging from 4.5-50.0%, compared with 45.5-81.5% on complete-overlap examples. Moreover, cross-view consistency remains around 50% across models, including recent proprietary VLMs, despite substantially stronger performance on spatial reasoning. Our results reveal a substantial gap between processing multiple images and integrating evidence across them, highlighting the need for evaluations that explicitly test scene-level multi-view understanding. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: OneScene-Bench is a controlled benchmark testing whether vision-language models integrate evidence across multiple views of one scene, covering unique object counting, cross-view consistency, and spatial reasoning. Counting accuracy drops to 4.5-50.0% on complementary views and cross-view consistency stays around 50% across twelve evaluated VLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-image evaluations do not isolate cross-view integration, because tasks can be solved by independent per-view processing without any cross-view correspondence.
AI.method: Counting is controlled by varying object overlap across views to separate per-view aggregation from instance-level correspondence. Consistency is tested with localized edits in shared and view-specific regions, to distinguish genuine scene contradictions from viewpoint and visibility differences. Spatial reasoning uses object relations that require combining evidence across viewpoints to compare physical proximity.
AI.result: Twelve open-weight and proprietary VLMs show counting accuracy of 4.5-50.0% on complementary views, compared with 45.5-81.5% on complete-overlap examples. Cross-view consistency remains around 50% across models, including recent proprietary VLMs, although spatial reasoning performance is substantially stronger.
AI.conclusion: A substantial gap exists between processing multiple images and integrating evidence across them, so evaluations must explicitly test scene-level multi-view understanding.

title: GradSplat: Gradients Inside the Forward Pass for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting predicts a scene from a few images, but our predictor is less accurate than its own Gaussians optimized per scene on those images. This gap lies mostly in the shape of the Gaussians, their scale and rotation, since optimizing the shape alone recovers almost all of it and opacity and color recover less. Gradient steps on the input views correct this shape, and the model holds these views at inference. Log-anisotropy correction changes the axis ratios of each Gaussian in log space at constant volume, and in-forward gradient refinement renders the Gaussians into the input views and applies the gradient of the photometric loss with a learned recurrent update, first to opacity and color and then to the shape. GradSplat is a feed-forward model that refines its own Gaussians by learned gradient steps inside its forward pass, with no target view. On both complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, it has the best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods and keeps its accuracy from $6$ to $42$ input views. Without fine-tuning, it is the most accurate on DL3DV and has the best PSNR and SSIM on ScanNet++. The code will be released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: GradSplat is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting model that refines its own Gaussians through learned gradient steps inside its forward pass, without a target view. It has the best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods on the complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols and keeps its accuracy from 6 to 42 input views.
AI.motivation: A feed-forward 3DGS predictor is less accurate than per-scene optimized Gaussians fitted to the same input images, and the gap lies mostly in Gaussian shape (scale and rotation), not in opacity or color.
AI.method: Log-anisotropy correction changes each Gaussian's axis ratios in log space at constant volume. In-forward gradient refinement renders the Gaussians into the input views, applies the gradient of the photometric loss through a learned recurrent update, first to opacity and color and then to shape.
AI.result: On both complete six-view RealEstate10K protocols, GradSplat has the best PSNR and SSIM among nine methods. Without fine-tuning, it is the most accurate on DL3DV and has the best PSNR and SSIM on ScanNet++.
AI.conclusion: Learned gradient steps on the input views, executed within a single feed-forward pass, can close much of the accuracy gap between feed-forward and per-scene optimized Gaussian splatting.

title: What do MLLMs know about 'Waldo'? Evaluating Visual Reasoning under Multi-Instance Multi-Object Challenges
summary: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have led to significant progress in visual reasoning capabilities. However, existing benchmarks curate image-question pairs pertaining to object categories with few instances, enabling trivial object referencing and limited visual ambiguity. In this work, we introduce MIMO-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs in a Multi-Instance per Multi-Object categories (MIMO) setting. Each image-question pair in our benchmark pertains to instances belonging to object categories with multiple instances. The presence of such similar feature distractors causes hindrance in basic visual reasoning tasks, necessitating the referring expression to be composed of multiple visual subtasks to uniquely and unambiguously identify the target object. MIMO-Bench comprises 3,802 image-question pairs across attribute binding and numerical counting tasks. Despite impressive performances on existing benchmarks, both SOTA open-source (InternVL, QwenVL) and proprietary (Gemini, GPT-5) models exhibit substantially lower performance on MIMO-Bench, highlighting their limitations in the MIMO setting. The benchmark will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: MIMO-Bench evaluates multimodal LLMs on visual reasoning where each image-question pair involves multiple instances of object categories that share similar features, requiring compositional referring expressions. Both open-source and proprietary models, including Gemini and GPT-5, perform substantially worse on it than on existing benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks use object categories with few instances, which allows trivial object referencing and limited visual ambiguity, so they do not test disambiguation among similar distractors.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 3,802 image-question pairs across attribute binding and numerical counting tasks, in which the referring expression must be composed of multiple visual subtasks to identify the target uniquely.
AI.result: SOTA open-source models (InternVL, QwenVL) and proprietary models (Gemini, GPT-5) show substantially lower performance on MIMO-Bench than on existing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: MLLMs have clear limitations in the multi-instance, multi-object setting, and the benchmark exposes them. The benchmark will be made publicly available.

title: AlbumVSR: Identity-Preserving Face Video Super-Resolution from a Personal Photo Album
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Nianyao Du and Xijun Wang contributed equally
summary: Severe blur, downsampling, noise, and compression can erase the identity cues needed to faithfully restore a person's face. We therefore use photographs of the same person as an external source of identity. AlbumVSR conditions a frozen, one-step streaming diffusion transformer on a personal album. We use four MagFace/CLIP set tokens to encode the album, and 64 texture tokens which come from a fused UV atlas rendered at the current window's estimated face pose. These tokens are appended to the transformer's cached cross-attention context. On an identity-disjoint VoxCeleb2 benchmark with heavy synthetic degradation, AlbumVSR raises ArcFace similarity to the ground truth from 0.586 to 0.670 and face PSNR from 24.98 to 26.71 dB. On the 91 test identities, its mean identity similarity is higher than that of all 14 baselines.

AI.tldr: AlbumVSR is a face video super-resolution method that uses a personal photo album of the same person as an external identity source, conditioning a frozen one-step streaming diffusion transformer on album and texture tokens. On a heavily degraded VoxCeleb2 benchmark it raises ArcFace similarity from 0.586 to 0.670 and face PSNR from 24.98 to 26.71 dB.
AI.motivation: Severe blur, downsampling, noise, and compression can erase the identity cues needed to restore a person's face faithfully, so an external source of identity is needed.
AI.method: Four MagFace/CLIP set tokens encode the album, and 64 texture tokens come from a fused UV atlas rendered at the current window's estimated face pose. These tokens are appended to the transformer's cached cross-attention context.
AI.result: On an identity-disjoint VoxCeleb2 benchmark with heavy synthetic degradation, ArcFace similarity to the ground truth rises from 0.586 to 0.670 and face PSNR from 24.98 to 26.71 dB. On 91 test identities, the mean identity similarity exceeds that of all 14 baselines.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning on a personal photo album preserves identity more faithfully than the compared baselines under severe degradation.

title: LightGenBench: A Benchmark for 3D Emission Generation
summary: Recent generation methods produce 3D assets with detailed geometry and rich textures. However, these assets are non-emissive: they reflect light but emit none. We study a new task, emission generation: predicting spatially varying RGB emission over a 3D asset's surface from its geometry, non-emissive materials, and a rendered view. To support this task, we introduce LightGenBench. Our benchmark makes three contributions. First, we curate a dataset of 37k artist-authored emissive assets in UV, voxel, and multi-view form. Second, we establish baselines across four method families: UV-domain, sparse-voxel, multi-view, and segmentation-based generation. Third, we design an evaluation protocol that measures where an asset emits and how, complemented by user-study comparisons on renderings with varying emission strength. Across the four families, the sparse-voxel baseline TRELLIS.2-Emission performs best because generating emission natively in 3D avoids the failure modes of the other representations, such as the fracturing artifacts of UV space and the occluded emitters that multi-view generation cannot see. However, TRELLIS.2-Emission only reaches an IoU of 0.271, leaving the task far from solved. We hope LightGenBench establishes emission generation as a benchmarkable problem for 3D generation.

AI.tldr: LightGenBench is a benchmark for emission generation, which predicts spatially varying RGB emission over a 3D asset's surface from its geometry, non-emissive materials, and a rendered view. Across four method families, the sparse-voxel baseline TRELLIS.2-Emission performs best, yet it reaches only an IoU of 0.271.
AI.motivation: Recent 3D generation methods produce assets with detailed geometry and rich textures but without emission, and no benchmark exists for predicting where and how a 3D asset should emit light.
AI.method: The authors curate 37k artist-authored emissive assets in UV, voxel, and multi-view form, establish baselines across UV-domain, sparse-voxel, multi-view, and segmentation-based generation, and design an evaluation protocol measuring where an asset emits and how, complemented by user-study comparisons at varying emission strengths.
AI.result: The sparse-voxel baseline TRELLIS.2-Emission performs best across the four families because generating emission natively in 3D avoids the fracturing artifacts of UV space and the occluded emitters that multi-view generation cannot see. It reaches an IoU of 0.271.
AI.conclusion: Emission generation remains far from solved, and the benchmark is intended to establish it as a benchmarkable problem for 3D generation.

title: Kinematic Causal Attribution: Black-Box Explanations of Motion versus Geometry for 4D Point-Cloud Video Models
summary: 4D perception models, which classify 3D point-cloud videos, are being built into robots, assistive monitoring and AR, yet before deploying one a practitioner cannot check which cue it relies on: how a body part moves, or what shape it has. 3D attribution is single-frame, video attribution is confined to RGB pixels, gradient maps need white-box access, attention is absent from state-space backbones, and point-level perturbations assume a point correspondence across frames that real depth and LiDAR data lack. We present Kinematic Causal Attribution (KCA), a black-box, interventional attribution method that queries only the model's outputs. Its freeze operator removes a region's motion while keeping its shape, and a shape-free proxy removes the shape while keeping the motion. Together they span a motion$\times$geometry cube for every tracked region, whose order-symmetric Shapley decomposition is complete and whose interaction is measured rather than assumed away. The operators rewrite per-frame point sets, so they need no correspondences, and a context-averaged estimator handles structures that span several regions. We validate KCA on the official PSTNet, P4Transformer and Mamba4D trained on MSR-Action3D. The decisive test is an audit: two binary tasks are built from real clips whose classes differ only in the motion or only in the shape of the same arm, and the motion share of the arm's importance follows the defining cue on all three backbones (0.83 vs. 0.60 on P4Transformer, 0.86 vs. 0.30 on PSTNet, 0.92 vs. 0.61 on Mamba4D), a distinction no single attribution map can make. The split costs no faithfulness: the necessity maps have the lowest deletion AUC on P4Transformer and PSTNet, tie with the best baseline on Mamba4D, and lose their correlation with the trained model's once the weights are randomised. Skeleton ground truth, re-sampling stability and cost complete the validation.

AI.tldr: Kinematic Causal Attribution (KCA) is a black-box, interventional attribution method for 4D point-cloud video models that separates how much a body region's motion versus its geometry drives a prediction. On three backbones, the motion share of an arm's importance follows the defining cue in an audit that no single attribution map can make.
AI.motivation: Existing attribution methods are single-frame, confined to RGB pixels, require white-box access, are absent for state-space backbones, or assume point correspondences across frames that real depth and LiDAR data lack.
AI.method: The freeze operator removes a region's motion while keeping its shape, and a shape-free proxy removes its shape while keeping its motion. Together they span a motion-by-geometry cube for each tracked region, whose order-symmetric Shapley decomposition is complete and whose interaction is measured. The operators rewrite per-frame point sets, so no correspondences are needed, and a context-averaged estimator handles structures spanning several regions.
AI.result: Validated on PSTNet, P4Transformer, and Mamba4D trained on MSR-Action3D, the motion share of the arm's importance is 0.83 vs. 0.60 on P4Transformer, 0.86 vs. 0.30 on PSTNet, and 0.92 vs. 0.61 on Mamba4D for the motion-defined vs. shape-defined tasks. Necessity maps have the lowest deletion AUC on P4Transformer and PSTNet and tie with the best baseline on Mamba4D.
AI.conclusion: The motion-geometry split comes at no cost in faithfulness, and it lets practitioners check which cue a 4D perception model relies on before deployment.

title: STRATA: Reinforcement-driven Active Sampling with Tri-paradigm Adaptation for Efficient 3D Spatial Transcriptomics
summary: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables joint characterization of tissue morphology and gene expression. However, 3D volumetric ST acquisition remains expensive. AI-driven methods offer a low-cost alternative but remain limited in accuracy, while recent 2D section-wise ST acquisition still rely on dense grid sampling, resulting in redundant measurements and undersampling of biologically informative regions. To bridge the gap, we propose STRATA, a reinforcement-driven active sampling framework with tri-paradigm adaptation for reconstructing dense 3D transcriptomic maps from sparse voxel-wise ST acquisition. STRATA constructs a 3D graph integrating H&E morphology with single-cell priors and employs a reinforcement learning agent to estimate morphological sparsity and transcriptomic informativeness, enabling budget-aware selection of informative spots. Given these sparse measurements, an adaptive tri-paradigm predictor combines retrieval, regression, and cross-layer imputation through lightweight fusion, dynamically weighting their contributions. Experiments across datasets demonstrate improved sampling efficiency and accuracy, particularly under low-budget settings. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: STRATA is a reinforcement-driven active sampling framework that reconstructs dense 3D transcriptomic maps from sparse voxel-wise spatial transcriptomics acquisition. It combines retrieval, regression, and cross-layer imputation with adaptive fusion, and improves sampling efficiency and accuracy, especially under low budgets.
AI.motivation: 3D volumetric spatial transcriptomics is expensive, AI-driven alternatives are limited in accuracy, and recent 2D section-wise acquisition relies on dense grid sampling, which yields redundant measurements and undersamples biologically informative regions.
AI.method: STRATA builds a 3D graph integrating H&E morphology with single-cell priors and uses a reinforcement learning agent to estimate morphological sparsity and transcriptomic informativeness, enabling budget-aware selection of informative spots. An adaptive tri-paradigm predictor combines retrieval, regression, and cross-layer imputation through lightweight fusion that dynamically weights each contribution.
AI.result: Experiments across datasets show improved sampling efficiency and accuracy, particularly under low-budget settings.
AI.conclusion: Learned, budget-aware active sampling combined with multi-paradigm prediction can reduce acquisition cost while preserving reconstruction accuracy for 3D spatial transcriptomics.

title: VEvo-Harness: Causally-Guarded Self-Evolving Harness for Agentic Image Generation
summary: The central bottleneck in visual generation and editing has migrated from achieving pixel-level fidelity to satisfying densely constrained user specifications through increasingly agentic workflows. Prevailing agentic generation pipelines remain shallow generate-verify-rewrite loops treating VLM judgments as coarse visual feedback, either discarding repair experience or admitting ungated updates that poison skill library. With memorize and govern periods left open, they degrade into ungoverned iterators of repeated trial-and-error rather than continual self-evolving harness. Towards this issue, we present \textbf{VEvo-Harness}, the first causally-guarded continual self-evolving harness system for agentic visual generation. VEvo-Harness introduces four coupled innovations: (1) \textit{a visual traceback} that densifies sparse judgments into root-cause attributions with a hierarchical verification tree; (2) \textit{a visual continual governance} that admits only causally valid skill patches through counterfactual dual-arm image generation replay; (3) \textit{a lifecycle-managed harness state} that hierarchically distills root-cause-anchored episodes across working, experience, and pattern tiers into a persistent skill library of routable and causally verified capabilities; (4) \textit{a heterogeneous sandbox policy} that orchestrates a diverse action space of repair primitives, dynamically routing cost-aware interventions based on root causes to select the most effective strategy. VEvo-Harness surpasses state-of-the-art agentic methods and rivals proprietary generators (\textit{e.g.}, GPT-Image, Nano-Pro) while maintaining the continual harness evolution and generalization.

AI.tldr: VEvo-Harness is a causally guarded, continually self-evolving harness for agentic image generation and editing, which admits skill updates only after they are causally verified. It surpasses state-of-the-art agentic methods and rivals proprietary generators such as GPT-Image and Nano-Pro.
AI.motivation: Current agentic generation pipelines are shallow generate-verify-rewrite loops that either discard repair experience or admit ungated updates that poison the skill library, so they degrade into trial-and-error iterators rather than continual self-evolving harnesses.
AI.method: Four coupled components are introduced: a visual traceback that turns sparse judgments into root-cause attributions with a hierarchical verification tree; visual continual governance that admits only causally valid skill patches through counterfactual dual-arm image generation replay; a lifecycle-managed harness state that distills episodes across working, experience, and pattern tiers into a persistent skill library; and a heterogeneous sandbox policy that routes cost-aware repair primitives according to root causes.
AI.result: VEvo-Harness surpasses state-of-the-art agentic methods and rivals proprietary generators such as GPT-Image and Nano-Pro while maintaining continual harness evolution and generalization.
AI.conclusion: Causal gating of memory and skill updates lets agentic visual generation evolve continually without degrading into ungoverned trial-and-error.

title: CLaW: Codec-Guided Adaptive Latent Watermarking for Traceable Diffusion Image Generation
summary: With the rapid advancement of text-to-image diffusion models, increasingly realistic AI-generated content has raised serious concerns about misuse and copyright infringement. Digital watermarking offers a promising solution by enabling user-level traceability, yet existing methods remain difficult to deploy at scale, hindered by costly model retraining or detection, poor effectiveness-fidelity trade-offs, and limited robustness to image transformations. To address these challenges, we propose CLaW (Codec-guided Latent Watermarking), a robust and efficient watermarking framework for traceable diffusion image generation with frozen diffusion backbones and inversion-free detection. Specifically, CLaW first uses a pretrained watermark codec to map each watermark message to a latent residual, enabling low-cost sampling-time injection. Then, the residual is injected within a late denoising window, where image semantics are better preserved and the watermark signal is less perturbed by subsequent denoising updates, yielding a better balance between watermark effectiveness and image fidelity. Furthermore, we introduce a decoder-guided adaptive injection mechanism that uses decoding confidence as feedback to dynamically calibrate watermark strength, reinforcing weak watermark signals and improving robustness under image transformations. Extensive experiments show that CLaW preserves high visual fidelity and achieves state-of-the-art robustness under image transformations, enabling reliable user-level traceability.

AI.tldr: CLaW is a watermarking framework for traceable text-to-image diffusion generation that injects a codec-mapped latent residual into a frozen backbone during a late denoising window. It uses decoder-guided adaptive injection and inversion-free detection, and achieves state-of-the-art robustness under image transformations with high visual fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion watermarking methods need costly retraining or detection, offer poor effectiveness-fidelity trade-offs, and are limited in robustness to image transformations, which hinders deployment at scale for user-level traceability.
AI.method: A pretrained watermark codec maps each message to a latent residual for low-cost sampling-time injection. The residual is injected in a late denoising window, where semantics are better preserved and the signal is less perturbed by later updates. A decoder-guided adaptive mechanism uses decoding confidence as feedback to calibrate watermark strength dynamically.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that CLaW preserves high visual fidelity and achieves state-of-the-art robustness under image transformations.
AI.conclusion: CLaW enables reliable user-level traceability of diffusion-generated images without retraining the backbone or requiring inversion-based detection.

title: Joint Rigid Alignment and Morphable Reconstruction from Partial 3D Face Scans
summary: Aligning a partial, real-world 3D face scan to a canonical representation requires solving two coupled problems at once: estimating the rigid pose that brings the scan into a common frame, and completing the facial shape in regions the scan never observed. Existing pipelines typically decouple these steps, running a generic point-cloud registration front end followed by a separate non-rigid fitting or deformation stage. Building on the GeoTransformer superpoint-matching architecture, we propose a single network that predicts both a rigid pose and a shape-complete point cloud in one forward pass: a cross-attention regressor, conditioned on transformer point features and predicted coarse correspondences, maps a partial scan to per-patch coefficients of a 3D morphable face model learned offline from a corpus of 8,000 identities. The resulting morphed template is then used, in the same forward pass, as the target for fine-grained Sinkhorn matching and rigid pose estimation, supervised purely by geometric alignment to ground-truth morphed geometry, so no hand-labeled coefficients are required. Against six classical and learned non-rigid registration baselines on held-out identities, our method leads the strongest ones by 3-4 times on per-vertex error and baselines that collapse the head onto the visible region by more than an order of magnitude, and is simultaneously the most accurate and fastest method on ground-truth-free scans from two independent real-scan datasets, NoW and NPHM. Code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: A single network jointly predicts the rigid pose and a shape-complete point cloud of a partial 3D face scan in one forward pass, built on the GeoTransformer superpoint-matching architecture. It leads six non-rigid registration baselines by 3-4 times on per-vertex error and is the most accurate and fastest method on NoW and NPHM real scans.
AI.motivation: Aligning a partial real-world face scan to a canonical representation requires both rigid pose estimation and completion of unobserved facial regions, but existing pipelines decouple these into a generic registration front end and a separate non-rigid fitting stage.
AI.method: A cross-attention regressor conditioned on transformer point features and predicted coarse correspondences maps the partial scan to per-patch coefficients of a 3D morphable face model learned offline from 8,000 identities. The morphed template then serves, in the same pass, as the target for fine-grained Sinkhorn matching and rigid pose estimation. Training uses only geometric alignment to ground-truth morphed geometry, so no hand-labeled coefficients are needed.
AI.result: On held-out identities, the method leads the strongest of six classical and learned non-rigid registration baselines by 3-4 times on per-vertex error, and baselines that collapse the head onto the visible region are worse by more than an order of magnitude. It is the most accurate and fastest method on ground-truth-free scans from NoW and NPHM.
AI.conclusion: Jointly solving rigid alignment and shape completion in one forward pass is both more accurate and faster than decoupled pipelines for partial 3D face scans. Code will be made publicly available.

title: Edited Endpoints as Partial Goals for Image-to-Video Generation
comment: 34 pages, 8 figures, 28 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Edited endpoint images make the target of an image-to-video transition explicit and can improve transition completion, but also preserve context in the source image's layout. Full-frame endpoint conditioning turns this preserved context into requirements on the video's final state, potentially inducing temporal artifacts. We measure discontinuity with Hard-Cut (HC), late background reversal with Background Motion Reversal (BMR), and motion suppression with Dynamic Degree (DD). These artifacts appear across five video models spanning training-free and learned endpoint conditioning, in model-specific forms. We study Partial, a selective conditioning scheme that constrains only an edit-relevant region estimated from image-editor attention and leaves the remaining terminal content to the video model. Across three backbones on TC-Bench-I2V, Partial reduces temporal artifacts relative to full-frame conditioning, with no significant difference in Transition Completion Ratio (TCR); on Wan2.2-Turbo, uniformly weakening conditioning does not reproduce these reductions. A donor-context intervention keeps full-frame conditioning and replaces only the context outside the edit-relevant region with the final frame of a Partial video. It lowers HC and BMR on HunyuanVideo-1.5 and lowers BMR while restoring DD on Wan2.2-Turbo, with no significant difference in TCR, so constraint extent alone does not account for these artifacts. Together, these findings suggest that edited endpoints should serve as partial future goals, although edit relevance does not guarantee future validity. Code and data will be released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Partial conditioning constrains only an edit-relevant region of an edited endpoint image in image-to-video generation, which reduces temporal artifacts relative to full-frame conditioning without significantly changing transition completion. The authors also show that the artifacts are not explained by constraint extent alone.
AI.motivation: Full-frame endpoint conditioning turns the source image's preserved context into requirements on the video's final state, which can induce temporal artifacts such as hard cuts, late background reversal, and motion suppression.
AI.method: Partial is a selective conditioning scheme that constrains only the edit-relevant region, estimated from image-editor attention, and leaves the remaining terminal content to the video model. A donor-context intervention keeps full-frame conditioning but replaces the context outside the edit-relevant region with the final frame of a Partial video. Artifacts are measured with Hard-Cut, Background Motion Reversal, and Dynamic Degree on TC-Bench-I2V.
AI.result: Across three backbones, Partial reduces temporal artifacts relative to full-frame conditioning with no significant difference in Transition Completion Ratio. On Wan2.2-Turbo, uniformly weakening conditioning does not reproduce these reductions. The donor-context intervention lowers Hard-Cut and Background Motion Reversal on HunyuanVideo-1.5 and lowers Background Motion Reversal while restoring Dynamic Degree on Wan2.2-Turbo.
AI.conclusion: Edited endpoints should serve as partial future goals, although edit relevance does not guarantee future validity.

title: Multi-level Constrained Learning for Underwater Image Enhancement
summary: Underwater image enhancement aims to correct color and recover detail degraded by wavelength-dependent attenuation, scattering, and noise. Paired-reference supervision constrains output similarity, but does not by itself specify the color mapping, the strength of local detail corrections, or consistency with the degraded observation. We propose MCL-UIE, a paired-supervised framework that addresses these requirements by constraining restoration operations and the training objective. Monotonic Chromatic Transform (MCT) restricts global color mapping in log-LMS space through positive diagonal entries and bounded cross-channel coefficients. Uncertainty-Gated Wavelet Reconstruction (UGWR) modulates high-frequency residuals with a learned confidence gate calibrated against normalized wavelet reconstruction errors. During training, Reference-Anchored Degradation Replay (RADR) renders the enhanced image and its paired reference using shared latent degradation proxies, encouraging both to reproduce the input. The three components share a restoration network that combines structured color correction, locally controlled detail recovery, and reference-anchored replay. MCL-UIE ranks first in thirteen of sixteen full-reference dataset-metric comparisons and produces competitive visual results on no-reference benchmarks. Objective ablations indicate that confidence calibration is most effective when combined with replay supervision. RADR is used only during training and adds no inference-time computation. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MCL-UIE is a paired-supervised underwater image enhancement framework that constrains the color mapping, local detail corrections, and training objective. It ranks first in thirteen of sixteen full-reference dataset-metric comparisons and is competitive on no-reference benchmarks, with its replay component adding no inference-time cost.
AI.motivation: Paired-reference supervision constrains output similarity but does not by itself specify the color mapping, the strength of local detail corrections, or consistency with the degraded observation.
AI.method: Monotonic Chromatic Transform restricts global color mapping in log-LMS space through positive diagonal entries and bounded cross-channel coefficients. Uncertainty-Gated Wavelet Reconstruction modulates high-frequency residuals with a learned confidence gate calibrated against normalized wavelet reconstruction errors. Reference-Anchored Degradation Replay, used only in training, renders the enhanced image and its paired reference from shared latent degradation proxies so that both reproduce the input.
AI.result: MCL-UIE ranks first in thirteen of sixteen full-reference dataset-metric comparisons and produces competitive visual results on no-reference benchmarks. Objective ablations indicate that confidence calibration is most effective when combined with replay supervision.
AI.conclusion: Constraining both the restoration operations and the training objective yields strong full-reference results, and the replay term improves training without adding inference computation.

title: COGS: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Attribute-Aware Object-Level 3D Gaussian Splatting Perception
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027, Datasets and Benchmarks Track. 20 pages, including references and supplementary material
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is increasingly explored as an input representation for 3D perception. Yet it remains unclear how current 3D architectures exploit heterogeneous Gaussian attributes. This ambiguity makes accuracy hard to interpret and limits principled architecture design for 3DGS perception. However, existing object-level 3DGS datasets lack the appearance variation or artifact control needed for systematic attribute-level analysis. We introduce COGS, a large-scale 3DGS dataset with 15,675 artifact-filtered and appearance-rich objects across 40 categories. Built on COGS, we establish COGS-Bench for object classification and attribute-usage diagnosis, complemented by external validation. Our benchmark shows that Gaussian attributes are not uniformly beneficial: selected subsets can outperform the full attribute set, and the effects of appearance, opacity, and covariance-related attribute combinations vary substantially across architectures. We further study this finding with HALO, a reference model that preserves attribute-specific evidence before hierarchical aggregation. Experiments on COGS-Bench and external 3DGS datasets demonstrate that COGS supports systematic diagnosis of 3DGS attribute usage, while HALO highlights the value of role-preserving attribute organization. Our dataset is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: COGS is a dataset of 15,675 artifact-filtered, appearance-rich object-level 3D Gaussian Splatting assets across 40 categories, with COGS-Bench for classification and attribute-usage diagnosis. The benchmark shows that Gaussian attributes are not uniformly beneficial, and that the HALO reference model, which preserves attribute-specific evidence, highlights the value of role-preserving attribute organization.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how current 3D architectures exploit heterogeneous Gaussian attributes, and existing object-level 3DGS datasets lack the appearance variation or artifact control needed for systematic attribute-level analysis.
AI.method: The authors build COGS, a large-scale 3DGS dataset, and establish COGS-Bench for object classification and attribute-usage diagnosis, complemented by external validation. They also study HALO, a reference model that preserves attribute-specific evidence before hierarchical aggregation.
AI.result: Selected attribute subsets can outperform the full attribute set, and the effects of appearance, opacity, and covariance-related attribute combinations vary substantially across architectures. Experiments on COGS-Bench and external 3DGS datasets show that COGS supports systematic diagnosis of attribute usage, and HALO highlights the value of role-preserving attribute organization.
AI.conclusion: Systematic diagnosis of Gaussian attribute usage is needed for principled architecture design in 3DGS perception, since attributes are not uniformly useful across architectures.

title: Seeing and Imagining as One: Unified Video Generation and 4D Perception for Embodied World Modeling
summary: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.

AI.tldr: GenSight is a unified embodied world model that uses a single pretrained video diffusion transformer to generate future video and predict dense perception (depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow) in one shared representation. It shows strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception.
AI.motivation: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world, and existing pipelines use separate modality-specific components.
AI.method: A unified spatiotemporal representation covers video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow, and a shared DiT backbone with lightweight task modulation predicts all modalities. All tasks are jointly optimized in a unified velocity prediction space. At inference it runs either multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions, or single-step dense perception from an observed video.
AI.result: Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception.
AI.conclusion: Unifying modality representation, architecture, and prediction space promotes cross-modal consistency and lets dense perception benefit from spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation.

title: DeCoRL: Decomposed Consistency Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Image Composition
summary: Multi-image composition (MICo) is a critical yet challenging capability for large-scale image editing models, where consistency degrades rapidly as the number of reference images increases. While supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip models with basic MICo ability, it provides only implicit supervision on the composed image and often fails to learn reliable object-level correspondence across multiple references. We propose DeCoRL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that improves MICo consistency by decomposing holistic MICo consistency into object-level consistency. DeCoRL first establishes instruction-relevant object correspondences across reference images and localizes the corresponding regions in the generated image. It then uses a VLM-based reward model trained on single-object consistency annotations to produce fine-grained, object-wise feedback, which is aggregated into a multi-object consistency reward to guide RL post-training. We further introduce DeCo-Bench, a benchmark covering compositions from 2 to 6 reference images. Experiments on DeCo-Bench and the public MICo-Bench demonstrate consistent improvements in MICo consistency.

AI.tldr: DeCoRL is a reinforcement-learning framework that improves multi-image composition consistency in image editing by decomposing holistic consistency into object-level consistency with a VLM-based reward. It is evaluated on the newly introduced DeCo-Bench and the public MICo-Bench, with consistent improvements reported.
AI.motivation: Consistency in multi-image composition degrades rapidly as the number of reference images grows, and supervised fine-tuning gives only implicit supervision on the composed image and often fails to learn reliable object-level correspondence across references.
AI.method: DeCoRL first establishes instruction-relevant object correspondences across reference images and localizes the corresponding regions in the generated image. A VLM-based reward model, trained on single-object consistency annotations, produces fine-grained object-wise feedback that is aggregated into a multi-object consistency reward to guide RL post-training. DeCo-Bench covers compositions from 2 to 6 reference images.
AI.result: Experiments on DeCo-Bench and the public MICo-Bench demonstrate consistent improvements in multi-image composition consistency.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing holistic consistency into object-level rewards is an effective way to improve multi-reference composition in large-scale image editing models.

title: Efficient Covariance-Aware Vicinal Latent Diffusion for Continuous Conditional Image Generation
summary: Continuous Conditional Generative Modeling (CCGM) aims to synthesize high-dimensional data conditioned on continuously valued scalar labels. However, existing continuous diffusion models face severe data sparsity under imbalanced and long-tailed label distributions, which can lead to visual artifacts and condition inconsistency. Moreover, inference-time classifier-free guidance and dense pixel-space integration introduce substantial sampling overhead, limiting practical deployment. To address these challenges, we propose CAViLD, an efficient latent diffusion framework for continuous conditional generation. CAViLD first constructs a purified condition-aware latent space through density-adaptive vicinal learning, auxiliary semantic regularization, and NIQE-guided negative data augmentation. It then internalizes the conditional guidance direction through an EMA teacher, enabling single-branch conditional inference, and introduces covariance-aware progressive distillation for label-dependent probability-flow ODEs, supporting sampling down to four NFEs. Experiments on RC-49, UTKFace, and Steering Angle demonstrate a favorable trade-off among generation fidelity, continuous condition consistency, and sampling efficiency.

AI.tldr: CAViLD is an efficient latent diffusion framework for continuous conditional image generation that addresses data sparsity under imbalanced labels and reduces sampling to as few as four function evaluations. It achieves a favorable trade-off among fidelity, condition consistency, and sampling efficiency on RC-49, UTKFace, and Steering Angle.
AI.motivation: Continuous diffusion models face severe data sparsity under imbalanced and long-tailed label distributions, which causes visual artifacts and condition inconsistency, while classifier-free guidance and dense pixel-space integration add substantial sampling overhead.
AI.method: The framework builds a purified condition-aware latent space through density-adaptive vicinal learning, auxiliary semantic regularization, and NIQE-guided negative data augmentation. An EMA teacher internalizes the conditional guidance direction to enable single-branch conditional inference, and covariance-aware progressive distillation is applied to label-dependent probability-flow ODEs.
AI.result: Experiments on RC-49, UTKFace, and Steering Angle demonstrate a favorable trade-off among generation fidelity, continuous condition consistency, and sampling efficiency, with sampling supported down to four function evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Covariance-aware distillation and a purified latent space make continuous conditional generation practical to deploy with few sampling steps while keeping fidelity and label consistency.

title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
summary: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence. Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations remain tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision, providing a limited learning signal for physical dynamics. To circumvent these limitations, we introduce \method{}, a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories. By parameterizing 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid, a unified Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) backbone jointly denoises both modalities under a rectified-flow objective. This formulation couples explicit geometric dynamics with visual evolution, effectively unlocking the physical commonsense embedded within pretrained video models. To empirically scale and validate this unified architecture, we train \method{} on a heterogeneous mixture of 1.44 million object-level samples spanning simulated and real-world domains. We further introduce WorldFlowBench, comprising 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources across simulated and real-world interactions, including spatial reasoning tasks. Across all three evaluation sets, WorldFlow achieves the lowest average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) among the evaluated learning-based methods. Notably, on the challenging SpatialCog set, WorldFlow achieves an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2\% reduction compared with the strongest external baseline. It also reduces ADE and FDE by 55.9\% and 68.5\%, respectively, compared with its flow-only variant. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: WorldFlow is a generative world model that jointly predicts future video and query-based 3D trajectories with a unified Mixture-of-Transformers backbone, trained on 1.44 million object-level samples. It achieves the lowest ADE and FDE among the evaluated learning-based methods on three evaluation sets.
AI.motivation: Existing video world models leave 3D dynamics implicit, action-based formulations are tied to specific robot configurations, and 3D motion prediction models use flow-only supervision that gives a limited learning signal for physical dynamics.
AI.method: The model parameterizes 3D motion as continuous displacement tokens aligned with the video grid and uses a unified Mixture-of-Transformers backbone that jointly denoises video and motion under a rectified-flow objective, unlocking physical commonsense from pretrained video models; the authors also introduce WorldFlowBench with 1,678 evaluation samples from 11 data sources.
AI.result: On the SpatialCog set WorldFlow reaches an ADE of 0.060 m, a 54.2% reduction over the strongest external baseline, and relative to its flow-only variant it reduces ADE by 55.9% and FDE by 68.5%.
AI.conclusion: Coupling explicit 3D motion with visual evolution in one generative model gives better physical prediction than video-only or flow-only supervision, suggesting a useful route to physically grounded world models.

title: PriorMaskMap: Robust Online Vectorized Map Construction with Biased Priors
summary: Online vectorized map construction provides autonomous vehicles with essential, real-time semantic and geometric scene understanding. While leveraging prior maps presents an opportunity to improve accuracy, they are often biased due to outdated information or temporary road changes. Existing methods, which typically treat priors as fully reliable or only consider limited noise patterns, suffer severe performance degradation when these priors are imperfect. To address this, we propose PriorMaskMap, a robust framework for prior-guided vectorized map construction. Its first innovation is a Prior-Aware Confidence Estimator (PACE) that evaluates the input rasterized map against current visual observations. It assigns confidence scores to regions classified as reliable, erroneous, or blank, creating a foundational mask that guides two subsequent branches. In one branch, the Dual-Prior Query Generator (DPQG) selectively filters and embeds both rasterized and vectorized priors to initialize informative queries from trustworthy map structures. In the other, the Confidence-Guided Prior Fusion (CGPF) module spatially propagates and refines the mask, using the refined version to govern the fusion of BEV features with the prior map, thereby providing rich contextual representations for the map decoder. Evaluation on the nuScenes dataset shows that PriorMaskMap achieves superior mapping precision over existing approaches and exhibits marked robustness when provided with priors containing apparent errors. Our code is released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: PriorMaskMap is a robust framework for online vectorized map construction that uses possibly biased prior maps, estimating per-region confidence to decide which priors to trust. It shows superior mapping precision on nuScenes and marked robustness when priors contain apparent errors.
AI.motivation: Prior maps can be outdated or temporarily wrong, while existing methods treat priors as fully reliable or only model limited noise patterns, so they degrade severely when priors are imperfect.
AI.method: A Prior-Aware Confidence Estimator compares the rasterized prior with current visual observations and labels regions as reliable, erroneous or blank to form a confidence mask; this mask guides a Dual-Prior Query Generator that filters rasterized and vectorized priors to initialize queries, and a Confidence-Guided Prior Fusion module that refines the mask and governs BEV feature fusion with the prior map.
AI.result: Evaluated on nuScenes, the method achieves higher mapping precision than existing approaches; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly estimating prior reliability and gating prior use per region makes map construction robust to imperfect priors, which matters for autonomous driving where prior maps are often stale.

title: Youtu-Parsing-Omni: One Encoder, One Schema, All Modalities
summary: We present Youtu-Parsing-Omni, an omni-modal parser that converts documents, images, audio, and video into structured records grounded in space and time, providing a perception layer for agents that read, locate, and cite evidence across modalities. Its design rests on one encoder for every modality and one schema for every task. Youtu-Omni-Encoder, initialized from a pre-trained language model to strengthen text reading, encodes all modalities with shared weights in a unified space-time coordinate system, and a few fusion layers let video frames attend to concurrent audio, bringing cross-modal fusion and temporal alignment into perception itself. OmniSchema unifies the outputs of all ten parsing tasks, allowing a single self-evolving post-training procedure, OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD), to provide a shared token-role-based objective across tasks. In each round, the model is trained on its own rollouts against token-level targets from a reference-conditioned copy of itself, which is then refreshed with the trained weights, so that the parser and its supervision co-evolve. With a single 5 B-parameter checkpoint, Youtu-Parsing-Omni achieves state-of-the-art performance on OmniDocBench v1.6 (96.96 Overall) and leads all open-weight models on OmniParsingBench (75.08 Avg.), with its advantage concentrated on audio and video. It also achieves the best overall chart-parsing score (95.02) and the highest exact chemical-fingerprint agreement among compared systems, and matches a dedicated optical-music model in character-level transcription of typeset sheet music while staying far ahead of general-purpose systems. Code and model weights are publicly available.

AI.tldr: Youtu-Parsing-Omni is an omni-modal parser that converts documents, images, audio and video into structured, space-time grounded records using one encoder and one schema. A single 5B-parameter checkpoint reaches state-of-the-art results on OmniDocBench v1.6 and leads open-weight models on OmniParsingBench.
AI.motivation: The abstract frames the need as a perception layer for agents that must read, locate and cite evidence across modalities, which requires cross-modal fusion and temporal alignment to be handled within perception itself.
AI.method: Youtu-Omni-Encoder, initialized from a pre-trained language model, encodes all modalities with shared weights in a unified space-time coordinate system, and fusion layers let video frames attend to concurrent audio; OmniSchema unifies the outputs of ten parsing tasks, and OmniSchema-Aware On-Policy Distillation (OSAD) trains the model on its own rollouts against token-level targets from a periodically refreshed reference-conditioned copy of itself.
AI.result: The model scores 96.96 Overall on OmniDocBench v1.6 and 75.08 Avg. on OmniParsingBench, with its advantage concentrated on audio and video; it also reaches 95.02 on chart parsing and the highest exact chemical-fingerprint agreement among compared systems.
AI.conclusion: A single unified encoder, schema and self-evolving distillation procedure can handle heterogeneous parsing tasks, and the code and model weights are publicly released.

title: MemoryFusion: Cross-Temporal Memory Learning for Multimodal Video Fusion
summary: Multimodal videos contain rich temporal cues that can facilitate faithful fusion. However, existing video fusion methods mainly rely on short-range temporal interactions, leaving valuable long-term information underexplored. Moreover, inconsistent fusion representations can cause flickering artifacts, undermining temporal coherence. To address these coupled challenges, we propose MemoryFusion, a two-stage framework integrating cross-temporal memory learning with progressive temporal refinement. Considering the complementary roles of adjacent and distant frames, the first stage combines a Short-Term Memory Bank for local temporal guidance with a Long-Term Memory Bank that preserves reliable historical information through a fusion-oriented update strategy. To mitigate temporal fluctuations, a Temporal Smoothing Module leverages soft motion cues for coarse background stabilization. Building upon the resulting fusion prior, The second stage further employs a lightweight 3D residual Temporal Refinement Module to correct remaining temporal inconsistencies while enhancing structural details. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MemoryFusion achieves superior fusion quality and temporal consistency over existing frame-based and video-based fusion methods. The source code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MemoryFusion is a two-stage multimodal video fusion framework that uses cross-temporal memory to exploit long-range information and suppress flickering. The paper reports superior fusion quality and temporal consistency over frame-based and video-based fusion methods.
AI.motivation: Existing video fusion methods rely mainly on short-range temporal interactions, leaving long-term information underexplored, and inconsistent fusion representations cause flickering artifacts that harm temporal coherence.
AI.method: The first stage combines a Short-Term Memory Bank for local guidance with a Long-Term Memory Bank updated by a fusion-oriented strategy, plus a Temporal Smoothing Module that uses soft motion cues for coarse background stabilization; the second stage applies a lightweight 3D residual Temporal Refinement Module to correct remaining inconsistencies and enhance structural details.
AI.result: The abstract states that MemoryFusion achieves superior fusion quality and temporal consistency over existing frame-based and video-based methods, without reporting specific metrics.
AI.conclusion: Combining short- and long-term temporal memory with staged refinement offers a practical way to make multimodal video fusion both high quality and temporally stable.

title: MRC-MMAgent: Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Role Collaboration in Multimodal Tool-Using Agents
summary: Multimodal tool-using agents augment vision-language models with access to external information and capabilities, enabling them to solve knowledge-intensive and visually complex tasks that cannot be addressed using visual context alone. However, existing reinforcement learning pipelines largely train single-role agents to search and answer using terminal rewards, overlooking how humans inspect retrieved evidence, reformulate queries, and revise conclusions during search. Consequently, they fail to optimize this self-corrective process over complete interaction trajectories. We propose MRC-MMAgent, a multi-role collaborative reinforcement learning framework that incorporates trajectory assessment and continuation directly into the executable agent loop. First, the framework establishes a multi-role collaborative loop that integrates solving, inspection, and continuation, enabling the agent to acquire evidence through tools, evaluate the preceding trajectory, and resume problem solving when the current answer is insufficiently supported. Second, we introduce a role-coupled learning objective that combines task success, interaction validity, and successful correction with full-trajectory policy optimization across the decisions generated by all roles. Extensive experiments show that, using only the original baseline training set without constructing additional datasets, our method consistently outperforms the corresponding base models and achieves leading or highly competitive performance across benchmarks.

AI.tldr: MRC-MMAgent is a multi-role collaborative reinforcement learning framework for multimodal tool-using agents that adds inspection and continuation roles to the solving loop. Using only the original baseline training set, it consistently outperforms its base models and achieves leading or highly competitive performance across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RL pipelines train single-role agents with terminal rewards, overlooking how humans inspect retrieved evidence, reformulate queries and revise conclusions, so they cannot optimize the self-corrective process over full trajectories.
