AI.method: A multi-role loop integrates solving, inspection and continuation, letting the agent evaluate the preceding trajectory and resume solving when the answer is insufficiently supported; a role-coupled objective combines task success, interaction validity and successful correction with full-trajectory policy optimization over decisions from all roles.
AI.result: The abstract reports consistent gains over the corresponding base models and leading or highly competitive performance across benchmarks, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing the whole self-correcting trajectory across roles, rather than only terminal answers, improves multimodal tool-using agents without constructing additional datasets.

title: Can Image Agents Complete Visual Commissions? A Benchmark and Modular Framework
summary: Visual commissions require image agents to integrate heterogeneous source materials, preserve requirements across dependent stages, and produce coordinated deliverables. Existing evaluations examine specific capabilities and execution settings, leaving end-to-end commission completion less understood. We introduce Visual Commission Bench (VCB), comprising 600 tasks across 12 categories and three complementary tiers, from capability-focused tasks to complete commissions. VCB uses 5,039 requirement checks and separate visual quality ratings to assess content correctness, visual realization, constraint preservation, and delivery completeness without prescribing an internal workflow. We present V-Protocol, a reference agent that dynamically composes reusable task, cognitive, and expression modules at inference time. Task modules organize delivery, cognitive modules derive content, and expression modules guide visual realization. The modules exchange structured intermediate artifacts, while a shared execution harness tracks artifact revisions and dependencies, manages tool execution, and checks completion. With the same controller and image generator as the agent baselines, V-Protocol achieves 69.0\% strict task success on VCB, compared with 42.0\% for SCOPE. On Mind-Bench, strict accuracy increases from 39.2\% to 45.4\%.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Visual Commission Bench (VCB), a 600-task benchmark for end-to-end commission completion by image agents, and V-Protocol, a reference agent that composes modular task, cognitive and expression modules at inference time. V-Protocol reaches 69.0% strict task success on VCB versus 42.0% for SCOPE.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations examine specific capabilities and execution settings, so end-to-end completion of visual commissions, which require integrating heterogeneous materials and preserving requirements across dependent stages, is poorly understood.
AI.method: VCB spans 12 categories and three tiers from capability-focused tasks to complete commissions, with 5,039 requirement checks and separate visual quality ratings; V-Protocol dynamically composes reusable task, cognitive and expression modules that exchange structured intermediate artifacts, while a shared harness tracks artifact revisions and dependencies, manages tool execution and checks completion.
AI.result: With the same controller and image generator as the agent baselines, V-Protocol achieves 69.0% strict task success on VCB compared with 42.0% for SCOPE; on Mind-Bench, strict accuracy rises from 39.2% to 45.4%.
AI.conclusion: Structured, dependency-tracked module composition is a promising way to complete end-to-end visual commissions without prescribing a fixed internal workflow.

title: Telling Is Not Seeing: Textual Personas Rarely Make Vision-Language Models Answer Like the People They Describe
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly prompted with personas, such as "You have low vision", to stand in for people in user studies. We ask whether a persona makes a model see like the person it describes. We compare persona answers with measured people with low vision, color blindness or hearing loss, and with simple rules that use only the facts the persona states. The persona never beats these rules, and it erases the real differences between groups and individuals. Describing blur leaves recognition unchanged in all 14 models we test, while blurring the photo lowers it as it does for people. Inside open models, the description changes neither the image information nor the answer probabilities. Yet the models know the effects they fail to show: they can estimate how blur and illusions affect people. Telling is not seeing: a persona makes a model say what it knows about people, not see what they see.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that textual personas such as "You have low vision" rarely make vision-language models answer like the people they describe. Persona answers never beat simple rules built from the stated facts, and they erase real differences between groups and individuals.
AI.motivation: VLMs are increasingly prompted with personas to stand in for people in user studies, but it is unknown whether a persona makes a model perceive the world as the described person does.
AI.method: The authors compare persona answers with measured responses from people with low vision, color blindness or hearing loss, against rule-based baselines that use only the facts the persona states, and they probe 14 models, including open models whose image information and answer probabilities are examined directly.
AI.result: Describing blur leaves recognition unchanged in all 14 models tested, while actually blurring the photo lowers recognition as it does for people; in open models the description changes neither image information nor answer probabilities, although models can estimate how blur and illusions affect people.
AI.conclusion: A persona makes a model state what it knows about people rather than reproduce what they perceive, so persona-based simulation should not replace measuring real users.

title: PicturePerfect: Diffusion-based Same-identity Facial Replacement
comment: Camera-ready version (ECCV 2026 workshop - Third Workshop on Foundation and Generative Models in Biometrics)
summary: With the growing success of diffusion models in computer vision, we explore their potential for same-identity facial replacement in photographs. Specifically, we propose a diffusion-based method, built on top of a pre-trained text-to-image model, that takes as input a portrait image of a person and a second reference image of the same individual, potentially captured under different conditions. The goal is to seamlessly replace the input face with the reference face, while keeping the background intact. Surprisingly, despite the clear real-world utility of this task, no recently published work has directly addressed face replacement in this specific setting. To support this goal, we construct a large dataset of image pairs depicting the same person under varying facial expressions and poses. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach produces more realistic and identity-consistent results than existing face reenactment models.

AI.tldr: PicturePerfect is a diffusion-based method for same-identity facial replacement that swaps the face in a portrait for a reference face of the same person while keeping the background intact. The authors also build a dataset of same-person image pairs with varied expressions and poses, and report more realistic and identity-consistent results than face reenactment models.
AI.motivation: Same-identity face replacement has clear practical value, yet the abstract notes that no recent published work has directly addressed this setting.
AI.method: Built on a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model, the method takes a portrait and a second reference image of the same individual, possibly captured under different conditions, and is supported by a newly constructed large dataset of image pairs of the same person under varying expressions and poses.
AI.result: Experiments show more realistic and identity-consistent results than existing face reenactment models; the abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models built on text-to-image priors are a viable route to same-identity face replacement, a setting the authors distinguish from face reenactment.

title: CASE: Concept-Aware Segmentation from Positive and Negative Visual Exemplars
summary: Few-shot semantic segmentation typically identifies target objects based on positive support examples of a single semantic class. In practice, however, positive cues alone are often underspecified: for instance, "red cars" may be confused with cars of all colors, "vehicles" may include cars that should be excluded, and "material-defined objects" may span multiple categories. Fulfilling precise requests requires positive exemplars to provide inclusion evidence and negative exemplars to act as intent-defining constraints for exclusion and disambiguation. We formulate this setting as Specified Visual Prompt Segmentation (SVPS), where the target concept is specified by both positive and negative visual prompts. In this work, visual exemplars refer to support-image regions specified by bounding-box prompts. To study SVPS, we introduce CASE (Concept-Aware Segmentation from Positive and Negative Visual Exemplars), a benchmark built on COCO and PACO. CASE encompasses six category- and attribute-level task families: exclusion, isolation, union, attribute exclusion, attribute isolation, and attribute union. We evaluate SAM 3 under this setting and find that, despite its powerful positive-only few-shot segmentation capability, frozen SAM 3 does not consistently treat negative visual prompts as exclusion evidence. To address this, we present Concept Prompt Adaptation (CPA), a conservative LoRA-based adaptation baseline that improves positive-negative prompt interpretation on CASE while remaining competitive under positive-only few-shot segmentation. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates Specified Visual Prompt Segmentation (SVPS), where a target concept is defined by both positive and negative visual exemplars, and introduces the CASE benchmark on COCO and PACO. It finds that frozen SAM 3 does not consistently treat negative prompts as exclusion evidence, and proposes a LoRA-based Concept Prompt Adaptation baseline that improves this.
AI.motivation: Few-shot segmentation identifies targets from positive support examples only, but positive cues are often underspecified, so precise requests such as "red cars" or "vehicles excluding cars" need negative exemplars to constrain the concept.
AI.method: CASE covers six task families (exclusion, isolation and union, at both category and attribute level) built from bounding-box visual prompts on COCO and PACO; the proposed Concept Prompt Adaptation is a conservative LoRA-based adaptation of SAM 3.
AI.result: Frozen SAM 3 does not consistently treat negative visual prompts as exclusion evidence; CPA improves positive-negative prompt interpretation on CASE while remaining competitive under positive-only few-shot segmentation. The abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Negative exemplars are needed to specify concepts precisely, and lightweight adaptation can teach a positive-only segmenter to use them without losing its few-shot ability.

title: ACD-GS: Asymmetric Curvature-aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for real-time photorealistic novel view synthesis. However, its training-time densification remains largely heuristic, often resulting in redundant Gaussian proliferation and inaccurate geometric reconstruction. Existing methods predominantly rely on first-order screen-space gradients to trigger cloning and splitting, which fail to distinguish true geometric discontinuities from high-frequency textures or noisy residuals. To address this limitation, we propose ACD-GS, an Asymmetric Curvature-aware Densification framework for compact and geometry-aware 3D Gaussian optimization. Our key insight is that second-order depth responses provide a more reliable structural prior for density control, enabling asymmetric regulation of cloning and splitting to better capture geometric discontinuities. Building on this, we introduce a multi-view photometric consistency constraint to suppress transient single-view errors, together with a capacity-aware adaptive regulation strategy that balances densification and pruning during training. Unlike post-hoc compression or quantization-based approaches, ACD-GS directly prevents redundant Gaussian generation during training, yielding inherently compact representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method reduces nearly 60% of Gaussian count and storage while maintaining competitive rendering fidelity, consistently outperforming existing methods across multiple datasets. Our code is available in this https URL.

AI.tldr: ACD-GS is an asymmetric curvature-aware densification framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that uses second-order depth responses to control cloning and splitting. It reduces nearly 60% of the Gaussian count and storage while keeping competitive rendering fidelity.
AI.motivation: Densification in 3DGS is largely heuristic and relies on first-order screen-space gradients, which cannot distinguish true geometric discontinuities from high-frequency textures or noisy residuals, leading to redundant Gaussians and inaccurate geometry.
AI.method: Second-order depth responses provide a structural prior for asymmetric regulation of cloning and splitting; a multi-view photometric consistency constraint suppresses transient single-view errors, and a capacity-aware adaptive regulation strategy balances densification and pruning during training.
AI.result: The method reduces nearly 60% of the Gaussian count and storage while maintaining competitive rendering fidelity, and consistently outperforms existing methods across multiple datasets.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware densification during training yields compact representations directly, without relying on post-hoc compression or quantization.

title: SymKL: A Unified Representation-Space Measure of Signal Degradation
summary: Quantifying degradation between a pristine signal and its degraded observation is fundamental to signal processing, yet existing full-reference measures are inherently modality-specific. We introduce SymKL, a unified full-reference degradation measure based on implicit neural representations (INRs). An INR is fitted once to the pristine reference and characterized by its diagonal Fisher information, which captures the local information geometry of the learned representation. Evaluating the Fisher information with the pristine reference and a degraded observation yields two parameter-sensitivity profiles whose symmetric KL divergence defines the degradation score. The proposed formulation requires only the reference and degraded observation, without knowledge of the corruption process or degradation severity, making it applicable across images, audio, and 3D data. We further derive an exact closed-form expression for the diagonal Fisher of SIREN, enabling efficient computation. Experiments on image, speech, and volumetric 3D benchmarks demonstrate that SymKL accurately tracks degradation severity, remains monotonic where conventional metrics saturate or fail, and provides a unified modality-agnostic measure of signal degradation. Code will be made publicly available after the review process.

AI.tldr: SymKL is a unified full-reference degradation measure built on implicit neural representations, comparing the parameter-sensitivity profiles of a pristine reference and a degraded observation through the symmetric KL divergence of their diagonal Fisher information. It applies across images, audio and 3D data and tracks degradation severity more reliably than conventional metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing full-reference measures are modality-specific, so there is no common way to quantify degradation between a clean signal and its corrupted version across signal types.
AI.method: An INR is fitted once to the pristine reference and characterized by its diagonal Fisher information; the Fisher information is evaluated for the reference and for the degraded observation, and their symmetric KL divergence gives the score, requiring no knowledge of the corruption process or severity. An exact closed-form diagonal Fisher for SIREN enables efficient computation.
AI.result: Experiments on image, speech and volumetric 3D benchmarks show that SymKL accurately tracks degradation severity and stays monotonic where conventional metrics saturate or fail; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: SymKL provides a modality-agnostic measure of signal degradation grounded in the information geometry of learned representations.

title: YOLOF-MLD: A Multi-Level Distillation Framework for Efficient Object Detection
summary: Efficient object detection on resource-constrained edge devices is essential for safety-critical applications such as fire-smoke monitoring. However, current lightweight frameworks, such as YOLO26, still rely on the parameter-dense multi-branch Feature Pyramid Network (FPN), preventing full exploitation of their lightweight advantage. Replacing FPN with YOLOF's single-input-single-output (SiSo) neck is a promising solution but causes substantial accuracy loss. To alleviate this, we propose YOLOF-MLD, a CPU-efficient multi-level distillation (MLD) framework that combines a YOLO26n backbone, a SiSo neck, and MLD. It aligns features at the backbone via sliced-semantics matching, neck with receptive-field matching, and response levels. On D-Fire and Annotated Fire-Smoke (AFS) datasets, YOLOF-MLD reduces the parameter count of YOLO26n by 35.7\% and achieves a 62.3\% speedup on Raspberry Pi 5, attaining 71.6% and 59.9% mAP@50, respectively, compared with 75.5% and 60.0% for YOLO26n. These results demonstrate a competitive accuracy--latency trade-off for edge deployment. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: YOLOF-MLD is a CPU-efficient multi-level distillation framework that pairs a YOLO26n backbone with YOLOF's single-input-single-output neck for edge object detection. It cuts YOLO26n's parameter count by 35.7% and gives a 62.3% speedup on Raspberry Pi 5, with a small drop in mAP@50.
AI.motivation: Lightweight detectors such as YOLO26 still use a parameter-dense multi-branch FPN, and replacing it with YOLOF's SiSo neck saves parameters but causes substantial accuracy loss.
AI.method: Multi-level distillation (MLD) aligns features at three levels: the backbone via sliced-semantics matching, the neck via receptive-field matching, and the response level.
AI.result: On D-Fire and AFS, mAP@50 is 71.6% and 59.9% for YOLOF-MLD versus 75.5% and 60.0% for YOLO26n, alongside the 35.7% parameter reduction and 62.3% Raspberry Pi 5 speedup.
AI.conclusion: The method offers a competitive accuracy-latency trade-off for edge deployment in safety-critical settings such as fire-smoke monitoring.

title: Anatomical Prior-Guided Routing for 3D Lung Tumor Segmentation
summary: Accurate lung tumor segmentation in computed tomography (CT) is essential for treatment planning, response assessment, and quantitative imaging analysis. However, 3D lung tumor segmentation remains challenging because tumors occupy only a small portion of the whole volume and exhibit heterogeneous appearances across anatomical locations. In patch-based training and sliding-window inference for 3D medical image segmentation, location-dependent heterogeneity is further amplified because cropped image patches provide limited global anatomical context, making it difficult for a model to adapt its feature processing according to the anatomical region from which each patch is extracted. To address this limitation, we propose an Anatomical Prior-guided Routing Module (APRM) for lung tumor segmentation. For each image patch, we obtain anatomical prior information of regional occupancy and deterministically select an anatomical routing gate. The selected gate then performs sparse feature routing over a shared expert adapter pool, enabling anatomy-specific feature adaptation while sharing expert capacity across regions. We evaluate APRM on two datasets with various backbone networks and demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline models. Furthermore, feature visualizations show that APRM produces different feature responses depending on patch location, indicating that the proposed routing mechanism effectively adapts feature processing according to anatomical context.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an Anatomical Prior-guided Routing Module (APRM) for 3D lung tumor segmentation in CT, which selects a routing gate per patch from anatomical occupancy priors and performs sparse routing over a shared expert adapter pool. It yields consistent improvements over baseline models on two datasets with various backbones.
AI.motivation: Tumors occupy a small part of the volume and look heterogeneous across anatomical locations, and in patch-based training and sliding-window inference cropped patches carry limited global context, so a model cannot easily adapt its processing to the region each patch comes from.
AI.method: For each patch, anatomical prior information of regional occupancy is obtained and an anatomical routing gate is selected deterministically; the gate performs sparse feature routing over a shared expert adapter pool, allowing anatomy-specific adaptation while sharing capacity across regions.
AI.result: APRM gives consistent improvements over baseline models with various backbone networks on two datasets, and feature visualizations show location-dependent feature responses; the abstract gives no numeric values.
AI.conclusion: Routing features by anatomical context is an effective way to adapt patch-based 3D segmentation to location-dependent heterogeneity.

title: PathCowork: Learning from real-world pathology practice to build AI copilots
comment: 56 pages, including supplementary information. Code, models and demonstration videos: this https URL
summary: Medical AI learns from the answers doctors record, but rarely from how they interpret the evidence to reach them. Here we introduce PathCowork, a framework that turns pathologists' narrated examinations into supervision for visual grounding and procedures that guide diagnostic AI agents. Synchronized gaze, narration and navigation link visual findings to the process of interpreting them. Across 48 sessions from 16 pathologists, the platform captured 1,028 minutes of slide review. Using these data, we trained PathCowork-1T for server deployment and PathCowork-27B for local deployment, with improved visual grounding. Across five organ-specific evaluations, agents combining this grounding with recorded diagnostic procedures achieved primary task scores averaging 17.9 and 24.1 percentage points higher than Claude Code and Codex, respectively, with shorter processing times and lower inference costs. Compared to the state-of-the-art multiple-instance learning AIs, the PathCowork agent-proposed regions achieved higher prostate-grading scores with limited slide labels. PathCowork can also help construct pathology AI benchmarks where questions derived from the recordings identified difficulties in recognizing viewing context and rejecting inapplicable premises. In summary, PathCowork proposes a new paradigm to scale up the data collection and train pathology AI through transparent reasoning from diagnostic sessions, opening a path towards systems that learn directly from routine clinical practice.

AI.tldr: PathCowork turns pathologists' narrated slide examinations into supervision for visual grounding and into procedures that guide diagnostic AI agents. Agents combining this grounding with recorded procedures average 17.9 and 24.1 percentage points higher on primary task scores than Claude Code and Codex, respectively.
AI.motivation: Medical AI learns from the answers doctors record but rarely from the reasoning that leads to them, so the evidence interpretation process in routine pathology practice is not used for training.
AI.method: Synchronized gaze, narration and navigation link visual findings to the process of interpreting them; 48 sessions from 16 pathologists (1,028 minutes of slide review) were used to train PathCowork-1T for server deployment and PathCowork-27B for local deployment.
AI.result: Across five organ-specific evaluations, agents with this grounding and recorded procedures average 17.9 and 24.1 points higher than Claude Code and Codex, respectively, with shorter processing times and lower inference costs; the agent-proposed regions achieve higher prostate-grading scores than state-of-the-art multiple-instance learning models with limited slide labels.
AI.conclusion: Learning from diagnostic sessions offers a transparent and scalable route to pathology AI, and the same recordings can help build benchmarks that expose difficulties with viewing context and inapplicable premises.

title: Calibrating Attention-Based Token Pruning for Efficient Multi-Image Synthesis in UMMs
summary: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) enable powerful multi-image synthesis but incur substantial computation from long visual contexts. While token pruning offers a direct route to accelerating inference, existing methods are primarily adapted from understanding tasks, suffering from insufficient reference image exploration, confused conditional guidance, and pooling-induced ambiguity that degrades generation quality. To address these issues, we propose CATP, the first training-free context-compression method tailored to UMM generation, which \textbf{C}alibrates the discrepancies of general \textbf{A}ttention-based \textbf{T}oken \textbf{P}runing for better quality-efficiency trade-off. Concretely, building on independent layer-wise pruning during denoising, we introduce Guidance-Consistent Pruning (GCP) to synchronize pruning decisions across conditioning branches, and a Taylor-Calibrated Attention Metric (TCAM) that derives a theoretically grounded second-order correction for pooling-induced bias. In addition, a Fast Scoring Operator (FSO) fuses the calibration into tiled online Softmax to reduce pruning cost. Extensive experiments across representative UMMs and benchmarks demonstrate that CATP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art token-reduction methods, achieving up to 2.09$\times$ attention-core speedup.

AI.tldr: CATP is a training-free context-compression method for multi-image synthesis in Unified Multimodal Models that calibrates attention-based token pruning for generation. It achieves a better quality-efficiency trade-off than state-of-the-art token-reduction methods, with up to 2.09x attention-core speedup.
AI.motivation: Unified Multimodal Models incur heavy computation from long visual contexts, and existing token pruning methods adapted from understanding tasks suffer from insufficient reference exploration, confused conditional guidance and pooling-induced ambiguity that degrades generation.
AI.method: Guidance-Consistent Pruning synchronizes pruning decisions across conditioning branches; a Taylor-Calibrated Attention Metric adds a second-order correction for pooling-induced bias; a Fast Scoring Operator fuses the calibration into tiled online Softmax to reduce pruning cost.
AI.result: CATP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art token-reduction methods across representative UMMs and benchmarks, achieving up to 2.09x attention-core speedup.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating attention-based pruning for generation rather than understanding allows substantial inference acceleration of multi-image synthesis without any training.

title: Regional Anchor Routing for Multi-Object Motion Transfer
summary: Compositional motion transfer requires a model to extract motions from multiple reference videos, and apply each motion to a user-specified object in one target scene. Existing methods normally struggle to reliably assign different reference motions to the correct target objects, thus a motion intended for one object may affect another. Meanwhile, some motion-specific tuning approaches are still facing another issue: they must run a new optimization whenever the reference video changes, making repeated transfers inefficient. To address these limitations, we propose RART, a framework that unifies object-wise motion extraction, target-region anchoring, and frame-aligned injection into a frozen video Diffusion Transformer for multi-object motion transfer. For each reference motion, RART extracts temporally ordered features from the masked reference video, and then conditions them on the target first-frame mask to form mask-anchored motion tokens. Frame-aligned motion cross-attention allows each generated frame to read only the motion tokens at the corresponding time slots, composing all object motions in one denoising process. During training, a motion-attention routing loss encourages each target region to attend to its corresponding motion tokens and reduces interference between objects. Therefore, RART can handle novel reference-target combinations without per-video optimization. Experiments show that RART achieves accurate motion preservation, efficient inference, and strong compositional generalization.

AI.tldr: RART is a framework for multi-object motion transfer that injects multiple reference motions into a frozen video Diffusion Transformer, each applied to a user-specified target object, without per-video optimization. It achieves accurate motion preservation, efficient inference and strong compositional generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing methods struggle to assign different reference motions to the correct target objects, so one object's motion can affect another, and motion-specific tuning requires a new optimization whenever the reference video changes.
AI.method: Object-wise motion extraction yields temporally ordered features from masked reference videos, which are conditioned on the target first-frame mask to form mask-anchored motion tokens; frame-aligned motion cross-attention lets each generated frame read only the tokens at its time slot, and a motion-attention routing loss during training encourages each target region to attend to its own motion tokens.
AI.result: The abstract reports accurate motion preservation, efficient inference and strong compositional generalization in experiments, without numeric values.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring motion tokens to target regions with frame-aligned injection enables handling of novel reference-target combinations in a single denoising process without per-video optimization.

title: Agent-Wise Test-Time Normalization for Camera-Based Cooperative Perception with Corrupted Collaborators
summary: Intermediate-fusion cooperative perception lets a vehicle detect objects beyond its own field of view by fusing features shared by nearby agents. When only a collaborator's cameras are degraded by fog, motion blur or exposure errors, the features it shares drift away from the training distribution while the ego input stays clean, and cooperation can become worse than not cooperating at all. Test-time batch-normalization adaptation, the standard training-free remedy, estimates statistics over the pooled batch of all agents and therefore normalizes both the clean ego and the corrupted collaborator with a mixture of two distributions. We show that this mixing harms even the clean ego: when the ego shares BN statistics with a corrupted collaborator, its detection from its own features drops by 3.58 to 6.68 AP@0.5 points although its cameras are untouched. We propose AgentNorm, an agent-wise test-time normalization that i) estimates the normalization statistics of every collaborator from its own current observation and ii) anchors the ego to its source statistics, so that the ego path remains exactly the original model. AgentNorm has no learnable parameters, needs no gradients or labels, is independent of the order of test frames, and runs locally on each agent without changing the transmitted features. On camera-based OPV2V with four fusion checkpoints and collaborator-only corruptions, AgentNorm raises AP@0.5 under severity-5 fog from 29.42-37.25 to 43.32-58.86 and outperforms pooled normalization by 5.53-12.94 points under fog and motion blur, at an extra latency of 2.3 ms per frame. On the real-world DAIR-V2X-C dataset, it outperforms pooled normalization in all ten infrastructure-corruption settings. We also report the cases it does not fix: occlusion, which removes image content rather than shifting feature statistics, and the case in which all agents share the same shift.

AI.tldr: AgentNorm is an agent-wise test-time normalization method for camera-based cooperative perception that estimates normalization statistics per collaborator and anchors the ego agent to its source statistics. On OPV2V with collaborator-only corruptions, it raises AP@0.5 under severity-5 fog from 29.42-37.25 to 43.32-58.86.
AI.motivation: When only a collaborator's cameras are degraded, pooled test-time BN adaptation mixes clean and corrupted statistics, which harms even the clean ego agent, dropping its AP@0.5 by 3.58 to 6.68 points.
AI.method: AgentNorm estimates each collaborator's normalization statistics from its own current observation and keeps the ego path identical to the original model; it has no learnable parameters, needs no gradients or labels, is independent of frame order, runs locally on each agent and does not change the transmitted features.
AI.result: On OPV2V with four fusion checkpoints, AP@0.5 under severity-5 fog rises from 29.42-37.25 to 43.32-58.86, and the method outperforms pooled normalization by 5.53-12.94 points under fog and motion blur at 2.3 ms extra latency per frame; on DAIR-V2X-C it outperforms pooled normalization in all ten infrastructure-corruption settings.
AI.conclusion: Per-agent normalization is a simple, training-free remedy for corrupted collaborators, though it does not address occlusion or the case where all agents share the same shift.

title: Robust LIDAR Sensor-to-Sensor Domain Generalization via Accumulated-Point Scene Completion
summary: We study domain generalization for LIDAR semantic segmentation. Deep neural networks achieve strong performance on 3D point clouds, yet real-world LIDAR exhibits sensor-specific sampling patterns that hinder transfer across datasets. In many applications, performance on completely unseen sensors is crucial. A model should preferably work on a new setup without prior access to its data or labels. To this end, we introduce a source-only training scheme that adds an occupancy prediction auxiliary objective. We aggregate source-domain scans into a simple world model and use it as the supervision signal, replacing single-scan standard segmentation training. A key property of our approach is that it does not alter the input scan. During training and testing the network consumes the same single-frame LIDAR input, only the supervision signal is enriched via the occupancy objective. At deployment, there is no runtime overhead as the auxiliary head can be dropped for pure segmentation, or kept to obtain scene completion alongside semantic segmentation. In an experimental evaluation across distinct LIDAR datasets, we demonstrate that a model's generalization to new domains can be significantly affected by how it is supervised. In certain setups, performance on unseen domains improves without any explicit domain adaptation (no target scans, no target labels, no sensor priors) and without prediction refinement. At the same time, our method maintains competitive source-domain segmentation performance and incurs no additional inference cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a source-only domain generalization scheme for LIDAR semantic segmentation that adds an occupancy prediction auxiliary objective supervised by aggregated source scans. The input stays single-frame, and performance on unseen sensors improves without target data or runtime overhead.
AI.motivation: Real-world LIDAR exhibits sensor-specific sampling patterns that hinder transfer across datasets, and many applications need good performance on completely unseen sensors without prior access to their data or labels.
AI.method: Source-domain scans are aggregated into a simple world model that serves as the supervision signal, replacing single-scan segmentation training; the network consumes the same single-frame input, and the auxiliary occupancy head can be dropped at deployment or kept for scene completion.
AI.result: Across distinct LIDAR datasets, generalization to new domains improves in certain setups without domain adaptation, target scans or prediction refinement, while source-domain segmentation stays competitive and inference cost is unchanged; the abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: How a model is supervised can significantly affect its domain generalization, so enriching supervision with occupancy from aggregated scans is a cost-free lever for sensor robustness.

title: FFAI: Flow Matching with Feedback Training and Adaptive Initialization for CT Reconstruction
summary: Although low-dose, sparse-view, and limited-angle CT involve distinct degradation mechanisms, all three pose reconstruction challenges due to limited measurement information and can therefore be addressed within a unified framework. In iterative image restoration with flow matching, prediction errors may cause inference states to deviate from the prescribed training path, while a fixed initialization may be unsuitable for inputs with varying degradation severity. We propose a unified conditional flow matching method that conditions on the initial reconstruction and combines feedback-aware training with degradation-adaptive initialization. During training, a teacher network simulates inference updates to generate shifted states, from which a student network learns to recover high-quality reference images, improving its ability to handle prediction errors. During inference, the starting time is selected based on the noise level or extent of missing projection data, and the noise added to the initial state is adjusted accordingly to adapt the starting point to the input. Experiments on public benchmark datasets show that the proposed method achieves better quantitative results than the compared methods across all three reconstruction tasks, effectively suppressing noise and artifacts while preserving anatomical structures and details.

AI.tldr: FFAI is a unified conditional flow matching method for low-dose, sparse-view and limited-angle CT reconstruction that combines feedback-aware training with degradation-adaptive initialization. It achieves better quantitative results than the compared methods across all three tasks on public benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Iterative flow-matching restoration can drift off the prescribed training path because of prediction errors, and a fixed initialization may be unsuitable for inputs with varying degradation severity.
AI.method: The model conditions on the initial reconstruction; during training a teacher network simulates inference updates to produce shifted states, from which a student learns to recover high-quality references; at inference the starting time is chosen from the noise level or the extent of missing projection data, and the noise added to the initial state is adjusted accordingly.
AI.result: The method achieves better quantitative results than the compared methods across all three reconstruction tasks on public benchmark datasets, suppressing noise and artifacts while preserving anatomical structures and details.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-aware training and input-adaptive starting points let a single flow-matching framework work effectively across distinct CT degradations.

title: BRIDGE: Learning Brain-Gut Metabolic Evidence for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) diagnosis may benefit from gut metabolic information associated with brain-gut interactions, yet existing models largely analyze cerebral glucose metabolism alone. Although whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) can provide paired brain-gut observations, routine brain examinations rarely include gut imaging, limiting direct use of this information for diagnosis. In this paper, we present BRIDGE (Brain and Gut Representation Integration via Distribution-Guided Enhancement), a two-stage framework for transferring brain-gut metabolic knowledge to brain-only diagnosis. Specifically, BRIDGE integrates a conditional brain-to-gut latent transport module and a disease-evidence-guided cerebral pathway to capture subject-specific cross-organ correspondence and disease-relevant cerebral representations. For the cerebral pathway, a large language model (LLM) helps organize literature-derived descriptors into human-approved semantic anchors that guide feature learning. Additionally, we introduce a counterfactual-guided residual fusion mechanism, which uses matched and non-matched virtual-gut evidence to supervise a confidence gate and dynamically regulate the contribution of transported cross-organ information. At inference, BRIDGE exploits complementary gut-related context using brain PET alone, without measured gut PET. Extensive experiments across public and private cohorts demonstrate that BRIDGE outperforms brain-only and cross-organ baselines, achieving AUC gains of 6.0% and 5.2% over its brain-only counterpart for CN/MCI and CN/AD diagnosis, respectively. Notably, its ability to transfer complementary brain-gut metabolic context while preserving brain PET as the sole inference input highlights its potential for clinically practical diagnosis. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: BRIDGE is a two-stage framework that transfers brain-gut metabolic knowledge from paired whole-body FDG-PET to brain-only Alzheimer's diagnosis, so only brain PET is needed at inference. It achieves AUC gains of 6.0% and 5.2% over its brain-only counterpart for CN/MCI and CN/AD diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Existing models analyze cerebral glucose metabolism alone, and although whole-body PET gives paired brain-gut observations, routine brain examinations rarely include gut imaging, which limits direct use of gut information.
AI.method: A conditional brain-to-gut latent transport module captures subject-specific cross-organ correspondence, and a disease-evidence-guided cerebral pathway uses LLM-organized, human-approved semantic anchors derived from literature descriptors; a counterfactual-guided residual fusion uses matched and non-matched virtual-gut evidence to supervise a confidence gate that regulates the transported cross-organ information.
AI.result: Across public and private cohorts, BRIDGE outperforms brain-only and cross-organ baselines, with AUC gains of 6.0% and 5.2% over its brain-only counterpart for CN/MCI and CN/AD diagnosis respectively.
AI.conclusion: Brain-gut metabolic knowledge can be distilled into a brain-only pipeline, making cross-organ information clinically practical without gut imaging at inference.

title: MorphSIG: Subject-Driven Image Generation via Decoupled Anchoring and Feature Transport
summary: We propose MorphSIG, a training-free framework that reformulates subject-driven image generation (SIG) as pseudo-video feature transport. MorphSIG contains two core modules: Progressive Decoupled Anchoring, which uses frequency-domain decoupling and structural scrambling during early denoising to break structural locking and enable a gradual transition from free composition to identity alignment; and Pseudo-flow Guided Feature Transport, which constructs a latent-space pseudo-flow field to mimic Image-to-Video temporal coherence and transport subject semantics precisely. To address stylistic homogeneity and the lack of ground truth in existing benchmarks, we further introduce a benchmark with diverse stylized subjects. Extensive experiments show that MorphSIG significantly improves pose diversity and subject fidelity over baselines without additional training. Overall, MorphSIG bridges static generation and dynamic propagation, providing a cost-effective paradigm for high-fidelity subject consistency.

AI.tldr: MorphSIG is a training-free framework that recasts subject-driven image generation as pseudo-video feature transport, improving pose diversity and subject fidelity over baselines without additional training.
AI.motivation: Existing subject-driven generation suffers from structural locking that limits free composition, and current benchmarks lack diverse stylized subjects and ground truth, which causes stylistic homogeneity.
AI.method: Progressive Decoupled Anchoring applies frequency-domain decoupling and structural scrambling during early denoising to move gradually from free composition to identity alignment; Pseudo-flow Guided Feature Transport builds a latent-space pseudo-flow field that mimics Image-to-Video temporal coherence to transport subject semantics. A new benchmark with diverse stylized subjects is also introduced.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show significant improvements in pose diversity and subject fidelity over baselines, with no additional training.
AI.conclusion: MorphSIG bridges static generation and dynamic propagation, offering a cost-effective paradigm for high-fidelity subject consistency.

title: MOSAIC-Flow: Orthogonal-Axis and Status-Conditioned Fusion for Missing-Sequence Completion in Brain Tumor MRI
summary: Missing-sequence completion is important for comprehensive brain tumor characterization, but cross-modal fusion can obscure sequence-specific contrast and lose fine-grained three-dimensional tumor detail. To address this challenge, we introduce Modality-aware Orthogonal-axis Status-conditioned Attentive Integration for Completion (MOSAIC-Flow), a unified framework for missing-sequence completion that learns a target-conditioned velocity field while keeping the seven acquired volumes fixed throughout the transport. Specifically, modality-aware stems independently encode each sequence, and orthogonal-axis refinement captures axial, coronal, and sagittal dependencies while retaining the three-dimensional representation. Status-conditioned prototype fusion uses compact modality and availability tokens to route and modulate pooled queries from the fused visual representation, enabling target-adaptive conditioning without dense voxel-to-voxel attention. A conditional flow matching objective transports target-channel noise toward the single missing sequence, while four Heun trajectories are averaged to produce the completion. Evaluation across structural, diffusion, and contrast-enhanced MRI in UCSF-PDGM demonstrates consistent whole-brain and tumor-region fidelity across all eight single-target completion tasks, with the strongest performance on structural sequences. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MOSAIC-Flow is a unified flow-matching framework that completes a single missing MRI sequence in brain tumor imaging, evaluated on eight single-target completion tasks in UCSF-PDGM.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal fusion for missing-sequence completion can obscure sequence-specific contrast and lose fine-grained three-dimensional tumor detail.
AI.method: Modality-aware stems encode each sequence independently, orthogonal-axis refinement captures axial, coronal and sagittal dependencies, and status-conditioned prototype fusion uses modality and availability tokens to route pooled queries without dense voxel-to-voxel attention. A conditional flow matching objective transports target-channel noise to the missing sequence, with the seven acquired volumes kept fixed, and four Heun trajectories are averaged to produce the completion.
AI.result: Across structural, diffusion and contrast-enhanced MRI in UCSF-PDGM, the method shows consistent whole-brain and tumor-region fidelity over all eight single-target tasks, with the strongest performance on structural sequences.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a unified solution for missing-sequence completion that preserves three-dimensional tumor representation, with performance strongest on structural sequences.

title: BEACON: Distilled Begin/End-Aware Structured Decoding for Continuous Sign Language Segmentation
comment: Accepted at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027. 12 pages, 4 figures, including supplementary material
summary: In segmentation-based continuous sign language recognition, an untrimmed video is first partitioned into lexical units; segmentation is therefore a means to an end---downstream recognition. However, segmenters are usually judged by local boundary detection rather than by the quality of the lexical segments and the recognition they enable. We present BEACON, a begin/end-aware segmenter that combines four-class Outside/Begin/Inside/End (BIOE) labeling, constrained Viterbi decoding over eight legal transitions, and boundary knowledge distilled from a binary teacher into a shared student. Under strict no-cut evaluation with validation-based model selection, BEACON improves segment-F1 by 14.58/14.59 points and boundary-F1 by 2.17/1.22 points, and reduces the downstream word error rate (WER) by 9.10/4.15 points relative to the state-of-the-art in the PHOENIX-14/BSL Corpus. To examine which segmentation metric better reflects downstream recognition, we evaluated five distinct architecture families. Segment-F1 aligns more consistently with lower WER than boundary-F1 in both corpora (Spearman $\rho=-1.0/-0.9$ versus $-0.9/-0.8$). These results support evaluating sign language segmentation in terms of segment quality and downstream recognition utility rather than local boundary accuracy alone.

AI.tldr: BEACON is a begin/end-aware segmenter for continuous sign language that improves segment quality and downstream recognition on PHOENIX-14 and the BSL Corpus, and shows that segment-F1 tracks word error rate better than boundary-F1.
AI.motivation: Segmenters are usually judged by local boundary detection, which may not reflect the quality of the lexical segments or the downstream recognition they enable.
AI.method: BEACON combines four-class Outside/Begin/Inside/End (BIOE) labeling, constrained Viterbi decoding over eight legal transitions, and boundary knowledge distilled from a binary teacher into a shared student. Evaluation uses strict no-cut evaluation with validation-based model selection, and five architecture families are compared to determine which segmentation metric better reflects recognition.
AI.result: Relative to the state of the art on PHOENIX-14 and the BSL Corpus, BEACON improves segment-F1 by 14.58 and 14.59 points, boundary-F1 by 2.17 and 1.22 points, and reduces word error rate by 9.10 and 4.15 points. Segment-F1 aligns more consistently with lower WER than boundary-F1 (Spearman rho of -1.0 and -0.9 versus -0.9 and -0.8).
AI.conclusion: Sign language segmentation should be evaluated by segment quality and downstream recognition utility rather than by local boundary accuracy alone.

title: DOSE: Dominance-Guided Ordinal Severity Estimation from Sparse Relative Annotations
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 8 pages, 4 figures. Adjust the counts if you add the supplementary material
summary: Medical severity estimation commonly relies on absolute grade annotations, which are fundamentally ordinal, yet existing methods often treat the grades as independent categories. Learning-to-rank methods, which can be trained using relative annotations based on severity comparisons of image pairs, can provide continuous severity rankings but cannot directly predict discrete severity grades. We propose Dominance-guided Ordinal Severity Estimation from Sparse Relative Annotations (DOSE), a framework for learning ordinal medical severity from sparse pairwise comparisons without using absolute annotations. DOSE aggregates the observed comparisons through a global comparison graph to estimate a dominance score for each image. Differences between dominance scores set cumulative margins in the embedding space, so that pairs with larger estimated severity differences are separated more strongly, and also generate pseudo-pairs that supervise a scalar severity head alongside the observed comparisons. The learned continuous severity axis is converted into discrete grades via label-free score calibration, with tie-anchored segmentation as the main calibration method. In the experiment, DOSE consistently outperformed pairwise-ranking baselines on ACNE04, IDRiD, and LIMUC under different pair budgets. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: DOSE learns ordinal medical severity from sparse pairwise comparisons alone, converting a continuous dominance-based severity axis into discrete grades, and outperforms pairwise-ranking baselines on ACNE04, IDRiD and LIMUC.
AI.motivation: Medical severity grades are ordinal but are often treated as independent categories, while learning-to-rank methods trained on relative comparisons give continuous rankings but cannot directly predict discrete grades.
AI.method: DOSE aggregates observed comparisons through a global comparison graph to estimate a dominance score for each image. Score differences set cumulative margins in the embedding space and generate pseudo-pairs that supervise a scalar severity head alongside the observed comparisons. Discrete grades are obtained by label-free score calibration, with tie-anchored segmentation as the main calibration method.
AI.result: DOSE consistently outperformed pairwise-ranking baselines on ACNE04, IDRiD and LIMUC under different pair budgets.
AI.conclusion: Ordinal medical severity can be learned from sparse relative annotations without absolute grade labels.

title: TactoHand: Learning Geometry-Based Dense Hand-Surface Interaction Fields from Video
summary: Understanding how humans interact with the world requires a representation of physical interactions at the hand surface. Tactile sensing captures these interactions, but collecting tactile data at scale requires specialized hardware. We introduce TactoHand, a model that predicts three dense hand-surface interaction fields---contact, proximity, and 3D force---from monocular video. We derive geometry-based contact and proximity labels and motion-derived force labels from eligible training data within a curated collection spanning approximately 50 million source frames. TactoHand uses a temporal transformer to aggregate visual evidence across frames, while three learned queries decode the corresponding hand-surface fields. A differentiable physics layer further constrains force predictions using observed object motion. Across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, TactoHand improves contact and proximity estimation over prior methods. In addition, physics supervision reduces position and rotation errors in motion rollouts, and the predicted contact and proximity fields improve downstream hand-object reconstruction. Together, these results show a scalable, low-cost path to learning hand-surface interaction fields without collecting tactile measurements. Code will be released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TactoHand predicts dense hand-surface contact, proximity and 3D force fields from monocular video, using geometry-derived labels and physics supervision so that no tactile hardware is needed.
AI.motivation: Understanding physical hand-object interaction requires representations at the hand surface, but collecting tactile data at scale requires specialized hardware.
AI.method: Contact and proximity labels are derived from geometry and force labels from motion, using eligible training data from a curated collection of about 50 million source frames. A temporal transformer aggregates visual evidence across frames while three learned queries decode the corresponding hand-surface fields, and a differentiable physics layer constrains force predictions using observed object motion.
AI.result: TactoHand improves contact and proximity estimation over prior methods on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. Physics supervision reduces position and rotation errors in motion rollouts, and the predicted contact and proximity fields improve downstream hand-object reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: The results point to a scalable, low-cost path for learning hand-surface interaction fields without collecting tactile measurements.

title: Operator-Aware Posterior Sampling for Multivariate Weather Downscaling
summary: Statistical downscaling is the task of reconstructing high-resolution meteorological fields from coarse inputs. A principled approach formulates downscaling as a Bayesian inverse problem, using a diffusion prior over high-resolution fields and incorporating the coarse field only at inference through a likelihood. This decouples the prior from the coarse source, allowing one pretrained model to adapt to different sources. However, two challenges limit this flexibility: (1) when coarse and target fields come from different reanalysis systems, no fixed coarsening operator can capture their relationship; and (2) guidance gradients can differ by orders of magnitude across variables, making a single guidance strength ineffective. This paper addresses both challenges within the guidance loop, leaving the prior unchanged. We learn the forward operator from paired data and normalize the gradient per channel. We show that this normalization corresponds to steepest descent under a block-max norm, allowing a single guidance strength across variables. Our code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes operator-aware posterior sampling for diffusion-based weather downscaling, learning the forward operator from paired data and normalizing guidance gradients per channel so that a single guidance strength works across variables.
AI.motivation: A pretrained diffusion prior with a coarse-field likelihood is flexible, but a fixed coarsening operator fails when coarse and target fields come from different reanalysis systems, and guidance gradients differ by orders of magnitude across variables.
AI.method: The method works inside the guidance loop and leaves the prior unchanged. It learns the forward operator from paired data and normalizes the gradient per channel, which the authors show corresponds to steepest descent under a block-max norm.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results and states only that the per-channel normalization permits a single guidance strength across variables.
AI.conclusion: The approach addresses both challenges without modifying the prior, so one pretrained model can adapt to different coarse sources.

title: DiFuse: Fusing Native Diffusion Representations for Spatial Reasoning in Unified Multimodal Models
summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) jointly support visual understanding and image generation, yet information flow between these two capabilities remains largely asymmetric: understanding representations routinely condition generation, whereas generative representations are rarely reused for multimodal reasoning. In this work, we investigate whether intermediate representations from a UMM's native diffusion branch can enhance spatial reasoning without compromising general multimodal understanding. We propose DiFuse, which selectively incorporates intermediate diffusion representations into the understanding pathway of UMMs. Through systematic layer-wise analysis, we identify which diffusion representations are most informative and where they can be integrated with minimal interference to semantic processing. Guided by these findings, DiFuse spatially aligns diffusion features with visual tokens and injects them into selected multimodal decoder layers via residual fusion. Extensive experiments on UniWorld-V1 show that, DiFuse consistently improves spatial reasoning over a matched SFT baseline while maintaining broadly comparable performance on general multimodal benchmarks. Further analyses show that these gains depend critically on the choice of diffusion representations, injection positions, and the preservation of spatial correspondence between diffusion features and visual tokens. Results on OmniGen2 further demonstrate the transferability of DiFuse across unified multimodal architectures. Overall, our findings show that native diffusion representations can provide complementary spatial cues for multimodal reasoning when selectively integrated in a structure-preserving manner.

AI.tldr: DiFuse injects intermediate diffusion representations from a unified multimodal model's native diffusion branch into its understanding pathway, improving spatial reasoning over a matched SFT baseline while keeping general multimodal performance broadly comparable.
AI.motivation: In unified multimodal models, information flows mainly from understanding to generation, and generative representations are rarely reused for multimodal reasoning, particularly spatial reasoning.
AI.method: Layer-wise analysis identifies which diffusion representations are most informative and where they can be integrated with minimal interference to semantic processing. DiFuse spatially aligns diffusion features with visual tokens and injects them into selected multimodal decoder layers via residual fusion.
AI.result: On UniWorld-V1, DiFuse consistently improves spatial reasoning over a matched SFT baseline while remaining broadly comparable on general multimodal benchmarks. Gains depend on the choice of diffusion representations, the injection positions and the preservation of spatial correspondence. Results on OmniGen2 show the approach transfers across unified multimodal architectures.
AI.conclusion: Native diffusion representations provide complementary spatial cues for multimodal reasoning when integrated selectively in a structure-preserving manner.

title: UniTele: Learning Device-Conditioned Degradations for Unified Smartphone Telephoto Super-Resolution
summary: Super-telephoto imaging on mobile phones suffers from complex, device-dependent degradations that are poorly captured by conventional handcrafted pipelines. Collecting large-scale aligned training pairs across different phones and diverse scenes, however, is both costly and difficult to scale. We therefore study whether device-specific degradations can be learned from only a small number of physical captures and transferred for training a unified super-resolution (SR) model. Our key idea is to factor degradation learning into two learnable components: one captures the device-specific imaging characteristics under well-resolved conditions, while the other captures the additional information loss and artifacts that arise in super-telephoto imaging. We build a paired benchmark across three phone brands (Huawei, Apple, and vivo) by photographing the same content at two display sizes and zoom settings. The larger displayed image is captured at the phone's maximum optical zoom setting, while the smaller image is photographed directly at the phone's highest native zoom setting through the phone's native imaging pipeline. The benchmark contains 519 training and 60 held-out pairs. We use the benchmark to learn device-specific degradation, then apply it to external images to synthesize thousands of additional pairs to train our UniTele SR model. Relative to the pretrained Qwen and FLUX backbones before adaptation, the full UniTele training recipe substantially improves paired restoration fidelity and perceptual similarity on the held-out benchmark and yields markedly more stable and visually faithful restorations.

AI.tldr: UniTele learns device-specific degradations from a small set of physical captures across three phone brands and uses them to synthesize training pairs for a unified telephoto super-resolution model.
AI.motivation: Device-dependent super-telephoto degradations are poorly captured by handcrafted pipelines, and collecting large aligned training pairs across phones and scenes is costly and hard to scale.
AI.method: Degradation learning is factored into two learnable components: one captures device-specific imaging characteristics under well-resolved conditions, and the other captures the additional information loss and artifacts of super-telephoto imaging. A paired benchmark of 519 training and 60 held-out pairs from Huawei, Apple and vivo phones is used to learn the device degradation, which is then applied to external images to synthesize thousands of additional pairs.
AI.result: Relative to the pretrained Qwen and FLUX backbones before adaptation, the full training recipe substantially improves paired restoration fidelity and perceptual similarity on the held-out benchmark and yields more stable and visually faithful restorations.
AI.conclusion: Device-specific degradations can be learned from only a small number of physical captures and transferred to train a unified super-resolution model.

title: FutureWorld: A Plug-and-Play Causal Next-State Predictor for Interactive Video World Exploration
summary: Interactive video world models aim to follow user actions while maintaining scene consistency over extended interactions. History-based methods reuse generated latents to preserve scene content, but three limitations of this reuse contribute to error recirculation. 1) The latent generated at each interaction is retained as history, potentially containing blurred details, geometric distortions, or semantic drift. 2) Although retrieved historical content matches the current scene, it can still contain errors that are carried into the next chunk. 3) New outputs then become history for later interactions, potentially reinforcing the same errors through repeated reuse. To limit this cycle, we aim to predict the future scene state from the current generated latent and the next action before generating the next interaction's video chunk. This future-state prior provides guidance for the next chunk, with the aim of reducing the errors carried forward from history. To this end, we propose a plug-and-play Causal Next-Chunk Predictor (C-NCP) with cross-model adaptability and prediction-guided modulation. We integrate C-NCP into four base generators and evaluate the augmented models across three benchmarks for interactive long-video generation and action-conditioned world modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency across diverse generation settings. The project page is at this https URL.

AI.tldr: C-NCP is a plug-and-play causal predictor that forecasts the next scene state from the current generated latent and the next action, reducing error accumulation in interactive video world models across four base generators.
AI.motivation: History-based interactive video world models reuse generated latents, so blurred details, geometric distortions and semantic drift can be carried forward and reinforced across interactions.
AI.method: Before generating the next video chunk, a Causal Next-Chunk Predictor takes the current generated latent and the next action to predict the future scene state, which then guides generation through prediction-guided modulation. The module is designed for cross-model adaptability and is integrated into four base generators.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks for interactive long-video generation and action-conditioned world modeling, the augmented models show reduced error accumulation and improved long-horizon consistency across diverse generation settings.
AI.conclusion: A future-state prior can limit the cycle of error recirculation in history-based video world models.

title: Intrinsic Distribution Matching
summary: One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution. Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network. We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision. A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly. We introduce Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which retains the full DMD correction and matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy, requiring no external feature encoder. Experiments use full-parameter and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B. At two network evaluations, IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across the five reported metrics. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Intrinsic Distribution Matching adds an explicit moment constraint to distribution matching distillation, using the generator's EMA features to match feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations for one- and few-step text-to-image generation.
AI.motivation: One- and few-step text-to-image generation has limited opportunity for refinement, and the learned score supervision in distribution matching distillation may benefit from an explicit constraint on moment statistics.
AI.method: A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies the statistics to constrain. IDM keeps the full DMD correction and matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average copy, requiring no external feature encoder. Experiments use full-parameter and LoRA tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B.
AI.result: At two network evaluations, IDM reaches 94.25% on Chinese LongText-Bench and 90.20% on English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show gains from the added moment loss, and generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across five reported metrics.
AI.conclusion: Explicit moment matching using the generator's own features improves distillation for text-to-image generation without an external encoder.

title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?
summary: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: this https URL

AI.tldr: BedBench is a controlled benchmark showing that vision-language models often answer individual 3D judgments correctly yet fail at exact per-color counting and at consistent use of the properties they recover.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use exact 3D object properties, a gap that accuracy alone does not reveal.
AI.method: The authors introduce BedBench, with thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. They evaluate twelve open-weight and four frontier models, apply targeted fine-tuning, supply per-color counts as text, and probe Qwen3.5-27B with image-removal controls.
AI.result: Humans reach 93.3% accuracy on per-color counting, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model from 3.0% to 68.6%, but its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. The probe recovers exact counts at 65.0% versus 3.0% for the model, and some apparent successes require no visual evidence.
AI.conclusion: 3D reasoning should be evaluated by exact correctness, consistent use and image dependence rather than by accuracy alone.

title: FlexTry-On: A Time-Efficient Framework for Multi-Scenario Virtual Try-on
summary: Virtual try-on has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, yet most existing methods are designed for a specific scenario, such as cloth-to-person or person-to-person try-on, and often require separate conditioning strategies and processing pipelines for different settings. We present FlexTry-On, a unified and time-efficient diffusion-based framework for diverse virtual try-on scenarios, including cloth-to-person, person-to-person, cross-domain, and in-the-wild settings. FlexTry-On adopts a common conditioning formulation, where a text-aware condition extraction strategy converts heterogeneous garment sources into a unified representation, and a dual-conditioning diffusion transformer jointly models garment appearance and person identity. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive performance on both cloth-to-person and person-to-person benchmarks while maintaining fast inference. Moreover, the same framework can be directly applied to unseen cross-domain scenarios without requiring separate architectures or scenario-specific processing pipelines. These results highlight the potential of unified and efficient virtual try-on frameworks as a practical step toward more flexible and widely applicable virtual try-on systems.

AI.tldr: FlexTry-On is a unified diffusion transformer framework that handles cloth-to-person, person-to-person, cross-domain and in-the-wild virtual try-on with a shared conditioning formulation and fast inference.
AI.motivation: Most virtual try-on methods target a single scenario and require separate conditioning strategies and processing pipelines for each setting.
AI.method: A text-aware condition extraction strategy converts heterogeneous garment sources into a unified representation, and a dual-conditioning diffusion transformer jointly models garment appearance and person identity.
AI.result: The framework is competitive on cloth-to-person and person-to-person benchmarks while maintaining fast inference, and it applies directly to unseen cross-domain scenarios without scenario-specific architectures.
AI.conclusion: Unified and efficient try-on frameworks are a practical step toward more flexible and widely applicable virtual try-on systems.

title: Annotation-Free Representation Learning for Polyp Retrieval in Colonoscopy Videos
summary: Colonoscopy is inherently comparative: reliable visual assessment of polyps often depends on complementary views acquired under different viewpoints and imaging conditions. Retrieving such views requires polyp tracklet representations, which recent contrastive methods learn from temporal cues but still build from manually annotated bounding boxes. We propose an annotation-free framework that constructs tracklet views directly from raw colonoscopy videos, enabling temporal self-supervised learning on full-procedure videos, including frames without visible polyps. On REAL-Colon, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on tracklet retrieval and re-identification, outperforming both self-supervised and supervised baselines. We then introduce few-shot polyp retrieval, a task closer to clinical use, where a few observations of a target polyp are used to retrieve its remaining tracklets: with only two examples, our method surpasses most competing methods given ten. Finally, we show that a modest number of unlabeled procedures suffices for competitive performance, making on-site model development more practical. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: An annotation-free framework builds polyp tracklet views directly from raw colonoscopy videos for temporal self-supervised learning, achieving state-of-the-art tracklet retrieval and re-identification on REAL-Colon and enabling few-shot polyp retrieval.
AI.motivation: Contrastive tracklet learning for polyps relies on manually annotated bounding boxes, and it cannot exploit full-procedure videos that contain frames without visible polyps.
AI.method: Tracklet views are constructed directly from raw colonoscopy videos, enabling temporal self-supervised learning on full procedure videos, including frames without visible polyps. Few-shot polyp retrieval is introduced as a task in which a few observations of a target polyp are used to retrieve its remaining tracklets.
AI.result: On REAL-Colon the method achieves state-of-the-art tracklet retrieval and re-identification, outperforming self-supervised and supervised baselines. With two examples in few-shot retrieval it surpasses most competing methods given ten. A modest number of unlabeled procedures suffices for competitive performance.
AI.conclusion: Removing the need for bounding-box annotation makes on-site model development for polyp retrieval more practical.

title: Look at Where You Think: Localization-Head Alignment for Fine-Grained Perception in Thinking VLMs
summary: Thinking vision-language models reason for thousands of tokens, yet still miss small details in high-resolution images. Zooming methods pay for extra inference passes, and outcome rewards never tell the model where to look at. In Qwen3.5-4B, we find that the bottleneck is selection, not seeing: a few attention heads, which we call localization heads, pick the evidence out of thousands of visual tokens; ablating four of them costs 13.2 points more than ablating four random heads, and their focus fades as the reasoning grows. We therefore propose Localization-Head Alignment (LHA), which makes attention a training signal: whenever the reasoning states a visual fact, these heads learn to look at the focal region rather than the background, as an auxiliary loss in both SFT and RL training. On benchmarks of V*, HR-Bench 4K and TreeBench, LHA lifts Qwen3.5-4B from 74.1% to 76.6% accuracy, the best single-pass 4B result we evaluate, ahead of multi-pass zooming and released 7B models. Alignment alone adds 1.8 points over otherwise identical training while shortening reasoning by 20%, and the gains carry over to Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

AI.tldr: LHA aligns a few attention heads called localization heads with focal visual regions during training, lifting Qwen3.5-4B to 76.6% accuracy on V*, HR-Bench 4K and TreeBench with a single inference pass and shorter reasoning.
