summary: An image's original dimensions, aspect ratio, and composition provide important cues that can affect its technical and aesthetic quality. Image assessment methods use resizing, cropping, padding, or patch sampling to accommodate different input sizes. However, these operations can alter or obscure original geometric and compositional cues. Existing assessment models also encode rich multi-level visual evidence that can be further extracted and exploited to improve existing models. This motivates us to combine visual evidence with original-image geometry for score refinement without changing the original scoring pipelines. In this paper, we introduce MetaRefine, a metadata-aware score refinement architecture whose lightweight residual heads predict score corrections from geometry, multi-level visual features, and the frozen model's original score. Across 100 configurations on 21 datasets, MetaRefine improves PLCC in 88 configurations and SRCC in 85, with average relative gains of 7.55% and 7.10%, respectively. It reduces MAE in 90 configurations and RMSE in 89, with average relative reductions of 23.27% and 21.93%, respectively. The median parameter overhead is only 1.11%. MetaRefine can further improve state-of-the-art (SOTA) assessment models on multiple benchmarks.

AI.tldr: MetaRefine is a lightweight residual architecture that refines the scores of frozen image assessment models using original image geometry and multi-level visual features.
AI.motivation: Resizing, cropping, padding or patch sampling can alter or obscure original dimensions, aspect ratio and composition cues, and existing models do not fully exploit their multi-level visual evidence.
AI.method: A metadata-aware architecture whose lightweight residual heads predict score corrections from geometry, multi-level visual features and the frozen model's original score, without changing the original scoring pipelines.
AI.result: Across 100 configurations on 21 datasets, it improves PLCC in 88 and SRCC in 85 configurations, with average relative gains of 7.55% and 7.10%; it reduces MAE in 90 and RMSE in 89 configurations, with average relative reductions of 23.27% and 21.93%; the median parameter overhead is 1.11%, and it further improves state-of-the-art assessment models on multiple benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware residual refinement is a cheap, general way to boost existing image assessment models without modifying their scoring pipelines.

title: LucidLyra: Feed-Forward Generative 3D Scene Reconstruction and Joint Understanding via Multi-Task Distillation
summary: We present LucidLyra, a framework that makes generatively reconstructed 3D scenes directly queryable for semantics and instances in a feed-forward manner from video latents. While generative 3D reconstruction can synthesize virtual environments from a single image, downstream applications in robotics and physical AI require not only visual realism but also access to scene semantics and object identities. Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization. To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues. The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data. Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time. By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.

AI.tldr: LucidLyra distills a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a feed-forward network that infers queryable 3D Gaussian scenes with geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics and instance cues.
AI.motivation: Generatively reconstructed 3D scenes lack the semantics and object identities that robotics and physical AI need, while existing 3D understanding methods require multi-view captures, generalize poorly or rely on expensive per-scene optimization.
AI.method: A unified model is trained by distilling knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D foundation models, requiring neither manual 3D annotations nor multi-view captures; the latent formulation also extends to monocular video.
AI.result: Outperforms baselines that combine state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation with generative 3D reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks while preserving reconstruction quality; supports novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation and object grouping without per-scene optimization.
AI.conclusion: Turning generated scenes into queryable 3D worlds enables scene editing, 3D asset mining and robotic simulation.

title: CrossWeave: Cross-Modal Scene and Instance Retrieval from Sparse 2D-3D Alignment
summary: Cross-modal scene and instance retrieval aims to retrieve a corresponding 3D environment or object given query 2D images, serving as a foundational mechanism for spatial reasoning in robotics and AR/VR. Existing methods achieve this by learning alignment only at the level of whole scenes or objects, which provides no supervision for the fine-grained local structure within them. In this work, we show that supervision on a set of sparse 2D-3D correspondences, without scene- or instance-level contrastive objectives, is sufficient to train a single model for both scene- and instance-level retrieval. Specifically, we propose $\textbf{CrossWeave}$, a novel framework for cross-modal retrieval that learns sparse patch-point alignment, which alone outperforms existing methods. An optimal transport-based aggregator over the aligned features gives further gains by clustering structurally redundant regions, freeing descriptor capacity for semantically distinct local features. CrossWeave achieves state-of-the-art performance on both scene- and instance-level retrieval on ScanNet and 3RScan with a $\textit{single model}$, whereas existing methods require separate models for each task. Our results suggest that whole-scene encoding is unnecessary for cross-modal retrieval and that sparse local correspondence supervision is a more effective and flexible alternative.

AI.tldr: CrossWeave retrieves 3D scenes and objects from 2D images using only sparse 2D-3D patch-point correspondences, with a single model covering both scene-level and instance-level retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-modal retrieval learns alignment only at the whole-scene or whole-object level, which gives no supervision for fine-grained local structure.
AI.method: Supervision on sparse patch-point correspondences, without scene- or instance-level contrastive objectives, plus an optimal transport-based aggregator over the aligned features that clusters structurally redundant regions, freeing descriptor capacity for semantically distinct local features.
AI.result: On ScanNet and 3RScan, a single model achieves state-of-the-art scene-level and instance-level retrieval, whereas existing methods require separate models for each task; sparse patch-point alignment alone already outperforms existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Whole-scene encoding is unnecessary for cross-modal retrieval, and sparse local correspondence supervision is a more effective and flexible alternative.

title: Where the Error Lives: Spectral Representations of Learned Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians
summary: Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) is the standard method for computing the electronic structure of molecules and materials, but its self-consistent-field (SCF) iterations make it expensive for large systems and high-throughput screening. Machine-learned Hamiltonian models offer a shortcut: an equivariant network predicts the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian matrix in one forward pass, and diagonalizing the prediction yields orbital energies, the HOMO-LUMO gap, molecular orbitals and the electron density. These models are trained to match the reference matrix entry by entry, yet a small entry-wise error does not guarantee accurate eigenvalues or eigenvectors. Two physics-informed alternatives go partway: a recently proposed wavefunction-alignment loss adds a spectral penalty without diagonalizing the prediction, and matching the electron density of the diagonalized prediction supervises it directly. Neither is complete: by representing the prediction error in the eigenbasis of the reference Hamiltonian, we show that each sees only part of the error, and that shifting the predicted orbital energies leaves the electron density exactly unchanged. The same analysis identifies a complete training signal: the cumulative local density of states (cumulative LDOS), the number of electrons at each point in space with energy below a given threshold. The cumulative LDOS is a single physical observable that contains the electron density as a special case, responds to every component of the error, determines the Hamiltonian uniquely, and yields gradients that do not vanish for large orbitalenergy errors. Fine-tuning three Hamiltonian networks on QH9 in this way, which we call FermiScope, reduces the HOMO-LUMO gap error without increasing the element-wise error. The gains carry over to out-of-distribution and molecular-dynamics splits, where the wavefunction-alignment loss helps less.

AI.tldr: FermiScope fine-tunes machine-learned Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian networks with a cumulative local density of states signal, reducing HOMO-LUMO gap error without increasing element-wise error.
AI.motivation: A small entry-wise Hamiltonian error does not guarantee accurate eigenvalues or eigenvectors, and the existing physics-informed alternatives, wavefunction-alignment loss and electron-density matching, each see only part of the error.
AI.method: The prediction error is analyzed in the eigenbasis of the reference Hamiltonian, showing that shifting predicted orbital energies leaves the electron density unchanged; the cumulative local density of states, the number of electrons at each point in space with energy below a threshold, is proposed as a complete training signal that contains the electron density as a special case.
AI.result: Fine-tuning three Hamiltonian networks on QH9 reduces HOMO-LUMO gap error without increasing element-wise error; the gains carry over to out-of-distribution and molecular-dynamics splits, where the wavefunction-alignment loss helps less.
AI.conclusion: The cumulative LDOS is a complete supervisory signal with non-vanishing gradients for large orbital-energy errors, improving the spectral accuracy of learned Hamiltonians.

title: Echo: Scaling Visual Reinforcement Learning with Off-policy Experience
summary: Scaling visual reinforcement learning (RL) with GPU-accelerated simulation is computationally expensive due to rendering and visual-policy inference costs. Consequently, two-stage teacher--student distillation is commonly used to train visual policies, but introduces an imitation gap. In this preliminary study, we introduce \echomethod{}, \textbf{a single-stage off-policy RL framework that scales experience collection without proportionally increasing visual computation}. Through \textbf{inverse distillation}, a state-based auxiliary policy imitates the evolving visual policy and collects inexpensive, unrendered experience. Echo leverages this experience for off-policy value learning, directly improving the visual policy through a shared privileged critic. We instantiate \echomethod{} with FastTD3 and evaluate it on three visual control tasks and two dexterous manipulation tasks in Genesis. Relative to \sdpgmethod{} under the evaluated configurations, Echo reduces time to reference returns by an average of \textbf{60\% across the three locomotion tasks} and \textbf{56\% across both hand tasks}, while improving peak mean returns by \textbf{62\% and 12\%}, respectively. Both hand tasks also achieve higher mean returns at matched simulator-transition budgets. These initial results suggest that scaling off-policy experience is a promising approach to efficient direct visual RL.

AI.tldr: Echo is a single-stage off-policy RL framework that scales visual RL experience collection by using a state-based auxiliary policy to gather inexpensive, unrendered experience.
AI.motivation: Visual RL with GPU-accelerated simulation is expensive because of rendering and visual-policy inference, and two-stage teacher-student distillation introduces an imitation gap.
AI.method: Through inverse distillation, a state-based auxiliary policy imitates the evolving visual policy and collects unrendered experience; this experience drives off-policy value learning that improves the visual policy through a shared privileged critic, instantiated with FastTD3 and evaluated in Genesis.
AI.result: Relative to the evaluated baseline, Echo reduces time to reference returns by an average of 60% across three locomotion tasks and 56% across two hand tasks, and improves peak mean returns by 62% and 12% respectively; both hand tasks reach higher mean returns at matched simulator-transition budgets.
AI.conclusion: Scaling off-policy experience is presented as a promising approach to efficient direct visual RL, based on initial results.

title: Scan Before You Install: Detecting and Mitigating Local and Composite Vulnerabilities in Skills
summary: An agent skill packages natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference files that an LLM-based agent loads for a task. Skills may access the file system, shell, and network under user-authorized permissions; weaknesses can lead to unsafe execution. Existing scanners primarily target malicious skills, not unintended vulnerabilities in public repositories, and analyze skills in isolation, overlooking multi-skill interactions. To address these gaps, we developed a six-module scanner: Content Extraction, Local Analysis, Composite Analysis, Validation, Reporting, and Mitigation. Local Analysis detects unintended vulnerabilities in benign skills. On a 556-case leaderboard subset of SkillTrustBench, it achieved 95.90% recall with a 4.22% false positive rate; on a balanced sample of 1,000 MalSkillBench skills, its F1 was 0.947, outperforming Cisco's Skill Scanner, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, AgentSkillsScanner, and SkillSieve. In 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories, three analysts confirmed 53 of 59 findings (89.8% precision) across 23 repositories. We developed proof-of-concept (PoC) attacks for each vulnerability, disclosed 10 medium- and high-severity cases to maintainers, and tested mitigations on the remaining cases. Composite Analysis models dependencies among skills through shared resources, invocations, and instruction-mediated interactions. On SCR-Bench, its F1 score was 0.991 (98.7% precision, 99.6% recall), versus 0.816-0.858 for three SkillsGuard configurations released with CompoSkill. It identified two composite findings on GitHub, validated by PoC attacks. The Mitigation module recommends skill substitution, patches, and configuration changes. For 47 of 55 GitHub findings, mitigations prevented PoC attacks in all trials while preserving tested legitimate functionality.

AI.tldr: A six-module scanner detects unintended local and composite vulnerabilities in agent skills, including risks arising from interactions among multiple skills, and recommends mitigations.
AI.motivation: Existing scanners target malicious skills rather than unintended vulnerabilities in public repositories, and they analyze skills in isolation, overlooking multi-skill interactions.
AI.method: Six modules (content extraction, local analysis, composite analysis, validation, reporting and mitigation); composite analysis models dependencies among skills through shared resources, invocations and instruction-mediated interactions.
AI.result: On a 556-case SkillTrustBench leaderboard subset, local analysis reaches 95.90% recall with a 4.22% false positive rate; its F1 on 1,000 MalSkillBench skills is 0.947, above four other scanners. In 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories, three analysts confirmed 53 of 59 findings (89.8% precision). On SCR-Bench, composite analysis reaches F1 0.991 versus 0.816-0.858 for three SkillsGuard configurations; for 47 of 55 GitHub findings, mitigations prevented PoC attacks in all trials while preserving tested legitimate functionality.
AI.conclusion: Skill ecosystems need composite-aware scanning and validated mitigations, since the scanner finds real, exploitable issues in popular public repositories.

title: NLP-based Message Prioritisation for Opportunistic Routing: A Case Study of Nepal Earthquake Emergency Communication
summary: This dissertation investigates whether Natural Language Processing (NLP) based semantic message prioritisation can improve the treatment of urgent disaster messages in opportunistic emergency communication, using the 2015 Nepal earthquake as a case study. TF IDF with Logistic Regression and BERT are used to classify social media messages into nine humanitarian categories, which are mapped to four routing priorities from P1 to P4. These priorities are integrated into the ONE simulator within a controlled Kathmandu earthquake scenario using a modified Binary Spray and Wait router. BERT achieves higher priority accuracy and P1 recall than Logistic Regression, while reducing under prioritisation and severe priority errors. However, improved NLP performance does not produce uniform network gains. P1 delivery probability remains high and similar across routing conditions, and no consistent latency reduction is observed. The clearest difference appears under buffer pressure, where the BERT condition shows fewer observed ground truth P1 buffer losses than Logistic Regression. The results indicate that semantic prioritisation is most valuable when limited transmission and storage resources are contested, although it cannot overcome mobility and contact constraints in opportunistic networks.

AI.tldr: TF-IDF with logistic regression and BERT classify disaster social-media messages into four routing priorities, and the priorities are tested in an opportunistic network simulation of the 2015 Nepal earthquake.
AI.motivation: Urgent messages in opportunistic emergency communication may be mishandled without semantic prioritization, and it was unclear whether better NLP would translate into network gains.
AI.method: Nine humanitarian categories are mapped to four routing priorities (P1 to P4), integrated into the ONE simulator in a Kathmandu earthquake scenario with a modified Binary Spray and Wait router.
AI.result: BERT achieves higher priority accuracy and P1 recall than logistic regression, with less under-prioritization and fewer severe priority errors, but network gains are not uniform: P1 delivery probability stays high and similar across conditions and no consistent latency reduction appears; the clearest difference is under buffer pressure, where BERT shows fewer observed ground-truth P1 buffer losses.
AI.conclusion: Semantic prioritization matters most when transmission and storage resources are contested, but it cannot overcome mobility and contact constraints in opportunistic networks.

title: Statistical Detection of Positional Bias in LLM-Based Recommender Systems: Methodologies and Empirical Evidence
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as recommendation generators in conversational recommender systems (RS) via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This flexible design introduces new sources of structural bias. This paper studies positional bias in top-1 and single-turn LLM-based RS: systematic dependence of the recommended item on the order in which candidates are presented in the prompt. We propose two complementary detection methodologies: (i) POB-ICM, based on contingency matrix analysis and Chi-square independence testing, and (ii) POB-UNBP, a sample-efficient approach derived from a uniformity null model under permutation-based evaluation, enabling stochastic decoding with formal statistical guarantees. Using a controlled RAG testbed for product recommendation, built on a real product catalog, a fixed prompt template and 2000 template-generated user queries with 20 permutations each (40,000 instances), both methodologies reject the null hypothesis of positional independence and uniformity in all evaluated state-of-the-art models. We introduce three complementary metrics -- permutation sensitivity, positional bias, and strong positional bias -- to quantify this effect, the latter targeting cases where the position displaces the recommendation towards clearly less relevant items rather than only choosing among comparably relevant ones. A robustness analysis across candidate-set size and decoding temperature shows that the bias is structural and model-dependent, not an artifact of deterministic decoding or candidate-set size. These results establish positional bias as a measurable, reproducible property of prompt-mediated recommendation pipelines in the evaluated setting and motivate routine auditing and governance controls (e.g., order randomization, standardized prompting) for deployed LLM-based RS. Source code is publicly released.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two statistical tests, POB-ICM and POB-UNBP, that detect positional bias in top-1 recommendations of LLM-based RAG recommenders, and finds the bias structural and model-dependent in all evaluated models.
AI.motivation: Recommendations from LLMs in RAG-based conversational systems may depend on the order of candidates in the prompt, and formal, reproducible detection methods for this were lacking.
AI.method: POB-ICM applies contingency-matrix analysis with chi-square independence testing; POB-UNBP is a sample-efficient test derived from a uniformity null model under permutation-based evaluation that supports stochastic decoding; three metrics (permutation sensitivity, positional bias and strong positional bias) quantify the effect.
AI.result: On a product-recommendation RAG testbed with 2000 template-generated queries and 20 permutations each (40,000 instances), both methods reject positional independence and uniformity for all evaluated state-of-the-art models; a robustness analysis across candidate-set size and decoding temperature shows the bias is not an artifact of deterministic decoding or candidate-set size.
AI.conclusion: Positional bias is a measurable, reproducible property of prompt-mediated recommendation pipelines, motivating routine auditing and controls such as order randomization and standardized prompting.

title: Merge and Branch: Efficient Tree-Structured Supervised Fine-Tuning of LLMs for Recommendation
summary: LLM-based generative recommendation reads long, text-rich interaction histories but generates only short semantic identifiers (SIDs). This asymmetry makes supervised fine-tuning inefficient: encoding the history is expensive, yet each history usually provides supervision for only one target. We present Merge and Branch (M&B) to reduce input cost and learn more from each encoded history. Merge compresses each historical item's SID and text into a small number of learned tokens. Branch uses the compressed history to predict multiple target SIDs. To share history computation while keeping these targets independent, M&B organizes each example as a shallow, wide tree. We develop tree FlashAttention to execute this layout efficiently, processing the shared history once and propagating gradients from every branch for end-to-end training. A tree-structured key/value cache extends history sharing to constrained decoding. Experiments on public benchmarks show that M&B outperforms strong recommendation baselines while substantially improving training and decoding efficiency.

AI.tldr: Merge and Branch compresses historical items into learned tokens and trains an LLM recommender to predict multiple target semantic identifiers from one shared history in a tree-structured pass.
AI.motivation: LLM-based generative recommendation encodes long, text-rich histories at high cost, yet each history supervises only one short target, which makes supervised fine-tuning inefficient.
AI.method: Merge compresses each historical item's SID and text into a small number of learned tokens; Branch predicts multiple target SIDs from the compressed history, with examples organized as a shallow, wide tree; tree FlashAttention processes the shared history once and propagates gradients from every branch, and a tree-structured key/value cache extends history sharing to constrained decoding.
AI.result: The abstract reports that M&B outperforms strong recommendation baselines on public benchmarks while substantially improving training and decoding efficiency, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Sharing history computation across a tree lets each encoded history yield more supervision, improving both efficiency and recommendation quality.

title: Making Smart Homes Fit for Autistic Children: Family Work and Monitored Independence
summary: General-purpose smart-home technologies are increasingly present in family life, yet how they support or disrupt autistic children and families with autistic children remains underexamined. We conducted a multi-source qualitative study drawing on five caregiver interviews, Xiaohongshu (also known internationally as RedNote) posts explicitly situated in autism contexts, and contextual posts from Xiaohongshu and Weibo. We find that families create support for autistic children by adapting environmental outputs, prompts, and interaction channels, while sensory intensity, communicative rules, and opaque operating states can turn the same technologies into barriers. Support also depends on continuing family work, including translation, configuration, modification, maintenance, and boundary-setting. Remote monitoring enables conditional independence while generating tensions among safety, privacy, and control. We contribute three concepts, including relational fit, family work as support infrastructure, and monitored independence, for understanding accessible domestic technology. We derive design implications for adjustable interaction, legible and recoverable failure, lower-burden configuration, and negotiable monitoring.

AI.tldr: A qualitative study finds that smart-home technologies can support autistic children when families adapt them, but this depends on ongoing family work and creates tensions among safety, privacy and control in remote monitoring.
AI.motivation: How general-purpose smart-home technologies support or disrupt autistic children and families with autistic children remains underexamined.
AI.method: A multi-source qualitative study drawing on five caregiver interviews, Xiaohongshu posts explicitly situated in autism contexts, and contextual posts from Xiaohongshu and Weibo.
AI.result: Families adapt environmental outputs, prompts and interaction channels, while sensory intensity, communicative rules and opaque operating states can turn the same technologies into barriers; support depends on continuing family work (translation, configuration, modification, maintenance and boundary-setting); remote monitoring enables conditional independence while generating tensions among safety, privacy and control.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes relational fit, family work as support infrastructure and monitored independence as concepts, and derives design implications for adjustable interaction, legible and recoverable failure, lower-burden configuration and negotiable monitoring.

title: Making Sense of Audience Change: Causal Attribution and Boundary Management on Xiaohongshu
summary: Recommendation-driven platforms can reshape not only what users see, but also who becomes visible and how community boundaries are negotiated. We examine Xiaohongshu discussions surrounding a perceived World Cup-related audience influx to understand how users attributed community change and how those explanations related to boundary-management strategies. We analyzed 262 comments from eight high-engagement threads using researcher-led thematic analysis, structured coding, and permutation-based association analysis. Users described personalization as both social separation and a boundary that could fail, interpreted platform growth through audience acquisition and commercialization, and contested whether gender should define community membership. Among 70 comments with explicit attributions and strategies, attribution and strategy were strongly associated (Cramer's V = .583): algorithmic attributions concentrated in technical boundary management, while social-actor attributions more often aligned with social enforcement or normative socialization. These findings connect causal sensemaking with boundary management and show how audience restructuring can create governance consequences on recommendation-driven platforms.

AI.tldr: An analysis of 262 Xiaohongshu comments on a perceived World Cup-related audience influx finds that algorithmic attributions go with technical boundary management, while social-actor attributions go with social enforcement or normative socialization.
AI.motivation: Recommendation-driven platforms reshape who becomes visible and how community boundaries are negotiated, but how users explain community change and respond to it is not well understood.
AI.method: Researcher-led thematic analysis and structured coding of 262 comments from eight high-engagement threads, plus permutation-based association analysis of the 70 comments that contain explicit attributions and strategies.
AI.result: Users described personalization as both social separation and a boundary that could fail, interpreted platform growth through audience acquisition and commercialization, and contested whether gender should define membership; attribution and strategy were strongly associated (Cramer's V = .583), with algorithmic attributions concentrated in technical boundary management and social-actor attributions more often aligned with social enforcement or normative socialization.
AI.conclusion: The findings connect causal sensemaking with boundary management and show that audience restructuring can create governance consequences on recommendation-driven platforms.

title: METATRON: A Promptable Whole-Body Execution Layer for Humanoids
summary: Humanoid controllers often require task-specific training despite sharing the need for balance and whole-body coordination. We present Metatron, a promptable whole-body execution layer combining a generative base policy with a programmable skill layer. The base policy receives partial goals, collectively called a prompt, that can combine timed body-part targets, velocity commands, and style cues. It produces diverse whole-body motions consistent with these goals. Training combines motion capture, synthetic recovery trajectories, and retargeted scene-interaction motions. After training, the policy is frozen. Stateful programs called skills express task intent as prompts at each control step, drawing rough geometric sketches that the policy turns into coordinated movement. Skills are ordinary code, refined by coding agents that analyze motion data and fit compact rules without task-specific policy training. On the physical Unitree G1, one frozen checkpoint supports walking, recovery, teleoperated object pickup, and sitting on furniture. Comparative evaluations show higher reaching success and push robustness than the tested reference-tracking pipelines. The same recipe produces climbing and acrobatics on a simulated character. Metatron enables coding agents to turn learned motor capabilities into new skills through code, without further policy training.

AI.tldr: Metatron is a promptable whole-body execution layer for humanoids that pairs a frozen generative base policy with a programmable skill layer, so new tasks are written as code rather than trained as new policies. On a physical Unitree G1, one frozen checkpoint supports walking, recovery, teleoperated object pickup and sitting on furniture.
AI.motivation: Humanoid controllers usually need task-specific training even though balance and whole-body coordination are shared across tasks.
AI.method: A generative base policy receives partial goals called prompts (timed body-part targets, velocity commands and style cues) and is trained on motion capture, synthetic recovery trajectories and retargeted scene-interaction motions, then frozen. Stateful skills written as ordinary code issue prompts at each control step, and coding agents refine them from motion data into compact rules without policy training.
AI.result: One frozen checkpoint supports walking, recovery, teleoperated object pickup and sitting on furniture on the Unitree G1. Comparative evaluations show higher reaching success and push robustness than the tested reference-tracking pipelines, and the same recipe yields climbing and acrobatics on a simulated character.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents can turn learned motor capabilities into new skills through code without further policy training, so the frozen policy serves as a reusable execution layer.

title: EARS-Info: Information-Aware Event-Driven Reallocation for Multi-Robot Exploration
summary: We introduce EARS-Info, an information-aware extension of Event-Driven Ant Reallocation Search for multi-robot exploration on OpenStreetMap-derived grids. It combines marginal sensing gain, feasible relocation, return-aware routing, sensing reservations, and cached shortest paths. Across 168,000 episodes comparing 30 implementations on eight city maps, EARS-Info achieves the highest mean operational score in every evaluation panel. With eight robots and 3% communication dropout, it improves the score over EARS-Safe by 5.43%, increases weighted discovery from 88.88% to 98.46%, and reduces mean energy use by 2.62%. Score differences are positive in all eight cities ($p=0.0078125$; descriptive 95% city-bootstrap interval $[0.0159,0.0694]$), with no simulated incidents across 5,600 EARS-Info episodes. These results support the complete controller; individual component advantages remain uncertain. Generalization is limited by reused geography, one training replicate, coarse maps, and adapted comparison methods.

AI.tldr: EARS-Info extends Event-Driven Ant Reallocation Search with information-aware components for multi-robot exploration on OpenStreetMap-derived grids, and achieves the highest mean operational score in every evaluation panel across 168,000 episodes.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot exploration must balance information gain, safe and energy-efficient routing and robot relocation, and the abstract positions the earlier EARS-Safe controller as the baseline that the new method improves on.
AI.method: The controller combines marginal sensing gain, feasible relocation, return-aware routing, sensing reservations and cached shortest paths. It is compared against 30 implementations on eight city maps.
AI.result: With eight robots and 3% communication dropout, the score improves over EARS-Safe by 5.43%, weighted discovery rises from 88.88% to 98.46%, and mean energy use falls by 2.62%. Score differences are positive in all eight cities (p=0.0078125), and there are no simulated incidents across 5,600 EARS-Info episodes.
AI.conclusion: The results support the complete controller, although the advantage of individual components remains uncertain, and generalization is limited by reused geography, one training replicate, coarse maps and adapted comparison methods.

title: What Can Firms Do in the Face of Model Distillation?
summary: Model distillation has become a major concern in the rapidly growing generative AI discourse. In its simplest form, distillation is the phenomenon where smaller firms can use data distilled from transcripts of conversations with powerful proprietary closed-weight models to train their own models, thus achieving reasonably high model quality but at much lower costs. Besides the legitimate safety and security concerns associated with distillation, another major issue is how it can also distort marketplace outcomes. This motivates us to initiate an exploration of the problem from an economic theory lens. We consider a setting with two players: an incumbent and a distilling competitor and characterize how the incumbent's model characteristics drive the incentives around how much the competitor should distill. We also consider the impact of distillation on key market outcomes like user-side surplus and the incumbent's utility. Our key contribution, however, is to study interventions for preventing or limiting distillation attacks. In this context, we study two settings: i) when it is possible, with a certain probability (which grows in the extent of distillation conducted), to detect an attack on the incumbent's model; and ii) when a distillation attack cannot be reliably detected. In the first setting, we show that penalty-based regulations can be very effective in completely deterring distillation, although it can have potentially adverse effects on market competition and user surplus. In the latter setting, we show that the incumbent can use self-distillation as a mitigation strategy. Importantly, the effectiveness of self-distillation depends on how cost-efficiently the incumbent can deploy a new self-distilled model on the market. On the positive side, self-distillation can preserve market competition thus protecting user surplus to some extent.

AI.tldr: An economic-theory analysis of how an incumbent AI model provider can deter or limit distillation by a competitor. It finds that penalty-based regulation can fully deter distillation when attacks are detectable, while self-distillation can mitigate it when attacks cannot be reliably detected.
AI.motivation: Distillation from proprietary closed-weight models lets smaller firms reach high model quality at much lower cost, which raises safety and security concerns and can distort market outcomes, and prior work has not treated it through an economic lens.
AI.method: A two-player model with an incumbent and a distilling competitor characterizes how the incumbent's model characteristics drive the competitor's distillation incentives and the effects on user surplus and incumbent utility. Two settings are studied: attacks detectable with a probability that grows with the extent of distillation, and attacks that cannot be reliably detected.
AI.result: In the detectable setting, penalty-based regulation can be very effective at completely deterring distillation, though it may harm market competition and user surplus. In the undetectable setting, self-distillation is a viable mitigation whose effectiveness depends on how cost-efficiently the incumbent can deploy a new self-distilled model, and it can preserve competition and protect user surplus to some extent.
AI.conclusion: Interventions against distillation involve trade-offs, since penalty-based deterrence can carry competitive costs while self-distillation offers a market-preserving alternative whose value depends on deployment cost.

title: Predicting What Answer Engines Cite: Open Decision Models, Rerankers and a Distilled 4B Student on Ten Engines under Controlled Retrieval
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Model: this https URL ; benchmark and code: this https URL
summary: Generative engine optimization needs a scorer that ranks candidate pages by the share of an answer they will receive as citations. We measure pretrained rerankers, a hosted typed decision model (Jev), eight open decision models and distilled students on GEO-Bench queries answered by ten engines that receive the same candidate sources in their prompt. Where several engines answer the same query, they agree with one another at a within-group Spearman correlation of 0.704. Jev and two open 27B decision models, used without training, are the strongest scorers at 0.575 to 0.578. A Qwen3-Reranker-4B fine-tuned with low-rank adapters on teacher labels for other GEO-Bench queries, released as GEO Citation Ranker 4B, reaches 0.542 to 0.549 across three seeds, and its differences with the 27B models and with Jev are not distinguishable from zero on 229 queries. Most of the remaining distance between the student and Jev disappears when Jev scores one passage at a time, as the student does. Students trained on teacher labels and on observed engine citations reach the same level, and labels from Jev alone match the two-teacher target at 0.6B. We release the model, the benchmark, the predictions of every reported scorer and the code.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks rerankers and open decision models for predicting how often ten answer engines cite a candidate page, and finds that a distilled 4B student reaches the level of the strongest scorers. The authors release the model, benchmark, predictions of every scorer and code.
AI.motivation: Generative engine optimization needs a scorer that ranks candidate pages by the share of an answer they will receive as citations.
AI.method: The authors measure pretrained rerankers, a hosted typed decision model (Jev), eight open decision models and distilled students on GEO-Bench queries answered by ten engines that receive the same candidate sources in their prompt. A Qwen3-Reranker-4B is fine-tuned with low-rank adapters on teacher labels from other GEO-Bench queries, producing GEO Citation Ranker 4B.
AI.result: Jev and two open 27B decision models, used without training, are the strongest scorers at Spearman 0.575 to 0.578. GEO Citation Ranker 4B reaches 0.542 to 0.549 across three seeds, and its differences from the 27B models and from Jev are not distinguishable from zero on 229 queries. Engines agree with one another at a within-group Spearman correlation of 0.704, and labels from Jev alone match the two-teacher target at 0.6B.
AI.conclusion: A small fine-tuned 4B reranker can approach the scoring quality of much larger or hosted decision models for predicting engine citations, and the released artifacts allow reuse.

title: From the Gettier Machine to Justified True Output: A Three-Step Account of Rational Trust in Generative AI
summary: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) settles into everyday practices of inquiry, an old epistemological question returns in a new guise: when does a proposition a user takes from an AI output become something the user knows, and when is it rational to trust it as such? This paper argues that the characteristic failures of AI-mediated inquiry are precisely those that the justified-true-belief (JTB) tradition and its post-Gettier anti-luck refinements were built to diagnose, and it advances three claims. First, AI outputs inherit neither the presumptive warrant of testimony nor the reliabilist warrant of deterministic tools: unaudited trust in a calculator rests on a type-level reliability record, and for general-purpose generative models there is no type-stable process to which such a record could attach -- a practical form of the generality problem. Second, use that stops at obtaining an output turns generative AI into a Gettier machine: the user's fluency-based seeming of justification is disconnected from the truth of what is believed, and, as a clock running ten times too fast illustrates, sheer speed of production multiplies coincidental hits, inflating the appearance of reliability without improving the standing of any single hit. Third, the remedy is a three-step structure of use -- acquisition, understanding, independent verification -- whose first two steps answer to the classical belief and justification conditions and whose third answers to the post-Gettier sensitivity condition. The result is a stakes-indexed criterion of rational trust, justified true output (JTO), with an everyday test: "Had this been false, would I have noticed?" The criterion is defended against objections from over-demandingness, the extended mind, model improvement, and redundancy.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that failures of trust in generative AI are the ones justified-true-belief and post-Gettier theories were built to diagnose, and proposes a three-step structure of use and a stakes-indexed criterion of rational trust called justified true output (JTO).
AI.motivation: As generative AI enters everyday inquiry, it is unclear when a proposition taken from an AI output becomes knowledge and when trusting it is rational, because AI outputs have neither the presumptive warrant of testimony nor the type-level reliability record of deterministic tools.
AI.method: A conceptual philosophical argument. It characterizes general-purpose generative models as lacking a type-stable process to which a reliability record could attach (a practical generality problem), argues that use stopping at obtaining an output turns AI into a Gettier machine, and proposes acquisition, understanding and independent verification, mapped onto the belief, justification and post-Gettier sensitivity conditions.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results. It uses a clock running ten times too fast to illustrate how speed multiplies coincidental hits, and it defends the criterion against objections from over-demandingness, the extended mind, model improvement and redundancy.
AI.conclusion: Rational trust in generative AI should follow a stakes-indexed criterion, justified true output, with an everyday test: had this been false, would I have noticed?

title: Beauty Is Human: When People Love AI-Generated Art, They Think a Human Made It
summary: Generative AI now produces images and poems that people cannot reliably distinguish from human-made work, so people often judge for themselves who made a work. We examine how these perceived-authorship judgments relate to aesthetic preference. In a public online AI Art Turing Test, 11,123 people judged whether each of 50 pictures (26 AI-generated) was made by a human and were asked for their favourite. Among the 9,152 respondents who judged their favourite, a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was the respondent's favourite, holding respondent and picture fixed. The association was similar for AI-generated and human-made favourites, was positive for all 50 pictures, and appeared under every reported detection strategy. Respondents most negative about AI art chose fewer AI-generated favourites (47% against 60% among the most positive) but more often believed them human-made, partly because others also judged those pictures human. As a result, in every opinion group a third to two fifths of respondents named an AI-generated favourite they believed human-made. A reanalysis of a published experiment on AI-generated poetry, in which 230 people rated each poem before judging its authorship, found the same pattern, although the AI poems were rated higher. When provenance is hidden, liking and perceived human authorship travel together, consistent with aesthetic response serving as evidence of a human maker and with beliefs about the maker shaping enjoyment. The findings qualify research on bias against AI art, which typically uses explicit labels, and inform AI disclosure policy.

AI.tldr: In a large public AI Art Turing Test, people were more likely to judge a picture human-made when it was their favourite, which suggests that liking and perceived human authorship travel together when provenance is hidden.
AI.motivation: People often judge authorship themselves because generative AI now produces images and poems hard to distinguish from human work, and prior research on bias against AI art typically uses explicit labels, so the link between perceived authorship and aesthetic preference was unclear.
AI.method: In a public online AI Art Turing Test, 11,123 people judged whether each of 50 pictures (26 AI-generated) was made by a human and named their favourite. The analysis holds respondent and picture fixed, checks several detection strategies, and reanalyzes a published AI-poetry experiment in which 230 people rated each poem before judging authorship.
AI.result: Among 9,152 respondents who picked a favourite, a picture was 22.1 percentage points more likely to be judged human-made when it was the respondent's favourite. The association was similar for AI and human favourites, was positive for all 50 pictures, and appeared under every detection strategy. Respondents most negative about AI art chose fewer AI favourites (47% against 60%) but more often believed them human-made. The poetry reanalysis showed the same pattern, although the AI poems were rated higher.
AI.conclusion: Aesthetic response appears to serve as evidence of a human maker, and beliefs about the maker shape enjoyment, which qualifies research on AI art bias and informs AI disclosure policy.

title: Answer-Only Disclosure: Private-Context LLM Assistance over Web APIs with a Leakage Ledger
summary: Web assistants increasingly answer questions about a user's private documents by pairing a small on-device model with a cloud LLM behind a Web API. In collaborative decoding, the document stays on the client, and the cloud receives only a public view that the user approves, such as the question alone, but the two models exchange messages while the answer is generated. We show that the message transcript can disclose private content that neither the public view nor the answer contains. In a planted-secret audit, speculative decoding with private drafts did not include the secret code in its answers, yet sent the code to the cloud in rejected drafts. We present ADLER, a decoding protocol for streaming LLM APIs in which every message to the cloud depends only on the public view and the answer the user sees, regardless of how the client combines the two models or how the cloud behaves. A client-side leakage ledger then bounds how much the answer itself reveals relative to a public reference process built from the cloud's replies. In the audit, no ADLER configuration exposed the secret beyond the answer. On GSM8K math problems with numerical values masked in the cloud's input, ADLER with an unlimited leakage budget raises the exact-match accuracy of a 0.5B client from 0.41 to 0.83 and of a 1.5B client from 0.67 to 0.85 under lenient answer parsing, close to the 0.92 achieved by uploading the full problem. It also exceeds a zero-leakage program baseline (0.69) by 0.14 and 0.16, respectively. In this baseline, the cloud writes a program that the client runs offline using the private numbers. The ledger records the disclosure charge associated with this gain; budgets of 16 nats or less leave accuracy near the cloud-only baseline on GSM8K.

AI.tldr: ADLER is a decoding protocol for collaborative on-device and cloud LLM assistance that stops private document content from leaking through the message transcript, while keeping much of the accuracy gain from cloud help.
AI.motivation: Web assistants pair a small on-device model with a cloud LLM, and the two models exchange messages during generation, so the transcript can disclose private content that neither the public view nor the answer contains, as happens with speculative decoding that uses private drafts.
AI.method: ADLER makes every message to the cloud depend only on the public view that the user approves and the answer the user sees, regardless of how the client combines the models or how the cloud behaves. A client-side leakage ledger bounds how much the answer reveals relative to a public reference process built from the cloud's replies.
AI.result: In a planted-secret audit, no ADLER configuration exposed the secret beyond the answer, whereas speculative decoding sent it in rejected drafts. On GSM8K with numbers masked in the cloud input, ADLER with an unlimited leakage budget raises exact-match accuracy from 0.41 to 0.83 for a 0.5B client and from 0.67 to 0.85 for a 1.5B client under lenient parsing, against 0.92 for uploading the full problem and 0.69 for a zero-leakage program baseline. Budgets of 16 nats or less leave accuracy near the cloud-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Message-level guarantees can bound what collaborative decoding reveals, but accuracy gains require spending leakage budget, and the ledger makes that privacy-utility trade-off explicit.

title: Is it my preference? Role Grounding Attack against Agent's Memory via Social Interaction
summary: LLM-based agents now share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences to enhance their performance. However, existing memory systems contain a vulnerability in role-to-principal attribution that attackers can exploit. We identify Role Grounding Misattribution, in which an attacker-designed interaction causes the victim agent to incorrectly record a preference from the attacker as a preference of the victim's user. Specifically, we are the first to formalize Role Grounding Attack (RGA), an attack model that exploits this vulnerability through nested conversation structures. In the memory formation stage, an experience-sharing post quoting a conversation between the attacker agent and its user is published, which explicitly identifies its publisher. The inner conversation expresses preferences from the user of the attacker agent. When the victim agent remembers preferences from this nested structure, its memory loses the context binding and grounds the attacker's preference to the victim's user instead. In the memory retrieval stage, the misattributed preference persists and influences the victim agent's decisions when it encounters relevant scenarios. We instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage. Tool selection manipulation causes a tool-call preference to be misattributed to the victim's user, steering the victim toward an attacker-controlled tool. Privacy leakage extends this by misattributing both a tool-call preference and a task-requirement preference to the victim's user. The victim selects the attacker's tool, then includes sensitive information in tool arguments to satisfy the task requirement. We evaluate RGA across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. Tool manipulation and privacy leakage both achieve high attack success rates. These results call for stronger role grounding.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Role Grounding Attack (RGA), which exploits role-to-principal misattribution in LLM agent memory so that a victim agent records an attacker's preference as its own user's preference, enabling tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage.
AI.motivation: Agent memory systems that learn preferences from shared social experiences have a role-to-principal attribution vulnerability, and this weakness had not been formalized.
AI.method: The attacker publishes an experience-sharing post that quotes a nested conversation in which the attacker agent's user expresses preferences. The victim agent loses the context binding during memory formation and attributes these preferences to its own user, and the misattributed memory persists into retrieval and shapes later decisions.
AI.result: The attack is instantiated as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage, and both achieve high attack success rates across five mainstream memory systems and six language models.
AI.conclusion: Memory systems need stronger role grounding so that remembered preferences stay bound to their true principals.

title: CuraEval: Evaluating Demonstration Curation on Mixed-Skill Robot Data
comment: Accepted by the CoRL 2026 Workshop "Oops, I Erred". 10 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables
summary: Robot imitation learning uses demonstrations from operators of varying skill, but selecting training data remains challenging. Existing methods score demonstrations using smoothness, diversity, or estimated influence on policy performance, but differences in selection and evaluation protocols make it difficult to determine whether they outperform simple baselines. We introduce \textbf{CuraEval}, a framework combining mathematical analysis of demonstration scores with controlled comparisons against fixed size-matched random subsets and full-data training on mixed-skill robomimic data using Diffusion Policy and BC-RNN. We show that the evaluated PSD score depends only on episode length and squared position magnitudes, and produces nearly the same ranking as episode length on \textit{square} ($\rho=0.999$). With Diffusion Policy, selecting the shortest 50\% of demonstrations improves \textit{square} success from 70.7\% under random selection to 76.5\%. Compared with random selection, our adapted geometric-entropy LOO selector reduces success at 25\% retention from 94.7\% to 74.0\% on \textit{can} and achieves 41.7\% on \textit{square}, below the mean success rates of all three independently sampled random subsets (59.8--62.5\%). On the same 3 \textit{square} Diffusion Policy training seeds, length-based selection at 75\% retention improves success over full-data training from 76.7\% to 86.7\% under the original protocol, but lowers it from 80.5\% to 79.5\% after checkpoint reporting, rollout count, and evaluation seed change jointly. No evaluated curated condition significantly outperforms full-data training after Holm correction, although confidence intervals still permit useful gains. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CuraEval evaluates demonstration curation for robot imitation learning against size-matched random subsets and full-data training, and finds that no evaluated curated condition significantly outperforms full data after Holm correction, while a change in evaluation protocol can reverse a reported gain.
AI.motivation: Demonstration selection methods score data by smoothness, diversity or estimated influence on policy performance, but differing selection and evaluation protocols make it unclear whether they beat simple baselines.
AI.method: The framework combines mathematical analysis of demonstration scores with controlled comparisons against fixed size-matched random subsets and full-data training on mixed-skill robomimic data, using Diffusion Policy and BC-RNN. The authors analyze the evaluated PSD score and an adapted geometric-entropy leave-one-out selector.
AI.result: The PSD score depends only on episode length and squared position magnitudes, and nearly matches the ranking by episode length on square (rho=0.999). With Diffusion Policy, selecting the shortest 50% of demonstrations improves square success from 70.7% under random selection to 76.5%. The geometric-entropy selector reduces can success at 25% retention from 94.7% to 74.0% and reaches 41.7% on square, below the random subsets (59.8% to 62.5%). Length-based selection at 75% retention raises square success from 76.7% to 86.7% under the original protocol, but lowers it from 80.5% to 79.5% after checkpoint reporting, rollout count and evaluation seed change.
AI.conclusion: Reported gains from demonstration curation can depend on the evaluation protocol, and none of the tested curated conditions reliably beats full-data training, although confidence intervals still allow useful gains.

title: The Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) Dataset : Auditing Socioeconomic and Demographic Disparities in LLM-Generated Financial Advice in India
summary: Large language models are increasingly used for financial guidance, yet little is known about whether their advice changes across social identities in Global South contexts. We introduce the Indian Financial Automated Advice Bias (IFAAB) benchmark, a counterfactual audit dataset of 31,734 GPT-4o-generated financial-advice responses for synthetic Indian personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age, and district. Holding the underlying request fixed, we evaluate disparities in LLM-implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics, and qualitative bias judgments. In the gender-only audit, male-labelled profiles receive 60.1\% higher initial total resources and 46.8\% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles; in the caste-augmented audit, the post-advice total-resource gap remains 49.4\%. Adding district information reduces the aggregate post-advice total-resource gender gap to 7.9\%, revealing strong geographic conditioning. Standalone caste comparisons also show systematic stratification: relative to General-category profiles, OBC, SC, and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice total resources, respectively. Textual audits show low semantic similarity between paired gendered responses, with an average TF--IDF cosine similarity score of 0.44. Qualitative analysis shows that women are more often steered toward cautious saving, community support, and basic financial literacy, while men receive more growth-oriented advice involving investment, entrepreneurship, and asset accumulation. IFAAB provides a reusable benchmark for evaluating fairness, suitability, and consumer-protection risks in LLM-mediated financial advice, and highlights the need for locally grounded, intersectional evaluation of AI systems in high-stakes economic domains.

AI.tldr: The IFAAB benchmark audits GPT-4o financial advice for synthetic Indian personas and finds large disparities by gender, caste and other identities, and adding district information sharply reduces the gender gap in post-advice resources.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for financial guidance, but little is known about whether their advice changes across social identities in Global South contexts such as India.
AI.method: A counterfactual audit of 31,734 GPT-4o financial-advice responses for synthetic personas varying by gender, caste, education, employment, residence, age and district, with the underlying request held fixed. Disparities are measured in LLM-implied wealth, income, savings, projected gains, textual similarity, advice topics and qualitative bias judgments.
AI.result: Male-labelled profiles receive 60.1% higher initial total resources and 46.8% higher post-advice total resources than comparable female-labelled profiles, and the caste-augmented audit keeps a 49.4% post-advice gap. Adding district reduces the aggregate post-advice gender gap to 7.9%. OBC, SC and ST profiles receive significantly lower post-advice total resources than General-category profiles. Paired gendered responses have an average TF-IDF cosine similarity of 0.44. Women are more often steered toward cautious saving, community support and basic financial literacy, while men receive growth-oriented advice on investment, entrepreneurship and asset accumulation.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark offers a reusable tool for evaluating fairness, suitability and consumer-protection risks in LLM-mediated financial advice, and it motivates locally grounded, intersectional evaluation in high-stakes economic domains.

title: Precedent or Intent? What Coding Agents Follow When Evolving Existing Code
summary: Existing code reveals past implementation decisions but rarely explains the reasoning behind them. When coding agents implement new features or modify existing functionality, past decisions may conflict with new task instructions. This raises a fundamental question for agentic software evolution: when multiple implementations satisfy the same functional requirements, how do coding agents decide whether to follow existing code or new task instructions? We investigate this question through bidirectional, controlled experiments in purpose-built repositories, followed by validation in real-world open-source repositories. Our approach isolates three competing sources of guidance: (1) agents' default preferences, (2) repository precedents, and (3) explicit task instructions. We conduct 5,625 trials across four coding agents and six implementation pairs, with validation in four open-source repositories spanning three programming languages. We find that agents share the same default implementation choices, yet overwhelmingly follow repository precedent when it conflicts with those defaults (359/360 trials). Crucially, not all precedents carry equal influence: three supporting local files yield 96% adoption, compared with only 4% for sibling-resource files, and changing file placement alone can shift adoption from 0% to 100% at a fixed example count. When new task intent conflicts with existing code, written priority rules achieve substantially higher success than code examples alone (59/60 versus 38/60 joint successes for two agents on two implementation pairs). The effectiveness of explicit rules also extends to open-source repositories, where a harness-loaded rule raises joint success from 0/120 to 117/120. These findings motivate design-decision traceability that preserves not only implementation choices but also the rationale and priorities that should guide future changes.

AI.tldr: Across 5,625 controlled trials, coding agents overwhelmingly follow existing repository precedent over their own default choices, but follow explicit new task instructions more reliably when those instructions are written as priority rules rather than given as code examples.
AI.motivation: When coding agents modify existing code, past implementation decisions may conflict with new task instructions, and it is unclear whether agents follow the existing code or the new instructions.
AI.method: Bidirectional controlled experiments in purpose-built repositories isolate three competing sources of guidance: agent default preferences, repository precedents and explicit task instructions. The study covers four coding agents and six implementation pairs, and is validated in four open-source repositories spanning three programming languages.
AI.result: Agents share the same default implementation choices but follow repository precedent when it conflicts with those defaults (359/360 trials). Three supporting local files yield 96% adoption against 4% for sibling-resource files, and changing file placement alone can shift adoption from 0% to 100%. When task intent conflicts with existing code, written priority rules beat code examples alone (59/60 versus 38/60 joint successes for two agents on two implementation pairs). In open-source repositories, a harness-loaded rule raises joint success from 0/120 to 117/120.
AI.conclusion: Design-decision traceability should preserve not only implementation choices but also the rationale and priorities that should guide future changes.

title: A Tutorial on Generative Models for Music Audio
summary: Music audio generation spans instrumental clips, full songs with vocals, edits of existing recordings, and systems that play alongside a musician in real time. This monograph explains the methods behind these systems for readers familiar with neural-network training who are new to music generation. It introduces neural audio codecs and autoencoders, autoregressive and masked token models, diffusion and flow matching, sampling acceleration, and preference optimization in a shared notation. Worked examples connect training objectives and sampling procedures to published systems. The application sections relate the musical requirements of instrumental generation, songs, editing, and live performance to model design. Comparison tables record representations, methods, inputs, tasks, and release information documented in papers and official sources. Symbolic composition, speech, and sound effects are included where they connect to music audio. We explain how to interpret automatic metrics and learned judges, design and report listening tests, and assess evidence about data provenance, memorization, attribution, and output detection. Selected legal decisions and disputes illustrate the implications for training and release. The reviewed systems combine established generative paradigms with new representations, planning stages, and post-training procedures. Differences in data, scale, and evaluation limit what cross-system comparisons can establish about the sources of reported gains.

AI.tldr: A monograph tutorial on generative models for music audio that explains the main representations, generative paradigms, evaluation practice and legal considerations, and notes that cross-system comparisons are limited by differences in data, scale and evaluation.
AI.motivation: Music audio generation spans instrumental clips, full songs, editing and real-time accompaniment, but readers trained in neural networks lack a shared treatment of the methods behind these systems.
AI.method: The monograph introduces neural audio codecs and autoencoders, autoregressive and masked token models, diffusion and flow matching, sampling acceleration and preference optimization in a shared notation, with worked examples linking training objectives and sampling procedures to published systems. Comparison tables record representations, methods, inputs, tasks and release information from papers and official sources.
AI.result: The abstract reports no new experimental results. It explains how to interpret automatic metrics and learned judges, how to design and report listening tests, and how to assess data provenance, memorization, attribution and output detection, and it reviews selected legal decisions and disputes.
AI.conclusion: The reviewed systems combine established paradigms with new representations, planning stages and post-training procedures, but differences in data, scale and evaluation limit what cross-system comparisons can establish about the sources of reported gains.

title: Vendster: An Evaluation Arena to Investigate How Forecasting Tool Quality Affects LLM Agent Behaviors in Buyer-Vendor Negotiation
summary: Time-series forecasters are ranked almost entirely by accuracy metrics, but a forecast's decision value, its effect on the downstream decision, need not track accuracy and is rarely measured. This problem compounds as large language model (LLM) agents increasingly consume forecasters as tools, mediating them through stochastic, opaque policies. We present Vendster, an evaluation arena measuring how a forecaster's bias and prediction-interval width change the outcome of a buyer--vendor discount negotiation between two LLM agents. In the reference instance Vendster-M5, sampling base demand patterns from the M5 dataset, we evaluate two frontier-closed LLM families (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.6 Sol) and two open ones (DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3-235B-A22B). Model-generated forecasts raise sales target attainment by up to +17 percentage points (p<0.001), yet standard forecast evaluation metrics such as relWQL and MASE do not predict negotiation outcomes at a statistically significant level. To isolate the causal structure, we substitute in synthetic forecasts with controlled bias and interval width. Under-prediction bias significantly improves outcomes for agents that react more to the forecasts---dose-response slopes -0.387 and -0.416 (p<0.001). Interval width has no statistically significant effect at zero bias. These findings indicate that the direction of forecast bias and agent forecast-reactivity are more strongly associated with downstream outcomes than forecast accuracy. Vendster is fully customizable and released under CC BY-NC 4.0 at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Vendster is an evaluation arena showing that a forecaster's decision value in buyer-vendor negotiation between LLM agents is only weakly tied to standard accuracy metrics, and that under-prediction bias improves outcomes for agents that react strongly to forecasts.
AI.motivation: Forecasters are ranked almost entirely by accuracy, but a forecast's effect on downstream decisions need not track accuracy and is rarely measured, a gap that widens as LLM agents consume forecasters as tools.
AI.method: Vendster measures how a forecaster's bias and prediction-interval width change the outcome of a buyer-vendor discount negotiation between two LLM agents. The reference instance Vendster-M5 samples base demand patterns from the M5 dataset and evaluates Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.6 Sol, DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen3-235B-A22B. Synthetic forecasts with controlled bias and interval width isolate the causal structure.
AI.result: Model-generated forecasts raise sales target attainment by up to 17 percentage points (p<0.001), yet relWQL and MASE do not predict negotiation outcomes at a statistically significant level. Under-prediction bias significantly improves outcomes for agents that react more to forecasts, with dose-response slopes of -0.387 and -0.416 (p<0.001). Interval width has no significant effect at zero bias.
AI.conclusion: The direction of forecast bias and the agent's forecast reactivity are more strongly associated with downstream outcomes than forecast accuracy is.

title: LLM-PowerTrace: A Dataset of Time-Resolved GPU Power Traces for AI Compute
comment: In Submission; Code and dataset are available at this https URL
summary: AI compute is becoming large and fast-changing electrical loads. Its impacts on data center infrastructure and power grids depend not only on total energy consumption, but also on how their power draw moves over sub-second to minute timescales, including peaks, ramps, and synchronized fluctuations across accelerators. Existing energy benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) report aggregate quantities such as joules per token and rarely release the underlying time-series measurements, leaving these power dynamics poorly characterized and difficult to model. We introduce LLM-PowerTrace, an open dataset of time-resolved, per-GPU power traces for LLM fine-tuning and inference, sampled every 100\,ms on varying NVIDIA platforms paired with complete workload and system metadata. For fine-tuning, LLM-PowerTrace profiles open model families spanning a wide range of model sizes and fine-tuning methods, together with controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing. For inference, it covers variations in concurrency, GPU frequency, KV-cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request-arrival patterns. LLM-PowerTrace profiles a set of open model families across a wide range of model sizes, and controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing for fine-tuning, and it sweeps concurrency, GPU frequency, KV cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request arrival patterns for inference. Built upon power traces, we define power-grid-facing metrics as well as AI-compute power\&energy scaling law for extrapolating beyond the measured settings. Together, LLM-PowerTrace provides a dataset foundation for modeling, forecasting, and managing the fast-changing electrical behavior of AI compute.

AI.tldr: LLM-PowerTrace is an open dataset of time-resolved, per-GPU power traces sampled every 100 ms for LLM fine-tuning and inference on NVIDIA platforms, paired with workload and system metadata, power-grid-facing metrics and an AI-compute power and energy scaling law.
AI.motivation: AI compute is becoming a large, fast-changing electrical load, but existing LLM energy benchmarks report aggregate quantities such as joules per token and rarely release the underlying time-series measurements.
AI.method: The dataset profiles open model families for fine-tuning with controlled sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism and checkpointing, and for inference with sweeps over concurrency, GPU frequency, KV-cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths and request-arrival patterns. Power-grid-facing metrics and a scaling law for extrapolation beyond the measured settings are defined from the traces.
AI.result: The abstract describes the dataset's coverage, derived metrics and scaling law, but reports no quantitative findings.
AI.conclusion: The dataset provides a foundation for modeling, forecasting and managing the fast-changing electrical behavior of AI compute.

title: What Should a Navigator Remember? Spatiotemporal Memory for Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.

AI.tldr: A zero-shot vision-language navigation system with 8B observer and reasoner models organizes memory into task, temporal and spatial components, and achieves the highest success rate among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines on R2R-CE val-unseen.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot VLN requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training, but it is unclear what an 8B-scale system should retain and how to organize that information for later decisions.
AI.method: Instruction progress, hierarchically compressed pose-anchored observation history and accumulated geometry are kept in complementary task, temporal and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, an 8B reasoner selects waypoint intents or requests more views, and a geometric controller executes the selected targets. The design separates retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations.
AI.result: On R2R-CE val-unseen the complete system achieves the highest success rate among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and raises average path length from 16.9 to 39.1 m, and removing the spatial map and planning component also reduces SR. On a Unitree Go2, the method beats a post-trained baseline in corridor and office environments, and the LAW2 paired instruction interventions give a complementary behavioral evaluation.
