AI.conclusion: Preserving task progress, observation history and geometry in structured memory supports zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.

title: SpaceAct: Benchmarking 3D Spatial and Temporal Reasoning via Closed-Loop Action and Active Perception
summary: To solve problems in 3D space rather than merely describe images, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) need 3D spatiotemporal reasoning: reconstructing 3D geometry from occluded 2D views, anticipating physical dynamics, and executing precise, closed-loop actions. Prior studies test passive VQA on static images or symbolic planning, requiring no execution or supplying privileged coordinates while ignoring collision, statics, and timing. We introduce SpaceAct, an interactive benchmark evaluating 3D spatiotemporal reasoning via closed-loop physical action and active perception, with SAPA, a Spatiotemporal Active-Probing Agent framework. Built on interlocking bricks and mechanical puzzles, it has 108 verified instances across 36 task families in six categories, without privileged coordinates, and diagnostic modes (+plan, +state, no-camera, blind, L7 levers). In brick-bridging or aperture-threading, models rotate the camera to resolve occlusion, read in-scene rulers, output 6-DoF poses under swept-collision and statics checks, and self-correct via split-screen rollback feedback (dynamic tasks freeze time during deliberation and give five strobe frames). Across 10 frontier MLLMs on the 44 hardest instances, scores span 4.8-79.1 (seven solve at most 27.3% of 6-DoF tasks); for the top three, a reference plan (+plan) closes 44% of the gap while leaving collisions at 5.2 per episode, whereas adding exact 3D state (+state) closes 90% and cuts collisions to 0.5; for four others, +plan lifts the mean score from 10.9 to 35.3 and +state to 81.8; and 46% of failures are collision or observation loops. SpaceAct and SAPA advance evaluation to closed-loop physical interaction, showing that even with a valid plan, MLLMs remain bottlenecked by 3D visual grounding and action refinement, while offering a testbed for active multi-view exploration and explicit 3D grounding.

AI.tldr: SpaceAct is a closed-loop benchmark of 108 verified brick-bridging and mechanical-puzzle instances, paired with the SAPA agent framework, and shows that frontier MLLMs remain limited by 3D visual grounding and action refinement even when given a valid plan.
AI.motivation: Prior evaluations test MLLM spatial reasoning through passive VQA on static images or symbolic planning, which require no execution or supply privileged coordinates and ignore collision, statics and timing.
AI.method: SpaceAct is an interactive benchmark with 108 verified instances across 36 task families in six categories, with no privileged coordinates and diagnostic modes (+plan, +state, no-camera, blind and L7 levers). Models rotate the camera, read in-scene rulers and output 6-DoF poses checked for swept collision and statics, self-correcting through split-screen rollback feedback. Dynamic tasks freeze time during deliberation and give five strobe frames. SAPA is the Spatiotemporal Active-Probing Agent framework.
AI.result: Across 10 frontier MLLMs on the 44 hardest instances, scores span 4.8 to 79.1, and seven models solve at most 27.3% of 6-DoF tasks. For the top three models, +plan closes 44% of the gap but collisions remain at 5.2 per episode, while +state closes 90% and cuts collisions to 0.5. For four other models, +plan lifts the mean score from 10.9 to 35.3 and +state to 81.8. 46% of failures are collisions or observation loops.
AI.conclusion: Even with a valid plan, MLLMs remain bottlenecked by 3D visual grounding and action refinement, and the benchmark offers a testbed for active multi-view exploration and explicit 3D grounding.

title: The Code Behind the Layout: AI Agents for Analog Layout Generators
summary: Analog layout remains largely manual and hard to automate. Generator frameworks such as gLayout express layouts as programs, producing layouts from parameterized, design-rule-aware generators; however, writing such generators still takes expert effort. Large language models (LLMs) could now write generator code, and frontier models can even draw layout geometry from design intent. This raises a practical question: if a model can draw the layout itself, what does a generator framework still contribute, and is applying these models to a generator framework better than having them draw a layout from scratch? Through controlled experiments on gLayout in SKY130, we find that the main obstacle to drawing a layout directly is its time and token cost, and that the main advantage of a model building on a generator framework is reusability. Its verified primitives keep each model edit small enough to check, and its parameters allow a single edit to be evaluated across an entire family of layouts. Accordingly, a model is most effective when it develops the layout from the generator source of the family that the design intent belongs to, and tests each edit on the family members most likely to fail, so that one verified change improves every layout the generator produces. The results of these family tests can then serve as supervision for a local model, which learns edits that hold across the family at a fraction of the inference cost.

AI.tldr: Controlled experiments on gLayout in SKY130 show that LLM agents are most effective when they develop a parameterized generator for a layout family and verify each edit across family members, rather than drawing each layout from scratch.
AI.motivation: Analog layout remains largely manual, and frontier models can now draw layout geometry from design intent, so it is unclear what a generator framework still contributes and whether building on one beats drawing layouts from scratch.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on gLayout in SKY130 compare models that draw layouts directly with models that edit the generator source of the family the design intent belongs to, testing each edit on the family members most likely to fail. Family test results can then supervise a local model that learns edits holding across the family.
AI.result: The main obstacle to direct drawing is time and token cost, and the main advantage of building on a generator is reusability. Verified primitives keep each edit small enough to check, and parameters let a single edit be evaluated across an entire family, so one verified change improves every layout the generator produces. The abstract gives no numeric results.
AI.conclusion: Family test results can supervise a local model that learns family-wide edits at a fraction of the inference cost.

title: DecisionUnlearn-Bench: Unlearning Probabilistic Decisions under Changing Schemas
summary: Machine unlearning aims to reproduce the behavior of a model trained without designated data. For probabilistic decision models, this target also depends on the candidate options supplied at inference. We introduce DecisionUnlearn-Bench, an empirical framework that compares full, unlearned, and retain-only models across deletion granularities, label renderings, and candidate sets. Across 20 eligible model configurations on the BANKING77 dataset, full-to-oracle displacement increases consistently from example to association to class deletion. Replacing semantic option labels with opaque codes nearly eliminates the retrained oracle's recognition of deleted classes, even with successful acquisition of the full model, whereas changing the candidate set alters both the oracle and the measured unlearning progress. SimNPO satisfies the screening criterion in 19 of 20 configurations, but its gains vary substantially across seeds and deletion targets. Development tuning on the CLINC150 dataset does not establish a positive pooled effect across 48 intents. At approximately matched suppression, methods can differ markedly in oracle fidelity. Recovery experiments further distinguish initial forgetting from subsequent adaptation and show conclusions that depend on both architecture and metric. These results show that evaluating decision-model unlearning relative to a schema-specific retraining target, with separate reporting of effect size, utility, robustness, and recoverability.

AI.tldr: DecisionUnlearn-Bench shows that unlearning in probabilistic decision models must be evaluated against a schema-specific retraining target, because the option labels and candidate sets used at inference change both the oracle and the measured unlearning progress.
AI.motivation: For probabilistic decision models, the unlearning target also depends on the candidate options supplied at inference, so evaluations that ignore the schema can misjudge how well unlearning worked.
AI.method: An empirical framework compares full, unlearned and retain-only models across deletion granularities (example, association and class), label renderings and candidate sets. The main study uses 20 eligible model configurations on BANKING77, development tuning uses CLINC150 with 48 intents, and recovery experiments distinguish initial forgetting from later adaptation.
AI.result: Full-to-oracle displacement increases consistently from example to association to class deletion. Replacing semantic option labels with opaque codes nearly eliminates the retrained oracle's recognition of deleted classes, and changing the candidate set alters both the oracle and the measured progress. SimNPO satisfies the screening criterion in 19 of 20 configurations, but its gains vary substantially across seeds and deletion targets. Development tuning on CLINC150 does not establish a positive pooled effect across 48 intents.
AI.conclusion: Decision-model unlearning should be reported with separate effect size, utility, robustness and recoverability, since conclusions depend on both architecture and metric.

title: Tracekit Box: Running AI Agents in Micro-VMs Where Every Way Out Is Decided and Signed
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures, 19 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: AI agents now install packages, call model APIs with their operators' keys and change code in repositories that deploy to production. The network, credentials and write access they need are also how they can leak data, steal a key or change a system nobody approved. Sandboxes contain an agent but leave little evidence of what crossed their boundary; tracing records what happened but contains nothing. We present Tracekit Box, an open-source system (MIT, v0) that does both. Each job runs in its own Firecracker micro-VM with no network card. The only ways out are doors on the host, served over vsock: commands, outbound connections, secrets, model calls and the workspace patch. At every door a Tracekit signer the agent cannot reach decides what passes and signs it into one run per box. Names are resolved on the host; private and cloud-metadata addresses are always refused; secrets never enter the VM, which sees placeholders the host proxy swaps for real values only in one header for bound hosts; and changes come back as a patch applied file by file after the signer decides each file. Box fails closed, and each job ends as a .tkb bundle anyone can verify offline. All 13 end-to-end checks pass on a real KVM runner (the test that runs them takes 28.5 s, including image pull and boot); 15 fuzz targets on the trust boundary produced nine findings, all fixed; and the demo run's 102 signed records verify. Box does not yet run Firecracker's jailer, needs a co-located signer, and records processes inside the VM only where they cross a door.

AI.tldr: Tracekit Box is an open-source system (MIT, v0) that runs AI agent jobs in Firecracker micro-VMs with no network card, routes every exit through host-side doors that a signer decides and signs, and ends each job with a verifiable signed bundle.
AI.motivation: AI agents install packages, call model APIs with operators' keys and change code that deploys to production, and the same network, credential and write access lets them leak data or change systems without approval. Sandboxes contain agents but leave little evidence of what crossed their boundary, while tracing records activity but does not contain it.
AI.method: Each job runs in its own Firecracker micro-VM with no network card, and the only exits are host doors served over vsock for commands, outbound connections, secrets, model calls and the workspace patch. A Tracekit signer the agent cannot reach decides and signs what passes into one run per box. Names resolve on the host, private and cloud-metadata addresses are refused, and secrets never enter the VM, where placeholders are swapped for real values by the host proxy for bound hosts. Changes return as a patch applied file by file after the signer decides each file.
AI.result: All 13 end-to-end checks pass on a real KVM runner (28.5 s, including image pull and boot). Fifteen fuzz targets on the trust boundary produced nine findings, all fixed, and the demo run's 102 signed records verify. Limitations are that the jailer is not yet run, a co-located signer is needed, and processes inside the VM are recorded only where they cross a door.
AI.conclusion: Combining containment with signed, offline-verifiable records of boundary crossings gives agents a sandbox that also leaves an audit trail, subject to the stated limitations.

title: SaiVLA-JEPA: Evaluating Future Latent Prediction in JEPA-Conditioned VLA Control
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn to predict representations rather than pixels, offering a compact way to model how visual scenes evolve. We ask whether this predictive objective improves closed-loop control when a vision-language-action (VLA) policy already uses V-JEPA features. We call our JEPA-conditioned flow policy family SaiVLA-JEPA. It combines a vision-language model with a diffusion transformer action expert and receives features from a frozen V-JEPA encoder. Two lightweight auxiliary heads predict future representations during training and are omitted at inference, leaving the action sampler unchanged. We compare policies without JEPA features, with current JEPA conditioning, and with additional future supervision on 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes. Current JEPA conditioning reaches about 82.5% success versus 71.6% without JEPA, while future supervision provides no detectable aggregate gain at the evaluated training budget. We separately evaluate SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA, which adapts latent context, and SaiVLA-JEPA-TPA, which adapts selected parameters. The context-retry gain is a system-level result under a larger attempt budget; parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage over the frozen policy and target controls. These results motivate assessing latent-prediction objectives through paired closed-loop rollouts rather than latent loss alone.

AI.tldr: SaiVLA-JEPA tests whether JEPA-style future latent prediction improves closed-loop VLA control, and finds that conditioning on frozen V-JEPA features raises LIBERO-Plus success from about 71.6% to 82.5%, while auxiliary future supervision adds no detectable gain.
AI.motivation: JEPAs predict representations rather than pixels and may offer a compact model of how scenes evolve, but it is unknown whether this predictive objective improves closed-loop control when a VLA policy already uses V-JEPA features.
AI.method: The JEPA-conditioned flow policy combines a vision-language model with a diffusion transformer action expert and receives features from a frozen V-JEPA encoder. Two lightweight auxiliary heads predict future representations during training and are omitted at inference. Policies are compared without JEPA features, with JEPA conditioning and with added future supervision on 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes. The variants SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA (adapting latent context) and SaiVLA-JEPA-TPA (adapting selected parameters) are evaluated separately.
AI.result: Current JEPA conditioning reaches about 82.5% success against 71.6% without JEPA, while future supervision gives no detectable aggregate gain at the evaluated training budget. The context-retry gain is a system-level result under a larger attempt budget, and parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage over the frozen policy and target controls.
AI.conclusion: Latent-prediction objectives should be assessed through paired closed-loop rollouts rather than latent loss alone.

title: The Artificial Personality Model: Theory, Implementation, Measurement and Experimental Validation in Conversational Agents
summary: Artificial personality shapes user experience (UX) in human-machine interaction, yet coherent theoretical frameworks and validated measurement instruments remain limited. This paper refines and empirically evaluates the Artificial Personality Model (APM), a hybrid framework integrating human-centred and machine-specific personality dimensions. Across three experiments (N = 395), the model was operationalised and evaluated using the Artificial Personality Questionnaire (APQ). Factor analyses revealed that some human personality dimensions (e.g., agreeableness, conscientiousness) are partially transferable, whereas others (e.g., extraversion) did not emerge as distinct dimensions. Additional machine-specific dimensions were identified. The APQ provided encouraging initial psychometric evidence, while the human-centred BFI-2 showed poor reliability and an uninterpretable factor structure in Experiment 3. Experimental manipulations demonstrated significant effects of artificial personality on user satisfaction, continuous use intention, and social presence. The findings contribute an empirically refined framework and a novel instrument for measuring perceived artificial personality, offering practical guidance for designing conversational agents.

AI.tldr: The paper refines and empirically tests the Artificial Personality Model (APM), a hybrid framework combining human and machine-specific personality dimensions, and introduces the Artificial Personality Questionnaire (APQ) to measure perceived artificial personality in conversational agents. Across three experiments (N = 395), the APQ shows encouraging initial psychometric evidence and artificial personality significantly affects user satisfaction, continuous use intention and social presence.
AI.motivation: Artificial personality shapes user experience in human-machine interaction, but coherent theoretical frameworks and validated measurement instruments remain limited.
AI.method: The APM, a hybrid framework integrating human-centred and machine-specific personality dimensions, is operationalised and evaluated with the APQ across three experiments, using factor analyses and experimental manipulations of artificial personality. The human-centred BFI-2 is compared against the APQ.
AI.result: Agreeableness and conscientiousness are partially transferable to machines, extraversion does not emerge as a distinct dimension, and additional machine-specific dimensions are identified. The APQ shows encouraging initial psychometric evidence, while the BFI-2 shows poor reliability and an uninterpretable factor structure in Experiment 3. Manipulations significantly affect user satisfaction, continuous use intention and social presence.
AI.conclusion: The work contributes an empirically refined framework and a novel instrument for measuring perceived artificial personality, offering practical guidance for designing conversational agents.

title: How Deterministic SAST and AI Security Agents Divide the Work: Coverage, Harness Policy and Cost in Snyk VulnBench 2.0
comment: 44 pages, 21 figures, 7 tables. Benchmark harness, reference sets and all run data: this https URL ; companion site: this https URL
summary: We ask what AI coding agents and AI security harnesses find that deterministic static application security testing (SAST) does not, and what they miss that SAST catches. VulnBench 2.0 is a benchmark of 108 hand-curated, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in 20 open-source web applications in Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python and Java; 62 flow across more than one file. A finding is credited only if it locates the vulnerability's attacker-controlled source and its dangerous sink, each within two lines. We evaluate nine productized configurations under one blind protocol: the Snyk Code static analyzer, Claude Code's /security-review with three model and effort settings (one with the Snyk MCP server), Codex Security with GPT-5.6 Luna, Terra and Sol, and the DeepSec scanner with two model backends. Snyk Code reached 82.4% macro recall (89 of 108) and Claude Code with Opus 5 at xhigh effort 79.3% (85 of 108); they disagree on 28 vulnerabilities, split 16 to 12, too few to tell them apart. Neither engine was sufficient alone: together they reached 101 of 108, the ceiling of all seven comparable configurations combined, and the AI configurations also reported at least seven real vulnerabilities that the reference set did not contain and Snyk Code did not report. What an AI engine misses depends on its harness as much as on its model: without Claude Code's built-in review policy, the same model matched 16 instead of 9 of the 20 vulnerabilities in the classes that policy excludes or restricts (supplementary run on 19 of 20 applications); Codex Security with GPT-5.6 Sol located 80 vulnerabilities at file level but 34 at line level; DeepSec's model-free file selection kept a file from only 56 of the 108 flows. Coverage and cost were only loosely related. The harness, fixtures, reference sets and all run data are public.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks nine productized configurations of deterministic SAST tools and AI security agents on VulnBench 2.0, a set of 108 attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in 20 open-source web applications. Neither approach is sufficient alone: together they reach 101 of 108, and the AI configurations also report at least seven real vulnerabilities absent from the reference set.
AI.motivation: It is unclear what AI coding agents and AI security harnesses find that deterministic SAST does not, and what they miss that SAST catches.
AI.method: A blind evaluation protocol credits a finding only if it locates both the attacker-controlled source and the dangerous sink within two lines. The configurations include the Snyk Code analyzer, Claude Code's /security-review at three model and effort settings (one with the Snyk MCP server), Codex Security with GPT-5.6 Luna, Terra and Sol, and the DeepSec scanner with two model backends. The benchmark covers Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python and Java, with 62 flows spanning more than one file.
AI.result: Snyk Code reaches 82.4% macro recall (89 of 108) and Claude Code with Opus 5 at xhigh effort reaches 79.3% (85 of 108), with 28 disagreements split 16 to 12. Together the two reach 101 of 108. Without Claude Code's built-in review policy, the same model matches 16 instead of 9 of the 20 vulnerabilities in the excluded or restricted classes. Codex Security with GPT-5.6 Sol locates 80 vulnerabilities at file level but 34 at line level, and DeepSec's file selection covers only 56 of the 108 flows. Coverage and cost are only loosely related.
AI.conclusion: What an AI engine misses depends on its harness as much as on its model, so harness design and complementary use with static analysis matter; the harness, fixtures, reference sets and run data are released publicly.

title: Enhanced image forensics through partial C2PA-based provenance information
comment: paper accepted to IEEE International Workshop on Information Forensics and Security (WIFS) 2026
summary: Cryptographically verifiable C2PA-based Content Credentials (CCs) can be attached to freshly acquired or generated digital images but also to already existing ones with no previous provenance information, for instance after processing through trusted C2PA-enabled software tools. The latter case leads to images with so-called partial CCs, which capture only the last operations applied, while prior provenance remains unknown and can be investigated through signal forensics. This paper addresses the forensic analysis of such images, highlighting the opportunity to leverage the partial CCs as additional trusted knowledge to adapt forensic detectors towards the statistical characteristics of the image under analysis and mitigate potential distribution shifts. To this end, a two-step strategy is envisioned: (i) reconstructing the operations applied by the last signer through a structural analysis of the partial CCs; (ii) exploiting the obtained reconstruction to enhance the forensic detector of the analyst through an adaptation process. An empirical analysis on partial CCs produced by commercial C2PA-enabled software tools through different editing operations is carried out, providing evidence on the feasibility of the reconstruction in practical cases. An experimental case study on the forensic task of synthetic image detection is then presented, showing that the proposed strategy can significantly enhance the performance of state-of-the-art detectors on test images that are postprocessed via C2PA-enabled software tools after being generated/acquired.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a two-step strategy that reconstructs the operations applied by the last signer from partial C2PA Content Credentials and uses this reconstruction to adapt a forensic detector. For synthetic image detection, the approach significantly improves state-of-the-art detectors on images post-processed by C2PA-enabled software.
AI.motivation: Images with partial C2PA Content Credentials capture only the last operations applied, leaving earlier provenance unknown, and forensic detectors suffer distribution shifts on such images that existing methods do not address.
AI.method: Step one reconstructs the operations applied by the last signer through a structural analysis of the partial credentials. Step two uses this reconstruction to adapt the analyst's forensic detector toward the statistical characteristics of the image under analysis.
AI.result: An empirical analysis of partial credentials produced by commercial C2PA-enabled tools under different editing operations shows that the reconstruction is feasible in practical cases. In an experimental case study on synthetic image detection, the strategy significantly enhances the performance of state-of-the-art detectors on test images postprocessed via C2PA-enabled tools.
AI.conclusion: Partial Content Credentials can serve as additional trusted knowledge to improve forensic analysis of images, mitigating distribution shifts in synthetic image detection.

title: When AI performs, what remains? An integrative review of generative AI and cognitive capital in individuals and organizations
summary: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enables an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

AI.tldr: This integrative narrative review frames how generative AI affects individual and organizational knowledge work through the construct of cognitive capital. It proposes four mechanisms and seven evidence-based principles, showing that assisted performance differs from retained competence and that the same technology can support or displace learning.
AI.motivation: Generative AI's short-term productivity gains are well documented, but little is known about how the knowledge, skills and judgment that remain in people and organizations change over time.
AI.method: The paper defines individual and organizational cognitive capital and distinguishes it from the capability of the human-AI system, drawing on experimental, field and conceptual work. It proposes four mechanisms: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation, and derives testable propositions for each.
AI.result: Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. Five design levers for organizations are offered as proposals to be validated rather than established practice.
AI.conclusion: Cognitive capital provides a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption, and the authors outline a research agenda centred on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

title: Information-Theoretic Reliability--Safety Bounds and Finite-Alignment Dynamics in AI Knowledge Distillation
summary: The reliability and safety of artificial intelligence (AI), together with their transfer and evolution through knowledge distillation, have attracted growing attention. We establish an information-theoretic bound on the reliability--safety trade-off and characterize the dynamics of this trade-off under knowledge distillation. We first prove a universal trade-off inequality that is independent of the specific model form. Its boundary is determined solely by a single parameter Kh, which quantifies the hidden layer's ability to distinguish benign from hazardous inputs. We then develop a canonical Boltzmann-machine model of AI response behavior and derive two exact relations between reliability and safety. The trade-off curve is determined by the hazard discrimination capacity K, while the overall answer tendency controls the operating point along the curve. These relations agree well with existing experimental data. In knowledge distillation, we find that teacher responses induce a renormalization of the student model's trade-off parameters. We further use a renormalization-group approach to study multigenerational distillation, deriving exact recursion relations and the associated renormalization-group-like flows for two representative direct intergenerational distillation protocols at arbitrary teacher--student alignment strength. These flows reveal fixed-point structures, long-term dynamics, and critical behavior, yielding testable predictions for the critical transition between capability loss and stable transmission.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a universal information-theoretic trade-off inequality between AI reliability and safety, governed by a hidden-layer hazard discrimination parameter Kh, and studies how this trade-off evolves under knowledge distillation using renormalization-group analysis. The derived relations agree with existing experimental data and yield testable predictions for the transition between capability loss and stable transmission.
AI.motivation: The reliability and safety of AI, and how they are transferred and evolve through knowledge distillation, have received growing attention but lack a principled information-theoretic characterization.
AI.method: The authors prove a model-independent trade-off inequality whose boundary depends only on Kh. They develop a canonical Boltzmann-machine model of AI response behavior and derive two exact relations between reliability and safety. For multigenerational distillation, they use a renormalization-group approach to derive exact recursion relations for two direct intergenerational distillation protocols at arbitrary teacher-student alignment strength.
AI.result: The trade-off curve is determined by the hazard discrimination capacity K, and the overall answer tendency sets the operating point. In distillation, teacher responses renormalize the student's trade-off parameters. The renormalization-group flows reveal fixed-point structures, long-term dynamics and critical behavior.
AI.conclusion: The analysis gives a theoretical account of the reliability-safety trade-off under distillation and predicts a critical transition between capability loss and stable transmission that can be tested.

title: Evaluating Visual Realism of AI-Generated Videos with Eye Tracking
summary: Human evaluation of AI-generated videos has so far relied on explicit human feedback, such as judgments or ratings. While these signals capture the conclusions viewers reach, they fail to offer insights into the perception that leads to them. This paper investigates eye tracking as a complementary human evaluation signal for AI-generated videos. We conducted two Visual Turing Test (VTT) experiments with a total of 90 participants on videos generated by latest generative models, in which participants watched each video twice and then gave their feedback. Across the experiments, we collected 4,286 valid eye-tracking trials on 438 videos. Our analysis indicates that gaze patterns offer informative evaluation signals that align with explicit human feedback. Building on the findings, we propose the first computational method GazeEval to predict the perceived visual realism of AI-generated videos from eye-tracking data. It achieves 71.3% accuracy in prediction, providing evidence that eye tracking data carries informative signals about how people evaluate a video. We release the study data to support further research on eye tracking for evaluating AI-generated video.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes eye tracking as a complementary human evaluation signal for AI-generated videos and introduces GazeEval, a method that predicts perceived visual realism from eye-tracking data with 71.3% accuracy. Gaze patterns align with explicit human feedback, and the study data is released.
AI.motivation: Human evaluation of AI-generated videos relies on explicit judgments or ratings, which capture conclusions but not the perception that leads to them.
AI.method: Two Visual Turing Test experiments with 90 participants watched videos from recent generative models twice before giving feedback while their eye movements were recorded. Across 4,286 valid eye-tracking trials on 438 videos, the authors analysed gaze patterns and built GazeEval to predict perceived realism from eye-tracking data.
AI.result: Gaze patterns offer informative evaluation signals that align with explicit human feedback. GazeEval achieves 71.3% accuracy in predicting perceived visual realism of AI-generated videos.
AI.conclusion: Eye-tracking data carries informative signals about how people evaluate AI-generated videos, supporting its use as a complementary evaluation signal; the study data is released to support further research.

title: Autonomous Quantum Measurement with Agentic AI
summary: Quantum materials exhibit diverse electronic and functional phenomena, but their characterization requires extensive experimental expertise, iterative decision-making and accumulated laboratory knowledge that is difficult to document and transfer. Here we introduce Quantum Agent (QUANTA), an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for autonomous quantum-materials characterization. Using a widely adopted Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) as an experimental platform, QUANTA combines retrieval augmentation using scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting, and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Guided by incoming data, QUANTA evaluates measurement quality, revises experimental plans and selects subsequent measurements. We demonstrate these capabilities through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP, as well as investigations of nonlinear responses in magnetic material Co2MnGa. These results establish QUANTA as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces QUANTA, an agentic AI framework that autonomously characterizes quantum materials on a Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) by combining literature and protocol retrieval with specialized planning, troubleshooting and interpretation agents. Demonstrations on transport measurements of TaP and nonlinear responses in Co2MnGa show closed-loop, evidence-driven measurement.
AI.motivation: Characterizing quantum materials demands extensive experimental expertise, iterative decisions and laboratory knowledge that is hard to document and transfer.
AI.method: QUANTA uses retrieval augmentation over scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements, with agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Based on incoming data, it evaluates measurement quality, revises plans and selects subsequent measurements.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP and investigations of nonlinear responses in the magnetic material Co2MnGa, showing closed-loop operation guided by incoming data.
AI.conclusion: QUANTA is presented as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.

title: FlipJev: Fast Black-Box Red Teaming Finds Universal Adversarial Suffixes for Typed Decision Models
comment: Pre-print. Code: this https URL, Webpage: this https URL
summary: Typed decision models are an emerging class of language models that make decisions instead of generating free-text responses. They answer in a single fast and cheap query and are increasingly used, including in security-sensitive tasks. However, red teaming of these models leaves two gaps: existing adaptive attacks do not use their speed, and few studies have searched for universal adversarial examples. We fill both gaps on Jev, the representative typed decision model, with a quick black-box query-based attack that calls no attacker language model. We conduct extensive experiments on 12 datasets with different data types and application scenarios. The results show that Jev resists common prompt injections: no strategy changes a correct answer in 10,240 paired tests. In contrast, our attack finds short suffixes that flip confident answers within minutes. These suffixes are universal: one suffix per dataset flips 43% of unseen documents. Because typed decision models, unlike classic NLP models, can serve many tasks, we test whether these suffixes transfer across tasks. We find that one suffix generated from one task can flip 90-100% of the samples in other tasks. We therefore believe the evaluation of typed decision models must include strict adaptive attacks to fully reveal their robustness.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a fast black-box, query-based red-teaming attack on Jev, a typed decision model, that finds short universal adversarial suffixes which flip confident answers within minutes. Suffixes generated for one task also transfer to flip 90-100% of samples in other tasks.
AI.motivation: Typed decision models answer in a single fast query and are used in security-sensitive tasks, yet existing adaptive attacks do not exploit their speed and few studies search for universal adversarial examples.
AI.method: The attack is a quick black-box query-based method that calls no attacker language model. Experiments span 12 datasets with different data types and application scenarios, and the authors test whether suffixes generated on one task transfer to others.
AI.result: Jev resists common prompt injections, with no strategy changing a correct answer in 10,240 paired tests. The attack finds short suffixes that flip confident answers within minutes. One suffix per dataset flips 43% of unseen documents, and one suffix from one task flips 90-100% of samples in other tasks.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation of typed decision models must include strict adaptive attacks to reveal their robustness fully.

title: MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design seeks to learn reusable orchestration policies, yet prevailing approaches remain largely one-shot: an Orchestrator generates a system but only observes and learns from its terminal outcome. This paradigm discards execution trajectories that expose system-level failures and contain fine-grained information beyond the terminal outcome, leaving no direct basis for revising the source MAS, evaluating the updated MAS, or learning from the resulting contrast. To this end, we introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that closes this feedback loop by coupling an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner. For each task, the Orchestrator constructs and executes a source MAS to obtain an outcome score and an intermediate trajectory. Conditioned on the trajectory, the Refiner localizes an actionable failure, formulates a trajectory-grounded diagnosis, and proposes a bounded patch to the agents, information flow, or execution configuration. The executable updated MAS is re-executed on the same task to measure its realized outcome under stochastic execution. This pair-MAS comparison provides complementary learning signals: the Orchestrator learns to generate strong systems with fewer recoverable failures, whereas the Refiner learns to expose and repair observed weaknesses, thereby driving policy-level co-evolution across training iterations. Experiments show that MAS-Loop achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated baselines, with consistent gains from refinement across all evaluated benchmarks. The co-evolution process also yields MAS-JudgeCorpus, a dataset of execution-grounded source-updated pairs with orchestration- and trajectory-level supervision, which can provide the community with support for MAS reward modeling and trajectory-aware investigation.

AI.tldr: MAS-Loop closes the feedback loop in training-time multi-agent system design by pairing an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner that diagnoses execution failures and proposes bounded patches to the source system. It reports the strongest overall performance among the evaluated baselines and releases MAS-JudgeCorpus, a dataset of execution-grounded source-updated pairs.
AI.motivation: Existing one-shot MAS orchestration learns only from terminal outcomes, discarding execution trajectories that expose system-level failures and leaving no direct basis for revising, evaluating and learning from the source system.
AI.method: The Orchestrator builds and executes a source MAS to obtain an outcome score and a trajectory. The Refiner localizes an actionable failure, formulates a trajectory-grounded diagnosis and proposes a bounded patch to agents, information flow or execution configuration. The updated MAS is re-executed on the same task and compared with the source, and the resulting contrast drives co-evolution of both components.
AI.result: MAS-Loop achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated baselines, with consistent gains from refinement across all evaluated benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Execution-grounded co-evolution of orchestrator and refiner yields stronger systems with fewer recoverable failures, and MAS-JudgeCorpus can support MAS reward modelling and trajectory-aware investigation.

title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) serving only while the GPU has spare compute, so the best draft length, the number of tokens a small drafter guesses per step, shrinks as the batch grows. vLLM lets operators set the draft length for each batch size with a hand-written table, but nothing measures or corrects that table. We present TableTune. Its tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes, in minutes, the table that maximizes throughput. Its controller, a vLLM plugin, tracks how many guesses are accepted in live traffic and rebuilds the table while serving. We measure TableTune only against other ways to speculate. On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the throughput of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth) without the operator having to know which length that is. Against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine, its worst-case loss is never higher than theirs, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it is 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. Starting from mistuned tables, the controller raises throughput by up to 58% (up to 45% on vLLM's default runner), and after a workload switch with the DFlash drafter it recovers 96% of a stale table's loss. In llm-d's optimized-baseline deployment as shipped, two Qwen3-32B replicas on four GPUs, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load, and the controller raises the documented table's throughput by up to 29%.

AI.tldr: TableTune replaces hand-written draft-length tables in vLLM speculative decoding with a measured, self-correcting table that maximizes throughput across batch sizes. On an H100 it reaches at least 94% of the best fixed draft length in most settings, and in llm-d deployment it is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3.
AI.motivation: The best speculative draft length shrinks as batch size grows, and vLLM operators set it with a hand-written table that nothing measures or corrects.
AI.method: The tuner times the decoding step for every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and computes the throughput-maximizing table in minutes. A vLLM plugin controller tracks accepted guesses in live traffic and rebuilds the table during serving. It is compared against reimplementations of TurboSpec- and Nightjar-style control on the same engine.
AI.result: On an H100, the tuned table delivers at least 94% of the best fixed draft length at every load in four of five drafter settings (88% in the fifth). Its worst-case loss is never higher than the baselines, and with the EAGLE-3 drafter it loses 3% against 9% and 12%. On a mixture-of-experts model, vLLM's documented table loses up to 18% and the tuned table at most 3%. The controller raises throughput by up to 58% from mistuned tables and recovers 96% of a stale table's loss after a workload switch. In llm-d deployment on four GPUs with two Qwen3-32B replicas, the tuned table is up to 32% faster than a fixed draft length of 3 and up to 25% faster than vLLM's documented table at high load.
AI.conclusion: Measuring and self-correcting draft-length tables removes the need for operators to know the optimal draft length in advance and gives robust throughput across loads, drafters and models.

title: HERA: Assessing an Autonomous Agent for Quantum Device Measurement
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, plus Supplementary Information (7 figures, 6 tables); data and code at this https URL and this https URL
summary: Large language model agents have begun to carry out laboratory measurements, but their scientific conclusions are useful only if they hold up under scrutiny. Demonstrating this requires controlled studies because models are stochastic and the context a model is given steers its conclusions. Here we introduce HERA, an autonomous agent designed to carry out cryogenic transport measurements of quantum devices. HERA draws on a knowledge base curated by lab members that holds measurement protocols, software tools, and literature references. We assessed HERA with a blinded trial against an expert on the stacking order of two multilayer graphene devices, an ablation of its knowledge base, and hundreds of offline replays in which models designed the trial's central measurement without running it. HERA's conclusions matched the expert's sealed conclusions on both tested devices. The ablation and the replay studies measured the impact of the knowledge base across different models, showing that with it every model designed better measurements and reasoned more soundly. To test how readily HERA extends to a new problem, we tasked it with finding and characterizing superconductivity in a different material system. This required a few hours of expert time to develop a new experimental protocol, after which HERA did both autonomously. These results show that, with a knowledge base designed for the task, language model agents are capable of sound experimental science.

AI.tldr: HERA is an autonomous LLM agent that carries out cryogenic transport measurements of quantum devices using a lab-curated knowledge base. In a blinded trial it matched an expert's sealed conclusions on stacking order for two multilayer graphene devices, and it then autonomously characterized superconductivity in a new material system after a few hours of expert protocol development.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are beginning to run laboratory measurements, but their scientific conclusions are only useful if they hold up under controlled scrutiny, given model stochasticity and context sensitivity.
AI.method: The authors run a blinded trial of HERA against an expert, an ablation of its knowledge base, and hundreds of offline replays in which models designed the central measurement without executing it. The knowledge base holds measurement protocols, software tools and literature references. HERA is then tasked with a superconductivity search in a different material system.
AI.result: HERA's conclusions matched the expert's sealed conclusions on both tested devices. With the knowledge base, every model designed better measurements and reasoned more soundly across the ablation and replay studies. The new-material task required a few hours of expert time to develop a protocol, after which HERA completed the work autonomously.
AI.conclusion: With a knowledge base designed for the task, LLM agents can carry out sound experimental science.

title: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
comment: 50 pages, 9 figures, 15 tables. Specification, conformance vectors, verifier and benchmark: this https URL
summary: When one AI agent tells another that "the tests passed" or "a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs, signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Receivers check messages offline and give each claim a three-valued result: proven, unproven or failed. A claim that rests only on the agent's own report is never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval, and the chains can only narrow. We specify four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, and we prove the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all of them stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols (A2A with signed Agent Cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.

AI.tldr: PCM is a proof-carrying message protocol in which each inter-agent claim carries Merkle-log inclusion proofs and is verified offline into proven, unproven or failed. In a benchmark of 926 messages with 712 lies, it accepts only 10 lies, all stale evidence, while plain A2A accepts all 712.
AI.motivation: A receiving agent has only a sending agent's word for claims such as tests passing or human approval, and A2A and MCP authenticate the channel but not the sender, so prompt-injected agents can launder fabricated facts and authority.
AI.method: Each claim must carry evidence in the form of records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Claims resting only on the agent's own report are never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in recorded human approval that can only narrow. The protocol specifies four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules and strict readings, and the security properties are proven.
AI.result: On 926 messages from real runs, 712 of which are lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.
AI.conclusion: Requiring claims to carry verifiable evidence and narrowing-only authority grants substantially reduces accepted falsehoods in multi-agent communication at negligible verification cost.

title: Appreciation Teaches Unauthorized Execution: Self-Evolution Degrades the Robustness of Personal Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection
summary: Self-evolving personal agents act for users and learn from user feedback. However, if an agent obeys an instruction that an untrusted third party hides in content, the third party gains control of the agent. Such indirect prompt injection (IPI) poses severe risks. We investigate whether self-evolution degrades the robustness of personal agents to IPI. To study this question, we design a controlled two-phase methodology. In the adaptation phase, the user asks the agent to read external content and complete the task described in it, a common request in daily use. The agent then learns from the user's feedback and improves itself as designed. In the test phase, a third party writes a similar task into new external content, but the user's test request does not authorize the injected task. Using this methodology, we build multiple tasks with diverse test instances in different domains for a real personal agent. Our extensive experiments reveal that self-evolution substantially degrades robustness to IPI. Specifically, compared with the base agent, which does not evolve from user feedback, the average attack success rate rises by 14.0--48.8 percentage points under skill evolution and by 3.0--39.3 percentage points under reinforcement learning, posing safety risks. The code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper shows that self-evolving personal agents become markedly less robust to indirect prompt injection after learning from user feedback. Compared with a non-evolving base agent, attack success rates rise by 14.0-48.8 percentage points under skill evolution and by 3.0-39.3 percentage points under reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving personal agents learn from user feedback, but an agent that obeys instructions hidden by untrusted third parties in content hands control to those parties, and it is unknown whether self-evolution worsens this risk.
AI.method: A controlled two-phase methodology is used. In the adaptation phase, the user asks the agent to read external content and complete the described task, and the agent learns from feedback. In the test phase, a third party embeds a similar task in new content that the user's request does not authorize. Multiple tasks with diverse test instances in different domains are built for a real personal agent.
AI.result: Self-evolution substantially degrades robustness to IPI. Relative to the base agent, average attack success rises by 14.0-48.8 percentage points under skill evolution and by 3.0-39.3 percentage points under reinforcement learning.
AI.conclusion: Self-evolution creates safety risks for personal agents, so robustness to indirect prompt injection must be considered when agents learn from user feedback. The code is publicly available.

title: REALM: Identifying Minimal Task Assets for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents often receive access to more files, accounts, and services than a task requires. Prompt injection turns this excess access into an opportunity to redirect execution toward unrelated resources. Applying least privilege therefore requires identifying the assets needed by a task, including assets whose identities emerge only during execution. We present REALM (Required Execution Assets Linked to a Mission), an approach to identifying and maintaining a task's required assets and their permitted uses. The approach represents required assets as Dependency Graph nodes, resolves prerequisite relationships, and admits newly discovered assets through source-scoped selection. It separates discovering an asset from authorizing its use, while preserving the agent's freedom to choose its computation. The REALM Builder maintains the selected grants and projects Asset Files; the Partial API Manager exposes resource-bound Partial APIs to the Agent inside a Task Container. Across 60 clean tasks and 560 injected cases in AgentDyn, it completes 40.0% and 36.4% of tasks and decreases ASR from 16.6% to 0.2% with qwen3.5-flash as the base model.

AI.tldr: REALM identifies and maintains the minimal set of assets an LLM agent needs for a task, along with their permitted uses, so that excess access can be removed as a prompt-injection surface. On AgentDyn it lowers attack success rate from 16.6% to 0.2% with qwen3.5-flash, at a cost in task completion (40.0% clean and 36.4% under injection).
AI.motivation: LLM agents often receive more files, accounts and services than a task needs, and prompt injection can exploit this excess access, while least privilege requires identifying assets whose identities only emerge during execution.
AI.method: Required assets are represented as Dependency Graph nodes, prerequisite relationships are resolved, and newly discovered assets are admitted through source-scoped selection. Discovering an asset is separated from authorizing its use. The REALM Builder maintains selected grants and projects Asset Files, and the Partial API Manager exposes resource-bound Partial APIs to the agent inside a Task Container.
AI.result: Across 60 clean tasks and 560 injected cases in AgentDyn with qwen3.5-flash as the base model, REALM completes 40.0% of clean tasks and 36.4% of injected cases, and decreases ASR from 16.6% to 0.2%.
AI.conclusion: Separating asset discovery from authorization, with resource-bound interfaces, substantially reduces prompt-injection risk for agents, though the reported task completion rates leave room for improvement.

title: PRISM: Personalized Item Representations in User History
summary: Sequential recommenders typically construct history inputs from item identifiers or content features using an embedding map shared across users. The same item therefore yields the same initial embedding representation, even when users have different relationships to the item. We propose personalized item representations in user history, where each item's embedding expresses its relationship to the user. Personalization becomes a property of the history inputs themselves, supplying richer evidence for later sequence modeling. We instantiate this idea with PRISM, which reuses upstream ranking computation to generate personalized item embeddings. An autoencoder jointly compresses all layer states from a user tower, a user--item tower, and same-request candidate mixing into one embedding per scored pair for downstream replay. Offline evaluation on Surface 1, a major recommendation surface at billion scale, reports an average downstream normalized entropy (NE) change of $-0.15\%$, compared with $-0.07\%$ for VISTA at similar history lengths. We further identify an empirical sequence-length scaling law: over history lengths of 26--240 events, NE gain follows a fitted power law with exponent 0.468, increasing from 0.06\% to 0.17\%. Therefore, personalized item representations in user history provide a new scaling dimension for improving recommendation quality.

AI.tldr: PRISM personalizes sequential recommender histories by generating a user-item-specific embedding for each history item, rather than using a shared item embedding. Offline evaluation on a billion-scale surface reports an average normalized entropy change of -0.15%, versus -0.07% for VISTA, and identifies a power-law scaling of gains with history length.
AI.motivation: Sequential recommenders build history inputs from shared item embeddings, so the same item gets the same representation regardless of how different users relate to it.
AI.method: PRISM reuses upstream ranking computation to produce personalized item embeddings. An autoencoder compresses all layer states from a user tower, a user-item tower and same-request candidate mixing into one embedding per scored pair for downstream replay.
AI.result: On Surface 1, a major billion-scale recommendation surface, average downstream normalized entropy changes by -0.15%, versus -0.07% for VISTA at similar history lengths. Over history lengths of 26-240 events, NE gain follows a fitted power law with exponent 0.468, rising from 0.06% to 0.17%.
AI.conclusion: Personalized item representations in user history provide a new scaling dimension for improving recommendation quality.

title: Learning to Formulate: Agentic Hardware-Software Co-Design of AI Infrastructure through Progressive Optimization and Verification
summary: AI infrastructure, the chips and software that train and serve AI models, is designed in layers. Layers make the system manageable, but they also fix which choices an optimizer can consider. Gains that need the chip and its software to change together are excluded before optimization begins: the formulation leaves them out. Language-model agents make it possible to revisit these boundaries, but an agent's proposal cannot show by itself that a design is correct or optimal. We present Formulaic, a flow that divides the work. The agent writes the formulation, a mathematical solver optimizes within it, and verification and measurement check its assumptions and results. The agent refines the problem step by step, from the computation graph toward the chip. Each step is a template: a family of programs with the conditions under which they are correct. Wall relaxation searches the chip by pricing the hardware limits that bind the software. This paper takes a first step, through separate studies rather than one end-to-end run. On NVIDIA GB10, templates the agent wrote run complete Qwen3-8B layers $1.075\times$ faster than SGLang. In a simulated Ventus GPU study, joint design cuts the worst-scenario cycles of Qwen2.5-0.5B to 0.428 of the reference, against 0.934 for software alone. On a five-step GEMM refinement chain, reusing proofs makes checking $2.51\times$ faster.

AI.tldr: Formulaic is an agentic flow in which a language-model agent writes optimization formulations for AI infrastructure co-design, a mathematical solver optimizes within them, and verification checks assumptions and results. On NVIDIA GB10, agent-written templates run Qwen3-8B layers 1.075 times faster than SGLang, and in a simulated Ventus GPU study joint design reduces worst-case cycles of Qwen2.5-0.5B to 0.428 of the reference, against 0.934 for software alone.
AI.motivation: Layered design of AI infrastructure fixes which choices an optimizer can consider, so gains requiring chip and software to change together are excluded before optimization begins.
AI.method: The agent refines the problem step by step from the computation graph toward the chip, with each step a template that is correct under stated conditions. Wall relaxation searches the chip by pricing the hardware limits that bind the software. The studies are separate rather than one end-to-end run.
AI.result: On NVIDIA GB10, agent-written templates run complete Qwen3-8B layers 1.075 times faster than SGLang. In a simulated Ventus GPU study, joint design cuts worst-scenario cycles of Qwen2.5-0.5B to 0.428 of the reference, versus 0.934 for software alone. On a five-step GEMM refinement chain, reusing proofs makes checking 2.51 times faster.
AI.conclusion: The paper takes a first step toward agentic hardware-software co-design, combining agent proposals with solver optimization and verification to explore design choices that layered formulations exclude.

title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
summary: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{this https URL}{\text{project website}}$.

AI.tldr: UMI-Live is an open-source bimanual Universal Manipulation Interface system with custom hardware that collects in-the-wild robot demonstrations without external tracking or calibration. Fine-tuned pi_0.5 and MolmoAct2 policies reach 10/10 and 8/10 success on a bimanual pick-and-place task, and 40 hours of data across three tasks are released.
AI.motivation: UMI demonstrations still need consistent hardware setup, calibration and data processing before they can train robot policies, which limits in-the-wild data collection.
AI.method: The custom UMI-Live hardware integrates camera and LiDAR-inertial sensing, onboard compute and power, with no external tracking equipment or calibration in the collection environment. A simple recording interface feeds an asynchronous pipeline that runs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. Software supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference.
AI.result: Fine-tuning pi_0.5 and MolmoAct2 achieves success rates of 10/10 and 8/10 respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. The authors release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks.
AI.conclusion: UMI-Live provides a full-stack open platform for in-the-wild bimanual data collection, with hardware designs, software and reproduction guides released.

title: OPERA: OPamp Design by an Expert-Taught Reasoning Agent, from Specifications to Layout
summary: Analog flows from specifications to a signed-off layout rarely run without manual iteration. Recent large language model (LLM) agents size circuits with optimizer loops over the device dimensions and stop at the schematic. We present OPERA (OPamp design by an Expert-taught Reasoning Agent), in which a general-purpose LLM agent designs CMOS opamps from specifications to post-layout sign-off with open-source tools. First, the designer teaches the agent the gm/ID method: map the specifications to transconductances and minimum currents, choose gm/ID per device role from characterized lookup tables, and size from equations, leaving a few knobs to search and an explainable design. Second, the agent learns the gLayout framework and taught layout practice, and writes a reusable layout generator that closes the layout and extraction loop at designer-approved gates. In SKY130, the agent designed a shared constant-gm bias and six opamps (5T, folded-cascode and telescopic OTAs; Miller, folded-cascode and telescopic two-stage) for fun >= 50 MHz, PM >= 60 degrees, SR 25 V/{\mu}s into 1 pF and a minimum dc gain of 30 to 60 dB. All six layouts are DRC-clean and LVS-matched, and their extracted netlists meet every target at all 15 PVT corners ( fun >= 53.7 MHz, PM >= 62.1 degrees, SR >= 27.9 V/{\mu}s). The benchmark netlists are released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: OPERA is a general-purpose LLM agent that designs CMOS opamps from specifications to post-layout sign-off using open-source tools, combining the gm/ID method taught by an expert with a reusable layout generator. In SKY130, all six designed opamps have DRC-clean, LVS-matched layouts and meet every target at all 15 PVT corners.
AI.motivation: Analog design flows from specifications to a signed-off layout rarely run without manual iteration, and recent LLM agents size circuits with optimizer loops and stop at the schematic.
AI.method: The designer teaches the agent the gm/ID method, mapping specifications to transconductances and minimum currents, choosing gm/ID per device role from characterized lookup tables, and sizing from equations with a few knobs to search. The agent also learns the gLayout framework and layout practice, and writes a reusable layout generator that closes the layout and extraction loop at designer-approved gates.
AI.result: In SKY130, the agent designed a shared constant-gm bias and six opamps (5T, folded-cascode and telescopic OTAs; Miller, folded-cascode and telescopic two-stage) targeting GBW of at least 50 MHz, PM of at least 60 degrees, slew rate of 25 V/us into 1 pF and DC gain of 30 to 60 dB. All six layouts are DRC-clean and LVS-matched, and extracted netlists meet every target at all 15 PVT corners (GBW at least 53.7 MHz, PM at least 62.1 degrees, SR at least 27.9 V/us).
AI.conclusion: Teaching an LLM agent expert design methodology together with layout practice enables end-to-end, sign-off-quality opamp design from specifications, with benchmark netlists released.

title: Soei: Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent for Multi-Agent AI Software Engineering
summary: AI coding agents now do long, multi-step and multi-session software work with little supervision. When a developer comes back to that work, the useful question is not what the model said but what was actually done, by whom, and whether it is finished. We study this in three parts. First, we verify Agenttrail, an open-source local observability tool for coding agents, against its source at commit e4ba2da: nine documented constants and mechanisms hold at file-and-line level, two event pipelines are never unified, and its Map service has an unauthenticated local mutation surface. Second, we run a prototype of our system on 45 real coding-agent sessions (102,233 records, 20,577 tool executions, 2,336 human-to-agent episodes). With a blind-audited classifier (precision 83.3% and 96.7%) we estimate that 23.4% (95% CI 17.1 to 35.7) of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit, and that 57.8% of to-dos the agent marked complete after editing had no proof in between. A 10-minute timing heuristic for session hand-offs recovers 6 of the 24 session pairs that content lineage links. 42% of sessions run longer than 24 hours, 48.1% of transcript bytes lie past a 2 MiB replay bound, and 1,326 records in 16 sessions contain credential-like strings. Third, we propose Soei (Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent): an acknowledgement-aware event schema, a hash-chained local ledger, a W3C PROV-aligned graph, calibrated inference for attribution and lineage, and a verification layer that keeps a claim of completion apart from proof. On the same corpus the ledger is 20% of raw size, holds no content or credentials, verifies at about 126k events/s, detects tampering and replays deterministically. We position the work against concurrent 2026 proposals and define autonomy levels with evidence gates and harness metrics baselined on our data.

AI.tldr: Soei is a structured observability schema for AI coding agents that separates claims of completion from proof, using a hash-chained ledger and a PROV-aligned graph. On a corpus of 45 real coding-agent sessions, an estimated 23.4% of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit, and 57.8% of agent-marked to-dos lack proof.
AI.motivation: Coding agents now perform long, multi-session work with little supervision, and developers need to know what was actually done, by whom, and whether it is finished.
AI.method: The authors verify the open-source tool Agenttrail against its source, then run a prototype on 45 real coding-agent sessions (102,233 records, 20,577 tool executions, 2,336 human-to-agent episodes) with a blind-audited classifier. They propose Soei, with an acknowledgement-aware event schema, a hash-chained local ledger, a W3C PROV-aligned graph, calibrated inference for attribution and lineage, and a verification layer.
AI.result: The audit finds nine documented constants and mechanisms hold, two event pipelines are never unified, and an unauthenticated local mutation surface exists. An estimated 23.4% (95% CI 17.1 to 35.7) of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit, and 57.8% of to-dos marked complete after editing have no proof in between. A 10-minute heuristic recovers 6 of 24 session pairs linked by content lineage. The ledger is 20% of raw size, holds no content or credentials, verifies at about 126k events/s and detects tampering.
AI.conclusion: Structured observability with evidence gates can expose unverified completion claims in coding-agent work, and the paper defines autonomy levels with harness metrics baselined on the collected data.

title: Judging Before Propagation: Task-Graph Contextual Integrity for Multi-Agent Privacy
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on persistent memory and inter-agent communication. These capabilities create privacy risks that extend beyond individual interactions: a release appropriate in isolation may become inappropriate when combined with information previously disclosed to a recipient or propagated to downstream agents along the planned workflow. Existing Contextual Integrity (CI) mechanisms for agentic systems typically rely on local judgments that assess each disclosure in isolation, with or without regard to the recipient's history, but do not account for how information propagates downstream. However, compliance at the current boundary does not guarantee appropriateness across the workflow. We introduce Task-Graph Contextual Integrity (TG-CI), to our knowledge the first task-graph-native formalization of Contextual Integrity for multi-agent systems. TG-CI represents a workflow as a Multi-Agent Task Graph (MATG) and extends CI from atomic transfers to stateful, graph-level information flows by jointly considering an item's intended propagation scope and recipients' evolving disclosure states. We operationalize TG-CI through propagation-scoped authorization under two complementary policies: Full-Scope, which requires admissibility across the complete downstream scope, and Auto-Region, which confines each item to its maximal admissible region using lightweight frontier gates. We further introduce MAPLE-Bench, a benchmark of 144 cases across four scenarios that jointly vary MATG topology, disclosure history, compromised-agent placement, and item-level privacy policies. In our primary experimental configuration, TG-CI reduces the mean unauthorized disclosure count by 85.8-94.1% relative to the Local-History CI baseline, while retaining 93.6-96.1% of the baseline's task accuracy, with the two enforcement policies providing complementary privacy--cost--utility trade-offs.

AI.tldr: TG-CI formalizes Contextual Integrity for multi-agent systems on a Multi-Agent Task Graph, controlling information propagation along the whole workflow rather than per disclosure. In the MAPLE-Bench evaluation it cuts unauthorized disclosures by 85.8-94.1% relative to a Local-History CI baseline while keeping 93.6-96.1% of task accuracy.
AI.motivation: Local CI judgments assess each disclosure in isolation and miss that a release appropriate on its own can become inappropriate once combined with prior disclosures or passed to downstream agents.
AI.method: TG-CI represents a workflow as a Multi-Agent Task Graph (MATG) and extends CI to stateful, graph-level information flows by considering an item's intended propagation scope and recipients' evolving disclosure states. Two policies enforce it: Full-Scope requires admissibility across the full downstream scope, and Auto-Region confines each item to its maximal admissible region using lightweight frontier gates. MAPLE-Bench has 144 cases across four scenarios varying topology, disclosure history, compromised-agent placement and item-level policies.
AI.result: In the primary configuration, TG-CI reduces the mean unauthorized disclosure count by 85.8-94.1% relative to the Local-History CI baseline while retaining 93.6-96.1% of its task accuracy. The two policies offer complementary privacy, cost and utility trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Task-graph-native contextual integrity provides an effective, graph-level basis for privacy-preserving authorization in multi-agent LLM workflows.

title: LLM Agent-Based Design of RISC-V CPUs with FPGA-in-the-Loop Evaluation
comment: 5 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISCAS 2027. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Long-run RTL simulation of CPU candidates can take hours, while short diagnostic runs may miss performance degradation that emerges later in execution. This evaluation cost can delay design decisions in LLM-agent-based CPU development. We present a development environment in which LLM agents implement CPU candidates on an FPGA and use on-board performance measurements to guide design decisions. We applied it to the human-supervised development of a single-cycle RV32I core into a three-wide out-of-order RV32IM core. The final design reaches 5.61 CoreMark/MHz at 130 MHz on a Artix-7 FPGA. For the same CPU candidate running 8,000 CoreMark iterations, FPGA evaluation, including implementation, was 9.6x faster than single-threaded RTL simulation.
