In one case, board measurements revealed long-run performance degradation in a candidate that improved in a short diagnostic run. The result guided candidate selection and led to RTL-based root-cause analysis and a fix.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a development environment in which LLM agents implement CPU candidates on an FPGA and use on-board performance measurements to guide design decisions, producing a three-wide out-of-order RV32IM core at 5.61 CoreMark/MHz and 130 MHz on an Artix-7.
AI.motivation: Long-run RTL simulation of CPU candidates can take hours, while short diagnostic runs may miss performance degradation that emerges later in execution, which delays design decisions in LLM-agent-based CPU development.
AI.method: LLM agents implement CPU candidates on an FPGA and use on-board performance measurements to guide design choices; in a human-supervised process, a single-cycle RV32I core is developed into a three-wide out-of-order RV32IM core.
AI.result: The final design reaches 5.61 CoreMark/MHz at 130 MHz; for 8,000 CoreMark iterations, FPGA evaluation including implementation was 9.6x faster than single-threaded RTL simulation; board measurements revealed long-run performance degradation in a candidate that improved in a short diagnostic run, which guided candidate selection and led to RTL-based root-cause analysis and a fix.
AI.conclusion: Measuring on the FPGA over long runs makes candidate evaluation faster and catches late-emerging performance problems that short simulations miss, supporting agent-driven CPU design.

title: Generative artificial intelligence prompting strategies among Chinese university students across academic tasks
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university learning, yet effective human-GenAI interaction depends not only on access to these tools but also on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts for academic tasks. This study examined university students' perceived GenAI prompting capability and reported prompting strategies. Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of optional comments. Students reported using GenAI across diverse academic activities and generally expressed confidence in their prompting capabilities, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts following initial outputs. However, prompting strategies showed limited sensitivity to task types: specifying output format was more strongly endorsed in a creative workshop preparation scenario than in a research-oriented assignment, whereas other matched strategies showed no adjusted differences. Students also commonly endorsed both concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset, suggesting that effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone. By contrast, fixed prompt templates received lower endorsement than other prompting strategies. In the adopted factor model, perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, while open-ended responses highlighted prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.

AI.tldr: A questionnaire study of 234 Chinese university students examines how they perceive their GenAI prompting capability and which prompting strategies they report using across academic tasks.
AI.motivation: Effective human-GenAI interaction depends on students' ability to formulate, evaluate and refine prompts for academic tasks, but how prompting strategies vary with task type has been unclear.
AI.method: Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations and qualitative coding of optional open-ended comments.
AI.result: Students generally expressed confidence, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts after initial outputs; strategy use showed limited sensitivity to task type, with output-format specification more endorsed in a creative workshop scenario than in a research-oriented assignment; concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset were both commonly endorsed; fixed prompt templates received the lowest endorsement; perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, and prompt-intent alignment was a common challenge in open responses.
AI.conclusion: Effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone, and aligning prompts with one's intent remains a practical challenge for students.

title: Data Provenance and Ethics in the Curricula of U.S. Health AI Education Programs
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Under review at PLOS Digital Health. Data and supplementary material available at this https URL
summary: Failures of deployed clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems have often originated in how their training data were generated. Whether the programs that train the health AI workforce teach practitioners to examine data provenance is unknown. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the publicly advertised curricula of health AI education programs at U.S. universities, identified through a structured multisource web search between April and July 2026. Two investigators coded coverage of data provenance (structural, dataset limitations, or data management only), ethics, and sustainability; collaborative structure; technical prerequisites; and the disciplinary background and gender of named instructors. The primary outcome was provenance coverage at the structural or dataset-limitations level. Of 43 candidate entries, 36 programs at 25 institutional units in 21 universities were included. Ethics was covered by 29 programs (80.6%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 65.0 to 90.2), data provenance by 8 (22.2%; 95% CI, 11.7 to 38.1), and structural provenance by 6 (16.7%; 95% CI, 7.9 to 31.9). None of the seven master's degree programs met the primary outcome, and no program addressed sustainability. Eighteen programs included team-based work, but only 5 assembled teams across clinical and technical backgrounds. Of 92 named instructors, 76.1% came from computational disciplines and 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities; among the 51 whose gender could be determined, 66.7% were men. U.S. health AI education programs widely taught ethics but rarely taught how clinical data are produced. None addressed the environmental cost of computation, and most instructors came from computational disciplines.

AI.tldr: A cross-sectional analysis of 36 U.S. health AI education programs finds that ethics is widely taught, data provenance is rarely covered, and no program addresses sustainability.
AI.motivation: Failures of deployed clinical AI often originate in how the training data were generated, but it was unknown whether programs that train the health AI workforce teach practitioners to examine data provenance.
AI.method: Publicly advertised curricula were identified through a structured multisource web search conducted between April and July 2026, and two investigators coded coverage of data provenance, ethics and sustainability, collaborative structure, technical prerequisites, and the disciplinary background and gender of named instructors.
AI.result: Of 43 candidate entries, 36 programs at 25 institutional units in 21 universities were included; ethics was covered by 29 programs (80.6%, 95% CI 65.0 to 90.2), data provenance by 8 (22.2%, 95% CI 11.7 to 38.1) and structural provenance by 6 (16.7%, 95% CI 7.9 to 31.9); none of the seven master's programs met the primary outcome; only 5 of the 18 programs with team-based work assembled teams across clinical and technical backgrounds; 76.1% of the 92 named instructors came from computational disciplines and 3.3% from the social sciences or humanities; 66.7% of the 51 instructors whose gender could be determined were men.
AI.conclusion: U.S. health AI education widely teaches ethics but rarely teaches how clinical data are produced, and none of the programs addresses the environmental cost of computation.

title: Rebuilding a Field's Open-Problem Catalog from the Literature: A Two-Layer Knowledge Graph, and Why Status Must Stay Proposed
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: A research field records its open problems in surveys, keynotes and community reports. Those are prose, written every few years, and nobody can ask them who works on a problem now or whether it was settled last year. We argue the problems should be data, and we build the system that makes them so: a hand-curated problem layer carried in unchanged, under an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links in one graph database and queryable from one language. A language model does four jobs -- per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdict, and idea generation -- each constrained to a candidate set so out-of-set answers are refused rather than stored. We report a study on two curated catalogs, database research (1,053 problems) and AI research (1,000 problems), each with a prior catalog-only graph. The rebuilt graph answers every question the catalog-only graph answered -- 47 of 47 on databases, 34 of 35 on AI -- plus questions the catalog-only graph refused: recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried, and outside papers bearing on a problem (336 problems, 770 works on databases). The capability we most wanted does not survive its own audit. Of 41 solves and refutes verdicts hand-checked against the papers, 9 are correct, 30 partly correct and 2 wrong; no refutes verdict (0 of 34) disproves an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closes the central question. We report that failure in full and draw the design conclusion: a status change must be proposed with its evidence and never applied, making the human reviewer part of the architecture. We close with the data-engineering problems this raises: entity resolution across curated and harvested layers, verifying model status claims, freshness under source quotas, and evaluation without ground truth.

AI.tldr: The paper rebuilds a field's open-problem catalog as a two-layer knowledge graph that joins curated problems to a bibliographic evidence layer, and finds that LLM status verdicts are unreliable enough that status changes must be proposed for human review rather than applied.
AI.motivation: A research field's open problems are recorded in prose surveys and reports written every few years, so it is hard to ask who works on a problem now or whether it was recently settled.
AI.method: Problems are stored as data in a hand-curated problem layer, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links to an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, in one graph database; an LLM performs per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdicts and idea generation, each constrained to a candidate set so that out-of-set answers are refused.
AI.result: On database research (1,053 problems) and AI research (1,000 problems), the rebuilt graph answers 47 of 47 and 34 of 35 questions that the catalog-only graph answered, and also answers questions about recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried and outside papers (336 problems and 770 works on databases); of 41 solves and refutes verdicts checked by hand, 9 were correct, 30 partly correct and 2 wrong, no refutes verdict (0 of 34) disproved an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closed the central question.
AI.conclusion: A status change must be proposed together with its evidence and never applied automatically, which makes the human reviewer part of the architecture; entity resolution, verification of model status claims, freshness under source quotas and evaluation without ground truth remain open data-engineering problems.

title: Can AI Agents Interface Clinicians and Complex Models?
summary: Background: Contemporary healthcare institutions generate daily very large amounts of data, which contain highly useful information for the improvement of work organization, planning and overall efficiency. While models and techniques to extract these insights are well known and constantly developed in mathematical biology, complex systems physics and data science, the adoption of these techniques among Clinicians and Hospital Administrators remains limited, mainly due to language and methodological divides. Objective: In this article we implement an AI Multi Agent System (MAS) that allows Users to use predictive models and make statistical analyses via natural language conversations. Methods: We developed EpidemIA, a training-free MAS endowed with a modular suite of epidemiological models written by human experts, executable on a single-GPU workstation. To avoid relaying sensitive data to third parties, the system uses locally an open-weights LLM as backbone for its two subagents. Results: Using a dataset of Emergency Department visits provided to us by IRCCS Sant'Orsola (Bologna) we test the model on a few typical use cases, demonstrating the possibility of performing both simpler statistical analyses and visualizations as well as more complicated epidemiological predictions based on dynamical models, through simple queries made in natural language. Conclusions: While still being a proof-of-concept implementation, EpidemIA showcases the transformative capabilities of LLM based technologies as an enabling factor in the widespread adoption of complex dynamical models, which is at present hindered by their steep learning curve.

AI.tldr: EpidemIA is a training-free multi-agent system that lets clinicians and hospital administrators run statistical analyses and epidemiological models through natural language conversation, using a local open-weights LLM on a single-GPU workstation.
AI.motivation: Hospitals generate large amounts of data useful for planning and efficiency, but clinicians and administrators rarely adopt complex epidemiological models because of language and methodological barriers and their steep learning curve.
AI.method: A multi-agent system with two subagents, backed by an open-weights LLM run locally so that sensitive data are not relayed to third parties, which invokes a modular suite of epidemiological models written by human experts.
AI.result: Using an Emergency Department visit dataset provided by IRCCS Sant'Orsola (Bologna), the system performs simpler statistical analyses and visualizations as well as dynamical-model-based epidemiological predictions in several typical use cases, driven by simple natural language queries.
AI.conclusion: As a proof-of-concept, the system suggests that LLM-based interfaces could help overcome the barriers that currently limit the wider adoption of complex dynamical epidemiological models.

title: Practical Assessment of Agentic Systems in Acoustics
summary: In engineering, applications of artificial intelligence have so far been largely limited to surrogate models and optimization tasks. Large language models changed this, as they can write software from a task given in words. Placed inside a harness, a system of components that lets it search for information and execute software, such a model becomes an agent that can take over recurring engineering tasks. This work measures how the model and the elements of the harness shape the performance and behavior of the agent in two common acoustic applications. In the first, the agent detects and locates faults in audio recordings from a vehicle interior with near-perfect accuracy. A benchmark on this task shows that a weak model sets a limit that no harness design can overcome, and that design choices take effect only once the model is capable enough to use them. In the second, a case study on the design of a metamaterial unit cell, the agent reliably finds designs that achieve a specified insertion loss over a given frequency range. The results aim to help the reader understand what each element of an agent contributes and how to design an agent for acoustic tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how the model and harness components of an LLM agent shape its performance in two acoustic tasks: fault detection in vehicle-interior audio and metamaterial unit-cell design.
AI.motivation: LLMs can write software from a task description, so placed in a harness they can take over recurring engineering tasks, but how each element of the harness affects agent performance in acoustics has not been clear.
AI.method: Two case studies: in the first, the agent detects and locates faults in audio recordings from a vehicle interior, with a benchmark varying the model and harness design; in the second, the agent designs a metamaterial unit cell that achieves a specified insertion loss over a given frequency range.
AI.result: The agent detects and locates faults with near-perfect accuracy; the benchmark shows that a weak model sets a limit no harness design can overcome and that design choices take effect only once the model is capable enough to use them; the agent reliably finds unit-cell designs that achieve the specified insertion loss over the given frequency range.
AI.conclusion: The results help readers understand what each element of an agent contributes and how to design an agent for acoustic tasks.

title: The Importance of Speech Genre for End-of-Turn Detector Training
summary: End-of-turn (EoT) detection has been studied mostly through features, models, and modalities, while the speech genre of the training data has drawn far less attention. We isolate this factor. Using one reproducible annotation pipeline, we build a matched pair of corpora, multi-turn human-human conversational and single-turn human-machine, and train the same streaming ConvLSTM EoT detector on each. Across four test sets the conversational model reaches up to +0.45 higher F1, driven by fewer false alarms on the mid-turn pauses and hesitations that are rare in single-turn corpora. This conversational-training effect is not specific to frame-level decoding. Under a matched complete-or-not test it also appears at the utterance level, across two encoders, but only on conversational test data. Testing only on single-turn speech, as most prior work does, therefore hides the benefit of conversational training data. Against open-source baselines, our 1.8M-parameter model attains the highest F1 on every test set.

AI.tldr: Training a streaming end-of-turn detector on multi-turn human-human conversational speech instead of single-turn human-machine speech raises F1 by up to 0.45, mainly by reducing false alarms on mid-turn pauses and hesitations.
AI.motivation: End-of-turn detection has been studied through features, models and modalities, but the speech genre of the training data has received little attention, and most prior work tests only on single-turn speech.
AI.method: A single reproducible annotation pipeline is used to build a matched pair of corpora, multi-turn human-human conversational and single-turn human-machine; the same streaming ConvLSTM detector (1.8M parameters) is trained on each and tested on four test sets, with a matched complete-or-not test at the utterance level across two encoders.
AI.result: The conversational model reaches up to +0.45 higher F1 across four test sets, driven by fewer false alarms on mid-turn pauses and hesitations; under the matched complete-or-not test the benefit also appears at the utterance level, but only on conversational test data; against open-source baselines the model attains the highest F1 on every test set.
AI.conclusion: Testing only on single-turn speech, as most prior work does, hides the benefit of conversational training data, so the speech genre of training data should be taken into account.

title: InferD: A Honeypot Framework for AI Inference Infrastructure
comment: AISec Workshop '26, ACM CCS 2026, The Hague, Netherlands
summary: Large language model serving stacks, commercial inference APIs, vector databases, and agent orchestration gateways are now ex- posed on the public internet and indexed by commodity scanners within hours of deployment. The threat characteristics of this sur- face are only beginning to be measured, and the honeypot frame- works that could measure it were designed for conventional net- work services rather than for AI infrastructure. In fact, emulating an AI service is a distinct deception problem: the observable behavior of the service, including model inventories, token formats, tool-call protocols, and authorization flows, must be reproduced faithfully, while the underlying computation, model inference and tool ex- ecution, must never occur. We present InferD, a low-interaction honeypot framework organized around a single principle we call deception without inference: every request an adversary can observe is answered from static response pools, and nothing an adversary submits is ever executed. InferD decomposes the emulation into four deception planes, transport, service protocol, vulnerability surface, and agentic session, adds a provenance plane that links a planted credential to evidence of downstream model-mediated processing.

AI.tldr: InferD is a low-interaction honeypot framework for AI inference infrastructure that answers every observable request from static response pools, so nothing an adversary submits is ever executed.
AI.motivation: LLM serving stacks, inference APIs, vector databases and agent gateways are exposed on the public internet and indexed by scanners within hours, but existing honeypot frameworks were designed for conventional network services and cannot faithfully emulate AI services.
AI.method: Organized around the principle of deception without inference, the framework splits emulation into four deception planes (transport, service protocol, vulnerability surface and agentic session) and adds a provenance plane that links a planted credential to evidence of downstream model-mediated processing.
AI.result: The abstract as given describes the framework design and does not report evaluation results.
AI.conclusion: Measuring threats against AI infrastructure requires honeypots that reproduce the observable behavior of AI services faithfully while never performing the underlying inference or tool execution.

title: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions
summary: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

AI.tldr: Using enactive theory, the paper argues that people incorporate LLMs both as tool-like enablers of skills and as identity-tied ways of languaging, and introduces the notion of susceptive sense-making for the extra semiotic labour caused by frictionless LLM services.
AI.motivation: Standard theories of technological impact on autonomy are inadequate for LLMs, which can induce linguistic interaction with humans in an unprecedented way, while traditional social cognition theories fall short because LLMs have neither autonomy, minds nor sociality.
AI.method: A conceptual analysis grounded in enactive theory, particularly the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent enactive accounts of AI, which treats LLMs as excorporated and excarnated phantoms of human languaging.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results; it offers conceptual advances, places the linguistic relation to LLMs alongside other linguistic artifacts such as religious books, and discusses particular forms this relation takes today.
AI.conclusion: Humans incorporate excorporated others, and the lack of friction in LLM services increases semiotic labour, which may affect the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans.

title: Accumulating Pruning Constraints: New Exact Polynomial-Space Algorithms for Max 2-SAT
comment: Project folder with Lean verification: this https URL
summary: We present deterministic polynomial-space algorithms that solve Max 2-SAT on $n$ variables exactly in time $\Ostar(2^{(1-\gamma)n})$, for a fixed $\gamma>0$, on several classes of instances whose clause density may grow with $n$. Our main tool extends the classic DPLL branching algorithm. When the search gives a variable its less promising value, comparing the two values of the variable yields a pruning constraint that is satisfied by some optimal assignment. Accumulating these constraints along each branch prunes all but an exponentially small fraction of the assignments. The classes are formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expander graphs and on graphs generated by a stochastic block model. In a semirandom formula, the pairs of variables that may share a clause are arbitrary, and the clauses on these pairs are random. For semirandom formulas and block-model graphs, the algorithms are still exact on every input, and the time bound holds with high probability over the input. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with such a running time for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances. Beyond these classes, the pruning constraints can be added to any branching algorithm for Max 2-SAT, and we expect them to be of practical relevance for general formulas, in particular for sparse ones, where each constraint involves only a few variables.

AI.tldr: The paper gives deterministic polynomial-space exact algorithms for Max 2-SAT running in time 2^((1-gamma)n) up to polynomial factors, for a fixed gamma > 0, on several classes of instances, by adding pruning constraints to a DPLL branching algorithm.
AI.motivation: Exact polynomial-space algorithms with such running times were not known for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances, whose clause density may grow with n.
AI.method: The DPLL branching algorithm is extended so that, when the search assigns a variable its less promising value, comparing the two values yields a pruning constraint satisfied by some optimal assignment; accumulating these constraints along each branch prunes all but an exponentially small fraction of assignments; the classes are formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expander graphs and on stochastic block model graphs.
AI.result: The time bound holds on these classes; for semirandom formulas and block-model graphs the algorithms are exact on every input and the time bound holds with high probability over the input; beyond these classes the pruning constraints can be added to any branching Max 2-SAT algorithm.
AI.conclusion: These are the first polynomial-space algorithms with such a running time for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances, and the authors expect the pruning constraints to be practically relevant for general and sparse formulas.

title: HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization
comment: 48 pages, including supplementary material; 5 figures and 13 tables
summary: Automatic operator design (AOD) has increasingly adopted large language models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific search and variation operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Yet most methods evolve the operators while leaving the process that discovers them fixed. This limits adaptation as new Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions change where and how the search should proceed. We introduce HEMO, which makes the AOD harness itself a self-evolving optimization target. HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and updates one module at a time, revising the logic that determines which experience to retrieve, which operators to improve, which parents to select, and how to formulate the orchestration of search steps. Downstream solution quality and runtime guide these updates, while a discounted UCB scheduler directs adaptation toward promising modules as their utility changes. A persistent memory filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across harness states, enabling successive states to build on accumulated optimization experience. Experiments across eight MOCO tasks and two structurally distinct evolutionary backbones demonstrate strong performance against conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based AOD baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks. HEMO extends automatic operator design beyond evolving individual operators to improving the search process that discovers them.

AI.tldr: HEMO makes the harness of automatic operator design for multi-objective combinatorial optimization a self-evolving target, updating one module at a time so that the search process improves along with the operators.
AI.motivation: Most LLM-based automatic operator design methods evolve the operators while the process that discovers them stays fixed, which limits adaptation as Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions change.
AI.method: HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and updates one module at a time (experience retrieval, operator improvement, parent selection and search orchestration), guided by downstream solution quality and runtime and directed by a discounted UCB scheduler; a persistent memory filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across harness states.
AI.result: Experiments on eight multi-objective combinatorial optimization tasks with two structurally distinct evolutionary backbones show strong performance against conventional evolutionary, neural and LLM-based operator design baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks.
AI.conclusion: Operator design can be extended beyond evolving individual operators to improving the search process that discovers them.

title: UPPAAi: Towards LLM-Assisted Modeling, Verification, Analysis and Synthesis
summary: For more than three decades, UPPAAL has supported the modelling and analysis of real-time and cyber-physical systems. Yet building a suitable model, formalising the intended properties, choosing analysis techniques and interpreting counterexamples remain iterative tasks that demand substantial expertise. Large language models (LLMs) can offer plausible explanations and even solutions, but they are not necessarily correct. We present UPPAAI, an extension of UPPAAL in which users construct, explain, debug and specify models in dialogue with an LLM. The guiding principle is that the user requests, the LLM proposes, explains and orchestrates, and UPPAAL verifies. UPPAAI exposes the UPPAAL editor, queries and verifier through a Tools API. We report on seven case studies, from explaining to a newcomer to learning a controller, covering timed automata, stochastic hybrid automata and strategy learning. LLMs proved to be extremely helpful in not just generating solutions but also pro-actively suggesting relevant UPPAAL features it was not asked about.

AI.tldr: UPPAAi extends the UPPAAL verification tool so that users build, explain, debug and specify real-time system models in dialogue with an LLM, while UPPAAL performs the verification.
AI.motivation: Building UPPAAL models, formalizing their properties, choosing analysis techniques and interpreting counterexamples require substantial expertise, and LLM outputs are plausible but not necessarily correct.
AI.method: The user requests, the LLM proposes, explains and orchestrates, and UPPAAL verifies; UPPAAi exposes the UPPAAL editor, queries and verifier through a Tools API.
AI.result: Seven case studies, from explaining a model to a newcomer to learning a controller, cover timed automata, stochastic hybrid automata and strategy learning; LLMs were helpful not only in generating solutions but also in proactively suggesting relevant UPPAAL features the user had not asked about.
AI.conclusion: Keeping the verifier as the final check on LLM proposals lets LLM assistance support the modelling and analysis of cyber-physical systems without accepting unverified output.

title: Learning Safe Flow Matching Robot Policies from Binary Feasibility Oracles
summary: Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for flow-matching robot policies that uses only binary feasibility queries and applies the same safeguard during training and inference.
AI.motivation: Flow-based action generation in robot foundation models does not guarantee physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance, and the problem is hardest when the feasible set has no analytic description and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles.
AI.method: Binary feasibility queries correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while local boundary information extracted from the oracle provides constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass; combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used in training and inference, without explicit or differentiable constraint models.
AI.result: On obstacle-aware robotic manipulation experiments, the policy achieves 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.
AI.conclusion: Safe flow-matching policies can be learned from black-box feasibility oracles alone, with forward and backward passes aligned between training and inference.

title: PhysCount: Do MLLMs Count Visual Appearances or Physical Entities?
summary: Images reveal appearances, but counting often asks about physical objects. A single entity may be visible directly, in several reflections, or through glass, so detecting every visible occurrence does not determine how many entities are present. Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate these two operations. We introduce PhysCount, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can distinguish what appears in an image from what physically exists in the scene. PhysCount contains 546 real-world images and 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups. For each group, annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed, and identify appearances of the same entity. Four complementary question families test the enumeration of appearances, the enumeration of physical entities, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance--entity correspondence. We measure both accuracy on each family and the proportion of groups answered entirely correctly. Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them. Even the strongest model answers every question correctly in only 13.36\% of groups. Performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes. Higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement. These results expose a gap between recognizing what is visible and correctly recovering the physical entities behind those observations.

AI.tldr: PhysCount is a benchmark of 546 real-world images testing whether MLLMs can separate what appears in an image from how many physical entities exist; even the strongest of 40 evaluated models answers every question correctly in only 13.36% of groups.
AI.motivation: Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate counting visible appearances, such as reflections or views through glass, from counting the physical entities behind them.
AI.method: The benchmark contains 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups; annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed and identify appearances of the same entity; four question families test appearance enumeration, entity enumeration, image-formation-specific counting and appearance-entity correspondence.
AI.result: Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them; performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes; higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement.
AI.conclusion: The gap between recognizing what is visible and recovering the physical entities behind those observations is a central limitation of current MLLMs.

title: RADIOlogy: A Single-Pass Approach to Training-Free Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Code available at this https URL
summary: Current zero-shot anomaly detection methods often rely on complex prompt-learning techniques or computationally expensive sliding-window strategies to achieve fine-grained visual alignment to detect small-scale anomalies. This reliance stems from the fundamental limitation of standard CLIP architectures, where [CLS] token attention and spatial patch pooling struggle to capture subtle, localized anomaly features. While prompt-learning approaches aim to bridge this gap, they typically require a large number of ground-truth segmentation masks from auxiliary datasets, which are often unavailable in specialized domains. In this work, we show an emerging property of multi-head attention pooling in vision-language models: remarkable zero-shot anomaly localization and detection right out of the box. We translate this property into a single-pass anomaly detection technique, RADIOlogy, that does not require dense, windowed execution and significantly outperforms other training-free baselines. Instead, the method relies on a simple contrastive scoring approach that compares the average similarity between vision features and a suite of normal and abnormal prompts. Furthermore, we leverage the agglomerative features of RADIO models to enhance pixel-level anomaly segmentation using a dense anomaly refinement pipeline. Finally, we show how the vision-language family of training-free zero-shot anomaly detection techniques can be applied successfully to the medical domain with minimal modifications. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: RADIOlogy is a training-free, single-pass method for zero-shot anomaly detection that exploits multi-head attention pooling in vision-language models, scoring images against normal and abnormal prompts and refining pixel-level maps with RADIO features.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot anomaly detection often relies on complex prompt learning or costly sliding-window inference, because CLIP CLS token attention and spatial patch pooling capture subtle localized anomalies poorly, and prompt-learning methods need many ground-truth masks that are often unavailable in specialized domains.
AI.method: A single pass computes a contrastive score that compares the average similarity between vision features and a suite of normal and abnormal prompts; the agglomerative features of RADIO models support a dense anomaly refinement pipeline for pixel-level segmentation; the approach is adapted to the medical domain with minimal modifications.
AI.result: RADIOlogy significantly outperforms other training-free baselines and shows zero-shot anomaly localization and detection out of the box from multi-head attention pooling; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The vision-language family of training-free zero-shot anomaly detection techniques can be applied successfully to the medical domain with minimal modifications.

title: Beyond Ground Truth: A Heuristic Unsupervised Quality Assurance Engine for Diagnosing Calibrational Blindness in Dental Segmentation
comment: Accepted at 11th IEEE Asia-Pacific Conference on Computer Science and Data Engineering (IEEE CSDE 2026), Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh. Copyright 2026 IEEE. 5 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables
summary: In real-world clinical settings, dental X-ray segmentation using deep learning methods suffers from reliability issues. Even when the segmentation quality is bad, deep learning models show high confidence in their predictions (calibrational blindness). Moreover, in real use, doctors do not have ground-truth masks to check their accuracy. To address this problem, we introduce a simple quality-checking engine called HUS-QA with three stages. We train it on the PRAD (Periapical Dental X-ray) dataset to build our SimCLR self-supervised ResNet-18 U-Net model, which generates the segmentation mask and then evaluates its quality. Our HUS-QA checks the segmentation mask quality without a ground-truth mask. Prediction confidence, edge sharpness, shape connectivity, and area-size penalty are the simple indicators considered in this research. Results show that standard confidence methods fail (r = -0.1394, p = 1.7864e-3, ROC AUC = 0.4275). By contrast, our HUS-QA shows a positive correlation with actual Dice scores (r = 0.4647, p = 3.7510e-28) and achieves a strong ROC-AUC of 0.8405. Therefore, HUS-QA serves as a practical tool for clinical quality control.

AI.tldr: HUS-QA is an unsupervised quality-assurance engine that estimates the quality of dental X-ray segmentation masks without ground truth, addressing the high confidence that segmentation models show even when their masks are poor.
AI.motivation: Deep learning segmentation of dental X-rays is unreliable in clinical use because models remain highly confident when segmentation is bad (calibrational blindness), and clinicians have no ground-truth masks to check accuracy.
AI.method: A three-stage engine built on a SimCLR self-supervised ResNet-18 U-Net trained on the PRAD periapical dental X-ray dataset; it combines prediction confidence, edge sharpness, shape connectivity and an area-size penalty as indicators of mask quality.
AI.result: Standard confidence methods fail (r = -0.1394, ROC AUC = 0.4275), whereas HUS-QA correlates positively with actual Dice scores (r = 0.4647, p = 3.7510e-28) and achieves a ROC AUC of 0.8405.
AI.conclusion: HUS-QA is presented as a practical tool for clinical quality control of segmentation outputs when no ground-truth mask is available.

title: Fight World Model: Customizable Combat through Visual Interaction Proxies
summary: A playable, programmable game world must maintain persistent state, enforce executable rules, and support extensible gameplay mechanics. Existing video world models can generate plausible combat, yet struggle to keep hit reactions and health updates consistent with game rules. We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), which separates rule-governed combat execution from video rendering. An executable engine maintains state and resolves interactions. A deterministic compiler encodes these outcomes and attempted actions in a spatially and temporally aligned interaction proxy. The proxy aligns action and skill windows, brief hit reactions, and persistent health by fighter identity and timing. These cues can be controlled separately to render interactions under modified rules. Identity-bound references preserve character appearance across side switches. We train FWM on FightWorld Corpus, spanning 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond the native game. It also allows character and arena customization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FWM, which outperforms existing game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, health-state consistency, and character appearance preservation. Our project is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Fight World Model separates rule-governed combat execution, handled by an executable engine, from video rendering, so that a video model can render fights that follow customizable game rules without retraining the renderer.
AI.motivation: Existing video world models can generate plausible combat but struggle to keep hit reactions and health updates consistent with game rules, which a playable, programmable game world requires.
AI.method: An executable engine maintains state and resolves interactions; a deterministic compiler encodes outcomes and attempted actions into a spatially and temporally aligned interaction proxy that aligns action and skill windows, brief hit reactions and persistent health by fighter identity; identity-bound references preserve appearance across side switches; training uses the FightWorld Corpus, with 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants and 15 arenas.
AI.result: Without retraining the renderer, the model supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond the native game, as well as character and arena customization, and outperforms existing game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, health-state consistency and character appearance preservation.
AI.conclusion: Separating rule execution from rendering makes game mechanics controllable and customizable in generated video.

title: L3G-World: Real-Time Infinite World Generation with Latent 3D Gaussian Memory
summary: Interactive world models generate visual content conditioned on user actions, yet maintaining spatial consistency over long-horizon exploration in real time remains challenging. Existing approaches rely on either temporal context or explicit 3D memory, both of which scale poorly because memory grows with the length of the generated stream. Moreover, explicit 3D memories condition latent video generators by re-encoding RGB renderings, which precludes real-time generation. In this paper, we introduce a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G) that combines the efficiency of feed-forward reconstruction with a compact, rapidly renderable scene representation. Building on this memory, we propose L3G-World, in which a memory updater and a video diffusion transformer (DiT) alternate autoregressively to generate spatially consistent worlds. The memory updater spawns Gaussians in newly observed regions and refines existing ones, so that the memory grows with scene extent rather than stream length. Each Gaussian further stores a VAE latent feature, allowing the memory to be rendered directly into the DiT's latent space without VAE re-encoding. Experiments show that L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to $38.6\times$ fewer 3D primitives, $3.2\times$ faster memory updates, and $359\times$ faster memory rendering relative to the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time world generation at 9 FPS.

AI.tldr: L3G-World generates long, spatially consistent interactive worlds in real time by alternating a memory updater over a latent 3D Gaussian memory with a video diffusion transformer, reaching 9 FPS.
AI.motivation: Interactive world models struggle to keep spatial consistency over long real-time exploration, because temporal context and explicit 3D memory both scale poorly with stream length, and explicit 3D memories must be re-encoded from RGB renderings, which precludes real-time generation.
AI.method: A Latent 3D Gaussian Memory combines the efficiency of feed-forward reconstruction with a compact, rapidly renderable scene representation; a memory updater spawns Gaussians in newly observed regions and refines existing ones, alternating autoregressively with a video diffusion transformer (DiT); each Gaussian stores a VAE latent feature, so the memory is rendered directly into the DiT latent space without VAE re-encoding.
AI.result: L3G-World achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and long-horizon spatial consistency, with up to 38.6x fewer 3D primitives, 3.2x faster memory updates and 359x faster memory rendering than the most efficient prior 3D-memory baseline for each metric, enabling real-time generation at 9 FPS.
AI.conclusion: Because the memory grows with scene extent rather than stream length, real-time world generation with long-horizon spatial consistency becomes feasible.

title: Probing Spatial State Representations in Visual Foundation Models
summary: An observer sees only part of the surrounding world, yet must keep track of what lies beyond the current view. Spatial perception therefore involves more than recognizing individual images: it calls for a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action. Do visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state? We study this question through four levels of spatial capability---spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability---using frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments. The resulting capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers, and prefix lengths: strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. Matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer to predicted features unchanged. Finally, goal-dependent candidate selection does not establish reliable continuous action utility: predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress. Across the four levels, object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial representations not only by what can be decoded from them, but by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively, and used for goal-directed action.

AI.tldr: The paper probes frozen features from ten visual foundation models for spatial state and finds that strong readout of the visible scene does not guarantee object persistence, future-feature retrieval or goal-directed action utility.
AI.motivation: Spatial perception requires a persistent spatial state that is updated under self-motion and used to guide action, and it is unknown whether visual foundation models provide representations that support such a state.
AI.method: Frozen-feature probes on ten representations under streaming egocentric observations of static indoor environments, evaluated at four levels: spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update and actionability; matched controls separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion.
AI.result: Capability profiles vary across tasks, network layers and prefix lengths; native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer unchanged to predicted features; predicted actions respond to goal changes, yet supplying the correct goal does not reliably improve progress.
AI.conclusion: Spatial representations should be evaluated not only by what can be decoded from them but also by whether that information is maintained beyond observation, updated predictively and used for goal-directed action.

title: SonoWorld4D: From One Video to a 4D Audio-Visual Scene via Diffusion Synchronization
summary: Recent progress in visual scene generation has extended beyond static 3D scenes toward the more challenging problem of generating dynamic 4D scenes from minimal input. However, sound, despite being intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events, remains largely unmodeled in prior work. We introduce Video-to-4DAVScene, a new task that turns a video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, and present the SonoWorld4D framework for this task. Given a monocular video, our method generates a 360 static background, reconstructs explicit motion trajectories of dynamic, sound-emitting foreground objects, and synthesizes a physically-grounded sound field consistent across multiple sources through dual-space audio diffusion synchronization. The resulting 4D scene supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial audio rendering. Evaluation on real-world dynamic scenes and a user study demonstrates SonoWorld4D generates 4D audio-visual scenes with perceptually realistic, physically grounded spatial audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.

AI.tldr: SonoWorld4D turns one monocular video into an explorable, time-varying 4D audio-visual scene, with a 360-degree static background, moving sound-emitting objects and a physically grounded sound field.
AI.motivation: Dynamic 4D scene generation has advanced, but sound, which is intrinsically coupled with dynamic objects and events, has largely been left unmodeled in prior work.
AI.method: Given a monocular video, the framework generates a 360-degree static background, reconstructs explicit motion trajectories of dynamic sound-emitting foreground objects, and synthesizes a sound field consistent across multiple sources through dual-space audio diffusion synchronization.
AI.result: The resulting 4D scene supports real-time novel-view visual and spatial audio rendering; evaluation on real-world dynamic scenes and a user study show perceptually realistic, physically grounded spatial audio consistent with scene geometry and visual content.
AI.conclusion: The Video-to-4DAVScene task, which turns a video into a 4D audio-visual scene, is shown to be feasible with the SonoWorld4D framework.

title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at The 2026 IEEE International Conference on Content-Based Multimedia Indexing (IEEE CBMI)
summary: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.

AI.tldr: The paper studies strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that detects and re-identifies luggage from multiple video streams in real-world environments. It examines how to select and merge views and shots of the same luggage and how training on different environment datasets affects overall ReID performance.
AI.motivation: Luggage re-identification matters for surveillance and luggage management, but existing approaches focus on appearance matching of cropped images under clean conditions, while occlusions, clutter and crowds degrade real-world performance. Strategies that exploit complementary shots and views from different video streams are overlooked.
AI.method: An end-to-end pipeline operates on multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. The authors evaluate variants for selecting and merging different views and shots of the same item, and for training on different environment datasets.
AI.result: The variants are evaluated on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments. The abstract does not report specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The study gives practical guidance on view and shot selection and merging, and on the choice of training data, for improving luggage ReID in practical applications.

title: TACOS: Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision for Visual Footstep Planning
summary: Humans navigate their environment based on their vision system, anticipating how the ground will respond before committing to a step. Self-supervised learning could provide legged robots the same ability, but the supervisory signal is typically chosen on intuition, and its effect on what the model learns is rarely examined. We present Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision (TACOS), which proposes a meaningful and consistent footstep instability score, based on the residual of a factor graph in legged state estimation. It projects the continuous score into preceding images to supervise a dense visual predictor. We propose two variants, a hard score that exploits hindsight and a causal soft score available immediately. Both metrics are compared against state-of-the-art alternatives in two independent evaluations that share no data or labels. On 1716 manually annotated contacts, both variants outperform every evaluated alternative at detecting instability and ranking its severity, improving pooled severity ranking by 28 % over the strongest baseline. On three outdoor test runs, our metric also trains the most accurate visual predictor, improving rank correlation by 58 % over the strongest alternative, and by a further 25 % when supplemented with onboard context. In a real-world experiment over a 50 m forest trajectory, the trained predictor handles non-geometric terrain properties such as mud and vegetation, while stepping around geometric obstacles like fallen branches. Code is available for reproducibility at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TACOS derives a terrain-aware footstep instability score from the residual of a factor graph in legged state estimation and uses it to supervise a dense visual predictor for footstep planning. Both score variants outperform the evaluated alternatives at detecting instability and ranking its severity.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised visual footstep planning for legged robots depends on a supervisory signal that is usually chosen on intuition, and its effect on what the model learns is rarely examined.
AI.method: The continuous instability score is computed from the residual of a legged state-estimation factor graph and projected into preceding images to supervise a dense visual predictor. Two variants are proposed: a hard score that exploits hindsight and a causal soft score that is available immediately.
AI.result: On 1716 manually annotated contacts, both variants outperform every evaluated alternative at detecting instability and ranking severity, improving pooled severity ranking by 28 percent over the strongest baseline. On three outdoor test runs, the metric trains the most accurate visual predictor, improving rank correlation by 58 percent over the strongest alternative and by a further 25 percent with onboard context. In a 50 m forest trajectory, the predictor handles mud and vegetation and steps around fallen branches.
AI.conclusion: The choice of supervisory signal materially affects the learned visual predictor, and a consistent, physically grounded contact instability score yields better terrain-aware footstep prediction than the alternatives. Code is made available for reproducibility.

title: Efficacy of Monocular Depth Estimation in Lunar Environments
comment: Accepted at the International Conference on Space Robotics (iSpaRo) 2026
summary: Recent advances in monocular depth estimation have demonstrated highly accurate 3D reconstructions within in-distribution terrestrial domains. This study investigates the efficacy of several state-of-the-art approaches to reconstruct out-of-distribution lunar environments using the NASA Ames Polar Optical Lunar Analog Reconstruction (POLAR) stereo dataset and Apollo 17 surface imagery. By leveraging these datasets, we establish a robust analog-to-field validation pipeline that evaluates quantitative performance against ground-truth physical analogs and qualitative performance against historical field data. Our results indicate that select state-of-the-art techniques can successfully generalize to produce high-fidelity relative 3D reconstructions of the unstructured lunar surface.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates several state-of-the-art monocular depth estimation methods on out-of-distribution lunar terrain, using the NASA Ames POLAR stereo dataset and Apollo 17 surface imagery. It finds that select methods generalize to produce high-fidelity relative 3D reconstructions of the lunar surface.
AI.motivation: Monocular depth estimation performs well in in-distribution terrestrial domains, but its ability to reconstruct out-of-distribution lunar environments has not been established.
AI.method: The authors build an analog-to-field validation pipeline that measures quantitative performance against ground-truth physical analogs in the POLAR stereo dataset and qualitative performance against historical Apollo 17 field imagery.
AI.result: Select state-of-the-art techniques successfully generalize to produce high-fidelity relative 3D reconstructions of the unstructured lunar surface. The abstract gives no numerical metrics.
AI.conclusion: Some current monocular depth methods transfer to lunar terrain for relative 3D reconstruction, a finding supported by an analog-to-field validation approach.

title: From the Superderivative to a Relative-Gradient Edge Operator
summary: First-derivative edge detectors such as Sobel, Prewitt, Roberts and Scharr measure absolute grey-level differences. We revisit the log-gradient magnitude, a relative-gradient edge operator, and motivate it by analogy with the superderivative, a multiplicative derivative in which the independent variable is perturbed multiplicatively rather than additively. In one and two dimensions the logarithm of the superderivative is a radial logarithmic derivative; its local, origin-free, isotropic analogue is the magnitude of the logarithmic gradient. The resulting operator measures relative rather than absolute change, giving an edge-strength map that is invariant under global intensity rescaling. We present the theory, show how the operator can be implemented in two steps---a classical gradient kernel plus a pointwise division---and compare it with standard first-derivative filters on synthetic images with ground-truth edges and on the official BSDS500 benchmark. We also study a parametric family that interpolates between the absolute gradient and the log-gradient; empirically, the best members are small intermediate exponents, which edge the classical kernels by a small but statistically detectable margin in the per-image metric and, with the same Gaussian smoothing as the single-$\sigma$ Canny, match it in ODS and lead it in OIS and AP, while the tuned Canny remains ahead in ODS. The single-threshold margin over the kernels does not replicate on the held-out test split, and the fully relative endpoint is never the best member, its ranking depending on the edge-map normalisation. The contribution is the construction and the invariance it buys, not a new state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits the log-gradient magnitude as a relative-gradient edge operator, motivated by the superderivative, and shows that it gives an edge-strength map invariant to global intensity rescaling. Its performance is comparable to classical first-derivative filters rather than a new state of the art.
AI.motivation: Standard first-derivative edge detectors such as Sobel, Prewitt, Roberts and Scharr measure absolute grey-level differences, so their responses depend on absolute intensity.
AI.method: The log-gradient magnitude is derived by analogy with the superderivative, a multiplicative derivative, and implemented in two steps: a classical gradient kernel followed by a pointwise division. The authors also study a parametric family that interpolates between the absolute gradient and the log-gradient.
AI.result: On synthetic images and BSDS500, the best family members (small intermediate exponents) beat the classical kernels by a small margin in the per-image metric and match them in ODS while leading in OIS and AP, but the tuned Canny remains ahead in ODS. The single-threshold margin does not replicate on the held-out test split, and the fully relative endpoint is never the best member.
AI.conclusion: The contribution lies in the construction of the operator and the invariance it provides, not in a new state of the art, and the ranking depends on edge-map normalisation.

title: EgoContact: Evaluating Physical Intelligence with Egocentric Video
summary: Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction. We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact's annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.

AI.tldr: EgoContact is a large-scale egocentric dataset of 22.5K manually verified interaction events for evaluating physical intelligence through future contact-point prediction. Current methods often struggle to predict precise contacts, and using the dataset as a memory bank improves an affordance-transfer policy's grasp success.
AI.motivation: Egocentric video is widely used to pretrain manipulation policies but has been underused as a validation tool for physical intelligence, in particular knowing where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction.
AI.method: The dataset contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, a semantic intent and pixel-precise contact locations, and is used to evaluate future contact-point prediction. It is also used as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy.
AI.result: Current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse in-the-wild scenes, even when multiple predictions are allowed. Using EgoContact as the memory bank raises grasp success from 14.2 percent to 31.2 percent in simulation and from 16 percent to 58 percent on a real robot.
AI.conclusion: EgoContact is a useful benchmark for precise contact prediction, and its annotated interactions can directly improve robotic manipulation through affordance transfer.

title: Fast rigid rotational alignment of voxelized 3-D density maps in sliced Wasserstein distance
summary: We develop a fast method for the rigid alignment of voxelized three-dimensional density functions over $\mathsf{SO}(3)$ using sliced optimal transport. Our approach efficiently transforms each density map into a tensor of one-dimensional quantile functions, taken from central slices over the unit sphere, such that the Euclidean distance of the transformed volumes approximates the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance. Our formulation is therefore compatible with existing, fast, voxel-based Euclidean alignment algorithms. We provide theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrating that the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance is a robust metric for comparing three-dimensional shapes and for computing their rigid alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fast method for rigid alignment of voxelized 3-D density maps over SO(3) using the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance. Each map is converted into a tensor of one-dimensional quantile functions so that Euclidean distance approximates the sliced distance, which makes fast voxel-based Euclidean alignment algorithms applicable.
AI.motivation: The abstract frames the need as a fast and robust metric for comparing and rigidly aligning three-dimensional shapes, with the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance as the candidate metric.
AI.method: Central slices over the unit sphere are used to transform each density function into a tensor of one-dimensional quantile functions, such that the Euclidean distance between transformed volumes approximates the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance. The formulation is compatible with existing fast voxel-based Euclidean alignment algorithms.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis and numerical experiments show that the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance is a robust metric for comparing 3-D shapes and for computing their rigid alignment. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The sliced 2-Wasserstein distance is a robust and practical basis for 3-D shape comparison and rigid alignment, and the transformation enables fast alignment with existing Euclidean tools.

title: Decoding Geometry, Not Tokens: Efficient VLMs for Robot Affordance and Trajectory Prediction
comment: IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027)
summary: Predicting where to grasp and how to move is fundamentally a geometry problem. Vision-language models treat it as language generation instead. They tokenize spatial coordinates into text and decode them autoregressively. This mechanism ignores spatial structure and truncates continuous precision. Errors compound across coordinate tokens during decoding. In this paper, we show that compact off-the-shelf VLMs with 0.5-2B parameters already encode rich spatial information in their intermediate hidden states. Autoregressive decoding is the dominant bottleneck for trajectory prediction, while affordance prediction depends additionally on feature depth and decoder architecture. We expose the latent spatial information with a lightweight, geometry-compatible prediction head that attaches to a frozen backbone. It reads features from an intermediate hidden layer, conditions a learned query on the task instruction and refines it via cross-attention over the visual tokens to regress affordance boxes and trajectory waypoints directly as continuous values, without modifying the backbone. We evaluate on ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K. Our 2B variant reduces trajectory error by over 60% and improves ShareRobot-Bench affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline. It approaches RoboBrain on trajectory prediction (0.251 vs 0.191 DFD) at 3.8x higher throughput. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for instruction-conditioned 2D geometric prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that compact 0.5-2B vision-language models already encode spatial information in intermediate hidden states, and proposes a lightweight geometric prediction head on a frozen backbone that regresses affordance boxes and trajectory waypoints as continuous values. The 2B variant reduces trajectory error by over 60 percent and raises affordance mAP by 85 percent relative to an autoregressive baseline.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models treat grasp and motion prediction as language generation, tokenizing spatial coordinates and decoding them autoregressively. This ignores spatial structure, truncates continuous precision and lets errors compound across coordinate tokens.
AI.method: A lightweight, geometry-compatible head attaches to a frozen backbone. It reads features from an intermediate hidden layer, conditions a learned query on the task instruction, and refines the query via cross-attention over visual tokens to regress affordance boxes and trajectory waypoints directly as continuous values, without modifying the backbone.
AI.result: On ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K, the 2B variant reduces trajectory error by over 60 percent and improves ShareRobot-Bench affordance mAP by 85 percent relative to the autoregressive baseline. On trajectory prediction it approaches RoboBrain, with a DFD of 0.251 against RoboBrain's 0.191, at 3.8 times higher throughput.
AI.conclusion: Autoregressive decoding is the main bottleneck for trajectory prediction, and the approach offers a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for instruction-conditioned 2D geometric prediction.

title: GC-LIF: Spiking Group-Equivariant Neural Network With Group-Coupled Membrane Dynamics
summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise event-driven, low-power inference, but on vision tasks they still acquire rotation invariance only through data augmentation. Group-equivariant CNNs build such symmetries into the architecture, yet a faithful spiking analogue is missing: a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron placed after a $G$-equivariant convolution can break equivariance through its membrane recurrence. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for this not to happen. The layer is equivariant at every time step if and only if the neuron parameters $(\beta, v_{\mathrm{th}})$ are constant along the joint orbits of the group action on the (group, space) index. We solve it in closed form, and it covers any elementwise stateful neuron. Its sufficiency half specialises a known result for equivariant recurrent networks; its necessity half rules out the heterogeneous per-neuron parameters common in SNNs. The per-channel parameterisation that satisfies it, Group-Coupled LIF (GC-LIF), is combined with $p4$ and $p4m$-equivariant convolutions and a spike-rate group max-pool into SGE-Net. On MNIST, KMNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, evaluating each checkpoint on the clean test set and all its group-transformed copies, SGE-Net trained without rotations is invariant under $C_4$ and $D_4$ and outperforms a plain SNN trained with rotations in nine of ten dataset-group pairs, whereas non-equivariant baselines lose up to $72$ percentage points in the worst case. Operator-level tests confirm the theory before and after training, and an analytical estimate places SGE-Net at $1.7\times$ the arithmetic energy of a standard CNN and $2.3\times$ below its ANN counterpart at eight time steps.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a necessary and sufficient condition under which a spiking neuron placed after a group-equivariant convolution preserves equivariance at every time step, and builds SGE-Net from GC-LIF neurons, p4 and p4m convolutions and a spike-rate group max-pool. SGE-Net trained without rotations is invariant under C4 and D4 and outperforms a plain SNN trained with rotations in nine of ten dataset-group pairs.
AI.motivation: Spiking neural networks acquire rotation invariance only through data augmentation, and no faithful spiking analogue of group-equivariant CNNs exists, because the membrane recurrence of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron can break equivariance.
AI.method: The condition requires the neuron parameters (beta, v_th) to be constant along the joint orbits of the group action on the (group, space) index. The closed-form solution covers any elementwise stateful neuron. The per-channel parameterization that satisfies it, Group-Coupled LIF (GC-LIF), is combined with p4 and p4m equivariant convolutions and a spike-rate group max-pool into SGE-Net.
AI.result: On MNIST, KMNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, SGE-Net trained without rotations is invariant under C4 and D4 and outperforms a plain SNN trained with rotations in nine of ten dataset-group pairs, while non-equivariant baselines lose up to 72 percentage points in the worst case. An analytical estimate places SGE-Net at 1.7 times the arithmetic energy of a standard CNN and 2.3 times below its ANN counterpart at eight time steps.
AI.conclusion: Group-equivariance can be built into spiking networks through a precise condition on neuron parameters, giving rotation invariance without rotation augmentation, at 1.7 times the arithmetic energy of a standard CNN.

title: Blind Video Denoising for Vocal Tract rtMRI using a Self-Supervised Ensemble
summary: Real-time magnetic resonance imaging of the vocal tract makes speech articulation directly observable, but the trade-off between temporal resolution and signal quality introduces substantial noise and obscures fine articulatory detail. Since clean references cannot be acquired for a moving vocal tract, supervised denoising approaches are not applicable in this setting. We propose a self-supervised denoising framework that combines spatiotemporal super-resolution learning with pseudo-supervision derived from a variance-stabilized non-local means filter. A dual-model fusion strategy balances noise suppression and preservation of high-frequency articulatory structure.
