Experiments on the USC-75 multi-speaker dataset under natural noise conditions show that the ensemble raises the signal-to-noise ratio by 11.9 dB on unseen subjects while attaining more high-frequency articulatory content in the frames. Among tuned implementations of anisotropic diffusion, block-matching filtering, non-local means and pre-smoothed non-local means, every configuration that achieves comparable noise suppression does so at the cost of high-frequency content or of structural fidelity. Under severe added Gaussian, Rayleigh and Rician noise, peak signal-to-noise ratio improves by 7.6 to 11.8 dB and structural similarity roughly triples. An ablation shows that the variance-stabilized pseudo-supervision is an essential element for denoising, and that the effect is attributable to the hard thresholding contained in the stabilization transform.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a self-supervised ensemble for denoising real-time MRI videos of the vocal tract, using pseudo-supervision derived from a variance-stabilized non-local means filter. On the USC-75 dataset under natural noise, the ensemble raises SNR by 11.9 dB on unseen subjects.
AI.motivation: Clean references cannot be acquired for a moving vocal tract, so supervised denoising is not applicable, and the trade-off between temporal resolution and signal quality in real-time MRI introduces noise that obscures fine articulatory detail.
AI.method: A self-supervised framework combines spatiotemporal super-resolution learning with pseudo-supervision from a variance-stabilized non-local means filter. A dual-model fusion strategy balances noise suppression and preservation of high-frequency articulatory structure.
AI.result: On USC-75 under natural noise, the ensemble raises SNR by 11.9 dB on unseen subjects and retains more high-frequency articulatory content. Under added Gaussian, Rayleigh and Rician noise, PSNR improves by 7.6 to 11.8 dB and structural similarity roughly triples. Tuned classical filters that reach comparable noise suppression lose high-frequency content or structural fidelity. An ablation shows the variance-stabilized pseudo-supervision is essential, and the effect is attributed to the hard thresholding in the stabilization transform.
AI.conclusion: Variance-stabilized pseudo-supervision is the key element for denoising, and the ensemble offers a better balance of noise suppression and articulatory detail than classical filters for real-time MRI.

title: Decision-Level Error Attribution and Depth-Aware Safety Evaluation of Monocular RGB Human Tracking for Autonomous Robot Navigation
summary: Monocular RGB tracking is useful for robots operating near people, but perception errors affect binary stop/proceed decisions in ways that geometric accuracy metrics do not capture. We examine how much decision error arises from the safety rule versus perception. We prove that lateral-only distance is a lower bound on planar distance: with accurate positions, it cannot miss dangers identified by the planar rule, but it produces unnecessary stops. We introduce a two-factor Shapley attribution separating rule and perception contributions, and further distinguish missed detections from localization errors. Experiments use ETH and UCY pedestrian videos with simulated stationary robots, disjoint calibration and evaluation pedestrians, and time-block bootstrap intervals. Across 898 pedestrians in three scenes, the lateral rule missed no dangers on annotated positions but achieved only 5.6-31.9% stop precision. In two scenes with RGB perception, calibrated ground-plane localization achieved 0.59 m and 0.51 m planar RMSE, compared with 1.72 m and 1.39 m for a geometric baseline and 0.81 m and 0.68 m for calibrated Depth Anything V2. Detection recall of 0.43 and 0.26 made missed detections the leading source of missed danger. A two-standard-deviation safety margin with ground-plane localization matched or improved on the lateral rule's missed-danger rate in all eight scene-threshold settings and reduced unnecessary stops in seven. All robot interactions are simulated, and outcomes are offline decision classifications, not demonstrations of collision avoidance.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how monocular RGB human tracking errors and the lateral safety rule each contribute to stop/proceed decision errors for autonomous robot navigation. It proves that lateral-only distance lower-bounds planar distance, and shows that calibrated ground-plane localization with a two-standard-deviation margin matches or improves the lateral rule's missed-danger rate in all eight scene-threshold settings.
AI.motivation: Perception errors affect binary stop/proceed decisions in ways that geometric accuracy metrics do not capture, and it is unclear how much decision error arises from the safety rule versus perception.
AI.method: The authors prove that lateral-only distance is a lower bound on planar distance, introduce a two-factor Shapley attribution separating rule and perception contributions, and distinguish missed detections from localization errors. Experiments use ETH and UCY pedestrian videos with simulated stationary robots, disjoint calibration and evaluation pedestrians, and time-block bootstrap intervals.
AI.result: Across 898 pedestrians in three scenes, the lateral rule missed no dangers on annotated positions but achieved only 5.6-31.9 percent stop precision. In two scenes with RGB perception, calibrated ground-plane localization achieved 0.59 m and 0.51 m planar RMSE, versus 1.72 m and 1.39 m for a geometric baseline and 0.81 m and 0.68 m for calibrated Depth Anything V2. Detection recall of 0.43 and 0.26 made missed detections the leading source of missed danger. The two-standard-deviation margin reduced unnecessary stops in seven of the eight settings.
AI.conclusion: Under RGB perception, missed detections are the leading source of missed danger, and the attribution shows where the error lies. All robot interactions are simulated and outcomes are offline decision classifications, not demonstrations of collision avoidance.

title: SymAnt: Grounding Long-Horizon Action Anticipation with Adaptable Symbolic Priors
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 18 pages (8-page main paper, references, and supplementary appendix), 6 figures, 9 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: As robots and intelligent systems increasingly interact with humans, they must anticipate long sequences of future actions from only brief observations. While purely neural models typically require extensive observations to predict future actions and remain difficult to interpret and adjust, symbolic priors offer a structured alternative. To this end, we introduce SymAnt, a novel neuro-symbolic approach that unifies the expressiveness of neural networks with the structured reasoning of scene and knowledge graphs. Given a short video, SymAnt performs a joint-search over both graphs to construct a symbolic context, enabling unified reasoning over spatial relationships, object attributes, affordances, and associated actions. This symbolic context serves as a prior for an iterative refinement process that progressively generates and improves the sequence of future actions. By grounding predictions in symbolic context, SymAnt anticipates long-horizon actions from short observation windows in a parameter-efficient manner, while enabling users to directly edit the underlying knowledge to adjust predictions without further training. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SymAnt, particularly when only short observation contexts are available, across five diverse datasets: Breakfast, 50 Salads, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA Gaze+, and Assembly101.

AI.tldr: SymAnt is a neuro-symbolic approach to long-horizon action anticipation that builds a symbolic context from scene and knowledge graphs for a short video and uses it as a prior for iterative refinement of future actions. It is evaluated on five datasets, with a focus on short observation windows.
AI.motivation: Purely neural anticipation models typically require extensive observations, and they are difficult to interpret and adjust, while symbolic priors offer a structured alternative.
AI.method: Given a short video, SymAnt performs a joint search over scene and knowledge graphs to construct a symbolic context covering spatial relationships, object attributes, affordances and actions. This context is a prior for an iterative refinement process that generates and improves the future action sequence. Users can edit the underlying knowledge to adjust predictions without further training.
AI.result: The abstract reports effectiveness across Breakfast, 50 Salads, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA Gaze+ and Assembly101, particularly when only short observation contexts are available. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Grounding predictions in symbolic context enables parameter-efficient anticipation of long-horizon actions from short observations, with interpretability and editable knowledge.

title: Micro-Edits: Computational Support for Fine-Scale Edits in Film
comment: UIST 2026 Best Paper Honorable Mention. Project page: this https URL
summary: In film editing, every frame matters. While macro, content-level edits shape the high-level narrative of a film, small local edits often control timing and direct visual attention. For example, editors can adjust the precise timing of clips to control the length of a meaningful silence, or cut to shots that highlight a specific character's reactions to important moments. These small, detailed edits are slow and tedious to make in standard editing tools because users have to map high-level narrative goals to low-level frame-by-frame adjustments. At the same time, these fine-scale adjustments, which we call micro-edits, can be nuanced and expressive, with different choices serving different creative goals. In this work, we start by conducting a formative study with professional editors to understand the structure of micro-edits and how they are used. We then derive a mathematical formalization for this structure to develop tools that leverage AI and optimization to make exploring micro-edits simpler and more efficient for users. Finally, we validate our tools in multiple user studies and a wide range of video examples.

AI.tldr: The paper studies micro-edits, which are fine-scale timing and shot choices in film editing, and presents AI and optimization tools that make exploring them simpler. A formative study with professional editors informs a mathematical formalization of micro-edits that underpins the tools.
AI.motivation: Fine-scale edits that control timing and visual attention are slow and tedious in standard editing tools, because users must translate high-level narrative goals into frame-by-frame adjustments.
AI.method: A formative study with professional editors characterizes the structure of micro-edits. A mathematical formalization of that structure then underpins tools that use AI and optimization.
AI.result: The tools are validated in multiple user studies and across a wide range of video examples. The abstract reports no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Formalizing micro-edits enables computational support that makes fine-scale editing exploration simpler and more efficient for users.

title: Hammering with Vampire in Lean
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Tool demonstration paper
summary: We present Vampire-Hammer, a hammer for the Lean interactive theorem prover that discharges goals using the Vampire automated theorem prover and reconstructs proofs checked by the Lean kernel. Vampire-Hammer uses the Lean-auto framework to process goals and premises before dispatching them to Vampire for proof search. Doing so, we rely on standard TPTP problem formats and annotated TSTP proofs that support proof reconstruction. With a 10-second budget on 196,083 eligible Mathlib theorems, Vampire-Hammer solves 21,158 problems not solved by other evaluated tools within the same budget.

AI.tldr: Vampire-Hammer is a hammer for the Lean interactive theorem prover that sends goals to the Vampire automated theorem prover and reconstructs proofs checked by the Lean kernel. With a 10-second budget on 196,083 eligible Mathlib theorems, it solves 21,158 problems that the other evaluated tools do not solve within the same budget.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not state the motivation explicitly. It frames the work as bringing Vampire's automated first-order proof search into Lean while keeping proofs kernel-checked.
AI.method: Vampire-Hammer uses the Lean-auto framework to process goals and premises before dispatching them to Vampire. It relies on standard TPTP problem formats and annotated TSTP proofs that support proof reconstruction.
AI.result: With a 10-second budget on 196,083 eligible Mathlib theorems, Vampire-Hammer solves 21,158 problems not solved by other evaluated tools within the same budget.
AI.conclusion: Vampire-based hammering adds substantial coverage over the other evaluated tools on Mathlib, with proofs reconstructed and checked by the Lean kernel.

title: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents for personal health read wearable data and recommend, but do not learn about the individual in a way that can be audited or falsified. We present EpiCoach, an agentic system that treats one athlete, a cross-country mountain biker, as the subject of accountable N-of-1 science. Claims about the athlete live in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry: each must issue a probabilistic prediction about a future session before it occurs, and its belief moves only through computed evidence from a logged statistical fit. Predictions come from a mechanistic digital twin inferred from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude: a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants, and a latent technical-descending skill state, measured on discovered trail segments. The agent prescribes the next training week as a constrained experiment maximizing information gain subject to load and safety constraints, around two instrument rides. We evaluate the system two ways over eighteen months of data. A rolling-origin replay benchmark shows the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, and the agentic loop matches a static model. A live prospective phase runs the weekly cycle: in its first three weeks the ledger sealed 20 predictions, scored 14, the descent forecast calibrated after one correction, the climb forecast pessimistic as the athlete improved, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice. Every correction is preserved in the registry, a template for auditable, falsifiable personalization in digital health. We release the registry, benchmark and protocol.

AI.tldr: EpiCoach is an agentic system that treats one athlete as the subject of N-of-1 science, using an evidence-gated hypothesis registry, a mechanistic digital twin and constrained experiment design. Over 18 months of data, the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not on segment time, and the live phase sealed 20 predictions in its first three weeks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents for personal health read wearable data and make recommendations, but they do not learn about the individual in a way that can be audited or falsified.
AI.method: Claims are stored in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry. Each claim must issue a probabilistic prediction about a future session before it occurs, and its belief changes only through computed evidence from a logged statistical fit. Predictions come from a digital twin inferred from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude, comprising a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants and a latent technical-descending skill state. The agent prescribes the next training week as a constrained experiment that maximizes information gain under load and safety constraints.
AI.result: In a rolling-origin replay benchmark, the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not on segment time, and the agentic loop matches a static model. In the live prospective phase, the first three weeks sealed 20 predictions and scored 14, the descent forecast calibrated after one correction, the climb forecast was pessimistic as the athlete improved, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice.
AI.conclusion: The registry, which preserves every correction, offers a template for auditable, falsifiable personalization in digital health. The authors release the registry, benchmark and protocol.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
summary: Despite growing capabilities, LLMs remain susceptible to prompt injections: malicious inputs that can manipulate or hijack models. In particular, it has recently been observed that LLMs can exhibit role confusion (Ye et al., 2026), where models attribute the source of text based on its style instead of its labeled role. Malicious text in tool outputs (for instance, a malicious webpage accessed by an agent) can leverage role confusion to impersonate the user, an attack we call role spoofing}. In this work, we seek to understand and mitigate role spoofing. We study how models track "who said what" in a conversation, showing that they use cues from both content (e.g., semantics and writing style) and structure (e.g., control tokens and formatting). We show that LLMs are highly susceptible to role spoofing attacks that combine both fake structure and content. Additionally, in a toy setting, we show that adversarial training which teaches the model to ignore content-based injections does mitigate content-based attacks but leaves the model susceptible to structure-based attacks. This can explain why frontier models, with increased resistance to many injection attacks, can still be susceptible to role spoofing. Finally, we propose a new method for detecting role spoofing using linear probes trained to predict roles in a conversation, and show that it is effective across different settings.

AI.tldr: The paper studies role spoofing, in which malicious text in tool outputs impersonates the user by exploiting LLM role confusion. It shows that LLMs are highly susceptible to attacks combining fake structure and content, and proposes a linear-probe detector that is effective across different settings.
AI.motivation: LLMs remain vulnerable to prompt injection. Role confusion, where models attribute the source of text by its style rather than its label, lets malicious tool outputs impersonate the user, and adversarial training against content-based injections leaves structure-based attacks open.
AI.method: The authors study how models track who said what in a conversation, finding that they use cues from both content (semantics and writing style) and structure (control tokens and formatting). In a toy setting they test adversarial training against content-based injections. They propose detecting role spoofing with linear probes trained to predict roles in a conversation.
AI.result: LLMs are highly susceptible to role spoofing attacks that combine fake structure and content. In the toy setting, adversarial training mitigates content-based attacks but leaves the model susceptible to structure-based attacks. The linear-probe method is effective across different settings. The abstract gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Resistance of frontier models to many injection attacks does not rule out role spoofing, since structure-based cues remain exploitable, and probe-based detection is a promising mitigation.

title: Bridging Neural Representations and Symbolic Semantics in Audio Classification
summary: Deep audio classifiers can achieve strong predictive performance, but their hidden representations remain difficult to interpret. Existing audio explainability methods often focus on input-level attribution, such as waveform segments, spectrogram regions, or acoustic features, and provide limited insight into what hidden neurons encode. Interpreting hidden neurons at the concept level can provide a more meaningful view of what an audio model learns internally. This paper investigates whether hidden neurons in audio classifiers can be associated with human-understandable symbolic acoustic concepts. A model-agnostic neurosymbolic framework is presented for analyzing the final hidden layer of audio classifiers, containing 32 neurons, through symbolic concept induction. The framework is evaluated on two audio classification settings: music genre classification using GTZAN dataset and musical instrument classification using IRMAS dataset. Results show that several hidden neurons can be associated with meaningful induced concepts, and most confirmed neuron-concept pairs are statistically supported using the Mann-Whitney U test. These findings suggest that symbolic concept induction is a promising direction for explaining latent audio representations beyond input-level attribution.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a model-agnostic neurosymbolic framework that associates the 32 neurons of the final hidden layer of audio classifiers with human-understandable symbolic acoustic concepts. Several neurons are linked to meaningful induced concepts, and most confirmed neuron-concept pairs are statistically supported by the Mann-Whitney U test.
AI.motivation: Deep audio classifiers can be accurate, but their hidden representations are hard to interpret. Existing explainability methods mostly give input-level attribution and offer limited insight into what hidden neurons encode.
AI.method: A model-agnostic framework analyzes the final hidden layer, which has 32 neurons, through symbolic concept induction. Neuron-concept associations are tested with the Mann-Whitney U test.
AI.result: Evaluated on music genre classification with GTZAN and musical instrument classification with IRMAS, several hidden neurons are associated with meaningful induced concepts, and most confirmed neuron-concept pairs are statistically supported.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic concept induction is a promising direction for explaining latent audio representations beyond input-level attribution.

title: AI in the EGI e-infrastructure -- Past experiences and future strategies
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure. Preprint of a paper submitted to the proceedings of the 28th Conference on Computing in High Energy and Nuclear Physics (CHEP 2026), to be published in EPJ Web of Conferences
summary: The EGI Federation has provided federated e-infrastructure services to European and global science for over 15 years. We review EGI's early experiences with AI in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects, which built digital twins in physics and environmental sciences and an image-analysis platform for aquatic research. We then examine how the AI landscape has changed since 2023 and argue that the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains, projects and questions. Building on these lessons, we present the AI strategy emerging from the EGI Federation Strategy 2026-2030, organised around three enablers: (1) an AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data and application resources across the continuum; (2) human skills to know what is possible with AI and how to implement it; and (3) trust, to run AI with confidence even in high-risk environments. We describe the projects implementing each enabler, including federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms and AI competence centres, and discuss a division of labour with EuroHPC's AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures and EOSC, in which EGI specialises in the customisation and long-term operation of AI for research.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews EGI's experience with AI in the interTwin and iMagine Horizon Europe projects and presents an AI strategy for the EGI Federation 2026-2030, organized around three enablers. It argues that the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains.
AI.motivation: Since 2023 the focus of AI in science has shifted from model training to adapting and applying AI to specific domains, projects and questions, and research e-infrastructures need to respond to that shift.
AI.method: The paper reviews early experiences in interTwin and iMagine and organizes the emerging AI strategy around three enablers: an AI-ready infrastructure connecting compute, data and application resources; human skills; and trust for running AI with confidence in high-risk environments. It describes projects for federated LLM inference, AI-ready data platforms and AI competence centres, and a division of labour with EuroHPC AI Factories, RAISE, research infrastructures and EOSC.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results. It describes the projects implementing each enabler and the division of labour in which EGI specializes in the customization and long-term operation of AI for research.
AI.conclusion: EGI's role is the customization and long-term operation of domain-specific AI for research, complementing other AI initiatives.

title: BURGER: Benchmarking and Understanding Robotic Generalization via Embodied Drawing
summary: How effectively can vision-language-action (VLA) models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviors as training data scales? Investigating this question requires large and varied robot datasets, whose collection on physical robots remains costly. We introduce BURGER, a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline for generating continuous drawing trajectories, both in simulation and the real world. In BURGER, an agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language, while each instruction allows an open-ended variety of valid drawings and stroke orders. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks, we evaluate five representative VLA models across data scales, language grounding, and multimodal behavior. BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of language grounding, spatial composition, and action generation, revealing distinct failure patterns across VLA models. Our experiments suggest that some VLA models can benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviors, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. Finally, we deploy a trained policy on a Franka Panda arm, demonstrating the ability to draw reactively under human intervention. Project homepage and code can be found at this https URL.

AI.tldr: BURGER is a language-conditioned robotic drawing benchmark with a scalable, prompt-driven pipeline that generates continuous drawing trajectories in simulation and the real world. Using 28,200 simulated demonstrations over 282 tasks, it evaluates five VLA models and reveals distinct failure patterns in language grounding, spatial composition and action generation.
AI.motivation: Investigating how VLA models learn diverse language-conditioned behaviours as training data scales requires large, varied robot datasets, and collecting them on physical robots is costly.
AI.method: An agent starts from the same blank canvas and controls a robot arm to draw the object or spatial composition specified by language. Each instruction allows open-ended valid drawings and stroke orders, and the pipeline generates continuous drawing trajectories in simulation and the real world.
AI.result: Five representative VLA models are evaluated across data scales, language grounding and multimodal behaviour on 28,200 simulated demonstrations spanning 282 drawing tasks. Some models benefit from greater task diversity and demonstration scale, capture multimodal drawing behaviours, and generalize to unseen compositions of familiar objects. A trained policy deployed on a Franka Panda arm draws reactively under human intervention.
AI.conclusion: BURGER supports fine-grained analysis of VLA generalization and reveals model-specific failure patterns, with some models benefiting from task diversity and demonstration scale.

title: From extreme weather to agricultural consequences with agentic AI
summary: Extreme weather is forecast days ahead, yet its consequences for agriculture remain hard to predict: a forecast says where a storm will strike, not which crops will suffer or how much is at risk, and the records that could tell span many sources. We present WxCrop, the first agent that judges agricultural hazards from physically interpretable weather indices examined by causal analysis, and the first that combines weather and agricultural information to predict crop loss reliably for past and forecast dates. We demonstrate it in Florida on hurricanes, freezes and dry heat, with a loss model calibrated on insurance records for each, and the same procedure extends to other hazards and areas. Three checks show reliability: the hurricane index detects recorded cyclone days with an AUC of 0.98, recorded losses in held-out years are reproduced to within 2%, and independent production records confirm the county rankings (rank correlation 0.63). Users ask the agent for each crop group's loss as a fraction of expected season value, every number sourced, so that governments, growers and scientists respond to agricultural disasters quickly.

AI.tldr: WxCrop is an agent that judges agricultural hazards from physically interpretable weather indices examined by causal analysis, and combines weather and agricultural information to predict crop loss for past and forecast dates. Demonstrated in Florida on hurricanes, freezes and dry heat, its hurricane index reaches an AUC of 0.98 for detecting recorded cyclone days.
AI.motivation: Weather forecasts say where a storm will strike but not which crops will suffer or how much is at risk, and the records that could show this span many sources.
AI.method: The agent derives physically interpretable weather indices, examines them by causal analysis, and combines weather and agricultural information. A loss model is calibrated on insurance records for each hazard, and users ask for each crop group's loss as a fraction of expected season value, with every number sourced. The abstract states the procedure extends to other hazards and areas.
AI.result: The hurricane index detects recorded cyclone days with an AUC of 0.98. Recorded losses in held-out years are reproduced to within 2 percent, and independent production records confirm the county rankings with a rank correlation of 0.63.
AI.conclusion: The agent offers a reliable, sourced way to estimate agricultural disaster losses that could help governments, growers and scientists respond quickly.

title: Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform: Data-Adaptive Window-Length Selection for Time-Frequency Analysis
summary: The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) characterizes the local frequency content of time-varying signals by evaluating the discrete Fourier transform over a sliding analysis window. The STFT is governed by a fundamental resolution trade-off: a short window localizes rapid transients in time at the cost of frequency resolution, whereas a long window resolves closely spaced harmonics at the expense of temporal resolution. The Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform (U-STFT) resolves this trade-off sequentially by modeling the analysis window duration as a data-adaptive state variable that indexes the number of hops included in the current observation interval. At each frame, a bank of candidate window durations is scored using normalized order-three Rényi entropy to quantify joint time-frequency concentration. A window length trellis aggregates the resulting $\mathcal{O}(3^M)$ candidate window schedules with linear complexity per frame, guaranteeing a cumulative mix-loss regret bound of $\mathcal{O}((k+1)\log M)$ relative to any hindsight window schedule with $k$ resolution changes over $M$ frames. By linearity of the Fourier transform, posterior expectation across the candidate bank yields a single spectrum equivalent to an STFT evaluated with a data-adaptive effective window, while an envelope-normalized synthesis stream guarantees exact overlap-add reconstruction. Evaluations on synthetic and marine bioacoustic signals demonstrate adaptive resolution tracking, enhanced spectral concentration, and exact time-domain invertibility.

AI.tldr: The Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform (U-STFT) makes the analysis window duration a data-adaptive state variable, choosing window lengths frame by frame through normalized order-three Rényi entropy scores. It guarantees a cumulative regret bound against any hindsight window schedule and exact overlap-add reconstruction.
AI.motivation: The STFT has a fundamental time-frequency resolution trade-off: short windows localize transients but blur frequency resolution, while long windows resolve closely spaced harmonics but blur time.
AI.method: Window duration is modeled as a state indexing the number of hops in the current observation interval. A bank of candidate durations is scored at each frame with normalized order-three Rényi entropy, and a window length trellis aggregates the O(3^M) candidate schedules with linear complexity per frame. Posterior expectation across candidates yields a single spectrum equivalent to an STFT with a data-adaptive effective window, and an envelope-normalized synthesis stream ensures exact overlap-add reconstruction.
AI.result: The method has a cumulative mix-loss regret bound of O((k+1) log M) relative to any hindsight window schedule with k resolution changes over M frames. Evaluations on synthetic and marine bioacoustic signals demonstrate adaptive resolution tracking, enhanced spectral concentration and exact time-domain invertibility.
AI.conclusion: Data-adaptive window-length selection can improve time-frequency concentration while keeping exact invertibility, backed by a formal regret guarantee.

title: Scalable Bayesian Quadrature via Operator-Adapted Features
summary: Kernel methods face two recurrent bottlenecks: the cubic cost of inverting an $n\times n$ kernel matrix, as in kernel ridge regression, and the evaluation of kernel integrals, as required in kernel quadrature. Existing low-rank kernel and Gaussian process approximations primarily address the former bottleneck, but do not control the downstream quadrature error when both the kernel matrix and kernel mean are approximated, particularly when the integrand lies outside the kernel reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We address both challenges through an operator-adapted finite-feature approximation. Specifically, we construct a finite-dimensional working kernel from the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a second-order differential operator. We establish convergence guarantees for the resulting finite-feature estimators in kernel quadrature, with extension to other related kernel methods. Our results show that, with $m \lesssim n$ basis functions, the truncated estimator attains the corresponding benchmark statistical rates. The theory covers fixed/random designs, noisy/noiseless observations, oversmoothing/undersmoothing regimes, and Matérn/Gaussian-type weights. We provide explicit error bounds that quantify the roles of the spectral cutoff, regularization parameter, lengthscale, sampling geometry, and operator boundary condition. We verify the convergence results in numerical experiments.

AI.tldr: Proposes an operator-adapted finite-feature approximation for kernel quadrature that builds a finite-dimensional working kernel from the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a second-order differential operator, and proves convergence guarantees for the resulting estimators. With the number of basis functions m of order at most n, the truncated estimator attains the benchmark statistical rates.
AI.motivation: Low-rank kernel and Gaussian process approximations address the cubic cost of inverting the kernel matrix but do not control downstream quadrature error when both the kernel matrix and the kernel mean are approximated, particularly when the integrand lies outside the kernel RKHS.
AI.method: A finite-dimensional working kernel is constructed from the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a second-order differential operator; the analysis covers fixed and random designs, noisy and noiseless observations, oversmoothing and undersmoothing regimes, and Matern and Gaussian-type weights, with explicit error bounds in terms of the spectral cutoff, regularization parameter, lengthscale, sampling geometry and operator boundary condition.
AI.result: With m of order at most n basis functions, the truncated estimator attains the corresponding benchmark statistical rates; numerical experiments verify the convergence results.
AI.conclusion: Operator-adapted finite features give a theoretically controlled and scalable route to kernel quadrature and related kernel methods, with error bounds that make explicit the role of each design and regularization choice.

title: Integrating multi-source local information for global undirected graph reconstruction via integer programming
summary: Graphical models are widely used to represent conditional independence structures, but learning them is challenging when data are fragmented across sources that measure different subsets of variables and may not be directly shareable. We develop a general framework for reconstructing a shared global graph from heterogeneous, partially observed sources. Our framework permits both the observed variable sets and source-specific distributions to differ. Under a source-wise faithfulness condition, local conditional independence graphs correspond to latent projections of the shared global graph, which is identifiable up to the equivalence class induced by the observed variable sets. The framework integrates raw data, estimated source graphs, or a combination of both, accommodating settings with restricted access to individual-level data, such as privacy constraints. We develop mixed-integer optimization formulations and scalable approximate algorithms for several classes of graphical models. Unlike standard high-dimensional analyses, our guarantees are governed by new combinatorial notions of signal strength that capture how information propagates across partially observed sources. Extensive simulations further show that integration can substantially improve estimation of source-specific projected graphs relative to separate source methods. Real-data application illustrates the framework's use with partially-observed sources of fatty acid measurements.

AI.tldr: Presents a framework that reconstructs a shared global undirected graph from heterogeneous, partially observed sources that measure different subsets of variables, using mixed-integer optimization and scalable approximate algorithms. Simulations show that integrating sources substantially improves estimation of source-specific projected graphs over separate-source methods.
AI.motivation: Data are fragmented across sources that measure different variables and may not be directly shareable, so the conditional independence structure cannot simply be learned from pooled data; standard high-dimensional analyses do not capture how information propagates across partially observed sources.
AI.method: Under a source-wise faithfulness condition, each local conditional independence graph is a latent projection of the shared global graph, identifiable up to the equivalence class induced by the observed variable sets; the framework integrates raw data, estimated source graphs, or a combination of both, accommodating restricted access to individual-level data, and its guarantees are governed by new combinatorial notions of signal strength.
AI.result: Extensive simulations show that integration substantially improves estimation of source-specific projected graphs relative to separate source methods; a real-data application uses partially observed sources of fatty acid measurements.
AI.conclusion: Integrating local information from partially observed sources can recover a shared global graph under restricted data access, and the combinatorial signal-strength measures characterize how information propagates across sources.

title: Metropolized backward sampling for conditional sequential Monte Carlo
comment: 12 pages + appendix. A Lean formalization was AI-generated after the draft of the paper was written as an experiment. I have subsequently edited the documentation of the formalization for better readability, and discussed the process, as well as difference between the AI-formalized and my original proofs in the appendix. this https URL
summary: Particle Gibbs samplers with backward sampling are widely used for sampling the smoothing distribution of state-space models, but, with few particles, the new trajectory often coincides with the current one at many time steps. A known but rarely used remedy replaces the random selection of the final particle by a Metropolis--Hastings move which avoids the current particle. We show that, with backward sampling, this remedy only helps at the last time steps, because its effect on the update rates decays geometrically with the distance to the final time. We propose instead Metropolized backward sampling, which makes such a move at every step of the backward pass, forcibly switching trajectories whenever possible. Additionally, we introduce a coupled version which prevents proposing the current trajectory, maximizing the chances of an actual switch versus the current trajectory and performing perfect sampling when the state-space model has no observations, a feature not shared by backward sampling. We prove that, at every time step, both methods dominate backward sampling as they update the state more often and have smaller lag-one autocorrelations than it does. Our methods are drop-in replacements for backward sampling, and can be used to improve any particle Gibbs sampler.

AI.tldr: Proposes Metropolized backward sampling, which makes a Metropolis-Hastings move at every step of the backward pass in particle Gibbs samplers, and a coupled variant that avoids proposing the current trajectory. The authors prove that both methods dominate standard backward sampling at every time step.
AI.motivation: With few particles, backward sampling in particle Gibbs often returns the current trajectory at many time steps; the known Metropolis-Hastings remedy for the final particle only helps at the last few time steps, because its effect on the update rates decays geometrically with distance to the final time.
AI.method: Metropolized backward sampling makes a Metropolis-Hastings move that avoids the current particle at every backward step, forcibly switching trajectories whenever possible; the coupled version prevents proposing the current trajectory, which also enables perfect sampling when the state-space model has no observations.
AI.result: At every time step, both methods are proven to update the state more often and to have smaller lag-one autocorrelations than backward sampling.
AI.conclusion: The two methods are drop-in replacements for backward sampling and can improve any particle Gibbs sampler, with the coupled variant additionally providing perfect sampling in the observation-free case, a feature backward sampling does not share.

title: Orthogonal Inference for Conditional Z-Estimation without Cross-Fitting: A Distributional Nearest-Neighbor Approach
comment: 36 pages (including appendices and references), 4 figures, 5 tables; supplementary material: 12 pages, 2 figures, 17 tables
summary: Estimating conditional parameters, such as heterogeneous treatment effects, often requires rich covariate adjustment, even when the parameters are reported along only a few dimensions. Fitting nuisance functions on the full sample makes all observations available for adjustment, but creates dependence between fitted scores and the observations at which they are evaluated, which is typically avoided by cross-fitting. We develop pointwise inference with full-sample nuisance predictions for exactly identified conditional moment equations, recovering conditional average treatment effects as a special case. We localize the estimating equations around the reporting point using distributional nearest neighbors (DNN), a U-statistic-based averaging procedure. Under sufficient conditions on the local design, orthogonality, prediction accuracy and quantitative deletion stability, the estimator is asymptotically normal, and a frozen-score jackknife consistently estimates its limiting covariance with nuisance predictions held fixed. In simulations, full-sample and cross-fitted inference perform similarly, with coverage shortfalls from nuisance approximation error, spatial bias and heavy studentized tails. An application to 401(k) eligibility using Survey of Income and Program Participation data finds similar estimates across nuisance prediction methods, with wide normal-reference intervals.

AI.tldr: Develops pointwise inference for exactly identified conditional moment equations using full-sample nuisance predictions, without cross-fitting, by localizing the estimating equations with distributional nearest neighbors. Under stated conditions the estimator is asymptotically normal, and a frozen-score jackknife consistently estimates its limiting covariance.
AI.motivation: Estimating conditional parameters such as heterogeneous treatment effects requires rich covariate adjustment, but fitting nuisance functions on the full sample creates dependence between the fitted scores and the observations at which they are evaluated, which cross-fitting is typically used to avoid.
AI.method: Pointwise inference uses full-sample nuisance predictions, with the estimating equations localized around the reporting point by distributional nearest neighbors, a U-statistic-based averaging procedure; a frozen-score jackknife, with nuisance predictions held fixed, estimates the limiting covariance.
AI.result: In simulations, full-sample and cross-fitted inference perform similarly, with coverage shortfalls arising from nuisance approximation error, spatial bias and heavy studentized tails; an application to 401(k) eligibility using Survey of Income and Program Participation data finds similar estimates across nuisance prediction methods, with wide normal-reference intervals.
AI.conclusion: Full-sample inference without cross-fitting is a viable alternative for conditional parameters, although its coverage is limited by nuisance approximation error, spatial bias and heavy tails in the studentized estimator.

title: A Spectral Boundary for Independence Learnability
summary: Learning independence is fundamental to statistical inference and machine learning, yet learning independence between entire time series by a test remains challenging when only a single observation record is available. Existing guarantees often rely on structural or mixing assumptions, while stationarity and ergodicity alone do not permit consistent testing. In this work, we identify a class-level boundary governed by shared nontrivial Koopman eigenvalues, which represent common persistent oscillatory frequencies of the two processes. When no such eigenvalues are shared, we extend shift-based rank calibration with finite-window dependence witnesses and a data-adaptive threshold to construct a deterministic, weakly consistent test with finite-sample false-positive control, without quantitative mixing assumptions. Conversely, we show that no possibly randomized test can achieve vanishing false-positive probabilities under every independent jointly totally ergodic law while consistently detecting every dependent jointly totally ergodic law with a shared nontrivial eigenvalue. This impossibility already holds for binary observations and persists within any prescribed nonempty open eigenvalue window, identifying a spectral obstruction to universal learning of full-process independence.

AI.tldr: Identifies a spectral boundary for learning independence between two time series from a single observation record, governed by shared nontrivial Koopman eigenvalues. When no eigenvalues are shared, a deterministic, weakly consistent test with finite-sample false-positive control is constructed, and no randomized test can achieve vanishing false-positive probability while detecting every dependent law that shares an eigenvalue.
AI.motivation: Testing independence between entire time series from a single record is difficult; existing guarantees rely on structural or mixing assumptions, and stationarity and ergodicity alone do not permit consistent testing.
AI.method: Shift-based rank calibration is extended with finite-window dependence witnesses and a data-adaptive threshold to build the test when no nontrivial Koopman eigenvalues are shared; the impossibility result holds already for binary observations and within any prescribed nonempty open eigenvalue window.
AI.result: A deterministic, weakly consistent test with finite-sample false-positive control is obtained without quantitative mixing assumptions; conversely, no possibly randomized test achieves vanishing false-positive probability under every independent jointly totally ergodic law while consistently detecting every dependent jointly totally ergodic law with a shared nontrivial eigenvalue.
AI.conclusion: Shared Koopman eigenvalues form a spectral obstruction to universal learning of full-process independence, so consistent independence testing is possible only outside that class.

title: Non-Asymptotic Confidence Regions for Separable Nonlinear Models
comment: Accepted for publication at the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026)
summary: This paper studies robust uncertainty quantification for separable nonlinear least squares (SNLLS) problems. We propose two identification methods, (i) Residual-Perturbed Gradient (RPG) and (ii) Global-Fit-Gap (GFG), to construct joint distribution-free confidence regions for both the linear and nonlinear parameters. By exploiting assumed group invariance of the noise (such as symmetry or exchangeability), we apply random perturbations (such as sign-changes or permutations) to build the regions based on resampling and ranking. We prove that both methods guarantee non-asymptotically exact coverage (type I error). Finally, we illustrate the constructions through two numerical experiments: (i) identifying generalized finite impulse response (GFIR) systems using Laguerre polynomials with an adjustable decay rate and (ii) fitting Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) models with variable knots and widths.

AI.tldr: Proposes two distribution-free methods, Residual-Perturbed Gradient and Global-Fit-Gap, that construct joint non-asymptotically exact confidence regions for the linear and nonlinear parameters of separable nonlinear least squares models, using resampling and ranking under assumed noise group invariance.
AI.motivation: Robust uncertainty quantification is needed for separable nonlinear least squares problems, where joint confidence regions for both the linear and nonlinear parameters are required without distributional assumptions on the noise.
AI.method: The assumed group invariance of the noise, such as symmetry or exchangeability, is exploited by applying random perturbations such as sign changes or permutations, and the regions are built from resampling and ranking.
AI.result: Both methods are proven to guarantee non-asymptotically exact coverage, that is, exact type I error control; the constructions are illustrated by identifying generalized finite impulse response systems using Laguerre polynomials with an adjustable decay rate and by fitting Gaussian radial basis function models with variable knots and widths.
AI.conclusion: Group-invariance-based perturbations yield exact finite-sample confidence regions for separable nonlinear models, demonstrated on system identification and RBF model fitting.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Blind Passive Beamforming in RIS-Assisted MIMO Systems
comment: Accepted at AIxNET 2026. 6 pages. Copyright may be transferred to IEEE after publication, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) are a promising solution for improving millimeter-wave (mmWave) communications by controlling signal propagation. Yet, selecting the optimal RIS configuration remains challenging due to the high-dimensional search space and signaling overhead. We propose a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework for blind passive beamforming, where a Deep Q-Learning (DQL) agent learns an adaptive policy to select near-optimal RIS configurations while sounding only few codewords, without channel state information. Results show that our approach outperforms Q-Learning (QL) and conventional baselines in convergence, performance, and overhead reduction.

AI.tldr: Proposes a Deep Q-Learning agent for blind passive beamforming in RIS-assisted mmWave MIMO systems that selects near-optimal RIS configurations while sounding only a few codewords, without channel state information.
AI.motivation: Selecting the optimal RIS configuration is challenging because of the high-dimensional search space and the signaling overhead required to estimate the channel.
AI.method: A Deep Reinforcement Learning framework in which a Deep Q-Learning agent learns an adaptive policy for choosing RIS configurations from only a few sounded codewords, with no channel state information.
AI.result: The approach outperforms Q-Learning and conventional baselines in convergence, performance and overhead reduction.
AI.conclusion: Deep reinforcement learning enables blind passive beamforming that reduces signaling overhead while still selecting near-optimal RIS configurations.

title: Optimal Neural Estimation for High-Dimensional Nonparametric Regression under Multisource Covariate Shift
summary: We study high-dimensional nonparametric regression under multisource covariate shift, where $\mathrm J$ sources of training data share a common regression function but differ in their covariate distributions, sample sizes, and noise variances. Our goal is to combine these sources to estimate the regression function accurately under a target covariate distribution. We propose an oracle weighted neural estimator and establish its minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors through matching upper and lower bounds. The resulting rate is $\mathsf n_{\rm eff}^{-2p/(2p+K)}$, where $p$ and $K$ denote the effective smoothness and dimension of the regression function, and the effective sample size is \begin{align} \mathsf n_{\rm eff} =\sum_{j=1}^{\mathrm J} \frac{n_j}{(1+\sigma_{\rho,j})\sigma_{\epsilon,j}^{2}}. \nonumber \end{align} Here, $n_j$ is the sample size of source $j$, $\sigma_{\epsilon,j}^{2}$ is its noise variance, and $\sigma_{\rho,j}$ controls the deviation between the covariate distribution of source $j$ and the target covariate distribution. We also develop an adaptive procedure that requires no knowledge of source noise variances or covariate-shift parameters. Under suitable conditions, this procedure attains the oracle minimax rate up to logarithmic factors.

AI.tldr: Studies high-dimensional nonparametric regression under multisource covariate shift and proposes an oracle weighted neural estimator that is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors, together with an adaptive procedure that attains the oracle rate without knowing source noise variances or covariate-shift parameters.
AI.motivation: Several training sources share a common regression function but differ in covariate distributions, sample sizes and noise variances, and the goal is to combine them to estimate the regression function accurately under a target covariate distribution.
AI.method: An oracle weighted neural estimator combines the sources; the effective sample size sums n_j divided by (1 + sigma_rho,j) times sigma_eps,j squared over the sources, where n_j is the sample size, sigma_eps,j squared the noise variance, and sigma_rho,j the deviation of source j's covariate distribution from the target; the adaptive procedure does not require these quantities.
AI.result: Matching upper and lower bounds give the minimax rate n_eff raised to -2p/(2p+K) up to logarithmic factors, where p is the effective smoothness and K the effective dimension of the regression function; under suitable conditions the adaptive procedure attains the oracle minimax rate up to logarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: The sources are effectively pooled through the effective sample size, and an adaptive weighted neural estimator can achieve the optimal rate without prior knowledge of noise levels or covariate-shift parameters.

title: Finite-Sample LTI System Identification from a Misspecified Finite Model Set
summary: We consider the problem of finite-sample identification of an unknown LTI system from a finite hypothesis class. In contrast to existing results that assume the hypothesis class contains the true system, we consider the misspecified setting, where the true system does not belong to the hypothesis class. We first characterize the resulting estimation target and its dependence on the data-generation scheme. We then establish a finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability that any identification algorithm must incur. Finally, we analyze the robustness of an existing exponential weighting-based identification algorithm to the misspecification and derive a finite-sample upper bound on its failure probability. Our results illustrate when using a misspecified finite hypothesis class can provide an advantage over identification without prior knowledge of the candidate systems.

AI.tldr: Studies finite-sample identification of an unknown LTI system from a finite hypothesis class that may not contain the true system, deriving a finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability of any algorithm and an upper bound for an exponential weighting-based algorithm under misspecification.
AI.motivation: Existing results assume the hypothesis class contains the true system, whereas the misspecified setting, where the true system lies outside the class, has received less analysis.
AI.method: The estimation target and its dependence on the data-generation scheme are characterized; a finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability that any identification algorithm must incur is established; an existing exponential weighting-based algorithm is then analyzed for robustness to misspecification.
AI.result: A finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability holds for any identification algorithm, and a finite-sample upper bound is derived for the failure probability of the exponential weighting algorithm under misspecification.
AI.conclusion: The results show when using a misspecified finite hypothesis class can be advantageous compared with identification without prior knowledge of the candidate systems.

title: Self-regularization and structural adaptation of NPMLE for Gaussian mixture models in all dimensions
summary: We establish structural properties of the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) for $d$-dimensional Gaussian mixtures whose means lie in a hypercube. We show that, with high probability, the NPMLE based on $n$ independent observations self-regularizes by fitting a mixture model with $O((\frac{\log n}{\log\log n})^d)$ components, achieving the optimal model complexity without explicit model selection. Furthermore, the NPMLE exhibits a structural adaptation property: For data drawn from a finite mixture, the number of fitted components is bounded in probability as $n\to\infty$. Our proof applies a multivariate Jensen-type bound to control the typical number of critical points of the KKT function associated with the first-order optimality conditions. The key step is to lower bound its gradient norm uniformly on complex spheres. We establish this lower bound by decomposing the KKT function into an empirical fluctuation term and a relative density estimation error term, combining small-ball probability estimates for the former with polynomial approximation and Hellinger error bounds for the latter.

AI.tldr: Shows that the NPMLE for d-dimensional Gaussian mixtures with means in a hypercube self-regularizes: with high probability it fits a mixture with O((log n / log log n)^d) components, and for data drawn from a finite mixture the number of fitted components is bounded in probability.
AI.motivation: The nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator of Gaussian mixtures is usually paired with explicit model selection to reach the optimal model complexity, and its structural behavior in all dimensions has not been established.
AI.method: The proof applies a multivariate Jensen-type bound to control the typical number of critical points of the KKT function from the first-order optimality conditions, lower-bounding its gradient norm uniformly on complex spheres by splitting it into an empirical fluctuation term and a relative density estimation error term, handled with small-ball probability estimates, polynomial approximation and Hellinger error bounds.
AI.result: With high probability the NPMLE fits O((log n / log log n)^d) components, and for data from a finite mixture the number of fitted components is bounded in probability as n tends to infinity.
AI.conclusion: The NPMLE adapts its own complexity without explicit model selection, reaching the optimal component count and exhibiting a structural adaptation property in all dimensions.
